People use ethe term "friend slop" rather loosely, Big Walk is actually a well-designed co-op game and doesn't fit the mold for that. Overall, fun game, I played with a group that had done a few puzzles without me, I almost got 6 hours. I spent my time playing this game with my directionally challenged friend. We would walk to random points of interests, then after solving puzzles I would often turn around to see my friend had wandered off somewhere getting lost. We would spend sometimes up to an time trying to regroup firing off flares until eventually meeting up again, where we would recount our respective journeys. We would then head off to the next point of intrest and repeat the process all over again.

 We managed to beat the game, as well as get all achievements and it was honestly some of the most fun I think I have ever had gaming. I initially thought I would most likely get bored from this game in the first 20 with it being a walking simulator/chat room but this game has so much more to offer. 

The puzzles are the perfect difficulty for me personally, allowing us to solve all the puzzles without requiring a guide or having a convoluted answer that I would never even think to do, instead they require either clever uses of the in game gestures to create systems to communicate an answer or being able to give clear instructions to guide your teammate through a puzzle. There was never an instance where I felt a puzzle was unfair to me, but it was never too easy either, creating a perfect balance of exploring and solving. Each puzzle sovled unlocked a new mystery to unravel, constantly keeping you hooked.

What I initally wrote off as a game I would probably refund after getting bored in the first 20 minutes with ended up being an amazing experience I got to share with a friend instead. If you're ever sitting on the fence about this game wondering if it's something you would even like, I'd highly reccomend grabbing a buddy and giving it a try, maybe you'll end up pleasantly surprised like I was. I would also reccomend taking the extra time to complete all the puzzles (including the challenge ones) in order to see both endings, it helps wrap up the experience as a whole. 

If I could go back in time to play this game from the start all over again, I would do so in a heartbeat. 10/10 would walk again.

Big Walk is a Big Experience
I love walking simulators, I love cooperative exploration games, I love puzzle games, and these days I love friend-slop games providing me activities to share and parallel play with friends online. 

So it's no surprise that I liked and whole-hearted recommend Big Walk. What was surprising to me is how much the experience really touched me. Without spoilers, the game reached further and deeper than I had expected, and ranged from silly slapstick moments to easy puzzles to challenging puzzles, all of which I loved although some have sound components that bordered on having accessibility challenges.

But broadly, boy is this an inclusive experience. It's wonderful how simply things like limited proximity based communication set up interesting challenges and immersive experiences, and delightful how many tools and toys and twists the game designers threw in around them. This is a true labor of love, a delightful intimate and cozy experience to share with the people you want to share more experiences with. 

Gaming could use more truly social and adventurous experiences like this!

Big Walk is perhaps the most fun I've ever had playing a co-op game. No matter what kind of friends you have, this game is bound to be a blast. The pre-made open world map the game takes place in is surprisingly beautiful and a breath of fresh air after the deluge of procedurally generated "friendslop" games that've been coming out in the years since Lethal Company's release.

The lack of any real threat helps this game focus on cultivating what have always been the best moments in these sorts of games: the interactions between friends. From slow walks on the beach, to screaming at your friends for fucking up their part of a puzzle, to getting an important item wrenched from your hands and kicked into the depths of the sea; all of it is pure, distilled, magic. This all culminates brilliantly in the final puzzle, which is maybe the best moment of any game this year.

The only possible negative is the lack of replayability. But, let's be honest, you aren't going back to these "friendslop" games after a few months anyways, so it's nice to see a game like this wrap itself up in a nice little bow and roll the credits.

review: Big fan of this game; I've enjoyed it so much. Getting suprised and challenged by different puzzles and such a laugh with the friends that I play this with.

I missed out on Untitled Goose Game when it was popular, but didn't really care for it. However now that I've played through the entirety of Big Walk, I really want to check out more of House House's projects, and for good reason.

Big Walk offers a great selection of puzzles that you must cooperate with your friend(s) on solving. Having been out of school for the last two years because of my apprenticeship/full-time job, I feel like my knowledge has been deteriorating, and it hasn't exactly boosted my confidence. Recently though, I've been greatly enjoying all the thought processes I've had while playing Big Walk. Sometimes a puzzle would take a sole minute to complete, whilst other times my friend and I would have to call it quits for the night and try the puzzle again the next day, or the next one after that if we still couldn't solve it. The joy and satisfaction of then completing said puzzle was indescribable.

I think the game design is pretty great too! The avatar which you play as is very simplistic, and is based on the best and the cutest parts of your average bird (as a hardcore bird lover, I LOVED this idea). Sometimes I also wonder if the avatars are inspired by an ice cream cone with three scoops, or a colorful snowman. Or perhaps both? 

I wanted to show my love for the Big Walk avatar by creating a Halloween costume 48 hours before a party. I wasn't planning on going, but after seeing all the inspiration online, I just had to try it for myself, and that might've been the best idea I've ever had lol cause I was met with a lot of compliments, and although I'm a very creative person working in the creative industry, I had never before made my own costume, so this experience gave me a lot of confidence, and also got me to do something fun.

I also recently decided to show my love for the Big Walk devs by sending them a letter. I included the best pictures I had of my costume in them, as well as four written pages about all the different feelings I had about Big Walk. In about four weeks I'll hopefully receive something in return!

Big Walk is a game that my friend and I are hoping to revisit one day when we have more people than just us two. I'm also hoping that Big Walk will eventually get more maps and puzzles, if that's what the devs want as well. Go, go! Buy it! Have a swell time!

Big walk is a game I genuinely was surprised by. 

From the first game trailer I saw of it on a Nintendo Direct, I was interested. When it came out, it was an instant buy. Played it for 8 hours straight that night with my friends, and it felt like time passed so quickly. There is so much to do, but it was great at points to just stop and fool around, or take sit down and take a rest in the game, chatting and looking at the horizon and scenery.

I really enjoyed this game so much that I've now gone through it at least 3 times, and each time it's a relaxing journey, because the game encourages you to slow down and enjoy the walk. There are a lot of puzzles, but sometimes there are random stops along the way where there's no objective. Just to sit and relax, like pit stops. 

I will say it is the type of game that I feel benefits from having more people/split off groups. Really comes alive when you see other people walking off in the distance. Meeting people and having a quick chat as you walk/switching off the group members every so often is so much fun, as it allows you to have what feels like very IRL interactions where you chat with one person and hangout with them awhile, and then chat and hangout with another. 

The ending made me cry. Such a simple premise but I feel like they set it up perfectly. 

Game ran smooth on my PC, no issues.

review:
I genuinely don't think I've ever played anything quite like BIG WALK. In fact, I'd go as far as saying it's the best game I've ever played. That's a pretty BIG statement, but I couldn't think of another game that deserves it. There is something incredibly special about this game. It's difficult to put into words because so much of what makes it brilliant isn't just one particular mechanic. It's the way everything comes together.

The world is a joy to explore. Being able to wander around aimlessly and discover things has been done by countless other games before, but to give me a game where getting lost makes the game even more fun? That's something I'll never get in any other game. It doesn't feel like I'm constantly being rushed towards the next objective. It's just a WALK in the park.

The world is much BIGger than I initially thought it was. Even after beating the main game, there are still puzzles and locations I haven't visited yet. The amount of thought and creativity that has gone into each puzzle that I've found accross the map is incredible. It doesn't feel like they've just copy-pasted every encounter (though the challenge mode ones are copies. but you'll find out why I love those when you discover them). 

The sound design is phenomenal, and I don't just mean the proximity chat shenanigans. The puzzles that rely on sound are clever, the music stations are fantastic and all the items you find have been lovingly worked on. I can hear every single bit of that love. 

Above all else, the thing that brings me the most joy in this game is the friends I've brought with me. BIG WALK on your own is simply that; a WALK. But a BIG WALK with your friends will be one of the best (or potentially worst) things you'll ever do. BIG WALK has designed it's puzzle to be played with a minimum of 2 people. but can be rebalanced for 3 or 4+ players. The fun that I've had bringing friends along and streaming our adventure is and will always be one of the best moments I've ever had in my 20ish years of gaming. 

I could go on and on about this game and what makes it so special to me, but ultimately, BIG WALK is just one of those rare experiences that you won't find anywhere else. This game reminded me of why I love videogames in the first place. 

House House has created something that I personally believe nobody else has. My only regret is that I'll never be able to experience it for the first time again. If you've got a group of friends, or just that one best mate you play everything with, then do yourselves a favour and go for a BIG WALK.

The shenanigans everyone gets up to are almost as great as the peaceful moments you'll share after a long hard day of tomfoolery. It's basically just a semi-open world multiplayer puzzle solver, but I need to acknowledge how much fun it is that we get to just do stuff at our leisure and basically complete the game how we like. [h3][u] Overall [/u][/h3]

Big Walk is SUCH a beautiful gem to come out this year. It's one of the few games I've played that manages to strengthens the bond of the friends I play with, while suprisingly not doing much in the game itself to achieve that! It essentially gives us an entire island to explore together, puzzles to solve as a team, tools to help communicate each other, and the toys to play around with. Everything else is left to us on how to approach the game, and that's been the greatest aspect of this!

There would be occasinal times, where we open up Big Walk JUST to hang out, and create our own fun, WITHOUT doing any objectives! Something as simple as a puzzle room [spoiler]where you wait 5-10 minutes to get your collectable, turns into a gathering party, discussing anything likes it our own little podcast[/spoiler]. Or something unassuming as a whiteboard, turns into a guessing game, as we figure out what's written behind ourselves, as whiteboards are attached to our backpacks. HELL, we'd even open up Big Walk JUST to take a virtual hike! Sure, we could've just hangout and play some little game in discord calls, or within any other hangout games. But something about Big Walk has just the RIGHT environment, tools, and vibes to make this our prefer way to connect together. There's always different intentions whenever we play this game, and its always something unexpected!

Another strong aspect of Big Walk that really works for me is its immersion. With how vast the island is to get lost in (and the challenges of re-grouping the team), how lushful the forest is to take a leisurely stroll, and how BREATHTAKING the scenary can be, whether taking in the sun setting/rising, or illuminating my flashlights/ball lamps during the night (with some GORGEOUS lighting!), I'm ALWAYS sucked into the game's world, and will be spending so many hours without me realizing it! Plus, with there being no threats to deal with at all, you're always in peace.

The only thing I will say is this: Big Walk is not for everyone. While we are the right group of people to have so much fun out of Big Walk. You might have groups that doesn't resonate as strongly with each other, and with what little gameplay this game has, or lacks the hype moments seen in other friend group games. For some, this game might come across boring, aimless, or lacks substance.

But in anycase, I STILL highly recommend Big Walk! Its an experience where friendships grows stronger and shines the brightest, bringing in great memories that I will ALWAYS cherish :)

An incredibly charming, relaxing, and beautiful game. 

Big Walk caught my interest as soon as I saw its first trailer over on Twitter. I enjoyed Untitled Goose Game (I played it on the Switch, not Steam) and the thought of a game about solving puzzles while interacting with friends seemed interesting, if not very novel. However, after playing through Big Walk in its entirety with someone very close to me, I found that this game is in fact very special.

The puzzles are easy to grasp but not so simple that they become effortless. Communication is key to working things out with whoever you choose to play with. What’s really fun about Big Walk is that you don’t feel the need to go from puzzle to puzzle, to rush through anything - the puzzles are spaced far enough apart to where you naturally discover them, or choose to set out on a specific journey in order to get to one, possibly even getting distracted by something along the way.

Losing yourself in the world of Big Walk is what made the game so special to me. Being able to naturally talk about our lives, what happened during the day, or whatever came to mind never felt forced. When we stumbled across a puzzle, we would do it, then move on to something else, starting up another conversation. It’s a relaxing, fun time all around.

Big Walk is a 10/10 for me, and I don’t think I’ll ever forget it.

Big Walk differs from many other multiplayer games in that the gameplay is very minimal: you just walk around and do puzzles. Compare that to a game like PEAK, which has more depth in its movement, requires more planning and strategy, and where there are many more mechanics and items.

However, what makes Big Walk unique is that it really heavily focuses on the multiplayer aspect.

- The puzzles, while often basic, require you to cooperate with other people to solve them, encouraging you to talk with each other.
- There is a lot of downtime as you walk from one location to another, motivating you to fill that silence with some conversation, much like a walk in real life does.
- The island is simple yet well made and nice to look at, which is a breath of fresh air in a time where video games seem to get ever brighter and flashier. This further incentivizes you to chat with others while traversing the digital hand-crafted nature surrounding you.
- While one player has the potential to carry multiple items, you cannot put anything on your own backpack or belt by yourself, meaning that others have to help manage your inventory and, in turn, you have to help manage theirs. This turns inventories and items into a common resource worth discussing, rather than just something everyone handles on their own.

A lot of multiplayer games, such as PEAK, Terraria, Valorant/CS2 (and every other competitive game), don't really feel like they are actually multiplayer. Oftentimes, it feels more like you are playing a singleplayer game *next* to other people, rather than *with* them, since the interactions with your peers are usually minimal or sparse.

This is where Big Walk shines the most: by heavily investing into the multiplayer aspect and rooting it into every part of the game, it feels like you are actually together in the same location, doing the same things for the same goals. All your actions are important, since if one person doesn't participate, the group cannot function, creating a sense of responsibility and togetherness. Combined with all the opportunities for conversation that the game provides, it makes Big Walk a great way to spend time together with friends, while also having something to do at the same time. I haven't found any other game that does this quite so well.

However, this does mean that if your group doesn't get along well, or doesn't have much to talk about, or is just here for the gameplay, then Big Walk could disappoint. Even the ending, which is praised by many, hinges on the players (at least somewhat) bonding over the course of the game. Without this, the game can feel weak, lackluster or tedious, since Big Walk without other people is essentially just a walking simulator with occasional puzzles.

In conclusion, if you are looking for deeper gameplay mechanics, it would probably be better to look at games like PEAK and KTANE. But if you have a group of people who like to talk, then Big Walk is a perfect way to spend time with them.

This was the biggest surprise of the year for me. It was far from my most anticipated game, and objectively not the best game I've played this year, but it was hands down the most fun and immersive experience I've had with a group of friends in a very, very long time.

Big Walk rewards you when you're curious, but also punishes you when you're not careful. A slight misstep may send you barreling down a hill into the jungle, without a way of communicating with your friends, forcing you to spend a significant amount of time attempting to reestablish contact. But that's a huge part of the fun, it rewards you with some of the best emergent gameplay I've had the thrill of experiencing in years.

And don't even get me started on the puzzles. They build so naturally on one another that you and your friend group will start being able to almost read each other's minds when you get to the harder parts. And trust me, it gets pretty hard towards the end, but when you beat the harder parts together you truly feel a sense of accomplishment that is nearly unbeatable, especially in a game completely lacking any kind of combat. All brains, no brawn, and shocked full of "friend slop" in the very best of senses.

Grab some close friends, go for a nice Big Walk, and always keep that walkie talkie close at hand!

[h1]Premise and synopsis[/h1]
Developed by House House (creators of Untitled Goose Game), Big Walk is a cooperative online first person adventure game for 2 to 12 players. You and your friends explore a large, puzzle-filled island, like a modern-day multiplayer Myst, relying on spatial proximity voice chat, physical gestures, and tools to navigate, communicate, and reach the end together.

[h1]Inspirations and comparisons[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Myst:[/b] Obviously.
[*][b]The Witness & Outer Wilds:[/b] Mirrors a hands-off, observation-driven puzzle design and emphasis on world discovery.
[*][b]Lethal Company & Content Warning:[/b] Shares the physical comedy of spatial proximity voice chat and goofy gadgetry, but removes the horror and high-stress time limits.
[*][b]Journey:[/b] Captures a similar sense of wordless camaraderie, emotional payoff, and shared traversal toward a distant goal.
[/list]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The core loop revolves around, well, walking together. You explore, observe, and solve communication barriers. Your voice fades over distance, muffles through walls, and crackles over walkie-talkies. When separated or forced into silence by specific puzzle mechanics, you rely on expressive arm flailing, binoculars, laser pointers, megaphones, flares, and whiteboards to relay clues across valleys and towers. Between puzzles, there is zero pressure. You can just hang out, watch the sunset, or kick your friend's binoculars into the ocean.

[h1]Art and technology[/h1]
Big Walk is an interesting visual experience. You've got geometric player avatars against a muted, sun-drenched landscape of trees and brush. The players and puzzles admittedly look like placeholders shoved into a pre-fab or purchased landscape template, which took some getting used to, but once I got some hours in I realized that this was intentional in order to keep puzzle and player elements obvious. The standout feature here is audio: directional proximity chat, environmental reverb, and subtle musical cues dynamically react to terrain and distance, making sound the star.

[h1]Singleplayer and progression[/h1]
There is no singleplayer mode, so bring a friend. The game is hours long and I have yet to see the end.

[h1]Multiplayer and grind[/h1]
Multiplayer is exclusively online co-op with full crossplay across PC, Mac, PS5, and Nintendo Switch 2 (no local split-screen). There is zero grind, no leveling, and no daily checklists. The entire experience is a handcrafted, finite adventure meant to be played at your pace.

[h1]Monetization and continuing support[/h1]
Big Walk is a traditional one-time purchase with no microtransactions, battle passes, or live-service hooks. House House has stated there are no plans for paid expansions or DLC, treating the game as a complete, self-contained release out of the box.

[h1]Reasons to buy this game[/h1]
[list]
[*]Brilliantly inventive puzzles that turn voice chat, distance, and non-verbal communication into unforgettable co-op moments.
[*]Relaxed, stress-free pacing with full crossplay and support for anything from a focused duo to a chaotic 12-player group.
[/list]

[h1]Reasons to not buy this game[/h1]
[list]
[*]Completely unplayable solo and lacks local split-screen, requiring at least one friend with their own copy and a working mic.
[*]Minimal replayability once your group solves the island's mysteries, and external apps like Discord ruin the core mechanics.
[/list]

**Big Walk: Highly Recommended**

I expected Big Walk to be a relaxed stroll with friends. It turned out to be much more. It comes from House House, the studio behind Untitled Goose Game, and it is a purely multiplayer game with no single-player mode, built entirely around teamwork and talking. It isn't another loud co-op game full of chaos. It is a longer open-world adventure where you wander a big world with friends and solve puzzles together.

The game's greatest strength is that nobody holds your hand. You have to talk things through, argue, try ideas and sometimes get completely lost. The puzzles rely on trust and on following your own gut. Light bickering and funny moments come up along the way, and they make it feel like a real trip with friends rather than a list of tasks. Proximity chat works great, because voices fade with distance and every meeting in the world feels natural.

Visually, the game is simple, calm and stylish. The landscapes look dreamy, which makes it easy to settle in. The music and sound design are pleasant and never get in the way of conversation.

**Pros:**
- excellent co-op that makes you actually talk
- original puzzles you solve together
- lovely visuals and atmosphere
- works with a small group or a big one

**Cons:**
- pointless without friends, since there is no single-player mode
- a lot depends on how well your group communicates, and a quiet microphone can spoil the experience

**Verdict:** If you have a group of friends who enjoy chatting, Big Walk is a great pick. **Highly recommended.**

review:
Booted up Big walk, and left with a bigger heart

I love to talk to people. Getting to know friends better, talking about your lives and sharing experiences. Orrr you can talk about straight bullshit

In Big Walk, you and your friends roam around an open world with puzzles scattered throughout. These puzzles require verbal and non verbal communication with one another, which either results in your group solving it really quickly or everyone sharing a singular braincell as they figure out what the actual f*ck the guy behind the soundproof glass is trying to convey

The beauty lies however, with the people you play with. You'll split yourselves up to get puzzles done, talk over the radio  about your newfound discoveries. Some guy is planning a route. Some other guy is goofing around constantly but then locks in during puzzle time. And some other other guy keeps getting lost so often you the group appoints someone to walk with them so they don't wander off again (me). And nothing beats that feeling of firing your flare, gathering everyone back together and sharing everything they've done. 

You'll sit at beaches, talk amongst yourselves atop a tower, or perhaps have a personal conversation with a friend who wandered off from the group, and you just so happened to find them while trekking through the forest. 

This game means so much to me, beyond words, and it's reminded me to hold my friends who value me close and dearly. You only live once. Text that friend of yours again. Call them, hang out with them, support each other through it all.

Because you only live once. And when it's everyone's time to say goodbye one by one, you know damn well you've lived a good life together.

So most of the time we ended up either with two people sharing a single job or one of us just watching. The game would have benefited so much if all the tasks were of that caliber.
The island itself is quite underwhelming. While it [i]is[/i] an open world, it just looks exactly the same everywhere. You won't get rewarded by new visuals when unlocking a new area. Neither is it fun to traverse. I'd imagine making it more nested, putting interesting paths here and there with some vistas or even environmental storytelling, adding some mystery would've made it much more enjoyable. But like this it makes the impression that is was just cheaply generated with the engine's default height map generator. Place some random vegetation and stones, and finally break the visual style by adding overly colorful assets that practically scream, "Look at us, we are the things you should go to." I know that the island is based on a real world national park or so but I wouldn't have guessed by its in-game representation.
There's a train which seemed like a big thing to us when we unlocked it. But is so annoyingly slow that we used it once for transport and once when I got separated from the others to use its radio. The lift was more useful but way to slow for our taste as well. So we ended up just walking most of the time.
I guess in the end our group is more used to escape room games with a high puzzle density, with [i]actual[/i] puzzles, and having something to do and something to see all of the time. Which, unfortunately, clashes completely with this game's intentional gameplay.

There has never been anything quite like Big Walk. It is a wonderfully crafted co-op experience that allowed me to explore the bush with a bunch of friends, get lost, and find my way back again, all while somehow never feeling isolated. From start to finish, the game offers up surprise after surprise, never failing to evoke a smile and always creating a space to enjoy time with friends in a way that nothing else (video game or otherwise) ever has. This game is something special, and I truly believe it will forever be viewed as a touchstone for what video games as a medium can accomplish.

Over Labor Day weekend I attended PAX West with a big group of friends/mutuals, and I suddenly was able to place a familiar feeling that was in the back of my head while playing through Big Walk.  

I played it with a group of 8-12 folks from a discord where some of us knew each other well, and some were more of a friends-of-friends situation. We sat down one day and played it for 8 hours to completion.

After walking through the convention floor for a few days, I realized that the experience mapped pretty close to how it felt playing with such a big group - even down to it sometimes being impossible to reach each other remotely for hours on end, thanks to the cell tower flooding. 

To elaborate - both as we explored the game world, and the convention center, way the grouping of our friends mapped up ebbed and flowed. Sometimes, the whole group is all there at once watching the same thing or playing the same puzzle; sometimes the group would break off into small groups to go off and try different things; and then sometimes you would see something of interest, get lost on your own for a bit, and then randomly stumble upon another faction from your group out there, doing something else entirely. 

The similar emotional experience to these events really struck me, and it had me thinking about how sometimes these social games can tap into natural human behaviors and patterns, whether intentional or not.

Big Walk is easily one of the most unique and authentic experiences I've ever had in gaming, it's the sort of thing that video games as an art form should strive to be; something to be experienced and invoke deeper emotions in a different way for every person that plays. It's a special game that quickly won my love.

First and foremost this is a co-op puzzle game, you explore this massive island that is able to guide you from place to place in such a natural manner that always prods a sense of exploration, where even getting lost is intended as there are any number of paths. The journey is as central to the experience as the destination.

All the puzzles are built around collaboration that heavily relies on communication, the real magic of the game comes during these moments as how you communicate varies. Puzzles can be verbal communication where you need to relay information from one another, group challenges where you need to work together to find the solution, or my favorite are the non-verbal puzzles where you have to think of ways to use your characters body language to communicate. There are so many great "aha" moments where the solution dawns on you and your teammate at the same moment that's often hard to replicate in other games, it's great.

The developers had to put a lot of trust into players in order to complete this game and it paid off immensely, one particular thing I love is in the patch notes they refuse to name items, but rather describe what the item does. I think the reason for this is they want each player to define their own experience; once art is shared it's no longer just yours, many people will walk away with a different experience. This idea is what Big Walk is built around.

Big Walk to me is something that captures a piece of what is the human experience; as development began during the pandemic it makes perfect sense to want to make something that on a deeper level is about having to invent new ways of communication to solve what are otherwise mundane tasks like counting or matching. After beating the game every person I've watched played Big Walk had a completely different way of communicating with their friends. It feels like if a game was 'one size fits all'.

I completed Big Walk with my partner and as a 2 player experience and we had a fantastic time and our screenshots folders are both overflowing with new memories together. If you can find at least one other person to share this experience with, please don't pass up on this one.

I would never define Big Walk as a "friendslop" game, but it definitely epitomizes the genre. Both friendslop games and similar titles, like the Jackbox games, focus on the relationships you have with your friends rather than the relationship each of you have with the game. A game like REPO doesn't have the most compelling gameplay loop until you add that chaotic interactions with your buddies, and the Jackbox games literally do not function without three or more players.

However, many of those friendslop games do not appeal to the quiet friends, the ones who are in the discord for idle chatter, but maybe can't fit a word in edgewise next to their friends' big personalities. Big Walk is a game that excels at giving a role and a voice to everyone (which is ironic, because oftentimes the game forces you not to use your voice). It catalyzes your relationships with your friends in such creative ways that ensures that, by the end of the game, you're surely going to be closer to one another than when you started it. Big Walk does well on letting players have fun with the chaotic energy that comes from a friend group, but really thrives in the many different ways it forces the players to learn to communicate with one another.

As someone who specializes in cultural rhetorics, Big Walk in many ways is about the creation of culture through one of culture's most important identifiers: language. Throughout the game, you find yourselves across vast distances only able to communicate by walkie talkie and flares, or right next to each other, separated only by a single pane of soundproof glass. The surprisingly emotive characters offer a lot to a player in communicating without words. Raising your hands, pointing, spinning, sitting, everything becomes more meaningful as you and your friend group begin to ascribe meaning to those actions. I genuinely think that a group of people that all speak different languages can come together to play this game and leave knowing how to communicate with one another.

I also believe the finale to be one of the most inspired moments in all of gaming. I refuse to spoil it, but it really brings together the whole experience as something memorable-- it truly tests the language you and your friends have created up until that point. If you love your friends, and you love to solve puzzles, then play Big Walk. I cannot put into words how special it was playing this game with my group of friends, and I really hope every person that plays it gets an experience just as meaningful as mine.

This was exactly what I look for in a coop (friendslop) type of game. The core gameplay loop, solving puzzles across the island, is engaging and interesting. The gameplay challenges lead to funny and frustrating moments with my friends, or moments of triumph where we all lock in and get something done. There is a ton of room for just bantering and chatting while playing the game. 

The overall puzzle quality tends to be fairly high, and there is rarely a moment when someone is just sitting around doing nothing. Smaller puzzles that are easier can either be made quicker with everyone helping out, or you can split into two groups and divide and conquer. The game's ending was super unique too, and was a really interesting choice to make that I personally found to be super fun and exciting. For a game like this, it does get weirdly cinematic at times, and the ending sequence(s) of departing the island made me feel a little moved I wont lie. 

Part of the fun is asking other friends who played the game in a different group how they solved this puzzle or that puzzle, or even watching a video of people playing and seeing how they solved it. The end result is obviously the same but the game leaves it fairly open to interpretation how one should solve the puzzles with the tools given. The choice of not having to do all of the puzzles if you only want to beat the game is also a really nice touch, since some people will probably find a few of the puzzles a pain in the ass (I know we sure did). The game is worth going back and completing fully though, even though a certain puzzle (purple golf) is really evil.

It became a routine with me and my friends for months. 

At first it’s pretty exciting, figuring out new ways to communicate and it reminds me a lot about my favourite puzzles on a Scouts hike. My friends and I were set loose all over the map. Then I had to learn to stay with the group, not get lost, and to make my needs heard (‘can I take a break’, ‘can I be carried’, ‘can we go there next’, ‘what do you want to do?’) Sometimes I still scatter wherever I want to, and take detours, and confuse my friends. Am I as patient with my friends as they are with me?

It’s a simple game and I’ve played slowly and I’ve played quickly. The controls are easy to pick up, so it appeals to people with very different tastes in video games.

I’ve had a lot of fun with friends. Even watching the sun rise and set and watching the stars. That’s one of my favourite parts, is having something to talk about, but sometimes it’s easy to get carried away with puzzles or travelling across the map. I like engaging with other people. 

But I also really like getting lost. And being keen to be found again. I like saying ‘I’ll meet you here’ and we each navigate there separately. I like keeping in touch via radios and walkie talkies and megaphones and laser pointers and flares. I like making meaning out of gestures and signals, and have it be understood, when formerly it didn’t mean anything. This is probably why Big Walk is best played with no spoilers and no prior knowledge, because then nothing has a name to it, it’s all there for you to assign a name to it. It’s so whimsical that you can nod your head or shake your head by moving your mouse or joystick.

If, by any means, the reviews of Big Walk have eluded you, let me preface mine by stating that I'm just as dumbfounded as you are for this glowing recomendation. I recommend playing as blind as you can, no cheating/looking on the internet, with a sheet of paper and a handful of pencils for note taking (just in case).

When this game first came out, I feared it would be another "friendslop" and that I would find immensely joyless and unfunny (as I find most of these newer coop games that revolve around organic, often slapstick comedy). So I got very puzzled when my posse all bought that on launch week and asked me if I wanted. So I went, mostly because we're all tired adults with real life stuff to do and a couple of hours to spare at the end of the day and I could use a new activity to do with my friends. 

To talk about Big Walk's strong points without getting emotional is a near impossible task, I wasn't expecting to find such a fine tuned experience structured in such a way that allows for the game to be played in small, gentle chunks. The game revolves around this giant, beautiful island, filled with communication-based puzzles that asked for us to become better at talking to one another, to use our powers of abstraction and improvisation to do stuff together (to my fellow Brazillian readers, it always felt like Olimpíadas do Faustão. If you're not Brazillian, look it up). The entire experience felt like a gentle afternoon of gathering your friends and not doing much but enjoying each other's company; a breathe of fresh air amidst the chaos of normal life. This game allows for these moments at the same time it also allows for high energy, carnival-feeling shenanigans that allow for genuinely funny moments.

I love me some good puzzles and I love me some mysteries, and having other people that also enjoys good puzzles and mysteries made the whole trip incredible. Some puzzles are genuinely impossible to solve alone and some puzzles will ask for you to find unusual ways to communicate. The mysteries are enticing and will steer you into some form of completionism without asking too much of you. As I said, none of us have that much free time and we managed to squeeze 24 hours to get 100% of the game by playing before we hit the bed.

It's one of my favorite games of the year, and it was one of the best times I've had with a coop game since forever. It felt like after school Payday (which may be an overly specific experience, but somewhere someone will relate and I love you for that), it evoked the nostalgia for easier, calmer days while providing clever puzzles that asked us to be bold, brave, patient and caring.

Big Walk is one of those games that reminds me why I love cooperative gaming.

The soundtrack and sound design are phenomenal and do an incredible job of creating an atmosphere that is both relaxing and immersive. The puzzles are genuinely fun, and working through them with friends feels rewarding without ever feeling like a chore. The proximity chat, once the initial launch issues were ironed out, was incredibly well implemented and added so much to the experience.

I also really appreciated how easy it was to put the game down and jump back into it another night without feeling lost or having to relearn anything.

Without spoiling anything, the ending sequence was absolutely phenomenal. Easily one of my favorite gaming moments in recent memory and something I wish I could experience for the first time again.

Big Walk doesn't need complicated progression systems or an endless gameplay loop to be engaging. It's a game that understands the simple joy of exploring, discovering things, solving problems, and sharing memorable experiences with friends.

If you have a group of friends to experience this with, I cannot recommend it enough. Go in blind.

Big Walk is a game that I can only describe as serene. It doesn't expect anything of you, and it doesn't force a pace. You can wander around a large, beautiful world, and even invite some friends along for the journey. There is no objectives that Big Walk will explicitly state for you, it's up to you to find your own goals and explore what you want to. There are all sorts of fun puzzles to do, but I find that Big Walk shines most at making the player curious. Throughout Big Walk, you will often be presented with various little gadgets you can fidget around with, and you may even find them useful for solving puzzles, or communicating with friends. It's a perfect game for picking up here and there and simply spending time with your friends in a beautiful, open world.

Side note, I just want to glaze this game's art for a moment. The environment in Big Walk is INCREDIBLE. It is so absurdly gorgeous, the graphics are amazing. This isn't to say that it's a very hardware intensive game, you can still very much get a pretty experience on a lower end computer, but the game is truly graphically amazing. And if that weren't enough, the audio design is probably the best in any game I've ever played. I cannot even fathom the time it took for every tiny little detail of this game's incredible soundscape. It's so immersive, with the wind in the trees softly shaking the leaves, or the sound of your little footsteps pitter-patter-ing along the ground. All of which are seemingly dynamic. If you walk on wood, you'll hear the hard claps of your character's shoes hitting the planks. If you walk in the sand, you can hear that sort of squeaky sound as your character walks through it. And that's just some of the sounds. This game is truly beautiful, and I'm honestly at a loss for words sometimes when I'm just wandering around, taking in the sights. It's a great little escape with friends, and a wonderful way to hang out over long distance. The only experience second to Big Walk is actual nature, so overall I give this an overwhelming recommendation!

Big Walk is a relaxing and enjoyable game with some interesting and creative puzzles. I enjoyed exploring the world, discovering new areas and figuring things out without being given too much direction.

The proximity chat is one of my favourite features, especially at night when it gets extremely dark. Getting separated from your friend can make things surprisingly difficult, particularly when you have no idea where they are. I liked how the game lets you use walkie-talkies, flash your torch or point a laser into the distance to help find each other. It's a simple mechanic that works really well and leads to some funny moments.

The moon mask puzzle was another highlight. I won't spoil anything, but working through it together was satisfying and probably my favourite part of the game.

One thing I would have liked is the option to explore the world in single-player. I realise the game is designed around co-op, so it's more of a personal wish than a criticism. Sometimes I just wanted to wander around on my own, take in the surroundings and revisit places at my own pace.

Overall, I'm really glad I played Big Walk. The puzzles are enjoyable, the exploration is relaxing and the co-op mechanics make it stand out.

Big Walk is a walking simulator, yes. It is a game where you get together with your friends, yes. And it's got puzzles. 

But it's more than that!

There's time to sit and think. There's time to talk it out and make a plan. There's time for you and your friends to get to know each other better. Where you and someone you may not have talked to much are separated from everyone else, and there is no fast travel. There is no shortcut. It's you and them, working together, providing company, bonding. 

Big Walk asks you to trust your friends, and build a better connection. To sit in a room together for five minutes. To do trust falls, to communicate, to work together like a team. It asks a lot of you, and what you get is an experience that you and your friends will remember forever.

Ideally keep whatever group you start with, and keep that same group every session. That familiarity and trust in each other is what'll make it all possible. 

I had a fantastic time and I'll treasure the experience! Give Big Walk a try with your friends, and do your best to make it to the end. It's so much more than what's on the surface, but you have to go through it together to see what I mean.

With a very hard cap on what you can do in this game, Big Walk is excellently designed so that you and your friend(s) get a good, nay, an excellent time together. You spend most of the time simply walking, fidgeting with whatever you have in your hands, enjoying the scenery and, more specially, the company you're with.
The rest of the game is a series of distinct yet familiar puzzles you and your friends need to figure out and coordenate together. These, too, are excellently designed, and they only get more fun and creative as you explore the island.

Big Walk is easily one of the must-have experiences for you and your friends to get, more so if you're fed up and tired with overstimulating medias. It's not a game you play for long, but it's a game that will stick to you long after you've finished.

This game was a once-in-a-lifetime, magical experience with 2 of my best friends. Something that looked so simple on the surface actually contained so much mystery, followed by intriguing discoveries and satisfying progression that fueled many nights of staying up longer than anticipated.

Very little is explained in Big Walk, leaving it to the players to build their own explanations for why these locations exist and what they mean, but even if you don't come up with your own answer for what it all means it's still amazing to get caught up in the awe of witnessing it all.

You're on your own to come up with solutions to the puzzles, and over the course of your playthrough you essentially will make your own language of both verbal and non-verbal "words" or cues to solve various types of puzzles and their re-iterations and variations. The final "level" imposes restrictions on communication that pose as a final exam to your system and it is a contender for the single-most satisfying payoff I've ever experienced in a video game. Short preface here. Gonna deviate from my regular format for this review. I want to tell a beautiful story. Using the proximity chat in this game is a must. Looking back on the experience as a whole, it would have been ruined by using discord to voice chat. Big Walk is the sort of game that you can only experience for the first time once, so don't ruin it for yourself.

Several months ago, I was convinced to get Big Walk by some friends. Normally, I’m not a fan of these sorts of games, but the concept behind Big Walk was intriguing enough.

We began our big walk with a group of about 8 people. It was fun. I got lost in the woods at night, we solved puzzles, and were having good conversation. By the end of the first ~2 hours, the group dwindled down to just me and my closest friend. Those who left early had decided the game was too boring and refunded it. My friend and I were captured by the ambiance of Big Walk’s island, and we chose to keep playing. The hum of the insects at night had jogged memories of camping, some I had not remembered for years. The soft crash of waves along the beach gave me nostalgia for a place I had never been to before. The ambiance and sound design of this game is truly stunning, and it helped immerse me in the experience.

Me and my friend played this game on and off. Sometimes we’d just do a puzzle or two, other times we’d get a little more done. There were setbacks, lost time, but it was fine. With each session, we’d inch closer to our goal of getting beyond the wall and to the black sphere. We got lost in the tunnels, enjoyed riding the chairlift and trains, we listened to the radio as we walked around between puzzles. We worked out how to solve the puzzles, sometimes having to come back to certain ones we didn’t have a viable solution for. The conversations kept flowing. Some times it was just conversations about getting to the next puzzle, other times it was regular conversation to catch up with each other. The hours we spent playing this game didn’t feel so long.

After several months of playing on and off, the day finally came. We solved the last puzzle we needed and got the key for the wall. We eagerly proceeded forward, wanting to finally see what was inside the sphere. The skills of communication we spent the last 10 hours building came into play. And when we had reached the finale, I didn’t want it to end. Familiar music played during the ending, and I was overcome with a somber feeling. Luckily, there’s post-ending content to go back and explore, and me and my friend have decided that after a break, we’re going to come back to Big Walk and see what else there is to explore. And who knows, maybe after that, Big Walk will become a digital third space to just talk about life while walking around instead of the sterile environment of a discord call.

Life is short. We are told we need to constantly be doing something productive, constantly moving forward to the next goal. Many games echo this sentiment. FOMO, battlepasses, constant grinding for the next achievement, the next level, it’s all ubiquitous in the modern gaming industry. Big Walk reminded me that sometimes, it’s okay to get lost in the moment for a bit. It’s okay to not always know where you’re going. Big Walk reminded me how many things in life are not possible without good friends. If my friend had chose to not stick with me through Big Walk, I would have never been able to get to the end of the game. I would have never been able to have a moment of introspection on my life. While some people might consider this game “friendslop”, It’s not. It’s an absolute gem of a game. This game has a level of quiet intentionality and thought put into it that I haven’t seen in years. This simple, silly game completely subverted my expectations. It gave me a new perspective on life and on gaming. It was a breath of much needed fresh air.

Thank you, House House.

Big Walk is one of the most original co-op experiences I've played. Rather than relying on obvious markers and constant callouts, the game teaches you and your friends to communicate in subtle ways. By the end, you're reading each other's intentions through small gestures and cues, and solving a puzzle together feels earned rather than handed to you.

The puzzles themselves are mostly original. Very few of them feel like recycled co-op mechanics, and each one makes you rethink how you're working as a group. The length is also well judged: long enough to feel like a complete journey, but it never drags or overstays its welcome.

My only real criticism is that the proximity voice chat range is slightly too small. Teammates who aren't far away can become hard to hear, which sometimes gets in the way of the communication the game is built around.

That aside, Big Walk is an excellent co-op game and easy to recommend to anyone with a group of friends willing to take it slow and pay attention to each other.

The visuals are a surreal blend of beautiful natural environments and deliberately artificial, primary-colored structures reminiscent of playground equipment that exist for no other reason than to give the players something to do.  There's no story or background lore to justify the setting, it's just a big island for you to explore at your own pace, full of problems to solve together, forcing you to invent new ways to communicate with your friends.  

If you intend to finish absolutely everything in the game, expect a single playthrough to take about 24 hours.  There really isn't any replay value unless you do another run with a different number of people, as the puzzles scale dynamically based on how many people are involved, but nothing else changes between playthroughs.

I only had two issues.  One is that the collision physics makes actually walking around the island often frustrating as you frequently get stuck on branches, small rocks, and tiny inclines that you don't see.  The platforming really could have used more work.  The other, which would be an easy fix, is that joining a friend's session requires you to enter a password every time.  It would be nice if there were an option to automatically allow everyone on your friends group, or remember a password you've entered once.

Small gripes aside though, if you're looking for a solid co-op experience, you won't find much better.  Each puzzle requires you to think creatively and work together in ways I've never seen in any other game.  There are some truly novel ideas here, and I hope other studios take notes from the design philosophy.

||I want to talk about my favorite challenge in the game that I think perfectly exemplifies what Big Walk is all about, the 30 minute room. It's an empty room with nothing but buttons that activate a large timer in the room that counts down from 30 minutes. There's no other puzzle or escape room in the room, it's just you and your party in a room for 30 minutes. When we realized what the challenge was, we just sat down and talked about stuff. Some silly things, some personal things, just talking. I think that it speaks volumes that I see a lot of agreement on how well designed this puzzle is because it strips down Big Walk's design to its purest aspects, which is your friends or just the people you play with. Big Walk presents itself as a game of challenges with your friends but there comes a point where you realize how little it really is about the challenges as everything in the game demands cooperation like with the challenges needing 2+ people minimum, the inventory management, and even picking your colors for your character. So much of the game promotes these small moments with your friends like a load of fun items to play with, nothing being named so each group will identify the collectible as something unique, and all the happy accidents where some random item you bring in actually being helpful to completing the challenge like a whiteboard that becomes integral to solving a challenge where you can see the other side but can't hear. We brought in a radio with us to the challenge playing track no. 2, ended up being a favorite for my group, and it did numbers on setting the mood and making us that much more comfortable with being open to each other and ties a bow on a moment that I'll never forget. Big Walk is a game about spending time with friends and fostering the moments we share together whether intentional or not and it's easily become my favorite game of the year.||

This game is great for a few reasons. The puzzles manage to find a sweet spot where you're not bashing your head against a wall to get them done, but you still feel a small, comfortable sense of accomplishment in doing them. The time spent navigating the beautiful island is fantastic for making conversation with your friends, and all the means of communicating with them spread around the island make getting lost more fun than cumbersome. Unlocking new methods of transportation make the game easier, but not faster, which is delightful for focusing on relaxing chats or taking in views while a train or chairlift takes you on your leisurely way. There's always a fun sense of unpreparedness, getting to your destination and wishing you'd brought a tool that would make a puzzle easier or a flashlight for getting back home, and then getting your hands on the items in question only to fiddle with them for a moment and leave again, empty-handed.

I sort of put off reviewing this one. It’s been difficult to review something that’s been tied to your friends so much. We had ten people cycle through it in total, but there’s been a core five of us all the way to the end.

Here’s what stuck with me after the credits: the time spent with my friends *was* the game in the end. Yeah, the puzzles were sometimes funny, sometimes clever, sometimes infuriating. But by the back half, the game for me was just spending time with people I like, and Big Walk was the thing we were doing while we did that.

Even the bits I thought at first were pacing problems turned out to be the point. The slow puzzles. The traversal, even the *vehicular stuff* giving you space to talk to whoever’s next to you. Getting lost from the group wasn’t an annoyance, it was just a thing that meant when you reunited you had something to say. A discovery, a funny story, a 'lads you’ll never guess what I just found'.

That’s what House House built here, and it took me a while to clock it. The game is the excuse. The walk is the thing.

Recommended for: people with friends. Especially friends you feel you don’t spend enough quality time with any more, or ones you’ve not played a game with in a while. Big Walk gives you a reason to be in a voice chat together for a few hours, and then it quietly steps out of the way.

An absolute delightful game to play with friends. Much fun was had in quite unexpected ways.

Friendslop is an incredibly easy, and at times applicable, label to toss onto cooperative indie games these days. Generally the phrase gets rubber stamped onto games with surface level impressions because they often feature an incredibly low barrier of entry, are low in development budget, and are frequently priced at a low-cost to the consumer so that it can attract entire friend groups as an online social activity. I do think the suffix "-slop" carries some connotations of carelessness, which can be very applicable to your Unreal Engine market place asset crammed flavor-of-the-week simulator game that you and your buddies can hop into for a few bucks & get an evening or two hours of fun with and that will eventually have a Roblox clone made of in a few days (assuming that it hasn't been derived of an existing one already.) But, I feel like "-slop" largely does a disservice in describing these games, and is used negatively in the form of rejection and detestment towards the seemingly cookie-cutter rubric that the easily approachable genre has. Regardless of my feelings towards the common haphazardly flinging of the subgenre label and the reckless connotations that it may imply, it's a name that has stuck within pop-culture.

*Big Walk* is a recent entry to the genre that features a, relative to the genre, hefty $20 per-person price tag, going against the grain of the typical pricing structure that others lean into. But, to paraphrase my friend Tucker's description of our time with *Big Walk*,  if many of these cheap turn-and-burn games are friend-slop, then *Big Walk* is friend-gourmet.

The game puts a heavy emphasis on audio & visual communication, to the point where the default sound settings feel a little egregious and overly suppressive. The unaided travel distance of in-game voice communication is rather intentionally shallow, almost to an unrealistic point. Initially it was incredibly extreme, but it was something the devs dialed a little bit back after launch, and does feel like it's at a sweet spot now. The voice proximity restrictions, though, really help elevate the ambiance of the world within the game with the way sounds can echo through caves or across canyons. It bring about a certain charm & warmth when you wander off and loose your friends, only to hear & seek them out later via the reverberations of their voice across the landscape, or hear them beep in via the walkie talkies, or for some like myself, adventuring off to a soundtrack with one of the radios strapped to their back. This relationship with sound, how empty it is alone and how much of a beacon small things can become is incredibly charming. Being able to identify who is around me because such-and-such person was always running around with a certain thing was a very fun aspect of the game, especially as people started to wander off in different directions. The game also pairs a handful of methods of visually communicating with one another via the use of flares, signs, light orbs, laser pointers & flash lights. At night in particular, they can be great signals for paths already trodden, signaling locations for far off lost friends or just straight up being a goofball with (a frequent occurrence among those I played with).

But these things alone are not simply enough to make a good game, or hardly a game at all. The secret sauce with *Big Walk* is all the ways that they use the prior mentioned restrictions & tools for communication in relationship to it's core gameplay loop; solving puzzles. While exploring the world, you'll come across random puzzles (as that is largely the only thing that seemingly exists on this island) that you must solve in order to receive these red bulbus things (note, my friend group referred to them as chuddlings, and seemingly each group of players had their own unique name of reffering to them). Among these puzzles are a handful of towers that have some chuddling-shaped boxes that are empty. It doesn't take a rocket scientist to figure out what you need to do from here.

The puzzles are plentiful, and all require a level of teamwork and coordination to complete. Each also typically offer some level of auditory or visual restriction between the group as well, and very little indication of what you need to do to solve it. It is *entirely* up to you & the people you play with to not only figure out what the game is asking of you, but how you are going to overcome it. This alone enables an immense level of personal creativity, as fundamentally you are working together to find a system to overcome this challenge. The solution to the puzzle will always generally be the same, but the way you get to that point is so incredibly personal to you, the tools you have brought with you & the people you play with. It was great fun to observe online the puzzles my friends & I had overcome, and to compare the difference in ways other players approached it. For example, we *never* used the sign, so our form of communication frequently became a shared method of signaling via player movement. While others may have lugged around a sign to write more specifically what you need.

*Big Walk* is an incredibly simple game at the end of the day, but the way in which it presents a challenge and then takes a step back is absolutely magical. The game becomes so much more of a catalyst for a shared social experience, making it easily one of the most memorable experiences I've had playing video games with my friends. I'll likely hold this game very fondly as the years go on, not because it was all that impressive graphically or mechanically, but more so because of the amazing social experiences that it allowed me to have with my friends. This social offering is what the crux of the genre should be, and I really hope more well polished social games such as this one emerge from the sea of turn-and-burn, $5 flavor-of-the-week games that so frequently blight the genre.

First of all, I don't want to overhype this game. Big Walk is simple little puzzle/exploration game where you and a few friends or acquaintances (A group of at least 4 is required) explore an island filled puzzles that mostly center around cooperation and communication. I suspect this game has about 15-20hrs of content. The puzzles are not difficult, because that is not the point of this game. This is a game built firmly on socialization. Some would describe this as "friendslop", but there is nothing "sloppy" about Big Walk.

Big Walk is an amazing experience. I struggle to find the proper words to describe exactly how well put together this seemingly simple game is. It is, in my opinion, one of the mostly perfectly designed games I've ever played. I have not experienced a single moment where I chafed against the game's mechanics, or thought it didn't absolutely nail what it was going for.

The sound design is amazing. Not just on a soundtrack level, although the few very simple little tunes you come across are certainly delightful, but on a mechanical level. This is a game that hinges on communication between players. It requires players to be able to chat and joke and collaborate on puzzles, and it's perfect. The echoes, the occlusion, the proximity, the overall quality, all of it is executed flawlessly. 

The puzzle design is very clever. All of them are perfectly designed to be solved relatively quickly with cooperation, and not at all without it. I don't think any puzzle took more than 15 minutes, but many only took our group about 5. And yet, none of them felt like let-downs. They were "easy", but they still felt satisfying to complete.

The world is beautifully crafted. It's not the most high-res, photo-realistic thing in the world, but it's exactly what the game needs. It's charming, it's interesting, and it never ones pulls you out of the game, because everything looks like it belongs.

The item system is equally charming. It's limited enough to give you meaningful decisions, and make everyone feel useful, without overburdening the players with too many choices, all while adding additional goals to the game.

The game gives you all the direction you need, while giving you basically none at all (at least, not overtly anyway).

Again, I don't want to oversell this game, because I would be heartbroken if anyone was disappointed with their playthrough. But it is easily one of the most well designed and polished games I've ever played.

If you want the best experience, I would play it blind, with a consistent group, and in short, regular sessions. Play with headphones and a good mic. DO NOT USE 3RD PARTY VOICE CHAT - The in-game chat works perfectly and using something like discord will pull you out of the game, break some of the puzzles, and be an actively worse experience.

Have fun, explore, and... y'know... be careful out there.

This game really struck a cord w/ me. I was pleasantly surprised by "Untitled Goose Game", a game I had no business liking as much as did, given my normal preferences, and given that, I knew this was going to be something special and entirely unique. Boy was I right. "House House" are among the most unique developers out there, always messing around w/ concepts nobody else has even thought of, and more than that: they make it fun too (not just unique for unique sake).
I played w/ a buddy of mine, and it was definitely outside of both of our normal wheelhouses, and we had some incredibly memorable experiences. I laughed more than I have in a long time playing "Big Walk". The game will adapt to how many players you have, except if you try to play by yourself. You can explore the island on your own, but until you have the puzzles solved (which takes at least 1 teammate), you'll be locked out of everywhere except the starting area, so this is exclusively a multiplayer game (2-12 players). But after completing it and opening up the environment, it's really a zen, chill environment to just exist in. 
The gameplay itself is based entirely upon communication, and the limits of NATURAL (not video-gamey) communication. It will cut you off from each other, and force you to use your avatar's body language to communicate the solutions to puzzles to each other. A particular favorite of ours takes away your ability to see, while your teammate(s) has to guide you through a precariously high obstacle course, where if you mess up, you fall quite a ways and have to climb back up and start over. 
In lesser hands, things like this would absolutely be more irritating than fun, but here, with "House House", it's a blast (if not sometimes a little irritating). 
If you lose each other, separated by even a few dozen feet, the proximity chat will slowly cut out, and if you get badly separated, you will need to use tools on your character, or in the environment to signal your location to your teammates so you can re-unite, assuming of course you don't cheat via Discord. I mean, we did a couple times, but we really tried not to, and it made the experience that much more memorable. 
If you have at least one friend you like to play games with, and are open to unusual gaming experiences, this is an absolute must try. Don't write this off as just another "friend-slop" title... It's so much more than that.

For me: game of the year. Maybe a top game of my life. But the experience here is dependent on factors and elements you may not have or enjoy.

Big Walk revolves around a few central things: friends, communication, exploration, and puzzles. On paper it doesn't sound that different from a what of might get deemed friendslop. But the suggested limitations and the canvas provided to paint on are what set Big Walk apart.

Talking solely through the game's voice system at times was annoying. You get used to hearing everything when you're on a video call. But here, it's like in life: we have to be near each other. That's some muscle-memory stuff to overcome. But the flipside, is that you are forced to find and use other ways of communicating. Either setting a plan and finding each other later, just gestures, finding a tool to help, or maybe some other option entirely.

Puzzles are usually some variety of "figure out how to communicate within limitations" but each puzzle elegantly adds to the catalog available. Some you walk in and understand immediately. Some you have to each trade roles or positions in before the light bulb goes off. Sometimes it's just a matter of one person gets it, but how to you untangle this abstract series of things and bring your friends along with you?

Exploration can be a bigger or smaller part of your experience if you like. I love a walk in the woods, down a riverbed, rain, shine. For me this captured the essence of "don't know where I'm going, but I gotta see what's over there". Even with the art style it felt alive and fascinating. 

I want to go on and on forever about how much I loved my time in this game. But you just want to know if you'll have a good time. I think if you enjoy wandering and puzzles, you will have a good time if you can form a group. Mine was not particularly methodical, and I personally am responsible for many delays. But it felt like an incredibly brief 20 hours together.  We started playing at launch. Took a long time with my group, usually in 1-2 hour chunks every week or two. Worth every moment.

One thing that really meant a lot to me was exploring how to create a functional vocabulary about what you're experiencing together. This is the part that shows the biggest humanity of the design of Big Walk. What do you call these red blobs you find? It both matters, and it does not. But the choice is emblematic of how the game works: you work together to make your world, and that gives it meaning for you. You now have some skin in the game, no matter how small. When you finally draw that to a close, it's like that bittersweet mood like finishing a life-changing book. The kind where you just can't bear to be done, can't bear to look for a next one just yet.

Since my group started playing, House House has opened up about some AI/LLM use in wrapping up production of the game. I want to acknowledge I'm aware of that and disappointed, I generally do not support a lot of AI/LLM use. At the same time cannot stress enough how much Big Walk feels like a deeply human game, made by people, with the clearest of intentions about connecting people. I think it is fair to consider where AI/LLM fits into the world in lots of ways. But I don't think in this specific case the art of the experience is damaged.

This is a very special game. The puzzles are varied and interesting, and as you progress through the game the devs iterate on the ideas presented in a very fun way. You will undoubtedly develop a unique language to discuss the puzzles with your group, and the development of that language is in a way the core of the game.

This game is a friendship building machine. It gives you many opportunities to slow down, periods where you might as well just talk, catch up, joke, whatever. review: 10 years ago, Unity had senior engineers that would help studios using their engine so that if a niche bug came up and your developers couldn't solve it, the studio could get support from their expertise and focus on building their game rather than tackle complicated technical errors. Allegedly even the founders would get into video calls to help people with their engine. That's all gone now. Unity has fired many of those people and pushed the rest of them out with their poor management. If House House made this game ten years ago, they would've had the support they needed to fix the bug. In the year 2026 though, that's no longer available. Unity told them they couldn't help, that it was impossible to fix the bug, and they used the only tool left to them, Claude. I think it's ridiculous to disqualify this game from game awards ceremonies because the industry the awards go towards is so severely rotten that there's no choice but to get senior engineer help from an AI that was likely trained on the portfolios of the senior engineers Unity has lost. This game isn't AI slop, it's a love letter to puzzling and co-operative gaming, and House House deserve an award for creating such a moving work that can be experienced with your friends or family, easily the best of the year. These devs do not deserve the stake that some people want to hang them on. As someone who doesn't use AI and hate how it impacts art and artists, AI as a tool will never fully go away, and if it makes you upset that we live in a world where it's quickly becoming non-negotiable to interact with AI agents to solve a problem, then you need to be taking that up with proponents of workers rights in your government and Unity itself for its garbage AI focused business tilt.

This game ended up being the catalyst for some of my favorite shared experiences with some of my closest friends. I feel honestly that it helped us to build a deeper connection and awakened dynamics between us that I didn't realize were possible. 

The puzzles in this game are incredibly inventive, thoughtfully constructed, and inherently collaborative. The game insists upon you communicating and problem solving and doesn't hold your hand while doing so. You are intended to take minimal information and use deduction, intuition, and trial and error to solve puzzles and understand the objective of the game in a way that always feels extremely rewarding.

The overall design of the game, I think, is genius. It is visually striking and beautiful while simultaneously being visually simplistic. The characters, objects, and buildings are all bold simplified forms scattered around a detailed landscape inspired by nature. There are no blinking lights or arrows, there is no big text wall of instructions, there is no voice-over narrative guiding you through the game telling you what to do. It's up to you and your friends to use the information and objects presented to you to figure it out. Because of this, the game presents itself uniquely to everyone who plays it. I really appreciate that the devs trusted the players to figure things out in a way that makes the overall experience feel uniquely personal and exciting to complete.

It's been a few months now since my friends and I completed Big Walk and I still remember it fondly. I think some of my favorite moments were when we all sat in a circle, unrelated to any puzzle or objective, and just talked. I found myself getting genuinely emotional at different points in the game, like riding the ski lift and watching the sunset, or when a solution finally clicked and we all celebrated together, or when I had to wave goodbye for the last time as we completed the game. Big Walk is peaceful, challenging, character defining, inspiring, welcoming, creative, and just wonderful. I love this game. 10/10.

Big Walk is a meditation on what it means to inhabit digital bodies with your friends. It can be described as an open world multiplayer game peppered with communication puzzles, but that discounts what it actually does. A lesser game would have given you a minimap or a compass showing you where all the nearby puzzles are. A lesser game would have given you item slots so you can take all the useful gear you find with you to help with those puzzles. A lesser game would have made going to the next area a simple process.

Instead, Big Walk is about making a plan with your friends and immediately losing one of them at night in the pitch black dark, and then spending 15 minutes trying to find them. Big Walk is about taking a really useful item with you and then falling down a small cliff and watching as that item flies out of your hands and rolls away down a much larger mountain. Big Walk is about yelling at your friends for coming up with the most convoluted system imaginable to solve a puzzle. Big Walk is about finding a new music spot and getting your digital body to dance awkwardly with your friends.

Big Walk understands that the point is not necessarily the puzzles, not even necessarily about communicating with, but just [i]being[/i] with your friends. And, without spoiling anything, in that way, Big Walk reaches for the sublime.
