Wonderful little puzzle game. Leave it to the Aussies to create such a comforting, low stakes adventure with your friends. This isn't a game you grind out or get obsessed with for a week before dropping. It's best enjoyed in small bursts, maybe when you've got a good meal at hand or you've just finished a stressful day, as it forces you to slow down. No manic sprinting around, no effect-and-sound laden action, no menu upon menu of collectibles or visual noise. You're just in the wilderness, hanging out with the lads or ladettes, and solving a few puzzles at your own pace. It encourages you to goof off, chat with people, or enjoy a companionable silence as you walk between areas.

But this is not just a "it's as fun as you make it" game, the puzzles at its core are communication focused. Everything is intuitive, usually reliant upon your friends putting their heads together to get around barriers in sight, sound, or logistics. One puzzle has you slap a vision-restricting helmet on one friend as the others guide them through a maze. Another has you use telescopes to find the locations of hidden buttons, and then find a way to signal for everybody to press them at the same time. None of the puzzles are extremely convoluted, yet they all feel rewarding, inventive, and never frustrating or agonizing. It really embodies the spirit of teamwork makes the dream work.

So, round up some friends, or make some new ones, and try and put this on the docket in place of a board game or movie night. It's well worth it.

November 11th - [b]Big Walk[/b] - 18h 24m - 8/10 - 100% - Started August 18th - 85 Days Taken - Got all of the beans and all of the achievements.

[b]Pros:[/b]
Big Walk stands out from other co-op puzzle games due to how intuitive it is and how much it laser focuses on the communication aspect of co-op games. I'll start with explaining the former. Once you're inside of the game, outside of the tutorial area, there isn't any text inside of Big Walk explaining what you have to do. This can easily leave players confused and unsure of what do, especially on such a large map, but the game steadily builds up its scale at a natural pace. In the beginning [spoiler]players are only able to explore a small area and are taught the mechanic that keys are the key to progression.[/spoiler] They go [spoiler]on a path which leads them to their first tower, from which they see 5 empty containers for 5 objects.[/spoiler] This clues them into the fact that the game's main gameplay loop is [spoiler]collecting objects and bringing them to the towers. Finding these objects (which I will be calling beans from now on)[/spoiler] can be quite daunting, especially on such a big map, but Big Walk circumvents this issue, by making brightly coloring each area that contains a bean, making it stand out from the realistic terrain. After players beat [spoiler]the first tower, they unlock the map room.[/spoiler] This teaches players that they'll [spoiler]unlock something new for every tower they complete. The subsequent towers unlock more transportation options on the island, making it easier to move around the island to reach the puzzles you want. The map shows them the layout of the island as well as the location of every puzzle and tower.[/spoiler] From there players can create their own plan and which order they want to tackle the towers. This highlights another one of Big Walk's strengths, which is the game's non-linear nature. If your group is stuck on a specific puzzle, you can skip that one and do a different puzzle instead. My group got the normal ending with 15 puzzles left over, which is plenty of leeway.

Now to address the puzzles themselves. They place a lot of importance on the co-op aspect of the game. All of them require good communication from your teammates in whatever form that may take. A lot of puzzles restrict your ability talk with your teammates. Maybe you can only talk to specific teammates or you can't talk at all and you have to use gestures to communicate. I found this very unique for a co-op game. Most co-op games require good vocal teamwork, so it's interesting to see a co-op game tackle the concept from a different angle. There are also puzzles that restrict your sight with your teammates and make you reliant on your teammates descriptions. It sounds quite simple in concept, but Big Walk manages to take this premise and use it for a large amount of puzzles, where each one feels unique in some way. Due to their unique style, the actual difficulty of the puzzles isn't that high for a puzzle game even though they don't feel easy either. This means that even your friends who don't play puzzle games can have a great time with the game. The best part of the game is the ending section [spoiler]inside the black orb[/spoiler] as it puts the skills you've accumulated over the course of the rest of the game to the test. You have to do the entire thing [spoiler]without being able to talk to your friends, without items that would otherwise help you circumvent that like signs and everyone looks the same so you can't even tell your friends apart.[/spoiler] It's a marathon with you having to do 7 puzzles in a row, but that just makes the end of the game that much more rewarding. To top it all off, the end of the game has a strong impact in the bittersweet way you have to say goodbye to your friends in game one by one. That's the regular ending, the 100% ending also fits the game very well. Rather than [spoiler]a bittersweet ending after a challenge gauntlet, you are prompted to reflect on your experience playing the game and what your favorite moments were. The game creates a moment where the fun comes from your friends rather than the game itself,[/spoiler] which does fit well with Big Walk's co-op focused gameplay style. 


[b]Neutral:[/b]
I found that orienting yourself on the island can be a little difficult, since it's large and you can only [spoiler]view the map in the map room[/spoiler] unless you take a map with you. This can be a bit of a problem if you're trying to locate a specific puzzle. The problem could've been exacerbated for me, because my friend group could only play every other week, so I couldn't memorize the map. For my playthrough it wasn't that big of an issue, since others in my friend group knew what direction to head in most of the time. Even then, I can't fault the game too much, since it's called Big Walk after all, so wandering around is a core part of the game. This problem, however does get worse the fewer puzzles you have left, because rather than wandering around the map and solving whatever puzzles you come across, you are instead seeking out specific puzzles you haven't completed yet. These puzzles are likely to be far away from [spoiler]the map room[/spoiler], so you either have to remember the key landmarks around each puzzle you want to complete or just take a screenshot, which is what my friend group ended up doing.


[b]Cons:[/b]
While I praised the puzzles in the positive section of the review. I wrote that section after the regular ending, before 100% completing the game. I realized that my friends had skipped all the more annoying puzzles in the game, which a big chunk of the puzzles we had left after getting the regular ending. What I liked about the puzzles we had done before is that they tested specific communication skills by confining you into small areas. However the puzzles my group had left were ones that spanned across larger areas of the map. For a few of them all you needed was enough walkie-talkies to be able to communicate with your friends and the puzzle became trivial. They just took a while to complete since you had to travel across the map to various points. During those puzzles, the only thing alleviating my boredom came from chatting with my friends rather than anything offered by the game itself. Which I know is just what I praised Big Walk for doing during the 100% ending. The difference is that in that instance it felt intentional, while with these puzzles it felt like an unintended side effect of the puzzles not being very interesting or entertaining. The most boring challenge for me had to be the one where [spoiler]you had to grab specific panels from other challenges and bring them to one location. It's not very interesting, since you just have to hope you remember where those panels are located and take them.[/spoiler]

[b]Overall:[/b]
After 100%ing Big Walk, I honestly wish that I had marked the game as completed after the regular completion. It would've left a stronger impression on me due to its stellar regular ending. Fully completing the game exposes some of the game's flaws that are masked by being selective about which puzzles you do and not caring as much where you're travelling, which are leniencies you're awarded during a regular playthrough. It's a small blemish on what is otherwise an amazing co-op puzzle game , one of the best and most unique ones in the genre. One that really uses its co-op aspect to its fullest potential.

I have unfortunately been able to fully finish the game (haven't gotten past the wall), as I've never had a stable group to play with unfortunately, but I think I do still have a good foundation on making a proper review.
The game is lovely. Playing it with either flat screen or with the VR mod, both ways are perfect. It's really nice just spending time with people and getting to know them more. I may be zoomer with Autism and ADHD, would make sense maybe that I would enjoy games with constant dopamin rushes and whatever, that couldn't be any further from the truth. It is a breath of fresh air from the usual chaotic co-op extraction games. Most of my playtime has literally just been sitting on top of one of the towers with someone, having a conversation, waiting for someone else to join us. With the people that I've played with, we've ofc done the usual puzzles, but most of these sessions have still been just discussing about things. I enjoy that a lot. I don't have to worry about some time limit, entities, any danger at all - it's just me, some other people, and chill puzzles. To some, the walking and traversal is irritating or boring or whatever other negative adjective. That's the part I enjoy, because I get to speak to people.

I'm really happy with my time spent in Big Walk so far. It is a game I would return to just to play with people I already know, just to get to know them better, even if I remember everything about the, the socialising aspect is what I come and play for mainly. The game is worth getting even at full price imo, especially if you have close friends that you do seriously have fun with.

The quality of this game's experience hinges a lot on how much fun you can have just talking to your friends while occasionally doing a (usually very well designed) puzzle.

That said, this game is an absolute masterpiece in game design and atmosphere and will stand as a shining example of what co-op games can do that other games can not.

---

While I don't have a personal connection to australian nature, I can still feel that House House have put a lot of effort and care into the environment. This care is best felt when you — whether by choice or circumstance — split off from your group and find yourself walking through various shrubs and bushes, frantically searching for a way to signal your position to your friends.

And this exact moment is what makes Big Walk so, so special: The moments of solitude and quiet reflection that happen between all the chaos of doing puzzles and difficulty of navigating the map on your two feet... they make you think. About friendship, cooperation (and lack thereof, sometimes...) and everything that led to this moment of you walking through virtual shrubs.

But that solitude, as quiet and lonely it may be, never ends up feeling crushing. Why?

Because at the end of your walk, no matter how lost you may feel... you know that your friends are out there, waiting for you to find your way back to them.

And when you do finally find your friends and you resume yelling at each other over the dumbest shit again... you realize that this game goes beyond whatever clever puzzle lies ahead of you.

There is no other co-op game (and even any game in general) that has made me feel like this, and maybe never will be.

If you know anybody who wants to play this with you, please... do them a favor and listen to them. You won't regret it.

---

Also, I am aware of the entire "House House used AI for this game!!" thing. As much as I dislike generative AI, they only used it for a fringe performance issue that not even the developers at Unity were able to solve (and nothing else!).
Now ask yourself, would you rather release this game in a terrible state (performance wise) and risk people missing out on an otherwise beautifully handcrafted experience OR use a morally-dubious tool to aid development AFTER already exhausting all other options at fixing it? 

The answer, to me, is obvious. GenAI is not an absolute evil, it is a tool. And if the people who use it know not to replace their passion and creativity with it, then I see no issue in using it as a last resort to an issue that could ruin this game's release (even if the people who profit off the tool are despicable).

Please, people, know how to have some nuance to your hate.

Big Walk is one of the most creative, thoughtfully crafted co-op experiences out right now, and it deserves to be judged on its own merits rather than on the tools that were used in the game's development.

The use of AI was justified and only a very minor part of the game code, not really related to the game itself, but rather the engine the game runs on. I think it is good they were transparent about their AI usage, though unfortunately that is easily taken out of context, this game is not AI-generated.

The creators used an LLM to help fix a bug. The AI suggested a fix that did not work immediately, so they had to try multiple times and make changes to the code themselves to make it work. So the final code was not even AI-generated; it was an AI-assisted solution to a problem that was not directly related to the game, but rather the Unity game engine and underlying code.

House House did their research, reached out to the creator of the engine that had the issue, and turned to this as a last-resort effort to fix it themselves after they were told it was not fixable. They were determined to fix it anyway, because they want to make the game the best it can be and make it a great experience for everyone.

They could have given up, but they didn't. This should be praised and rewarded regardless of the tools that were used, especially in this day and age where a lot of developers release games full of issues. Big Walk is a true labor of love, and it shows.

People complaining about AI are ignorant, perhaps willfully, about how much AI is already in development.

Unity and Unreal almost certainly use AI by default in their development now. Godot, as a large open-source project, would be hard-pressed to not let AI-created material into the engine, even if only accidentally. There are limited options you'd have if you insist on an AI-free engine.

If you're willing to forgive that, then what about bugfixing? That's what this whole thing is about, after all: they used AI to fix bugs.

In the Unity engine. The engine that, as discussed, was almost certainly made at least partially by AI. That puts you with a fun little problem, with a few solutions.

One, you scrap the game you've been working on for god knows how long because you now have to migrate to another engine.

Two, you burn an untold amount of man-hours trying to track down the problem in a bunch of code that's probably poorly documented or undocumented so you can fix it.

Three, you ask the thing that can read the code ten thousand times faster than you can to point you at the right places.

AI is going to stay in coding forever. It's one of a handful of places where it's legitimately useful. And, yes, it has major downsides. Those need to be addressed in better ways than an attempt at wholesale banning that does not have popular support. You're not winning popular support.

I didn't have any intention of getting this game, but the controversy induced me to. That this game is charming, carefully considered, and extensively labored over is self-evident. The fact that House House used AI to fix a single bug really does not matter. It matters even less when you have the facts, and they are, as I understand them, as follows:

- House House realized the game was losing frames at sunrise and sunset
- They traced this to a lighting bug with Unity
- They consulted the Unity team to fix it
- The Unity team determined there was no fix for it
- House House asked AI how to fix it
- AI offered several ideas which House House then pursued
- Eventually, after some iteration, House House successfully implemented one of these AI ideas and fixed the sunset/sunrise bug

As to whether AI assisted in implementation or if it was purely the progenitor of the idea, I do not know, but the fact is, to go by what House House has said, the AI generated material in this game constitutes this single engine-bug workaround -- approximately 10 lines of code in a project of 10's of thousands. It is absurd to demonize or punish this group for such a trivial thing.

AI is icky, but AI is also everywhere. You interact with its products daily. This is not fatalism, it's fact. If a developer, or anyone trying to solve a problem anywhere for any purpose, has exhausted their options and consulted the human experts, why should they not then consult AI? It is a tool to be used, and in a situation where no human is able to solve the problem, then there is no human marginalized or put out of work by AI's consultation, so I would argue this is the most appropriate time for its use.

Yes, AI presents myriad potential and active harms. Yes, we should protest and oppose this. But we need to be reasonable, we need to be proportionate, and as evidenced by this ridiculous Big Walk outburst, we need to recalibrate ourselves on what the acceptable and unacceptable uses of AI are.

---------------------
regarding disclosure:

As I understand it, Steam requires only that the inclusion of AI-generated assets in a published game be disclosed. Code that is partially or entirely the product of AI does not need to be reported. No disclosure was required of House House, and so they made none, so it cannot be said that House House failed to comply with the rules. When the issue of their AI-use became a matter of (extremely limited) public interest, they made a disclosure. I don't see how they could reasonably have been expected to do any better.

[h1]The use of AI does not warrant the hate this game got recently[/h1]

Let's clear the air about what's happened if you haven't already heard about it. The developers of this game used, dare I say it, [b]generative AI[/b]. [i]*Audible gasps and the sounds of shattering glass*[/i]

So why doesn't this game deserve any hate at all? TL;DR - it's because the AI was only used to fix a performance tanking bug that even Unity Engine's own engineers couldn't fix.

Let's get just a little more in-depth here:

[h2]What was the bug?[/h2]

Unity utilizes a rendering framework called the Universal Render Pipeline (URP), which controls how graphics, lighting, and most importantly [b]shadows[/b] are rendered on your screen when you play the game. The big in question is more accurately defined as a limitation of the engine, and how it renders [b]shadows[/b]. 

If you've played big walk, you know that the day/night cycle of the game is fairly frequent, and an important part of the gameplay loop. So what does this have to do with the limitation of the engine?

The issue was causing shadows rendered behind the player to render at an infinite distance which, in short; [b]caused the game to run around 50% [i]slower[/i] during both sunrise and sunset for around 20 seconds.[/b] This is not an insignificant amount of time. In fact, 20 seconds of performance impact feels a lot longer than it actually is when you're playing a game. If you don't believe me, Take a game you're used to playing at a crisp 60fps, and then limit your frame rate to 30fps. You're going to notice a difference, I'm absolutely certain of it.

Now then:

[h2]What did AI actually generate in terms of code?[/h2]

Generative AI, in order to fix a limitation that Unity's own engineers were unable to fix, wrote for House House a grand total of [i]*drumroll*[/i]... 10 lines. Less than 0.1% of all the game's code.

Ten total lines of code were written, and then modified by the developers to better fit their game and what they wanted it to do, and all for the sake of making the game BETTER for everyone playing it.

[h3]Heads up fellas, this next one is gonna sting...[/h3]

Generative AI has been used terribly since its inception, but the argument that every single use case is unnacceptable simply isn't true or fair. AI can and has been used as a tool to do good, and in a way that doesn't steal from others or cause harm to the careers of those in the different industries involved.

This is an example of industry giants being unable to solve an issue for a smaller indie studio, and the studio taking matters into its own hands not for the money, but for the players. House House did not cut its workforce and start using AI instead. They did not replace a single programmer, artist, voice actor, or any part of their staff and place AI where they once sat. It was the very programmers of Big Walk that utilized the powerful tool at their disposal to fix something that no other avenue they attempted was able to fix.

As a tool, AI has become commonplace. The only thing we CAN do is keep the use of Gen AI responsible. Keep people accountable not for using it [b]at all[/b], but rather for using it [b]properly[/b].

one little detail i liked was just hitting and rubbing stuff with our little mitts, and hearing the different surfaces react :)

This is like one of the best use cases for AI. the game was actively coded like 99% of the way by hand, and they tried EVERY other avenue before turning to AI as a last ditch effort. If we yell about small potatoes like that, we're gonna get nowhere with AI sentiment in the larger public.

I’ve been gaming for a really long time, across pretty much every genre, and I can honestly say Big Walk is one of the best co-op multiplayer games I’ve ever played.

It’s built around teamwork and talking, and it really tests that. The proximity chat, walkie-talkies, gestures and all the little tools mean you have to communicate. When things go wrong, you’ll quickly find out who your real friends are. It put my friendships with my closest friends to the test, and we came out of it laughing. It was entertaining from start to finish.

The challenges are spot on. They’re never cheap or frustrating, and they always need everyone working together. Finishing a puzzle as a group feels earned.

I also want to give the team credit outside the game itself. They’ve taken a public stance on the Palestinian cause, which is really brave. Many studios stay silent on it, so seeing a developer speak up takes real courage, and I truly appreciate it.

I’ve seen some backlash about AI being used for a small bit of bug fixing. Honestly, that’s completely fine. It doesn’t take anything away from the game’s creativity or heart, and the developers don’t owe anyone an explanation for it.

If you have a group of friends and want something that will make you laugh, argue and work together, get Big Walk. 10/10.

The game is well paced, and satisfied me for its price point, although if I had only aimed to play it through once (probably the more sane way to do it, as the game is not really replayable at all), I would perhaps have been more satisfied with about 20% off. As it stands though, I have passed my completely arbitrary metric of 1 hour of fun per dollar I spent on the game, and more.

As much as I do not approve of the use of AI in general, the way it was used in this game is as close to ethical as you can get. The artistic vision remains human, and no jobs were replaced with chatbots. Time and effort were spent on this game, and it shows through. It is unfortunate that the game has been tied into the ongoing debate on the ethics of AI (or lack thereof) for so little. Ultimately, it is a usage of AI I am comfortable, albeit not elated about. I didn't want to leave a negative review on such a great game, but I'm feeling inclined to do so since my request for a refund was denied. I did not know that AI was a part of the development process when I purchased the game. It was not disclosed on the store page. I understand that it was "only used for debugging to avoid crunch time" and wasn't used as a substitute for artists or the creative process, and I understand that many game devs use AI far more than this one, but I am extremely disappointed to learn House House stooped to using AI tools instead of delaying the game's release, or fixing bugs after release with a patch.

Here's the thing about this seemingly trivial use of AI in an otherwise wonderful masterpiece of a game: it sets the stage for less passionate devs and AI investors to say "Look at Big Walk, that game's a work of art and it used AI! AI IS THE FUTURE OF GAME DEVELOPMENT!!!" without the context of how little it was used. It gives AI techbros ammunition in their war to justify the creation of effortless slop. If AI tools are standard in game development, data centers get made to facilitate their use, local neighborhoods suffer from the energy drain and noise pollution, water supplies are evaporated as cooling, and space that could otherwise be used for leisure or nature gets filled with RAM-hogging server racks whose only function is to "increase productivity".

I don't want my money supporting projects which used AI in any capacity, if I can help it. Unfortunately, since I spent my money already, played several hours, and can't get a refund, my only option is to leave a negative review warning others about the issues I have with the game. It's truly a shame too, if not for the AI usage, this game would hold a spot in my heart for my entire life as a beautiful creation of passion, celebrating what it is to be human, solve problems, and communicate with others. Instead, my memory of the game will be forever stained by the devs' decision to cut corners in debugging just to meet a deadline.

And to those who would defend the use of AI as a "tool to help reduce crunch time in game development": that's simply not how anything works in the world. Only in the honeymoon phase of a new tool does it actually make the life of the workers easier. As it becomes the norm, the expectations shift and crunch time remains. Just look at how anything else is. Peoples' lives haven't become more leisurely or relaxed as tech has sped up menial tasks; the opposite has happened and people are more impatient and rushed than ever. Tech has increase speed and productivity immensely, even without AI tools existing, and yet none of that has actually made people live more fulfilling lives. None of it has made the life of workers easier. Rather, their employers simply demand more of them.  AI tools will not eliminate crunch time, they will simply result in even stricter deadlines that account for any increased productivity that could be gained in the first place. The only way to avoid crunch time is to not have a deadline at all and to accept that it takes time to make a work of art and it takes time to solve problems that may arise in code. Sadly, patience doesn't pay and investors hate waiting for returns; the economic systems we live in simply don't allow for the true elimination of crunch time, and AI tools will not change that.

Big Walk is a masterpiece of human connection, and the recent wave of negative reviews fixating on its developer's incredibly minimal use of an LLM completely misses the forest for the trees. This is a game built entirely around authentic cooperation, empathy, and joy—qualities that shine through every hand-crafted inch of its open world.

To dismiss a project that took six years of passionate, independent development because the studio used an AI chatbot to debug roughly 10 lines of code is not just unfair; it shows a profound misunderstanding of how video games are actually made.  

Game development is a notoriously grueling, deeply technical process where progress often grinds to a halt over the most obscure engine problems. For decades, the solution to these roadblocks has been trawling through dead forums, outdated documentation, and endless pages of source code just to find a workaround for a stubborn bug. Using an LLM to research a solution to a difficult technical problem with third-party code is simply the modern evolution of that exact same process. It is a ridiculous double standard to consider researching a tricky game engine problem via an LLM any different from looking up the same solution on Stack Overflow. It is an extension of traditional problem-solving, only far more effective.   

When a small independent studio like House House is trying to bring a brilliant vision to life, getting stuck on a coding issue doesn't make the game more "authentic"—it just drains time, budget, and morale. Finding a cost-effective, efficient way to solve these highly specific technical hurdles allows the developers to focus their limited resources on what actually matters: designing puzzles, building the world, and refining the experience. The fact that they could untangle a messy code problem efficiently directly benefits both the developers' well-being and the quality of the product the consumer receives.Big Walk has an undeniable soul. The proximity voice chat, the playful communication tools, and the sheer brilliance of its shared adventure didn't come from an algorithm; they came from a team of human beings who wanted to make something special. Punishing an indie studio for utilizing a modern research tool to fix a bug is absurd. If you want to support independent art, play this game and judge it for the profound, beautiful experience it actually is.

A solid game, do recommend. As others have mentioned, it's definitely a your-mileage-may-vary for enjoyment (one person in our group tried it out and determined it wasn't their thing early on), but if it's your flavor it's good.

Pros
- does a decent job of early game guidance/education while still giving a lot of freedom in how you choose to progress for the bulk of the game
- puzzles are enjoyable, generally intuitive, varied, but also build on each other in a nice way
- with many of the puzzles, you/your group have flexibility in how you choose to approach them (comparing the group I played with to some actual plays, there were definitely different mindsets in how we thought about some of the puzzles)
- the way the player avatars move/animate/emote is delightful
- end game was great, post-game was fun
- pacing is very relaxed

Cons
- pacing is very relaxed (this is a YMMV thing); overland travel is pretty slow, and the other transportation options likewise are not quick; this is fine, but calling it out here since it may frustrate some
- getting stuck on environment geometry is sometimes weird in how it stops you from jumping, and isn't necessarily the clearest as it's happening
- as others have said, definitely check your audio setup so you can hear and be heard
- unless there's something that allows the puzzles to change on replay, replayability is low unless you're speedrunning; for the price one playthrough is reasonable

Big Walk is the co-op game from the Untitled Goose Game people, and it’s basically “go for a long walk with your friends and solve weird puzzles while yelling at each other.”You drop into this big, pretty Australian island as these little colorful stick figures with long noses. There’s no solo mode. You need at least one other person (ideally 3–4 friends) and the game’s own proximity voice chat. Discord ruins half the fun because half the game is losing each other and then inventing stupid ways to find each other again.Most of the time you’re just wandering around, messing with tools (walkie-talkies, flares, cowbells, megaphones…), pointing wildly, and trying to figure out whatever weird puzzle the island threw at you. The puzzles are actually really good — clever without being mean, and they force you to talk and coordinate in funny ways. Failures are usually hilarious instead of annoying.It’s chill, silly, and weirdly wholesome. You’ll laugh a lot, get slightly lost a lot, and probably end up with inside jokes that only make sense to the people you played with. The ending even hits harder than it has any right to.If you’ve got a small group of friends who don’t mind a slow, talky co-op game, this is an absolute winner. Just don’t play it alone and don’t use Discord. Go for the walk. ~grok

Yes, House House DID use GenAI. No, it wasn't a lot. It is still aneurysmically frustrating that the people who claim others haven't read the article are the ones who've themselves failed to parse the information. I will also cite the relevant paragraph:

[quote]In the final stretch of Big Walk’s development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs. In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.[/quote]

It was not used for "one last-minute bugfix". The one specific example [b]that they happen to cite among an unspecified number of "difficult technical challenges"[/b] amounts to about 10 lines of manually modified code after their own troubleshooting and official Unity support had failed them. A project of this size could easily have upwards of 1 million lines of code. I know they probably weren't thinking too specifically when citing "0.1%" as their reference, but 0.1% of 1 million is already 1000. Let's take them at their word that it's "well under" that number; let's say 500. 500 lines of manually reviewed AI code, under which the game probably performs better than it would have otherwise. Is that a breaking point for most people? Probably not. But where exactly [i]is[/i] that point? Where exactly do consequences fall, for whom, how, and to what degree? What is the message that is sent when we excuse its undisclosed inclusion, in an otherwise heartfelt and quite well-designed indie gem?

I have what I would say are sensibly complicated feelings on the matter. Does it diminish the fun I've had with the game so far? Absolutely not. Will I still finish my playthrough? Yes. Do I understand the temptation to fall back on those tools at the tail end of a 6-year dev cycle when even your engine's official support process claims what you want is impossible? Sure. Will I be holding any future House House game up to closer scrutiny? Very.

Would the foreknowledge have stayed my hand from a purchase? I'm not sure, but I'd have expected the disclosure up front in good faith from the studio that's recently made a moral grandstand of delisting their games from Microsoft platforms as part of the BDS boycott - which to be clear, is itself [i]a good thing,[/i] but to do so while trying to conceal any use of the tech that is making so many people's lives and livelihoods so much more difficult makes it feel a bit performative. Not to mention their publisher is Panic, a studio that has taken a no-holds-barred hardline stance of [b]ABSOLUTELY NO AI[/b] for games released officially under their label on their own handheld console, the Playdate. This has gotta be uncomfortable for them too, even if disclosure of this level of usage is seemingly not technically required by Steam's current policies.

There's a well-worded if lengthy article [url=https://www.clockworkworlds.com/a-couple-of-posts-about-ai-and-the-igf-awards/]here[/url] that does a good job of encapsulating the murkiness of AI use in this particular case. It's a comparatively minor infraction, but still not a decision without consequence. The more edge cases we let in, the less they're regarded as edge cases, and, well. I've seen the decades-long slide of where horse armor got us, and at this point it's only in retrospect that someone can look back and ask "how the hell did we end up here", assuming the presence of assorted $100+ exclusive skins in various games even occur to them as abnormal anymore.

Big Walk is a fantastic game. I'd still recommend it, generally speaking. I just feel burnt that the devs didn't trust people to be able to make up their own minds about this if they'd been upfront about it and decided asking forgiveness outside of their primary sales window was better than transparency while still inside of it.

Big walk released the day after I had a pretty intense surgery. I was bedbound for a few weeks, and felt very alone and isolated. Big Walk not only gave me a game to play, but a way to be together with my friends in a way that a Discord VC can't.

The game itself is a simple premise: co-op puzzle platformer collection. Solve puzzle, get reward, turn in reward, unlock more puzzles, get more rewards, etc.

That honestly wasn't the "point" of it, though. The point was that it truly felt like a long walk in the wilderness with friends. No strict itinerary, no racing to the end to "win", just exploration. So many of our sessions started with us saying we were going to do something, and never getting around to it because something interesting, beautiful, or silly took over.

I've never had so much fun playing a co-op game and separated from the group, wondering how to find them, while knowing we're not "accomplishing" anything. 

I hate the term "friendslop" generally, because I can think of nothing more important than spending time with your loved ones. Big Walk in particular would be "slop" in the way that spending a beautiful afternoon at the park with your friends is "slop".

The only downside is that I'll never be able to experience this game again. It's not some infinitely repeatable, programmatically generated experience where you can just start a new run and goof off some more. We've seen everything there is to see together. We've even gone back into the world just to hang out and goof off and that honestly didn't feel much different than playing it!

But I know one day will be the last time we log in together. The last time we lose our flashlight off a cliff in the middle of the night. The last time my partner BLASTS the train horn for 45 seconds. One day, the experience will really be over. And that's ok.

I'll cherish it forever.

I'm writing this as I had previously left a negative review due to my issues with the use of LLMs to assist in bug-fixing near the end of the game's development as disclosed by the devs. While I still do not condone the use of AI in any part of the development process, House House was put in a very unfortunate position due to a lighting error in the Unity game engine, which both Unity and Engineers told them was impossible to fix. Using AI was a last ditch effort and it managed to produce a result that the team could build off of to fix the 'impossible' bug. The only instance of AI usage in the game is about three lines of code, which would not have been needed had Unity actually gave a shit and tried to help. I really loved Big Walk, and that's why I was so upset that Ai may have had a big role in it, hopefully seeing this review saves you from all hoops I put myself through!

With that stuff all cleared up, I can now say in full confidence that I cannot recommend Big Walk enough. The game is delightfully charming and you can feel the love House House put into every last bit of it. The game itself is simple, but it goes a long way with its mechanics. Most of the fun will come from walking and talking with your friends! For me, some of the best moments in this game was when me and my buddy were just headed from A to B and yapping at each other :]

Putting it simply, Big Walk is a simple and personal game, having a good time with your friends always comes first and I can promise you that it'll leave you with some great memories :3c

I am torn.  More than other games, this is a game where you need to bring your own fun (aka Friends).  So I suggest not bothering with strangers for this one.

There is no time limit, there is no score, there is no fail state that I am aware of.  There is no motivation to do anything except wanting to discover more things.  The “puzzles” are better described as “cooperation opportunities”.  My group has not yet done everything there is to do, however none of the “puzzles” that we have encountered so far were challenging at all if you can manage to work together.  So it’s more like hanging out with your friends with a vague direction to it.

My gripes so far are:
1. For at least one person, there is a strange tendency for feeling somewhat ill while playing.  Adjusting the FOV seemed to reduce the effect
2. Undisclosed AI use for fixing a performance issue.  I personally oppose the technology.  Yes, it’s already everywhere.  Yes, I already have to use programs that contain AI-generated code.  That doesn’t mean that I like it.  If you think that it is fine, tell us.  If you are ashamed because you feel that it is not fine, then don’t use it.
3. The world looks very pretty but moving through it is surprisingly clunky.  Slopes that look like you could not scale them are no problem, others that you feel you should be able to scale, you cannot.  Frequently, you may get briefly stuck on some random plant or branch on the ground.
4. I strongly suspect that the replay value is low, from what I have seen so far.
5. I am not entirely sold on the choice of music.  It tries to sound “human”, but ends up sounding artificial.  Luckily, for most of the game there is no music, unless somebody brought the radio along.  I think Black Metal would have been an interesting contrast and would have been strangely fitting as well as more memorable.  Imagine the sunset scene from the trailer but Venom is playing.  Much better.

Positives:
1. As I said: It does look pretty and motivates to take a walk in a nice place in reality.
2. Friend games are very often fun because hanging out with friends is fun.  This game is no exception in this regard.  I am having fun.

This game is a wonderful experience. It is more than a game, it is a mechanism for fostering community and friendship. It is a conduit of socialization disguised as a walking simulator / puzzle game. This game is not technically complex, nor are the puzzles absolute brain teasers. What makes this game compelling and alluring is the unique interpersonal experiences that will accompany each playthrough.

Through the usage of proximity voice chat and the sound physics, it generates a very unique and real experience that feels very much like the Big Walk that it claims to be. I've only played this game once but I will no doubt return for the sake of community and closeness it so easily fosters.

As for the actual gameplay and experience, every dynamic in this game is about teamwork, not the individual. Inventory management becomes a cooperative dynamic by limiting players from interfacing with their own inventory. Having to juggle items for either communications sake or dealing with long distances, all these unique restrictions allow for playful dynamics to emerge on their own. Twisting around to stop your friend from putting the item on your backpack. Being the friend that has the privilege to handle the aux cord and messing with the music like a DJ. Fiddling with various items because of the sound they make. Standing atop a mountain and shouting to hear the echo with your friends. It's about hanging out with the gang.

This is friendship in a trench coat, disguised as a puzzle/walk video game. The raw emotion I felt when I finished this game with my best friend was genuinely unmatched.

If you had asked me last week what my game of the year would be, I’d say Big Walk. But in light of the recent disclosure of Large Language Model usage, I feel very conflicted about it.

Big Walk became a special place that I enjoyed with my friends. It gave me a space to hang out with friends, solve puzzles and explore. It brought us together and created a sense of closeness despite how far apart everyone was.

But now those memories feel tainted. I feel lied to. There is a lot to unpack here.

The usage of AI in Big Walk is not the most egregious case. House House estimate that less than 0.1% of Big Walk’s codebase is LLM generated. Assuming that is true then it puts the game far from the realm of AI slop that a lot of recent reviews have mentioned.

I understand that many people feel similarly, but I don't think it's fair to call this game slop when there are far bigger offenders out there. That's not to say I’m happy about AI usage in Big Walk (I'm absolutely not), but I’m not going to label this game as slop. It's contaminated, but it's also not a complete incoherent mess.

This whole incident highlights the problems with LLM use. From the way it scrapes knowledge, to replacing experienced people. It’s being pushed so much that it makes finding reliable information harder as communities become more closed off to protect themselves. Therefore, making the tool more enticing and exacerbating the issue.

Does it make it right for House House to use LLM’s? No. With how things stand, the usage of LLM’s is unethical on many fronts. If the LLM could generate a solution to the bugs the developer had, then it means that it’s scrapped data of someone solving that problem or at least having a similar one. Sure, it’s probably faster than delving though countless forums to find the answer you’re looking for, but it’s at the cost of tainting your work, causing harm to the environment and fuelling the mass plagiarism machines that technology companies keep pushing for.

I cannot deny that Big Walk is an outstanding game in its own right. Its well-designed puzzles, gorgeous environments and fantastic sound design work so well to create a whimsical and fabulous experience. I can tell it is a lovingly produced game at its core. But that has all been undermined by the usage of AI and the fact that they hid it from us till they had no choice but to reveal it.

This is one of those moments where I wish I could give a mixed review for a game. I still thoroughly enjoyed my experience and the time I spent playing Big Walk, but its impact has significantly been diminished in light of the news. I fear that this is likely going to be a continual issue throughout the industry and is looking to get worse before it gets better.

[h1] Big Walk, AI, and Moral Superiority [/h1]

[h3] Big Game [/h3]
Big Walk is such a unique and beautiful game, with tons of passion put into it, and it shows.
From the sound design and music, to the visuals, to the puzzles and how they were implemented, to the fact that they built three different versions of the puzzles depending on the amount of players, to the itmes and how the players can interact with them, to the fact that it is a game where hanging out with your friends is the most important part.
Everything about this game oozes with joy.

[h3] AI Usage & Disclosure [/h3]
[b] AI Usage [/b]
I believe that a lot of people have the wrong idea about AI, and that they clump it under one umbrella to be all bad, no exceptions, and that it is overall ruining everything, which is obviously not the case.
For context about how AI was used in this game, it was not gen AI for assets or anything, it was an LLM, chatbots, that was used on a bug that House House dev team were not able to find a solution for after extensive researched on their own, then directly contacted a Unity (the engine the game was made with) engineer who told ultimately told them that what the House House dev team wanted to achieve was not possible, then only after that did they use an LLM, and after multiple tries gave them a possible fix, that they had to modify a bunch, it worked, AND it was only about 10 lines of code at the very end of the game's development; Which in my view, is a very valid use, and is one of the things that AI is properly made for.
You can read [url=https://bigwalk.game/faq/#ai] House House's announcement on it [/url].

[b] Disclosure [/b]
This is definitely a mistake on House House's part, and while I understand their concerns of "voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as “inevitable”" that was stated in their post on their website, but that should not them from being upfront about it, and it leads me to feel like a reason they did not disclosue it from the beginning, is the fear of backlash from uninformed people, which leads me to my next point. 

[h3] Moral Superiority [/h3]
People who are review bombing, are either misinformed, or just want to bask in their sense of moral superiority.
The first is not an excuse for someone's ignorance, you are responsible of informing yourself.
And the second is unfortunately just how a lot of people are like online nowadays, a lot of them without even realising it because they just want to be the "good people" and turn a lot of things into a black and white argument in the process. 
Which I believe, a lot of these people that are acting out of the sense of moral superiority, are the same people that House House was afraid to disclose that information because of, which I am not using as an excuse for them not disclosing it, they still should have been honest about it.

[b] All In All  [/b]
Review bombing the product out of ignorance and the feel of moral superiority is a very irrational thing to do, and games like these do not deserve this type of backlash for something that they aren't even wrong for.
And I hope the people that are wanting to leave a negative review about the game, just stop and think for a minute and maybe inform themselve in the process.

Big Walk is probably the most original, deepest and most HUMAN game of the last ten years. More than 30,000 reviews already explain why, so I won't. I'm here to cancel out one of the negative reviews being dumped on this page. Let me explain what's happening, since the people bombing it haven't bothered with it. Late in development the game had a shadow-culling bug inside Unity's URP: performance dropped by about 50% for roughly 20 seconds at every sunrise and sunset. After several dead ends, a chatbot suggested a possible approach, which the team then rewrote into about 10 lines of code. That is well under 0.1% of the codebase. No AI art, no AI audio, no AI writing, no AI design. Nothing you see, hear or play was generated. (and I wouldn't be against it either, by the way)

That's the crime: ten lines of rendering plumbing that make the game run properly on your machine.

And the studio told this voluntarily. Steam's own rules don't require disclosing coding tools at all. House House disclosed anyway, said plainly that it isn't an endorsement of AI, and even apologized. Their reward is a wall of thumbs-down that has nothing to do with the game. Congratulations: you have just taught every studio on Steam that honesty gets punished and silence is free. 

On the one hand, I think House House deserves it, since they themselves admitted their fault: “Well, yes, we betrayed you! Our code is impure!” Next time, maybe they could be less political and and choose their friends and enemies more carefully.

I've been a game programmer for 35 years, starting in assembler and that was pure Aryan code, not like those dirty compiled languages like C++ or C#. Jokes aside, nobody has "hand-made" the code you run in decades. Compilers rewrite everything we type into machine code no human wrote. Engines compute culling, bake lighting and build LODs algorithmically. The noise suppression on your Discord call is a neural network. So is DLSS. So is the recommender that put this store page in front of you. You were fine with all of it until someone handed you a word to be angry at.

If you want to defend human creativity, the dumbest possible target is one of the most hand-crafted games of the decade, that put humans into a deep connection, made by an independent team whose livelihood depends on how this page looks. [h1]The Hard Truth About AI in Big Walk[/h1]

Big Walk is one of the most beautiful, refined, and enjoyable games I’ve ever played. From the moment I started exploring, it was clear how much thought went into making this world feel special. The atmosphere, the presentation, and the experience as a whole all come together in a way that kept me wanting to see what was around the next corner.

It’s the kind of game that reminds me why I love games in the first place. It has personality. It has charm. It feels like something made by people who cared about the experience they were creating, and in my opinion, they did an incredible job. Big Walk does everything perfectly for what it’s trying to be.

[h2]The AI conversation has gotten out of hand[/h2]

What’s frustrating is seeing the conversation around this game get swallowed by anti-AI slander instead of the game itself. People are allowed to have concerns and ask questions about how AI is used. Those conversations matter. But it’s gotten to a point where some people see the letters “AI” and immediately dismiss the entire project, without giving the actual work or the people behind it a fair look.

A tool being involved doesn’t automatically erase the creativity, decisions, effort, and care that went into making something. Look at the finished game. Look at how every part of it comes together. There’s a reason Big Walk feels as cohesive and polished as it does.

[h2]We need to be more thoughtful about what we support[/h2]

AI use is going to become more common whether people like it or not. That doesn’t mean we have to blindly support every use of it. It means we need to pick and choose what we support based on [b]how it’s being used[/b], rather than treating every use as equally bad.

There’s room to criticize harmful practices while still appreciating a game that clearly has so much personality and care behind it. If we refuse to make that distinction, we end up tearing down good work over a label instead of judging it on its own merits.

[h2]Give the game a chance[/h2]

At the end of the day, Big Walk gave me one of the most enjoyable experiences I’ve had in a game. It’s beautiful, polished, memorable, and full of the kind of charm that makes a world feel worth spending time in.

I think it deserves a conversation about more than one part of its development. Judge it for the experience it actually delivers. For me, that experience is something special, and I absolutely recommend it.

Big Walk is my favorite multiplayer game of the year. Lots of clever mechanics at play, and plenty of satisfying teamwork to be had. I wouldn't describe any of the puzzles as overly difficult; the age-old advice of "the simplest answer is usually the correct one" applies throughout. I wouldn't call this a negative since you can basically spit in any direction and uncover another brain-teaser to tackle. My group of five spent about 45 minutes trying to execute a trickier puzzle, but that was our fault we took so long - the game made it quite clear what the solution was from the beginning.

The buildings and characters are lovely, a simplistic style set in a detailed, beautiful rendition of the Australian bushlands, which I thought was an interesting contrast. The lighting in Big Walk is gorgeous, and the shadows add a near photo-realistic finish. Sometimes you might fall a little behind from the rest of the group, and in those moments where it's just you, the sunlight filtering down through the foliage, the kookaburras singing, and a basic direction in mind... Beautiful, just beautiful. It's very easy to feel alone, sometimes even intimidated by the vastness of the wilderness, even when you know your friends are just around the corner.

The ending was something that my friends and I still fondly reminisce about, even months after completion. Tears were had, laughs were had, and lovely lasting memories were made - I'd recommend this game to anybody with a handful of friends and a few hours to set aside during the evenings. The game's upper limit of 12 players sounds like it has the potential to be ridiculous in some really great ways, but I can't say for sure if Big Walk would have left the same impact had I experienced it that way. 

I believe the adage "Less is more" absolutely applies in this case. Knowing what I know now, and if I were to go in blind again, you would be hard-pressed to convince me to join a lobby with more than 6 friends. I feel that this is the upper-limit before the group begins to fragment, and that introduces the potential to miss out on some puzzles entirely because 50% of the team is off solving them and doing their own thing. Of course, splitting up is undoubtedly the right move with that many players, since the majority of puzzles only need 4~ players to actually solve them, sometimes fewer. If you're not okay with taking turns and sitting out occasionally while the rest of the group tackles a puzzle, splitting up is unfortunately the correct move. This isn't to say it would be inherently unfun, but I feel strongly of my opinion that it wouldn't have been the same experience. Still fun, but a focused, cohesive group really, really shines here.

Hiding AI usage during development is a quick and efficient way to lose the trust and respect of your players. This is even more damning when you wait months after a very successful release to come clean about it. 

"In the final stretch of Big Walk’s development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs. A single point of a percentage of AI code, regardless of how modified it ends up being, is still AI usage and needs to be declared before/upon release. [h3]An Absolute Friendgem[/h3]

What makes Big Walk so unique compared to some other coop adventure games, is that the emotional core of a playthrough comes entirely from travel, puzzles and atmosphere.
With its simple puzzle rules, rich ambience, but no story or characters, *you* and *your friends* are the main focus of this adventure, whether its for puzzle solving or walking around.

The game also makes great use of friction, sometimes with your friends, sometimes *between* your friends, to give the journey ups and downs and make it truly memorable.
Someone's accidental slip will turn into a multiplayer slide down the mountain.
Monkeying around behind soundproof glass will turn into body code langage.
Splitting up, intentionally or not, will turn into stories around a proverbial campfire.
It really feels like a hike with friends.

The puzzle design is very strong too, with a lot of simple rules that are easy to grasp while still bringing a fair amount of headscratch. The main mechanic is "communication in all its forms" all the way to the end.

In the end, Big Walk is a beautiful work of art and game design, about finding utter joy in the very pure idea of "being on the same wavelength as your friends", in a way no other coop games did for me.

Probably my favorite game of the year, and definitely my favorite coop experience so far.

So, let's rip the band-aid off: AI was used in this game's development. But would it surprise you that I don't think that's the biggest problem here?

Compared to other cases of its use, the use of it in Big Walk is comparatively tiny; used in the closing stages of development and for a problem that seemed unfixable by normal means and was, at least [i]supposedly[/i], only done as a last resort (I say [i]supposedly[/i] because people apparently found solutions for it quickly when they were informed of what the problem was, to say nothing of Unity's tech support being laughable at the best of times). In some situations, you could even look past it or come to some degree of understanding, even if it's fairly negative in nature.

In the context of something like this, the AI usage is, surprisingly, NOT the main contributor for my negative review (although it definitely does not help its case, natch).

The problem lies in the fact that House House decided not to inform its playerbase of this detail right from the start. They may not have needed to at its release time since apparently it was before Steam's AI disclosure thingy became mandatory, but even after that point, no changes on the game's page are visible that discloses this information. If they had provided this detail from the start, there would no doubt be disappointment - but people who could look past it would still play it, and people who would stick to their values would look elsewhere, same as it is in many other cases. But that detail was not made apparent up until a certain point recently with the IGF, and had that certain point not played out the way it did... would House House have let that detail slip at all?

Especially baffling since, as indie developers who seemingly took a stance of ethical development (at least, if the other negative reviews here are anything to go by), House House should well have known that dipping your hands into the AI pool in any capacity is considered a poisoned chalice at the best of times these days. I have no clue why they felt that this risk needed to be taken, given the damage to reputation that you risk just by doing so, let alone doing so and keeping quiet about it. Even delaying the game to deal with the issue at hand would have served the game better in the long run (even if folks would get a touch annoyed about it, but they'd more than likely get over it in that case).

I'm not of the belief that AI usage itself is what is making people turn against this game and its developers. It's the simple fact that it was used and House House did not see it fit to disclose the information until it was forcibly outed. Some will be more than content to say it's a knee-jerk reaction to AI being used, but this case isn't just an AI-centric issue; people, by nature, don't tend to appreciate being lied to or deceived. And yes, the prior argument about it being before the mandatory disclosures still applies, but a lie of omission is still a lie.

What really sucks is that the game - at least, the amount I've experienced with friends - is genuinely fun. But House House have effectively instilled upon themselves a PR nightmare because of a scenario that may well could have been diluted or even avoided outright had they been honest from the beginning - or had been willing to ask out for alternative solutions so as to circumvent whatever problem it was that kicked this chain of events off.

As a result of all of this, Big Walk and House House will now have asterisks next to their names and reputations in the wake of Big Walk's controversial revelations. After all, if they were prepared to keep people in the dark about AI usage in this game, then the question has to be asked: what else are they willing to keep us in the dark about?

Buyer beware.

For those unaware, House House recently disclosed that AI was utilized towards the tail end of Big Walk’s development. [https://bigwalk.game/faq/#ai]

They claim the intent was for bug fixing, and that less than 0.1% of the code was touched by AI. Neat. I no longer have high praises to sing of this game.

This comes with a lot of disappointment, the biggest, of course, being the utilization of AI in any regard. I’ve seen the excerpt House House gave as to how they were “out of options” to optimize a problem they were having, with Unity engineers being unable to provide guidance in their situation. I refuse to believe, however, that the only option remaining was an inherently predatory and destructive technology founded upon stolen data. People in the game industry have been able to ship games for 20+ years without the need of an AI to solve problems. In fact, many cases saw solutions brought forth through the joint efforts of QA testers and coders alike; humans, not AI. I don’t doubt there were troubles in the making of this game, but there is no sob story that will ever legitimize the use of AI in my eyes.

But the biggest disappointment of all? How House House decided to disclose this, or more accurately when. You’ll notice the Steam page doesn’t currently list an AI notice of any kind. The only one available is on the Big Walk website, a whole 3 months after release. And the only reason such a disclosure exists now is because of Big Walk’s subsequent disqualification from any accolades at the Independent Game Festival. Otherwise, the company believed their usage of AI just fell below the requirements to disclose anywhere. This is striking, especially since just under a month ago House House announced without hesitation that Big Walk would not come to Xbox consoles as a part of a pro-Palestine boycott against Microsoft. I was glad to see them wearing their beliefs and morals so proudly, but it’s clear now they chose to highlight what fit their image while hiding their shame until they couldn’t anymore.

It’s a shame; this game has so many things I would’ve praised from an emotional and functional perspective, but it feels crucial now more than ever to be against AI, no matter how minimal it’s use may seem.

Big Walk is an absolutely brilliant game plagued by being involved in a discourse it did not even create.

From an art perspective, Big Walk invites people into open spaces to be able to creative explore the game while providing some guidance on where the players should look. The scale of the game was carefully crafted to give it the right sized feeling that makes you feel like you actually CAN get lost while also providing all of the tools to be found.

From a gameplay perspective, the controls are responsive, but do take a bit of getting used to. It's cleverly designed to allow you to use your motion to communicate which is well executed in the puzzles that one will need to complete if you want to see the end of the game.

Puzzles escalate over time to give you enough to get things moving, while also encouraging thinking outside of the box. Later puzzles become increasingly complex, but build off the lessons your group has learned over time.

Once you start to look at the game granularly, you start to realize how clever the world-building actually is and how almost every single piece of the game was carefully considered as it was built.

It's hard to compare this game to any others within it's genre. One could try to loop it in with the "friendslop" genre, but slop this isn't. The controversy, if you call it that, stems from the fact that they used one AI chat bot to give them an idea of where to solve a problem they had with shading after they had already consulting a Unity developer on the issue where they couldn't even figure out the solution. Once they had a direction, they still wrote the code from hand and made absolutely sure every single artistic detail was left to the actual hands of the artists for them to craft.

This game, after all, was made by a very small team of highly dedicated and passion people willing to take a chance on themselves rather than going with the status quo in game design and development. They took a chance that most other indie developers can't take to the extreme they did, and now they are being chastised over a small little detail in how they did it. People like to focus on the wrong things, but claim they care about the humans on the other side. It's clear they don't.

Pick up Big Walk if you want a nice and relaxing game to play with friends and acquaintances. If you like to stop and smell the roses every once in a while, this will be a unique experience for you. If you want quick satisfaction, then this one might not hit the spot.

In a day and age where the term "friendslop" is used to refer to anything with proximity chat and co-op, this game managed to surprise me quite a bit. The game oozes with attention to detail and love that the developers put into every nook and cranny of the pretty sizable map. Progression is rewarding and with certain group dynamics the game also has good replayability (although I have yet to start my second playthrough). 

Now as of today, there has been some controversy regarding the usage of AI for the development of the game. While I personally hold an anti-AI-stance when it comes to all things art (such as music and drawing), the usage of AI for this game, as detailed on the House House Big Walk FAQ page, was minimal and reasonable as far as coding (or rather debugging) goes. Should they have disclosed this earlier? Yes. Do I see why they didn't, as people tend to get very dismissive as soon as AI is mentioned in any context? Also yes. Their usage of AI is not required by steam to be disclosed. They could've and maybe should've but there are valid reasons as to why they didn't as even now some people scream slop and vibecoding, despite the very detailed explanation as to how AI was used (debugging a performance error that was less than 10 lines, while rewriting the LLM provided code). You can view this any way you want, if any usage of AI during video game development is a no-go for you, that is fine, but I urge everyone reading this to make an informed decision and read the FAQ before letting this drive them away from a game that I consider to be one of the best of it's genre.

We started off as quite a large group with nearly 10 players, which resulted in some people getting to do less puzzles and each group only experiencing about half of them while progressing through the game. In my opinion, the game is best enjoyed with a group of 4 players, start to finish, for that reason. 

The puzzles are fun and varying in difficulty, some requiring more mechanical finesse (i.e. using the dropkick feature to launch items to a teammate), some require more thinking. The first playthrough took my group about 10 hours (again with around 10 players for a good chunk of it, but also with a few breaks) and we did not do every puzzle. 

I want to highlight the atmosphere and sound design especially, the game is beautifully immersive despite it's cartoonish looks, the world feels gigantic around you and the sound design emphasizes that greatly. You can get lost in the landscapes easily, especially at night and coming across all the different structures and items feels organic and rewarding.

I have had tears in my eyes playing this game, both from laughter and the deeply touching ending. I cannot recommend this game enough. It is a beautiful experience start to finish and with the right group of people it is unmatched in what it sets out to do and achieves.

They did not disclose this though, they did so claiming that Steam technically does not require devs to disclose LLM usage, but not claiming something because you are technically not required to does not make that lack of disclosure good or right.

Disclosing it now because they were forced to by a stricter award platform then making a statement about supporting human creators after the hype has died down and people have likely completed the game multiple times feels performative at best.

I cannot recommend Big Walk due to a borderline deceptive action such as this, even if they had their reasons, House House still lied by omission and denies customers a right to understand what they're buying.

Updating this review about a day or so after the fact, mostly because I feel dissatisfied with only having the heat-of-the-moment quip I have. I believe I can be more nuanced in my take and should probably do so. Keeping the original part of the review up above because that feels right to do I think.

I'm well aware that in House House's FAQ, they've stated that the amount of code reliant on the usage of an LLM is under 0.1%. They used it to crack a difficult bug that was causing slowdowns at certain times of day due to shadow casters not being culled correctly. Despite House House's attempts to reach out to a unity engineer, they could not find a solution and relied on an LLM to help brute force there way into a solution by having it spit out code and modifying it to help the game.

This does mean there's one thing I do want to concede on, and probably should have brought up in my initial review. If there's a way that ai should be used? That's the one.

However, were that the entire story, I wouldn't have been (and continue to be) bothered by this. Now this is where I dive into a bunch of moralistic mumbo-jumbo so I'll leave my proper recommendation now and get into the weeds afterwards...

Big Walk is a beautiful game. I bought it for me and my boyfriend so we could play together. We live a good few states apart and Big Walk has helped us feel closer than ever despite the sprawling expanse of land between us. Beyond that, the idea of turning a part of Australia's beautiful nature (Wilsons Promontory National Park to be precise) into the stomping ground for the players is a kind of map design that's inspired me ever since my childhood playing Pokemon and getting to feel the vague sense of visiting somewhere I otherwise had little opportunity to. It's the kind of thing that even spurns me to research and appreciate my own backyard a bit more and enjoy the nature around me. You can feel how every rock and tree is placed deliberately in Big Walk. The sound design helps me sink into my screen and forget where I am; little details like the sounds of local fauna, the squeaking sand as you step across some of the beaches... There's so much of this game that ai simply CAN'T make. The game's inspired and full of love for both the land it's molded after and the sense of connection it's meant to facilitate. If you're someone who can get past the how and the why for their miniscule usage of ai, then by all means. It has my glowing recommendation.

...I, however, would not have bought this game if I knew about their application of ai prior to the game's release. This is, if you can't tell, the part where I babble on about things that are entirely constructed around where I draw the line on a very very large, very very complicated issue. I'd dip now if you're not interested in this sort of thing, and take my recommendation as a souvenir.

Everything that bugs me about this entire situation is entirely to do with one VERY load-bearing statement that's a part of the same FAQ response mentioned prior; "This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as “inevitable”. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards." Quoted directly.

I do think House House put themselves into a kind of no-win situation. They either don't reveal their use of ai prior to and during the Independent Games Festival and live with the lie for even longer at the risk of it being uncovered later with a potentially worse reaction... Or what they DID do and be open and honest about it and let the internet do as it pleases with the information. Now what? Well that's where we all have to take our own stance with what we have available, being House House's FAQ, the timing of when it was put out, and whatever personal thoughts and experiences we have on ai as a whole.

Beginning with their statement; while it does read as not being in-support of ai, I personally am weirded out that there's still not really a stance definitively taken in the FAQ? Yes, they're in support of those attempting to limit the harm genAI is having on videogames and everything else and all that... but not once do they directly state what House House themselves want to do about it. I don't like that. Anything that I could/couldn't assume from that will only be answered once they have an actual policy towards ai in place. I'd quite like if they made that policy public knowledge, once it gets made.

The statement DOES mention that they worry about the normalization of ai via putting the disclosure out; that's the closest we have to an official 'yay,' 'nay,' or 'maybe' we have. But, again, it also doesn't state whether or not they will use ai in any capacity going forward, or how they will should they decide to do so. It's just vague concern on it helping normalize ai. So that's the only string I have to really harp on, and OH BOY is it one that grinds my gears. If House House is concerned that disclosing the usage of ai will help normalize the technology as a whole, then they shouldn't have touched the LLM at all, full stop. They shouldn't have put themselves in the position to need to worry about it. They used the tool willingly and knowingly; that's normalizing. Even if it's a case of desperation and hindsight being 20-20, that's deserving of criticism. I'm sure they could have cracked the bug given enough digging around online, or at the very least rubber-ducking for long enough. Yes, unhelpful unity engineer, I'm sure that's a frustrating experience, and who's to say how long the programmers at House House were beating their heads against that issue; that doesn't make a decision that's contrary to the one definitive worry House House names in the FAQ suddenly not a contrary decision. 

As a whole with their FAQ statement; it feels counterintuitive to the one section of the entire disclosure that actually gives me solid information on how they feel about ai usage. I see a lot of "it's not THAT bad," and sure, definitely isn't that bad compared to the far more egregious uses of ai in the world. Unfortunately, when you suggest a standard you want to uphold yourself to in the same breath that you break that standard, it makes me raise a brow. Again, I'm hoping we get to see what their internal ai policy will look like once they have it ready.

Now, the timing of when this was put out is another sticking point. There's a sizeable number of people who dislike generative ai and LLMs enough that they don't want to touch the stuff with a 10-foot pole. I'm one of them. Knowing ahead of time whether or not genAI or LLMs were used in any part of making a game is something that determines if we buy a game. I understand Steam's policy only covers "visual" ai, and not the code of a game; that's a can of worms to criticize a different company with, though. (I have learned there's a character limit. Continued in comments, I guess? I'm sorry. I got a lot I want to say about this.)
