Idyllic and quietly joyful, [i]Big Walk[/i] encapsulates a long laid-back* hiking trek with friends with abundant time for idle chitchat and the occasional intrigue of a good thinky puzzle (*mood may ultimately vary depending on your companions.)

Oddly in my opinion, this cooperative open-world game's biggest strength lies in its proximity chat / in-game audio system. Not only is it well implemented but half the fun is discovering all the things that affect speech and communication methods. Particularly the puzzles where the goals are often simple (e.g. getting the correct tiles in the right order) but the real challenge derives from the obstacles that inhibits communication. It could be soundproof walls, blindfolds, or even sheer distance, but that always made it for a more unique puzzle experience where the solution becomes less of an a-ha moment and more something you slowly strategize for with your party.

Overall I highly recommend [i]Big Walk[/i] for any group (especially if it's a group of 4 or more!), especially with its thoughtful cooperative design which deeply contrasts with the increasingly common cooperative games that are more built on the silliness of chaos and hijinx.

Big Walk is a fun game for sure and I think every group will be able to enjoy. That being said, I'm feeling like I got caught on the tail-end of the hype surrounding it. People were flaunting this as one of the best games they've ever played or their game of the year.

I'll start with the highs of the game:

First and foremost, the Australian wilderness-based environment is absolutely stunning, the sound design is great, and the music is so unbelievably unique.

Hanging out with friends was a blast of course and we got to have some nice and fun conversations.

The puzzles themselves started out amusing and interesting. You stumble around with the ways to solve them and utilizing what you have and it's fun to start.

With all of these, it was a good experience, but I feel like there's a lot of shortcomings with the game.

From the puzzle perspective, I feel like it falls short. I will say, that the puzzle aspect was what I was looking forward to the most and working through these with my friends. As I said, they start off fun, but a lot of the puzzles stay the exact same as you see them from beginning to end with the slightest twist on them. Unfortunately, this twist is usually not enough of a twist that it can't be solved with the same methods used in other ones. At a certain point because of this, the accomplishment of the puzzles doesn't really feel good anymore and just kinda feels like minutia. [spoiler] In my opinion, the most interesting twist on all of this only comes at the ending puzzles, which you get one taste of and that's it [/spoiler] Thus, from a puzzle game perspective I wasn't really impressed.

I enjoy obviously hanging out with friends and having chit-chats, which is the main point of this game (the journey is what matters, not the destination). However, I feel like I can have fun chit-chats with friends just by being in a Discord call, playing another game, or just actually hanging out. Unfortunately, I think due to the rise of "friendslop" games such as Peak, REPO, Lethal Company, etc. it took away a lot of the novel feeling this could have captured, even if it was being developed before the explosion of the genre (granted I wouldn't call the game slop in the slightest).

I think that Big Walk is more of an experience rather than a game, and everyone's experience will be different. From my perspective, it's a fun time, but it's not a game changer in any respect. I wasn't getting complex puzzles and I was going to be talking with friends anyways. I think everyone's mileage may vary, but I didn't really feel like I got a lot out of it that I wouldn't get elsewhere. I do think most people will really resonate with it, though.

review:
Big Walk - despite being apart of the "friendslop" genre acts more as a vessel for you and your friends to have fun in. It is a masterclass of game design. The puzzles never feel repetitve or boring and are solved slightly differently by each party of people that play.

Throughout the entire journey - beginning middle and end the game never forces you to do anything and that's the beauty of it.

This is my GOTY. I 100%'d it and I would gladly do it again and again. Thank you House House for an incredible game.

---*---AI Discussion---*---

The use of AI in this game should have been disclosed - however, like all things there is nuance to this and iot needs to be discussed with care. Big Walk is a game with so much love and care for game design put into it that anyone calling the game "slop" is exaggerating. Yes, AI was used in theis game. Not to make the game, but to improve the player experience. Fixing a bug that Unity said was "impossible" with 10 lines of modified Opus code to make the game not slowdown when the sun sets is objectively in the best intrest of the player. 

I hate AI as much as anyone else and think it is a plague on gaming but raising pitchforks at House House over this when you can go on the Steam or Itch or Gamejolt homepages and find infinite games made in one click with no care for the end user or experience. This game is not comparable to any of those games.

All modern games have *some* AI use whether the dev chooses to or not. Engines like Unity (most likely Godot) certainly have some AI code in there somewhere; should every game that releases be called "slop" too?

Am I disappointed that AI was used? Yes.
Do I like not having a gauge of how much AI was used in production? No.
Do I think that Big Walk is slop and House House is malicious by proxy? Not at all.

Be reasonable about what is being hated on. The use of AI here is disappointing and realistically should've been told to consumers beforehand, but not world ending. We should be flaming "developers" who "create games" entirely is AI and pass it off as honest work and only repremand House Hosue for being dishonest about their AI use on launch. They have already willingly disclosed their AI use, they have acknowledged how it is unacceptable to mislead consumers. It's best to move on to other things. Big Walk is a great game. Lets leave it at that.

This game is one of the greatest examples of innovation, especially when it comes to a massive co-op experience. While the game has really entertaining bouts of exploration and just chilling and chatting and catching trains, the biggest appeal for me were the puzzles. They're fiendishly clever, but not impossible. They're group efforts and I was delighted that "quarterbacking" wouldn't solve many of them, you need the whole group for figuring out the puzzles and then also to execute the solutions. (Avoid spoilers about the puzzles as much as you can, so you can discover everything with your group.) They're kind of like the best kind of escape room puzzles, but with some really clever twists like disallowing speech, hearing or sight, limitations that would be harder to implement in a real life escape room. A lot of the puzzles will also reward your creativity, as you try to come up with the best plan for communicating with your team. "See here, when I do this dance it means the Chaos Undivided symbol."

Also since there's no fear of death in the game, the worst that can happen is that someone gets lost in the wilderness and probably stumbles on to something unique which the rest of the group has missed. There are plenty of in-game items that will help lost players get in touch with the rest of the group like walkie-talkies and signal flares. If you're tired of helicopter parenting in co-op games, this is the one game where you can just relax and let skilari fall off a mountain.

I wouldn't call it friendslop, as this thing is polished as all hell and everything is hand-crafted with really thought-out meanings. The years it took making this shows.

Huge recommend, and easily one of my new favorite games of all time. I fully completed this game with a few close friends and I enjoyed every single second, from the puzzles and progress, to the long walks and times of mischief, to even getting lost in the night and fighting with my friends about how to solve something.

If the term 'friendslop' turns you away from this game, don't let that affect your view of it, because to me it kind of strays away (pun intended) from the usual format that would make a game friend slop. It's too unique and well crafted to even be considered anything close to 'slop', and in my opinion, shouldn't have the term applied to it in the first place. The friend part of the term, however, absolutely applies.

For me, this game strikes a similar spot that games like Minecraft or Stardew once did for me, where you kind of spend hours doing seemingly mundane tasks to progress to an overarching goal, and yet somehow, you end up enjoying all of that time that could otherwise feel boring. They achieve this by having your friends be the entertainment, and making you have fun with them and their company in-game, rather than the game itself providing that 'fun' for you during those tasks. It tricks you into enjoying your friends, more so than just playing another game with them.
 
What makes this game stand out in this aspect however, is that the game uses this entire concept as its foundation, and builds almost every single detail off of it. Everything from the unconventionality of some of the objects to the speed of which certain things move will give you many opportunities to bond and appreciate the time you spend with your friends. Not to mention, the puzzles are beautifully constructed with this concept in mind, many of which will require you to think in a way that puts you into the minds of your friends, and require you to figure out ways to work with them and communicate with them, especially the ones near the end, which no spoilers, are the cherry on top for an incredibly unique and unforgettable experience.

Big Walk is a very enjoyable co-op puzzle experience, with a few great moments that make it feel extra special.

The puzzles in Big Walk are a very solid foundation, there's a lot of variety in there, but they all rely on that one big aspect of a co-op game: communication. Although most puzzles are straightforward enough to be easily understood, there were definitely a couple where we scratched our head figuring out a system how to communicate a way to solve them, especially if talking was not an option. I also appreciated the fact that the puzzles could be adjusted from groups as small as two, up to 4+ players, which made everyone feel useful in the puzzles (which especially as a group of 3 can sometimes be hard in co-op puzzle games).

Speaking of communication, the proximity voice chat was definitely a lot of fun, the filters and the echoes made it feel quite naturaly and lively. Exploring the beautiful island looking for new puzzles and items was a big part of the experience (it's called Big Walk for a reason). Sometimes the proximity seemed a little too close, losing half sentences as other people were talking while we were walking somewhere, but maybe that's more on me for straying from the group just a little too much. Still, it was a great experience to stumble upon a nice vista, especially as the sun was setting, and just watching it for a bit before continuing on.

And then there's the moments that make it feel a bit extra special. The finale is definitely a standout, absolute fantastic capstone on this game and it felt absolutely amazing. But then there's also the 5 minute house, and finding secret radio stations, that just led to memorable moments and felt very rewarding.

Overall, Big Walk is a great co-op puzzle game, that's playable with varying group sizes, and it's got some special moments that I'll remember for quite a while. Definite recommend!

I fell in love with Big Walk when I saw the first trailer for it and had patiently waited for its release. When it came out I didn't know if I would even have anyone to play it with me so I held off on buying it and just enjoyed watching others stream it or post videos playing it, living vicariously through them and their friends. I finally broke and bought the game and begged my friends to play it with me and since then it has been nothing but giggles and joy. I love Big Walking! I love the puzzles, I love how so many of them rely on teamwork and finding new and funny ways to communicate with your friends. I love the landscape and the ambience, sometimes I just sit by the water and watch the stars because it is so beautiful and serene. I love the Walklings so much they are so silly, I love how expressive they are for being four circles and some spaghetti noodles. The buildings and the props are so stylistically fitting being as colorful and whimsical as the Walklings while still maintaining a true-to-life feel to them to fit in with the realistic trees and water. It has been such a delight just wandering around the world, climbing mountains, falling off cliffs, and getting lost in the woods or the tall grass. The ski-lifts and the monorails are also awesome, perfect for just taking in the view without fear of getting stuck between boulders. I cannot talk about Big Walk without mentioning the sound or the music though. The sound effects are- like the props/items- a perfect blend of real-life forest noises and silly *pops* and *thunks* or wiggly wobbly for when you take a tumble. The music is so wonderful, it feels as though it was made by the Walklings themselves!! 

Overall, this game has been perfect. In a world full of leeching, disgusting AI Slop and every other game being a (with love in my heart) cookie-cutter first-person-shooter battle royale with daily log in rewards and pay to customize cash grab, Big Walk is a much needed breath of fresh. clean air. This work of art is- without a doubt- one of the most lovingly created things on this blue planet. I hope I am not wrong in saying that it is obvious that the developers did not just put their blood, sweat, and tears into its making but also their love, hope and joy. Big Walk is inherently a hopeful game. It hopes that we take time to laugh and work together with our community. It hopes that as we play, we notice how beautiful our forests and oceans and mountains and rivers are. It hopes that our curious minds are not completely lost to an age of relentless, fast-paced content, and that it still itches to learn and discover ("what's over that mountain?" or "what happens if I push this button?"). It hopes to show that good things are not built at lightspeed at the prompting of a generative bot, but from people coming together with an idea and one question: "how can we make this work?" and the determination to find out. 

Big Walk creators of any and all extent, thank *you* for making this video game. What you have done for not just the gaming industry and its community, but for people and the world we live on, is impossible to quantify. I hope you never doubt how important games like Big Walk are and how valuable your craft is not just as a career but as something that we are lucky enough in this universe to cultivate and watch flourish. There could be a world out there with no computers, no video games, no Big Walk; maybe we are the only world that has them at all! How lucky am I to have the odds that I do to live in a world at a time where your work exists and I may experience it. 

12/10. I love you Big Walk.

This might be the best multiplayer game I've played. So much fun and memories to be had with such relatively simple mechanics.  I have great memories of the conversations we had on the way to objectives, of forgetting the egg on the ski lift, and just barely missing the train and rushing, which is to say it doesn't fall into a trap of engineering situations designed to guarantee a quick laugh with deaths, jumpscares, or wacky situations like other types of games in this genre. Not that there is anything inherently wrong with that, but this game is different, valuing communication and problem solving in a way that a lot of "get in-get out" MP games like phasmo or repo don't. 

Most puzzles are relatively simple but don't have any guidance. This combo leaves it feeling fair and respects the player's intelligence. Too hard of puzzles would leave the solution unfair without guidance or too easy with guidance. Big walk manages to find that good middle ground to find these puzzles and ramps them up in difficulty as the communication and knowledge between players grows. To support this, the emoting system and objects provided work perfectly and surprised me with how many different ways we could find ways to communicate with each other just by changing poses or using an item in a unique way.

TLDR: on paper this game should suck, instead I found it to be one of the strangely more meaningful experiences I've had all year, fully reccomended. 

Full review:
This game is Fascinating.

In theory, it *really* shouldn't work. 
Yes the puzzl are pretty satisfying to solve, and not that hard most of the time, and the game has *fantastic* sound and environment aspects going on.

But in theory, it *should* be undercut by the fact tha many of it's puzzles *should* feel tedious, and you are stuck walking around a large enough gameworld rather slowly, with rather janky physics frequently tripping you up and getting you a tiny bit stuck, requiring you to jump or finagle your way around a bit.

In practice though, all those problems I just mentioned are actually *Strengths* of the game.
That's because this isn't a standard issue puzzle game, it's true agenda is to almost trick you into being social playing it, and bring you closer together with whoever you are sharing your big walk with.

The puzzle design leans into this in obvious ways of course, with communication puzzles being it's standard form.

But even the tedious ones only add to this, I can't explain exactly why, but it felt *satisfying*, even *rewarding* to persevere through them, something about sharing the difficulty with my brother turned what should have been terrible puzzles into some of them most satisfying wins I've ever had.
I think this effect is completely intentional.

Even the Janky movement helps, it makes walking through the environment feel more real, which combined with it's excellent natural setting and sound design, ended up part tricking my brain into feeling like I was actually *outside* playing it.
The fact that walking through it sucked just a little bit actually made it feel *better* by making feel it feel like a bit of a pain in the ass, just like walking is in real life.

It's absolutely fascinating, and I find myself genuinely missing the experience, a part of me wants to go back to the island.

All in all, this game is absolutely fantastic, easily in my top 10 for the year, even though on paper, it shouldn't be.
Goes to show that when it comes to game design, theory can only get you so far.

The term "friendslop" doesn't really describe this game. Sure, you need "friends" to play it but it's not slop. I'd call it a "friend-enhancer". When people hear "friendslop" they imagine games like PEAK, where the player and their troop has the unified goal of climbing towards the peak whilst overcoming the hostile environments they traverse through. It takes trial and error to finally reach the top, but that learning process is what makes that game fun -- since it's amusing seeing your friend fall off a cliff because they touched a weird mushroom while the doppler effect does its thing. Games like that are popular with streamers because they allow the opportunity for funny moments to happen, which means you can make viral online clips on the internet and make other people laugh. There's nothing wrong with games like that, but to fit Big Walk within that genre doesn't sit right with me.

I'm not claiming that Big Walk doesn't have funny moments, it absolutely does -- but it's up to the you and your group to create those moments. There's no scary monsters that make you scream, nor are there explosives that ragdoll you. You're just in an island alone with your friends, and then you just need to use your imaginations to create the fun. You create nicknames for items and landmarks in the game with your group, you have little inside jokes that are born here, sometimes you distract from the objective and sit down for a moment and talk about stuff -- whether it be your pet peeves or your hobbies. The ultimate goal of the game is to finish all the puzzles, but there isn't any pressure for you to get it done ASAP. You and your group just play the game at your own pace while taking in the natural environment that you're at. 

I called this a "friend-enhancer" earlier and I'd like to get into what I mean by that. I think, to truly appreciate this game, you have to be with the right people. It can be someone you already have a strong bond with, or a friend-of-a-friend you only recently met. And you need to go for the full 100% to appreciate it and you and your group need to agree on this commitment, so you must choose carefully. If you can't find anyone like that, don't bother playing this game until you can find that person. People want public matchmaking and I completely understand why this game doesn't have it, because playing with strangers would defeat the point of this game. There's no guarantee that you will have the same level of loyalty compared to playing with a friend.

I played this game with one other friend, so it was just the two of us. Throughout this experience, we were faced with complicated puzzles -- some had an easy to understand solution, others required much more strategic thought and planning to them. No matter the difficulty, the game requires the cooperation of both of us to progress the game, so we're forced to stay and talk to each other and talk things through. We would come up with ways to complete a puzzle, and experience that satisfaction seeing our plan be perfectly executed.

When not doing a puzzle, we would have to walk and explore the rest of the map to see what to do next. Those moments allow for small talk to happen. Sometimes we'd even just put the objectives on hold and go sit at the beach and just talk. It's that part of the game where our friendship gets to deepen and we begin to truly understand each other. We'd learn about each others hobbies, our hot takes, gossip, fandom discussions, favorite video games, jobs, real life, etc. When I finished playing this game, I feel like I deepened my understanding of my friend as a person, even though I've never seen this person in real life, but I knew that despite that -- they were a real human being who has goals and ambitions they want to accomplish in their life, just like me. It's a very personal experience, and with that in mind -- it just makes the ending of the game hit even harder.

The sentimental value this game provides make it unique from "friendslop" games. You rarely get those kinds of interactions with your friends in a game like PEAK because you're too distracted talking about which paths you want to take to climb the mountain while being forced to climb it quickly because you and your troop need to find food before you all turn into cannibals. I love PEAK, but to put in the same genre as Big Walk just doesn't make any sense. This is not a friendslop game. You will play this game and you will come to understand why I feel so strongly about the term "friendslop".

As I said earlier, go find someone you really trust or someone you'd like to get to know better. This may take a while, but take as long as you want because this game isn't going anywhere. I promise that when you find that person or group, you and your group won't regret playing this game, and that you will come out with an even stronger friendship than before.

This game was an absolute treat to play with a small group of friends (personally, I recommend four at most as the puzzles only really accomodate up to that number of players at a time.) It is very obvious that the devs spent a number of years building and polishing this game because not a single bug was encountered the entire game, aside from the issue of the quiet mic unless at close distance (which the devs immediately patched on day 2 from release).

 The sound design is wonderful with the squeaky sand on the beaches and songbirds, as well as the design of the island's landscape and fauna, carefully placed to match that of real australian bushlands, which altogether; feels very cosy. I can't really think of a single puzzle that made me and my friends frustrated, they were all enjoyable and even the most challenging ones felt fun and rewarding to complete.

Something this game does very well is forcing you to slow down and take things easy, and reminding you that its okay to take your time getting from A to B, as it lets you just hang out with your friends as you travel together! It feels like a breath of fresh air from the constant activity that a lot of other multiplayer games provide that can be overstimulating as they ultimately aim to be clipped for social media. Big Walk doesn't feel like it was really made for social media, but to be enjoyed privately with your friends :>

This game was made with a lot of heart, and its very clear that the devs cared a lot about the direction they wanted to take. I hope House House continues to create more games like this or even inspire other developers to create games that have this similar feeling of warmth and charm.

Big Walk is a bonding adventure in an open air museum that is as fun as you can make it. It’s best experienced with as little prior knowledge to the actual mechanics as possible, because figuring it all out together is part of the fun. You play online with friends, you hang out on a beautiful island, and you solve puzzles together. If that sounds good to you, then stop reading, assemble a group of pals and get walking. But if you need a little more pushing (or if you’ve already finished) then read on.

The game starts off in a playground that teaches you all the controls, and that’s just about the only instruction you get. You can run, jump, sit, kick, move your arms, and pick up objects (including each other). Hoisting your friends over your head and yeeting stuff across the room is immediately fun. Once everybody’s ready you head out to a lush island with colorful manmade structures scattered around; it feels a lot like a sculpture park. All over the map you find self-contained puzzles with no instruction, and hanging above you is your prize for completion: the Gourd. Find enough gourds, bring them to a tower, unlock new ways to explore the island. Simple as that.

The joy in this game comes from discovering new things with your friends. I had a crew of eight people I would hit up to play every Tuesday, and we would usually get about 4-6 players a week. We felt like geniuses every time we solved a new puzzle, and we chanted every time we got another Gourd. But we also spent a lot of time in between puzzles basking in whatever pleasures the island afforded us: going for a night swim, climbing mountains then jumping off a cliff, dancing to music, firing flares, sitting on a tram and watching the landscape go by. There were a lot of silly moments when one of us got lost and we had to find each other, or when we had to navigate without any light, or when someone quit out of the game and their avatar became a corpse that you could carry with you. Whether you’re actively solving puzzles or just passing time, the island of Big Walk is a serene and entertaining place to hang out.

The puzzles themselves take a few basic premises and build on them in creative and challenging ways. Most of them rely on one or all people having limited information and needing to communicate with each other under a set of restrictions. They are occasionally speed- and precision-based, but most of them are tests of the mind, so knowing your team and working collaboratively is priority number one. I saw someone online joke that their next corporate retreat should take place in Big Walk, but it really is a fantastic look at what roles everyone assumes in a group setting and how you and your friends approach the method of problem solving. I spoke to a member of my Big Walk crew irl today and she said to me, “you really like explaining things.” I hadn’t really thought about that, but I was definitely often the one to gather everyone together and lay out what we all knew. So you need to figure out what works for the group and what doesn’t.

And it’s especially interesting to see what happens when the group doesn’t work, or doesn’t have the proper tools to complete a task. This only happened with my crew once: we didn’t have enough walkies to talk to each other for a task that required us all to be in separate places on the island. We thought we could make it work, but after like 45 minutes of trying we didn’t end up completing it and had to log off. It was disappointing, but we all learned from it and never had an issue like that again, because we planned better and checked in with each other more. And that’s a wonderful thing to come from failure.

I’ve seen people say that this falls into the category of “friendslop” but I just want to emphasize how far that is from the truth, because Big Walk is anything but sloppy. So much polish went into making this game, from the day-night cycle to the way sound travels depending on what kind of space you’re in. The devs were very careful to design each puzzle with certain ideas in mind, so even if there are usually multiple ways to solve one, they knew exactly what was and what was not possible. The music is excellent, and the simplicity of the presentation seems to appeal to everyone I’ve played with or talked to about it. I even got a little emotional when we reached the end. There’s still more to do, though, so I’ll definitely be going for 100% completion.

God, what a fantastic game. I don’t play a lot of online co-op, but I could tell from the first trailer that this one would be special. Glad I was right. I’m grateful to have a group of friends that wanted to do this with me, and I would absolutely play another House House co-op experience if that’s what they choose to do.

This game came out during a very impactful part of my life. There are two big things going on in my mind. I'm about to start transitioning, and I just got the date for when I graduate from college. Big news!! 

I had already been playing Big Walk before this news came out. It was much after I started my journey through Big Walk that I finally knew when I was going to get my degree. I first heard about the game when it was initially announced some time ago, and I urged about 7 of my friends to get it. Starting a world with your friends can begin pretty silly, but it took completing the first puzzle to make me feel like this baby chicken hatching out of an egg and squinting my eyes as I bask in the sunlight. The peacefulness of the tiny tutorial bubble suddenly expanding into an entire world, and only seeing little baby steps to...something. It was really great.

From then on, you and your small world of friends and discovery continues. Taking more and more baby chicken steps, sometimes sitting together listening to strange tunes, having quiet talks, getting lost & found, making mistakes, experimenting with gadgets..it all leads towards that "something."

In this seemingly giant world, you learn a lot about your friends and yourself. You also become proud of your shared achievements and how well you mix with the people you love. For me, real life was continuing between sessions, changing how I saw the events of the game. Cycles between friends beat it in 3 months. Especially towards the end of that time, a lot changed in both of the worlds I was growing through.

The biggest impact I felt was that, with what was going on in real life, I noticed that all of my own baby chicken steps were about to amount to something. Starting college & working towards transitioning were new worlds to me that expanded my bubble. And when you're working step-by-step, you can only look as far as what you have to do today, tomorrow, or next week. It is only when you see the end that you can properly consider that every new assignment & project was taking you somewhere. And when you get there, when you finally feel like you've mastered this new world, it is terrifying. The bubble that once appeared limitless and unfamiliar begins to show the next one.

Big Walk is a game about journeys that begin unclear and daunting, so much so that many might begin them but many don't see them through. It is about those who have the courage to keep moving and do that thing they set themselves out to do, and the connections they make along the way. Let that be new connections or existing ones that become much deeper. Sometimes it might even mean the people who start with you and sadly stray off of your path. As I said above, you end up learning a lot about the people around you. And eventually, as with every journey, the chapter ends. Do you still have the courage to start the next?

In this transitionary period of my life where I will enter a bigger world, I am hesitant. I have become comfortable doing what I do every day. However, I know the time passes anyway and that I will regret staying here too long. I just need a little time to look around me before I enter another new world of baby chicken steps.

My thanks go out to House House for throwing this unexpected journey at me.

The game is meant to be played on separate systems which I highly recommend with headsets.  Proximity chat is key here and honestly is better for it.  A variety of tools are at your disposal, like radios, to help navigate the more difficult puzzles but ultimately communication is entirely up to you.  You can even use the game's hand gestures to work through the solutions.

A cozy puzzle game was not on my bingo card of games to play with my oldest but here we are still plugging through the final few puzzles before we put the game down.

Anecdote:
My oldest and I got to the last run of puzzles at the "end of the game" and, without spoiling, worked together extremely well as a team with how we communicated.  It was a heartwarming moment when we made it to the end only for my oldest to turn around and ask if we could then solve the other puzzles we missed.

This is one of those games where you can only truly ever play it once.

This game isn't just a multiplayer puzzle game, but it's a game that is designed to get you to learn more about the people around you. You will learn their favourite colour combinations, their favourite items, their roles within the puzzles and that isn't even touching the surface of what you'll find out about them during the quiet moments of the game. 

I love the design, how you and your friends are meant to have moments where you work together so tightly, but then it forces you to be apart to complete puzzles. I loved the idea of getting lost, or someone else getting lost, and having to contact them throughout the map to see where they were and feeling relieved when you finally are reunited with them. And I love how the game lets your friendships and relationships blossom and grow even further because you're meant to fill the silence. The only noises you hear are from the Australian wilderness, or occasional music or the ocean itself, but this gives you a gentle nudge in order to talk to those around. In an age of technology, where everyone is so separated by phones and machines, a game like this really does bring people together so easily. 

There are so many unspoken things about this game as well. You will eventually be given roles unknowingly. Someone will find a route, someone will dive head first into the puzzle.. someone will get lost.. a lot.. and someone might even end up holding the light. But that doesn't mean you're useless, it means that you're a team, a group, and I find it so beautiful. No one takes charge, no one competes. Everyone takes the game at their pace and enjoys one another's company.

I'm going to miss playing this game. We would hop on the game after horrible days of work or uni, just to then relax and do some puzzles together. We would laugh, joke and just talk. Just walking around and stumbling across a puzzle was so magical, because every one of them was unique and we always wanted to figure out what it was together. We 100%'d the game today, and it is truly one of the best games I have ever played. I was finding it so difficult to convey why this game is so dear to me, but then I realise that it's because of the people I played it with. The people you play this game with make it matter the most, and it's truly a testament to your friendship and relationships. At the very final moment, I could feel that there was an atmosphere in the air that no one really wanted this to end, we wanted to keep playing together. If you take my advice, please play it with those who are dear to you. It's so unforgettable, take it at your own pace and learn about the people around you rather than the game itself.

A cute, hilarious, whimsical multiplayer puzzle game that spits in the face of rapid consumerism. A pleasant 3rd space. Really spins what makes a multiplayer game fun on its head. 

Performance: Ran well on my laptop and runs well on my dual monitor PC. A little stuttering when the game first came out that has since been patched. I have not had connection issues and have never crashed. 

Gameplay: A large map that is pretty free to explore once you leave the tutorial zone with unique structures and foliage that catch the eye and make you want to continue exploring. Premise is vague enough that it sparks curiosity rather than confusion. Puzzles are engaging and at times challenging but leave room for creative problem solving rather than having one strict linear answer. The game gives you plenty of context and gives players a good idea of the game limits so that players can come to their own logical conclusions when solving more difficult puzzles. 

Graphics: The game is set in a robust, lush Australian inspired national park with amazing sound design that altogether suck you into the strange, beautiful world of Big Walk. Not a lot of detail is lost when you reduce the graphics to lowest and it is still very enjoyable. Blows you away on high settings. 

Re-playability: I value games with good re-playability and despite a lot of the puzzles being similar between servers there is still a lot of fun to be had when playing with a new group of pals. Seeing others feel whimsy and intrigue is part of the fun of Big Walk. 

If you enjoy unique puzzles, exploration, hanging out in digital spaces and multiplayer games with a dash (the smallest dash) of existential horror then I would say this game is for you.

I'm playing this in a group of myself 43, my 9 and 11 year old and their 15 year old cousin. This was enjoyable for all of us. It IS slightly bit of a walking simulator, but it also is a big puzzle game. Try TRY not to cheat. 

There is nothing else like this game and part of the fun is working through the frustration and figuring out how to do things even when you have some kind of limitation. When you're done, that's it. Each of these puzzles were handcrafted and special. Sure some worked on similar mechanics so you will never experience that first time of trying to figure out wth you're supposed to do. 

Having a Big Walk helped me learn many things. It helped clarify how people think and how to distil information down in clear and concise units. It helped me slow down and just experiment. I've always loved co-op games and this was definitely a love story to coop. I learned the strengths and weaknesses of my teammates. 

I had much better planning and I knew for the most part when a certain course of action wouldn't work. It was funny to me which team members pitched certain ideas but as I (tried) to walk them through their thought process to see how their plan would (or wouldn't) work. But I have a horrible sense of direction and I relied on my teammates to lead me and we saved so much time over than "just Dad being in charge and calling all the shots". 

I also learned how super powerful we humans are just because we can communicate, and how there are actually many methods of communicating. Both audio and words have their own strengths and weaknesses. 

I also learned how important having a common language was. Some picked words not specific enough, like "structure". Others were not preferred and therefore not used, causing us confusing (ie., I first elected to call the places you put the "Idols" (our term for the gourd/bell/figurine thing) in "Temples". Our group didn't like that term and kept calling it other stuff until we all agreed on the term "Blue/Red/etc Tower". Otherwise we all just were calling everything "thing" and no one knew what we were talking about!! 

I also see how weak we are when we get separated. It was definitely a certain feeling of falling and getting separated and then not seeing your group, wandering for 15 minutes alone wondering if you'd ever see a soul again. And then that feeling of joy and relief when you see a team member and everyone finds each other again, promising we won't get separated or get interested by something and leave the group.

This is what games are and what they should be. AI could not make this, I am convinced. Any copies will be shoddy. AAA gaming could never make something like this. This is entirely different from everything else on the market and I understand why now.

Big Walk questions and twists one of the fundamentals of online gaming, that has just been standardized for decades: how do players communicate with each other? 

When proximity chat games got popular last year, my mind went crazy with the possabilities for clever game mechanics using your friends voices in innovative ways. I am settling in for a showing of ‘Melania’ and the theater is PACKED!

Earlier, a bystander asked if I was heading in to see Avatar, and I stopped dead in my tracks.

“Avatar? No, son,” I curtly replied. “I don’t watch woke movies. I’m here to see the groundbreaking documentary about our incredibly talented First Lady.”

The man’s two little girls began jumping up and down, pulling on his sleeve, and begging, “Daddy, we want to see Melania!”

“But. But…” he stammered, “I thought you girls wanted to see Zootopia 2?”

Their father was scrambling, stressed out, and disoriented.

Tears began to well up in their eyes.

“But…” I said in a hushed tone, “I happen to have a few extra tickets with me, and I’d like you and your dad to have them.”

They jumped for joy and began hugging their father. He looked relieved as he wiped the sweat off his brow with a smile.

I handed him the tickets and pulled him close. “Raise these girls right,” I whispered. “Teach them to be classy conservative women of faith like Melania, don’t let them become like Meghan Markle. Capisce?”

He hugged me and thanked me profusely. “What are you going to do now?” He asked. 

“Don’t worry about me, son,” I told him, with a twinkle in my eye. “I’ve already got tickets to the next showing.”

That said I think some of the puzzles genuinely feel like padding in terms of what they offer as an experience, the 5 minute puzzle and the puzzle where you carry pieces one at a time across a mini gondola are frankly kind of silly. The 5 minute one in particular kinda boggles my brain because like I assume the idea is "just chill with your friends" but I am already chilling with my friends, its just a 5 minute time waste for a another red piece. 

But I do think a wide majority of the puzzles are either solid or really cool and make good use of the multiplayer format, although I only played with one person, I can't exactly speak how this goes with a 3 player or 4+ group. 

The highlight is easily the final segment past the wall with its core gimmick which I won't spoil here, I haven't done most of the bonus puzzles but they seem like harder versions of others you find throughout the game and I am excited to see the rest. 

My only other complaint is that some of the games collision with rocks and trees get really annoying at points when you are trying to navigate and at points I wish you could move faster, even if it was like an unlockable thing, I understand the game wants you to take your time and chill but it's still something I personally felt was dragging at points. 

Otherwise very solid game, friend gem.

My friends and I had an absolutely splendid time playing Big Walk. There's a seemingly sizable misnomer that this is a co-op game in a similar vein as Lethal Company or Peak (especially since it's bundled with Peak), but it's simply not that type of game, and I've seen it ascribed more accurately to VR Chat. This is a great place to walk and talk together; to hang out with your friends in an environment that isn't a sterile voice chat like Discord, with the ancillary activity available of being able to solve puzzles and explore the island. The puzzles themselves aren't any sort of logic puzzle like you'd find in another, typical puzzle game either. The puzzles in Big Walk are tests of your the communication abilities between you and your friends through various restrictions, like having to describe shapes without being able to point out the shape to your friends, or a one-way intercom and a lightbulb. So if you're bad at puzzles normally, don't let that dissuade you from playing. Precisely because these aren't logic puzzles either, I see replayability being reasonable as well, with the same or different groups of people having to come up with different or refined communication strategies.

It's hard to describe what makes Big Walk so great. It's a very simple game and I think that is what makes it beautiful. Everything has been made with the goal of immersing you in the atmosphere of the game:
- There's no music, only the sounds of nature around you, unless you carry a radio
- There's no minimap: you find your way around the island using landmarks and - if you're lucky enough to have one - a big foldable map
- The sounds of talking are wonderfully blended into the game. They're quieter if you're far apart and delightfully loud through a megaphone - and the echoes in tunnels are wonderful
Once you've wandered your way around the island and found yourself a puzzle, it's a new kind of experience every time. Something to solve and argue with your friends about. 

This is a game about walking, but the most memorable moments I've had in the game (so far!) have been when we were just sitting around doing nothing, just enjoying the vibes

the secret to all of this is that, simply put, humans are social creatures, and this game knows exactly how to use that to its advantage, even in ways you don't realize. there are so many subtle tricks the game pulls to get you to work together with your friends, even for the tiniest of aspects. 

sure, it's easy to say that the (smartly designed) collaborative puzzles are great at pushing people together and that they could easily carry an entire game, but the "Big Walk" itself, AKA the traversal and exploration, is what truly makes this game so unique.

there's so much i could say about all the ways this game accomplishes that, but to keep a long story short, Big Walk embraces everything that most other similar games would try to skip, speed up or make as convenient as possible; turning any regular game mechanic into a spark that can start up a conversation between you and your team mates.

and to top it all off, the brilliant design work put into this game is packaged nicely in a game with beautiful graphics, a striking art style and amazing sound and music. so grab a friend, two, three, as many as you can gather, and enjoy the best game to come out in 2026.

One of the best Co-Op games ever made. This is a game that takes full advantage of proximity chat to give you a unique experience. I have played plenty of co-op games before, but none quite like this. On its face, Big Walk is simple. It's a sandbox game where you explore an island with your friends and solve puzzles to progress. However, the magic of Big Walk is that every aspect of its design is so intentional and so smartly done to make you rely on your friends. Even something as simple as using a backpack requires your friends to help you, you cannot put items on the backpack without someone with you to put it on your back and take it off. There are also moments where the game will force you to separate from the group, and that sense of isolation and loneliness makes the moments when you reunite with friends all the more special. I had an amazing time exploring this world with my friends and when it was all over, I felt at the same time both sadness and joy. This is truly a special game and if you have a group to play it with, you will have an amazing, unforgettable experience. The kind of game I wish I could wipe my brain and play it again blind. The final gauntlet of the game is an incredible concept executed perfectly, and really filled me with such appreciation for the group and amazement at how the game taught all of its concepts. 

10/10, it's my Game of the Year so far.

Big Walk presents an experience that is one of a kind. It marries three concepts expertly to create an unforgettable 15-20 hours of playtime: open world exploration, puzzles, and co-op play. The open world is gorgeous and functionally fantastic, the puzzles are engaging, fun, and never get old, and the progression pushes you to keep exploring, even after the credits have rolled.

The open world is a monumental achievement, and rivals every other open world I have experienced and beats all of them, easily. I played this with one other person for 95% of the game, and every new session we would plan out where we wanted to go and what we aimed to achieve, only to get distracted by another building in the distance, or a spot of bright color peeking through the tree line. It would derail our adventure in the best way imaginable, helping us discover new sections of the map and pushing us into the unknown. The open world is expertly crafted to keep you moving, tailored to your curiosity and your groups sense of wonder. The visual design of the environment is not to be glossed over, by the way. It's a gorgeous natural landscape with plains and hills and mountains and rivers and beaches and ravines. The flora is pulled directly from the real world and feels familiar (if you've touched grass recently). 

Special shoutout to the audio design: the ambience is a masterclass on foley and field recording, bringing the world to life all around you. The music is playful, the sound design of the various items you can interact with are satisfying, and the implementation is a technical success, hands down. 

The puzzle design has brought me the most fun I've had with puzzles, ever. And I don't enjoy puzzles much. A good chunk of the early puzzles are straightforward, and get you familiar with the tools at your disposal. And this skillset only evolves as you sweep the island for more puzzles, culminating in an incredible final set of puzzles to cap it all off. It's clever, it's unique, and it doesn't feel like your hand is being held through any of it. It's all on you and your friends to get through it. Nobody gets to be hero, but everyone gets to share in the spoils. And we came out feeling pretty damn proud of ourselves.

Big Walk is an excellent experience that is a must-play if you enjoy some light hearted co-op adventuring or puzzle solving. There are some serious long term memories I made playing this one with my friend, and I doubt any other game will come close to this experience any time soon. 10/10

Big Walk is a one-off experience like nothing else. It's clever, cute, genuine, and soulful; and unabashedly designed by human beings with an obvious appreciation for [and understanding of] the chaos and complexity of interpersonal communication. Which, in 2026 (the year that OpenAI started proposing "guardrails") is deeply refreshing...

Also, can we talk about how delightful it is to play a game that was designed to be played once, and [i] only [/i] once? Don't get me wrong -- there's some fun Roguelite-Card-Battler-Extraction-Shooter-Royales out there. But in an era of gaming when so many titles are published with the hope of going viral and existing forever, with planned DLC's, VIP stores, and Battle Passes hoping to "capture the market", it warms my heart to see people out here makin games that are distinctly NOT designed for infinite replayability or getting people pathologically addicted to them.

The world of Big Walk is not procedurally-generated every time you start a new run; it also doesn't require an email, password, access to your kernel, and the forfeiture of your identity to a tech conglomerate that's also funding a g*nocide; and it wasn't made-in-a-corporate-lab to be farmed for clips till it's no longer trending. (Not that they haven't had plenty of positive press.)

House House could have spent the last seven years making "a game that keeps you coming back". Instead, they have handcrafted a finite world in which you and a group of (ideally) friends can embark on a unique journey through mind and back; a world where the POIs are only interesting until you have found them, then they're just Points; a world where the puzzles are meant to be solved and then (mostly) forgotten; a world where laughter and frustration and elation are constants; a world where whoever who holds the orb of light can become The One Who Holds The Orb Of Light and whoever's got the best sense of direction becomes Le Navigator Supreme (iykyk); and also a world where the game closes when you press exit.

And then, at the end, it's over. That's it. Once you have finished the game, there is no more game.
And in my opinion, that sort of finality is a necessary thing to feel every now and then.
 
tldr; idk man, it's real good.

Simply put, Big Walk is a game about solving puzzles on an island together. The puzzles you'll do require communicating effectively with your friends. 

If you're in a group of four or less, the puzzles are almost always going to require every player present. This means that nobody can be left behind. This means that nobody will be forgotten. As somebody who is often forgotten, this mechanic meant more to me than anything any game I've ever played before has ever done. Playing this game with some people I wanted to get know better was the first time I can remember not having to fear getting left behind by friends.

I realize now that, this is a game. Like any game, my friends could have stopped playing with me at any moment. Some did, but some stayed. Some people joined midway through, and in the spirit of Big Walk, we explained to them how the world worked so they could be on the same page as everyone else.

At the end of this game, I cried in the way one would cry as though they were saying goodbye to their friends knowing it was the last time they'd ever see them again. This island felt like a place I really went to, really left, and really want to be invited back to again. I am not certain that any team of developers could find the way back to that place like House House and Panic did.
Big walk indeed, very good.

I very rarely write reviews, but I wanted to put into words how much I loved this game. As someone who tends to play a lot of (but not limited to) shooters and action games, this game was a breath of fresh air for me, and I think it was for the group I played with as well. We have played a multitude of so called "friendslop games", games that are made specifically to gather friends to complete a repetitive challenge to see how far you can get. Think Lethal Company, REPO, Murky Divers, Content Warning, and to some extent PEAK (which in my opinion is in a different league, especially since PEAK has a proper win condition as opposed to the others that are in the "how far can you loop a run before getting torn a new one" category). I think that Big Walk is a take on this "genre" so incredible that I don't think it belongs in the category. 

To start out with, from the moment this game was announced, during and after playing it through fully, I was in love with the style. The theme from the trailer stuck with me for months to come and the choice to make an acapella accompanied by minimal instrumentals could not have been better. The music in-game was also such a treat to hear. It felt so lovingly hand-crafted, coming across a radio channel or speaker monument was always such a pleasant surprise. I could almost hear the smile on the composers face as they made these little tunes. The almost photorealistic terrain combined with the bright, colorful characters and objective structures creates such a unique visual element that I haven't really seen in any other game. Not only is it incredibly endearing, it also helps a lot with visual clarity while wandering. I did greatly enjoy being able to spot my bright yellow friend through thick foliage, or seeing a structure from far far away. It also helps to balance the mood of the game. If everything had been just photorealism, I think this game would be significantly less endearing. I love my stupid little pink chud ant/bird/thing player character.

Alongside the visual aspect, the sound design and foley for this game was nothing short of phenomenal. The amount of detail and care put into every little movement, click, thunk, thud and more made the experience feel so much immersive and personal. The sounds of flares popping in the night sky, soft pitter pattering of you and your friends feet, the gentle lapping of the waves as you watch the sun set over the ocean with your buddies beside you. I especially enjoyed the object and structure specific sound. The sound the orb lights make when you turn them on (and kick them!), the noise the little red gourds make when you place them into the tower slots. Wandering over to someone in a room and tapping on the glass to get their attention was my personal favorite sound, which also bring me to my next point. 

This game really stands out to me more than others due to how it handles communication  A lot of co-op puzzle games nowadays have very straightforward puzzles and communication mechanics. One series that comes to mind is the We Were Here games, which I did very much enjoy. In the We Were Here series, you almost ALWAYS have a way to vocally communicate with your teammate. Big Walk actively takes that away from you during many puzzles and nudges you into using other means of communication, such as the gesture system, or as I said before, tapping on glass (or other materials.) Nonverbal communication was implemented in such a creative way that it barely felt restricting. The gesture system was a fun little mechanic that added a LOT to the overall feel of the game. It forced us to all collectively reevaluate how we would commune and strategize during puzzles. It's such a simple thing, but it makes a huge difference in player interaction. 

I know I've said a lot already, but I have one more important thing to add. I think that there is one particularly special thing about this game; It just feels so indescribably human. Part of what I'm going to say is inspired by another review I read recently, but I think I have some other bits to add to it. Big Walk comes across as an incredibly simple game, but it is really so so much more. While playing this with my friends, I felt like we were brought together a lot more than we would be on other games. Big Walks unique yet simple twist on how you communicate with each other and interpret what the others are saying make the time you spend with your friends so much more personal. Adjacent to what was stated in the other review (Posted by user "grape" on September 23rd), it makes you ask questions like "how would YOU describe this object to someone who can't see it? would others agree if they heard it? is it accurate enough to transcribe to a drawing? how can I communicate this without using my voice?" Questions like these and how we as a group answered them really made me feel closer to my friends throughout my time playing with them. Minor spoilers ahead, but at some point in the game you lose both your ability to speak and the ability to see which player character is which. When we hit this checkpoint, I had become so used to each of my friends mannerisms in the game that I could clearly distinguish which was which with no problem. The way one barely talked, so his beak would always be short. The way one would always b hop alongside me, and gesture more often than the others. The way the one who was on controller would always turn a bit slower than the rest of us and move in smoother arcs. Again; The game brings you together like no other game has in the past. "We like to walk, we like to talk, we like to work together." I couldn't have said it better myself. 

In the end, this is one of my favorite multiplayer co-op games that I've ever played. The team at House House has created a truly beautiful game, one unlike any other game you will ever play, and that I can guarantee. Thank you, House House, for making such a wonderful experience.

I enjoyed the majority of my time with Big Walk. There is a thoughtful use of proximity voice and puzzle design that gives the game an enjoyable flow of splitting up to explore, finding each other to solve puzzles, and then splitting up again. I thought the end sequence was a perfect conclusion, with surprising emotional oomph.

My group didn't engage much with the post-game, as we felt the bonus puzzles strayed too far from being tricky to feeling like tasks. Stuff like, "Repeat this older puzzle to move a heavy ball, but over ten times the distance." Or, "Sit and wait for 30 minutes." Meh. Also, it's way too easy to get caught on the smallest deviations of terrain in this game, in particular when travelling uphill.

These small complaints aside, Big Walk was a cool game to experience from the start to the main ending, and that's a good amount of time to have fun. I would recommend it, but it's a bit expensive at full price (especially since everyone needs their own copy), so I'd say wait for a sale.

I’m so glad to have gotten to experience this game with my friends. Big Walk is so clearly made with love and passion, and that love is infectious. I felt so close and connected with my friends, all of whom live many hours away (if not in different countries entirely) in a way that I’ve never seen achieved in any other game. It’s a way to feel like you’re truly there with your friends, solving puzzles, laughing, and exploring just like if you were doing it in person. 

Thank you, Big Walk. For giving me and my friends a place to play together. For giving me connection. For bringing friends closer together. For making me appreciate what and who I have around me. For making me smile. For making me feel less alone.

I don't typically write many reviews, but Big Walk is possibly the most meaningful multiplayer experience I've ever had.
I cannot express enough how beautifully crafted this game is. From the sound design to the puzzles and the gorgeous landscapes, I was completely immersed and in love with this world from the second I stepped out of the tutorial room.
Now for spoilers, because I must talk about my favorite moments:

[spoiler] [h1] THE ORB [/h1]  Funny enough, one of my favorite sections of the entire game was when we were all mute and couldn't see each other's colors. It wasn't because I didn't like talking to my friends (honestly, I did miss their voices by the end of it), but this section completely removed all language barriers. Even though my friends all speak fluent English, I realized in that moment that no matter what language a player speaks, this section is completely doable. We were stripped down to nothing but nameless bodies with no identifying features and no vocal abilities. I thought that was incredibly cool and special in a world where we are often so separated by language and region.
[h1] The Endings. [/h1] Both the initial ending and the 100% completion ending were incredibly meaningful. On our way to the end-credit TV, we talked about the puzzles in the Orb and guessed who did what in each section, because we genuinely had no clue who was who! We sat through the entire credits sequence, which is something I rarely do, because I wanted to know the names of every single person who put their heart and soul into this project. Getting to say goodbye to my friends as they each walked out the door felt so bittersweet. In that moment, I thought it was the end of our journey and that we had seen all the game had to offer. (Boy, we had no idea what was actually in store for us next!)
Upon completing all the puzzles for 100% and unlocking the final room in the spawn area, we found ourselves in a small room with a stage and a chair for each of us. This moment genuinely made me tear up. We each took a turn on stage to share our favorite memory from our big walk. When I say that this game has forever changed me, I truly mean it. I will forever cherish the memory of my first walk with my favorite people in the whole world. <3
[/spoiler]

I want to give you a genuine thank you. If any single one of the devs, or anyone who had a part in creating this game, reads this review: thank you for creating something so beautiful. Big Walk is hands-down one of the most memorable co-op experiences you can dive into with friends and family. It strikes a rare balance between charm, accessibility, and clever design, making every dollar and hour spent on it feel completely justified.

At its core, the game thrives on pure team coordination. The puzzles and challenges aren't just arbitrary roadblocks, they are specifically crafted to demand real-time communication, observation, and working together. The mechanics are delightfully simple and intuitive, allowing players of almost any skill level to jump in and start contributing immediately, yet the gameplay loop remains consistently engaging throughout.

That said, the experience does have a couple of minor rough edges. You will occasionally run into random, unexpected physics collisions that can feel a bit awkward during movement. Additionally, the physical map you carry around in-game could definitely use some quality-of-life improvements, as navigating with it can feel slightly clunky at times.

However, these small critiques barely detract from how polished and joyful the rest of the game is. What truly elevates Big Walk is its final act: the ending sequence is absolute perfection. Reaching that last act and climax makes every initial puzzle, detour, and trial feel immensely rewarding. It brings the entire experience together in a way that leaves everyone talking about it long after you finish the game. If you are looking for a fantastic co-op or a game with your close friends or a title for your next game night, Big Walk is an absolute must-play.

10/10 - An absolutely fantastic game and undoubtedly the best co-op experience I've ever had. Big Walk is a game I'll remember fondly forever for a multitude of reasons.

Gameplay is perfectly simple - the game doesn't have a busy HUD, doesn't expect you to remember any over-the-top combos or intricate mechanics, it just asks you to explore with friends and engage with the puzzles you find. You can point (forwards, left, right and up), you can crouch, jump, run, pick things up and throw them - and that's about it. 

It is visually striking, far more than I realised when the first ever trailer dropped, and in a time when everything is all about pushing graphical fidelity to the absolute max, I loved how the game effectively balances simplicity in design with gorgeous lighting and playfulness in the worlds signposting and puzzle illustrations.

Audio is superb too - there's no spoken dialogue, just voice chat between you and your party members, but the general ambience, quite bizarre soundtrack and immensely satisfying sound effects give the island that you explore a very unique feeling.

Length-wise the game doesn't outstay it's welcome, my group clocked around 27 hours overall finishing the main game and then seeing everything else through to 100%, with a fair amount of time spent trying to figure things out but generally making steady progress as we went. I'm hoping the huge success means there's a chance for future DLC, and even after 27 hours I'd love to jump in with my group and tackle some more puzzles.

Additionally, playing on PC with my friends playing on PS5, we encountered almost no issues bar maybe 3 connection issues (which is likely down to my terrible internet, as host).

Big Walk is the latest game from Playdate, a company that is known for Untitled Goose Game. Which I have to admit, it is HARD to follow up something iconic which is why when I heard about this game back in 2023 during the Game Awards I was curious. Even back then it was a weird game, not a grandiose AAA game but a game that emphasized one thing. A game for you and your friends. As the date got closer and closer, the game didn’t really say much more than that. It just showed people talking and walking around this island. But put our trust in Playdate we would and it was WORTH it.

When you first enter Big Walk and join a group (or host one) you are taken to this tutorial island that uses pictograms to tell you how to play. This is also where you’re likely to meet up with everyone. Everyone is represented with these avatars that do have arms and legs segmented on 3 balls. The characters look cute. As you talk you realize there is proximity chat that gets quieter pretty quickly and there is also NO music. As you finish there is one way to go. As you walk in it quickly becomes night and you can’t see anything except for some glowing orbs that you can pick up and hold as a light source. You arrive and you get your first challenge, customize the colors of your character. The catch is that you can’t do it yourself, your other friends have to customize your character. So you point out what colors you want to be and they have the ability to grab the paint brush and make you that color. It’s really clever cause it introduces the thing that is the center of this game: Communication.

As you continue on this island you’ll find puzzles, each puzzle will give you an object shaped similar to a pear and after a bit you’ll find a place to put the pear shaped objects and once you do you’ll get a key which after more exploration opens up the rest of the island. The puzzles are nice and can be categorized by its limitations, like limiting the ability to see each other, to talk to each other, or limiting the environment around you. Each puzzle basically plays on the communication between the two of you and how you can speak. These puzzles are rarely hard but they’re hard enough that they force you to talk to your friend in weird ways or communicate in strange ways. It’s kind of fun as you work together cause with each puzzle you solve you get to know your friends more and how they think and communicate. And with each puzzle you win just a bit more. Which is further cemented by the exploration.

The island is huge. Walking in will take multiple ingame days and it would be a pain if that wasn’t interesting but the game does everything in its power to make it interesting. There are puzzles all over the place to give you bits of story, however the best part is just that you’re walking with your friends and chatting with them. What makes this game fun is the fact that this game has stories you create with your friends all over the place. The game lends itself to this with the fact that there is little music in the game which gives space to walk as if you were in the real world taking a walk. The game is intentional about all of this placing trinkets to communicate via walkie talkies, or megaphones, or flares to shoot in the sky. The game puts just the right amount of limitations in it (like a full day night cycle that slows you down in the night) to make this game feel vibrant and alive. It genuinely feels like I am indeed doing a big walk with my friends as I play.

People say frequently that this is the Breath of the Wild of co-op games and there’s a lot I agree in that. However I think many people think about it as the fact that there are puzzles to solve and that’s what makes it similar, but I have to disagree. What makes this game so special and Breath of the Wild so special is that it creates so many opportunities to create a story. BotW was interesting because everyone had a unique story that they were so excited to tell you. The puzzles are a part of it, sure, but it’s often the most random encounters that got you there.

One day early on in the game we didn’t carry a light source and the sun was setting. So instead of trying to walk around effectively blind we sat down and just caught up on the top of a hill. Just watching the sunset and then the sunrise before getting up and moving around. During that night we chatted about every small thing that had happened in our life, our woes with our jobs, what we were cooking that night, etc. When the morning came around it just felt like we were a bit closer. This is a game where you walk with your friends, and it’s one of the best games I’ve ever played.

[i]Big Walk[/i] is essentially like taking a long hike with your friends, except you also had to solve puzzles to keep going down a trail (with the puzzles becoming more and more difficult to communicate effectively in). And also if you and your friends were very tall birds.
