Games best played exactly one time are a subject I've written on many times, but I'll scream it from the rooftops if I have to: Games are experiences. Some experiences ought to be once-in-a-lifetime. Big Walk is such an experience. I advise anyone reading this who hasn't played it yet to avoid spoilers like the plague. But you won’t find any spoilers here, so keep reading!

Basically all you need to know going in is: this is a game about communicating with friends; one to eleven of your chums, lovers, or complete strangers. Communicate and solve puzzles.

The trials of long-distance Big Walking

I won’t harp on it for too long because we ironed out the wrinkles eventually, but we did encounter some game-stopping technical mishaps. 1,500+ miles of distance between players does induce noticeable latency. We managed, but it was noticeable. Cross-platform compatibility was also a bit sketchy, and we took quite some time to find the weak link. I joked in the first hour of our first session, “maybe this is the first puzzle?” Nobody laughed. :( But did you know that AirPods can make you sound like a jet engine?

Setting the scene

How do I even begin to talk about the magic of this game without spoiling it? Well, for one, Big Walk is the third release from House House—the developers of the devilishly charming Untitled Goose Game (2019). From the now-two games by them I’ve played, I keyed into a few ideas that carried over from their last game:

    Everything is unbearably cute
    Fierce commitment to simplicity of play; elegance in the controls
    No idea overstays its welcome
    Music is baked into the identity of the game

So there is this vague idea of what a House House-y game looks and feels like. Both Untitled Goose Game and Big Walk are marketed as ‘puzzle’ games. And that’s about the extent to which the games are similar. Except birds. Both games feature birds.

“Call me Maddy Primarycolors”

The game features no name tags, you distinguish one another with the random assortment of body colors initially assigned at the start. Very early on though, in the tutorial area, you are given a palette to choose from. I opted to have my player character’s bird body use the primary colors: red, blue, and yellow. Inadvertently, perhaps subconsciously, I matched my character with the splotches on the game’s logo and one of the ‘mascot’ birds featured on the game’s banner...which, in retrospect, got me thinking about the logo as a primer of what’s to come. Simplicity. Pure and distilled.

The setting of the game is a love letter to the wilds of Australia, in the form of a realistic scan of Wilsons Promontory National Park. Quite a beautiful rendition, I'll say. But the landscape is also filled with abstract geometric shapes, boldly colored and starkly contrasting the natural beauty, just begging to be explored. The whole map is a toybox designed with a brutal efficiency to evoke discovery and delight. Every piece of the game’s world beckons, and I jumped for joy at every little detail.

Music & Soundscape

Big Walk's music is absolutely integral to the game's identity, but in a much more personal way than Untitled Goose Game. Whereas Goose Game employed a suite of Claude Debussy's Préludes for piano (to incredible effect by the way), Big Walk has an original soundtrack. I would describe it as organic, orchestral electronica. Weird, angelic, carnal music from somewhere deep. It's only ever presented diegetically (through in-game speakers), dynamic to the time of day, and each track is specific to a region of the game's map. Sublime.

And when we're not bobbing our heads to the beat of those odd tunes, our ears are filled with the excellent soundscape provided by Em Halberstadt's foley work. Every way to interact with each object has a different sound, and every object sounds different. Contextual reverb in tunnels, long-distance echoes, wildlife noises, machine cacophany, omnious hums, irresponsibly loud horns, I could go on. It's not something we ever talked about in our appreciation the game in our playthrough, except perhaps in remarking how spooky a kookaburra call sounds in pitch dark, but the sound design is Big Walk's (ironically) quiet hero.

Big (and small) Puzzles

As much as I would love to gush about the puzzle design in the specific, you'll just have to take my word that they are spectacular. Some puzzles are similar to others. Iterations on a core idea; however, nothing ever felt stale. There are recurring symbols seen everywhere, a sort of alphabet of shapes. We developed the common language and thought processes through our shared experience that enabled us to be a better team by the end.
Who Big Walks?

    "I mean, this is a long walk." "...a Big Walk, even."

If you know, you know: we called our mysterious objects ‘schnozzes.’

What made Blue Prince (my favorite game of 2025) special was its willingness to take risk in its game design. That game catered to its niche audience and was willing to ostracize players to do it. When a developer understands its game is designed for a very particular type of person, that’s when video games can really soar. So it is with Big Walk.

But what kind of person plays this game? Me, obviously. The five people who played with me, to name a few more. I would say five friends, but two of the players in my group were strangers to me at the start of our journey together. Maybe that makes my playthrough of Big Walk a little unorthodox. But this is an unorthodox kind of multiplayer game! Playing it (and organizing to play it) is a test of commitment. Players unwilling to play together on a dedicated schedule are probably not the kind of players Big Walk attracts.

That’s not to say you can’t goof off. Big Walk never lets you stray too far from a new adventure, and we had frequent tangents inside of tangents inside of side quests. I’d say we were only seriously puzzling for about half of the roughly 18 hours it took us to reach the end of the game.

    "It kinda makes you caked up O_O"

The other 9 hours, we were just messing around. Getting lost in the dark. Tootin’ horns. Carrying around useless trinkets from the last session. Chucking said trinkets off cliffs. Chucking actually useful objects off cliffs. Jumping into random holes without looking first. Finding the most insane positions to pose our li’l guys. Seeing how far we could stretch our stringy arms.

    "It's time for the key!" "Keeeeeeeeey! Keeeeeeeeeey! KEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEY! WHOOO! WHOOO!"

We just took a Big Walk, is the point I'm trying to make. We set aside the time in our lives to experience this weird and wonderful thing together. No matter how we spent that time, it was special. In that sacred shared space we created for just us, we welcomed in all the emotions, frustration, jokes, whimsy, even meditated silence.

Disappointed though you may be, dear reader, I won’t ruin your Big Walk by sharing spoiler-y details of the hilarity, rage (oh my gosh THAT puzzle), triumph, and tears we shed there. It was just for us. I hope you can find a similar crowd, or even one close friend, with whom you can share this experience. Because if you and your group enter Big Walk with the same curiosity and spirit of adventure, you will create a wholly unique set of memories.

The details in the gestures, your snoot changing when you're talking, the eyes, pointing and looking and jumping--it's everything you need to tell your friends what the heck you want them to do to solve the puzzle when they can't hear you!

They--step by step as this kind of game requires--teach you the basics and then switch it up when you've got a solid grasp on it, all without being frustrating like some games can struggle with, especially multiplayer puzzle games. I figured I’d never play this game due to the MP-only nature of it. But then I had some friends singing its praises, and so I convinced my wife to try it with me, since it seemed really chill and not too demanding controls-wise

And wow, what a game! While it’s mainly about walking around a big Australian-inspired island with others solving puzzles, the whole premise of it is built around proximity chat, getting lost, focusing on what you can/can’t hear from other players, planning, and sharing stories. The unique and novel ways it uses these things to create some really neat puzzles, situations, and exercises to deal with is pretty inspired

It really comes down to figuring out ways to best communicate with others, sometimes through simple in-game gestures and coordination. Sometimes you can’t see and need the other player(s) to guide you with their voice. Sometimes you can’t hear, so it’s all about visual cues/motion/instruction. It’s just really natural and organic, and because you just walk (or lightly jog), there isn’t any time pressure for 99% of the game. There are a small handful of timer-based ones, but they are very rare.

Just like Untitled Goose Game, this is very polished despite its simplistic look. I don’t think we ran into any bugs, the online connectivity works flawlessly, and the world itself is quite lovely to look at, with global illumination and day/night cycles. Sound design is minimal, but is atmospheric, convincing, and can be quite charming, as are the character animations/expressions. The final section is also one of the most memorable and sublime experiences I’ve had in any game.

Do not bother checking reviews or video essays about this game. 

If you love games and have good friends, convince them to play this together and experience it for yourselves.

As the trailer puts it, this is a game about "walking and talking," but it is much, much more than that. It strips video games down to their most basic elements to create an experience built around connection and shared moments.

As you explore, solve puzzles, or simply wander around trying to find each other, you'll grow closer to your friends, you'll laugh at the different ways everyone approaches a puzzle (or fights over how to solve it xD), and you'll feel like you're genuinely there with them. The simple character designs and wide array of emotes do wonders to convey this feeling. Using them feels surprisingly natural, almost like communicating with your own body.

Sadly, this is the kind of game you can only truly experience once. There's little replayability, and the challenges aren't randomized. Everything is handcrafted, which makes every discovery feel fresh and sparks your curiosity as you explore. And that's also what makes the game so special.

It's a lot like life itself, you only get to experience these moments once, but you carry them with you long after they're gone. You'll look back on your time with this game and talk about it with your friends about the fun adventure you shared, just like the memories of a fun trip together.

I'll carry this game in my heart for a long, long time.

So take your time, and be ready for Big Walks and Big Talks.

Big Walk is an incredibly well designed co-op game. The experience of planning something out with your friends, splitting off to get items, gathering for the rendezvous, solving a puzzle together, splitting off to locate a new puzzle and return the key to a slot, getting separated and spending a night wandering alone, finding a tool to communication and having that flare of joy when you successfully coordinate with far away friends and reconnect. Every aspect of the co-op features is amazingly well tuned.

Communication is the heart of the game, and House House did a fantastic job making it interesting and enjoyable. The variety of tools to communicate lend the system a surprising depth, and a depth that is very fun (and important!) to utilize when something inevitably goes wrong and someone gets separated. The communication features are so good I find myself wishing other games had this level of love and care put into their communication features, just so I could spend more time using them.

I also adore the art style; the mixture of semi-realistic terrain and plastic-esque structures, items, and characters is so great. It is easy to get lost in the terrain, easy to spot points of interest due to the contrast in style, and reasonably easy to spot items and friends. The sound design also deserves a big shout-out: the way sounds are muffled depending on the surrounding surfaces is really fun, shouts echo across valleys, the ambient noises and steps sounds are lovely, and the items noises are distinctive and pleasant, which is a necessity for how often your friends will repeatedly spam them (barring some which seem purposefully designed to be annoying, such as the bells).

By far the most frustrating aspect of the game for me is navigating the terrain. It is rather rough at points and I got stuck and stopped even from jumping by the awkward terrain at points. It's by no means a deal breaker, but I leaves me wishing I had a climb ability to reset my position and force myself out of strange spots of terrain.

[h3]A true gem in the ocean of endless shallow co-op games[/h3]

COVID-19 created a huge demand for online co-op games to play with friends, and it started with interesting and unique games like Among Us or Phasmophobia, but as years go, there are dozens of same soulless idea-less and just boring games that you wouldn't bother completing after a couple of hours.

Honestly, I'm kind of tired of the same-thing but different-flavour co-op games that can occupy your time, you feel that you enjoy it, but then it just hits you: the time you spent with your friends is good. But the game actually sucks. There are either quota horrors where you collect a bunch of scrap, or museum exhibits, or whatever things, and then repeat until you die, or looking for a ghost in a spooky place that looks like Phasmophobia, plays like Phasmophobia but worse, or just any kind of "numbers go up" pointless things as drug-dealing, supermarket managing, or any other business simulator that just leaves you with a thought that you have wasted a bunch of your time chasing quick satisfaction from becoming a mafia boss when you started as a crook.

Anyway, you see, there is a huge choice of games that people play and talk about, and all of them focus on fun in the moment, but leave you with nothing at the end.

And Big Walk is different. It is different in everything: the puzzles, the interaction, the art style, the moments it creates just for being there. It feels like a proper adventure, not just "hey there are 50 fun co-op puzzles". It feels like true exploration, discovery and discussion with your friends. It feels like a real hike, with getting lost and found, spending a night in a strange place and being happy that you have found your friends again.

Big Walk is chill and it took us 30 hours to complete, but in the moment we never had time to just relax (well, except two places) - you are always doing something, going somewhere, and talk with your friends. Yes, you are in fact having a lot of time just to talk to people, and the game doesn't try to force you having fun every second and hit you with a bunch of content so you don't scroll TikTok for a second. This game is keeping you interested while staying not rushed at all. And slowly completing even the most annoying puzzles was fun at the end.

You know, this is like PICO PARK level of creativity in regards of collaboration, with a huge new layer of voice-based puzzles, and a warm moments in between that make it a jorney instead of another puzzle game.

This is one of the best unusual co-op games that I have played, and definitely in a Top-3 of my 2026.

This is one of the most beautiful games I have ever played. It is masterfully designed to not only convey gameplay mechanics with no words whatsoever, but also to foster unique, sometimes very close conversations with those you are playing with in a manner that is so natural that it feels like the game isn't even doing it. It's not until a puzzle forces you to lose a method of communication with your friend(s) that you realise how excellently this game has been designed to guide your actions and communication without making a single thing feel forced. Each puzzle feels as if it may be frustrating initially but every time you find yourself figuring it out in such a satisfying and natural way with just enough head-scratching to make it satisfying without making it tiring.

I played this game with a single other friend, which meant that each interaction was far more personal; this made the ending (which I will not spoil whatsoever) even more meaningful. We often found ourselves looking around simply for the sake of it despite our relatively fast pace with the puzzles, or stopping to chat [spoiler](one puzzle forces you to sit and talk for five minutes; we ended up talking for twenty)[/spoiler]. 

The one thing I will say about the ending is that it's brilliant, and very touching. As you progress through the game the realisation that you are indeed emotionally attached to it and the puzzles, routines and interactions you have within it begins to nag at you; you'll most likely ignore it at the time and just continue working through the game because of how much you know the feeling brought on by said realisation would affect you emotionally. The ending forces you to confront that feeling. 

You may not realise how fond of and emotionally attached you are to this game while you're playing it. As I said before it may poke through at some moments, but you will probably try and ignore it for fear of its emotional weight. For instance a quiet walk into the unknown with just the sound of music and the voice of your friend to punctuate it, or maybe even just sitting and watching the sun whilst the birds chirp. The game is able to build an incredibly strong relationship with you and the people you're playing with slowly but surely in the background, until the ending finally drops the weight of this on you all at once, releasing a flood of emotion.

This game is able to entice you in with the promise of a fun puzzle game to play with your friends and will end with you having tears rolling slowly down your face. It's brilliant, and so wonderfully well-considered. It deserves your attention.

Big Walk was one of the greatest, most enjoyable, and most interesting experiences I've ever had playing a video game. No other game I've played (or experience I've had at all, for that matter) gives a better insight into learning how other people interact, how they work through and solve problems, and how they bond with each other. For almost every puzzle in the game, no clear solution is given and players are forced to figure out their own solutions to the problems. It was fascinating to watch and listen to my friends discuss (and sometimes debate about) how to approach the problems in front of them, whether intended or player-created-- like accidentally dropping the red-object-of-rotundness acquired from a puzzle in a very high up, secluded location down into the forest below in the middle of the night with no way to find it until reconvening with my party to go searching for it together (or dropping things off of a chair lift because of a cat hitting someone's right mouse button...). I learned how my friends like to work through the puzzles and adapted my solutions to them based on that. We spent just as much time just talking, bonding, and playing pranks on each other as we did actually solving the puzzles and acquiring the various items and unlockables scattered across the map, and that was one of the most fun parts of the whole experience.

The developers put incredible attention to detail into every aspect of this game. The sound design in particular was fascinating, with so many surfaces in the game seeming to have been programmed with their own unique sounds that change based on how you interact with them (for example, if you use both hands to touch a glass surface and drag them around, the actual sound of the hands sliding on the glass changes based on how fast or slow you drag them or how far away your hands are from you, and each hand creates its own unique sound). This attention to detail extends to all the puzzles, the map design, and all the hidden little secrets scattered around the map.

The only complaints I have about the game are that there isn't more of it and that I can't play it again for the first time. It was genuinely a 10/10 experience through and through. Finishing all of the puzzles and unlocking every secret was bittersweet, because I was excited to have explored and enjoyed everything the developers had created, but I was sad that there wasn't more left to complete. I hope that they make more of this type of game in the future. It doesn't necessarily have to be the same formula, but anything that offers the same type of social experience that this game offered, especially with the ability to solve problems or complete puzzles together, would be nothing short of incredible. If the developers release DLC for this game or any future games like this one, I would buy them with no hesitation. Big love for Big Walk.

Oh boy. I feel that Big Walk stands as a one-time, long experience. It's a journey that's built on distances of walking. There's a lot of air to fill and places to explore, areas to get lost in, places to dance, and new items to find. "Where the hell did Jeff go he was right there!"

Big Walks' puzzles are exceptionally unique, each one unlike the other. If you've played with varying people along your save, you may find each person is unique in what they excel at during a puzzle. And if not a puzzle, then they likely discover great skill in their sense of direction, leading a group, excelling better with a friend, or making everyone laugh (or maybe getting lost). Everyone has their "thing" at some point. Big walk has a brilliant way of allowing everyone to actively need each other to solve a puzzle, forcing everyone to work together and not against each other. The puzzle designs themselves can make a tricky puzzle extremely satisfying to solve together. It really feels like an enjoyable group effort, even if some of them almost involved ripping each others heads off over tea kettles.

The game indirectly encourages you to spend time in other peoples company, having mild chit-chat or deep discussions along your way. When in good company, traversing long distances to get somewhere doesn't feel so long after all. A hike or walk in person can be quite similar, I reckon. It's like It doesn't seem like much at the time, but delicately becomes a memory to look back on. And It can never quite be re-experienced the same way, even if re-visited. It's fleeting but cherished. I personally feel that Big Walk is a memory to look back on, even if you've had varying people join you along the journey.

The game also does a good job of creating the desire to discover. It wouldn't be much if it was just a big map of random puzzles scattered around to bump into if there wasn't a sense of learning and unearthing some mystery, or even some secret areas.

I really cannot recommend this experience enough. It's unlike any other game I've played with people. There's an overwhelming sadness that it's over, but it was absolutely worth it.

In recent times, the online community has started to associate certain games with the word "Slop" be it "Friend Slop", "Quality Slop, or "Gooner Slop". In my opinion, this has messed up many people's perception of many games, especially game developers. They pump out these quickly made games that you can play with a couple of friends and then never open again. The Big Walk is none of these. The Big Walk is an amazing game about putting down your phone, being patient, and taking everything in. It's not meant to be speedran through or blindly played. The Big Walk is an experience you can't share with everyone; sometimes, it takes a special person to understand it. Now, I may not define the game as especially "fun" I would rather use the word "entertaining" to define The Big Walk. It's like watching a good YouTube essay or your favorite TV show; it's nothing like a competitive shooter.

When my friend told me about The Big Walk, I admit I was a little uncertain about playing it. I thought it would be one of those "Friend Slop" games that you'd only play once, but nonetheless, he convinced me to play it. That was one of the best choices I made. I found myself laughing, screaming, waiting, crying, and, of course, walking. In only nine hours, I made some core memories that I'll cherish forever. I realized during play that I felt relaxed and calm as well; my perspective of life and morals has definitely been altered a little bit because of this game. You should step back and think: Are you happy with where you are right now? Are you content with the direction you're taking your life right now? Do you admire life? Those are all questions I found myself asking.

The Big Walk also has amazing music design. The music is out of this world, and walking around with the radio or finding the peculiar speaker setups is definitely one of my favorite parts of this game.

If you are going through a weird or difficult time in your life, I would definitely recommend The Big Walk to you. Put your phone down, find a special person to walk with, and take a breather. For me, The Big Walk is a life experience. What does The Big Walk mean to you?

Note: I want to preface this review with the fact I play mainly strategy games, and occasionally shooters and such. This game was really not my cup of tea and I got it because of a friend group wanting me to play with them. While I am not complaining for no reason or bias, I did find serious issues with this game that while individually small added up.

To start the hype over this game was ridiculous. People were acting like this game was giving you a meaningful social resurrection and it was the best indie game since Fallout, Rimworld, PVZ1 Etc. It is very much a cooperative puzzle game. You walk around the map (incredibly slowly), talk a bit, and solve a puzzle to either get a red duck head or a purple one. This collectible exists in quantities in the double digits and are strewn across the map. Find the head, solve associated puzzle to unlock, carry to depository, unlock new feature, repeat. That is what you will do for a playthrough, a playthrough that took my group of five 12 hours to complete. That's right 1 with a 2 following it. So the core loop of gameplay is there so check on that. Next around the map you can get modes of transportation to unlock (A train, Catacom... I mean tunnels, ski lift...) That's it. You can also find all sorts of tools to play around with like flashlights, light orbs, maps, compasses, and (my personal favorite) a flare gun. 
With that basic gameplay out of the way let me talk about what I liked.
-Getting lost was more fun than actually staying on trail.
-Exploration was cool and the visuals are quite good, not to mention the environs are based off the Australian wilderness which is a nice easter egg.
-The tools/toys were well designed and fun to discover the different types.
Now those were all good things, here are my nitpicks that I think make this review collectively negative
-Absolutely no replay ability, once you do the puzzles the first time there is no point in playing another playthrough. 
-Because of above reason, the price is expensive, I give this game 10-15 dollars max, there is cheaper software out there which plays better than this. You are buying a basic 20 dollar, one time use, social experience, nothing else.
-Puzzle Design: This will be somewhat of its own paragraph because the puzzle design was hit or miss. They all challenge you with the same loop, find a way to communicate without talking, seeing, hearing etc. Naturally this gets repetitive 5 hours into the game and you realize that their creative team began to get lazy. Then there are puzzles in which how they got pass playtesting is beyond me. Here are some the best hits of causing you frustration: Find a box halfway across the map using coordinate grids that the game doesn't show you well. (How you are supposed to remember those numbers without outside communication is beyond me). Find a button camouflaged (I kid not) halfway across the map behind a bush to open a box. Take a ball that makes you stuck in place across the map to a slot. Wait in a room 30 minutes (Huh?). Scavenger hunt for pattern sticks around a zone and then guess a random pattern the game doesn't tell you. The combination of this audacious puzzle design and lack of creativity is my main problem with this game.
-Meant for another time: The devs said they made this game for during covid, well guess what? It released many years after covid, and also guess what? We can talk in real life now. It felt like they were so intoxicated by their "genius" idea that they thought the lack of covid would make a covid game that addresses covid problems relevant in a time without covid.
-Voice chat is insanely quite and they thought it was "some of the best voice chat systems in the industry" it basically gets very quite five feet away which is not how sound acoustics work in real life.
-Everything is slow: You can "sprint" although you're not getting anywhere, the ski lift and train aren't much better, not too mention you can't jump more then two inches without clipping onto invisible boxes, movement, which is integral to the game is not very good.
-Gigantic for content, huge storage for an indie game, should be like 1 Gig max, I bet the other 2 gigs are map assets, guarantee it.
-Lack of things to do: A social game should have social activities other than puzzles, like seriously give us a mini game or something. Again there is nothing to do after you beat the game.
In conclusion this a writing of frustration at multiple heavily shaky game mechanics, and series of bad development design has led me to write this review. Don't get me wrong it is a good idea. It just has too many problems. I think the amount of hype they stirred up was well played because this game just has easy to overlook problems. I probably will backlash for this but I have to address these issues.
While you can enjoy this game (and based off the 90+% of people who enjoy this game on Steam people like it a lot,) I can't ignore what seems like dev oversight (or maybe undersight?) I enjoy this game as any other person but I am giving this review to show what this game lacks. If you like the positives listed above and don't care for my negatives than give the game a try! Think of this review like a "positive but here are some obvious negatives."

Breaking tradition to leave a review before fully 100%-ing a game, because this will possibly be the only ever instance I am completely sure nothing can change my opinion for the worse.

When you play this game, make a rule for everyone to see the whole puzzle together before going into separate rooms and closing down the soundproof door.

The art direction is in the expressiveness of the deceptively simple gestures, in the silly noot noot nose or the way someone jiggles like rock candy in a jar with every keystroke when they type. The sound design is in your blob hand impatiently thudding the solid glass, in the scream echoing through the valley when someone and their IKEA ball lamp boings down a hill, in the pitter-patter of many little marching feet rustling through the grass to bring you home. The game design is in the way puzzles are scattered like discovering 40 lego sets over a national park, in the way no one holds your hand through the playground but your friends', in the way everyone celebrates simultaneously as the confetti pops and the rubber foam bean flies into someone's face.

The mountain is vast and beautiful, but not too perfect to require a supercomputer, not too wild to be truly lost from the diligently crafted and secretly guiding terrain, and not too grand to ever forget that your friends are right here with you.

When you end this game, make sure everyone is here to experience the whole journey together before, one by one, we go our separate ways and close the chapter in which our lives were once intertwined.

[b][u]cons[/u][/b]
- movement is kinda jank. very common to get stuck on a random rock when climbing uphill
- easy to get separated from your group with no way to catch up. see above
- proximity chat fades out way too quick. if you're a few metres behind your friends, you cant hear anyone anymore. see above
- if you get lost without a radio (especially at night), it's very hard to find your group. see above
- sound balancing needs more fine-grained controls. if you have a friend whose mic is too loud/quiet, you cant adjust it (on neither the speaker's nor receiver's end)
- "right click to drop item" becomes annoying. it's easy to accidentally drop something important. rebinding doesnt fix this, since that adds an additional input method instead of replacing the original
- train and ski lift are too slow
- not enough parkour or movement-based puzzles
- most puzzles only need a handful of players to solve. in a large group, a lot of puzzles feel like you're just watching or reduplicating effort
- a lot of puzzles feel like just another variation of telephone


[b][u]neither[/u][/b]
- cannot play solo
- low difficulty (side note: great for people new to gaming)
- music is okay, but not very memorable
- not much story
- replay value is (probably) low. but so is every puzzle game, so i dont consider this a real con
- a lot of movement mechanics are underutilised (e.g. crouch, throw). it's easy to forget they exist. only a handful of puzzles require it. not really a con, just lost potential
- default mute/push-to-talk is V, which feels really terrible ergonomically. but this is easy to fix with a rebind

It took my group ~19 hours give or take some idling here and there to 100% the BIG WALK. I assure you that this game, with good friends, is genuinely amazing. It's not a "FRIEND GAME" in that sense of buying something for 4 bucks you play for 4 hours twice, but a legitimate experience had over many sessions. Playing with randos would not be fun. I guess if that's how you gotta do it that's how you gotta do it, but I believe you need a game system and dudes to be with.

I never enjoyed a puzzle game more than this. It's really less about the PUZZLES than communicating with your friends how exactly to SOLVE the puzzles. What do you name these shapes, how do you reference these sounds with motions, you know, talking about the WAY you'll solve it together rather than HOW you'll do it. 

And that's the genius part. There was never a moment with my group of four where someone DIDN'T have the best idea on how to go about something or solve a big problem. 

I really could just heap praise on this game forever, I already wish there was more to play. 

In terms of similarity to other games, I can't think of any. There's stuff like Peak but that's not a game you really... play together, it's like a game where you can help or hurt your friends but the way you talk with them and the way you interact is just not the same. It's similar for many, MANY co-op games. You're doing your own thing together. This is a game for friends in every sense of the expression.

In a current sea of "friend-slop games", Big Walk seemed like it could easily be pooled into those types of games.  But this was one of the most surprising releases this year.  I played with just two other people and had some of the most fun I've ever had in a game.  The world is beautifully simple, with the realistic landscapes, forests and beach sides, juxtaposed by the clear bright colored goals that the game wants you to bump into.  Even with these bright landmarks its easy to get lost, and accidentally get separated from your group since your voices don't carry far.  But that was part of the joy was just wandering even if it meant getting lost, and trying to find ways in-game to bring yourselves back together.  These moments in other games would normally feel like its wasting my time, but its part of the charm of the island you're stuck on, and which friends you brought along with you to embrace the tough moments.

The puzzles are brilliantly setup to have you learn and build upon what you've done before.  This means I recommend playing with a group that wants to play this from front to back, because you will get a lot out of it as you reach the late game puzzles.  The biggest thing that sets this game apart is how its all presented.  There is an incredible detail to the sound design, and some moments in this game had me emotionally overwhelmed in ways that are hard to explain without spoiling.

You know that feeling as a kid, where you first get to go outside with your family to a place that isn't the city? Like visiting a farm or your family that lives in a world different than your own? Sure there were woes, like the wifi is pretty bad or the toilets are stinkier, but the exploration? The newness of it all? To have an inkling that the world is so much bigger?

Many adults lose that feeling. The sense of a grand adventure, the drive of simple curiosity. We often find ourselves bogged down by work, by bills and the pessismistic reality. We are reminded everyday that the worst of humanity is currently driving its direction, where our livelihoods and future are being shaped by those who live in the past.

Big Walk is that long forgotten feeling, as a game. When you get lost from your friends, sure it sucks, but, at the same time, you might have discovered something else. Like that little creek, or a new way up the mountains. You can hear the sound of your friend's flare, the light that guides you back to your buddies, but sometimes you feel like ignoring it all because you happen to face a direction where the awe of a setting sun just happens to grab you.

This game is like being able to meet with spirit of a childhood long ago, when everytime was new and the adventures were as small as going to a different part of town or entering the backyard of your friend. When it's over, sometimes, you feel sad, because you know that, after the game, that feeling will be gone. You are back to the hollow world, where kindness is few but needed plenty, where you'll go back to a soulcrushing workplace, where you feel like your life has lost all its meaning.

But, I hope that feeling never goes away. Life gets more beautiful when you reunite with your childhood self. You want to show it more things, more stuff it never got to see. You want it to see the change of the world because you can hear it laugh and ask and enjoy the moments as they are. I can't go back to a time of my youth, nor can I see into a future yet put into place.

What I do know, is after a Big Walk, I feel like, I should enjoy my present, and go on another one. Just this time, away from the computer.

There is something so special about this game. If you choose to play it, I highly suggest you play with people you've known very well for a long time.

It's honestly kind of exciting compared to something like Lethal Company or REPO. It feels kind of alive, especially when playing with multiple friends. The pacing is perfect and the time walking between puzzles can fly by quick when you take in the scenery. The proximity chat is good for what it is even when compared to a something like PEAK. It requires you to stay close with your group to communicate effectively when your hands are full, having to sacrifice storage for long distance communication which is a fun trade off. It's also very reliant on 100% of your group cooperating, leading to hilarious moments you or your friends might cause. 
The puzzles may feel randomly placed and scattered, but that is once again fitting for the game. It is enjoyable to stumble across a puzzle that requires one way of communicating, and then not too far from that you encounter another puzzle that is vastly different. No obvious cohesion between puzzles drives players to wonder what may come next. Even the character customization is something that puzzles the players that first discover it. They seemingly "stumble" upon it and then have to figure out how it works, once again emphasizing that this journey will not be done alone. The simple customization allows players to display themselves without wacky hats and costumes, and that is a necessary type of customization that does not take away from the aesthetic of the game. 
The developers highlight cooperation and dependency, peaceful environments that welcome delightful walks and talks with your friends, and a simple yet engaging game.
I love to say it, but this game makes Content Warning (another friend-slop game that is vastly different) look like a different friend-slop game, with different a environment, different character customization, and different tasks (huh, wow!). Big Walk makes driving 40 miles per hour through the Mojave Desert feel like a boring adventure (because driving that slow for that long would be boring). It puts the "friend" in "friend-slop".

I played this game with my boyfriend of two years now. While we complained in the beginning of having nobody else to play with, by the end, we realized all we really needed was each other. I loved that, with every puzzle we came across, they were still able to be accomplished by just the two of us. It showed us how great our teamwork is, even when we couldn't see or hear each other - or both! 

This game is for the patient, for the calm. It's a game to be slow with, to take your time and take in the sights and sounds of the world around you. Walking and talking is the best way I think that anyone could describe it. The puzzles are wonderfully crafted (screw that last one where we had to take that heavy ball across the WHOLE ISLAND!) and so creative, the landscape is so beautiful and the way the atmosphere feels so different between day and night is fantastic. 

While, yes, most of our conversations were filled with talks about the game, puzzles, and the island itself - as well as talks about the shared custody over the little babies we collected - it also gave us this time during our late nights to just... talk. Be human. Connect. It's a game that shows and tests just how strong your connection to other people can be, and how well (or terribly) you can connect and communicate with those people. 

I understand that there will definitely be a portion of people who won't like or be able to appreciate this game, but I feel like that's primarily because they're accustomed to the quick satisfaction and dopamine that comes with quick, high focus games (ex. CoD, CS, sports games, etc.). A lot of these games are designed to push you in and out of matches as quick as possible, where every decision is life or death (win or loss), and I think that makes it hard for players who only play these games (or primarily play/prefer these games, because I play every game I mentioned and still loved this one) to be able to appreciate the slowness and patience that comes with this one. 

This game will hold a special place in my heart for the rest of my life, I think. I only spent around a day's worth of time actively playing it, but wow. I got really emotional by the ending, and the true ending especially, because it's a reminder of how little time I'm able to allocate to the people around me that matter, and how much more important it is to me to do that. Thank you, Big Walk, for letting us take our time and exist together. And to my boyfriend, thank you for experiencing this with me.

[spoiler]Not being able to hear, Not being able to see, Needing additional people to communication between 2 or more people, etc.[/spoiler]

This game promotes Cooperation, Exploration, and Communication. 
If there's a Object in the distance, Odds are you can walk to it, explore it, and then backtrack to grab your friends who got lost.

The map feels large and as you progress through the game, More areas Open up, Shortcuts/Paths get unlocked.
I never felt like I was lacking content to explore.

If I was forced to choose my least favorite part, it would be that the movement on slopes seems to be a little wacky.
There are Hills that my friends could climb with ease, where my character's legs just stopped working. 
If they made slope movement a little more consistent I would be hard pressed to find an issue with this game.

If you have a pretty consistent friend group, and want to just vibe and have a good time, this is a great game to pick up.

Point of the game is to Cooperate and Socialize with friends.

I do not play many new games a year, but this game is easily my pick for game of the year. This is a game that really emphasizes the intrinsic fun of hanging out with your friends. 

It would be easy to lump this game in the pile of “friendslop” but I think that there are a few qualities that really separate it from a game like Lethal Company or Peak. This is not to say that those games are bad or not fun. It is just that the type of fun to be had with Big Walk feels fundamentally different. Most of the “friendslop” games that I am familiar with tend to use a hub world that you use to then select an area (often procedurally generated) to go visit and complete an objective before heading back to the hub world to do it again. 

Big Walk is not like this. The world of Big Walk is not procedurally generated. It is a very intentionally designed world. There is going to be a lot of walking through that world because there is no hub world or fast travel. The objective is to solve puzzles, but there is no quota/deadline. There is no run to fail whenever things go badly. The game wants to be taken at the player’s pace.

The puzzles in the game are all very well designed. I would not say that they are difficult, but they are incredibly satisfying to solve. The reason why they’re so satisfying is what makes the game so special. You do them with your friends. The entire game wants you to talk and hang out with your friends. The puzzles are all about communicating with them. Everything on the map is so spread out so that you have time to be with your friends. 

I played through this game with a long-time group of friends. The game felt reminiscent of back when we were able to hang out and do stupid shit in person all the time. I love my friend and I love that this game was able to be this much fun with them. This game had us genuinely emotional by the end of it. 

TLDR:
An amazing walk and talk simulator in an open world where you solve puzzles. But more than that, it’s about hanging out with your friends. Play it with the right group of people and it can be a surprisingly emotional experience.

A unique and lovely game about solving puzzles and spending time with your friends in a big, beautiful world. 

Big Walk is the canvas, you and your friends bring the paints. Your experience will only be as good as the people you get to spend your time in it with. Luckily for me, I'm blessed with wonderful friends who are all on the same wavelength. Well, for the most part. 

The puzzles themselves are fun tests for your collective communication and puzzle solving skills. My group found them rewarding to solve together, with a few satisfying "ah-ha!" moments, as every good puzzle game should have. 

You're given just enough tools - whether it be a radio, a flare gun, or even just your character's body - that you still get to rely on your creativity to solve problems together.

The real meat of the game, in my opinion, is the time spent between the puzzles. There's a lot of walking. It's called Big Walk after all. All of that walking gives you plenty of time to talk. Whether it's catching up, shooting the shit, ridiculous banter, or just simply enjoying the scenery, ambience and music. 

Even getting separated from your mates and trying to find them again is greatly enjoyable. 

This is why it really matters who you choose to share this game with, as your experience can only be as good as the company you play it with. 

I think this whole game is the closest I've gotten to replicating the same feelings I get from spending time out and about with friends in real life, especially being in nature, than I've gotten from any other game I've played.

My friends and I played this game over the course of a couple of months, so it served as one of our main methods of hanging out together throughout that time. 

Now that it's over for us (with a personally quite emotional conclusion), I'm glad I got to play this lovely game with the people I did. It'll be an experience I think we'll remember for a long time.

I hope if you're planning on buying this game, you'll have a similar enough experience to the one that we shared.

this concept is already a beautiful idea, but the actual execution is remarkably well done, the game never compromises on its central idea and remains focused throughout the whole experience. the way that the different puzzles, and eventually the endgame, work to push this idea to its extreme is wonderful.

the choice to use no text outside of the tutorial and pause menu, to not show players names, to require multiple people to access your "inventory", to require asking another player to customise your look, to have no fast travel, and so many more of these small "inconvieniences" all work to encourage communication and getting to know one another even outside of the game's puzzles 

(ending spoilers) [spoiler]the final puzzle all but asks you to create a vocabulary for a constructed sign language, and then communicate those signs and their definitions to one another with just your characters' body language. the entire final section to me represents the culmination of the game's central idea. by now, you don't need to speak, you don't need to be able to indentify eachother by looks or voice: when i played, even with the game's simplified characters and our new made up methods of communicating, we could still identify who's who through all the little ideosyncrasies we noticed in our friends. of course i know who the person who ran ahead and sat on the button is, of course i know who's the one who got a little lost, of course i know the person who took charge and started telling people where to stand. Big Walk's final section strips away almost everything from your arsenal of communication, and yet, the little group of friends you've slowly been growing closer to remains unimpeded, with patience, focus, and empathy, one can understand another.[/spoiler]

big walks ending- despite how silly, abstract, and bizzarre the whole experience was- is entirely sincere. even with its weird ungrounded aesthetic, the game is deeply earnest from beginning to end without a hint of irony. when we reached the final section, after debriefing over the game's credits, we came across a sign that, if you've played this game before, you would understand how its mere 7 words of tutorial made us emotional.

Big Walk is one of the most deeply special games i've ever had the priveledge to experience, and you will come out of it closer than ever to the people you played with. it is a game that is in love with its own thesis: communication and connection.

Without a doubt, Big Walk is the most enjoyable cooperative game I have every played. Puzzles are technically easy enough for those with even the most basic 3D videogame experience to accomplish, but require enough thought and care to feel rewarding when you've figured them out. The scenery and ambience are truly a delight and the music rules. The tools provided are intuitive and helpful; who doesn't love using walkie-talkies?!

Admittedly, your "enjoyment" from this game will greatly depend on the folks you play it with. As a 35 year old with four younger brothers, this was a great chance for all 5 of us, in three states and two different countries, to be together in a way that felt like we were goofing around in the backyard as kids or out hiking as a group for the first time without our parents as 20-somethings. The ending of the game - I won't spoil - was way more emotional than I thought it would be, especially as the eldest of the group and the game host. Find one-to-four people you like and spend a couple days plodding about and be better for it.
Unforgettable experience, it's legit one of the best games I've ever played and actually CARED to finish 100%.

Big Walk, at its surface, is a heartfelt, calming puzzle/adventure game you work on with your friends. But at its core, Big Walk is a strong willed story about friends getting closer and believing in yourselves, and each other. The journey and challenges you face together as friends is less of a fun, silly adventure, and more of a thoughtful trek across a non-linear path through each others minds. When most games of this sort would make everyone in the group hate one another, this one will bring you all together.
This is the second game that has brought me to tears.
10/10

This is a great game, and I had a lot of fun playing it with a group of friends. Our group of four felt like the perfect number — it really builds on teamwork, communication, and shared problem‑solving. You can play with two or three people, but I genuinely think four is where the game shines the most. At times it almost feels like a giant escape room, which is honestly one of its strongest points.

For the most part, it’s an amazing experience, easily close to a 10/10.

I only have two real gripes.
First, the “wait” missions ruin the flow and the enjoyment. They don’t add anything, they just stall the fun and break the momentum.

Second, this is a very much a one‑and‑done game. The first playthrough is fantastic, but the replayability drops hard because the puzzles don’t change. It becomes difficult to play again without feeling like you’re spoiling the experience for anyone who hasn’t done it yet. So make sure you’ve got a good group for that first run, because that’s where the game truly shines.

Big Walk uses its puzzles, map, and mechanics to push and pull your group, constantly breaking you apart and bringing you back together in new configurations as you play. Even the surprisingly short range of your voices works toward this. No other game I’ve played has kept my friends so motivated and moving while still giving us so much room to interact and connect with each other.

Playing Big Walk with my friends has been a wonderful experience. We’ve laughed, shared, and bickered with each other for dozens of hours, and so much of that time has felt genuinely precious to me. We’re finally nearing the end, more than 20 hours in, and I already ache at the thought that we won’t have an excuse to hop into a game together for a few hours twice a week anymore.

If I could offer one piece of advice to anyone looking to play Big Walk, it would be this: play with as big a group as you can manage. Four is great, but I’d pull in anyone you can convince to join. One thing I noticed while reading the negative reviews was how often they came from people who had played with only one or two friends. I don’t think that necessarily gives you the full picture of what makes Big Walk work. The game thrives when you get pulled into your own little adventure with a good friend, or even with someone who, up until then, was simply an acquaintance. It’s easy to look at Big Walk as a game that gives you a space to hang out, but what makes it special is how deliberately it creates that space.

I cannot overstate how good this game is. 

What I believed was going to be a relatively short, PEAK-esque experience of playing it once or twice with friends, quickly developed into a compelling, fun way to break the ice, so to speak, with my best friend. 

The game is a lot about walking. The puzzles are far apart one another in the first place, and when you find one, it will often require walking of its own. But it never feels empty, or quiet, even with only two players. Mostly because, I didn't want it to be quiet. I am spending time with my friends and whether it's silly jokes or talks about relationships or life goals or anything like that I would like there to be something in the air other than the little pitter-patter of two sets of feet. And so the game is, too, about talking. My first playthrough was only myself and one other; we didn't get much use out of the walkie-talkies or megaphones (not to say we didn't get any use!) but even still, the game provided a very unique, earnest, natural environment to talk about whatever you want.

There’s a really nice balance to it. One moment you’re genuinely trying to work something out together, the next you’re doing something completely stupid for no reason, and then suddenly the game gives you a quiet little moment where you stop messing around and just take in where you are.

And the ending ties all of it together beautifully.

It made me realize that Big Walk was never really about reaching the end in the first place. The destination matters, but most of what stayed with me were the completely unplanned moments along the way — the laughter, the frustration, the discoveries, the stupid conversations and the shared feeling of experiencing something together.

With the wrong group, it might just be a strange little walking game.

With the right one, it becomes a memory.

And I think that’s kind of beautiful.

Genuinely magical experience in a lot of regards in how it's another big group co-op type game but with a lot of aspects that have a level of handcrafted, curated finesse usually reserved for games that at most are only 1 or 2 players. I feel like we're in a bit of an era of games where a lot of developers have understood that playing most games with friends ends up as a wonderful time, and use this concept to allow for games that in some regard, feel extremely fundamentally flawed due to the co-op experience often offsetting the emotional response to such issues. This isn't to say that the experience gleaned from such titles is necessarily a bad or even lesser one, those feelings are still real, but it's nice to see a game that truly asks you to engross yourself in it while also going out of its way to intentionally curate an experience that relies on the foundational assumption of "you're playing this with friends"

Big Walk is an incredible time for many reasons, but it most thoroughly shines through in the sheer lengths it goes to to make everything feel like this wonderful adventure with your friends, each design decision revolving around this, whether it's the puzzles, tools or even methods of navigation and general map design. Rather than a game focusing on crafting a lot of individual big moments to laugh about and revel in with friends, the more holistic approach of this game leads to it feeling like a real digital shared space, especially when factoring in the different ways you're asked to slow down. Methods of transportation are all very slow and feel quite distinctive from one another in spirit, but this all is in service of this continued striving to make each other connect and also to make you really soak in all the finest details of the world you've been dropped into. Whether it's walking while having to traverse uneven terrain and stop once night falls, the slow, isolated and scenic gondola, or the feeling of waiting with your friends at the nearest train station, the vast majority of the best moments of Big Walk take place in the empty spaces between when you're 'doing things', which becomes an increasingly profound feeling when even most of the tools can be used in silly ways to further pass the time with each other. Probably also helps that you all get to look like the silly drinking bird gadgets while doing all of this, just an inherently pleasing thing to look at.

Walking across a big patch of Australian bushland in game form was also a nice time in itself, so many times where it felt like I myself had once wandered through extraordinarily similar areas in my own life ultimately led to a comforting sense of familiarity in my journey. It also made the stark contrast to the brightly coloured playground-esque structures where the puzzles would always be placed feel all the more striking, having these elements of plasticky artifice standing out in areas that otherwise felt so real. The puzzles themselves are also a lovely bit of fun, usually making use of some form of reduced capability of communication as the crux of the problem, leading to increasingly ingenious methods to express core concepts with what limited tools you're given. Some of my favourite iterative design in this regard is whenever you're given what is functionally an identical puzzle to earlier but with restrictions not to how the puzzle must be solved, but in your forms of conveying information, eventually culminating in everyone being able to understand each other through nothing more than a series of stupid looking arm movements. Turns out all you really needed to do to make one of the best multiplayer games out there was make a simplified The Witness and let you explore that world with friends <3.

I didn't expect legitimate "Walking Simulator: The Game" to become the highlight of my friend group, but here we are.

Video games often confuse "playing together" with simply sharing screen space while chasing objectives. In [i]Big Walk[/i], that convention is completely upended. Instead of handing you weapons, inventories, mini-maps, or crafting systems, it gives you binoculars, radios, and a bunch of bushland with one thing in mind: [i]talk to each other[/i]. What follows is one of the most refreshing, hilarious, and bonding cooperative experiences in recent memory.

[i]Big Walk[/i] transcends the typical "friendslop" genre. It's not about the puzzles, the pretty scenery, or the objectives scattered across the world. Those are just the excuse. What it's actually about, is you and your friends or loved ones scattered through a building or hillside, trying to describe what you're looking at to people who can't see your screen. That's the whole game, and it's absolutely magical.

The best part is nobody has the full picture, splitting information between players. It sounds simple, but it changes how you talk with everyone. You describe, negotiate, gesture (badly), and occasionally just make noises. Watching a group of grown-ass adults develop an entire improvised sign language for "the squiggly thing" was one of my favourite memories this year.

What else really gets me is how naturally the game just turns into genuine hangout time. We were just wandering, pointing things out, and getting distracted. That, to me, is the real achievement with this game. It doesn't simulate friendship, it just gives friendship room to happen organically.

There's also something oddly comforting about how forgiving the game is. There's no fail state, health bar, or punishing you for walking off (which means "mistakes" are pure comedy instead of frustration), and messing up is just as fun as succeeding, so the vibe stays light and cheerful the entire time. It's low-stakes in the best way, which naturally makes people looser, sillier, and way more willing to just talk to each other instead of tunnel-visioning on objectives. 

[i]Big Walk[/i] is an extremely rare multiplayer experience that values actual human presence over engagement metrics, successfully capturing the warmth of a weekend getaway with your friends. It's a masterclass in cooperative game design that understands what truly makes multiplayer games memorable: the people you play with. If who you play with matters more to you than the game itself, [i]Big Walk[/i] is built entirely around the idea, and it nails it.

This game is essential for anyone who loves cooperative adventures, and is easily one of—if not [i]the[/i]—standout achievement of 2026.

Gameplay loop, as experienced by my group:

1. Agree on a plan
2.Walk 4 feet
3. Someone sees a rock
4. Group splits into 4 factions
5. Proximity chat becomes a horror movie of distant screaming
6. Repeat until credits

review:
In the society full of shorts, reels, and low attention span, Big Walk teaches us that it is not all about the destination... but the journey along the way. We played music over a megaphone, thrown people off lifts, and thrown blobs off mountains. 

The puzzles were intricate, fun, and required teamwork and social connection. Particularly when words could not speak for us. Beyond that, this game is slow but all of the time in between puzzles truly make the experience. 

We laughed, we chanted, we screamed, we walked, and we did it. Together.

Big Walk is a game truly special to both me and my small group of friends. One I can't even fully formulate into words. Even when it was shown during a Nintendo Direct in June, I laughed it off and continued with my life. But, when the game first released, its praise was insane. Like a damn 91 on metacritic. "What the hell? What do you even do in this game?" And upon convincing 3 of my friends to buy it with me, I was blown away. The creativeness, the ingenuity, the friends you play with. These factors all made this game truly something memorable. Now, 24 hours later, I've attained every achievement. You never really expect a game like this to make an impact. You expect it to be lighthearted, fun, but breeze through it in 5 hours. This game BLEW that expectation out of the park. Sure, your frames per second may not hit 120, but that doesn't matter as long as you're truly enjoying yourself with people you know and like to spend time with. After 100%ing the game and doing everything there is to do, I'm truly left in a state of awe and contentment. All the puzzles we overcame, all the memories we shared, truly made me appreciate the people around me. Even better, the puzzle design was immaculate, with not a single puzzle feeling bland or stale. As this is my first game by House House, I'm truly blown away and would 100% recommend. You can't put a price tag on the happiness of friendship. Peak Gaming.

So there's this thing that myself and a couple of friends did in Minecraft a long time ago, it was a temporary hardcore server where our only method of communication was through the voice chat mod we had installed, and we weren't allowed to talk about what we had done in-game outside of the game.
It created an atmosphere that I hadn't really ever felt in any multiplayer game before, the obvious intent of the idea was that it would create a sense of dread and loneliness that comes with wondering whether or not your friends were still alive, and that certainly was present, but it also had an especially unique effect of enhancing those moments where you were around others and sharing your tales, that emphatic joy upon seeing a nametag you hadnt read in hours, maybe even a group of players you hadnt seen yet. It gave this liveliness to simply just seeing other players and interacting with them that has stuck in my head ever since we played. I would've figured it'd take years before there was a game that could synthesize and capture that experience with all of its heart and intent. But upon seeing the initial trailers and marketing for Big Walk, a quiet enthusiasm was building in me.

Given the trends in online co-op multiplayer games recently, it was hard to think a game like this was going to try and be anything beyond being just funny, which I'm not opposed to! But I hope the previous paragraph illustrated what kind of feeling I was really hoping this game would try and capture. And it seems silly of me to have worried about that now, because Big Walk is multiplayer co-op excellence, it is in love with the intricacies of in-game communication, expressed in ways that are playful and complex at the same time.

There is a delicate care given to how this game sounds in particular, obviously the voice chat sounds beautifully grounded in the environment of the game world, but the ant-like characters (Or "walklets", as I've seen them called) have a certain plasticity in how they look and feel that in contrast with the realistic environment, has a really soft and playful energy, it's able to elicit that warmth and joy that I felt in the first paragraph almost inherently.

And of course what I love so much is how intentionally all of this was done, its a game who's core experience is tied to the act of splitting up and reconvening to share your stories with eachother, and it knows this. [spoiler]It all cumulates in the finale where it manages to create this experience without spatially separating any of the players. It had me actively in awe when I realised what the game was doing.[/spoiler] This is one of the most beautiful multiplayer games I've ever experienced and I hope it's seen as a classic in the years to pass.

This is genuinely one of the best games I’ve ever played.

It’s an incredible game to play with friends because it actually gives you time to just be with them. You talk about random things along the way, solve problems together, and simply keep walking forward as a group.

At first, I thought a game like this would probably have a lot of boring moments. But once I actually played it, those moments didn’t feel boring at all. Instead, the game felt incredibly chill and relaxing. Even one of my friends, who usually gets restless pretty easily, was completely fine with the slower pace.

The level design is also extremely well done. It makes great use of the player's common sense and natural curiosity. Even though the game rarely tells you exactly where to go or what to do, you can usually observe your surroundings, understand what the game is trying to communicate, and figure out how to move forward naturally.

The controls are simple and easy to understand, but the mechanics can still be used in surprisingly effective ways when solving problems. It never feels unnecessarily complicated, but at the same time, it doesn't feel shallow either.

Visually, the game might not be the most technically impressive or flashy thing out there, but its atmosphere is incredibly charming. The peaceful environments and the relaxed feeling of simply walking through each area somehow made conversations with my friends feel more open and personal.

Maybe I'm just imagining that part, though.

One thing I especially want to praise is the sound design.

Sound is extremely important in this game, and they absolutely nailed it. The ambient sounds of each environment, the way distance affects how you hear other players, and how sound itself becomes part of the gameplay all work really well together.

But my favorite part is probably the soundtrack.

I've loved the music in this game since I first heard it in the trailer, long before the game was even released.

The UI is also excellent. It gives you exactly what you need without covering the screen with unnecessary information. It's clean, easy to understand, and fits the overall theme of the game perfectly.

Big Walk may not be a game with spectacular graphics or gameplay constantly trying to pump you full of dopamine every few seconds.

But to me, it's still an incredible game.

It's the kind of game where you can invite a few friends, walk around together, talk about things that happened in the past, talk about what's going on in your lives right now, solve little problems along the way, and help each other overcome whatever obstacles you run into.

This game doesn't ask you to constantly run toward the next objective.

It doesn't ask you to fight through life-or-death situations or overcome some massive challenge every five minutes.

It simply gives you a place to walk with someone.

Someone willing to share their stories and experiences with you.

And someone willing to keep walking beside you.

[b] Big Walk [/b]  — 10/10

My only small disappointment is that you can't play it alone.

Sometimes I honestly wish I could just enter the game by myself, wander around, solve a few small puzzles, and simply take in the atmosphere.

But then again...

If that were the case, I guess it wouldn't really be a [b] Big Walk [/b] with friends in the first place.

Big Walk already has enough buzz and praise that I don't really even need to tell you that it's fantastic. It was already eye catching on reveal three years ago, announced near the advent of the term "friendslop", delayed to 2026 during the proliferation and usage of such classification, now having arrived as some sort of bright colored knife to cut through the fog. Furthermore, so much of its charm is easily visible on first glance that it requires little words to describe what it's about and even fewer words to describe how good it is.

You solve puzzles on an island with friends. It's fantastic. 

However, as simply does Big Walk present itself, its in equal brilliance that it's magic almost only works through that simplicity. Before solving puzzles, Big Walk is about communication. The puzzles are simply the obstacles in which communication is directly stretched and strained. I say this as while I found no one puzzle particularly hard, it's a difficulty that is scaled based on your own ability to communicate with the people you are playing with. Your ability to transcribe, use tools, your ability to understand and interpret. I’d say less than half of Big Walk is puzzles, the majority of the time you're either walking and talking on a stroll to the next objective, trying to get a hold of someone to find out, or simply hanging out! 

Big Walk asks,

"How do you personally interpret this symbol, this drawing?"

"How would you describe it to someone who can't see it?"

"Without words, how would you do it?"

And what I mean by simplicity rears its head here. As Big Walk prods your brain about how you perceive and express, the other people people around you pick up on that, they in a sense understand you better. Picking up on ticks, movements, tendencies of the people around you, attributing it to them, all of which is amplified by the limited tools of communication provided. Becoming in sync in such a way does Big Walk not only bring you together for a shared activity, but also bring you together in a sense of understanding.

And it's all in this giant freeform sandbox of what I assume is a loving and endearing ecological recreation of the developer's home country of Australia, sonically backed by an incredibly tender and human soundtrack.

Big Walk doesn't require so many words to illustrate it's brilliance, but there's such a deep understanding and brilliant exercise in, as cheesy as it might sound, what makes us human. We like to walk, we like to talk, we like to work together.

Big Walk is as human as walking. Big Walk is as human as doing a funny little dance. Big Walk is as human as getting lost. Big Walk is as human as getting found. Big Walk is art like Pacman is art. Big Walk isn't about asking the smartest person in the room to solve a puzzle, it's about getting a group of people to work together to achieve a common goal. And I think that’s very human.

Big Walk is a shockingly simple concept for a game, but it does it really well. It's essentially just a co-op puzzle adventure game with proximity chat. While it may be given the title of being a "friendslop", its the most pure in this concept as it focuses on the game being a playspace to coexist and talk but still have a united endgoal so it doesn't feel aimless, as in theres an incentive to play it from start to finish. This is a big selling point to consider since many friendslop games usually go for a more endless gameplay loop.. that you play until your group gradually one by one gets tired of and drop off.

While it may sound like the game doesn't "try" then to be entertaining like Lethal Company or Repo, it has a handcrafted map with cleverly puzzles that are very akin to escape rooms, and the games simple movement system allowing things like tripping and dropping what you're holding, getting seperated from your team and need to somehow figure out how to show everyone where you went, does still create unique and memorable moments.

Many puzzles play on putting spins on how you communicate. Maybe you can only talk and need to describe what you're looking at, maybe you can no longer talk and you need to gesture to describe what you're looking at.. maybe you need to gesture to describe a sound you're hearing... you'll have to be on the same wavelength as your friends, or be willing to laugh at the fact that maybe you and your friendgroup isn't good at talking about simple things
