[h2] Friendship Is a Truly Chaotic and Beautiful Thing [/h2]

When I saw the first trailer, it looked like another “friendslop” project with some interesting puzzles. But for some reason, my heart was beating differently. Maybe it was because there were already too many typical 4+ player co-op games around me. But this one felt… pure. And I was more right about Big Walk than I expected.

This game is not slop. It is an incredible gem because of how well its ideas work together.

A short description would be simple: a co-op puzzle adventure with proximity chat. For some people, that alone is already a red flag, but here it actually serves a purpose. Almost every puzzle requires some form of verbal or non-verbal communication with your friends, so using Discord would ruin a big part of the experience.

Another important part is splitting your group into smaller teams. This creates moments where you unexpectedly find each other again or try to contact friends somewhere on the other side of the world. The game gives you tools like portable walkie-talkies and towers with radio sets. I even have a story about this.
I got separated from one friend while the other two were doing puzzles somewhere else. It was night, and I felt genuinely lost and lonely.
Then I found a huge blue tower and thought I could contact someone from there. I climbed to the top and called through the radio.
No answer.
Maybe the other group was busy? I started flashing the tower light and speaking into the radio. Then suddenly, I heard my lost teammate. He had found a walkie-talkie because he heard my voice coming from one lying somewhere in the woods.
I guided him toward the tower. Then someone flashed a light back at me, not from the tower, but from the forest. That was our second group. I kept flashing the tower light and pointing a laser toward them. In the end, all of us met at the blue tower and spent time there during the night, sharing what had happened to each of us during the previous two hours.
That was the first moment when being separated made the adventure much more personal. It felt less like we had simply regrouped and more like four people had returned from their own small adventures.
The game lets you fail at “staying together”, but it never turns that into a “mission failed” moment. Instead, a new invisible objective appears naturally: find your friends again.

One of my favourite parts is how you start naming things in your own way. The game only explains basic actions. Everything else becomes your own interpretation.
We called the puzzle keys “pears”. I later saw groups calling them “dolls”, “babies”, “thingies”, “eggs”, and many other things.

The same happens with puzzle symbols. Three circles might become “three balls” or a “snowman”. A diagonal line with a circle became “Sisyphus” for us because one friend called it that once, and somehow everyone accepted it. The same thing happens with communication itself.
Sometimes we used crouching: two crouches meant the second button. Sometimes we imitated sounds. Sometimes we used a simple Morse-like system: one blink for yes, two for no.

As we progressed, we became better and better at understanding how each other thinks. During the first puzzles, we had to reset them, explain who saw what and figure out everyone’s role.

Later, we could enter a puzzle and almost immediately understand who had the information, who needed it and who had to act.
The downside is that our communication became almost too efficient. After several hours, we understood the structure of most puzzles very quickly. The setup kept changing, but the basic formula often stayed the same.

Because of that, we slowly stopped reinventing the way we worked together. We were mostly using a language we had already created.
The final made me realise this most clearly because it suddenly takes that comfort away. Verbal communication becomes unreliable, the usual roles disappear, and it becomes unclear who should guide, interpret or act. For a moment, we felt inexperienced again.
That is what makes the finale one of the best experiences I’ve had in gaming. It doesn’t simply make the puzzles harder; it challenges the communication habits we spent the whole game building. I only wish the main game did that more often.

Another important point is that you simply cannot progress completely alone.
Some puzzles require one player to press a button so another can reach the reward. If you are already holding an important item, someone else may need to carry the “pear”.

My favourite example is the pouch and backpack system. They hold one item, but you cannot equip or remove them by yourself. Another player has to help you.
These mechanics make cooperation physically part of the game instead of something you do only because playing with friends is fun.

I also want to praise the sound design and music.
Almost every interaction has its own sound: tapping on glass, jumping on different surfaces, using vehicles or completing puzzles. The soundtrack impressed me the first time I heard it and continued to do so throughout the playthrough.
While travelling, we listened to songs through the in-game iPod, with tracks you actually find while exploring. Because of that, some songs almost feel earned.

Some of my favourite moments were not even connected to puzzles.
Sometimes we just sat together with music in the background, looked at the stars or sunset and talked about what had happened to us, what was new in our lives or just random things.
We were not trying to progress as quickly as possible. We were simply enjoying the moment.

Big Walk never rushes you to finish it. It gives you puzzles, situations that make you depend on your friends, and then enough space to relax and simply exist together.
Maybe the best proof of how well Big Walk worked for us is that it made almost my entire friend group interested in the same adventure.

Even when someone could not join, we continued as three or four people because nobody wanted to stop playing. But when we reached the end, we all agreed to wait for the last person before finishing the game together.
Instead, we spent that time completing optional puzzles and exploring hidden places.

The game never forced us to do that. We simply felt that after everything we had experienced together, finishing the journey without everyone there would have felt wrong.


These are my “whys”.
Big Walk is the best co-op game I have ever played with my friends.
If you are looking for a new experience to share with people close to you, especially if you do not always have time to spend an evening just talking with them, this is one of the best games you could choose.

If I had to describe this game in one word, it would be *charming*. The character models and the cartoonish looking structures scattered around a fairly realistic looking island seem a bit out of place at first, but it works for the game, both aesthetically and functionally, as it is easier to make out the colourful models on the fairly subdued background.

But all that is secondary - this game is all about wandering around with your friends, getting lost, getting found, solving puzzles, arguing about the solutions, having these quiet moments interrupted by some idiot constantly holding the train's siren button, throwing items at one another, figuring out the layout and debating the game plan. Rather than being a great game, Big Walk's design funnels you towards making it a great game in a way that no game I know does - and that's what makes it great. Most puzzles we solved had us asking whether this was what the devs intended.

I have no intention on writing a full analysis, this game is only as great as your friends are, and my experience was fantastic - I LOVE MY FRIENDS.

Big Walk is many things. It is a puzzle game that forces you and your friends to figure out ways to communicate under heavy restrictions. It is a fun space to occupy with your friends, goofing around and chilling. It is a game about splitting up and coming back together. It is a game about being isolated sometimes, and pushed together other times. It's a game about trust. It's a game about patience, and possibly frustration, and being alone, although not necessarily about being lonely. It's a game about being raucous, and about being contemplative. It's a game about completing goals, but also a game about stopping to watching the sun rise, or sitting in a puddle to splash the water with your hands. It's a game about not always being a part of the conversation, and knowing that's okay. It's a game about isolation and intimacy.

I have played in a tight-knit group of 3, as well as a far-flung group of 8, and I think both have their strengths. If you like chaos and the joy of repeatedly scattering and reconvening, I think 8 is the perfect group size. If you prefer a quieter, simpler experience, 3 or 4 is a lovely time. None of the puzzles are hard conceptually; it's all about you and the people you're communicating with. 

Something to note is that, whenever you start a new session or resume an old one, you're given a choice of "player count," either 2, 3 or 4+. This is not a player limit, but a cap on how many people it might take to complete any particular puzzle. Depending on your group size and dynamics, it may be worthwhile to set this value to "3" even if you have 5 people playing.

I will recommend it but not for full price, let me explain why.
It is overrated and respectfully do not agree with the philosophy this game tries to thrust on to you, but it's fun when you are playing with people you enjoy eating time away with. 
Most of these puzzles are not intellectually challenging whatsoever, but communication and having a notion of how your friend(s) articulate themselves is imperative to completing many of the puzzles. 

There even some puzzles, that are not puzzles at all- and more akin to a way to stretch out the game's length- which I see as wasted potential to add actual puzzles or something more interesting. You can not convince me that being forced into a small room under a timer or having to pass down a heavy ball across the map is fun or interesting over just being unnecessary and a lame attempt on encouraging people to interact more with each other than they already do on Discord or on any other co-op/friendslop game. 

Another grievance is that despite walking being a big part of this game, your in-game model weirdly 'snags' with much of the terrain of the world which is immensely frustrating at times when you absolutely have to walk through rocky areas. I love the designs of the guys but I do admit they feel very out of place with the realism of the island they reside in and makes me contemplate on the story behind designing them.

It would be nice if they expanded the game as it is not that long or allowed a mod workshop at least for puzzles as a way give the game a true quality of life once you've completed the game. In most scenarios, you do not really interact with objects beyond as a means to solve puzzles, illuminate areas, and ultimately proceed with the next section of the world. So with that being said, what is the incentive for me as the player to keep this game installed if once I fully completed it, will having nothing else to do minus walk around and witness a sunset or sunrise? Not sure. You can do the same thing in something like VRCHAT.

Maybe I do not have a whimsy or the emotional sensitivity to grasp the point of this replaying this game once you have completed it, but I'm just genuinely wondering if as a consumer, was this TRULY worth 20 dollars for what it offers compared to other friendslop games such as Peak, REPO or Lethal Company....? The aforementioned games are all cheaper and frankly- have way more to offer in terms of dynamic gameplay and encourages more proactive engagement amongst friends than this.

Take that for what you will.

There are 2 types of puzzles, Red Gourds and Purple Gourds. the red are the normal puzzles. but on the mountain range to the south there are harder versions of certain puzzles which give you the Purple Gourd. [spoiler] I say gourd because there are actual keys [/spoiler] most puzzles are match symbol types, but there are sound puzzles, mime puzzles and 2 dreaded ones IYKYK. this leads me into the small issues i had.

You can get stuck pretty easy on rocks and sticks which in the night but even in the day get you lost from your party quick. Night time is DARK. it's so hard to see without a light source so navigating without is very difficult. A few puzzles made you hunt for a hidden location but were fairly close, the worst one was a sound one where it wasn't easily understood where to go. Other than that the puzzles weren't unfair. But the biggest annoyance was the lack of audio controls. trying to fine tune them was difficult and making people louder just wasn't working. 

Other than that, play with friends you work well with and can laugh off stressful moments. The ending was so bittersweet in a good way really making you feel like you were saying goodbye. A fantastic game.

Big Walk is beautifully made and has some of the most satisfying sound design i've come across in recent games. It's definitely worth the experience if you plan to play with a group of 4+ people, as I've done until the first ending. 

Unfortunately a lot of the general gameplay experience doesn't feel as polished as it should be, especially considering the price of €18,99. 

For 2-3 players, it takes a long time to get certain puzzles done, especially if you intend to 100% the game. Puzzles become repetitive after a while. Travel around the island is excruciatingly slow - which is alright for the first 10 hours of gameplay but becomes incredibly tedious once you've completed the 4 towers and are only really missing 5-8 bulbs (some of which have objectives located on opposite ends of the map). 

There's certain issues with moving up mountains or from rock to rock. Sometimes your character will get stuck in a seemingly flat space and lock you in place for several seconds before you're allowed to attempt another jump. The physics on the train carts are inconsistent. The proximity reach is small and would benefit from volume-distance-balance, the utter lack of visibility at night makes certain terrain unplayable for 10 minutes at a time. Your character cannot access the items slotted in their belt or backpack, which sometimes makes long-distance puzzles in 2-3 player lobbies extra annoying to complete. 

Most of these things could be fixed easily by adding better night vision balance, a dynamic proximity bubble, fixing certain movement issues and possibly extending daytime and shortening night time by a few minutes each. The train could allow for accellerating when all in-lobby players are on the same wagons or add fast-travel after the first ending altogether, so that people will have an incentive to 100% the game, as it otherwise has little replay value. 

Probably an enjoyable game if your friendgroup consists of 4 or more people that will always be available to play, but expect to run into some frustrations during the second half of your run and preferably wait to get it on discount.

Big Walk is a wonderful little game, and it provides one of the most enjoyable experiences I've had in a while.

In the midst of games that can feel too large and too full of too much to do, Big Walk is truly a breath of fresh air. It offers a variety of many puzzles and challenges, but it does so in the perfect way - nothing feels dreadful or unenjoyable. In fact, Big Walk has a way of slowing players down the perfect amount. A slow (yet helpful to traverse the world) ride on the chairlift or train forces players to pause and enjoy the view while chatting with the friend beside you. I can't recall a single moment that I wasn't in awe of the game's beauty and scenery. And when you arrive at your destination, you can hop right off and jump back into exploration and puzzles. The balance of taking things slow and working through tasks is perfect, and it really allows players to appreciate the game, and their time with friends, to its fullest.

The puzzles and communication are really well-done. They offer lots of room for creativity and collaboration, and plenty of room for fun. The mechanics introduce exciting new ways to communicate, and the gradual introduction of new items and mechanics rewards players just enough to help them out, but still leave them with a challenge. Whenever a new puzzle came up, I was excited to jump in and work through it - each one felt just challenging enough, as well as extremely fun. And the rule of no outside communication is a good one - the limited and strategic communication in Big Walk makes the game all the more fun.

Everyone's saying it, but it's true: Big Walk is the opposite of friendslop; it's a shiny friendgem. Rounding up friends for the game is necessary, and so rewarding. The game revolves around communication of different forms, and downtime creates chances for chatting and goofing around to take center stage. From solving puzzles to enjoying the view together, Big Walk was made with friendship in mind. In my playthrough, it even fostered new friendships. A group of busy people across 4 timezones literally marked their calendars each week for Big Walk, and we loved every second. What started as roping in a few extra people to join the game turned into new friendships that are extending into other games and beyond.

In short, Big Walk is beautiful - for its scenery and its ability to bring people together. I eagerly awaited this game since its announcement, and every second of waiting was worth it. Big Walk is a beautiful gem in a sea of games, and absolutely worth your time.

One of the most singularly focused games I've ever played, and an actual delight to play with friends.  The game is about cooperation and spending time with each other, and almost every aspect of it comes back to those two core identities.  Want to carry more than one item? Better have a friend put a backpack on you.  Want to access what's on your backpack? Need a friend for that too.  

Nothing can be accomplished alone.  There are so many puzzles and each one has a unique way of getting you to work together.  Modern generation games tend to hit you with stimulus after stimulus to keep you engaged, but despite having moments of "Well, we gotta sit around for a bit.", I never felt that it was disrespecting my time.  It always felt completely intentional, a break from solving puzzles just to talk to your friends while you watched the sun set.

There are many ways to communicate with each other, but all of them have their own limitations. Walkie Talkies, but there's only two of them, so you have to be in pairs.  A flare gun to signal a specific timing.  A megaphone to talk to others from far away (but they cannot talk back to you).  The game often deafens you for puzzles so that you have to gesture to one another to convey an idea.  

Each time we discovered a new location we were all excited to find out what our new task was, and often times felt incredible once we came up with a solution.

Overall, one of the best multiplayer games I've ever played.  If you have between one and three friends, even if they don't play games, this is a slam dunk and an easy purchase.

Legitimately one of the most introspective and emotional games created, truly something special, no other way to describe it.

review:
[h2]Review[/h2]

Orientate your way through 45 unique puzzles, each testing different and often obtuse forms of communication: VoIP, radios, walkie-talkies, laser pointers, flare guns, gestures, lights, symbols, shapes, sound, music, and more. Get lost, sabotage each other, and try to conquer the game’s various puzzles while creating memorable moments along the way.

While [i]Big Walk[/i] has plenty of content, the sense of accomplishment is a distraction from its true goal: creating memories. The games various systems and puzzles push for cooperation and communication which breeds socialization. Choose your companions wisely, because once you’ve finished the game, you’ll never be able to recapture the same experience twice.

[i]Big Walk[/i] gives you all the tools you need to have fun with friends, but it works best with people who are happy to simply spend time together, regardless of whether you’re actually making progress. Some of my most memorable experiences came when we weren’t progressing at all: pressing a button to extend a puzzle’s timer, getting lost or separated and using the game’s various tools to find each other, putting a mask on a friend that obscures their vision and watching them run off and get lost, finding an item a friend kicked down a mountain, Mission Impossible jumping on and off trains, or trying to fit too many people onto a ski lift and watching one fall off.

I truly believe that if you pull through to see the true ending you’ll leave this game reminiscent of time spent together and melancholic as it comes to an end, but I know a lot of friends groups will end this one early wondering what the point was.

[h2]Addressing Criticism[/h2]

House House (developers) took a gamble on true connection and it’s telling that most negatives reviews have very little time played and most streamers couldn’t enjoy this one.

Only 1/5th of groups finished the base game, and only 6.5% got true ending, so most people complaining about price didn’t finish the experience in its entirety. I personally value games not based on hours, but instead overall experience, and I think this one is worth full price hands down. I got 21.6 hours having fun and not rushing, but you could easily do it in 15 hours if you’re not sabotaging or mucking around. 

I genuinely think anyone who didn’t enjoy this game missed the forest for the trees.

The games limitations of night being too dark, VoIP being too close, having limited carry slots or ways to communicate across distance… These ‘limitations’ or ‘points of annoyance’ is what create memorable moments. Getting lost and trying to reunite. Dedicated roles based on who’s holding what items. Sticking together and helping everyone get to the next objective. These things would hold very little weight if it was easy to traverse and communicate. It’s unthinkable for me to see the games enforced limitations that breed the necessary environment for cooperation and socialization be seen as a negative.

Others talking about how the puzzles are easy to figure out but hard to accomplish due to the games restrictions… Like yeah, that’s the point. Trying to say the puzzles should be hard to figure out and easy to solve once you have figured it out is missing the point. The game at a fundamental level is about cooperation and communication, while the puzzles limit how you can cooperate and communicate in order to create challenge and memorable solutions. Like one puzzle could have entirely different solutions based on the people involved and the ideas they come up with. One puzzle could need a laser pointer, but without it you still have gestures… But what gestures do you use? That might be entirely different based on your specific group. Or using the lights to communicate, how many blinks yes or no? What do you describe the room as? The individual shapes as? That’s going to be unique to every group. Some might communicate long distance using telescopes and gestures, walkie-talkies or radio, laser pointers or flares, the sound of the flare or the direction of where it’s going. There are many times where nothing was communicated beforehand, but the journey defined how we thought about things, and that allowed us to solve puzzles regardless of preplanning.

Then there’s people saying ‘why buy this game if the point is about entertaining yourselves and having fun with friends? You can do that in any game or in Discord!’… This is quite frankly the biggest misunderstanding. You could have fun with friends in many ways, but this is just one specific way to do it. I personally value unique experiences with friends, and I’m sure many people do which is why they buy the newest friends slop that comes out instead of just replaying the same games over and over. What [i]Big Walk[/i] does differently makes it stand out among other games, a quality experience that doesn’t quite fit the same mold as rogue-like co-op friends slop games that frequently get pumped out. It really feels like House House put a lot of love and thought into this experience, and if you’re asking ‘what’s the point? I could just go play another game!’ then what about this game in particular makes it less valued than choosing another experience?

To lead off of that: complaints that the game itself isn’t fun and that it’s your friends that are, and the game adds nothing to that experience. This I find disingenuous and you usually see it coming from people with an hour in the game. They’ll complain about hours of walking, but they themselves haven’t done the hours of walking. They’ll complain about systems they’ve barely had time to get used to or interact with, or puzzles they have yet to see. ‘Lack of direction’ in a game where every puzzle has a purpose. For those who might have this opinion that have seen and interacted with the games systems, it feels like they are lying. You played a game whose entire identity was built around ‘how can we make communication and cooperation the forced mode of operation’, and you cannot understand how the game is positively impacting or creating socialization between friends? Most puzzles require the entire group – the game is actively pushing you guys together to have fun… If you’re getting lost or your friends are leaving you behind or actively not including you or giving you a role, you have bad friends – that’s not the games fault. The game does everything in its power to make sure that doesn’t happen and disincentivizes uncooperative play, so if you cannot figure out how the game adds to or benefits socializing with your friends…

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]

[i]Big Walk[/i] is one of the best social experiences I’ve had in gaming. Its only downside is the attention span of those unable to just sit down and enjoy a game with friends. The best puzzle in the entire game was a 5 minute timer, and if you don’t get that, you’re probably a very boring person.

Probably hard to say anything that hasn't already been said about this game, but... it's a one-of-a-kind experience, to be certain. It's not your ordinary friendslop - it consists entirely of hand-crafted communication puzzles in a hand-crafted map. Cooperating with your friends in developing protocols, brainstorming the solutions and executing them together is like no other game on the market.

Beyond the core gameplay loop, though, is an incredible level of attention to detail and a profoundly welcoming and contemplative atmosphere. The game world is mysterious, beautiful, and has many secrets. The sound design is minimalistic yet maximalistic - every little physics interaction has foley, from stepping on sand to a polo ball rolling into a rock to the sound of your arm stretching out like rubber. Yet, it makes sure not to take too much space - leaving you and your friends plenty of 'negative space' to fill in with conversation of any sort you choose.

The way you exist in this space is so organic. Every little way you can interact with the world feels natural, physical. And that, of course, extends to all the different ways you can communicate with your friends... or fail to. Getting lost is part of the experience, but so is getting found again. And the tools you find encourage forms of cooperation and communication that are... I wouldn't say "realistic", so much as they "feel real". Tactile. Concrete. Saying "over" when you stop transmitting on a radio. Popping a flare to signify something you determined beforehand. Leading your friends back home or to a puzzle via a laser pointer from a vantage point. Communication, verbal and nonverbal. It makes you feel like you're really occupying that space.

The most magical thing about Big Walk is how it feels like... a world of its own, where you and your friends almost seem to be together, physically. Enjoying every moment for what it is. Deciding what to do together... soaking in what's all around you. It ALMOST matches up to the feeling of hanging out in person... which is something video games seldom accomplish.

This game is worth playing all the way through. I encourage everyone to play through its ending, which is magical beyond description and worth going into blind. I rate this game a solid 9/10, and would recommend it to just about anybody, and it's a solid contender for game of the year, in my opinion.

Super sick surreal open world coop puzzle game. 

The puzzles are mostly chill and are designed to require cooperation with your friends, but they also scale the puzzles to your group size, which is cool as fuck. 

The crown jewel of this game, though, is its incredible sound design (with one caveat). Audio is generally the most neglected and underrated aspects of games. The sound design in Big Walk, though, elevates the shit out of the game. 

The caveat, though, is in the proximity-based voice chat. The game is designed around having a very limited hearing radius. Limiting your ability to communicate with your friends is critical to the game. This is great. What I don't understand, though, is why the game is so absurdly quiet. They've already patched the game once to boost maximum voice volumes without extending the voice drop off radius, but this made the voices in the game go from being unplayably quiet to barely playably quiet. I have to crank up my system volume to ear blast levels to comfortably hear someone speaking right next to me. God forbid I get a message from someone in another program while I'm playing, my poor ears will just be fucked.

Aside from that, incredible game, extremely fun with friends.

A truly wonderful experience from beginning to end.

Large Hike is, from its beginning moments to its final ones, a game about you and your friends. The environment is a canvas where you make your own story, where you explore, discover, see beautiful things, but more than anything else, it's about sharing those moments. It's about poking around, talking to each other, and finding a colourful building in the woods. Exploring it, examining its insides, theorizing about what it means. Figuring out what the puzzle wants from you, figuring out how to communicate that to each other, and the moment of triumph when the circle flashes green and the confetti drops.

There's no story, no lore, save the friendship you bring to it. My only criticism is that I wish there was more of it, more time with these silly little characters in funny puzzles. As I said, Large Hike is a canvas, and in the end, it's painted with the colours you brought into it, much like the characters you control.

The entire final puzzle run had me grinning from ear to ear. It's one of those rare games that I think should be an absolute must-play for any human being, and the closest thing I can compare it to is Outer Wilds.

Much like Outer Wilds, Big Walk is all about the joyful experience of discovery, but rather than learning about the universe around you, it's about discovering the bonds between you and your friends by inventing new ways to communicate with each other. 

It's a genuine work of art, and I cannot stop smiling at all the memories I made with my weird little gooseball buddies in pursuit of those beautiful gourds.

A genuinely fun coop experience!

In a landscape full of meh friendslops that I can't stand anymore, Big Walk is such a refreshing surprise.
This game is genuinely chill, funny, creative, and incredibly well thought out. I'm usually not a puzzle person and yet I just really enjoyed it!

The puzzles constantly find different ways to make you communicate and cooperate with your friends. Sometimes you're the one solving the puzzle, sometimes you're trying to figure out what the hell your friend is trying to tell you through chaotic signs, and somehow both are equally fun.

The whole game has such a great aesthetic, very simple but beautiful environments, relaxing music, and really nice ambient sounds that make wandering around feel satisfying, especially when you're on a BIIIIIIG walk trying to find your way around the mountain!

It's a really nice game to hop on after a long day to solve a couple of puzzles. There’s no pressure, no need to optimise everything and no constant feeling that you should be progressing. You can explore, mess around, solve puzzles, get distracted, and chit chat with your friends.

TLDR: I went in being very sceptical and expecting an average quickly kinda boring little coop game and came out thinking “yeah, we need more games like this one.” Genuinely had such a good time. Absolutely recommend.

review: Great Walk

This.. was an truly experience unlike any other. 

The store page and all of these reviews, cannot express the indescribable feeling this experience gives, many come close, but none can quite reach the feeling of playing it youself. It may quite well also be a feeling that can only happen once, it's essence, cant be repeated. This game may not match your tastes in game, it likely wont change your tastes in games either, but it is one that can resonate with you, no matter what you usually play. 

This game is more than the talking, more than the walking, more than the puzzles, and more than the joy as you go through it all. But is it the combination of all of these? Is it the journey? Is it the friends we made along the way? Some may say it is, and they're not wrong either. But for me, its about the people, the ones you go on this big walk with, and a big walk it is.

Although this game seems like you need a big group for it and can certainly be experienced well with one, the truth of the game may only be able to be discovered as a duo, like what another review said, "its easy to lose sight of what matters in crowd, but when its just the two of you - Big Walk turned out to be not about puzzles, but about an amazing psychological experience". 

Although it is quite different to any of my other favorite games, the experience alone, has quickly spearheaded its way to first on the podium. Even if it in the future, some other game usurps its place; this experience shall forever remain, etched into my soul. 

Once your journey is over. At the end of it all, you'll take a lean back, maybe look away from your screen, and think to yourself: That.. was a good walk.

Big Walk is a game that will surprise you with big feelings. Playing this with a dedicated group of friends will stimulate your communication chops and sense of adventure and mystery. I think the most interesting thing about it is the complete lack of violence or hostility. A lesser game would feel the need to fill the map with dangerous critters or scary monsters. Big Walk is capable of providing moments of genuine unnerve without resorting to the fear of "losing a life", all with its immense scale and the sense of discovery as you traverse a world that keeps getting bigger.

But more than any of that, it rewards collaboration in a way that other cooperative indie games just don't. There is no incentive, big or small, to independence. Every game design element is deliberate and laser focused in its mission to encourage outside-of-the-box cooperation and communication. Not to mention every puzzle nails or comes damn close to nailing the perfect balance between challenging and rewarding. It is a game that invites sincere engagement and rewards you with both a great game and an experience you will remember fondly with your friends.

Big Walk is an incredible game that plumbs the depths of human communication. The puzzles primarily facilitate this, often requiring you and your knucklehead friends to figure out ways to encode information in unique and novel ways. This is sometimes easy, sometimes frustrating in an utterly enjoyable way as you wonder just how what you communicated wasn't clear. It's really fun.

Between puzzles, you and your friends will chitchat, schmooze, shoot the breeze. You'll talk about nothing and everything. After all, what else is there to do but talk?

Beyond this, I think Big Walk beautifully explores time. The game is in no rush, and it expects you to be on the same page. The map is large and relatively difficult to traverse. You will get your Big Walk. Even with the transportation methods you unlock as you progress through the game, it takes minutes to cross the island. This can be sort of frustrating at first coming from a place where instant gratification is the norm, but over time you learn to slow down. And it's really nice to allow the minutes to tick by. The landscapes are enjoyable to look at, the ambient sounds are calming, and you always have a friend or two with you. And when you inevitably slip into silence with someone by your side, you learn to love it. No words need to be exchanged. The simple being present with someone you care about and enjoying a shared experience is warm and fuzzy.



SPOILERS:
There were two specific moments where the game said something about time that really meant something.

The first was when, for one of the "challenging puzzles," the game locked myself and four friends in a room for 30 minutes. At first, it was a little ridiculous. Half an hour is not an insignificant amount of time to spend in one room.  Despite this initial trepidation, we ended up playing 20 questions. It was stupid, but I loved it. There was no game in that moment. Just myself and my friends who I have known for years enjoying each other's company. The timer very quickly faded into the background. And then the thirty minutes was over. Maybe a little too soon.

The second moment was the first ending of the game. After spending some time in the final tower completing various puzzles that rely on the communication skills you've built with your friends, you're spat back out to make one final Big Walk to the turnstile that leads you off the island. I don't know. For whatever reason this simple act of having my friends walk one-by-one through the turnstile and waving goodbye made me really emotional. It really is strange. A friend walks through the turnstile and it closes behind them. You wave through a pane of glass and say your goodbyes and then they walk into a white tunnel, never to return. 

Even though we were just one Discord un-deafening from talking to each other again, I really felt like I was saying goodbye to someone I wouldn't see for a while. And in some ways, it's true. We were saying goodbye to the shared experience of Big Walk. We were saying goodbye to our ability to simply allow the minutes to pass by while we enjoy each other. Our lives get busier each year. Finding the time for our last session of Big Walk took us multiple weeks. We just can't spend time together the way we used to. 

And for that, I'm incredibly grateful to Big Walk for giving me time with people I cherish.

After spending so much time walking around, getting lost, messing around, laughing until we couldn’t breathe, and just enjoying being together, reaching the end felt like saying goodbye to a little world that had become ours. It sounds dramatic, but I genuinely felt like a piece of me was being ripped away when it was over. And honestly, the best part of Big Walk was getting to experience it with all my friends. Finally being able to get everyone together in one game and just exist in the same space was something I didn’t realize I had been missing so much. We weren’t always doing anything important. Sometimes we were just wandering around, getting distracted, doing stupid things, or making each other laugh over the smallest stuff. But those moments ended up meaning the most to me. There’s something so beautiful about a game that gives you an excuse to spend time with people you care about. Big Walk gave me a place to make a few last memories together before we all went to college, and I think that’s why the ending hit me as hard as it did. I wasn’t just finishing a game. I was finishing a little chapter of our time together. I’m going to miss loading into this game and seeing everyone there. I’m going to miss the stupid conversations, the chaos, the inside jokes, the random adventures, and all the moments where we completely forgot what we were supposed to be doing because we were having too much fun. I love this game so much, but more than anything, I love what it gave me. It gave me memories with people I care about, and I genuinely couldn’t have asked for a better way to experience it. Some games are fun. Some games are memorable. And then there are games that become attached to a specific time in your life and the people you shared them with. Big Walk is one of those games for me. I miss you all so much. Thank you for being such amazing friends. I’m so incredibly grateful I got to take this walk with all of you. ❤️

i've re-written this review about half a dozen times by now, over the course of a whole month (I'm slow, forgive me). Each time, the word count has gone up. I kept reaching further and further for concrete, practical, *tangible* demonstrations and explanations for my near 15-hour experience with the game. Each time, I failed.

It shouldn't have been this hard - the game is distinctly well-designed in everything from its inventory system to its composition. Early on during my group's sessions, I called it a "game design game" in the way that everything feels laser-focused on being Just Right, from how it blends simplicity with open-ended problems ranging from the actual puzzles themselves to the act of navigation itself, creating beautifully emergent gameplay (check that off your bingo board...) and making downtime a core part of the experience itself. The game almost effortlessly commands your attention without you even realizing it; it explicitly wants you to stop and take a look around, to spend as much time as you need. Time to explore. Time to figure out what's next. Time to goof around with your friends. Time to take it all in. Time to stop and think. Time to wave goodbye.

It's silly to admit, but this game about giant clay-bird-people collecting [papayas | effigies | babies |???] is a very emotional game at its core. A very personal one, too - no experience is universal, of course, but still an ironic observation given one of its pillars of design being co-op. It just struck a very particular chord with me, one that I had been half-heartedly tugging at myself without even realizing.

I don't know if it hit any one of my friends as hard as it hit me. I don't know if it hit *anyone* as hard. But there still is a deep, underlying sense of emotion weaved into the very fabric of Big Walk, a pang that echoes back with each and every connection made. A moment etched into our memories, even long after we go our separate ways. An invitation to sit and appreciate the good times, if not for just a little longer. A quiet reminder of the people we will cherish for the rest of our lives.

Hello! After heavy consideration between this and another game I played this year, I've decided my Game of the Year belongs to this game. This game is something so special that I'm writing a review for it, which is something I normally don't do nowadays. This is a one-of-a-kind game that I am incredibly glad to have experienced all the way through to the end with my friends, and a game that anyone with a friend group, big or small, should play. 

I've wanted to play this game since I saw one of the announcement trailers, but I'm not a very talkative person and don't have a microphone, so I wasn't sure if I would be able to fully enjoy the game with my friends. Thankfully, there is a very well implemented proximity text chat system, which every multiplayer game with proximity voice chat should have.

While walking around with my friends and looking for puzzles there was a sense of exploration and discovery that I haven't felt as strongly in other games compared, and sharing it with them made each and every moment feel special. We came across some puzzles that had us stumped for a bit, or took a lot of effort to complete, and that shared feeling of finally figuring them out, going "OOHHHH", working together to complete them, and sense of accomplishment after felt amazing. We're so smart.

There were many moments in the game where we lost each other or got lost together, which felt less like a hinderance in the pacing of the game and more like an integral part of what makes the game special. There are many ways you can find your friends or help them find you, and many different ways of communication so you're not lost and alone the entire time. The few moments where I was lost and alone felt like I was taking a brisk walk through nature, taking in the sights, rather than actually feeling lost. 

In the final portion of the game we [spoiler]had our vocal cords removed and had to rely solely on body language, which we all did amazingly with. We were like books with how easily we were able to read each other, and the puzzles were incredibly well done and well thought out.[/spoiler]

That's another thing I love about this game, all of the puzzles are so unique in their own ways, some with many different ways you can solve them, intentional or unintentional, and are incredibly thought out and fun to solve. Each puzzle solved feels like an accomplishment and not just "oh we did it".

We also [spoiler]went for the post-game stuff, and did everything there was to do, saving probably the most fitting puzzle for last. After a long 21-ish hours we had finally reached the true end of the game and shared a moment in the void together before closing the game for the final(?) time.[/spoiler]

This is one of those games that can only be experienced once, and the worst part of the experience is that it ends. If you can, and your friends are up for it, please play this game with them. I'm sure you'll all enjoy it. After all,

The sprawling walk with its accompanying soundtrack only heighten the experience further, making basically everything around the island an aspect of an adventure and curiosity. 

There's also the interesting human aspect that's important to this game. Around the island there're hotspots where you and your friends can sit, relax, and chat. These hot spot are not super frequent and spotting them not only piques curiosity, but, forces a conversation to be had. Whether it be on the spot itself or a different subject entirely. This idea of 'hey, relax, take your time' is prevalent around you. A subliminal message that's thrown at you whenever you go. As to why it is unique here, is simply because of how it corelates to the puzzle design in itself.  

In Big Walk you will have 'senses puzzle', puzzles that rely on some aspect of your senses. You also have communication puzzles, how would you convey information to another friend if your tools of conveying are limited. And then you have teamwork puzzles, where your team is forced to come up with a solution on how to get an objective done. There're more, but the point is that they all flow perfectly together. 

And these hotspots re-enforce that idea. Sometimes without even noticing you would be practicing a tool that would be used in an upcoming challenge, or, a hint at what is possible to do within the game. It is simply incredible.  
I cannot recommend this game highly enough, buy it!

Big Walk is a fantastic way of connecting with your close friends with many opportunities for discussion during quiet exploration and working together to solve puzzles where collaboration is paramount to success.  

After finishing the tutorial area you're given free reign to practically the entire island and can enjoy a fun go-where-the-wind-takes-you style of non-linear progression.  Despite the large scale it's very easy to find places of interest thanks to the high contrast between the semi-realistically detailed island and visually striking puzzle entrances + more using solid bright colors to catch your eye.  This however is completely turned on it's head once it turns nighttime, aside from a small light around your player the map turns nearly pitch black.  There are of course ways to remedy this beyond simply waiting for daytime but does create moments of interesting friction if you decide to take certain items over others.  Getting lost is also fairly fun but not particularly beneficial considering the lack of solo puzzles that are available, thankfully there are many systems in place that allow you to roughly pinpoint players so you can fill in the gap of what you've been up to.

The puzzles feature enjoyable problem solving with enough restrictions to make you scratch your head on some.  From our experience as a group of 4 we were able to solve most of these on our first attempts after a brief discussion beforehand.  The puzzles featured in the game's finale and post-game sections however can offer a bit more difficulty in these regards in more ways than you might think.  Getting stuck on any puzzle is quite unlikely thanks to the simple fact that this is a co-op game, either one player  ascertains the correct approach or you put your heads together and work things out.

The memories Big Walk has given our group are priceless and I thoroughly appreciate how different this game feels to it's contemporaries in the genre.  What a special experience!

This game is something truly special. On the surface, it's a fun puzzle sandbox to take with friends, but there's one particular aspect of the game that makes it truly memorable: the ease in which you can get separated from your friends and lost. The game relies very heavily on proximity voice chat to complete its experience, but the thing is, the range of the voice chat is *very* low. If you go further than about 15 feet away from one of your friends, you will not be able to hear them anymore. But that's okay, because you'll be able to keep track of them visually, right? Well, maybe during the day, but even then, the terrain and foliage in this game can be so dense and variable in their height that it can be surprisingly easy to lose sight of people. And that's before nighttime. When night falls, it is near impossible to see anything beyond a few feet in front of you without a light source.

So you can quickly lose track of people if you're not sticking together and paying close attention to your positioning. The short voice chat range means you will eventually have to rely on non-verbal means of communication over longer distances. Big Walk provides plenty of those in the form of hand signals and items. But it's also very easy to lose items if you're not careful, because you can only carry one of them at a time under normal circumstances and if you end up dropping them somewhere in dense foliage or in the dark, it might be a struggle to find them again.

These things don't really seem like much at first, but as you explore the island, travel over more complex terrain and split up to cover more ground, these can suddenly become bigger problems. One would think that would dampen the fun of the game, but it's quite the opposite, because this is in fact what makes the game special: limitations. How do you circumvent these limitations? You work together with your friends. You keep an eye on each other, decide who carries what valuable item and how they're used. You can either stick together like glue, or set up systems for long range communication and signaling, like with laser pointers, radios, flares and what not in case you split up to take on multiple puzzles, or if someone gets lost.

This ends up reinforcing the social experience of the game massively and makes for a lot of dynamic moments. There is no scripted path, no fast travel, no tutorial outside of the starting hub, no strict team mechanics and no warning message for when things go wrong. Everyone in this game makes their own unique experience, deciding who they want to travel with, how they want to work together and what kind of stories they want to make and share with each other. This is what makes Big Walk a truly special game. One of 2026's best, in fact.

In a world that feels increasingly hostile, chaotic, and divided, Big Walk reminded me of the quiet joy of connecting with friends. Beyond its beautiful landscapes, playful puzzles, and simple premise, what stays with me are the small, ridiculous moments: watching someone tumble down a mountain on their butt, singing while the train arrives at the next station, saying something without words through a clumsy dance, walking beside someone in the dark, stopping to look at something beautiful, getting stuck in a room talking for half an hour about whatever is happening in your life, or laughing at something that would mean nothing to anyone else.

As we grow older, time has a way of scattering us across cities, careers, relationships, and lives that become increasingly heavy. The friends we once saw every day become people we have to make plans to see, and those plans fail more often. Perhaps that’s why these simple moments feel so precious. There is a quiet kind of beauty in having nowhere else to be for a while, nowhere to be but here, right now.

Big Walk understands something I think games can sometimes forget: they don't always need to take us somewhere new. Sometimes they just need to give us a reason to stay together. A world to wander through, something to laugh about, and a few hours during which the distance between us seems to disappear. And when it ends, there is a strange sadness in knowing that you can never quite experience that first walk again.

This is a game that is about communication. 

There's the obvious: using hand signals in puzzles when you're too far away. Finding a system to communicate when one group is missing information. Practical things.

Then there's some less obvious things: the complete silence and isolation if you lose your way from the group, separating from the group enough naturally so you and one other person can have an unintentionally private conversation, being stuck in a room together for 30 minutes.

The game runs the gamut of how we communicate. For practical reasons, End-Game:[spoiler]the complete absence of your previously most powerful communication tool of voice[/spoiler], for fun, and even just silence. 

It's a very human experience and really got me to reflect on and appreciate our evolution of communication as a species.

The game's hesitation of giving the players shortcuts also help to contribute to this feeling of wistfulness. Traveling between puzzles is as much of the game as the actual puzzles. Planning a route, dealing with rocks/obstacles you didn't know were there, finding dropped objects, and finding lost people all make traveling fun and unexpected. Furthermore, the shortcuts all feel like natural parts of the world. There's no teleportation, just a tunnel through the mountains for example. That being said, the train rarely felt worth using. These parts could feel like a chore but it didn't for me. It felt like a fun outing between my friends and it shocked me how realistic it felt.

There's a few puzzles I think are downright bad ([spoiler]Finding the correct music station, the scavenger hunt to get 4 parts of puzzles from all across the map, and the long heavy shotput purple puzzle[/spoiler]) but the rest are amazing, especially in the last area. 

I would definitely recommend playing this with people you know if possible. Finding out how your friends communicate and think is part of the fun.

Pretentious language on the store page and "10/10 IT CHANGED MY LIFE" reviews made me a little suspicious, but Big Walk turned out to be great. It is an open world co-op puzzle game with a big emphasis on communication. Its challenges are pretty simple, but they do not feel banal because you are allowed a great deal of creative freedom. Like, if you need to signal a number to your teammate who can see but can't hear you, you may develop a simple sign language beforehand (like one hand to the side is 1, one hand up is 5 etc). But you may as well simply flash your lantern a certain number of times. It's up to you. 

And the game always presents you new obstacles to work around. What if you can't see other people? What if you can't talk? What if you are separated or very far away from each other? What if you need to be highly synchronous? What if everyone has just a partial piece of a solution? It's fun to develop your own unique ways of organizing and communicating. And in the end, things that you've learned are put to the test, and everything comes together in a very beautiful and satisfying way.

This is my game of the year. Every single aspect of the game is designed with attention and care, creating emergent gameplay that bring you closer to the people you love. The finale will stick with me for a long time. You know that a game is good when it creates a massive discourse about whether the label "friendslop" has excessively pejorative connotations. 

It is insane watching people hate on this game and review-bomb it based on objectively wrong pretenses. 

House House did not hide AI usage. Valve changed Steam's AI disclosure policy eight months before the release of the game and it explicitly does not apply to this kind of thing, only applying to generative art. Use of LLM-generated code is not required to be disclosed, let alone something as superficial as rubber-ducking and bug-fixing. 

They voluntarily disclosed their use of LLMs after a portion of IGF jurors released a statement pledging not to vote for any game that used LLMs in any capacity whatsoever, viewing the technology as fundamentally unethical. The IGF juror statement was prompted by "a significant increase in the number of submitted games developed with generative AI tools," not Big Walk itself. Big Walk did not receive a nomination that prompted them to disclose their AI usage; game developers have to submit their own games to the awards and House House disclosed marginal LLM usage in response to be transparent and let the jurors make their own choices. 

I fully understand the issue the jurors have with LLMs but in an era where LLMs have been crammed into every single IDE, search engine, spellchecker, and website, I do not think it is a productive use of anyone's time to act like one of the best games of the past decade is somehow irreparably tainted by superficial LLM usage. The game engine itself has LLM-assisted code in it! 

They even tried going to get assistance from the developers of the game's engine and used AI when that failed. House House has already pledged to develop a clear policy on use of AI code assistance going forward. What do you want at that point? A land acknowledgement but for Stack Overflow? 

They could have disclosed far more than Valve requires, but close to a supermajority of developers utilize code assistants in some form. House House did not fail any disclosure they should have been expected to make. The thing people are getting mad about, viewing anything to do with LLMs as fruit of the poison tree, would not change in that case.

I wish House House the best of luck in both the IGF and the Game Awards. They deserve it.

A well put together game that is best experienced with around 3 or more friends who stick together and keep everyone involved with the puzzles and exploration within the game. If playing with like-minded people it can foster some feelings of being closer as a result of communication and the required teamwork for majority of the puzzles in the game. Note that whoever hosts the game will need to host all future sessions of the game unless you want to start over and have to figure out which save file/host you want to use for your sessions.

That said, if you have friends who are bringing in prior knowledge or go off on their own to retrieve items on their own (whether they've played this game already or not) or if you have friends who make unilateral decisions without involving everyone, you may find this game rather frustrating.

Also, it's online only and there's no single player accommodations. So if you miss something with your friend group then sorry you've missed it until you get another group together - hence my noted frustration with friends who make unilateral decisions. Try not to be that friend who undermines the experience for others.

The environment and aesthetics of the game are pleasant; scenic views abound, the lighting of the flashlight against trees at night is particularly very realistic/striking, and the puzzles are all bright toy colors so it's hard to miss them except for if they're hidden by trees or hills.

The puzzles themselves are fairly fun and range from rudimentary or just waiting around for a bit to puzzles that require teamwork without talking or puzzles where a person is blind and must be guided to objectives. 

While I think the game is worth the price, it might be best to wait for it to be on sale if you have friends who are skeptical about it or undermine the experience for others as discussed previously. Otherwise, you may find yourself with buyers remorse due to a less than ideal experience.

In the age of friendslop (complimentary), Big Walk is a true friendgem.

It’s hard to put into words what makes playing this game feel so special, but it had me in tears by the end. It really feels like you’re going on a journey with your friends, because of what it asks of you. There were times when half our friend group got split up, and it’d be an hour before we saw each other again, but that separation became part of our Big Walk story we were telling together.

In most cases, the puzzles in the game were pretty intuitive to work out with some thought, and I love that the developers clearly considered multiple ways a group could solve a puzzle, giving the flexibility for that to happen rather than locking you into one way of reaching the solution. Two of my friends, on one of our split up excursions, developed a number system using the different ways you can hold up and out your arms, and it helped us through so many puzzles. When we reached the final puzzle gauntlet, where we couldn’t communicate with our voices or even know who was who, we all immediately knew that the ‘patented number system’ was going to be our way through this challenge, and it helped us immensely. In another puzzle, we literally just had to wait in a room for five minutes, and spent that time arguing over a recipe.

Big Walk’s sound design is impeccable, some of the best I’ve experienced in a game, aside from the proximity chat being way too quiet at launch. Voices carried and echoed differently depending on whether you were in a tunnel, a vast canyon, or just a normal room, and combined with all the ambient sounds and music fading in and out, it made the world around us feel real. Visually, I love the character designs and the way you could customise your characters, and important landmarks or puzzle locations always stood out clearly from the environment, without ever feeling out of place or uncanny.

The world is so intricately designed, opening up in different ways with each tower we completed. Shortcuts could be unlocked to make it easier to progress each time we started a new session. At the start of each session, we’d try to plan where we’d go using the map, only to get immediately side-tracked most of the time by something we spotted on the way to our actual destination. 

The progression items, like tool belts and backpacks, were incredibly useful, and always seemed to arrive right when we needed them. I know some people had gripes with this, but I personally love that you need someone else to help you put them on and take them off, another small way the game makes you rely on each other. If I had to wish for any other progression item, it’d be some form of headlamp. A lot of the time, if we were playing and it got dark, we’d just wait out the night, which was nice sometimes, since we’d all just sit down and talk while we waited. Other than that, we’d normally have a dedicated flashlight guy.

I think if you have a group of really good friends you’d love to spend time with, Big Walk is a great way to do it. It’s a game that gives you and your friends the tools to make fun and talk shit with each other, while also giving you the chance to come up with intuitive and fun methods to work together to solve puzzles and explore, in a way that is wholly unique to your friend group’s playthrough of the game.

Big Walk isn’t a game I’ll remember for its puzzles or its map, though both are excellent. I’ll remember it for our ‘patented number system,’ the nights spent waiting for the sunrise, and the ridiculous shit we talked while walking. It’s a friendgem in the truest sense, less about what you’re doing on the journey, and more about who you’re taking it with.

review:
When Big Walk was first announced, I rolled my eyes and shrugged. The announcement videos made it feel like it would easily fall into the friend-slop trap, and in my head I had already tidily dismissed it as "PEAK but slow, low-stakes, and not about climbing anymore." I loved Untitled Goose Game, and appreciated the charm it had, so I at least saw some appeal in a new House House game, at least enough to buy it when a few groups of friends picked it up on when it released.

I'm very pleased to admit that not only has it shattered the middling expectations I had for it, but is one of the best games I've played all year, and brought some of the most memorable experiences I've ever had playing a game. It demands some patience, but its simplicity makes it one of the most refreshing games I've found in years.

The art style grew on me midway through playing, as did the sometimes-goofy physics, as well as how close people really have to be to hear you at all (though the game provides many other ways to remedy this by communicating in other ways). The struggles are part of the fun, but not in a rage-baiting way, they're just genuinely parts of the obstacles of the game you have to engage with, and House House seems to get that.

The game is very accessible for those who need it as well, allowing the skipping of some puzzles. We also found that it's perfectly playable even without a mic, as written chat messages are readily visible at a distance above your head, and even carry through things such as radios or walkie-talkies. I'd genuinely recommend this game for anyone as it's not too difficult, can be picked up and set down even if you only have an hour or so to play, and works in any size of group. Having a group of 5 or 6 friends felt perfect for me, but the game is a fine experience even if it's just you and a single other friend/partner/kid/parent/whatever.

The ending [spoiler] is absolutely best-in-class. I've never seen a better ending for a game, and I could write a whole review on the last hour of gameplay alone. It was weirdly heart-wrenching for me and my friends. [/spoiler]

My friends and I will continue to play and ravenously discover what secrets remain. We spent hours together, walking, getting lost, finding each other, and making progress, and I hope we get a few more together.

In the age of slop Big Walk is something real. A truly special experience with the right group of friends.

It took my group of 5 around 40 hours to completely finish the game. Some nights we would log on intending to complete puzzles but instead spent hours just hanging out, dancing to the game's soundtrack, exploring, getting lost, finding each other, then getting lost again. The game trusts you to find enjoyment in simple things like stumbling across a new song to add to your collection, or a place to just sit and chat. These things would probably be pretty uninteresting on their own but sharing that sense of discovery with your friends is magic.

The basic character models are a huge part of the charm. Because the emotes are so simple everyone finds creative ways to use them and your group will develop their own individual mannerisms that are uniquely theirs. There are moments where the game makes it hard to tell who is who through various (spoilery) mechanics, but even then I could pretty reliably tell who my friends were by their frantic waving, pointing and jumping around.

To add to the chorus of people saying exactly the same thing - Big Walk is truly about the journey rather than the destination. 100%ing the game was bittersweet, and we truly didn't rush, especially those last few sessions where we knew we were approaching the end. When you do finally finish, you get a satisfying sense of closure knowing that the experience is over and that you will all move on to whatever comes next. We might return to the island again to just hang out but nothing can recreate the experience of exploring it for the first time.

I expected a nice distraction for a few nights but this one is really really special. There's honestly nothing else like it.

This game is genuinely a once in a lifetime game. While there aren't enough words that can describe the feelings that this game brings me, I can describe the game itself while not spoiling too much. 

1. First and foremost, the people you play this game with will directly facilitate how much fun you have. While most other "friendslop" games rely on your friends to do the heavy lifting, the puzzles in this game are quite challenging at times. By providing a mix of straightforward solutions and plenty of obscure solutions, you are genuinely excited walking up to whatever puzzle or challenge you stumble across. If you have friends that give up or get salty easily, maybe don't play this game.

2. The game has a TON of walking as the name implies, while you can unlock things throughout the game, your main traversal will still be walking and talking. Filling the down time with friends etc.

3. While there isn't necessarily a story, there does seem to be some sort of lore or contained miniature story that takes place throughout the game. Even if you prefer story driven narratives, I would still recommend you try it.

4. There is a small bit of psychological horror to the game. If you manage to get separated from your group, especially at night. It can be quite nerve wracking. Even if you know there's not really a way to lose or die, every twig breaking or small noise from the darkness surrounding you fills you with a sense of unease.

Finally, I will give my personal experience with this game. It is genuinely something special and will stick with me just as much as a family vacation, or other memorable life experience. I've laughed the hardest I ever have playing Big Walk. It makes you feel a little bit of everything, you get so lost in the world and experience of it all that the time flies by. All those memories and moments are then wrapped up with possibly the best ending I have seen in a multiplayer game.

It is cheesy, but the phrase. "Don't cry because it's over, smile because it happened." applies to this masterpiece. It truly is one of those games that you will wish you could forget, just to experience it again.
If this game doesn't win best multiplayer game at TGA, I'll pull a Big Sad.

Need more games like this. No handholding, just good game design, both providing freedom as well as a basic form of fundamental structure to give you clear goals. You can tell how many things are deliberately designed the way they are in order to give the players a very specific experience when playing with your friends. 

My biggest complaints has nothing to do with the game, but performance. Game gives you many settings to change so it WILL run on most systems, but overall optimization when you don't want the game to look like it's running on a Playstation 2 is poor. Partially understandable because a lot of the world is deliberately rendered in, so that, for example, you can see what your friends are up to halfway across the island if you have binoculars. 

If you insist on using "friendslop" terminology, I'd say what differentiates friendslop from a friend-gem is the deliberate design that doesn't just require working together with friends, but actively encourages it, in both bigger and more subtle ways. Big Walk is a masterclass in this, and one of the ways in which it surpasses most other "friendslop" titles.

The only other thing I'd personally like changed is the belt upgrade. I like that backpacks are intentionally only equippable and interactable by your friends, but I feel that a belt should differ in your ability to interact with it yourself, once its been put on you. If the number of items is limited to specific ones such as flashlights or walkie talkies, that would be fine too.

A lighthearted and fun game to play with your friends!

I was positively surprised how much fun I was having as we solved puzzles together!

Every few years, a game comes out which is truly special; it's brilliantly designed and stands-out amongst everything new-ish on that current market.  Big Walk is that game, right on time.
Big Walk is a game relying on cooperation of players, at least 2 are required by the puzzles scale up to require 4 players (and you can have up to 12 playing at once).

The entire game is about exploring and figuring things out. Everything. Everything from even [i]what to do[/i] to [i]how to[/i]. There are no instructions, no guidance, absolutely no hand-holding; things don't even have names/labels... so your friends can name things as they will to identify things and you create your own "culture".

I will not spoil anything at all in a review, because the game is about exploring and solving puzzles together and figuring it all out [b]is[/b] the game.

In playing, you'll find brilliant designs; from the puzzles themselves to the communication methods (there is a short drop-off of proximity voice chat, intentionally, so you use the multiple communication methods, like radios, provided) to the SOUND DESIGN.
Often overlooked, the work that goes into really good sound design, like in Big Walk, is huge and it shows. And it matters here in a big way... being able to shout from up high into a valley and be heard, hearing footsteps, using walkie talkies to find each other...

Aside from the obvious things, the game feels good to play and having control over your each of your character's arms independently lets you be expressive -- it reminds me how fun social interactions in VR are, and perhaps because I was playing through the game with my friends group whom I first met in VR that's why I make that comparison.

The main issues I had with Big Walk are:
[list]
    [*] Travelling around isn't that fun or interesting. Movement is kinda slow, running doesn't feel that fast. I seemed to constantly get stuck on the environment and even the smallest incline was a struggle. You can't bunny hop your way up a mountain like in Skyrim.  [spoiler] There's a train, and it seemed like this was going to be way more useful than it actually was - it's painfully slow. [/spoiler] 

    [*]  There's a day/night cycle, but I found that this only made the game even more frustrating. It gets dark every 15-20 minutes, and when it gets dark - it's pitch black. It got to the point where I'd find a lit up building when it was getting dark and just stay there for 20 minutes while i browsed my phone.

    [*]  The game supports 12 players, but it feels like it's clearly meant for 4. I was in a group of 5 and it felt like the only useful thing I could do was to bring a lamp everywhere so that the group could see. I missed the first few puzzles in the game because I'd joined late, so it felt like i was at a big disadvantage later on since the later puzzles become more complex and expect you to have knowledge of how prior puzzles worked. 

    [*]  I had the vibe that the game didn't know what it wanted to be. Some elements felt like they were taken from a survival game, while the game itself looked like it was trying to be a cozy game without too much challenge (not having a HUD with a minimap but instead having to take a physical map and compass with you, only being able to carry one item at once, etc). 
Even the environment gave me that "Unreal/Unity store asset" uncanny valley feeling, completely disconnected from the cartoonish players and buildings. The environment felt like it was taken from an asset pack (albeit a high quality one), and didn't give me the feeling that this game had been in development for 6 years.

    [*]  When you fall from a high place, you'll drop the item in your hands. It's novel the first time it happens, but frustrating when it's happened for the 5th time.  There's a scanner you can use to try and help find an item on the ground, but I found it to be completely useless and easier to instead reload the server and find wherever the item had respawned. 

    [*] Game was a bit pricey at £16 when it could be completed in around 10 hours. If the movement was faster, less backtracking was involved and empty space was removed then I   feel like there'd be around 8-9 hours of content to 100% completing it.
Also optimisation wasn't great, I had around 30 fps which wasn't too stable.

They say "it's about the journey, not the destination", and that's very true with Big Walk. Sure, there's a bunch of escape room-esque puzzles to complete, and an obvious destination to eventually meander towards. At its core though, Big Walk is a game that invites you to slow down, take in the sights, and have a chat about things, whether that's a puzzle solution, orienteering strategy, or, perhaps, about life in general. Merely taking is not the only method of expression, though, and the nature of the game means you may find your connection with whoever you play with grows just that little bit stronger by the game's conclusion, which I did not expect but am nevertheless grateful for.

It's a fairly unique game all things considered, so grab some friends and/or family, make some room in your schedules, and play this from start to finish blind. I'm really glad I went on this walk, and you will too.
