[b]⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ – A puzzle co-op game that comes highly recommended!! 🚶‍♂️🤝[/b]

[b]🤝 Brilliant co-op game to play with friends[/b]
[b]🏆 Felix’s TOP 10 co-op games[/b]

[b]Big Walk[/b] is an engaging and incredibly entertaining co-op game for [b]young and old alike[/b] – and it’s particularly fun with up to [b]4 friends[/b]. 😄

What makes the game so special for me is the [b]communication[/b]. 🗣️ Communication takes place exclusively through the game itself and is deliberately restricted or even completely blocked in many puzzles. This suddenly makes [b]non-verbal communication[/b] extremely important.

Moreover, that’s exactly where some of the funniest moments come from. 😂 You try to show your fellow players what they’re supposed to do, but of course they understand something completely different, and in the end everything turns out completely differently than planned.

What I particularly like is that [b]things don’t always go smoothly[/b]. Moreover, of course, at first it’s always someone else’s fault. 😜 🤝 Teamwork and team building are the key here!

However, that’s exactly what makes it so appealing. Over time, you learn to look out for one another, understand each other, and find solutions together. As a result, you actually grow closer and closer as a [b]really good team[/b] during the game.

For me, that’s why Big Walk isn’t just a great co-op game, but almost a [b]fantastic team-building exercise[/b]. 😄

[b]🧩 More puzzles, please![/b]
I really hope that [b]lots more puzzles[/b] will be added – ideally as DLC. In my opinion, the gameplay offers incredible potential for further creative challenges.

[b]🛠️ A small request for the 2-player mode:[/b]
There’s one thing, however, that I’d like to see changed: [b]The scaling to two players doesn’t quite work as well for me as it does with four players.[/b]

The main issue is the [b]rucksack and belt[/b]. You often need a second player to stow items on the belt or in the rucksack, or to interact with them. However, if there are only two of you playing and you have to split up to tackle a puzzle, this can be rather impractical at times.

The [b]belt[/b], in particular, is also often used for the walkie-talkie, so that you have your hands free and can talk to each other over longer distances. In two-player mode, this is a bit of a shame, because it means you can hardly use the belt for anything else.

In two-player mode, it would be great if you could [b]put down the rucksack and the belt and then load them or take items out of them independently[/b]. This would allow you to split up more effectively when tackling puzzles, without certain items suddenly becoming unusable.

[b]🏆 Verdict[/b]
A really great, creative and, above all, [b]fun co-op game[/b] that, thanks to its unusual communication style, ensures plenty of chaos, laughter and, at times, a touch of frustration. 😂

If you’re looking for a game where you can puzzle things out together, have a good laugh and bond as a team, you should definitely check out [b]Big Walk[/b].

Big Walk is a fine exemplar of the term 'friendslop'. 

The gameplay is excrutiatingly boring. Whatever scarce puzzles are scattered around the open world are very trivial, some of them even undeserving of being called puzzles in the first place. In fact, one of the 'puzzles' expressly demands that you simply AFK in a room for 5 minutes; yes, that's it.
That said, there is a smaller subset of interesting puzzles that require inter-player coordination and communication through limited means. Trying to pass an obstacle course while blindfolded and relying on teammate guidance is genuinely a cool concept. Unfortunately, not too much is done with it: they are relatively short and don't pop up often, most puzzles you'll encounter are basic information asymmetry games.

The traversal itself of said open world is not much better off. The character get frequently stuck on ever-so-slightly jutting geometry, uneven surfaces, objects etc. The 'sprinting' is closer to 'walking' and 'walking' is crawling. When you take away the slow movement, the world itself is actually not particularly big -- or varied, for that matter. It's mostly just sparse jungles, a tiny mountain range and a few fields. You get access to the funicular and a railway system later on, but with how slow they are, it's hard to say if they were put there as a placebo or just a capral tunnel syndrome therapy so that you don't have to hold W all the time.

The items are only in the game to make crossing the distances less painful, or skimming off some time from the puzzle solving. Realistically, you won't even be able to use them that much. Why? Your character can only carry a single item at a time. You can carry two additional items - one on a packboard and one on a waistbelt (only small items can fit on a waistbelt). The catch - you can access neither of these on your own. Want to use a walkie-talkie attached to your belt? Whoopsie-daisy! If you're playing with only 1-2 extra members, you'll all be hauling the keggles (keys that you earn for completing puzzles to make further progress) and using exactly zero items. You don't really need them, though - almost all puzzle chambers have intercoms or integrated chambers for you to exchange information in. Nights are fairly dark, but not dark enough to require a torch. Flare guns and walkie-talkies are grand and all but the world is not big enough to get seriously lost in, and the landmarks are very conspicuous.

The bottom line is, that Big Walk is a random assortment of simple semi-puzzles, spaced apart across a smallish island that you slog through with a team. The magical bonds of friendship are supposedly the glue that are to keep the entire game creakingly coming together, but having people to talk to while you're doing pretty much nothing of value is in no way the game's merit. Might as well just play Minesweeper in co-op.

[b]Big Walk[/b] is a very nice game that drops you into a large map filled with challenges, designed for multiplayer around asymmetrical puzzles.

[h3]The Good:[/h3]
- [b]Great as a duo:[/b] I strongly recommend playing it as a 2-player co-op (haven't tried with more). It's very enjoyable, never chaotic, easier to schedule long sessions, and you don't really miss out on the 4-player experience.
- [b]Puzzles and exploration:[/b] The puzzles are simple, varied, and genuinely fun to solve.
- [b]The main ending:[/b] It's enigmatic and cryptic without any real explanation, but it fits the overall style of the game, so the main ending worked fine for me.

[h3]Exploration downsides:[/h3]
The fast-travel and transport options end up feeling like pointless gimmicks. The train is only used for a single challenge, and the chairlift doesn't have a station at the spawn point, forcing you to hike halfway across the map just to reach it. It slightly ruins progression by making you walk everywhere even after unlocking tools meant to speed up travel.

[hr][/hr]

[h3]Why the negative review? The 100% completion is a chore.[/h3]
A friend and I decided to go for 100% completion before finishing the main story out of fear of getting softlocked (by the way, if you're reading this before playing: don't worry, you won't get softlocked). Basically, this means clearing the big green room with its 15 extra totems (on top of the 5 towers that each require 5 totems).

- [b]Content that literally doubles (or more) playtime:[/b] Totems are scattered all across the map, and some puzzles force you to backtrack across the entire world.
- [b]Zero payoff:[/b] If it added a cutscene or extra lore/explanations, it might be worth it. But without completely spoiling it: aside from a [i]"thank you for playing"[/i] message, the credits music, and an achievement, [b]you get absolutely nothing else[/b].
- [b]Total burnout:[/b] During our last few sessions, we had to force ourselves to keep playing. It dragged on, became tedious and repetitive, and ended with zero satisfaction—borderline disgust.

[b]Bottom line:[/b] The base game is cool, but [b]do not bother going for 100%[/b]. Unless you're an obsessive achievement hunter, completely skip the big green room; otherwise, it will ruin your entire experience.

An overhaul on the proximity chat making it more forgiving and easier to hear others would help a lot

-Day & Night Cycle: Why is there night? NO puzzles that i know of use the night time or darkness. Maybe give the host the ability to turn it off. BIG WALK is a remarkable game that manages to transform something as simple as walking into an extraordinary experience. Beyond its beautiful visuals and enjoyable gameplay, there is something deeply peaceful about it almost meditative.

Playing with friends makes the experience even more enjoyable, because the journey itself becomes a shared memory: conversations, laughter, unexpected moments, and all the little things that happen along the way.

But in my opinion, one of the most special things about BIG WALK is the sense of tranquility it provides. When your mind is overwhelmed and life begins to feel intense, the game gives you a chance to simply stop for a moment, breathe, explore, and let your thoughts drift away.

Not every game needs to offer constant action or endless challenges. Sometimes, the ability to slow down, enjoy the journey, and simply exist in the moment can be the most meaningful experience of all.

That is why I highly recommend BIG WALK to everyone especially if you are looking for a peaceful, beautiful, and enjoyable game that you can experience and share with your friends.

I played the entirety of this game with a four person group, which is the number I recommend the reader should also play with. This review very lightly spoils the first 30 minutes of the game at most.

This game is extremely unassuming. The description on Steam and the other reviews will make you think this is a "stop and smell the roses" type of game. And for the first hour or two, that's exactly what it is. You'll do the tutorial together and cross the initial valley while goofing off with your silly little characters. You'll spend 30 minutes at the color station messing with each other and finalizing your character's colors. You'll be a little bit lost while you figure out the first puzzle before the big bridge. And the bridge itself is full of the kinds of moments this game likes to make, like a bench next to an area full of speakers playing peaceful music, placed in an orientation so you and your friends can watch the sunrise.

Then you'll start solving the many puzzles spread out across the island. The cozy and slow vibe will give way to a more goal-oriented type of gameplay, in which you and your friends will mostly go from point A to point B, puzzle to puzzle, tower to tower, etc. Of course, you'll still get lost. You'll lose items in the darkness, goof off and be silly with your friends, and have all of the other types of evocative, emergent fun that this game can provide, but it won't exactly feel the same as the first hour. Don't get me wrong, the island has plenty of fun little spots and alcoves that feel designed and at the same time natural, and the puzzles do a good job of challenging your team's communication skills without being repetitive or frustrating. But ultimately, at some point, you'll probably fall into the opinion of, "Yeah, this is a cozy little puzzle game. It's not bad, and I'm having fun with my friends."

If you're like me, you'll wonder why this game's following is so fervent. Why is Instagram so full of fanart of this game? Why do the all of the reviews gush so much about the game? Sure, you'd recommend this to any other gamer, especially at the price point that it's at, but what's the big deal exactly? It's not boring, but it's no masterpiece.

And then you'll get to a very specific point in the game, perhaps 7 or 8 hours in. The game hints to you: there's more to this experience than meets the eye. Even at this point, I wasn't necessarily convinced that this was a 10/10 experience or anything...

My recommendation to the reader would be: you absolutely must finish this game to the end. The developers stick the landing so unbelievably well. They somehow deliver on two incongruent promises the game makes: there's something weird about this island to discover, and the game is still about "stopping and smelling the roses". My last 2 hours were some of the most fun I've had in a "friendslop" type of game in a very, very long time. The presentation of the final moments of the game is pristine and beautiful, and the game becomes, in many ways, a work of art. Every aspect of the end is simple, clever, humbling, compelling, and enchanting. I felt like my connection to the three people I had played the game with had been nurtured and focused upon without even really being the main point of the game. At the end of the 12 hours I put into this game, I found myself chatting happily with my friends about what we had just experienced together, and looking forward to our return to complete the island's challenges in its entirety.

I get it now. I get why people were so hyped about this game, and why so many love it. I strongly believe that most games, especially the massive story driven titles we expect from the biggest studios, frequently fail to deliver a satisfying ending to the game in both narrative and gameplay aspects. Big Walk, however, nails it so well that I immediately had to rush to the Steam page to leave this review. I wholeheartedly recommend this game; it's an experience that is well worth the money and the time. You owe it to yourself to put aside the easy dopamine hits and brain rot and just get walking.

What a weird and positive experience this was. I tried this game with 3 different sets of people, and ended up doing a full 100% playthrough with my 2 kids (crossplay on Steam, PS5 & Switch 2). 

It was a great (even educational) test for them both (10 & 13 years old) on topics like orientation, communication, memorization & collaboration. I would strongly encourage all parents to play this game with their whole family, and it will as well be a good test of patience & endurance, mostly for the parents ;)

The variety of the puzzles was broad, and surprisingly novel (for a big chunk of them at least). The puzzle weren't complex to understand, the challenge is how to communicate the answers to each other. Though, some of them were tedious yes, but somewhat contributed to the game's charm?

The only 2 downsides I could find about this game were the inventory management (even if you could find a few upgrades), and the voice range (too short, and talking louder had to impact when at distance). There are no real ways to go around them sadly, so you just need to accept these 2 limitations when playing. Oh also, nighttime was initially very annoying, but we quickly learned to be prepared when we were seeing it coming.

So, you need to be in a good & specific mindset to play this game, and ensure everybody in the session shares it. You need to accept to be lost sometimes, and to trust the game with all its strange mechanics that you will find a way to find each other again without cheating (also, setting plans and meeting spots is something you learn as well while playing). Sometimes, you'll need to be a bit creative when you can't communicate what you're trying to say, and again, that's part of the game. Trust the other players, be patient, and know that you'll figure this out with them.

This is a wonderful game experience. Even though the game doesn't have a direct storyline, there's a deep, rich story that makes you think about the themes behind the game.

The game makes you think about what it means to communicate, how we communicate, and how we make do with the limitations given to us. There's whimsy, beautiful scenery, and lots of opportunities to spend time with friends to just enjoy the experience.

The world is open, yet the experience is finely curated. Everything was placed with intention, there's lots of little secrets and interesting things to stumble upon no matter where you go. There has been plenty of talk about this being a 'friendgem' rather than 'friendslop', and I'd happen to agree, this is arguably the best co-op game of the past few years. Over the past few years, I've generally grown tired of competitive play, monitoring my meaningless statistics, and being rage baited by Slavs in matches. I think this game arrived at a perfect time, I was looking for something to play with my friends where I wouldn't have to necessarily worry about pulling my own weight or having to one-up another person in my group. 

Big Walk provides players with a meaningful experience, yet all you do is walk and talk, and it is peak.

The game forces you in establishing communication and bonding together. Puzzle-solving is mandatory, so working together is ultimately the best decision you'll make, and this forms comradery. It is immensely satisfying to amongst your friends cheering and jumping in a circle after finishing a puzzle.

I think it is ultimately best to not talk about gameplay as it's truly important to experience the game blindly and with your friends. No stats, no sweatiness, no leader-boards. Just hanging out with friends, messing around, making each other laugh and enjoying the journey.

I quite enjoyed our walk.

What I will say though regarding the ending, is that the ending to this game is heartfelt, and makes the journey all that more meaningful. I will detail my experience of the ending in the spoiler bars below:

[spoiler] As we crossed the Great Wall of Big Walk and finished the puzzles inside the abyssal orb, we got to the end, one by one we were instructed by the game to exit the game through a gate corresponding to the colours that we picked for our characters. I ended up being last, I don't know if this was because I was the host or it was just luck. However, watching my friends exit and leave the proximity chat, and overlooking a sunset slowly dimming was a fantastically meaningful moment. I'm not particularly literate and I'm not an especially gifted writer, but I say without hyperbole, that this was probably one of my favourite moments in a game over the past decade. [/spoiler]

For how hyped it is, I can't believe how mid this game is in execution (not in concept). I think the fact so many people love it is more a testament to how overstimulated and desperate for something quiet to do with friends everyone on this godforsaken internet is than any actual indicator of the game's quality. 

The puzzles were so far apart and getting to them took so long, and then we would get there and they are puzzles for babies that take about 5-10 minutes to do. Which is fine! The challenge is supposed to be communication, and I think them being harder would have been even more unfun--getting to them was already frustrating, and being stuck on a puzzle would have been miserable. 

But like, we’d play for an hour sometimes and only have done one puzzle and held down the W button. Which i know other people can enjoy but it just. Was so uninteresting to me. Especially when 90% of the landscape is about as exciting as a Unity asset pack.

"But what about talking with your friends! The game is about walking and talking!" The proximity chat is bad. Like, really bad. I already struggle sometimes with hearing my friends, and the concept that we would be able to walk and talk when we are navigating a hostile landscape of sticks and rocks while only being able to hear each other if we are actively riding each other's asses is... it's ambitious for sure! The walkie-talkies helped a bit, but it's a bit silly to be using a walkie-talkie when the person you're walkie and talkie-ing to is maybe ten feet away from you.

When a game is this pared down and intentionally simple, the base aspects really need to be as tuned as possible, and Big Walk just. Doesn't deliver on its most basic concept: being able to walk and talk with your friends, because the walk and talk is constantly interrupted by "I can't hear you" and "wait I'm stuck on something".

Sorry, Noel and Dakota, love you guys and every moment we spend together is precious and etc etc, but every moment of this past the first three or so hours was miserable.

Anyway. TLDR: Play We Were Here, A Way Out, Content Warning, Portal 2, or Tabletop Sim if you want something to do with your friends while just talking. Hell. Play Wizards 101 with your friends instead.

The mechanical description of Big Walk is a coop-focused puzzle game that utilizes proximity chat and character gestures and other novel approaches for communication.  As the name suggests, it involves a large amount of walking but what it's ABOUT is actually the small things you do in meantime.  Catching up on one another's day, goofing around with the various items and gestures, splitting the party and getting lost in the dark.  Stronger than any individual feature or puzzle, Big Walk's greatest strength is the way it acts as a landscape for you and your friends to have fun and make memories.  

I can't stress it hard enough that this game needs to be played with the built in Proximity Chat.  To use Discord or any other voice chat undermines both the puzzles and the experience as whole.  The game formally supports 1-4 player but I would don't think you can get the true experience with any fewer than 3.  I played with 3-5, depending on the day, and I thought that made for a solid experience, but if we had had 6+, I think some of the puzzles would have been too cramped with multiple people being unable to contribute.  

If you enjoy unorthodox, coop puzzles and have the friend group for this game, I can't recommend it enough.

This is honestly one of the best games 2026 has had to offer. Going in I fully expected another 'friendslop' experience that might have proven to be fun for a couple of days, maybe a week tops.... oh boy.... was I wrong.

Starting up the game and immediately coming to realise that the proximity chat is unforgiving in regards to the voice drop off was a strange but welcome surprise. Without a voice chat as harsh as this, the game would lose its charm. You really can lose your friends at a single wrong turn and that really adds to the experience. 

The puzzles are where this game shines in my opinion. Each one is cleverly crafted to utilise teamwork and communication often without the voice chat. The developers are clearly masters at puzzle crafting and it really shows. I was especially impressed with the ability to choose between playing with 2 or 4 people with the puzzles changing to match your choice.  

And then there's the ending. No spoilers of course but wow, something new and unique that played with every emotion I have.

Bravo House House, bravo. I'll remember this game for a long long time.

Great game that definitely deserves all of the positive attention it's getting. My friends and I had a great time with this game and I feel like it was a breath of fresh air for the otherwise stagnating multiplayer co-op game genre.

For one, this game is great at making the best out of your time. One person may be the best at communicating an idea, but you still need someone who can interpret that idea, and another who can execute things well. Inventory management is a team effort and so is making progress in the game. Everything is kept just ambiguous enough that the unique perspectives and ideas of your friends can inadvertently help you make progress even when you are seemingly lost. You will have fun with your friends and you will also get mad at them for making such simple mistakes. The whole journey is the point of the game, and I won't deny that that is the best element the game has.

The game's artistic identity is there. The various music areas throughout the game are kind of meaningless and I much preferred the regular music in the game. The visuals were striking in their simplicity, but I felt like it was starting to get old after a while. Dynamic weather would have added more to it, as the day-night cycle was starting to wear thin near the end of the game. The visuals of the characters was done well; they are cute and fun without being too in your face about the game's quirkiness. The color coding was great but the last area should have been white instead of green, but that's a minor visual identity issue.

The gameplay is good enough. The tunnels were the only main complaint I had about progression; I think we only used them once and even then I felt like the train, which is too slow in my opinion, was adequate enough. I understand that the game is called "Big Walk" but there were too many moments where I felt like getting from across the map just took too long.

The puzzles are great. Some of the later puzzles were a mixed bag. The "final" area was great, but our group actually missed the ending because we thought we had to go back to the main part of the island after we beat it. There should be a better way of communicating where the ending is to the player. The post-game puzzles are a mix of great and... terrible. One is just a long wait in a boring room. Realistically speaking, everybody in the group would rather just tab out than find something to do in a small room. There should have been some items to entertain you for a while. The first waiting room isn't bad since it's short and a unique change of pace. Some of them like the golf puzzle was absolutely *awful*, and I can't understand why the developers would intentionally put something this painful and unintuitive in the game. I felt like the "blindfold" puzzles were pretty poorly-designed, too. Not much to it besides yelling at your teammate to turn slightly to the left.

The game missed out on a few good opportunities. There could have been better tool unlocks as you progressed, but inventory space + radio is pretty much the best way to get things done. There should have been more puzzles that involved physical teamwork vs. communication and a few more puzzles that utilized unique tools to get things done. In the end, most of the puzzles felt very similar in DNA, with a few unique ones that stood out. This isn't such a big problem; the game is still great either way, but I can't help but think the game ultimately held itself back in too many areas which stopped it from being a masterpiece. Tons of tools in the game went unused because they felt utterly pointless. The game's best puzzles are the ones with a unique premise or interesting tools. Grabbing teammates, sitting, gesturing, etc. isn't utilized as much as it could have been.

This game's biggest weakness is the payoff at the end. Both endings are pretty lacking in substance and makes this game feel painfully close to The Witness rather than its own thing. We get a credits sequence that could have at least been interactable in some way and a white door that marks the ending of the game. This ending is decent but I felt like it could have used more fare. The evil orb entity isn't really explained and doesn't need to be, but I felt like we could have had a more conclusive sense of satisfaction other than "Oh, you beat the game, but there's more to do!" The secret ending is far worse. You sit down, read something about appreciating the journey with your friends (well, duh!) and then the screen goes white slowly. Maybe this would have hit hard if this was the last time ever seeing your friends, but it wasn't, and our first thought afterwards was "is that all there was?"

I thought the game was setting up a sort of grand puzzle or revelation with the position of the lamps (think like the ending in The Looker... lol). Unfortunately we didn't get a "everything comes together" ending, or even something more meta. We got a slightly preachy ending about appreciating your friends. That's nice, but I think the game's world, design, and mystique inherently promises a larger payoff than what we got. It's disappointing and admittedly hurt my experience of the game.

I still think Big Walk is a great game and I am hoping for the developers to potentially explore the idea further in a DLC someday. The sphere was easily the best part of the game and I felt like it helped bring together all the lessons my group learned quite well. The only issue is that this game, like the Witness, promised more of a payoff than it actually delivered. Games like this deserve some kind of Outer Wilds type crazy ending. Instead, I was disappointed and hoped for more. Still, the experience and journey itself was easily the best part of the game for me.

Big Walk does such an amazing job of quietly "teaching" you in the background-- about the game itself of course, but surprisingly, also about your friends and their quirks and strengths. I could probably write a lot (a LOT) about this game and all the aspects it succeeds at, but I'd be incredibly hard pressed to find any cons beyond a very subjective 'deeply impatient personalities might not be able to tolerate the lulls between puzzles, which can be compounded if the play session is... to be blunt: composed of a bunch of boring people.'

The music is used to sparing but great effect; items feel strong but not broken; 'upgrades' keep pace with the expanding game map excellently; lobby creation is seamless; I don't think I encountered even a single bug the entire time; the puzzles are a perfect, and I do mean perfect, blend of difficulty ranges that still never leave you feeling unsatisfied or irritated or utterly lost; the environment is beautiful and the studio's love for their homeland shines through; controls are simple and smooth; audio is crisp; and perhaps the most satisfying thing of all is that wacky stuff you'd THINK shouldn't be doable usually is. Want to stack a pile of people all sitting in chairs 5 high? You can. Want to write "kick me" on an enormous sign, and put it on your friend's back? You can. Carry around a disconnected friend's KO'd body? Yep. Pick up your friend minding their own business in a chair and fieldgoal kick them off a tower? Yes. The game isn't massively intricate such as a Baldur's Gate 3, but it doesn't need to be; within its own ecosystem you will constantly find new ways to do things and it never stops being fun.

It sounds a little stupid to say "this game made me feel something", but like, it DID. It did do that, in spades. This is a game you can never experience for the first time twice, and you'll forever wish you could: so do yourself a favor and go experience it once. Big Walk is about the destination *and* the journey. It's puzzles, but it's so much more than just puzzles.

In a market saturated with low stakes, shallow, generic looking and mindless co-op games that are more about clip farming than gameplay, Big Walk somehow manages to stand out greatly.
The main distinction you can make is in the pacing. While it's common for games like this to have something trying to kill you or a time limit of some sort, Big Walk fully allows you to approach it at your own pace, often even encouraging you to simply take a break and hang out for a bit. Not to mention it's also way more elegant with its co-op aspects than similar titles. A lot of the time you'll see a game trying to force a reaction out of you, or set you up for an easy joke and this just doesn't happen here: it doesn't feel like you have to be funny all the time for the game to stay entertaining.

What also puts it in the spotlight is its focus on scripted and curated challenges rather than randomly generated and repetitive tasks. The "Puzzles" in the game are not really about finding the solution: it's obvious what you need to do just by looking at the setup; no, the interesting aspect is finding a good way to approach it together: you may know how you'd want to solve it but does that sit right with your friends? Is it a clear enough way of conveying information across? Does someone else maybe have a better idea on how to tackle this? It's honestly an incredibly refreshing gameplay loop that leaves you wanting more even after you've completed everything. Hell, with the way the game is structured I wouldn't be surprised if they even included the few tedious puzzles on purpose just so you could bond over how annoying they were. 
After a while you stop seeing the map as something the developers made for you to explore and start seeing it as a giant playground that you can have fun in with your buddies. And just when you think you've seen it all it delivers one of the most elegant and ethereal endgame sequences I've ever seen.

Big Walk doesn't claim to be a stupid and funny game and it doesn't pretend to have an incredibly engaging gameplay loop by including a sad excuse of a singleplayer mode, because it just does not need to. What you see is what you get: a big world for you and your friends to hang out in and I can guarantee you it's a fantastic time.

I've never seen my gaming group so excited to continue a game before. I've certainly never seen a game quite like this. Not in the sense that it rejects categorisation, but that when trying to think of a game to compare, it to feels like comparing apples and oranges.

Big Walk excels at the wonder of discovery and the elation of cracking a puzzle and builds the experience to be enjoyed with friends.

House House clearly understand that strong level design is crucial for an exploration game.
Big Walk balances having enough visible points of interest to avoid feeling directionless and lost, but not so many as to feel overcrowded.
Instead of a ubisoft tower marking everything on a map, climbing a tower gives you a great view of places to check out around you to then (perhaps with a friend using a laser pointer) figure out how to get there.

Even if you get split off from your group without walkie-talkies, there are numerous tools to navigate. For example you can head for one of the towers (which all have radios and flares) or you can follow music from a radio a friend's carrying nearby.
There was one time my group figured we wouldn't need walkie-talkies, immediately split in two, then got separated further before regrouping. XD

Puzzles have a good approach of introducing elements that some puzzles use before you find trickier variants in the wider world, whilst keeping things fresh and interesting. As with the rest of the game (barring control and whiteboard tutorials), puzzles are presented wordlessly for players to poke at and figure out how they work.

The game handles progression in some interesting ways. It has the soulslike IKEA approach of unlocking shortcuts between places. There's also a monorail and a chairlift which follow set routes. So instead of 'fast travel' making the world feel small, understanding the layout of the island continues to be useful for figuring your way around.
Exploring the island also finds you more literal tools for navigation options. It's certainly appreciated that the game has a luggage zone at spawn for picking up what everyone was carrying at the end of the previous game session.

And of course there's room for prattling about, taking it easy on the chairlift seeing the island from above, enjoying one of the radio zones, or jumping down a big hole to see what's down there.

Touches like different sound effects based on what surface you're walking on and animations on character eyes when interacting with different items (including having them stolen :P) add to the charm of the experience.

Big Walk makes me wonder if we seeing a Golden Age of party games.

Big Walk is a solid game. You and your friends will need a lot of patience and good communication skills to explore the island and solve its puzzles. So far so good: the puzzles are interesting, the way the game presents new information is clever, Figuring out how the island works is exciting.

Now, the bad: the pace can be too slow at times. First, you better beg that nobody wanders off on their own, or there's going to be a lot of lost time. The sharp drop-off in player voice range makes it easy to get lost and separated from the group, delaying everyone. Players who are alone can't even access the items in their own belt and backback. This is just one of the multiple ways the game will force the group through periods of waiting, backtracking, and general downtime. It can be frustrating. On that note, I think the developers should consider increasing the distance at which players can hear each other's voices, as well as the speed of the chairlift and train.

Overall the game can provide a good time with friends, especially if you're looking for a casual experience.

Soren Kierkegaard said that life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards. So is the case for Big Walk.

Big Walk is an open world puzzle game by Melbourne-based studio House House (Untitled Goose Game).

The game requires a minimum of two players. There’s almost not a single puzzle that can be solved alone. Puzzles are adjusted for 2, 3 or 4+ players. Having the maximum of 12 players on the map is an incredible experience. Whether it’s splitting up to focus on different areas, or just having a large group of people solve a single puzzle. Also, as male friendships tend to be activity-based, it’s an opportunity to catch up with friends. The main challenge is getting a group of 30-year-olds together at the same time. 

The puzzles have two elements to them. Figuring out the rules of the puzzle, and solving it. The epiphanies in Big Walk largely come from figuring out the mechanics, rather than the steps of solving a puzzle. One example was a puzzle where one side had access to a series of tiles that were either marked or unmarked, and the other side had to copy this input. The only way to communicate was a gymnasium room in the middle, that only one side had access to at a time. We agreed beforehand that we would leave kettlebells on the floor’s tiles to indicate which tiles were marked. Most of the puzzles are relatively simple compared to the range of puzzle games on the market. The difficulty typically comes from communicating with your teammates.

The replayability is hampered from knowing how puzzles are meant to be solved. But you still need to work together as a team to solve them in different playthroughs. Furthermore, I’ve played with three different groups, and in each group I’ve experienced unique puzzles that I didn’t find with the other groups.

The game is slow in a very deliberate way. We used a walkie-talkie to tell some friends where we were on the map. They made their way to us by train. Occasionally we get separated, and use flairs or radios to find each other. As you complete puzzles on the island you unlock pieces of infrastructure you get around, a train, a chairlift and some tunnels. You can also find tools to help you. Players could use Discord, the developers could have added teleporters, but these would detract from the game’s delivery. 

Players walk around a 1/20th scale model of Wilson’s Promontory in Victoria. The game’s spawn area welcomes you with a native tree. You hear kookaburras in the distance, the sand squeaks when you walk on it, the river is red from tannins, the coastal rocks have an orange lichen on them. Australia imports a lot of culture from the United States and the United Kingdom. Over the years the word bushwalk has been crowded out by the word hike. Yet here is a distinctly Australian game that is doing numbers overseas. 

All the skills you have taught each other come together at the end. There’s a lot more I want to say about this, but I won’t. Going into the endgame blind is a blessing. It puts the rest of the game into a greater context.

As someone who likes games where you solve puzzles on an island I already thought Big Walk would be for me. But it isn’t just a great game, it’s a special game.

I would definitely recommend this game for anyone who is interested in grabbing a group of friends, and going off in a grand, hillariously amazing adventure. This game runs great with my P.C., and I've happened upon no issues while playing. 

 This game engineers your group to be as social and as cooperative as can be. Limited movement opportunities allows gameplay to focus on the characters within your group, rather than the gameplay itself, which makes for natural moments of hilarity and socialization. This is amplified by the amazing communication structure built within Big Walk, thus encouraging people to stick together, and discouraging solitary movement.  

However, this is not to say that being alone in Big Walk is detrimental to enjoyment. In fact, I found great pleasure and adventure attempting to re-locate with my group, by utilizing the great locating tools placed along for this exact purpose. Additionally, the fantastic visuals of the game aid in creating enjoyment, regardless of the presence of friends or other players.

Similarly to their other projects, House House has again, killed it with their art direction and environment. The beautiful Austrailian setting, sprinkled with cartoonish arcitechture and player models, creates this wonderful experience, filled with child-like imagination and a sense of wonder. Many times, I have found myself scrolling through community-made artwork and posts, always wanting to see more of these little circle people adventuring the world, leaving nothing but excitement and joy.

In summary, Big Walk is of Big Value, and I urge anyone who has a friend group willing to take a trip through the beautiful scenery (and make more friends along the way), buy this game immediately, and have Big Fun in House House's lastest Big Game.

Another entry in the 'friendslop' genre. Played this game with a group of 4, and I have to say I really enjoyed my time with this game. Definitely not for everyone as it's quite slow-paced, but If you like the idea of a relaxing, exploration + puzzle game to play with your friend group it's a really good experience.

In terms of puzzles, I will admit that the beginning section is a little bit of a slog, due to the very low difficulty of the puzzles at this point in the game. But if you can get past that point, the puzzles are probably what I enjoyed the most out of everything. Sure, there are some misses here and there (looking at you, golf ball puzzles. Easily my least favourite puzzles in the entire game), but more often than not the puzzles are bangers that require cooperation. I won't spoil much, but the puzzles in the black dome near the endgame are undoubtedly my favourite ones. They will throw you for a loop and take a bit to figure out, but they're really fun to do once you get the hang of it.

On the exploration side, I was expecting to get bored travelling from one place to another. But honestly? In the end I kinda enjoyed the downtime. There's something melancoly about traversing forests and mountains of this size. The movement on rocks is a little jank, but trying to find paths to head to the next destination wasn't a challenge I expected to like. There are also times where you may accidentally get lost by wandering off, and my friend group often had to find ways to locate the lost person or meet up somewhere.

On a side note, please set the lobby password to something secure. Despite not having a proper public server browser, it is possible for modders and hackers to see active lobbies currently. We had a hacker join our game once since our password was weak, but thankfully he just wanted to troll by placing ominous messages around. However, from what I've heard there are malicious hackers who want to ruin the experience by either speedrunning all the challenges or sabotaging by taking key items away, so do keep watch for unknown people joining your lobby (Pause Menu -> Moderation -> Session Details, all currently joined players are listed. I'm going off of memory, so the menu order could be wrong).

Overall, if you have a group of friends to play with (4+ is ideal, but duos and trios are still quite good), I'd say this is a solid pickup. It's the type of game where you would only play once, but have an enjoyable week with your friends with.

8.0/10. Twelve hours, two players, in-game voice only, no Discord, and we only looked up four puzzles in the whole thing.

Playing it honest is the point, because the puzzles are hard enough that you have to describe things to someone who can't see what you're seeing, and you're bad at that before you're good at it. By hour eight we had our own conventions, words for shapes that don't have words, a tone that meant "I've got this, stop helping." Hour eight was also when we got to the highest point on the island with all the towers lit and could see everywhere we'd been, which is probably the best thing I've done in a game this year.

The complaints are real though. For a game about walking, rocky ground will eat you, and you'll spend a while wedged between boulders or failing the same little climb four times. The gourds roll away and getting one back is stress with no puzzle in it. You can only carry one item until you find the backpack and two until the hip pouch, so go find those early. And it spends twelve hours building a mystery about who made this island, then has no plan to answer it, so go in knowing what you get is the walk.

Play it in as few sittings as you can, since only the host saves and every new session costs you momentum. Buy it for the specific person you're going to play it with. We came out liking each other more than we went in.

Big Walk was a great, lo-fi co-op experience, best summed up as an exploration game with puzzles akin to what you'd find playing an escape room.

With my playthrough consisting of 4 other friends, most of the puzzles did not feel too mind-bending or frustratingly challenging. They are more focused on collaboration and creative thinking, However, the final series of puzzles can certainly test groups of people. Overall, the game puts you in situations that get you to think about different modes of communication, so listen to friends and come up with ideas together!

Theres a few other things I wanna praise - starting with the sound design. The squeaky steps that your feet make on the sand, or rubbing your hand against the glass is an unneeded but amazing attention to detail. 
The explorable open world is a gorgeous location reminding me of trail walks in Tasmania and Western Sydney which I really appreciate.
A swell reminder that our most valuable moments with others can very well be found within the unexpected and ordinary occasions that we initially believed to lack significance.

I think there's very few perfect games in the world, and I think Big Walk is one of them.

In a way very few games are ever able to, it flawlessly executes what it sets out to do - being a lighthearted, discovery-and-adventure focused game to play with some friends. It features a world that starts small but feels big, and keeps getting bigger until it feels impossibly large, thoughtfully brought closer together by various ways to Big Walk a little less and never feel impossible or strenuous to traverse.

The puzzles are never alien or frustrating, but intuitive, fun to solve, and at their hardest still get that "eureka" dopamine hit when somebody figures out a mechanic you're missing. In many cases, they are more about communication and cooperation than they are about requiring exceptionally puzzle minded people - even the best of us who love puzzles and escape rooms found ourselves playfully yelling as we failed to describe the correct spiral shape we needed to across a walkie or a wall.

The puzzles became a way to direct where we walked, so that we could share moments together, whether that was game-driven incidents like falling off a cliff or shenanigans and pranks we played along the way. Megaphones became singalongs, glowing orbs became deities we refused to leave behind, maps were thrown in the sea because we preferred to get lost.

The "friendslop" (affectionately - I love the genre) boom results in a lot of games where the joy is in the chaos and the time limit. It's something special to get to engage in an experience so focused on unknown and discovery, on failing and problem solving with your friends, and taking your time be design to enjoy the world around you as you take thousands of plodding steps together.

It took me and my friends about 13 hours to complete. If your friend group is particuluary smart and organized, you could probably do it in 8

Each puzzle revolves around communication, either not being able to see your friends, not being able to hear them, both, or much more. Each puzzle HAS to be completed with your friends, with a few exceptions. Additionally, each puzzle is so well done, there was rarely one that didnt confuse us the first minute we looked at it. They are all a perfect level of difficulty that really makes you think.

You go across the island collecting "pears" as my group called them, and as you do you are more easily able to explore deeper into the island. 

GO IN BLIND. If you have a group you can spend a couple hours playing with once or twice a week, you'll have an amazing time.

I dont want to say anything else, except to play this with friends you love, or friends you want to get closer with. It has been a long, long time since a game has made me think, laugh, cheer, and get emotional as much as this game has. I'll remember playing this for a long, long time.

Deep Rock Galactic is one of my top favourite games because of the co-operative aspects, and I *love* playing with my friends most of all. That said, Big Walk is now definitely among my top 5. If you need a much more peaceful game experience and you just want to vibe with easy company, this is it. It is similar to PEAK in a few aspects:
*You explore.
*You talk via proximity chat.

Of course, this games comes without all the hazards of peak. What it does come with is a wide assortment of very creative and silly puzzles that can be solved in a multitude of ways, and even if you have already done that puzzle on another playthrough, the real replayability of this game is your friends. And you don't even have to do puzzles. There are plenty of ways to chill out and just relax. 

In most exploration games with proximity chat, getting lost and separated is generally very bad. However, in this game, getting lost is an aspect of the game that you must embrace - because it's not necessarily a bad thing. You can wander around and explore things the rest of your party hasn't, and there are so many ways to regroup with your friends anyway. You absolutely should not use a discord voice chat for this game, because it is very clear that the devs worked very hard on communication in this game, and I really admire that they made the text chat proximity based as well.

This goes on to my next point: sound design. I absolutely adore the sound design of this game. The sound is amazing. I love the squeaky sand (which apparently comes from Australian beaches - I didn't know that), I love how the glass sounds when you punch it with your fists. I love the popping noises of picking up signs and other objects. I love how the strength of your imminent throw is represented through intense rumbling and visual shaking. I could go on about the sounds, but it is a real treat.

The map design itself is awesome. I love the aesthetic of the characters mixed in with a semi-realistic environment. This adds so much character to the game. I love that when it is dark, you can still see the eyeballs of your friends' avatars, as if it were a cartoon. I love the visual design of the puzzles themselves. They are quite colourful, but not in an overwhelming way.

Most importantly (but not least), bring your friends. That is the whole point of this game. DRG is fun. Lethal Company is fun. REPO is fun. PEAK is fun. But those games all have share the same problem: you don't really get to *enjoy* your friends, at least not in the way this games allows. All of those are great games and are fun with friends, but if you need a break from danger and action - and dare I say frustration - this game is it. We needed a game like Big Walk. This game is cute, charming, and very clever. Absolute genius. Well done, House House.

review: I LOVE THIS GAME
It was phenomenal, it was emotional, and it was funny as hell. I don't regret a second of it.

In this post-covid era, I believe Big Walk came out in a perfect time where connections and interaction between friend and even family became lesser with how busy and messy the world right now unlike during covid where interaction and connection were something we really held onto because there wasn't much else we could do.

I think this game capture the essences of that connection we once experiencing during covid. My favourite part of this game is the atmosphere where you felt and experience the game it's like you were there in real life. From those sand sound to even the glass squeking noise.

After letting the ending sink in, I think if I were to characterize this game with one word it would be nostalgia

When you look back at where you started and see all those lantern paths being lit up, or the building lights that were left on, maybe from finishing a puzzle or failing it, it feels like looking back at memories. It reminds me that I was there. I experienced those moments. I struggled through those puzzles, laughed at the stupid moments, and eventually made it to the end.

It's not just that you finished a puzzle.
It's that you were there.

My only negative to this game in my opinion, is how the difficulty ramps up. The two-person and four-person gameplay feels very different with the four-person puzzles having a certain charm that the two-person puzzles don't quite capture.

If there were ever to be DLC for this game, I really hope some of that charm from the four-person gameplay could be distilled into the two-person experience. Not everyone has a large group of friends to play with, and I think bringing some of that magic into two-player would make the experience even better.

All in all, I think Big Walk is my favourite game I've played so far. It gave me an experience that I didn't know I was looking for, and I think the devs really delivered on what they set out to do

Big Walk is a deeply wonderful and unique experience. Playing it with fewer than four players is almost a disservice, if I'm being honest, as its less a "game" and more like a meditative hiking trip through a very big escape room.

I suggest picking one group to stick with for one entire playthrough before playing different sessions with different folks. Every group tackles this game differently and there's more to it than you'll likely see in one organic playthrough, so it's absolutely worth revisiting with new faces, but there is no getting back that feeling of seeing everything for the first time with a full squad of intrepid explorers.

While obviously this Big Walk was designed to be played with friends, it can't be understated just how much thought went into making this game a blast with friends. While initially a lot of the mechanics seem cumbersome (practically 0 inventory, low proximity mic range, the slow movement speed), once you get accustomed to it, they compliment each other nicely to let you slow down and just talk with your friends as you explore. 

I also really appreciate this was made with a definitive end. While i enjoy a lot of the "friendslop" games, I did get a little bit tired of them having no real end. It can feel sort of incomplete at times. Big Walk has a really nice ending that sort of exemplifies what this game is all about, and it feels like a complete journey that I thoroughly enjoyed.

Unfortunately, there will be some people who just bounce off of this. But if you have some friends who are patient and don't mind just chatting and walking around, this is a really good game to give a shot with them.

What's funny is that when I got this game, before playing it, I went on a 50-mile hike on the PNW coast for 6 days and then on the day that I got back, that's when I started playing (as if I hadn't already walked enough).
Big Walk itself is a game where you hang out, discover, explore, and puzzle-solve with friends. It's really simple. I only played it to full completion one time with a singular friend. Would I claim I've gotten the full experience that comes with playing with a group of 4+ people? No. But did him and I have a good time coordinating and puzzle-solving? Of course. Games like Big Walk are meant to be enjoyed methodically, slowly, and strategically, so I definitely feel like I had a good experience there.
The only nitpicky-type stuff I found while playing was that some puzzles are more tedious and time-consuming than puzzling. The puzzle where you [spoiler]have to bring the heavy ball allll the way across the entire map, one where you have to wait 30 minutes, and one where you have to bring the square tiles from all around the island [/spoiler] are so utterly grueling that the puzzles start to get almost frustrating in my opinion ([spoiler]I know 2 of the puzzles I mentioned are technically harder versions of existing ones and therefore not required[/spoiler]). Also, just some technical stuff: I wish voices were a bit louder (and you could hear people from further away) and I wish the game was a bit more optimized for pc.
Personally, I had a good time. If you're patient and like social, puzzling, non-friendslop games, this game is for you.

There's not a lot I can say about Big Walk that hasn't been said by people with better ways of writing reviews. House House has created a game that masterfully combines several enjoyable tropes - the thrill of exploration, the fun memories of being with friends, the mystery of being in a new world - into a neat little package that creates what is truly a unique gaming experience.

This is a game that can be played by any groups of people regardless of skill as long as they are able to communicate effectively. There are no big brain teasers or tests of dexterity. Everything comes down to how well you can play charades with a limited ways of explaining yourself. Because of this, the closer you are to the people you are playing with, the easier the game will be. That said, nothing was so difficult that my personal group couldn't immediately figure out what to do or how to arrive at an answer.

Beyond just what you do, the world you explore is so interesting and mysterious. Modeled after the beautiful Australian outback, there is seemingly something new over every hill and every corner. The thrill of this exploration is that over time you and your group come to memorize the land and make it your own. Nicknames for landmarks and items you encounter. Attention was clearly given to making sure that you enjoy being in that world. 

Beyond that, the enjoyment you get out of this game largely depends on your group. If you have people you can play with that are attentive and fun to be around, Big Walk will truly be a unique gaming experience you've never had before and will never forget. I know that that's the case for me.

This game is a 10/10. Wish I could wipe my memory and play it all over again with my friends, as it's one of the most enjoyable multiplayer gaming experiences I've ever had. 

At first glance, it seems like another cute friendslop game with prox chat. It is not. It is an open world puzzle adventure game, where you solve puzzles that requires you and your friends to communicate over distances where sound drop-off is a huge factor. Using poses, visual cues and clever-thinking, there are often multiple solutions to the puzzles you find. Usually, the theme is sound-based puzzles or sight based puzzles requiring some clever ways to communicate answers to one another. The map is incredibly well-designed and as you progress you uncover multiple new ways to traverse it, making it feel even more interconnected. You find things like backpacks and belt loops to store items on your person, but it requires another player to place them there or remove them. EVERYTHING in this game is designed to cause you to interact with your fellow players to make progress.

Half the fun of this game, is trying to formulate an objective with your friends to make puzzle progress, only for half the group to get distracted playing with flare guns or walkie-talkies, or riding the ski lift. You get impatient and try to go to the objective yourself and then you get lost. You try to find your friends again to no avail. You stumble upon a curious area with speakers playing vibey music and decide to watch the sunset. You ponder. 

It's dark now and you forgot to bring a flashlight. You wander through the darkness and hope to reach your friends. You see a flare get set off from a nearby tower, and stumble your way through the dark in hopes of reaching something familiar. The sound of walkie talkies being spammed and people RP'ing reaches you, the warm glow of a lightbulb ushers you into safety like a beacon, and you know you're home and safe again. 

And that's the game. Super meditative, puzzles requiring co-operation and AMPLE room for shenanigans to take place along the way. Many, many moments to simply sit, take in the view and vibe with your crew. 

These devs put so much thought, love and care into this game and it shows. The final run of puzzles to the end was such a delight. The initial "ending" was very sweet and wholesome. The 100% puzzle completion ending, even more so. Truly a gem of an experience that I wouldn't trade for anything. Thank you House House for creating such a lovely experience for your players.

Big Walk is technically a co-op puzzle game, but that undersells what it actually does.

Most puzzles are not difficult because the solution itself is obscure; the fun is figuring out how your group is going to communicate that solution. The group might stick together or spread across the island, and voice chat may be enough for one puzzle, while another requires an improvised system of your own.

That is probably what the game does best: it creates situations where [b]players have to improvise[/b]. Different groups will solve the same problem in different ways, and the puzzles are designed around that.

[h2]Puzzle solving[/h2]
Mechanically, [b]the puzzles are mostly simple but they work very well as social puzzles[/b]. Some ideas are repeated in different variants and a couple can get tedious, but even then our group usually found ways to solve them faster, or in increasingly stupid ways. Both were fun.

[h2]Exploration[/h2]
Exploration also works well. The island looks nice, especially around the sea, and there is enough going on between puzzles that [b]walking rarely feels like dead time[/b]. You chat on the train, lose items in ridiculous ways, fall somewhere stupid, or suddenly realize one teammate has disappeared.

[b]Getting separated is part of the fun[/b]. You might have to reunite without direct communication, or trust that whoever got lost is doing something useful somewhere. At night this becomes especially funny because it gets VERY dark.

Navigation is handled well. You are not buried in waypoints, but you gradually find tools. [b]It gives you enough information without making exploration automatic[/b].

[h2]Planning[/h2]
Movement is simple and mostly smooth, aside from occasionally getting briefly stuck around rocks or trees. The physics and random objects are more important because they give you room to experiment. [b]Even things that seem pointless can become useful[/b] if your group decides to include them in some unnecessarily complicated plan.

[b]Big Walk is also very forgiving of bad ideas[/b]. A stupid solution can take much longer than the obvious one and still be worth doing, because it becomes the version everyone remembers.

[h2]Group size and progression[/h2]
I played in a team of five. [b]Four probably feels ideal for most puzzles, but I can see larger groups working especially well[/b] when the team needs to spread out. I do not think the game depends on already having a long history of chemistry with your group.

Progression is handled nicely. The spawn area teaches you the essentials and most other things are left for you to figure out. [b]Later puzzles build on the communication habits your group has already developed[/b]. The last building is probably the best example... No spoilers. :)

[h2]What sticks with you[/h2]
The things you will remember most are not specific puzzle solutions. Rather, the accidents, bad plans, weird communication solutions and funny moments between people. Although those moments come mainly from the players, Big Walk is good at creating the situations that let them happen.

I was planning on buying this game the moment I saw the trailer, since I LOVED Untitled Goose Game and the House House devs / Panic team in general and wanted to support their next game. I've played this on all 3 'modes', with my partner as a duo, with a trio, and with 5-6 friends. I have currently finished one full playthrough with my duo at the time of this review.

I had TEARS finishing this game.. to the point I didn't WANT to finish it LOL. You will NEVER forget the emotions you experience during your first playthrough and I don't think I'll ever be able to replicate it. It is an unforgettable first experience, and I would do anything to re-experience it for the first time all over again.

This game challenges you to work together, think outside the box, and utilize empathy and self-regulation skills. As similar reviewers have expressed, this experience really is truly special with the right person/people. Everything from the simplicity and cuteness of the characters, the multiple methods possible to solve puzzles and goals by working as a team, to unique landscapes and scenery that favour slowing-down and taking things in. Along with a perfect and addictive variety of music creates a 
 one-of-a-kind, generational game. 

The different communication options, in verbal and non-verbal methods, was so polished and thought out with so much love and attention to detail. From arm signals, to the openness in creativity of how you choose to communicate with different items, the game challenges you to stop and think. The ending was such an overwhelmingly rewarding experience because it built-up EVERYTHING you learned throughout the entire game and tests that knowledge to see what you learned and if you were paying attention. I felt so much pride as all the hours paid off, and you can't describe the feeling you get when everything just clicks.

Lastly, as mentioned earlier and deserving of credit, the soundtrack really is the cherry on top of this entire experience. It is genuinely incredible and fits the vibes of the characters and setting. From the menu music to the stations, it is perfection. I have been listening to it outside of the game for weeks now. 

It's hard to describe but this feels like such an 'old-soul' style of game. You learn to appreciate downtime / taking your time. I honestly believe anyone who calls this game 'boring' does not understand the message behind it. There is no need to rush or zoom through challenges at all. With a timeline today where life and social media is so fast-paced and shortening our attention spans, this was such a breath of fresh air and teaches us to take a minute, slow down, and appreciate simple things.

Thank you so much for giving us such a genuinely rewarding gaming experience. It's evident that the devs created Big Walk with so much passion in mind for both gaming and friendship. THIS is what gaming with friends is all about. The option to do everything or nothing at all.. all at your own pace. Collaborate, learn together, separating and later reuniting with stories to share.

No true punishments, no ordered task-lists, and no restrictions. 

Overall a 10/10 unforgettable gaming experience with the right person/people. I will be voting and rooting for you guys and the lil' walklings at all incoming gaming awards!

I have a hard time making friends.

I'm neurodivergent. For a few years now I've been trying to expand my social circle, going to different get-togethers and events so I can get out of the house and talk to people. And it's working! I can actually talk to people in the same room and have interesting conversations (or just listen in and learn something new). One opportunity to shoot the breeze I remember fondly was about, of all things, John Waters, and whether his movies have still aged well.

I have a hard time keeping in touch.

I don't use Facebook anymore. I used to message my old classmates on that site, but eventually I lost connection with almost all of them. Sooner or later I want to delete that account, knowing full well I'll lose all contact with those people if I do. It made me think about if those people I shared a teacher with -- reading from the same books, doing the same homework, taking the same tests -- were actually my friends. Actually, what [i]is[/i] a friend?
After I have these in-person conversations, I usually forget the names of who I was talking to, exacerbated by my lack of social media, making further communication impossible until the next meetup. At least I have Discord. That's where most of my friends are, and it's easier that way because we don't have to talk face to face, just through text.

[i]But you didn't answer your question. What's a friend?[/i]
Easy now.

I have a hard time fitting in.

Most of the time, I'm not in a Discord server for very long because I feel like I don't belong there. It only takes a second for me to realize that these are the guys I'll be sticking with for the rest of my life, or that I'm sticking out like a rusty nail and I need to get out of there. With that in mind, I've found a small group of communities I can gel with, carefully curated from a lifetime of figuring out my tastes and my place in the world. I'm in one particular Discord server with a few friends. We've been somewhat active there for a while. When we saw the announcement trailer for this game it stood out from everything else. Something about the weird bird creatures drew us into this odd little world, and we knew the day the game came out we would jump right in, and that's what we did. Little did I know how such a simple little game could make me rethink my entire life... wait, I'm jumping the gun. Back on track. 
You play as these little bird dudes walking around this big island. On this island there are a lot of puzzles to solve. You have to communicate with your teammates to get through each puzzle, usually by talking. However, sometimes you have to talk to them in different ways, like light signals or flares, or through a walkie-talkie if you get separated from the party. It seems pretty simple on the surface.

I have a hard time finding solutions to a problem.

Even before I started gaming, I was a puzzle freak, and for a short while I was really into Mensa. Yeah, the high IQ group. I never took their test, though. Does anyone remember when they made decks of cards that had 75 puzzles apiece on them? They had word puzzles, number puzzles, logic puzzles, "riddles and conundrums"... for some reason I was really into those things and I carried them around everywhere I went, like a comfort object. I guess I was more happy that I had them in my hand or my pocket rather than actually solving the puzzles on the cards. Not here. We enjoyed savouring our aha moments, rejoiced when everything came together, and flailed our arms in celebration waiting for the apple to fall (Yeah, we call those red things apples.)
Big Walk isn't primarily a puzzle game. You don't teleport to another location on the island when you finish one. You have to go the long way, walking across the terrain. You may as well chat it up with your group. That's where the real beauty of the game lies. It's those moments in between, where you talk about how you came up with your solution... and then drift off into anything else that's on your mind. It's a game about sticking together and knowing each other better. My friends aren't really one for deep conversations, and that's okay. Goofing off is what we do and that's what makes us happy. There was one particular puzzle (if you know you know) which devolved into a "therapy session" involving throwing chairs and rubbing our hands on the glass after we realized it makes a funny noise. We're just a few dudes clowning around.

I have a hard time sticking with the pack.

I think I got lost the most out of everyone else in the group. During one long trek to regroup with them, a thought came to mind. These guys really are my friends. I may not be into the same games or media that they are, but just being in their presence and getting a little silly was what made me feel like a part of their own little world. I'm the guy in the corner who tries to mull things over in my head and then suddenly runs up to the others telling them about the epiphany I had. I'm the guy who just wants to cheer everyone on.

I have a hard time letting go of things.

The pit in my stomach is still there a day after we finished the game. I wish I could experience Big Walk for the first time again. I wish I could wipe it from my mind and take my sweet time wandering around and embracing the scenery. I wish I could be amused again when we first trod across the squeaky sand.
Before I wrote this review, I sat down at my computer and thought about the adventure we had. Then I thought about how it ended. It fills me with some dread at first. These friendships are ephemeral. They're not gonna last forever, but we like to believe they will. It's not how long these friendships last, it's what we do with them. Knowing that there has to come a time when our journey on the island will come to an end makes me wish the moment was longer, becoming a shiny glass tube stretching out on both sides into infinity. Then it explodes like a Prince Rupert's drop, in pieces on the ground, never to return.
I stared at the screen for a few moments, thinking about how wonderful this friend group really is. We each played our part, we screwed up, we fixed it. All of us together, enjoying the moment on our big walk. I knew that we would be sticking around for a long time after. I was genuinely happy I found the people I belonged with. I finally fit in.

I still see the birds in my dreams.

And [i]that[/i], dear reader, is what a friend is.

This game was so special. I had mixed feelings before starting this game with the worry of it potentially being a bit too boring for me and my low attention span. I was entirely wrong. This game was so full of lighthearted fun and had me a bit emotional as we reached the end. I can definitely see how this game would not be for everybody but I think it's definitely worth giving it a shot. More than anything, I think the people you play it with make all the difference. I played with my two best gaming friends and it just makes it so much more fun. It's so much different than playing other games that are more action heavy. One of our fondest memories is actually the 30-minute patience test where had our "therapy" session and actually ended up playing "never have I ever".

Of course this game is not perfect structurally. The first issue I came across was getting stuck almost too often. It felt very challenging to walk through terrain at some points due to the characters getting snagged on rocks and random pieces of ground that we didn't think were actually too steep to climb. Alongside that, if you try to jump when you get stuck, its basically impossible. It feels like the jump mechanic gets locked when you're stuck making it really tough to move or get out. The second issue I found was with the voice chat feature. Now, this could be entirely based off the microphones of my friends but I did find at times that it was almost impossible to hear someone even if they were right next to me. It was not a consistent issue, and again, could be related to their personal audio. Third, my group felt that the daytime nighttime cycle was a bit disproportionate. It felt as though nighttime was 2-3 times as long as daytime. My only other comment - not entirely a complaint - was about the puzzles themselves. I do wish there was a bit more variation in the puzzles instead of multiple of the same ones. I am a big puzzle game fan so that may just be my preference. 

Other things like getting lost, places taking a while to get to or to complete, etc. are definitely all on us and how we chose to engage with the map. I do love that there were more puzzles than required for all the towers and not secluding all puzzles to one specific tower to encourage a bit more freedom of choice of what puzzles you wanted to do and when. I also loved the addition of challenge puzzles. It was such a fun surprise to see the purple peanuts? blobs? kongs??? The items to collect and use along the way were super fun - despite us often choosing to carry and orb light instead. I loved the tunnel feature and the little rave surprise! Most of all, the black ball was so much fun! We were unsure what to expect going into it but were so locked in working out way up the sphere. The end was super and sentimental and its the those details I really appreciate in a game. Thank you for allowing us to sit together one last time talk about the fun we had. I hope everyone gives this game a try and have yourself a relaxing big walk. My 2026 GOTY!

Im 20 as of writing this, Ive had bad years in my life but Ive been currently going through an incredibly bad one, going through a blindside break up, loosing my grip on what it meant to be "me", trying to find my purpose in life and then having to walk away from my friend group of 4 years.
