My older sister who wrote a review just before mine, told me to get this and we would play a group of 3, My sister, My sisters friend who lives in America (Im European) and me. 
The few things Ive looked forward to in my life currently have been, playing Big walk with a stranger and my sister, therapy and  driving lessons. I wont explain why I look forward to the last 2 as its not really the point of this review, but big walk, was the only thing that made me laugh again, and properly laugh. It made me feel that I wasnt alone, even though there was only 3 of us within this large island, we filled it with our laughter, our voices and the pitter patter of our feet as we marched onwards into our next challenge. Ive played "friendslop" before, with my old group, yeah it was fun at times but we regularly got heated at eachother, or I would feel bad for not being good enough at the game, in one game, I got stuck always playing the engineer as that was the job nobody else wanted and I was the only one willing enough to fill that role (the game was barotrauma, my self-made title was reactor-bitch), after a while we would move on to other games, like competitive shooters. 

This was the only game that never made me like I was less than somebody else, that I was struggling to keep up with my group or actively holding them back. The game is designed in such a way where performance isnt based on something like aim or movement tech, but on communication. There is no punishment for failing, only the opportunity to have a laugh and trying again. I never was stuck in a role, or stuck in a loop of failing. There is a challenge, for the sake of the game I wont say what it entails, but when you reach it, if you reach it, do NOT pick up your phone and start scrolling, just sit through it with your group, it is the PERFECT litmus test (props to you House House, very clever). In the 3 player version of the game, there is no challenge that a single person can do alone. Each one requires everybody. The puzzle is too difficult? There's puzzle skipping, don't have it enabled? just take a detour, do different puzzle and try again later. I dare to say that this game is almost perfect.

I have the privilege of saying that I played this game at the time of my life where I needed to play it, not when I wanted to. I also have the privilege of saying that this game is more than worth the price tag and that it thought me things that I needed to learn that this point in time, and thought me things that I believed I had lost within myself. More importantly, Big walk thought me that I was never alone while playing it, my new friend might hundreds of kilometers away, but we shared this experience together, My sister and I did as well, all three of us deserved to walk to the credits of the game. And you should too, with the right group. 

Yes, the game has a lot of walking. No, there isnt a battle pass and there arent levels to grind. Yeah, its incredibly refreshing to play this game and lastly, yeah i fucking cried at the end of it, i had to get up off my lazy ass and go hug my beloved sister. This game genuinely helps you get closer to the people you play with and it helped me find a part of myself that I thought I lost for good. Be good to eachother and please enjoy this game.

After playing through Big Walk with three friends, I can say this is one of the most uniquely special games ever made. I don't know what I was expecting when I heard the creators of Untitled Goose Game were making a big multiplayer game that used voice chat to explore a mysterious island, but this is one of the memorable gaming experiences of my life.

So much thought went into the design of the island, the design of every puzzle, the sound design, the end game, and pushing the constraints of proximity voice chat and the limited (but surprisingly flexible) gestures. Even though we all looked like weird little blobby guys, I've never felt so immersed in a game before. I wanted to stay in there, hanging out with friends, sitting by the beach, waiting for the sun to rise.

I don't want to spoil anything, but I'll just say that this game was meant for four players. You can play it with two or three, but the puzzles are too simple and minimalist, and you can't really split into groups. 4-6 is ideal. You'll want to play with the same core four people from start to finish if you can.

House House made this game for groups of friends, not strangers, and I think that's the way to go too. The hardest part of this game was getting four dads to hang out a couple hours a night over a couple weeks, but we made it work. By the end, I think we all felt closer because of it.

I didn't expect that kind of progression in the game, which was unexpected but not a negative.

The game has lots of fun puzzles and things to discover, and the game feels very grounded. It often gets you and your friends to just be in the moment, rather than constantly be focused on just progressing. The puzzles also often put that to the test, while also testing you and your friends ability to communicate, with the game also offering a lot of different ways for you and your friends to communicate, other than just speaking. I do wish the voices in the game were slightly louder though, or at least offered some way to increase the volume. Both me and my friends felt it was often hard to hear eachother even when standing just about a meter from each other in game. I do get that they wanted to limit how much you can speak so that you are urged to use other tools to communicate, but that short of a distance limiting your ability to hear felt a bit extreme. Although while the puzzles are fun, I will say that there are a few puzzles which I did feel was reused way too many times. I won't mention what or why, for the sake of not spoiling it, but you'll know it if you play it.

The graphics of the game is okay, it's definitely unique, with partially being realistic and partially being stylised. I like the style, however I do have to mention that the graphics is nowhere near good enough to justify the performance this game demands. Sure, my PC is closer to mid tier these days, but I've seen Roblox games that look more graphically impressive than this game, and my PC is absolutely roaring playing this game. This leads me to believe that this game likely isn't very well optimised, and instead might be built on the assumption that it will be played on a high tier PC, an assumption which would be weird since this genre of games are very oftenly played on low tier PCs.

Overall I would definitely recommend this game, it's a lot of fun and is one of the more unique gaming experiences I've had in some time now. Personally, I'd rate this game a 7/10, and I would have rated it higher if the performance of the game was better, and there was just a few less of the repetitive puzzles. But if you have a high tier PC and don't mind a few repetitive puzzles, then this would probably be an 8 or a 9 out of 10 for you.

These are questions I held in my head the entire time I was playing it. And then 2 unbroken weeks straight passed where we played the game for multiple hours each night.

Big Walk knows EXACTLY what it is. It is very clear the team at House House created a super specific design philosophy meant not to challenge, frustrate, or farm for funny moments, but instead make you communicate with your friends. Every puzzle is a communication challenge. Every WALK is a communication challenge. Sometimes you are on a train or ski-lift and you have nothing to do but talk. Sometimes the devs lock you in a room with nothing to do but talk. And every single time any of this happens, it is nothing but a treat. 

Big Walk took our group averaging around 6 people about 11 hours to complete, with an ending that left a few people in our group teary-eyed. I didn't know that was possible in a non-story driven game. It then took another 11 hours to fully complete the game.

Completing the game left my group with only one thing left to say: "I can't wait to do it again"

[h1] Sometimes, you just need to take a walk. [/h1]

Whether the experience is something profound to you, or just another way to hang out with your friends/family one more time, Big Walk is a game where it's up to you to find enjoyment in something seemingly pointless: there's no enemies to kill, no big reward to chase. Just a place to explore with things to find, and the freedom to go wherever and however far you wish.

The game isn't here to grab you by the eyeballs and throw you into some [i] grand adventure [/i] you'd be a fool to miss out on. It's here to be a place for you and the people you enjoy spending time with to have another opportunity to do just that: spend time together. 
The ways you communicate, joke, plan, and more are unique things only [i] you [/i] can experience in the moments you share. Every step, every word, and every approach is part of the journey you share with whomever you chose.

Maybe you just want to goof around with your friends for a while. Perhaps you and a sibling haven't had a chance to spend much time together in years. Maybe there's people from far away you'd wanted to spend some time hanging out with. 
Whatever the reason, big or small, this game easily landed itself as my favorite way I've spent time with people online.

It reminded me of being younger, when the things I would do for fun didn't need to help me master a skill or earn an accolade. No need to feel cool, or skilled, or smart. A joyous moment could be as simple as frantically waving my arms at a friend from afar, and seeing them wave back in the same erratic manner. It's laughing together when something dumb happens, or idly chatting while you're walking from one place to another. It's sharing that "oh shit" look when the thing you needed rolls down the mountain and out of sight. It's struggling to figure something out and shooting ideas back and forth. It's taking a moment to rethink your approach when what you were doing wasn't working at first.

Some of the best memories are the simplest ones, memories of just having experiences together. If you want to have a few more, Big Walk has my enthusiastic recommendation for your next adventure.

review:
My group hit credits yesterday on Big Walk after 14.4h of game time, though we have more content left to do. Lots to say about it, but I'm struggling to put it into words in a way that fits a Steam review. Here's a gist.

Big Walk is a unique, very well crafted experience that derives its concept from the combined aspects of social interaction, immersion and physicality that defines the newly born 'friendslop' genre and executes it beautifully. Playing Big Walk with my friends felt to me like being on a real trip with them. Yet its appeal isn't just a gimmick: the puzzles that make up the progression of the game are plentiful and engaging, and they tie perfectly with the rest of the experience, making the game worth its price for your friend group.

There's not a lot to nitpick about in such a cleanly designed, focused game that meets its goals so well; though I will remark on the limited settings available. There's no way to adjust individual voice volume for other players, nor are there separate graphics settings, only presets. I also experienced some small graphical bugs, mainly flickering lighting in some situations, which could be due to me playing on Linux. Some of my friends had issues connecting to our lobby a couple times as well. These issues were incredibly minor in my enjoyment of the game, and some of the lacking settings can be made available using mods.

This may sound odd and uselessly dramatic, but I think Big Walk may earn itself a small place in the history books. Friendslop (I've started liking the name) is a budding genre that people still struggle to agree on a definition for. Some might say genres are fake and bad and we shouldn't care about them anyway, but I think they have an importance both to consumers looking to find more games with the elements they enjoy, and to anyone who wants to hone in on what makes a certain set of games special, what gives them their unique appeal. Big Walk, by being friendslop without following the usual run/match-based structure found in other defining friendslop games, helps codify the term by keeping their unique aspects as the sole common denominator and making them the focus: minimalism, physicality, dynamic social interaction, emergence. I like these games a lot because of those factors, so I am happy that this is happening. 

I think we'll remember Big Walk for a long while, and I think there will be more games that will follow suit and do some of the things it's doing.

Absolutely love this game. The visuals are nostalgic, with the beautiful realistic environments paired with the simple abstract artificial structures, like those exercise machines found on nature trails.
The sound design is soft and light, with the sounds of nature in the environments, and very playful in regards to character and object interactions. The music invokes a sense of wonder, silliness, and sometimes even comfort.
There's a lot of walking (that's a good thing), and while there are modes of transport, it doesn't take away from the vastness of the world, nor make it feel like an automatic faster option compared to walking there yourselves.
The puzzles are very engaging. I feel the puzzles are actually a great way to build communication skills with people, and they are applied in an appealing way that doesn't make new tasks feel too difficult, but instead prompts the want to understand and find a way to solve it.
No spoilers, but especially near the end, moments of the game feel kind of ominous, which only made me more curious and want to do more. I love how the game never directly tells you what your goal is, you more so explore and figure out pretty much everything on your own, making the game feel very fulfilling.
Only personal negative remarks is that there was one puzzle we avoided because we struggled to find a reasonable way to solve it, the puzzle in question being one with lights(?) facing many different directions, that when activated, will show a random amount of faces that you have to count, and then put the correct number into the answer box. There was only two of us, so we weren't confident we could correctly do it on our own, thus we avoided it.
That being said, I again love the open exploration approach with how the game never forces you to do anything, it's more like you're on a grand adventure with your friends, seeing what the world has to offer, enriching yourselves with little puzzles and picturesque biomes. :D

review:
I really enjoyed it.

I loved how the game made you interact with your friends while also letting you just sit back and talk. There were no timers, and nothing forced you to go to the next mission. If you and your friends just wanted to sit on the beach and watch the sun rise or set, that was totally fine. The map was kept relatively plain so you could focus on spending time with your friends.

With jobs and responsibilities, you don’t get a lot of time to spend with friends. Even when you do get to game together, it’s often a shooter or another fast-paced game where you’re locked in and talking about the game rather than your real lives. Here, you could work through problems together while still having time to talk about your lives and relationships.

And when the game did get down to business, the puzzles were great. They made you find new ways to work together. You had to put your brains together to solve a problem. You and your friends got to cooperate, enjoy yourselves, and work towards a common goal.

I also enjoyed the vastness of the map, which gave us plenty of time to talk.

My only criticism is that some of the puzzles were quite easy. If we could get a hardcore mode or something, that would make this game a 10/10 for me.

review:
It’s rare that you find a game that delivers as perfectly on its vision as Big Walk does. If we judge a game by how well it executes on the thing it sets out to do, this one is essentially flawless, a masterpiece.

The first thing Big Walk does is present you with [i]instructions[/i].
“Big Walk is a game about talking to your friends,” it reads whilst asking you to test your microphone volume. “Once you begin, Big Walk should be the only way that you communicate, so please: No voice calls, no talking face-to-face, no looking at other players’ screens. Thanks, House House”.
It’s a surprisingly candid request on the part of the developers, and sure, there’s no safeguards in place to stop you from defying it. But make no mistake, this message [i]is[/i] a compass pointing directly to the best experience possible.

Big Walk manages to excel at two things. One is capturing the essence of nature in Australia, and the other far more impressive one is to give you and your friends a platform to have a good time together; the puzzles littered throughout the game are merely a means to that end. 
You could also argue that point number two is the whole conceit of the “friendslop” genre, but Big Walk is so much more. It’s a defined experience, a campaign, that you go through together, but it’s built in such a way to really draw those experiences out. We played in a group of five and had an amazing time all together, but often Big Walk will require you to split off into smaller groups to complete objectives or maybe just fetch an item and bring it back. 
Some of the best moments of Big Walk are actually going on Little Walks with one friend - out of proximity of your teammates, being able to just have a small, quiet conversation as you traverse the landscape. And it’s not like this is a super secret conversation or even one related to the game at all, but just like - “Hey man, how’s life been?”.
In my playthrough, one of these Little Walks came about because a puzzle’s design encouraged the group splitting up to complete the objective much faster, so me and one friend took off on our little sidequest. We’d both had busy lives lately, less time to play games lately - much less together - so we’re just having a grand yap, completely oblivious to the fact we were heading in entirely the wrong direction. We got very, [i]very[/i] lost, it was extremely funny when we realized what we’d done, and this was a [i]highlight[/i] of my 16 hours with the game. Journey, not destination.

And that brings Big Walk to its biggest hurdle: This is a game that [i]must[/i] be played with friends - actual friends with bonds between you. It cannot be played solo in any capacity, and there is no matchmaking system in any form. Sure, you could go onto a Discord server and LFG, but I can’t imagine playing this with strangers would be a great experience. In that scenario I described earlier, unless you absolutely win the LFG lottery, getting lost feels like an inefficiency; potentially even wasting time. You might even be berated by the rest of the group for making them wait. It might still be a [i]good[/i] game played that way, sure - it’s still very well designed no matter what - but it certainly wouldn’t be [i]special[/i]. And the game I played was incredibly special.

Big Walk is a unique, joyous experience that only wants to make sure you and your friends have a great time. Grab people you care about, respect the requests the game makes of you at the start, and set aside around 15 hours. Enjoy working together to solve the puzzles, stopping for a minute to take in a sunrise together, occasionally steal a key item from your friend and boot it off a cliff for a laugh. Just enjoy this space purpose-made for you to enjoy each other’s company.
I mourned our playthrough when it was over, and I am supremely jealous of anybody who still has this experience in front of them. 
Just an absolute triumph of a game that I expect we’ll be talking about for years to come.

I don't usually write actual reviews for games but this is an exception.

I played this game with my childhood best friend (K) and their partner (L). Me and K have been best friends since fourth grade, and both of us are in our first year of college together at the moment.
I was a bit skeptical of this game simply because of the "friendslop" games that have been coming out at nausium but both K and their partner had gotten it for free and I was able to get it at a discount, so I thought why the hell not. 
My first thought was how unique the game looked, and how much you really had to rely on your friends for the entirety of it. We didn't play it every other night, we just played it when we could. With me moving away for college in just a couple weeks, all the packing, prepping, and time I spent seeing my friends in person didn't let us have a lot of time to play it all the time. When we did though, it was so much fun. 
I was the designated map girl, if that's important to this review.
As time went on, we couldn't finish the game by the time college for me came around. Moving 2 hours away from home was a big change, and there was a lot of things I had to get used to, and so I didn't have time to play this with them, but I always thought about it.
I major in aviation, flight operations specifically. This made me busy during my first two weeks of school alongside me having to sign up for clubs I was interested in such as photography and an honor group for aviation.
This second week of school I had the time to play big walk for the weekend, and it was on the day I'm writing this review we finished it.
The black orb for me was emotional. Not being able to hear each other or even know whose who was an odd departure from the norm the game presented, but it was interesting.
We could only use hand signs and body language we developed through doing these puzzles together, and in the end it didn't take us long to complete it. Once we finally realized we could hear each other then, we already started getting emotional.
K has been one of the only people in my life that I could say is one of my best friends, I've known them for what feels like my entire life and there hasn't been a time where we weren't close.
Although L only became K's partner in the past year, I've still gotten close to them naturally. I would say they're also a close, if not best friend of mine.
Once we got to the end, where it was the door leading to the light, they said they couldn't enter into it, and I realized I could. The sign right before told me the controls on how to wave, and I realized what it was.
One person at a time, waving goodbye at the rest before they leave to go on their own journey. One after the other leaving to live their life, but not forgetting the people who are behind them.

I almost cried when I finished this game, because when I looked back at L & K, it reminded me of how I left them, I left them to go on my own journey, paving my own future in college. But despite how far I am from them, they'll always be behind me.

So, I've played 30 hours in this game on a server hosted by my partner. We opened it up to a couple other friends on occasion, but for the most part it was the two of us. I had a beautiful time learning the puzzles with them, it wouldn't have been the same if it was anyone else. Learning the mechanics of the game together, finding each other when we got lost, figuring out how to communicate when we may not have words or visuals or body language or something else we may usually choose to use... it was all a lot of fun. 

Some notes from my experiences:
 == The Puzzles ==
Some of the puzzles we thought would be easy were challenges, some of the ones we avoided for looking challenging were a breeze. Some of the ones we tried to rush took a long time, some of the ones we thought would be tedious went by quick. There's no real judging the ease of a task at a glance.

You CAN finish the game without completing every puzzle, and you can avoid the ones you feel will be tedious if you want. However, if you're going to see the game to the "Big Ending", Every puzzle NEEDS to be completed. 

That being said, you do not have to complete a puzzle the first time you try them. If you start a puzzle and realize you're fundamentally on different wavelengths with your partner, it's GOOD to take a step back, reconvene, and talk about where the fatal error is and how to resolve it. Additionally, don't be afraid of throwing around the puzzle materials. Everything that isn't being held by a player will reset to its original position when the server is closed and opened again.

 == Environment ==
Me and my QPR live in a more arid place, so the environment in the game is pretty familiar to us (though with more trees). Maybe it's because it's a more familiar type of environment, but I really felt at home in the game. The graphics aren't groundbreaking, but the textures are beautiful. The puzzles stand out against the landscape by being really sleek and vibrant, but I don't feel like their inclusion takes away from the nature aspect.

Now, idk if I would say I'm disabled, but I will say that walking half a mile in the sun has given me heart palpitations so bad I thought I was dying once. Either way, I am not the kind of person who SHOULD be going on hikes irl, at least not until I sort whatever is happening to my body out. Being able to share this experience in, what feels like, nature was kind of beautiful. As wonderful as it would have been if it was real life, it was excellent as the 'next best thing'. 
I do recommend this game for people who like the beauty of nature, but feel held back from truly enjoying it from a lot of the aches, pains, and possible health issues it can bring with it. Someone who really wants to BE in nature may feel insulted by the simulacrum; you won't be able to feel the wind or the temperature in the game (which may feel jarring), there is no mechanic to scale rocks, you cannot see birds, bugs, or any other animals (though you can hear them), I don't think the moon will rise at night, no way to set trails, and no survival mechanics. 
That being said, that just means this game won't satisfy you if you're only looking to buy it for some of these things. At least from my pov, it was excellent without it. Just... keep in mind that if you're looking to buy this for a disabled friend who wants to go on a hike in real life, they may feel somewhat disappointed if its missing anything they feel is quintessential to their experience feeling "right".

 == Navigation ==
My partner has a kinda... Unfortunate internal sense of direction, and while mine is great, I have a tendency to wander off. It is intentional game design that sound doesn't travel very far between players, so it's easy to lose someone if you don't have a way to keep track of them. 
Now, we played with just two people. I can't attest to the ease of keeping track of other players if you get 11 of your closest buddies together. Sound-wise, there are portable radios and megaphones you can carry if you need to communicate in a pinch. If you want to make your location known, ANY light is good at night, just flash it a bunch and if you're in line-of-sight you'll be spotted instantly. I will say that keeping track of where stationary flares & radio sets are can be a godsend in a pinch. If you've given up on finding your partner, trek to the nearest flare and signal your location. 
If you're comfortable always keeping something in your hand, you may have an easier time than we did, but personally, carrying something all the time would make me anxious that I'd lose or forget it. Our method was essentially to put me on a leash; we got a backpack, stuck a radio attuned to a music station on it, and my partner was able to tell if I started to wander off bc the music would suddenly start to fade. It wasn't a perfect system, but it gave them assurance I wasn't too far if I was out of sight.
Other than that, I would say that it was REALLY easy to find our way around the environment. There's a handheld map you can study and a room-sized map that tracks your progress for you. Most things that are color-coded also have shapes that are specific to them, so your colorblind friends don't have to worry. There's large towers at different points of the map that can act as waypoints; if you ever feel lost, you can find your way by scaling it off the location of the tower. This is another bonus to the puzzle rooms being bright and unnaturally shaped, they made them easier to find on the map.

This game can be a challenge if you have a set goal, but it's not your enemy.

 == Sound Design ==
I spent 90% of my time playing this game with a radio strapped to my hip, and lemme say the soundtrack for this game is beautiful. Idk if there's anything else to say. It's completely original music with no lyrics and eccentric instrumentation (didn't hear any wind, string, or percussion instruments I recognize if memory serves), and it works incredibly well with the environment around it.
Sound design is an essential part of the game. Part of the premise of Big Walk hopes that you'll be able to listen, and encourages it with the proximity chat being the only encourages method of communication for the game. While you may only be putting on your headphones to hear your buddy, the nature sounds are Stunning, they really help to ground the environment. I'm pretty sure they play different animal sounds depending on the area, too, which helps to really section the map in your mind.

 == Silly Anecdote ==
My partner and I are both OCD (not a metaphor), which presents in different ways. For the most part, we're very understanding about the other's preferences and are able to navigate doing things in a way that makes us both happy. The BIGGEST argument we got into during the ENTIRE game was AFTER finishing the final puzzle. It was over them wanting to put a tool in a circle & me taking it OUT of the circle bc I wanted to stand the thing up vertically and we didn't realize what the other person was trying to do. It lasted 2 minutes and we spent the rest of the game laughing about it.
That being said, if that was the biggest conflict we had during the entire 30 hour period we played this game, even though we both have a clinical diagnosis that's bound to butt heads (as it did here) about particularities, I want to emphasize how Good this game is at fostering communication and making you sit down and reflect. The game wants you to get along, and everything about it is like... MADE to make you feel at least a little at peace. Don't quote me on that, lol, maybe my partner is just the best and I'm attributing too much to the game <3

I don't usually write reviews on Steam, but Big Walk is genuinely one of the best gaming experiences I've ever had (Nier Automata, you're still up there!). 

I had the absolute pleasure of playing this with nine close friends at launch, and then completing the game with three of those same friends and we all loved it. I got really emotional after finishing it. I don't want to share my own experience with it or spoil it, as I think that's one of the major appeals with seeing this game till the end. Trust me, it is so so worth it.

In your group of however many are playing (minimum is 2, and maximum is 12...!), you complete really well-crafted puzzles which scale depending on how many people are playing on the save file of the host. You do some major big walking and take in the Australian scenery (this game is based on a real place! - Wilson's Prom). [spoiler] To help with big walking and traversing the map, you can unlock and take the train, or a gondola (ski lift) if that's more your thing.[/spoiler] These all take you around to coloured towers that aid you in completing the game. Each tower has a certain number of gourd-like objects (my friends called them babushkas, some folks call them babies, nipples, dolls, whatever picks your fancy) that you fill up, usually 6, which itself makes a very satisfying sound!

There are items that aid with helping to communicate over large distances from your friends to solve puzzles, but I think one of the unique aspects with the puzzles themselves is you can find your own way to solve them based on your own terms set out by yourself or your group of friends.

From the outside, this game seems like it's another "friendslop" experience, (which I personally don't agree with) but when you start playing, and getting in to the environment, you overlook this label and see that this game is something else entirely. Nothing at all like "slop". You take in the time you spend with your friends in game and it is a genuine joy. In terms of communicating in game, there is, of course your voice, and a text-chat, which keeps messages above your player for around 20-30 seconds. I have used it once in a playthrough, which only shows up when you're nearby players, otherwise it shows up as (inaudible).

I want to give a brief shoutout to the wonderful sound design and music. The ambience and music of the world really adds so much to this game. The voice effects of your fellow walkers when you're in certain rooms delay, echo, reverberate and muffle, all of which sound incredible, which is why in-game prox chat is a must.

There can be funny moments of course, you're spending time with your friends in game (our group done torch rituals at 2:30am, telling scary Watchmojo stories at a campfire, along with other silly shenanigans that I'm not going to share). [b]You will have your own experiences that will be entirely unique with your friends during your playthrough.[/b] [i](Or random fellow big walkers - shout-out to r/bigwalk's LFG threads).[/i] The whole experience of the game is a journey. Completing puzzles with your friends, but having to rely on each other for pushing buttons, or doing communication through certain puzzles, and the sheer joy with a blast of confetti as you complete a puzzle. Then collecting the gourd-like object to aid in filling up the coloured towers which draw you closer to completing the game, bit by bit. It seems silly at first, but as you progress with the game, the discovery of new areas and landmarks you come across is wonderful. You can tell the small development team put a lot of love and care into the placement of things.

Once again, I'm not going to spoil the ending of this game, as I personally think you should go in blind to it. It's such a special, emotional experience, and is worth all the effort of completing the puzzles with your friends (or random big walkers) by your side.

Thank you, House House, for crafting an amazing game that has now become a core memory for me.

Edit: it's November 2026, and I still regularly think of this game. What an experience!

The Big Bore - People are obviously allowed to like what they like. And judging by other reviews, this game seemed widely enjoyed and rated oftentimes as 'the best game of this genre'. Everyone appeared to be having deep chats and finding out more about themselves, creating deep and meaningful bonds with their friends. So we all buy the game, and play it for some time. And the challenges are OK, but ultimately require a lot more menial walking across empty land than we would have liked (that may be on us, given the title of the game).

Most of the clips I had seen of the game were really the only exciting (used very liberally) moments. Otherwise, we were forced to stay right next to each other in order to be able to communicate through game chat. This is where the Big Talks are supposed to occur, and throughout the playthrough, we tried our best to keep the conversation going, but this is a group who play very regularly - deep chats can and have been had in other dynamics (Discord, which is free, real life??) and nothing about this game really cultivated anything deeper than some coordination and teamwork at times.

After about an hour, we got ready for the second level, and until then nothing had been said about the game, yet we all unanimously agreed it was time to request a refund. The game isn't the worst game ever, but it was not fun. People may say "you clearly didn't play with the right people" or "you went into this game with a negative mindset". We were excited to play this, and we ended up disappointed. The premise people should pay £15 to play a game so devoid of pace, in a lifeless setting only alleviated by your friends who have to be directly next to you or else you won't hear them, is silly. 

On a separate note, this isn't a dig at the developers, myself and friends absolutely love PEAK. It's a great game. What drove me to write this review was the flocks of people harping over this game as if playing it awakens some deep bond between yourself and your friends. Please!

Big Walk is an uniquely fantastic coop puzzle game for 2-12 people (who aren't in the same room as each other!).

Without spoiling too much you're left to roam an Island to find and solve puzzles using proximity chat, various poses and a lot of teamwork to solve (usually) relatively simple puzzles. If that's something that sounds fun, and you have people to play with, you probably don't need to know any more to go check it out.

I will say the game is purposefully slow, the island takes a long time to get across, there's points to stop and reflect, the game is as much about those moments between puzzles with friends as it is about solving the puzzles themselves but I can see that being frustrating for anyone who just wants to get the game done as quickly as possible.

You can set up the puzzles to be solvable by 2, 3 or 4+ players and you can play with up to 12 players, we did the whole game with just two of us and had a great time throughout, there's not too much replayability though, so hopefully we get a sequel, or something similar, from the devs in the future!

[h1]Big Game, Big Heart[/h1]

[b]Big Walk[/b] is a game with a shocking amount of depth and thought put into despite its simple premise: Explore the island and solve puzzles scattered throughout, preferably with close loved ones who you can consider family. Completing the game together from front-to-back seems to have this effect where bonds will strengthen and will make you appreciate life and the company of one another more than ever, something not many games ever achieve.

Despite being a puzzle game, arguably the most important aspect of the game is the exploration. There is a lot of quiet time in-between puzzles and this is where many of the greatest moments tend to occur, assuming you are with the right people. The island is beautiful, there is a lot to see, and it gives you time to hangout and talk about literally anything. The exploration is non-linear, giving you total freedom to see  That's what makes the game special; The nothingness and atmosphere of it all. It's clear that [b]House House[/b] designed it with a lot of intent and thought despite being so simple.

The puzzles, the part that people may associate the game with more. They are insanely well-made and, while not incredibly hard, are designed for teamwork and communication like no other. Every single time I found a new puzzle with my sisters, we were excited to check it out and see what type of challenge they'll present to us because each one was so different from the other.  While not every puzzle was a homerun (ex. coordinate puzzle), they were so intensely outnumbered by the amount of banger puzzles that it didn't affect the game for me. They were the definition of fun, probably the funnest puzzles I've ever experienced in any game ever.

There is also another aspect to the game that isn't talked about much: The soundtrack. It's very poignant, and some of the radio stations play some gorgeous tracks that almost make you contemplate life. Listening to the music now after completing it is very emotional now, which brings me to the last aspect I want to talk about...

The ending. I will not go into too much detail, but the game ends on such a bittersweet, heartfelt moment that puts life into perspective. It tied everything together and gives this sense of appreciation toward the people and world around you. It's a perfect ending that is designed to be very emotional in the best possible way.

This is a must-play, and the potential GOTY of 2026. It's fun and accessible to everyone, and was clearly made by a team of passionate devs who knew what it meant to enjoy the little things. Bring your closest people, and prepare to go on your big walk. You won't regret it.

[h1] This game is not for everyone. But it's for people who like chatting with their friends, [/h1]

Big Walk is one of those games that seem like [i] 'friendslop' [/i] on the surface. But underneath it's nothing like Lethal Company or Peak. Big Walk is a game focused on communication and trust. In some puzzles, you can't talk to the other person/group. You have to use your body to communicate. [b] SOMETIMES YOU CAN'T SEE OR HEAR [/b] and you have to rely on a system with your friends. This game is also not a streamer game. This is a friend game. I personally don't see this as a friendslop game but more as a friendgem game. The main point of the game isn't the puzzles, it's the reward of trusting your friend to finish a puzzle with you.

[h2] (SPOILERS BEWARE) [/h2]

[spoiler] In the final part of the game, when you completed all the towers, you are rewarded with going in the final black tower. In it, you press two/four buttons to open the door. When they're all pressed, a cutscene is present for ONE PERSON ONLY. That person gets to see and, when it's over, is responsible to tell the truth of what they saw. Sure they can clip it, but in a true game of Big Walk, they won't. During the final stretch of the game, you go into the big black ball. There are several layers to the ball, there's one catch: YOU CAN'T TALK THROUGHOUT THE ENTIRE THING AND EVERYONE TURNS GREY. You and your friends are trusting each other to communicate. You don't know who is who but you trust everyone can trust each other. It can take hours or minutes, you just need trust. [/spoiler]

Big Walk will not win game of the year :(

[h3]Post-Normal Ending[/h3]
This might be the greatest coop game I've ever played. However, you do have to go in with the right mindset to get the intended experience.

1. This is not a "friendslop" game. It is casual and you can goof around like in those kinds of games, but it doesn't have the typical replayable gameplay loop. Big Walk is a full campaign with a beginning, middle, and end that can really only be experienced once.

2. This is a slower-paced game by design. There's a reason the "Games like this" tab is recommending Flight Simulator, Truck Simulator, and VR Chat rather than something like Peak. Understand that it's more like going on a hike with friends and complete some puzzles along the way. It's a nice time.

3. I played with 7 ppl, which I thought was a good number. I'd imagine it's best to play with 4-8, as a lot of the enjoyment is splitting up into groups, solving puzzles separately, and reconvening to move onto the next "chapter". That being said, check out other reviews from groups of 2-3 or 9-12. They may have still had a fantastic experience, albeit different than mine.

4. View the playthrough as sessions, similar to a DnD campaign. Specifically, try to get all the same people every time you hop on the game. It's more fun for everyone to experience every milestone, especially the end.

With all that being said, have fun!

[h3]Post-100% Ending[/h3]
Beating the normal ending felt like the perfect pace. It's slow, but there's constant progression and you're able to reach major milestones each session. And to top it all off, the ending was generationally fantastic.

However, I think if you're trying to get the 100% ending in order to achieve the high you got when beating the normal game, you'll probably be let down. The pacing was a bit slower since we avoided the more tedious puzzles to reach the normal ending. The new puzzles, however, were great.

I still love the game, and if you and your friends want to continue playing and get the 100% completion, it's not a waste of time. It just won't feel the same as the normal ending.

Nearly 10 years ago I moved across the country and happened to meet a group of new people with basically all the same interests as me. We immediately became friends, and since that moment we have played games online most evenings. Even though each of us moved for college, we continued to share our love for games and have used it as a way to stay connected. 

Over time the games we play have changed, and each of us has gotten busier and busier. Recently our "rotation" of games has gotten very small and most nights we end up playing one of three games. That was, however, until Big Walk came out. We saw the early trailers for it, and decided we wanted to try it out when it released. Even though all of our schedules were crazy and rarely aligned such that all of us could be available, we carved out an hour here and there to play the game. 

To be honest, my initial impressions of Big Walk were mostly boredom. I'm a big fan of fast-paced, competitive multiplayer games. Think Overwatch, CS2, Escape from Tarkov, etc. The idea of just walking around a world with zero dangers, and solving puzzles with my friends was kinda underwhelming at first. Having to walk from puzzle to puzzle, slowly chipping away at them in frustration at how stupid I didn't realize my friends really were made the game hard to enjoy. That is, until we hit "the room of many lights" puzzle. I won't spoil it , but it involved having to figure out a way to communicate which specific light was flashing in a room that was full of lights (all over the walls, floor, etc.). My initial reaction was frustration as I assumed I was being very clear in my explanation. Finally after about 15 failed attempts, I forced all my friends in the room and we talked it out. We created these complicated mnemonic devices for explaining exactly which light was which. We walked back to our rooms, and proceeded on a generational run of puzzle solving. 

This puzzle is literally one of the most memorable moments I have ever had with my friends. I watched as each person did their part with masterful precision. We flew through the rest of the puzzle in a single attempt, and realized in that moment that the key to success was communication. Communication. It was such a simple thought. Of course we had been talking to each other, but we hadn't been communicating. By taking the time to walk through the puzzle, we were able to ensure that every member of the team understood it in full. Once we knew what we were each doing, solving the puzzles became fun.

Every new puzzle was a new opportunity to communicate and work together. Even the walking from puzzle to puzzle became an experience that can't be explained. Navigating the rough terrain in search for some random colored box that someone SWORE they saw from the top of a nearby mountain became an opportunity to learn more about the people I have known for nearly a decade. Having to work together to fit pegs in holes or throw balls at each other presented a new opportunity to discover how my friends thought. Slowly over time that frustration and boredom turned to excitement and appreciation. Each failed attempt was a chance to improve how we worked together. Each solved puzzle was a chance to rejoice and compliment each other.

All of this means nothing compared to the end of the game. Big Walk is one of the very few games that I was legitimately sad to finish. I won't say a word about the ending because I want you to experience it with your friends for yourself, but I genuinely believe that Big Walk's ending will remain a top 3 video game ending for me. As my friends and I crested the hill having finished the game, I felt a sense of love for my friends that I have not felt for years. Real, genuine love. Love for who they were as people. Love for the way each person thought. Love for every frustration. Love for each time one of them took the item out of my hand, threw it off a mountain, and we all had to take a 20 minute detour to go find it. And though our friendship will likely return to how it was before, there will always be a part of each of us that remembers this experience and the love that we felt for each other. 

Big Walk isn't a game about solving puzzles. It is a game about walking. Even more, it is a game about the people walking beside you. Big Walk doesn't refer to the distance. It refers to the experience. 

I know that someday, probably sooner than any of us would like, getting everyone online for games will become harder. Most nights will turn into once a week. Once a week will become once a month. And before you know it, you haven't talked to your friends in years. That is normal. It is what time does. 

But for ten hours, Big Walk gave us something back. 

For ten hours, I felt like I was back in high school playing Minecraft with my friends without caring that it was 3AM. For ten hours, the distance between us disappeared. There were no jobs, no different cities, no obligations. There was just a group of friends wandering through a new and exciting world, trying to remember how to be friends. 

I started Big Walk wondering when it was going to be fun. 
I ended Big Walk wishing I could go back and play it again without remembering anything. 

That might be the biggest recommendation I can give. 

If you have even one friend, play Big Walk. It will change your friendship, if only for a brief moment. Some day, you will have forgotten how you solved each puzzle. But, you will remember who walked beside you through it all. 

My only recommendation is to go into it blind, and hold yourself to that.

review:
I'm blessed enough to have 10 friends to play with. We're from the same city, and we've known each other for almost 25 years. We've played a ton of games together over that time, and the friend-slop explosion has been a major boon for us. Over the years we've built careers, moved, started families- life happens. Games are how we stay close through it all.

It is difficult to describe how special this game is. The puzzles are creative, the scenery is beautiful, and you're constantly filled with a natural drive to explore more- but I think the most captivating aspect of big walk is its ability to get you laughing, talking, and spending heartfelt, focused joy with your friends.

I imagine I'll play this again when my kids are older; I think it would be fun to play with them. But even if I never pick it back up, I can say without a doubt that this is one of the important games in our lifetime.

In a sea of games often described derogatorily as friendslop, House House has produced a certified, one-of-a-kind friendgem.

If you have a tight group of friends you like to play co-op puzzle and exploration games with, I cannot recommend Big Walk enough. In my personal opinion, it's easily GOTY material. This game is up there with Outer Wilds in terms of "games I wish I could play for the first time all over again", if that's any indication of quality.

Whether it's getting creative with communication to solve the game's puzzles, or simply finding a place to sit and relax for a moment in the breathtaking environment, it's the perfect game for enjoying spending time with friends. It's very plain to see how this was born from the pandemic's isolation and the need for a digital hangout space, and House House has done incredible work with a deceptively-simple premise. The soundtrack by aksfx complements the game very nicely, and I'd always bring a radio along to bring the music with us wherever we went.

Without spoiling anything, the final gauntlet of puzzles is where the real magic happens and where the game's mechanics shine brightest. I'd wholeheartedly recommend a blind playthrough, where you can come up with your own vocabulary for everything in the game. Especially the little objects you get for completing puzzles.

Also, I'm a huge fan of the design of the ingame characters, who I've been calling "walklings". Goofy little bird-faced guys.

Enjoyable puzzle game focused on communication and how it can be limited. I don't think its a 10/10, but it was fun for me and my friends, which is by far the most important metric. Oh, and the characters are rather cute.

Movement on terrain can feel awkward, especially with walking being such a focal point, and the performance leaves a bit to be desired for such a visually simplistic game. Proximity chat's falloff could also stand to be increased by at least 50%.

I am making this recommended, because it has a lot of good qualities that make it fun for most people, but for me there are a number of issues that make me a consistently frustrated. 

The game expects players to act as a coordinated group and to play simultaneously. The party I play with, however, lives in different timezones so starting simultaneously is an unreasonable expectation. 

I find that whenever I get separated (such as jumping into the game after everyone has started), I find it very difficult and takes a very long time to get back together, and wandering around by myself in a game meant to be played together isn't particularly fun. 

In such scenarios, certain items are critically necessary to navigate, such as walkie talkies and flashlights. However, I can only carry one item at a time. So either I have to walk around alone with no means of communication, or stumble around in the dark whenever it gets night. 

Even when I do have light, it is almost impossible to see where I am supposed to go when it is dark. If I am unfortunate enough to reach a watchtower at night, I have no choice but to wait until dawn because I cannot see which direction to go. 

Then there are the rocks. There seems to be some kind of invisible walls over large rocks, even ones that are clearly short enough to jump on (almost looking like stairs). The end result is that even when I do know which direction to go (by a friendly flare or landmark), I cannot walk in a straight line because of the rocks getting in the way. By the time I walk around it, then I am completely turned around and have no idea where I'm going. 

Then after going through all of that, when I do catch up with my friends they've already analyzed most of the puzzles, so I spend most of the time passively watching as they already figured out what they are supposed to do. 

On top of that, I keep running into a bug where my game disconnects, but only from everyone else's perspective. I don't see any issue or error message, but apparently everyone else in the server cannot either see or hear me, until I leave and rejoin.

review: peak friendship game

This game is something new. At least: to me it was. It may be to you too. It's not just nice scenery and strangely addicting puzzles. It's also a refreshingly new way to be together. Over the last decades, technology has allowed us to hear each other, ALWAYS. This game, for many, will be the first time technology enables them to NOT always hear each other. And the immediate social effects are profound.
For example: its amazing to see how something as "simple" as proximity voice chat —The sound of your voice can only be heard by those who are close to you in game— leads to people automatically walking in pairs, each having their own conversation, while they're hiking with a bigger group. Big Walk may not be the first game to have proximity voice chat, but it is an example of how this game perfectly places (non)communication at the core of its experience.
If you have no idea what I'm talking about, or you do but you have never experienced it, Big Walk is the game to try.

Big Walk is a big game about little things. It's about the conversations that come up out of nowhere while hiking through the middle of nowhere. It's about catching up with your old friend to see how life's going, while also catching up to see what they found over the hill. It's about coming up with secret codes that only you and your friends would understand. It's about campfire stories and running gags and inside jokes. And while you find yourself up so late that it's early, you'd definitely let the hours melt away again. Because when your journey eventually comes to a close, as all journeys do, you wouldn't get upset that it's over, you'd smile because it happened.

This game restored my faith in humanity.

No, really. When did you last really talk with someone? Like, [i]really[/i] communicated? Something that wasn't just a trite injoke or some kind of obvious truism that barely even needs a speaker to be heard? When did you actually feel like the act of communication has resulted in the idea in your brain being actually properly transferred to whoever's listening, the way you intended?

You know Lapras, the Pokemon? Because it's so rare, its in-game description talks about it desperately crying into the void, hoping that another of its kind will hear, sparing it from the excruciating loneliness. When I saw Big Walk on the store page I almost immediately added it to ignore. I've had my fair share of friendslop games, played them with many different people, and sure, they're fun. But what does this bring to the table? Oh, so it's like PEAK but with walking? Sure, sure, maybe this'd be fun with the right people. I love games where I get lost in the wilderness, and I do enjoy company, but come on. Enough of that.

And then a friend that I've been trying for a very long time to get to play something with me mentioned being interested in this. Why not? Might as well.

The name "Friendslop" fits so well because the games themselves aren't particularly well designed. The balance is usually wack, and the fun you're getting from the game isn't from the great design or whatever, but from the fact that you're with your friends, getting into all kinds of social shenanigans; the game being merely a backdrop - an excuse to hang out.

Big Walk is not like that. The design is bespoke; artisanal. Look at the price tag. There's a reason it costs this much. Friendslop games are comparatively easy to produce, and get most of their sales from the fact that multiple people will buy them. Here, the initial buy-in is unusually steep.

Ever played Portal? You know how the entire game is kind of its own tutorial without ever feeling tutorial-y? How it wonderfully explores the puzzle space of connecting two different places?

Big Walk is like Portal. Except instead of exploring puzzles of connecting places, it explores the puzzles of communication.

The name is almost misleading. Sure, there is the Big Walk - you'll likely spend most of your playtime on the road. Exploring, or going to a known location, or travelling between one mode of transit to another. But its genius lies elsewhere: in the very idea of a communication puzzle - and the execution of these puzzles.

How do you explain a sound?
How do you describe a random scribble?
How do you explain a very precise location to someone who can't see what you can, who can't hear what you can, using someone who can't see either as your messenger?

How do you agree on a complex strategy without being able to use words at all?

I can't write too much about the game's most powerful moments without spoiling. The beginning might seem a bit simple; the game takes a while to get going - if you're a bit picky about what games you consider good, you might start out unimpressed. But trust me: when it is time to say goodbye, your voice will tremble, your heart will burn with the love for your fellow man, your eyes will shine like they did on the first day you ever experienced happiness in your life.

For me in particular - for a glorious moment, I screamed, and the voices of my fellow Lapras screamed right back at me. I was not unique or exceptional. When the push came to shove, all my friends sprouted wings, and I finally felt at home. We were all equal. We were all divine. And I'll always know that the wings that my friends sprouted back then aren't gone - they're still there, just perhaps folded, hidden under their everyday clothes.

Of course, the game expects you to actually have friends in the first place. Friends that you actually enjoy talking to. The more the merrier; I'd say the sharpest experience you can have is with 4 players. You obviously can't play it alone, but I can easily see a group of 10 or more people enjoying this adventure together.

That said, with all the positivity, only 14% of players got to the end of the game. I can kind of understand why: you need to give the game a chance, and you need to actually get along with your friends. My group was wonderful, but I can very easily imagine even the smallest amount of toxicity explode into an unbearable sh*tstorm when the going gets tough. It's also kind of an anti-game; giving you negavite QoL and benefiting from it. If you're the kind of person who values convenience and results over everything else, you'll likely have a bad time.

Even one more person will do. Someone who you'd like to know better, perhaps. Or someone you'd like to force to listen to you screaming "My Heart Will Go On" via a megaphone directly into their ear while you're stuck on a ski lift.

Oh my goodness, this is one of the best games of all time. I loved playing this game, and especially with a group of 4 friends. 100% on every level recommend anyone to play this game with friends, its such a good icebreaker, and the ending is so beautiful.

Big Walk is a big playground, setting you loose with pretty sparce instructions other than go out and walk around. The island map is full of odd puzzles and locations, and the core loop of the game has you collecting rewards from these puzzles in order to unlock progression and ease-of-access to other sections of the map.

The puzzles themselves are simple enough, and often rely on matching tiles or synchronizing actions between players. As a result, the crux of playing and progressing in the game is based on you forming strategies and methods of communication between you and your fellow players. The "escape room" style of a lot of puzzles share a similar (sometimes redundant) framework, but you'll begin to develop cadences and shorthands with your group helping you navigate the more complex puzzles based on habits and methods developed and tested in the game's early locations.

The sound design, controls, interfaces are all very minimalist but masterfully executed, and player inventories are limited to what you can hold in your hands. Storage upgrades can be found across the island, but only other players can store or use what gets put in your pack. Coordination and cooperation are key. 

The proximity chat can sometimes be annoyingly short-range, and you will get separated from your group at one point or another, but Big Walk also provides you with tools like walkie-talkies for long range communication, or maps, laser pointers, flares, lights, and so on to help find your way again. Take things one step at a time, and maybe discuss a spot for your group to rendezvous at before anyone gets too lost. 

The core game can be beaten in 8-10 hours moving with some efficiency, but exploring every nook and cranny to complete every single puzzle will likely double that time. There's no real reason to rush, and it's time well spent if you're spending it with friends. 

The game doesn't have a story per se, but it does have an ending, and it was one I found uplifting, emotional, rage-inducing, cathartic, and deeply, deeply rewarding to have shared with my friends.

This is a game that you have to play with the people closest to you. 

I would recommend playing in a team of 3 or 4, with people you consider family. I would also highly recommend playing only with proximity chat; if you play while using a VC outside of the game, trust me, you'd ruin your experience. Only use your external VC if you have been stumped on a puzzle for too long, or if someone somehow disconnects by accident.

Slow down. Relax. This is not a game where you run around, try to complete everything as fast as you can, and get some kind of power trip. It is a slow-paced, adventure puzzle co-op that was made to strengthen the bond between you and your loved ones.

Some say that the puzzles are "too easy", but the difficulty isn't the point. The point is that you spend time with your loved ones. You solve these puzzles together rather than have one person do all the work.

And as you reach the ending of the base game, you start to understand this message more. It was a very heartfelt game, made by passionate, caring creators, and it feels sad knowing me and my siblings have finally reached the end.

In a world dominated by greed and pride, where people have grown increasingly more hostile towards each other, where everything is starting to feel more cold and less human, Big Walk was a breath of fresh air that shed a little light on humanity, and reminded us that there is still beauty and love in the world. And it all starts with the people closest to you.

Lastly:

While me and my siblings have always been close, this game reminded me why family is so important to us, why our parents always told us to love and care for each other.

When we put our hands together for the first couple times, it was originally just a silly, fun thing our older sister did. But when we reached the end, and we put our hands together for the last time, it was a tender moment that made me not wanna let go. 

We finished this at 25-32 years old, and yet, in that last moment, it felt like we were little kids again, always together.

Fantastic game full of wonder and discovery. Wandering around with friends, figuring out the puzzles, and enjoying the scenery as we talked and planned what to do next was just a wholesome good time from start to finish. Communication with your teammates is key in everything from coloring your own character to solving puzzles separated from each other by distance or walls or sound-proof glass - figuring out all the ways you can bridge gaps and cooperate will make you cherish bonds with your fellow players more and more whether they're friends you've known for a long time or randoms in an open session. It's just entirely charming and delightful. Play Big Walk!

There's really only one thing I could wish for it doesn't currently have - some way to take a photo of your whole group, like a selfie camera or large mirror where you can all stand in a row. It makes sense for the style of the game that you can't normally see yourself in third person, but for a game celebrating cooperation I think getting a group pic even if it's an endgame feature would be a great memento.

I know it sounds a bit soppy but this game was truly a special experience. Every step of the way it felt like it had been carefully designed to maximise opportunities to interact positively and meaningfully with your friends. 

It manages to give every kind of person something to do - sometimes it’s ok to be a passenger princess and sometimes you need someone who will lock in on the puzzle, but either way everyone is included. The game does a great job teaching you how to solve increasingly intricate puzzles by introducing the mechanics to you a little bit at a time, so while some puzzles were harder than others I always felt like we had the tools to succeed. Equipment is dotted around the map in such a way that you’re never out of what you need for long and you have ways to find each other if you get lost. It kinda felt like being a kid again - exploring the map, finding shiny new toys, pressing buttons and letting your curiousity lead the way. 

There is a lot of walking, as you’d imagine, but this was our opportunity to discuss what we were doing, catch up on gossip, roast each other and generally piss about. There are also some places deliberately set up so you can take a break and talk, which we almost always did, because the game was showing us that rushing to the end was not the goal.

Speaking of the end, it was absolutely perfect for the journey we had been on and actually made me kind of emotional, not gonna lie. We sat and watched the credits together and all we could talk about was how much we had enjoyed the whole thing. It was a super polished experience and the sound design in particular was incredibly immersive.

Thanks to the team for making a game like this! It’s not for everybody but for people who love their friends, and especially people like me who may not get to hang out with their friends as often anymore, it was a great experience.

At time of writing this review, I have completed the core game. It took my 3-9 friends and I maybe 9 hours, all told, with the rest of my playtime on a few starts and stops with various subgroups of us, and I imagine there'll be a fair few more hours after this review is posted. But if the metric of what a game is for you depends on the hours played, this may not be the game for you. I'll keep it short and sparse, to keep it relatively spoiler-free while still talking about the things I want to talk about.

The game I've played most recently that I would compare it to is Chants of Sennaar, a delightful little language-learning puzzle game. At the outset, I compared it more to ARMA 3, a game that is about communication, in the sense of ability to coordinate and narrate with a shared language in order to achieve goals and objectives. But that presumption has been challenged as I've experienced more of the game, as I've identified some challenges wherein relying on existing patterns and modes of communication will absolutely fail you. Some negative reviews identify these challenges as shortcomings of the game, but I would propose that they are shortcomings of the player. 

I still think "arma for pacifists" is a pretty decent elevator pitch for what the experience is, being a walking simulator with some communication puzzles scattered about, but I no longer think that it is the whole of the game.

Things the game does well: it is visually stunning. Every ridge you crest reveals a new surrealist landscape. The items and puzzles are very clear and easy to see. While I didn't check in directly with the colorblind pal, there weren't any glaring issues that popped up, so that was good. The music is also excellent, and suits the tone of the game well.

Things I might complain about: Some visual issues with lighting that caused the screen to go haywire when certain particle FX were triggered. Not game-breaking, though, all I have to do is look the other way and beg my friends to shut the dang thing off.

The thesis of the game is communication, and it is about building a shared language and understanding with your fellow players. If you don't have friends you can do that with, you have my sincere condolences. If you do, this is a game you should get and play post-haste. 

If you're one of my old pals and you're reading this review, you should invite me, too, or at least we should make some time to talk about it if we've both played.

Using whatever tools you can gather, and with as many friends as you like, explore and solve puzzles together. How and when is totally up to you, as you can just spend your time exploring on the big island for hours, if you wished.

Playing this involves just so much...communication. So much talking, and so much time spent just walking, encourages you to have conversations as well. I talked about big and small things, the books and movies me and my friend both liked, and stuff that's been going on in our lives. 

I honestly wanted this to just keep going on forever, more island to explore and more puzzles to solve together. 

There were so many triumphant moments, like agreeing to solve a puzzle completely on vibes, and the absolute joy when we managed was amazing.

I love as well that, because of the nature of many of the puzzles, there's no reason you can't continue to play it, with new groups of friends, or in new ways. The things you discover will be different, the way you solve the puzzles will morph and change, and you'll have a totally unique experience. 

Honestly, this is my game of the year. The simple act of walking and talking brought tears to my eyes more than once, and is probably one of the most emotionally beautiful experiences I've had.

Big Walk is a big game that is big fun. I genuinely believe that I have grown closer with my friends after playing this game. Every single puzzle is amazingly thought it making sure everyone gets involved and feels important. Granted I played this game with 2 other people I'm sure that the 4 player mode is just the same. None of the puzzles felt hard but I think that plays to the game's strength. Some puzzles do require some decent planning and forethought but none felt too cumbersome to complete. There are a handful of puzzles that do not feel as intriguing as the rest of the game but that is a given in pretty much any game like this. The walking part of Big Walk is brilliant. There never really was a moment when I felt like I was bored with the exploration of the island. As you progress you unlock more and more ways to traverse the island. The way they are laid out makes each one important and you want to use them all. Planning out your route on the map multiple steps at a time using multiple traversal methods and landmarks feels great. Having a physical map that you have to unfold and read with no indicator of where you are makes it all the more satisfying to get to where you want to go. Multiple times we had to stop in the dark and have someone shine a flashlight on the map while the other 2 figured out where we were and where we needed to go. No matter what you are doing you have to involve your friends to help. You can not access your additional inventory nor even put it on without someone else helping you. Without spoiling it during the ending section of the game the mechanic there took me by such surprise and felt so satisfying to get through. this game is genuinely a masterpiece. i'm glad it didn't fall into the genre of creating chaotic moments and rng for the sake of funny clips, because it feels so much more genuine and fun when something funny happens between you and your friends *naturally*. it really highlights how close you are with your friends, when you can entertain yourself with very minimal tools.

like when me and a friend had to wait at the start of a puzzle where multiple buttons across the map had to be pressed. we had to wait for a solid like 30 minutes, but we were just sitting in foldable chair items, looking through a telescope and eventually talking through a walkie-talkie, and just generally creating our own fun with the lost art of simply chatting with each other. no other game that i know of can make doing nothing fun, because nowadays most coop games are designed so you always have something to do that is either engaging or makes everyone laugh. that's fine, but an experience that lets you enjoy not just the exciting moments but also the quiet ones, while still having fun gameplay, now that's a rarity.

this is all without even mentioning the puzzles !! the puzzles are SO fun. when you hear this is a game about "walking" it probably sounds really boring. but it is, in fact, a game about "communication". or in most cases, the lack of it. in some puzzles, you have to pose for signals, others you have to point to a puzzle piece. some you have to figure out a way to communicate across large distances, or on the other side, not being able to talk to someone right next to you. an extremely interesting part of the game is figuring out how to reconvene with bigger groups of people who have split. 

in my case, i played with 5 other people, so we often split up into groups of 2 and used what little tools each group got to bring everyone back together. maybe that's a walkie, maybe that's a laser pointer, maybe that's a flare, but it's always fun to try and get everyone together, and even more fun to hear about what happened while you were split off. like this time all 5 of my friends were stuck in a puzzle for 5 minutes and signaling with poses and flares, while i observed from a watchtower using some binoculars, not knowing what they were doing at all. only for, when i tried to go to them and got lost, someone found me and told me they were literally just messing around because waiting WAS the the puzzle. so i just spent 5 minutes watching them and another 5 minutes getting lost just for a quick laugh, and it was awesome.

it's hard to describe how fun this game was to play with friends, how fun it was to complete puzzles, and how fun it was to experience the ending. and we're not even done, since there's some extra content for completing every puzzle on the map. this isn't a game you play for 2 hours just to get funny clips, it's a game that genuinely helps you bond with who you play with, and it being a handcrafted game elevates what's already a fun puzzle game into a one-of-a-kind experience that will forever stay in your and your friends' minds as a special moment.

at least for the time being, i have to say Big Walk is my Game of the Year.
