Is Big Walk a good game? Yes!
Is Big Walk a great game? No!

Big walk is an open world adventure explorer game where solving puzzle challenges allows you to progress. You can play solo or with a group, I would definitely recommend playing with a group. I played through Big Walk with a group of 4 and this felt like just the right amount of people. With groups, you can split up and not feel useless. "Progressing" in this game can be unlocking new areas, unlocking new modes of transport, or finding new tools to use. The new areas are cool, the tools are hit or miss, the new modes of transport are not cool.

Since this is an adventure game, having more to explore and not knowing what secrets it holds is what makes the game interesting. When you spend all this time trying to unlock something, only to find out that the thing you just unlocked is quite literally worthless, it takes a bit of the magic away. The train is the perfect example here, You first unlock the train and it's this big grand thing where it's like "WOW this will let us explore so much more!" only to realize that the train literally moves at the same speed as the player character does, it only moves in a single direction, and it comes by so rarely that it will feel like an eternity waiting for it. Seriously, waiting for a train / metro in real life takes less time than waiting for the train in this game, then once on the train you have to wait AGAIN to get to where you want to go. It's always significantly faster to just run where you want to go. Also, since the train only moves in one direction, you will find often times that it is going the opposite way that you are trying to go.

On mobility in general, running around feels alright, but running around is the ONLY thing that feels good. There is a "slide" mechanic where you can slide down slopes or hills, you will do this probably once and then never again. It has never felt good to use, notably in one of the buildings where the only way out is to go down a massive slide, the end of the slide kind of levels out and your character immediately loses all momentum probably halfway down the slide. These kinds of moments simply don't feel fun, when I see a massive slide I want to see my character going fast as heck and flying out the other end, only letting me get halfway there is insulting.

The puzzles themselves are very interesting. I think they perhaps could be a bit more creative here, there seems to be a specific way the devs design a puzzle to be solved which can be completely bypassed by simply pointing and motioning "yes" or "no". There are some puzzles where they specifically restrict communication, whether its by preventing players from speaking to each other or seeing each other, these are the ones that are the most interesting and yet they are rare.

Overall, yes I think the game is fun. Puzzles in a group will bring out the social dynamics, your friends will butt heads and argue but that is what makes it fun. There is more than one right answer for a lot of the puzzles and if people have differing opinions or ideas then you see how it plays out in real-time, so being a spectator can be just as fun. The only downsides to me are that they seem to make the game a bit too "casual" and slow for literally no reason.

One of the most incredible games I've ever played. I've been excited for this game since it was originally announced. A co-op puzzle game where the main mechanics are communication and cooperation between friends? It sounded incredible (as long as you have friends to play with), and it exceeded my expectations.

I've found there's kinda two modes to play this game: Small Group, and Big Group.

[h1] Big Group (>6 players)[/h1]
Big Group follows a lot of the formula of Small Group, but tends to be much more chaotic and progress is made by small groups splitting off rather than everyone working together. It's more what you'd think if you think 'friendslop', basically, and is a lot of what you'll see on big group livestreams and such. I'll be mostly focusing on a smaller group for my review, since that's how I played, and how I think it should be played.


[h1] Small Group [/h1]

When playing with 2-6 players (aka the 'designed' player count), the game is pretty concise and streamlined. Walk around with your friends, talk casually, stop for a few minutes to enjoy a nice view. Then look down the hill- There's something there! Let's go check it out! You go, and every time, the process is the same. You work together to figure out the goal of the puzzle, you make a plan together for how to solve it, then you spend a few minutes enacting the plan.

That formula is executed [i]perfectly[/i]. Each of the puzzles are bite-sized enough that you can figure them out fairly quickly, but they're usually involved enough that it takes at decent bit of coordination and effort to execute them. Even when the party is distracted for one reason or another, the game's cozy atmosphere lends to just sitting and waiting until everyone's ready.

The puzzles are wonderfully unique, too. I never walked into a new puzzle feeling it was 'just another one of these kinds of puzzles'. Some puzzles overlap with mechanics, but ones that share ideas usually each have a unique and massive twist that cleanly separate them. And the ones that don't share mechanics with other puzzles feel like stand-out special treasures, every time, without fail.

You'll find useful (or sometimes just fun!) items as you adventure around, there's a natural progression to the game, and a wonderful ending to discover. The world feels like it was made for you to explore, but in the same way a nature park does (wow, what a surprise), not in the way video games typically do.

There's no skill-based puzzles, and all the puzzles and game mechanics work with either the in-game voice chat or text chat. The game is extremely accessible. It is a little chunky on the PC specs side, but my partner managed to play the entire game on her laptop without a dedicated GPU while staying over 20fps. Due to the game never needing high response time for puzzles, she never once complained.

If you have a friend group of size 2-6, and you're the kind of people who can be in the same room for longer than 5 minutes without arguing, I can't recommend this game enough. You will grow closer to your friends, and find that your teamwork and cooperation grow more and more with each completed puzzle. No game I've played has come anywhere near the level of real human connection that this game does.

No matter what happens, what the next puzzle requires, or what items you do or don't have, you can always rely on what you've learned together to make it through.

I have never had more fun walking around, solving puzzles, and having long visits with my friends. It is chill, thought provoking, and goofy and I would recommend it to everyone. I've played 16 hours and will continue to enjoy punting objects off tall places.

Big Walk is truly a game about walking AND talking. I want to emphasize the talking part. The game performs best when you use it as an opportunity to connect. Big Walk helps its players connect by presenting mildly easy puzzles with some increasing difficulty. I think the best puzzles were when there was room for misunderstandings, such as the audio puzzles.

The game also does an amazing job at creating an atmosphere. From the sound design to the visuals of the environment, you truly do feel like a part of a different world. I also appreciate that there isn't a direct story, giving space for imagination and creativity. The map room gives just enough direction for the player, but the journey is what creates the experience. It's fun figuring out how to carry everything, manage items, find new things to experiment with, and open the modes of transportation. I for one enjoyed the night cycle as a challenge of sorts. If we didn't have a light, my boyfriend and I would just sit together and talk.

Big Walk is also an easy game for most people to understand. The controls aren't too difficult, allowing players to instead focus on the communication aspect of the game. Having the controls directly available in the ESC menu was also appreciated. Having a smaller crosshair option also was great.

I think that Big Walk is the type of game that gets stronger with more people. The bigger the lobby, the larger the chaos and opportunity for separation. For my boyfriend and I, we wished that we had more opportunities to use the radio towers, speakerphone, or walkie talkies more often. With more people, there would be more hands to carry these additional items.

Yet, I still think Big Walk has a legendary status as a multiplayer game. As someone who plays a lot of co-op with my boyfriend, I found that Big Walk ensures that neither player feels left out of solving the puzzle. In games like Portal 2 co-op, you can easily communicate and ping exactly where things should go, defeating the purpose of it being "co-op". All of this made Big Walk a great experience and I can't wait to play it with more people.

Big Walk is a game that, after an initial period of feeling like it has genuinely interesting puzzles to explore within an open world, very quickly shows a tendency towards tedium, overreliance on the premise that you are playing this game with friends, and a lack of *anyone* during the development process of this game had the confidence to tell anyone else that a mechanic or concept is not actually fun.

Looking past the game's incredibly restrictive in-game voice chat distance, you will quickly find it is incredibly easy to lose track of other players. This feature, for some reason, is one that the devs leaned too far into. You quickly struggle to feel like the goals you accomplish have meaning, with most rewards simply being means of getting around the map to avoid the incredibly boring and tedious navigating through the map that the game is obsessed with. The nights are far too dark, which the game seems to think it is fine, because you can find methods of illuminating your surroundings rather easily... but doing so means you have to sacrifice valuable carrying space, even assuming you don't accidently drop and lose your light source because you happened to step down a narrow drop.

The game invented a staggering amount of problems that it constantly forces upon players, with the expectation that the players would want it. Spend dozens on minutes looking for a puzzle. Find frequent tedious puzzles that require you to further spend dozens of minutes going to a location to solve the puzzle itself. Get given a reward that you must then further spend a dozen minutes carrying to slot into a node, and then repeat this process until you are given a key, which you must spend several minutes carving to then bring to another location to unlock features that make the game slightly more tolerable. Unlocking ways to navigate the map more quickly,

In theory this loop could be rewarding, but even these 'faster' methods of traversal are excruciatingly  slow, making the loop itself feel unrewarding. You then repeat this loop, to be rewarded with another dozen minutes of walking.

The game seems to think that in order to be fun, you need to be playing with many of your friends. That might not sound bad, but ultimately doing anything with your friends *should* be fun. If it is the only way for your game to be fun, then your game is NOT fun. Big Walk is a Big Disappointment. It is unrewarding, overly punishing, the world is annoying to navigate.

The game does not respect your time, and is undeserving of it.

Big Walk is both everything I imagined and hyped about based on their trailers, and at the same time so much more. This game is truly a one-of-a-kind experience, to the point that the only kind of vibe guide I could give you is if "A Short Hike" was experienced with good friends, but that's still far from close to describing it. 

From the get go I'd like to set the expectation that this game is less-so a puzzle game and more of a communication game. If you're even somewhat used to puzzle games you WILL find Big Walk puzzles sit comfortably on the easy side of the spectrum, they are not that clever in their design nor do they give that big eureka moment puzzle games are based around, and thats because they're not supposed to be.

Big Walk's puzzles are less so about figuring out what to do (since that will become apparent almost immediately with most puzzles) and more so about figuring out HOW to create systems or roles for your friends to complete a given task together, the satisfaction comes both from how fun it is to organize that with people you love hanging around with and from finally coming together and executing your plan flawlessly, every puzzle complete feels so much like an accomplishment, not of problem-solving but of teamwork and cooperation.

On the exploration side, I love Big Walk's both understandable and unapologetic map design, you WILL get lost and you WILL get separated, and I have never experienced a game where I genuinely had fun when I ran into problems like losing my friends. And that's because the game gives plenty of fun tools to find each other again, none of these tools really solve your problem or make the challenge easy by themselves, but they make the task of finding each other an always manageable and always exciting side quest whenever it does happen.

Aesthetically, I can say big walk is quite beautiful in a very organic kind of way. While there are some clear "look over here for good view" spots, Big Walk's beauty is more so found by the people who take the time to breathe and really look around them with patience. The dry forests making silhouettes and ominous tunnels at night, the looks and sounds of morning sun entering the jungle, the sunset hiding over the mountain or setting under the sea on the beach. Blink and you'll miss them, but sit, and you will bathe in them.

If you have a a close group of friends this game is a MUST. But I would also recommend it for any group of friends who could use a slower, binding experience. On my case, I first finished the game with two friends from the town I left behind last year, friends I love deeply but that I am yet to be as intimate as some other friends. Big Walk gave us and excuse to gather but did not give us something to be distracted from each other, instead, it asked us to talk to one another, sit with one another, work with one another, and in the process, get to know one another on a very particular way. This with all the time and silence in the world for friendship to grow and become stronger.

The challenge before the ending made us smile and laugh with so much love for each other and what we had built over multiple sessions, to realize how much we had gotten to know each other due to the kind of challenge we just went through. (I'd be more specific but its a small spoiler) it really felt like a type of relationship that this group had not yet experienced, and a change was certainly made from it.

I cannot and will not stop recommending this game, it is a LIFE changer, but unlike other life-changing games like Outer Wilds, this game will not change you, it'll just give you space, for you and your friends to grow and change on your own.

[i]Big Walk[/i] is an open world puzzle game with emphasis on communication, both verbally and through body language. That is a wildly reductive statement, because I feel [i]Big Walk[/i] is also an incredible litmus test for your own capacity for communication. This game helped me understand more about myself and the friends I have around me, and caused me to genuinely rethink how I present myself to others. 

The way I would pitch [i]Big Walk[/i] to someone is "imagine if [i]Myst[/i] was cooperative". You're given this large island to explore, several tools to aid in exploration, and given the loose goal of completing a series of puzzles. The game communicates all of this to you almost wordlessly, which is an achievement in and of itself, but the real victory is in one major word in the prior sentence- "loose". [i]Big Walk[/i] does not provide strict ways to explore the island, interact with your fellow explorers, or how to use the various tools provided to you. Instead, it combines them with a positional audio system and a gesturing system to create an incredibly robust hiking experience. As a testament to how well this works, I found myself making in-game eye contact with everyone I was speaking to constantly, as body language and voice combined to heavily immerse me within the game. Having to plan out routes, using landmarks for orientation, and radio sets for long-distance coordination is incredibly fun and immensely satisfying once it works out. 

The actual puzzles you can stumble onto tend to be quite strong as well. They begin simple (put a ball in a hoop, match some symbols) and escalate into fairly complicated affairs. One puzzle is a game of broken telephone where everyone is given a piece of a pattern and must pass it around, one is a cooperative obstacle course, another requires two teams to coordinate on a pattern by using a team of go-betweens... and so on. The puzzle variety is incredible, but what's even moreso is that none of the puzzles introduce "new" mechanics. You're never pressing new buttons or combining them in ways you haven't before... You have your voices, your hands, and your own understanding of communication as the only tools you need, creating some really magical scenarios. The finale in particular has some of the best puzzles I have ever seen in a videogame, with a setup to doing them that is genuinely inspired.

The best thing [i]Big Walk[/i] does though, and the reason why I think it's probably my game of this year, is that it offers a glimpse into the psyche of the people you care about. Moreso than anything else, [i]Big Walk[/i] has forced me to think about the ways I communicate and the sentiments I project to other people. How will X person take this statement? How do I explain my reasoning behind this puzzle to Y person, who generally struggles with (concept)? Our plan for this puzzle isn't working, how do I figure out a solution with person X 
 and Z? There's so much to do, so many ways to overcome communication hurdles, and so many layers to each puzzle that you simply have to communicate well... and sometimes, you won't! You might need to pass off responsibility to your friends, who have brains that are more tuned to the puzzles around you. Conversely, there are times where you'll need to assume authority as you come to grips with a puzzle faster than everyone else.  As well, there are times where a friend of yours will wander off, because the range for audio is really small and it's very easy to get lost in the dense foliage. How will you meet up with them? What signals will work, using the tools you currently have? I found myself thinking about how I communicate to other people, and how to manage my communication effectively, in a limited design space. I found the first two hours of [i]Big Walk[/i] so frustrating because I hadn't yet realized that my own ways of communicating were stunted in certain ways that would not work for this game, but by the end, I found that frustration give way to an appreciation for my friends. Moreover, it fostered a genuine change within myself, and got me to think about my friends more than I had prior. I wouldn't say it got me to foster empathy for them, but rather it forced me to step outside of myself and think about their view of the world.

I don't think any game like [i]Big Walk[/i] has ever got me to genuinely reconsider an aspect of myself, let alone in such a low-key way. It is one thing to be a strongly-designed puzzle game with great mechanics, it is another to foster empathy and understanding for the other people in my life. House House have achieved something monumental here, and I think [i]Big Walk[/i] will go down as one of my favourite games of all time as a result.

If I had to describe this game in a single word, I couldn't. Not because there is no word in any language that has the magic this game will cast upon you.

This game is what a beautiful heartbreak feels like. This game, this experience rather, places you into a world and gives you a single, human directive. Explore. 

You walk around looking like an inbred Dodo searching for a direction, a landmark, anything that resembles the "yellow paint" that gaming has become. Don't get me wrong, it provides that, but it does it in a unique way. It can be best described with the phrase "Oh! Wait! What's that?"

The island you inhabit, your challenger and rival, the silent sentinel to your hours of solving clever puzzles in a world that is filled with so much ambiance and love that you can't stop yourself from uttering, at least once, "Man...that's beautiful"

Soon enough, trees look familiar, the way the river flows is enough to tell you where exactly on the map you've wandered to. You'll know, just by facing a mountain where to go. And you will do so with a ravenous hunger for "What's next? Have we been there?".

This game was made with so much love that the word itself loses meaning. Little details sprinkled into the very silly characters that you pilot that make them an extension of you. A vessel for you to implant your little habits, the way you jump or run that is so specific to your play style. Even the way they sit is different depending on the terrain. There is not a single moment in any of the hours displayed here where I had wished for the game to end soon. In fact, I wish it lasted two times as much.

I played in a group of four friends. We didn't expect much at first, after all, it's just a little puzzle game. By the end we had come to a single, unanimous agreement: This was the best gaming experience we have had in the past few years.

I simply can not describe this piece of art with words fancy enough to do it justice. When you play this game, you will fundamentally see the souls of everyone at House House and what it truly means to create a game, to create and to adore in such a basic human way that it needs no complexity, only emotion. I can't recommend it enough. 


Even if you think you and your friends wouldn't like it. Or if you think that it's simply not your genre. Give it a shot. You have nothing to lose but an experience like none other to gain that you will realize, with a heartbreaking certainty, will never happen again

TLDR; big walk is a 4/10 game with lots of issues.

[h3]PUZZLES[/h3]
For a game that's advertised as playing with your friends and talking to your friends I feel like I did none of that. 
When I played, I played with my friend group of 8 which often resulting in us having to break up into micro-groups to complete puzzles which often meant I would not be talking to half the people I was playing with or wanted to play with for lengthy periods of time. The game is obviously catered to a small friend group of 4, having all the puzzles either taking 2 or 4 people to complete, meaning that regardless of the fact my friend group was larger, the core mechanics of the game require you to split up to complete puzzles in smaller groups. I find this stupid considering... the core advertisement standpoint is hanging out with your friends.
The puzzles were the only halfway decent thing about this game, I found them entertaining and although some of my friends lack any amount of intelligence in order to complete them, that was funny and part of the charm I'd argue and you can't hate on a game for your friends being dogshit at it. However, and that's a pretty big however, the system in order to get the "babies" as we dubbed them, was terrible. They are not colour coded to the towers so you accidentally take them from one area to bring them to the wrong tower, finding the puzzles in the open world is frustrating as although you unlock and gain transportation walking is a much faster way to get around despite this. 
The ability to not talk to your friends for some puzzles is actually quite cute and resulted in a lot of funny moments, however SPOILERS!?!?!?!?! [spoiler]the last section of the game genuinely made me want to pull my own hair out. For the last 2 hours? Or so? Of the game you are mute, you cannot type, you cannot talk. And they take away all your items so you cannot communicate with a whiteboard either. They also strip your character of any colour so you cannot identify who your friends are - unless they have very unique movements in the game lolol. This means you are literally sitting in silence, banging your head against a wall until you can somehow figure out how to complete the puzzle. As I said before, your friends being bad at puzzles is charming and not at all a fault of the game - however in this point it's hard to alleviate that frustration as you cannot crack jokes or poke fun at your friends and simply watch them run around like headless chickens until the end.[/spoiler]
The game also drags. so. badly. The first 2 towers are enjoyable, it gets a bit old during tower 3 and 4 due to frustration with the game (which I'll get into). But then. The evil obelisk?!? Ok this came out of absolutely nowhere but..oki….Oh okay and now there's Even More Babies to collect. Cool! Oh and now there's an evil orb of doom and despiar..and then the last section of the game I already complained about. It sincerely did not need more than the 4 towers, it just made it for an unneeded lengthy experience.

[h3]WALKING AND TALKING[/h3]
The proximity in this game is sincerely horrendous, I would be chasing my friend who cannot be further than a couple meters ahead of me attempting to get their attention and they could not hear me, nor could I hear my friends behind me. This voice chat was consistently terrible, in the trailer they spoke of having finetuned the proximity chat and featured all the ways to make it better such as the echoing in caves or the various tools to communicate from afar, yet despite being in tunnels or caves my voice did not travel at all, nor did my friends. The megaphone was found way too late into the game which is the only saving grace in the game, but even then there's only a small amount in the game and I shouldn't have to rely on a megaphone to hear my friends that SHOULD be within earshot.
The open world was also really poorly crafted, the nature enviornment although pretty, suffers a lot from crappy collision issues. Me and my friends would constantly find themselves getting trapped within small pockets or between rocks, and generally struggle to move around. 
The day night cycle was a horrible addition, on paper its cute, but if you're out in the wilderness you cannot see jack, and you have to constantly fumble around to find your way. Puzzles and towers do have light bulbs near them, however they are not turned on by default, so if you find yourself in the forest at night Good luck! 
You may argue "but items,,!" Which leads into my next paragraph.

[h3]ITEMS[/h3]
The item and inventory sorting mechanics in the game was also terrible.
Backpacks were a beautiful find for me and my friends, to be able to hold more than one item, except they weren't. You the backpack wielder cannot actually obtain any of your items on your back, and in fact you have to be helped to wear the backpack in the first place. This causes a lot of frustration as you have to ask your friends to give you items on your back that you should be able to reach, and then coupled with the voice proximity issues has you being ignored as you're desperately trying to get the item on your back. Being unable to access the items on your back is such an unneeded addition and makes item management incredibly frustrating.
Fanny packs were a much welcome addition, and I do not understand why you'd even put backpacks in the game when they're so finnicky and at times wortheless, when you had a better inventory managemnt system already within the game? It doesn't make sense unless you wanted a sense of progression..but why? You don't!! Need that for inventory management!!!
An argument for the nighttime cycle is light bulbs, yet you cannot even put light bulbs on your back which is SO stupid, you have to either hold them above your head meaning you cannot walk through doorways and get stuck on surrounding nature, or have it hide the majority of your screen. When you could just...have it on your back like a normal game.
Item management was impossible, you have all these core items, the megaphone, walkie talkie, lights and yet you have to sacrifice your hands to hold them and in some cases forego them entirely because its night-time and you cant see a thing but you need to grab Something to see, which wouldn't be a problem if you could access your own backpack!!

[h3]WHAT THEY COULD DO TO CATER TO SPECIFICALLY BOREDOM ON STEAM[/h3]
Fix the collision..please….god it's so frustrating to get caught on stuff. Actually have your beautifully finetuned proximity chat like you advertised in your trailer and clearly did not follow up on making, please have the ability to access your backpack or forego them for fanny packs instead because its ridiculous I cant access anything on my back, and also make it so you can equip backpacks yourself. For the ending of the game SPOILERS!!! [spoiler]please make it so you have a mix and match of puzzles where you can communicate to your friends for some, and others you can't, as the gimmick gets very tiring very quickly and I just want to talk to my friends in the game about talking to your friends.[/spoiler]

This game is the real deal, and unlike other friend games that have come out recently this one doesn't get up all in your face. You just get some friends together, have a chat, and explore at your own leisure without worry and enjoy some surprisingly beautiful scenery (also the player avatars are the best, I love these nerds). The Mac build is also commendably stable and easy to run without any of the hassle.

If you want a co-op game that lets you go with the flow, has fun puzzles, and actually respects your autobiographical memory when it comes to the adventure, then Big Walk is the experience for you.

For the first 2 hours, Big Walk is a lot of fun. You mess about with the mechanics, get wowed by the pretty landscape and feel an easy natural progression with the puzzles. A lot of the enjoyment comes from just being able to split off into little groups have your own conversations and mini adventures then reuniting to progress. It almost feels like a perfect multiplayer environment to socialise and chill.

Unfortunately, this all breaks down overtime due to some fundamental issues with the game. Two of its primary mechanics, walking and talking, are severely hampered by an awful voice/proximity chat and horrendous climbing/collision when travelling. If a friend is even roughly 3 metres away they start to become either really quiet or straight up inaudible which obviously makes conversations while walking hellish. Also as stated, when getting around you will just get caught in random tiny rocks, rendered motionless by tree branches and just generally slowed down which doesn't help with your friends voices being consequently impossible to hear either. Getting around the map, while initially fine due to everything necessary being within a decent range of the current tower being progressed suddenly got much worse as the puzzle locations became harder to determine and transport the blobs back. The train and gondolas intend to relieve this but they move marginally faster than just walking causing exhaustion nearing the end.

Other issues include the Day/Night cycle which can make for some pretty sights yes but good luck if your not at a tower or a puzzle when its night-time cause you will not be able to see anything. There are lights scattered about the environment but as the game went on these became less frequent. Now granted you could lift one of the lights and carry it around with you but those become few and far between. Now if you wanted to put an item on your backpack, you need to not only find one of the few and then someone else needs to put the stuff on and off you. This makes item management a nightmare. On a lesser issue, the game also seems to spend a lot of its puzzles removing the ability to talk which is fine for some small puzzles but can get really boring and frustrating as the gimmick causes extended periods of time in silence when the game is meant to be about talking.

There is definitely things to enjoy about Big Walk and even as a group we felt immense accomplishment when finishing puzzles, took the time to sit and have chats, laugh at all the stories we would hear when regrouping and make eachother rage a little by doing something stupid. While it does facilitate an atmospheric and amusing multiplayer experience, the foundational aspects of the game are done so poorly that a more worthwhile adventure should be found elsewhere.

[i]Going on a Big Walk with my friends was my favorite gaming experience of 2026.[/i]

[b][u]INTRODUCTION[/u][/b]
While I think the recently coined 'friend-slop' is a really affectionate genre descriptor for a lot of these recent co-op indie hits, I think it just doesn't quite do [i]Big Walk[/i] justice. This is a game that was so meticulously crafted, refined, and massaged over the last seven years to be a truly one of a kind experience with the people you are closest to.

[b][u]THE REVIEW[/u][/b]
[i]Big Walk[/i] is a game that isn't focused on replayability or capturing your attention, but harnessing the already existent relationship of your party members to stretch and grow it over the course of a ten to twenty hour journey.

Perhaps the most impressively paced video game of all time in a sense that is kind of indescribable. The balance between actively solving puzzles, downtime, time separated, and time planning is just excellent. Despite being obviously entirely player-driven, it always felt so perfectly curated for our group. While riding on the train or waiting for our other party members to reach a location, we get the chance to just sit down and have a chat about our day. When the party is separated, we get to tell each other about our adventures when we reunite. 

While solving puzzles we are challenged in the most diverse, interesting, and human of ways. And in most scenarios, communication is the true puzzle. Having to figure out how to communicate intricate shapes, directions, yes, and no through the most unconventional of ways. No challenge ever overly painful or tedious, but the sense of accomplishment once we conquered our inept ability to communicate was such a high and ultimately so wholesome. The excitement we all feel with all of our arms raised in the air as we walk away with our prize each time is truly unforgettable.

The atmosphere of the island always provided us with a sense of wonder through its sound design, lighting, and music. Despite the game having not a single point of danger or loss-state, you still never wanted to get separated from the crew for fear of getting lost or stuck alone in the eeriness of the night.

On a technical level, this game is impeccably polished. Despite some very minor initial issues audio levels upon launch, this is one of the most polished games I've played in recent memory. Relatively never experiencing so much as a slight bug, let alone something that genuinely effected our gameplay. Every puzzle so clearly playtested into the ground.

[b][u]CONCLUSION[/u][/b]
[i]Big Walk[/i] is a game that is so systemically polished, directionally refined, and beautifully paced to provide you and the people closest to you with a truly one of a kind gaming experience. An experience where you are deeply challenged to communicate in unorthodox ways but also encouraged to have simple chats about your day in between. All while discovering and solving a massive wonder-filled island. A journey that doesn't ask you consume it again as you and your party can only really feel it out once.

Playing this game with three of my closest, lifelong friends was one of my most special gaming experiences in recent memory. A simple, sentimental, and absolutely unforgettable game-of-the-year-level co-op experience that I will look back on fondly for years to come.

[i]Go on a Big Walk with your friends. You won't regret it.[/i]

This game is supposed to be on the slower side but it also makes it so you genuinely have to interact and have conversations with one another. This game is about solving puzzles and strengthening friendships. You know I didn't really get this game at first. It felt like it was just wandering around with friends with the occasional thing to do interspersed throughout. But after having finished it, I can easily say that Big Walk is one of the best games you can play with your friends Period, and that it does some things that other hangout games are either too afraid to do or try to optimize you out of doing.

Big Walk is a Big Game. It took a group of 3 of us 22 hours to 100% it, and most of that time was wandering around lost with very little direction. The number of times one of us would run off in the hopes of making it to the same spot as the others, before getting very very turned around and ending up at a random location where we could shoot off a flare, or say something on the walkie-talkies is easily in the dozens, but getting lost really is what makes this game special. Big Walk isn't afraid to make you wait around, or have no idea where you are, or show you something you can't do because you found it alone. None of the puzzles have instructions, you just have to figure them out for yourself, and there were several times where we had to look around at different sections of the puzzles to try to piece together what they even wanted us to do. Hell, my favorite puzzle was a room with a couch and a chair, a light, a locked door, and a big clock on the wall and that's it.

I think Big Walk is special because it makes you a better communicator. I've never felt like I was particularly bad at that, but there were plenty of moments where I needed to figure out a different way to explain something I had learned to my friends, or in several cases had to do so without being able to speak to each other at all. We spitballed ideas, debated about what routes we should take, tried to solve puzzles, and then tried to solve those puzzles again when our first boneheaded idea failed. It asks you to learn to talk to the people around you, the people you care about, better. It doesn't meet you where you are, it says "here is something to improve about yourself, and here's the play place for you to do so". If self-improvement is ever your goal, as it is mine (and as I personally believe it should be for everybody), play Big Walk. It will not disappoint.

Charming, whimsical, surprising, delightful, clever, unbeatable good vibes. 100/10, no notes.

The premise alone was enough to hook me from the start - what's not to love about wandering around in a serene, gorgeous open-world with my favorite pals, gabbing through proximity voice chat, solving cooperative and creative puzzles, and having abundant opportunities for unexpected discoveries, shenanigans, and goofy mistakes?? I was constantly delighted and surprised by the things we stumbled across, the strange and beautiful aesthetics, and the funky and immersive soundscape of the game. You can really feel the love, joy, and whimsy the creators put into every inch of the game. The puzzles felt challenging but solvable, each unique and requiring its own creative solution. It's a perfect game of "show, don't tell" + "FAFO" - you just kind of wander around, experiment, learn, and figure things out together. What a true delight at every moment.

The final arc of the game was both ominous and grand - [spoiler] a surprising but not unwelcome tone-shift in some ways to the lighthearted, easy-going nature of the main puzzles/map [/spoiler]. The final puzzles were SUCH a great, satisfying capstone to everything we had learned and built together as a Big Walk party. We utilized not only all the technical skills we had learned, but all our little group's own unique language of gestures and communication. We all truly felt they were some of the best puzzles of the entire game, and SO rewarding to figure out together.

The very end was surprisingly poignant... why I am I crying [spoiler] watching each of my friends go through a turnstile gate??? [/spoiler] It's not very often you come across a game that perfectly combines silliness, puzzles, mystery, unstructured fun, beauty in every form, [spoiler] very light eldritch horror(??) [/spoiler], and genuine heartfelt emotion. My only wish is that I could forget absolutely everything about this game... just so I could go back and re-experience the entire thing for the first time in all its wonder. I will be thinking about this game, our journey as friends, and its ending for a long, long time.

Playing video games as a social experience really is the main way I've been able to consistently enjoy my time with them. I grew up on Halo multiplayer split screen with my brother, then I played Payday 2 with some of the same friends I played Big Walk with. I played A Way Out, It Takes Two, and all sorts of other remarkable games in the co-op genre. Recently I've even been trying out some of your more friendslop games, Peak and Gamble with Your Friends. Even when I've struggled to motivate myself to get through story games, co-op has been there.

Big Walk is so unlike any of these other experiences. It's slow paced, rewards teamwork and attention to detail. This game doesn't strike me as friendslop. A lot of people have been calling it a friendgem game, which is a sentiment I agree with. The puzzles are wonderful, simple and easy to understand, relying more on effective communication and overcoming certain barriers together rather than intensive problem solving, and yet it still feels so rewarding. Finishing the puzzles and slowly making your way across the map while simply hanging out together made for such a refreshing experience in a genre that has been dominated by chaotic games for the last few years.

The game really makes the best use of proximity chat that I've ever seen. The way it uses it for puzzles and general exploration is fantastic. Getting lost can be scary, since there's very little on the island, but it adds a little more unpredictability to the dynamic in a way that games like Peak simply don't achieve. 

The ending really really hit me and resonated with me. I just had to sit for a second and appreciate what I had just experienced. Big Walk is so much more than the sum of its parts, and I would have a hard time not recommending it to anyone who has a group of any size to play it with. I am interested to see how replayable it is, however I imagine with different groups it would be fun to run through again. There's a whole set of unique memories to be made with each run, each session. Funny moments and quiet moments. My game of the year so far.

[h1]The Pitch, I Guess? [/h1]
Big Walk is a series of simple "telephone" style puzzles [i]zhuzhed[/i] up by taking place in a walkable environment with friends. It sounds decently promising, but the catch is that the puzzles are mostly repetitive tedium, the island it takes place on is dull and onerous to traverse, and the very small range of proximity chat as well as many puzzle designs (particularly for a group of any size other than 4) eliminates most of the fun of playing with your friends.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]"Puzzles" [/h2]
To call the activities on the island "puzzles" is actually probably giving them too much credit. They bear more of a resemblance to teambuilding exercises, where incomplete information (like, say, the order of a set of symbols only one group can see) is passed between groups, compiled, and compared to the right answer. The only things being tested are your ability to communicate your part of the information efficiently and your patience in seeing the solution to its logical conclusion. This style of puzzle is then repeated over and over, with variations on who has what info and what communication tools you can use to compile that info, but the puzzles are so fundamentally similar that there's nothing interesting about these remixes. And yes, that includes the purple ones; there was no meaningful iteration in those either, despite representing ostensibly harder versions of previous puzzles. In all but a handful of puzzles, the METHOD of solving the puzzle is intuitable near instantly, while the solutions still require minutes of busywork in the form of delegation or arm waving or discerning what symbol is on what individual tile written in invisible ink.
The exceptions to this style of puzzle require even less thought, with tasks ranging from short obstacle courses to grueling backtracking to sitting in a room doing nothing while a timer ticks down. Having taken the time to finish a world 100%, there is nothing satisfying or novel in here for groups who have played games together before, with the possible exception of the normal ending sequence, which removes[spoiler]the artifice of the island for a bit and gives you a few earnest attempts at (still mostly rehashed) puzzles in a row before shoving you out to view the sunset. I literally got stuck inside a turnstile in one of those final puzzles and had to restart and rejoin the game to progress,[/spoiler] and it was STILL the most competent and enjoyable part of the game.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]The Island Sucks, Man [/h2]
If the island itself was charming, it might have been worth something to look past all that and immerse myself in the walk, but for the life of me, I can't imagine thinking that's true. The environment has so few interactive elements apart from the spaced-out puzzles, and there's just too little of an attempt made to liven it up aesthetically past the look of a default Unity asset flip. The only items I remember us finding ON THE ENTIRE ISLAND that exist solely to be whimsical are a couple of lawn chairs! It should have been a goal for it to be fun and interesting to just vibe anywhere on the island, with little vignettes of animals and scenery, or goofy items, or maybe fun little hiking activities like fishing, but instead it's largely devoid of character or beauty or ambition and just feels too big and EMPTY. It's rounded out with poor geometry (even on intended paths), a train that runs slower than you, a tunnel system that's also slower than going over the mountains (which exists solely to hide stuff somewhere permanently dark that people wouldn't want to go), and a day night cycle that exists solely to make sure a massive chunk of your playtime is holding w and mashing space bar in the dark to climb the mountain in front of you that you can't quite see.

[hr][/hr]
[h1]So Again, Why Big Walk? [/h1]
I struggle to answer what the game brings to the table or why I would recommend anyone play THIS game specifically. If you're goal-oriented, the slog of trekking with a group to each puzzle will wear you down, then the puzzles themselves are mostly the same rehashed mind-numbing pantomimes, then eventually you have to hike to another location to drop off the key items you've gained. If you want to take in the sights, well, there simply ARE no sights! If you want to walk and talk with your friends, the game actively works against that, because you'd better stay within a couple feet of each other, try to not get stuck on every twig and rock, and forgo any puzzle you come across that in any way splits you up (which is most of them). If you want to have fun, your only option is the fun you and your friends already brought with, and at that point, why not go play something else?

Getting lost, finding friends through various means, and finding new ways of cooperating to figure out a puzzle made for some of the most fun I've had in a co-op game. I played mostly with three or four close friends, and honestly, I think an even bigger group would make it more chaotic and even more fun. Most of the puzzles themselves are fairly simple. The real challenge is communication, coordination, and gradually learning how your friends think.
We had so many stupid, chaotic, hilarious moments while solving things that I really regret not recording our sessions. Now those moments just exist in our memories, which is strangely fitting for this kind of game.
My biggest complaint is the traveling. I understand what the developers were going for: long walks give friends time to talk, joke around, and just hang out together. Unfortunately, my group often responded to this brilliant social opportunity by silently walking across the map for several minutes or more. Even after unlocking the monorail and ski lift, movement still felt slower than I would have liked. A few drivable vehicles could have added a lot of fun.
The final section, however, completely changed how I felt about the game.
For most of the game, being close to each other allows you to communicate normally. Then the final challenge takes that away. You lose your normal means of communication, everyone looks the same, and suddenly you have to rely almost entirely on the habits and unspoken understanding you've built up throughout the rest of the game.
Somehow, my friends and I understood each other well enough that we didn't get stuck for very long.
And then came the ending, where everyone leaves one by one.
As the host, I was the last person left behind. It looked lonely, but everyone had turned around and waved goodbye to me before leaving. I didn't expect a silly cooperative puzzle game to make that moment genuinely emotional.
The hardest puzzle in Big Walk isn't anything the developers designed.
It's finding several friends who are willing to spend hours walking with you, communicating without getting angry at each other, building that strange little sense of teamwork — and somehow all being free at the same time.
Most of the game: 9/10.
The final communication-less section: 12/10.

I wanted there to be more puzzles, more areas to explore, more pointless moments with friends. More opportunities to get lost or to rescue a lost friend. More train rides. Reflecting on this, I realized why. I wasn't just trying to create more game... I was trying to create more time with my friends.

Big Walk is a game about enjoying each others company and getting lost in the moment. Its about coming up with silly systems to communicate when you can't simply talk to each other, and then lighthearted bickering to figure out what went wrong the first time. Its about finding a solution together, and celebrating every little win with cheering and victory dances. Its about dancing to music together, and mapping out your next destination, and chatting on the train. Its about your friends annoying each other by sneakily placing music radios in each others backpacks or snatching things out of each others hands. Or derailing a plan by throwing each other off cliffs.

Its about the little moments together... and I never wanted those moments to end.

[h1] I have no friends; but I must Walk. [/h1]

Do you ever stop and realize you're making memories? Memories so fond, funny, and friendly you typically only realize it as such until it's time for it for it all to come to a close? Big Walk, for me, encompasses this feeling nearly perfectly and I am beyond description that I had the opportunity to enjoy it.

I don't have friends. Nonetheless any friends that would have wanted to play Big Walk with me. The first couple of days I owned this game I could not play because I literally could not [i] pay [/i] for someone to play with me. It was extremely disheartening. Especially as someone who already suffers from pretty bad Major Depressive Disorder, I don't even want to begin describing what it was like to be unable to play a game I had been looking forward to since it was announced simply because there was not a soul who wanted to spend time with me. So, in a rare act of desperation, I turned to crossing my fingers and hoping the randoms I met from posting on a mega-thread for the first time wouldn't be a disappointment.

Writing it down hardly does this game justice, but I'm going to damn well try. Meeting new people, learning and exploring this incredibly designed and beautiful land chock full of secrets and puzzles just waiting for you to find it. Everything from the tools to the shortcuts feel incredibly purposeful and well thought out. The map is just big enough to get lost even if you know it's nooks and crannies, but not too big as to be overwhelming. It always felt like there was another hill to climb, not a mountain blocking the way. The freedom of choice is something I can only really akin to Breath of the Wild in the sense you can go anywhere, do anything in any order, and not be hindered or held back in the slightest. It's a world that wants to be seen, and you will be more than happy to indulge in everything it has to offer. But, around about half way through the journey, you'll realize the ultimate trick this game offers has been hiding in plain sight all along.

The puzzles? The exploring, landmarks, and progress? That's not what this game really wants you to do. It wants you to make memories. To [u] remember [/u] your time in this world. To cherish it. Not just playing, but enjoying the time I spent with all these wonderful people I had the absolute pleasure of meeting. I genuinely felt I was exploring a new land surrounded by people who were just as thrilled as me to see what was in store for us. Spending hours learning about all these people you travel along side with felt like I truly was on an adventure, and nothing could hold us back because we were together as a team. The teamwork of solving these puzzles in such creative and intriguing ways is so incredible that I fondly remember the time we spent brainstorming how to solve the puzzle together more than the actual puzzle itself. Then, as all things do, it came to an end. It's hard to talk about it without spoiling a thing, and if you've made it this far into the review, if you don't do anything else [b] please [/b] do the ending blind. It's been quite a while since a game has struck me on such an emotional chord, and the people I had the pleasure of playing with only amplified it. Going back for the 100% amped it up twice fold. I legitimately teared up during both the endings.

I will never forget my time with Big Walk. Nor will I ever forget the memories of the time I spent with the dozens of friends I was graced with along the way. Josh, Lemming, Brent, Mal, INK, and of course, Mr. John Bigwalk himself. Every single person, even the ones whos names were never given or heard, I'll remember them. All I can do is hope they remember me as I wave goodbye.
Thank you to everyone I ever had the pleasure of meeting and even letting this journey be possible.
Thank you to everyone at House House for the wonderful experience I was able to enjoy beyond words. It means more to me than I think anyone will ever truly know.

Genuinely one of my new favorite releases. Me and my friend just beat it tonight after a little less than 10 hours, but I know there are still maybe another 6 to 8 out there for us to 100% the game. We both got it during the 25% sale so here is my opinion.

1. It is slow, but I do not think it is boring
The game is for sure slow, slower than a lot of other games in the friendslop genre. Me and my friend play a lot together, whether it is Peak, Lethal Company, or Repo (the first two we may have over three hundred hours between us). Big Walk is certainly way slower than that. Instead of having the objective to survive like the other two, Big Walk is all about traveling around and enjoying the journey. There are no real stakes. Completing puzzles and adventuring is all at your own pace, and the island is your oyster.

2. The puzzles are really fun! Most of the time...
We really enjoyed the puzzles, especially the ones at the end. Collecting doodles (as we called the little red things shaped like our heads) was fun, and we became a well oiled puzzle solving machine by the end of the game. Cutting off ways we could communicate or certain senses were always our favorites. That being said some of those puzzles definitely are not for the faint of heart. Especially ones where we have to travel really far to solve it. That being said if we did not want to do a puzzle we could basically just skip it since the island is full of them.

3. It always has a great atmosphere
The game is always a vibe, and is pretty cozy most of the time. Most of our time spent looking around or checking landmarks was awesome, and I LOVE the sound design in this game. Besides voices that is, I hate not being able to hear my friend when we go only a little distance from one another.

4. The inventory is a little clunky
Playing with only one other person means that 2/3 items you carry on your person once you get inventory upgrades are exclusively ones accessed by the other person. Meaning me and my buddy were each others walking loot chests, whatever we wanted to use the other person had. Which is pretty fun do not get me wrong, though it would appeal to me more if there were more people on our island, so we could carry more needed stuff.

Overall the game is solid, my only critiques are making it easier to hear your friends and that I dislike that I cannot grab items from my own belt. It is my belt! But yes it is a great puzzle game to sink a few sessions in with your friends, I think you should get it!

I don't think I've ever played a game like this before.
It's nothing but good vibes with friends you take along with you on your way to explore an island full of outdoor aesthetics, cozy atmosphere, and mystery to unfold.

Big Walk allows for players to just walk around and sit and enjoy the world if they so wish to, and (or) make progression in solving thoughtful puzzles that utilizes communication skills.
Communication is a major part of this game and it works for both those with and without microphones. 
There will be times where the game cuts off player's verbal and text communication where only visual body language is needed instead. Furthermore, there are times where the game sets up on side of a puzzle for essentially translating a message from visual and (or) audio queues where the other side needs to decipher it.
Conversely, sometimes there are puzzles that have you just sit in a room and wait where it has spots to sit in. This sets up a nice break from the tough puzzles for just a time to be social with friends for a bit. 
It even has several receptives for stimming such as glass tink sounds when you tap on glass, squeaking sounds rubbing hands on walls, and so many fun lil objects to play around with.

Big Walk is a wonderful experience and best played with at least 1 or 2 friends but the more the merrier. (up to 12 players in one game at a time!)
It truly is a one of a kind experience and it will definitely be different for reach friend group you play in.

I walked [i](pun not intended)[/i] into this with great expectations with my group of 6 friends, and while they were continuing to enjoy themselves past the 1 hour mark, I found myself increasingly frustrated with a game that advertises "walking and talking" as one of its main selling points. The proximity voice chat not reaching beyond a couple meters led to countless moments of frustration where I did not receive a response, often feeling like I'm being aired or ignored. I don't want to have to repeat myself several times just to be able to butt in on conversations that I often missed because of the complete lack of volume sliders - as someone that is hard of hearing, not being able to adjust individual channels seems like a massive oversight as the SFX drowns out all the voices.  This often led to moments where I felt incredibly lonely or isolated, which is fine once in a while, but with how often this happened it seemed very counterintuitive for a game that's supposed to be played together with friends.

I understand that the slow walking and travel pace is intended—the game's title makes that very clear—but I think it hurts the game more than it benefits it. If you get split up, it ends up taking far longer than it should to group up again. This only added to the feeling of isolation I felt while playing the game, while also throwing FOMO into the bag, since there's little point in waiting for others to group up given the time it takes to do so. The day and night cycle and inventory system do not help the case for this either, as they hinder progress when splitting into smaller groups with item slot pressure (even with backpacks and the like), with the night further exacerbating this due to needing a light source of some kind. 

There are other issues in the game that other Steam users have put more eloquently than I have. I did have fun with this game, but not enough to justify the investment ($20 per player!), and I probably wouldn't even recommend it for when it goes on sale. I'll edit my review if anything changes.

There are very few games that are capable of pulling an emotional force as powerful and as symbolic as Big Walk. What some call gourds we call pairs, beyond the wall was the Tungsten Ball, we flailed our arms around in unfunny memes, laughed, failed a few puzzles, but we always came back every Sunday because this game is just that much fun. In a landscape dominated by "friendslop" and a time dominated by online friendships where attention spans are short and time together fleeting, you can look to Big Walk as a testament to defying that stagnant status quo. The answer to the question can you really consider yourself friends if simply going on a walk together, whether in game or in life isn't enough for you. Here the answer is an emphatic yes: impossible to complete on your own and necessary to have friends passionate enough to spend hours together to simply explore and soak it all in. It's a feeling sorely missed in most games in this genre, in the industry in general, and I'm glad Big Walk soars in treading its own path, one horse clop(?) at a time.

Really could use volume sliders though, environmental noises and BGM tend to overwhelm the proximity chat at times. 9.5/10, genuine Game of the Year contender and deserves to be played to the end at least once with a friend group.

Day/night cycle only causes frustration as players can only carry one item in their hand at a time. Backpacks are excluded because only your friends can access it and a few puzzles require players to be a medium to large distance away from each other, meaning whatever's on your backpack is inaccessible. 

At night time, it's very easy to fall off a cliff and lose the gourd in your hand and be unable to get it back as the shrubbery, trees and steep inclines means it can be hidden in a bush or roll all the way down a large hill, essentially softlocking the game, so this encourages players to wait it out, which would be very boring.

The entire map being open world is not good as it is very easy to get lost and not know where to go, made worse by the fact that you can only carry one item at a time and also night time as well.

Getting separated from the group can happen easily, but regrouping can be very difficult because of night time and only being able to carry one item at a time.

Rebinding keys doesn't really rebind the key as I would expect it to, instead now you have 2 keys that do the same thing.

The distance from which you can hear other players from is far too little.

Another thing with only being able to carry one item at a time is that quite a few items are basically required for navigation and communication, mainly being the walkie talkies (again, this is very important because quite a lot of puzzles require the players to be far enough away to not hear each other, or have walls that block sound). The store page of the game says that there is a required minimum of 2 players needed to play, so if you play with one other person, then deciding what items to bring with you is a nightmare as there are about a dozen other items useful for communication and navigation. So basically the game is actually ENCOURAGING players to use external voice chat because not having to bring walkie talkies everywhere means being able to carry a different item instead, like the compass, map, GPS, directional torch or a gourd. 

Lastly, THE TRAIN ISN'T EVEN FAST!!! WHY

I knew about Big Walk long before it released. It looked interesting, but I wasn’t convinced the game will be special. That was until I heard the main theme of the game for the first time, and I knew we are up for a treat. 
So let me tell you: the game is special. 

[h3] What a game map man [/h3] 
The game map was made with the help of a lindar scans 3D map of Wilsons Promontory National Park. I never saw such a beautifully crafted and detailed game recreation of Australian nature. The dev team crafter around 100 native plants, that are all faithfully places on the map. And don’t get me started on nature sounds the team has recorded them self. The whole sound design of the game is so damn good. From the insects buzzing, and bird songs to the button clicks, or just the way the voice echoes in certain areas. 
No matter where you go day or night the game looks great. The sunsets are the prettiest in my option. It really makes you wants to just sit down and take it all in. Gosh Australia so beautiful. 

And then you have the silly plastic looking structures that looks so out of place and ridiculous in the realistic nature. They grab your attention easily; you can’t miss them. They look like they are out of smooth plastic, and really remind me of children playground. That is how the whole game feels. A playground you and your friends get to play in. 

[h3] the puzzles [/h3]
I am surprised by the variety of puzzles. They all feel like “keep talking and nobody explodes, but you don’t get to talk most of the time and instead franticly gesture to your friends.” In the best was possible. For example, there is a puzzle where you need to describe sounds you hear to your friend, but they can’t hear you, and need to pick the right sound out of many. Or you might observer them with binoculars, while they show you the right pose you must select in the sequence. Or you need to work together to press the right buttons at the right time. The result is an entertaining cycle of planning and execution. The worst that can happen is you all regroup and talk the puzzle over. 

The solutions are mostly randomly generated. So, there is a lot of replay value. You might remember how to solve it, but you don’t know the solution, and the person you play with might not know how to execute it efficiently, or understand what you want from them. The game is perfect at creating and exploiting communication gaps, and making you understand how your game partners think. By then end you learned a lot about your friends, and yourself. And it feels great to see a puzzle and just execute it perfectly no words needed.  

I can’t even imagine the chaos that must occur if you play on 4+ player map. That is another thing. The puzzles come in 2, 3 and 4+ (up to 12 players) variant. The puzzle change to accommodate differently sized groups. This ensures the best experience and adds more replay value 

[h3] the end will stay with you (no spoilers) [/h3] 
This game is a journey. You will spend hours with your friends on this puzzle filled island, overcome challenges, collect items, spend cold night together, get lost and found and especially you will do a LOT OF WALKING. [i] I love hiking [/i] SO once you can finally get behind the big wall and enter the ominous big black sphere. The journey changed you all. You are now bonded, and have a deeper understating of yourself. And the fuffing ending man. I will never forget that that ending. Some journeys you can take only once in your life, and by the and all you have is memories you share with the people who walked with you.

In a world of friendslop, Big Walk was touted to me as a friendgem. But that's not right; in fact, it's THE friendgem.

On a more sincere note, Big Walk is one of those one-in-a-million amazing games, a unique experience that makes you -- even during the game -- sit back and marvel at the sheer quality and awe of the moment. The atmosphere is impeccable, although that was never in any doubt for me since the first trailer for the game dropped. It's a relaxing venture through nature that also boasts an incredibly high-quality puzzle game.

Except for when it's not REALLY relaxing. It's never stressful, but there are moments of... weight. Of impact. Of significance that will stay with you perhaps forever. The ending of the game is majestic, truly one of the best gaming experiences I've ever had; upon finishing the... main quest (as it were), the game was an immediate favorite.

If you want me to list cons, things to be wary of, the only one I can think of is this; I wish the talking radius was larger. That's it. I have no other complaints. The radius is not ridiculously small, but when walking out in the woods it can be hard to make sure people can hear you. Early on it was causing me some very mild anxiety, but that's on me and was exacerbated by the fact that I was playing with a group of six people. Still worth having that many friends to play with, but it was at times frustrating due to the number of people.

It is perhaps an empty buzzword in this context -- 'an experience' -- a fancy way of saying it was a cool game, but perhaps it isn't. If you're looking for something fast and distracting, for adrenaline and immediate gratification, look elsewhere; there's nothing wrong with any of that, but you simply won't find it here. If you're interested in meaning and are willing to earn it, however, then you're in the right place. Big Walk is a fantastic, life-altering experience to be shared with a careful selection of friends. As a preface, it's not my place to police who gets to experience Big Walk, or how you experience it. With that said, I would encourage that selection to be comprised of people who are committed to be there for every step you take. Beyond that, it's up to you what comprises friendship. My subjective injection is that I hope the composition has people who are thoughtful and care about you. People who are good people. Friends that are good friends.

There is no moment in Big Walk that is [i]the moment.[/i] If you're perusing these reviews trying to gleam what exactly that magic moment is, you won't find it through text. The best attempt I can do at transcribing Big Walk into text is the feeling of fond reflection after you've had a vacation or big outing with your friends. And really, it sort of is! The developers, [url=https://househouse.com] House House, [/url] being based in Melbourne, Australia have created a digital homage to the protected lands known as [url=https://www.parks.vic.gov.au/places-to-see/parks/wilsons-promontory-national-park] Wilsons Promontory [/url] south of Melbourne. This facet, along with the stellar sound design, create a real space for you to explore with your friends. The lands of Big Walk are vast and immersive. (As an aside, this game came out in a brutally humid two week stint of summer. While I've never been to Australia and by extension "The Prom," I'd like to imagine the feeling of taking my headphones off at night after a session while experiencing the facsimile of midwestern humidity added to the experience.) This immersion will strike you within minutes of playing and familiarizing yourself with Big Walk, and naturally, you won't even know it happened until it's time to wrap up for the session. 

Big Walk is fun, it's whimsical, and its play is childlike. None of these aspects are spoken or instructed to you. There's not a game-mandated station where you blow bubbles and take a nap. There's no signposts telling you platitudes like [i] the world is a hard place, be kind... enjoy nature... [/i] But being lost in a forest by yourself at night, only to have a flare from a near (or far!) tower light up the world around you in stunning firework display, that's wonder. As I've learned, it's also comfort that your friends are there, and they're thinking about you in one way or another.

A pet peeve of mine is the unhealthy attachment gamers can have to messages in a game -- dialogue or a boss battle that speaks on the heart or ambition of a character. A serious, deeply rooted motif of a game that's to be studied and reflected. Some nitwit online will read into it too much, get too attached, claim a game saved them, make a lengthy diatribe video essay, so on. I don't think that's possible while taking your Big Walk. I think the things you'll feel in this experience are so innately human, and so innately rooted in communication, such that speaking the things you feel almost feels pathetically obvious. You're taking the time to digest these various moments in ways you always should have been. It's my understanding that good communication is routed through the vessels of compassion, understanding, and patience. Big Walk possesses all of these facets, with some of them often manifesting in a literal way. I haven't touched on the puzzles at all in this review, but we left every puzzle that is born from this mantra grinning with arms to the sky, yelling "That was so fun!" to each other as we reunite from our often necessitated separation. 

Big Walk is a space for you and your friends. It is refined and ceaselessly beautiful in its ways. It is not razor sharp with wit, it is vaguely rounded and smooth, much like the... things, you will be collecting in the experience. Succinctly speaking, gathering your friends for Big Walk is not, "Would you like to play Big Walk?"

It is instead, "do you wanna go on a big walk with me?"

[h1][b]Recommended:[/b] Big Walk[/h1]

In a deluge of friendslop games aimed primarily at streamers, it's refreshing to see a title bucking the trend and trying to do its own thing. Well, not exactly - despite, on paper, being aimed at groups of friends who want a chill co-op experience, [b]Big Walk[/b] still owes a lot of its success to going viral on streaming platforms like Twitch.

The intent is still clear, though. In Big Walk, you play as one of up to twelve vaguely humanoid… things exploring a strange island filled with secrets and puzzles. There are no enemies to fight, no character death, and no real fail state either. The entire game is intended as a relaxing hangout with your friends, where you can walk around, chit-chat, and occasionally solve a puzzle or two.

To that end, Big Walk completely eschews the RNG that has become pretty much synonymous with friendslop games, opting instead for a more deliberate, hand-crafted approach. And it shows - all the puzzles feel purposefully designed, all the secrets and Easter eggs are there because someone wanted to put them there, and there are even several points on the island whose sole purpose is to just sit down, relax, and look at a gorgeous vista.

Speaking of puzzles, despite there being quite a few of them (somewhere around 50 by my count), each manages to feel fresh and interesting. Most of the solutions are really intuitive, and they rely just as much on communicating with your teammates as they do on using logic and deduction.

The ending is a particular standout. It plays almost like a "best hits" compilation, using the mechanics you learned from all the previous puzzles to offer new and inventive challenges. There's also a really clever twist I won't spoil here, that is definitely worth completing the game to see. Hell, it even gets genuinely emotional at the very end, which is something that even narrative-focused single player games often struggle to do.

All of this is presented in an extremely charming and inviting art style. The music is fantastic, and the devs deserve extra props for making it completely optional - if you want to play it, you have to pick up a radio and physically choose your favorite track. And the juxtaposition between realistic and detailed environments and abstract, cartoony characters and props never stops being funny.

Of course, nothing is ever perfect, and the same goes for Big Walk. One very obvious downside is the abysmal voice chat range, which is really odd in a game that's supposed to be all about communication and cooperation. Not being able to pick up whatever you're carrying in your backpack or hip holster yourself feels like an odd limitation, and it can get fiddly even with a friend helping.

And then there's the amount of bugs and general lack of optimization. I get that game development is a hectic process, and sometimes you simply don't have the time to put those finishing touches by the release date, but my PC was overheating more that it did with Far Cry 5.

Finally, Big Walk's greatest strength is, ironically, its biggest weakness. The fact that the game is hand-crafted instead of relying on RNG is great, but it also means that, once you've seen everything there is to see, there's no real point in replaying it. I'd be curious to see how many people end up returning to Big Walk once the hype dies down, but my guess would be not that many.

Ultimately, my recommendation for Big Walk really depends on who you plan to play it with and the vibe you're looking for. If you're buying it so you and a group of friends can chill and wind down as you talk and do some light puzzling, go for it - the price is more than justified by what's on offer. And if you're expecting some Chained Together, REPO, or whatever the hell else is the friendslop game of the hour style bullsh*ttery, maybe give this one a skip - I'm sure there are better options out there.

This game takes what's fun about going on an actual walk: the social, the exploration and the accomplishment of overcoming obstacles - and places it in a cute little digital world.

The Australian setting is convincing and realistic. To the point that I get a little nostalgic for these spaces that don't exist. But I cannot understate how the simple design language allows for imagination and fluid thinking to fill the gaps. There's so much detail in the landscape but when the puzzles take centre stage, the space is simple and its up to you, the player to communicate in any way possible. This gives simple mechanics like waving your arms so much depth and meaning. 

You end up feeling like you and your group of friends develop in game personalities and roles. Feeling like a genuine 'adventure' with your friends, where everyone has their dynamic with other people. The unlocks and items feel like the right amount of practical and realistic. Bringing a sense of excitement to a backpack or a key unlockable.

Honestly, the last hour of the game is the highlight. Brining together all you've learnt with your friends that you've all gone on this journey with. Something just clicks and you realise how far you've come.

The ending gave me that sense of... What now? That very few games give me. Waving good bye to this one was tricky and genuinely worth the purchase.
