As a 4-player co-op experience with friends this might be the easiest game recommendation of 2026 so far. The trailers explain the game perfectly as a game about walking and talking and exploring and getting lost and finding each other and sharing experiences etc. What you may find is some of the mechanics are crafted in a way to influence these moments happening, for example the walking isn't the smoothest it could be which can lead to someone falling off the side of a cliff and you then all have to jump off after them or press on and meet up later. 
The game has a super simple inventory system where you get three slots (Hands/Back/Belt) however the only one you can manipulate is the Hands slot, the rest is for your friends to manage this includes storing and retrieving. This is fine as long as you move as a group however there are times where you will want to separate and losing access to these inventory slots and whatever items you may have in them can be frustrating.
You will find yourself having a lot of time to reflect on the game so far.

As a 2-player game I find it harder to recommend, having played it after the 4-player variant I've noticed that it is slightly inferior in many regards. It is still a fun and fine romp but the *magic* that the 4-player has is missing.

From this point on the review will be venturing into spoiler territory (nothing major but examples are needed). I think the way they implemented 2-player is wrong. Throughout the game you will find items to help you in your journey, the most powerful of these is the walkie talkie which allows for cross map communication provided you are not in a restricted area. The problem with this is that the item needs to be in the Hands slot in order to send information, when placed in a belt or backpack you can hear one-way however, which makes the device not as useful as it should be. A few times you will need to travel to separate distant parts of the map to complete a puzzle at which point one of you will be awarded a macguffin and need to dispose of the walkie talkie until the macguffin can be deposited. This means that solitude is forced rather than being a random occurrence. Another issue I have is that the puzzles are altered to facilitate 2-player solving in a bad way. Instead of using the plethora of tools the game provides you with all of the puzzles that needed to be changed are done so in a way that means the items are not necessary.  For example there is a puzzle that requires two players to be locked in separate rooms and need to communicate the solution from one to the other, in 4-player you would have one or two people in the gap between the rooms to telephone the message across however 2-player adds a tunnel that lets then speak directly, but we found that the megaphone item can be used to talk across the gap making the extra players unnecessary. I think the team missed an opportunity to have tools be the replacement for missing players making them a key part of the game and not just a toy to play with. Another situation that is quite common is that the group will be split in two and will need to wait for one group to do something to the other can do something else, which in 4-player means splitting off into pairs and having a nice chat while you wait for your turn but in 2-player means that you must wait in silence. Finally, very early on in the game you will encounter a mirror which is used to see yourself as you change your colours but it is not used in any puzzles whatsoever.

Big Walk is a game I’ve heard about since it was first announced. I was immediately hooked on the art style but didn’t think much of it when it was teased, and I kind of just saw it here and there on State of Plays or Nintendo Directs and went “oh it’s that game!” and moved on with my life. Unfortunately, when it comes to co-op games, the term ‘friendslop’ shows up, and sometimes it’s valid. Ever since games like R.E.P.O. and Lethal Company hit the scene, the amount of unoriginal co-op games released trying to not even be a game meant to be fun, or even co-op games that last for maybe... 2 play sessions at most, hurts my wallet so much, and it’s genuinely upsetting to see a sea of unoriginal games and games that are only meant to be games meant for streamers to play or a quick buck, and that’s it. But with that being said, Big Walk is the anti-friendslop game. On the surface, it looks like a friendslop game, but deep down it is one of the best gaming experiences I’ve ever had in my life. This game was in development before friendslop was even coined, and this game set the standard for the friendslop games; I don’t even wanna engage with any other games in that term. 

Big Walk is about you and a group up to 12 people playing as these.. Bird circle things? (It’s hard to even say what these things are lmao) Exploring this vast open world and doing puzzles. When I say this map is huge, I’m not kidding. I haven’t had this much fun exploring an open world since Breath of the Wild; the amount of discovery you can find in this world is overwhelming yet breathtaking at the exact same time. You unlock parts of the map by solving puzzles and getting these pear-shaped orbs (My friends and I called them jellybeans), and you unlock the towers and grab the key, which unlocks more parts of the map or helps you to get to places faster, or gives you stuff to help you on your way. The main gimmick of Big Walk is communication, and the puzzles range from holding a button at the same time, to listening to sounds to solve a speaker puzzle, to being locked in a muffled room where you can only communicate with whiteboards, a puzzle where you get put on a mask that blinds you, and your friends have to navigate you to finish the puzzle, to grabbing a tomato bomb where you have work with your team to put it in the pot before it breaks and so much more. Those puzzles I’ve mentioned barely scratch the surface of how many there are, and all of them are not bad at all in the slightest; there is not a single bad puzzle, and the final puzzle at the end is one of the coolest things ever and made me think of the ending of 2001: A Space Odyssey. The puzzles are seriously some of the best I’ve experienced in gaming history, and I’m not even a fan of puzzles in gaming because I suck shit at them, but I actually loved doing every puzzle with my friends.

The open world seems bland, but you slowly open up stuff to make stuff faster, like a gondola and a train to make moving around faster, but imma be honest, just actually walking and exploring the open world was enough to make me go in awe. There’s even moments to sit and relax like a beach and a puzzle that locks you in a room for 5 minutes (and a 30 minute one in late game) to just... hang out with your friends. And doing these with my irl friends was genuinely fun and hard-hitting ngl. Even hanging out with my friends and solving puzzles and exploring this world and unlocking stuff was hard-hitting for me, as I haven’t seen my friends in years since I moved away and I haven’t had a game where I reflect on friendships with irls and even online friends, and it became a personal game to me in that regard.

The soundtrack is one of my favorite soundtracks of all time, next to games like Nier Replicant, Earthbound, Hollow Knight, Majora’s Mask, etc. The way a lot of the tracks are acapella songs because of the theme of communication, the theme song for the game ‘Jumping Voices’ is one of the most beautiful songs I’ve ever fucking heard, and the base game has so many amazing songs that range from different feelings. The way I just sat and reflected on the music is a good way of saying ‘yeah this soundtrack fucks hard.’ 

I also want to say that my friends and I couldn’t put the game down for how good it is and I love my friends to death, this game is really a special game with 3 or more players and even though that not a lot of people have friends to play this game, it still is an experience at least once in your life if you garner a group of friends or even strangers. But to my friends, thank you for playing this with me; this was an experience I will never forget, and to House House, thank you for making an important game in my life, definitely one of the best co-op games I have ever played. I hope this wins GOTY at the Game Awards because it’s probably going to be my GOTY for 2026, and I NEVER nominate multiplayer games until now. Big Walk is what I wanted a co-op game like this to be: fun with friends, fun gameplay, exploration, a banger soundtrack, and an experience you will never forget. Big Walk is a 10/10 masterpiece and hell, I’m just itching to play it again.

This game is not "Friendslop", it should absolutely be played co-op but it differs from typical "Friendslop" in some pretty major ways, if you are unaware of what those differences are, you might fall into the scenario of feeling like you wasted your money on a bad game. My goal is to try and give you my understanding as to what those differences are in hopes that i can help guide you towards making a more informed decision

This is what my interpretation of "Friendslop" games is.

 In most games that have earned the title "Friendslop" the generic pattern of gameplay is pretty much, load into scenario with friends, attempt to achieve whatever goal has been set (i.e. Climb the mountain, achieve the daily quota, make enough money to get to the next level, figure out what ghost haunts this location, etc.) the process through which you achieve this is typically where the friendship aspect comes in, as most of these goals require teamwork to accomplish, alongside the need for teamwork is obviously the ability to sabotage just as much as you help. Thus the typical balance is born, lock in and work together to achieve your goal or mess around and achieve some pretty hilarious outcomes because the game, either openly or covertly, support the actions of sabotaging your teammates, never in a malicious way but just little things that in the bigger picture have plenty of genuine purpose, yet they also heavily contribute to the reaction and outcome of certain moments in game (i.e. deathchat in things like lethal company or repo, the ghost form in peak etc.) these things should be in the game for a multitude of reasons but it is undeniable that they enhance the experience of messing with your friends by offering a suitable outlet for the reactions to take place and be experienced by members of the group, this is an inherent part of what makes these games so popular, alongside this is also the fact that most "Friendslop" games offer some form of tension or buildup, this puts pressure and keeps the roughhousing within a certain range because there are genuine consequences to not putting in effort to accomplish the overall mission (i.e. failing if you don't reach the quota for the day, the mist creeping up on you in peak, time limits on making decisions, monster spawns increasing the further you go in repo LC etc.) all of these small things work together to form the pacing of what a typical "Friendslop" game is, this concoction of game elements works exceedingly well at creating an environment where funny moments, clip worthy moments, content worthy moments, all happen on a more frequent basis in comparison to other games as well as forming its own unique niche in the gaming genre as a whole. 

I would offer the comparison to board games like Monopoly, Uno, Life, Chutes and Ladders, all games that work best when played with 4-5 friends who all enter with an understanding that the fun comes from the competitiveness of the players themselves working within the confines of the rules the game has set to enter into a scenario where the reality of picking the funniest option over the best option is almost always the most socially accepted and chosen answer (i.e. Uno reverse, Go to jail card, etc.) 

Big Walk is not that, Big Walk is putting together a jig-saw puzzle.

Big Walk has certain aspects that make it very similar to other "Friendslop" games, proximity chat, generalized goal set from the start, a basic requirement for at least two people to get the best experience, even the way your character moves and looks reminds you of a typical game of this genre, and it certainly delivers in those aspects, the foundation of this game is as solid as every other gamer of this kind out there, however it immediately begins to differ after we look past those aspects of its foundation. 

There is no tension. 

There is no reason to rush at all, no big monster is chasing you, no big timer is counting down to doomsday, no need to open a safe room everyday or to avoid certain areas of the map, it doesn't encourage messing with your friends or have anything that specifically puts your group in a scenario where not working together is funny for longer then 2 minutes, it is exactly what the name of the game says it is, one Big Walk, you solve puzzles along the way and have fun conversations with your friends. Excitement comes from finding a new puzzle, a new [spoiler] backpack or belt [/spoiler] or finishing a tower, nothing gives you a nudge to continue messing with your friends over just having a good time solving puzzles together, it is a slow, calm, lazy walk through some of the most fun and interesting puzzles I've done in a long time. If you come into this game with the perspective of walking into a game like repo or peak or lethal company than you are going to be in for a rough time. This game does not want to be anything like the "rouge-like"esque games mentioned above, where levels are new each time, things are reset and randomized to form new experiences, yes, but it also sets the stage again for more funny moments to happen. Big Walk is one experience throughout, if you've finished a puzzle then its done, if you've finished a tower than its done, there is no infinite loop to this game, it has a defined ending and is constantly walking you towards that, the experiences that you have while playing in the leadup to the end all grow exponentially more important and meaningful when you've finished the game. You will never have the experience of solving that puzzle for the first time ever again, and you will never have the same experience you had when you saw the old man in repo for the first time, but repo tries to give you as many opportunities as you want to have some spectacularly funny moments with that old man, Big Walk lets the puzzle rest. 

This game is at this point in time my game of the year, I adore everything about it and i think that this team should feel exceedingly proud of their work and the product that they ultimately created. This is ,in my eyes, a work of art that is genuinely one of the most unique experiences of my life. A game that I think everyone should give a try at least once and has brought me more joy and happiness then I initially would have ever though it would. A true 10/10 in my heart, Big Walk is an amazing experience and I hope that I helped you make a decision on if you want to try this game. If you wind up not getting it, great, play the games you think you'll enjoy. if you wind up getting it, awesome, I sincerely hope you have as good of a time as I did while playing.

This is an incredibly good open world cooperative exploration/puzzle game.  The trailers alone didn't really pique my interest at first, in part because open world games have kind of lost their charm to me over the years.  Things like objective markers, a fully interactive world map, and a fast travel system (while usually intended as quality-of-life features for players) feel like they can detract from the experience of simply exploring a vast open world.  

Fortunately, Big Walk is noticeably devoid of most of these features (at least from what I've seen so far having only gotten a few hours in), which I think contributes to an open world experience where the journey truly is just as engaging as the destination.  No objective markers means you and your friends need to figure out what your objective is on your own.  No interactive world map means you need to use more rudimentary and challenging forms of navigation (such as an incomplete paper map with no live markers for the players, or just the good-old-fashioned method of climbing to a high place to look around) just to figure out where you are.  And no fast travel means you have to walk everywhere; and while in other games that might feel tedious, this game makes it interesting!  

Another thing I want to highlight is how much the game emphasizes [i]learning as you play[/i].  The tutorial gives you the basic controls and gameplay mechanics; but after that, there is very little direct instruction the game gives you.  There are no NPCs or signs explicitly telling you where to go, what to do, or how to use that new tool you found.  It is all left entirely up to you and your friends to discover through trial and error.  If you like "Outer Wilds" (as I do) for its emphasis on learning about the game as you go, then you very well may like this game.

I noticed that a lot of the early negative reviews for the game pointed out how limited the range for the in-game voice chat was.  And when I first started playing, I too was a bit taken aback by it.  Essentially, in most locations in the game, you can only hear people at their full volume when they are within about 20 ft of you; as you get further away, your ability to hear each other plummets until you can't hear each other [i]at all[/i] beyond 30 or 40 ft.  It seemed ironic to me that a game that sells itself on being all about [i]talking[/i] with your friends made it so hard to do exactly that.  But as I played, I realized that that was part of the magic that made Big Walk so fun to play.  With such a restricted voice chat system, players are encouraged to find unique and interesting ways to talk to each other.  In that sense, figuring out [i]how[/i] to communicate with each other is one of the core challenges in the game.  If you want to talk with your group, make sure to get everyone close together so you can hear each other (my group got into the habit of, after completing a main objective, having a "group conference" in which we would all huddle together to discuss what to do next).  If you want to go ahead of the group, take a megaphone with you so your friends can hear you from farther away.  If you get separated, go back to that clearing where you remember you all previously played with that button that shoots fireworks into the air, where you can now use it as a way to signal to your friends where you are.  Or as a last resort, climb up to the tallest nearby peak and speak loudly, and your voice will echo across the landscape, allowing people to hear you from much further away.

Overall, I highly recommend Big Walk as a game that is fun in a way that very few open world games truly are.

In an endless deluge of "friend" games trying to capitalize on the terminally online streamer audience, Big Walk stands out as one of the most engaging and poignant experiences you can have with your buddies online. Though it shares a lot of its DNA with those games - proximity chat, funny gestures  - nothing feels tacked-on; everything that seems like a gimmick actually has a use. Brilliant sound design, neat puzzles, and a ton of fun.

I first heard about this game when it was announced during the Nintendo Direct back in June and I was interested in playing it. Kind of forgot about it for a bit until one of my friends suggested playing it. I didn't really know what to expect when we first loaded in but it was a lot better than I was expecting. I thought this game would be more linear in a sense that you are taking a big walk down a path. But was pleasantly surprised to see that it is open-world. It's so fun walking around trying to find puzzles. Speaking of, all of the puzzles were really fun to try and solve. None of them felt impossible and it was very satisfying to solve. They were not rage-inducing either. If you got frustrated it wasn't at the game, it was at yourself (or your friends). Even my friends who aren't into puzzle-solving games had fun with these puzzles. No matter what obstacles got in the way. It is so much fun trying to find out how to solve it. If you are looking to play a game with friends that doesn't include a ball or a gun. I would heavily recommend this. A very chill experience, and one of the best games of 2026.

The Big Walk is a fantastic co-op experience. If you enjoyed games like Portal 2, you'll likely enjoy this too. The art direction is simple but appealing. The puzzle design is deeply creative. The pacing may seem slow at first, the game really is about soaking in the atmosphere and taking time with the world. It reminds me of the problem solving of an escape room, but focuses on genuine logic puzzles rather than hunting for hidden keys. The limitations, from communications to unlocks, are synergistic and justified; it never feels frustrating. Highly recommend to anyone who likes teamwork games.

I tried. I really, truly tried to find the appeal in this, but I feel like I am being gaslit by the overwhelming amount of positive reviews. Big Walk doesn't feel like a video game; it feels like an elaborate social experiment specifically engineered by the developers to study the behavioral habits and patience thresholds of simpletons. Strip away the colorful aesthetics and the hype, and what you are left with is one of the most painfully boring, simplistic, and artificially drawn-out puzzle simulations ever created. The mechanical loops are incredibly basic, yet they are stretched across hours of agonizingly slow traversal. The entire product is cleverly disguised as a fun, cooperative experience to share with your friends. But let’s be entirely honest: the game itself contributes absolutely nothing to that equation. If you are having fun, it is entirely because you and your friends are forcing yourselves to joke around to survive the monotony. original review:

The best part of most "friendslop" games is the friends. But usually, being with your friends is detrimental to your success in the game. If I stand on a landmine in Lethal Company for the bit, at best I'm burning time and at worst I create a huge problem. The quota, timer, and money system means that, especially a few moons in, you actually have to play the game or risk loosing your save file.

Big Walk, on the other hand, has no such problem. Even if you chuck a Macguffin off of the mountain, that's not a failure condition. Worst case scenario: that one puzzle resets when you reboot the game. Best case scenario: you and your friends have this moment of finding the  Bambino together. 

This means that you're actually free and encouraged to goof off, get lost, and not "play the game." 

And it's so much fun. If you have the means, I highly recommend it. Especially in parties with 7+ people. You can actually do some divide and conquer, accidentally or intentionally, or just have a chaotic mass of friends all trying to solve the same puzzle together.

You kinda do need friends tho. But it's mechanically a very simple game. Excellent first 3D game material if you have any non-gamer friends.

[h1] Cons: [/h1]
1) The volume. There's only the OVERALL volume slider. You can't customize how loud the game is as opposed to the players, let alone how loud each player is for you. Normally the game doesn't have much music going on and you only have quiet ambiance, so it's usually not a problem, but when you enter an area with louder music or if you're carrying a radio around, it can be hard to understand what everyone else is saying at times, especially if one friend is louder than the others. From my understanding they have updated it so that the player voices are louder, but I still feel we should have sliders for this.
2) The trains. Out of all the fast travel elements, the trains are definitively the least helpful with how slowly they run. You need it frequently in late game to cross vast distances without having to climb up and over several hills, and can spend a lot of time waiting for the train and then on the train waiting for it to reach your destination, to the point where you may feel like it would have been faster if you had simply walked. This would easily be fixed by having a fourth train unlocked or their speed increased in late game. That said, the wait isn't the worst, so it's far from the end of the world.
3) The day-night cycle. While there are many things during the day that you can do perfectly with no trouble at all, a lot of those things become a lot harder during the night. You can bring lights with you, but it only lights up a small radius around you. If you're trying to spot a puzzle location but it isn't an obvious building, you might completely pass it. There are also certain puzzles where you'll need to be finding/holding an object that's not a light, so if you don't wait for day, you'll be stumbling around unable to see since you can only hold one item (this might not be a problem with more people). I understand they want the immersive experience the day-night cycle provides, and I agree that it might be lacking without it, it just feels a little painful as is. If they had something more interesting going on that was unique to nighttime, like a puzzle or item you could only get then, or something atmospheric like stringed lights in different areas, then I believe it would be much better.
4) The rocks. Yes, the stray rocks and sticks. About half of your exploration will be following paths or flatter surfaces, but the other half is climbing around mountains that have a lot of tiny rocks and sticks, etc, to get your poor character's feet stuck on. You get stuck a lot more easily if you're holding a large item in particular, as the additional hitbox also proceeds to get stuck on stray rocks and sticks. You get used to it and learn what will and won't be feasible after a while, but I wish there were fewer small objects to get stuck on.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]
1) The gesturing. It's really funny looking (in the best way), and you'll frequently use it in instances where you can't talk to each other, so you'll just be wildly gesturing at your friends and they'll be laughing their butts off at you.
2) The noises for specific things. I'll keep this one vague as some of the best ones come with spoilers as context, but the sound design for things like wiping your arms against the glass (yes I'm bringing it up again), handling items in puzzle rooms, and completing objectives are the most satisfying sound effects I've heard in a while. They could've kept it very basic, but it feels like instead of just doing that, someone had a field day making the most fun sounds they could come up with and it perfectly enhances the gameplay and the fun overall.
3) The achievements. Now I mention this because if you have any idea what the achievements are like for Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, and/or Halo, you'll start to wonder how bad getting all the achievements for a game will be, and if you should just cut your losses, throw your completionism in the garbage can, and not worry about it. I'm very happy to say that this game has none of the absurdly hidden achievements that force you to resort to googling, and that you'll likely end up with all of them by the time you're done no problem.
4) The freedom of choice. The game starts with a tutorial section before opening up the vast majority of the map, so once you're through with it, you can pretty much do things in any order you want. This has become increasingly common with the popularization of open world games, but I find they did it particularly well here in that any objective you find, no matter how small, adds up to the main objective as a whole and feels rewarding in the process instead of some things feeling like a drop in the pot you would only bother with for the sake of completionisting (looking at you, Koroks).
5) The flexibility of the puzzles for the player count. Each time you open up the same world you're asked how many people are going to be playing. This means that if you want to, you can use the same world despite the changing number of friends you can round up that day. The puzzles adapt accordingly to allow for more or fewer people to have a role in them, although some of them will remain as only needing two people just for the type of puzzles they are. This means that if one of your friends isn't able to play in your four player world but the other three want to continue, they can continue to make forward progress that session by switching to three player puzzles (you will have to rejoin the world) before swapping the world back for when the fourth player rejoins the group sessions, etc, and is incredibly useful.

Overall, I absolutely love this game and would recommend it so long as you're okay with puzzles on the easier end, lots of walking, and that one friend who keeps walking off and getting lost for about an hour, and finally, thank you to my friend for sacrificing her feet to the rocks and sticks as she carries me around in the dark.

You. Can. Sit. In. This. Game.

I went into this game on a whim with zero expectations, just to find myself 22 hours later reaching 100% completion with my best friend. Needless to say, I absolutely loved this gem of a game. 

[h1] DISCLAIMER [/h1]

To begin, I do want to preface this with a warning that this game is not for everyone and is not suited for every group. This game does not aim to suck your attention for every minute of every hour, and you will find yourself often in moments of just... silence. As the trailer itself puts it: "This is a game where you walk and talk with your friends." If you are not one for these silent pauses that exist in the distance between objectives, I would advise going into this game cautiously if at all. Most importantly-- I'd suggest going into this game with a friend(s) that you can make fun with moments that even may seem like "nothing."

As a note, I did purely play this experience as a duo and have not experienced what gameplay is like in a larger group setting.

[h1] PUZZLES [/h1]

A complaint I see often of this game is the simple nature of the puzzles. However, I personally found myself being especially fond of these puzzles. While they follow a similar formula and you may find yourself encountering similar gimmicks, by no means is any puzzle the same as another. If anything, I find that the puzzles do a great job building off of these core mechanics. Taking an easier foundation and expanding it through slight tweaks or added challenges. However, I would not describe these puzzles as "difficult." My friend and I had little to no issue solving any puzzles with the exception of a few of the endgame. Please do not go into this game expecting the challenge of a lifetime. The difficulty does not stem from the puzzle mechanics itself, but rather through how you communicate with your group. Something that I imagine only increases the larger the group you may have.

[b] !!!!SPOILER WARNING FOR ENDGAME (POST CREDITS)!!!! [/b]

The only puzzles my friend and I adamantly disliked were the puzzles included in the endgame, post credits scene. I won't go into too much into detail to avoid spoiling the experience, but these puzzles are what I deem to be straight "tedious." Taking between 30 minutes to an hour of walking, looking for the objective, or even sometimes just sitting. While my friend and I did make use of this time (for one we literally just watched an episode of a show), these puzzles did leave us more annoyed than satisfied upon competition. The good thing is that these puzzles are a minority in the majority of puzzles that are excellent. It only makes up about maybe 5% of them.

[h1] TERRAIN AND TRANSPORT [/h1]

The terrain of this game does admittedly leave room to be desired. If you're going into this game with the expectations of exploring wonderous landscapes, I'm afraid you will be disappointed. While I found the world itself to be gorgeous (likely due to the high-quality graphics), by no means was the exploration itself the pinnacle of my experience. However, endgame (or pre-endgame, depending how you look at it), does offer quite a surprise in the means of worldbuilding and suspense. Both in atmosphere, storytelling, and overall mood. I would highly recommend playing just to experience this moment for yourself. 

The actual "open world" aspect is also executed very well. The game never gives you a moment to be overwhelmed by the sheer size of the map and the countless objectives littered across it. With the use of the tutorial area, the locked transport systems, the blocked off walls, the game does an excellent job at narrowing down the world into your field of vision. Allowing you to approach it at your own pace. This is notably aided by unlocking more areas, tools, and transport through completing the main objectives. 

My biggest gripe with the landscape mainly comes from the smaller obstacles that you will no doubt be finding yourself slamming into every five seconds. Littered across the land is countless rocks, sticks, logs, and sometimes even STAIRS that serve as constant roadblocks to you trying to get literally [i] anywhere [/i] . My gameplay consisted of never-ending jumping just to avoid stubbing my bird person's toe every other step.

Transport is a mixed bag for me, though remains 80% positive. For majority of my gameplay, I didn't find myself actually using transport enough to make a proper note on it. This being primarily due to mainly sticking in one area as we worked to complete the main objective: the tower. It worked well enough when we used it and it was a ton of fun going about actually unlocking each means of transport. It's akin to restoring life back into a forgotten world, it's actually pretty neat. Transport only actually becomes annoying when you start approaching endgame (post credits) where you find yourself having to travel significant distances.

[b] Spoilers for Transport Systems (I go into specifics here) [/b]

The tunnels were by far the best and the method we used most often to get around the world. The sky lift was also great, though more situational in comparison (not to mention just fun). The train, however, often felt rather useless in actually saving you time. First, you have to wait for the train to arrive at a given stop. Which can take upwards of what feels like five minutes. Then, once actually on the train, it takes even longer to even reach your destination at all. Often leaving you wondering if it would be faster to simply walk. The only benefit of the train system is knowing exactly where you're going, being able to avoid stumbling in the dark during the night and not having to deal with the rocks and sticks on the ground. My main desire with the trains is for them to either be faster individually or add another train entirely. 

[h1] Day and Night Cycles [/h1]

I, with no amount of exaggeration, absolutely DESPISED the day and night cycle in this game. While I understand that it is likely meant to add to the realism of the experience, this did not take away the pure frustration that stumbling around at night subjected me too. While you do have light sources to provide a counter to this sight limitation, often times I found its assistance rather useless. When we had a light source at all, it's range of vision only assisted enough to prevent you from slamming into a rock or falling off a cliff directly in front of you. I would often times find myself walking blindly for five minutes, just to realize I had been walking myself in circles the entire time. Sometimes, you are also unable to hold onto any light source due to having to hold onto objects related to a puzzle (or walkie talkies for communication). Often times, my friend and I found ourselves just sitting on a hill waiting for day to come.

I imagine the day and night cycles would hold more value if it actually added anything worthwhile to the gameplay itself. Be it through smaller decorations or light sources (akin to lighting up the red lights on the stumps as you go) or even puzzles that have mechanics based around this cycle. Without this, the day and night cycle mainly feel like an annoying time waster without much depth behind it.

[h1] Miscellaneous [/h1]

This game is just filled to the brim of charm, having a ton of smaller things that enhance your experience as a whole. My personal favorite was the gestures, being able to wave your arms around like a mad man will never not bring me joy. Not to mention the ability to SIT? I've never been so satisfied. The sound design, character models/customization, music tracks, and the little blobs/gourds are also some of the little details that make this game that much more memorable to me. The AFK animations are just to die for.

By far, this is one of the best experiences that I've had in a long while. Despite my gripes, the pros of this game far outweigh the cons, and I cannot recommend it enough.

A really REALLY incredible game. It took me and my friends a few weeks to complete it all, coming together in the evenings in groups of four or sometimes as a duo. Every time, we found something new, did a new puzzle or collected some important info. 

In an era of competitive games and where social pressures are rampant, this game really is a breath of fresh air. Things are designed intuitively, with heart and soul and there are little messages left by the makers that really do hit home. This game was definitely made with love. 

It isn't without its faults. The landscape is, admittedly, a bit same-y but also frustrating in places. It'd also be nice to have gadgets like ladders, maybe a grappling hook for picking up friends or a way to not have the gadgets fly out of your hand after a small drop.

The trains are also way too slow and being able to not access your pocket/backpack is really annoying. I understand that it's all about teamwork, but when you know you have a walkie talkie on your back and your friend is trying to contact you, it becomes frustrating. 

So, is it a perfect game? No, but it's damn close. If House House continue to make another one, why not call it Bigger Walk, I'm sure they'll nail it by polishing little details and adding more and better gadgets along with ways to interact with them.

I think this game has found an interesting niche in the puzzle genre: the puzzles are similar to Zachtronics puzzles, in the sense that the solution is invented rather than discovered. We see a puzzle, and spontaneously create a plan to solve it, whether that be a particular way to move our arms or a signal to be transferred via lightbulb.

It is simply fun to trust your friends have understood your bizarre, arm-waving messages through soundproof glass. Rather than being frustrating, accidental miscommunications are heartwarming and funny. We regroup, laugh, discuss what went wrong, and try again.

I have only seen a single puzzle that I didn't think was good, namely one where we had to distribute four people far across the map and pull a switch at the same time. It was just tedious to organise, took far too long, and couldn't have been understood in its entirety without walking the whole distance.

The game is excellent. Get it. Play it with your friends. Do it. Now.

Overall though, I had an excellent time with this game, and I hope I'll be able to wrangle more of my friends together to play it all over again. Big Walk is an easy recommendation; anyone who enjoys solving puzzles with friends will absolutely want to play this one -- very accessible to all skill levels. House House has knocked it out of the park again with this title, which I think is best described as "Lost, but cozy".

The entire thing plays like a big, casually paced escape room. It encourages you to play with the objects in the world, learn what they do and make connections between things. It deeply encourages the players to think through how to best communicate nuanced information with limited means, in a way that requires creativity -- you'll find tricks, techniques and solutions unique to you and your friends, like inventing interpretitive dances to relay complex shapes or sounds (that is not an exaggeration).

Perhaps the best bit is that this is all couched in a picturesque, mysterious island that encourages you to learn natural landmarks and routes and appreciate the landscape entirely in its own right. The stakes are low, the pressure is low, but the challenges are novel and satisfying to tackle.

Honestly, there is virtually nothing here that doesn't feel absolutely thoughtful and lovely. There are some  times when navigating a particularly brushy, rocky or steep area that you can get a little stuck and that takes some time to acclimatize to, and it's easy to sometimes push things around unintentionally as your body collides with other players, objects and the environment matching the space it actually occupies (so holding something in front or above you can sometimes bonk on things unexpectedly) -- but those concerns are easy to get used to and move past. Early patches also show that House House is aware of some of the small sticking points and is making a point to try and address them (and other similar issues, like quiet microphones).

Give this one a try; set aside a few hours for you and some friends to get a little lost. You'll be hooked in no time.

A smattering of weak, derivative corporate team-building exercises dumped into a generic forest prefab setting. It's a poorly optimized game that chews on GPUs if left unchecked and looks nasty at anything under "High" settings. The proximity voice chat has poor range (even after a patch), and there’s only one volume slider for everything, making it an auditorily unbalanced/unpleasant experience. 

Most of the puzzles are intuitive situations turned into time-wasters or dead-simple problems given complexity through limiting basic communication. No twists and turns or unique mechanics, just games of telephone, hot potato, and trust exercises. You’ve definitely seen it all before. There’s nothing clever or satisfying about walking a distance to relay a symbol or being trapped in a room with an answer that needs to be translated into pointing or nodding. Collectively, these are ideas that don’t hold enough water to last a puzzle game of this moderate length.

While peaceful, all the uneventful hiking and limited range of voice chat promoted less conversation and more confusion. Numbly holding "W" on the keyboard to traverse these unremarkable hills isn't likely to spark meaningful banter, especially if you can’t hear each other from beyond a few meters. The game isn’t doing its job as a host if it leaves it up to you all to entertain yourselves for extended periods.

The one unique thing that Big Walk does facilitate is a type of analog group exploration as you gather around a map with a flashlight and laser pointer aimed at regions of note. However, we found these storage limitations to be annoying despite the game’s mechanical insistence on them. Creating a scenario where one player has to be the "map person" or "dedicated flashlight holder" is one way to incentivize delegation, yet having to leave items behind in the wilderness or constantly returning to towers to deposit idols drags the game down. Plus, being the single person with a single basic responsibility for hours of trekking and puzzle solving is no fun. Pouches/backpacks do exist, but there are not enough of them to meet the pace at which you find new idols/items. 

Nowadays, there are so many other options for cooperative games, puzzle ones or otherwise. As the social co-op genre continues to expand and diversify, Big Walk fails to stand out as anything more than a barren walking sim punctuated by brief distractions of inconsistent quality. The entertainment value of Big Walk scales with your party size, but keeping everyone dedicated to the campaign is like keeping a large D&D crew together. Starting over with a new crew isn’t fun since there’s nothing less interesting than replaying a spaced-out puzzle game where you already know the solutions. I can’t see a scenario in which I’d recommend Big Walk over a large number of social co-op games that let anyone enter and play at any point, especially considering that this game is twice the price of any of its peers.

This is my honest review after 100%ing the game:

My friends and I have been waiting for this game to release since it was first announced, and I'm going to be honest, it was worth it. When the game finally released, my 4 other friends and I got ready and started the journey for an experience I will never forget. And now that we have finished it, I was not disappointed throughout the whole run.

Big Walk is a journey. The walking, the puzzles, the communication, and the friendship we felt and built throughout the journey are truly one of a kind, and I enjoyed every moment of it. There were so many memorable moments and emotions that I felt while playing. The laughs when dumb things happened, the confusion when trying to solve a puzzle, and the excitement when we finally completed it. We even argued during some of the puzzles and laughed it off right after we finished them.

A lot of the puzzles in the game are very good and require communication and teamwork with your friends to figure out how to solve them. The fun part of solving the puzzles is the discussions you have with your friends about how to solve them. This is where communication is heavily relied upon. When you finally complete a puzzle after scrambling together ideas on how to solve it, the feeling is really something else.

While these are the good points of Big Walk, there are also some negatives I want to point out, particularly some of the puzzles in the game. While there aren't many, a few of them are rather tedious to do. When I completed a puzzle, I would have rather done it with all of my friends beside me. I won't mention what the puzzle was, as I would recommend experiencing it firsthand yourselves.

In conclusion, Big Walk is truly a phenomenal game. The experience that I went through can't be replicated in any other game I have played. When I finished the game, I felt saddened because the journey was finally ending. Even after years have passed, I will look back at this game, and it will always remind me of the fond memories that I created with my friends. I can't recommend this game highly enough if you want to experience it with your friends.

[h1]A FriendGem Game: A duo Playthrough Review[/h1] So a quick intro, Big Walk is a game where you land a giant island with upto 1-12 friends (I played this game with a duo). The game session's difficulty changes with number of friends - so one time you can make a session of 4 friends then the next you can do with 5 based on availability or whatever. The giant world is filled with structures (evident from their style) which has puzzles to solve whose keys are used to unlock towers which furthermore unlocks different ways of transportation across the world. Now let's go into the key features of this game and what I liked and disliked about it. [h3]World Navigation[/h3] Pros: So this is by far my favourite thing in the game. This game doesn't hold your hand AT ALL except the starting area after which you are on your own to figure out and interpret everything on your own. Its a very immersive world which can be explored with various tools like walkie talkie, flares, lasers and obviously a map. The night times is ACTUALLY NIGHT TIME, you cannot navigate without a light source. But with duos especially you have to keep in mind what to bring because you can only use what is in your hand and not access your belt or backpack on your own. But there will be countless HILARIOUS moments in this game especially because of this Later on as you progress you unlock the train, skilift and tunnels to improve your navigation speed across the island. Cons: I really think flares should be more accessible early in the game as it is one of the best ways to tell where to go to your partner and where they are right now + the utility of global light source but it. Now the biggest problem for me is the transportation. THEY ARE VERY FUCKING SLOW. I get it what people say that it is "not your type of game", "you need to have patience", "talk with your friends" and shit but idc the transportation, especially the train is absolutely trash because it is lowkey slower than walking. It needs to have 2 way trains or a faster switch. Ski lift is also slow but it takes you directly to towers and on top of mountains - so it makes sense. Navigating in the dark is fun, using spatial awareness and remembering landmarks and stuff BUT... We literally used to go do chores when we sat on a transportation. The exploration aspect diminishes very quickly when you have to go through the same areas multiple times to fetch the keys or solve puzzles you missed. Sometimes I just want to play the fucking game and progress man... this is biggest culprit that "slows" the pace of the game imo. P.s. Also give me more things to fidget in areas like train and do stupid shit and add more easter eggs. The world could be made way more interactive for how bizarre it is. [h3]Puzzle Variety[/h3] Pros: I liked the puzzles. There is a decent amount of thinking (not at all hard though). There were a couple of puzzles which we had interpreted in a wrong manner (like the audio hearing one) which needed some guidance. But I liked the ending puzzles a lot [spoiler] where you fully get muted [/spoiler]. I dont know whether the puzzles get much more harder with bigger groups or not but in duos it was very easy Cons: This game had a lot more potential - I could suggest easily 10-20 more different types of puzzles . Some features like talking through radio towers or using the whiteboard or even lasers are barely used for any puzzles. And the purple egg puzzles are literally copies of the puzzles you have solved before just slightly harder. I really hope that this game has few free updates like Peak to do more with the game. Some puzzle ideas: [list] [*]There could have been a morse code or some cryptographic puzzle that needs to be communicated across towers using the radio or telegraph. [*]There is a common occurance of "press this button on the wall" which is repetitive. One could have easily been a simon says puzzle [spoiler] (the one near the yellow tower - the purple stage one) [/spoiler] [*]There could have been a morse code or some cryptographic puzzle that needs to be communicated across towers using the radio or telegraph. [*]Make more lock rooms with interesting mechanics like where you get blind or get stripped of materials. Maybe do one where you have to use the chalkboard but you cant write actual words. [*]Doing a guess the difference kind of room. [/list] ... I mean the list can go on and on... [h3]Style and Audio[/h3] The style is definetely VERY unique which I find very cute and is a big part in finding out landmarks over the world. You can easily distinguish and tell that it is from this game. There audio system definetely needs a range increase but apart from that that its REALLY good. Voice echoes in ravines and tunnels, certain puzzles have glass that cuts audio but you can tap the glass and stuff. I dont know to explain but its VERY GOOD. Also the menu sound is lowkey iconic lol [h3]Story[/h3] I mean the "story" is not existent tbh. DO NOT Compare it with any Hazelight studios game. Its main story is to spend quality time together with your friend. The ending sequence and puzzles were hella cool though. [h3]BUGS[/h3] The game is actually very fucking polished overall. But I did face the following issues - [list] [*]On day one of launch I faced a few disconnections from the game but it never happened afterwards. [*]There is a puzzle where there is a gate through which you cant bring items in or out of. But somehow I took out one of the items out of the gate which was essential for the puzzle. And because we were doing all puzzles in one zone, we had to restart and revisit this place again only to solve this. Which was pretty annoying. [*]In the starting red tower where you add the red egg key in the glass box. I was annoying my duo with opening and closing the glass box and he dropped the egg in between opening and closing the egg literally glitched inside the wall or something - disappering. Had to restart for this as well. [*]The interactions in the train is HELLA glitchy, all interactable hitspots come and go. [/list] [h2]Overall thoughts[/h2] Overall this game is a fucking banger regardless of my complaints. It is not the game of the year I was thinking it would be and what the internet is saying but I REALLY ENJOYED this game. I think the game is way more fun with 3-4+ friend group as the game is not about rushing but laughing, talking and "walking" with friends through out the journey. That being said it is very important to KEEP YOUR EXPECTATIONS IN CHECK with this kind of game. It is supposed to be a chill puzzle game and it will have a long downtimes (which I personally dont like but the puzzle and world aspect kept us engaged enough) where you talk and do stupid shit. [spoiler] I mean there is a puzzle where you have to sit for 30 mins doing nothing to get one key ... [/spoiler] which can tell you what kind of stuff they want you to do. I want to see more from this game though. Would recommend if it fits your style.

If you can plausibly find any reason to acquire 3 other people to play it with; nay, not acquire, simply find, you needn't know them well.

Big Walk evolves the friendgame genre by making the friends portion not just a vestigial suggestion in which the game is 'Technically you can play me on your own, but friends are a large part of what makes it fun.'

No, this game says 'Some puzzles require 4 people to coordinate. That's the point'

So, why does that matter? What magic does it invoke by turning 'friends suggested' into friends required?

It makes you interact with them. The structure of the game is optimal when you play in a large group of mixed intimacy friends. Because as long as you have one person who will just fuck off into the wilderness to inspect weird thing they saw in the distance tm, the game itself will provide a playground in which for you to generate time together.

The puzzle difficulty ranges from 'I hold this button, you walk far away' to 'We much geocache 4 people to press buttons at the same time' And the game benefits from this.
The interaction system is what carries the game, reliance on your friends is baked into the very interaction modes. When you find a backpack, you can't put it on yourself, you can only put it on someone else. To take it off, same thing; when you find something,  your hands will be occupied carrying it, so that's it, each person can carry one thing. So to have more things, you need more people, or you need a backpack to hold the thing, which you won't be able to access, so the thing is mostly for your friends.

Anyways, if you can manage it, find someone to join and play with, be chill and get to know them, let yourself experience walking around digital grass and enjoy whatever funny shit happens.

I went into Big Walk expecting a funny little co-op game about walking around, getting lost, solving puzzles, and screwing around with friends. I did not expect it to hit me emotionally the way it did. The communication in this game is genuinely something special. Between the proximity voice chat, walkie-talkies, pointing, waving your arms around like an idiot, and the moments where the game makes you figure things out together, you slowly develop this weird little language with the people you're playing with. There were so many moments where we understood exactly what someone meant without really needing to explain it. And the emotional range of this game is honestly incredible. One minute we were frustrated and completely confused, the next we were celebrating with this huge sense of proud excitement because we finally figured something out, and then five minutes later we were absolutely just lost in the woods with no idea where anyone was. 😂 It somehow turns all of those feelings into part of the experience: frustration, confusion, excitement, pride, laughter, panic, and those quiet moments where you're just wandering around together. The puzzles are fun, the world is beautiful to explore, and sometimes the best part is honestly getting distracted and doing something stupid with your friends instead of whatever you were supposed to be doing. But the ending...

*No spoilers. Seriously, experience it yourself.*

The entire final section was amazing, but the *very end* caught me completely off guard. After everything we'd gone through together, all the frustration, victories, getting separated, getting lost, finding each other again, and laughing at complete nonsense, those last few moments suddenly gave the whole experience so much more weight. It was simple, beautiful, bittersweet, and somehow enough to genuinely bring me to tears. Big Walk isn't really just a game about walking or solving puzzles. It's a game about spending time with people. About getting frustrated together, figuring things out together, feeling genuinely proud when you finally succeed, laughing at stupid things together, getting completely lost in the woods together, and eventually realizing that the walk itself was the important part. Absolutely amazing. Please play this with people you care about, and please go in blind. 💛

Sharing this adventure with my closest friends and my partner touched a place in my heart that I did not expect. Whether we were sitting together on the train, riding the chairlift or listening to the beautiful music by the beach, there were moments when we simply stopped and took everything in. We weren't rushing to the next objective or searching for answers. We were just there, together, appreciating the world around us. By the end, I remember saying that I could never play this game with anyone else. The memories we have made feel too precious to recreate, and in a strange way that made the ending feel even more bittersweet. Some experiences only happen once, and perhaps that is part of what makes them worth cherishing. Thank you so much to everyone at House House for creating such a beautiful game, and for giving me something I could share with the people I love. I may never experience this journey in quite the same way again, but I will always be grateful that I got to experience it with them in the first place.

review: One of the best party/group games I've played since the couch co-op days of Gauntlet Legends on N64.

Big Walk is an incredible game. Its the perfect amount of play and teamwork that reminds me of playing with my friends on summer vacation. It scratches an itch through both gameplay and its music. *chefs kiss*

It's like an escape room, except I wasn't stuck with people I hated nor did I want to disown my friend at the end.  

Big Walk was a beautiful, simple, and adorable game.  Is it exciting? Not really.  Do I think there could be some improvements? Yeah (I got stuck on so many rocks). But during this gaming trend of "everything needs crafting and resource gathering", it was a breath of fresh air.  Puzzles ranged from light head scratchers to wholesome & goofy; it was a nice "existing together" game after a long day of work.  It was a good reminder of how in sync my best friend and I are; I can only imagine it'd leave others either feeling the same, or help strengthen weaker areas of creative communication.  

The biggest downside is, I don't really see much replay value in it after completing everything; nor do I want it to fall into the other obnoxious trend of "buy some dlc".  If it gets a free patch of some new puzzles or a new area, that'd be awesome... however, I'm also fine with appreciating it for what it is.

If you enjoyed playing games like Journey, Peak, and It Takes Two I strongly encourage you to buy this; full price.

This is one of those games that you can only experience to the fullest once. It was truly a beautiful experience, I loved every second of it until the very end (honestly I teared up). It's a must-play for me and a co-op gem.

Overall, it's a really charming game. The island and scenery look beautiful, things like the foliage, the mountains, skies and specially the water. You can perfectly stand in there for a bit to simply admire the scenery around you. Also helps the fantastic day-night cycle and how dark the night is.

All that paired with the silly-looking characters which I adore. They fit so well in this realistic world and are full of charm thanks to the many details they have like the eyes and mouth which reacts to many things (opening the menu, falling, being muted, writing...). Also the freedom of being able to move the arms freely and being able to sit anywhere it's fantastic.

The actual gameplay is great. I love just exploring around and going through different places in search for the next puzzle, all while talking around or even getting lost. Just like the game says on boot, absolutely do not use any external tools for communication. Getting lost and going onto a solo adventure until you can reunite with everyone is honestly quite fun (+ most of the puzzles are built into in-game communication).

Regarding the puzzles I enjoy them, there's quite a lot of unique challenges and it has been pretty fun figuring out how to solve them or straight up creating ways of communicating to express the things we see better. Again, this game has really nailed communication both verbal and non-verbal.

Like honestly I don't have many complains about it, game requires solid cooperation so I understand why you can't access your own backpack / belt for example. Really the only negative I have is that the collision for climbing is quite terrible, it's pretty hard to climb them without getting stuck.

Now that the audio sliders have been added, my only minor complain left is the voice chat range, it could be increased just a little bit more. And to add to that, the voice quality is great but sometimes they would become muffled or robotic for a brief moment, unsure what causes that.

Aside from that, this game is a wonderful experience. Played it with 2 of my closest friends and we had an absolute blast.

But! There's still more to see, so I'll indeed return and explore some more after this break :')

UPDATE: We came back and after 14 more hours of gameplay (we took 18 to reach the credits), we reached the 100% completion and truly finished our Big Walk. Again, fantastic game and lowkey sad that it's over, but at the same time really happy that I had this experience.

If you can get a permanent group to play this with, don't hesitate. Go for the credits then push for the 100%, it'll be worth it.

This game puts you and your friends in the role of colorful, ambulatory drinky birds with big, juicy butts. The gameplay is simple: walk around talking with your friends and solve little puzzles together while playing with toys, taking each others toys, painting each others bodies, violating each others corpses, and other wholesome activities. You can also solve puzzles that dot the landscape, ride around on trains, and satisfy your need to explore together, or alone. 

The game is elegantly designed to steer you towards interacting with others, even when it does not clearly move forward any kind of goal. 
For example, while exploring with friends, we encountered a small room furnished with furniture, four buttons, and a large clock on the wall. When the buttons are activated, the clock starts a countdown and the door locks shut. 
Some scrambled for clues as they thought this may be an escape room scenario or a puzzle need to be solved expediently. But it turns out, the game is just asking you to sit and chill with your friends for a minute... just kick back and the couch and tell some fart jokes or whatever... just for a few minutes. When the timer runs out you are free to go and you even get a little prize! A weird butt-plug thing that *vibrates* a little when you shake it! Neat!

Most importantly, its about hanging out with other people and communicating in a colorful sandbox world when people are becoming more and more isolated (ironically by technology).  
The game is not pretending, or trying to be anything that its not. 
Nothing is superfluous, and yet nothing is required. 
Everything has a place, and there is a place for everything that is.

Just have some fun with your friends.

Big walk is a game where you and a group of friends go around an island and have fun exploring it in any way you like. It's also a game, about communication - you'll find a big variety of ways to do that and sometimes you'll have to get creative. If you have people in your life, with whom you enjoy spending time then do yourselves a favor and play big walk. <3

I can't really describe this game in a way that does it justice. The game is so simple at its core - you group up with your friends, go on walks and do puzzles occasionally - mostly very simple, communication based puzzles. 
At first, that seems like all there is, and that's kinda true, but due to the nature of having no fast way around, you end up being stuck with each other just walking to your next destination or aimlessly wandering around, with little to do other than talk or fiddle around with the items you picked up. 
Me and my friends got into so many natural conversations, really bonded and got closer to each other - came up with our own little fun games with the few gizmos we had.
There's a lot of puzzles that don't have one correct solution, and every time it's so satisfying when you mutually come up with a creative way to solve it.
And without spoiling the ending, it comes to one of the most beautiful experiences I've experienced in a game.
Every minor inconvenience or slip up was frustrating at first, but that's what makes it more memorable. There's no "easy fix". You have to work together, and when you finally put your efforts together, it really feels great to move forward again.
You and your friends are all characters in your own story that's being shaped naturally by your successes and failures.
Make sure you play this game with people who are special to you, as this game is a really special, one of a kind experience.

I don't know if I can effectively communicate how this game feels, but I'm gonna try.

I spend an hour or so going around and doing a couple of puzzles with friends, and we'll be laughing and joking through it all. Then, I'll have a moment on my own or just when things get quiet long enough for me to realize I'm having the purest, most innocent fun I've had in ages. 

Then I look around me and realize just how beautiful the landscape I'm traversing is. Again, it's not because the graphics are absurdly detailed or because I'm pushing my GPU to its limits, but I can sense the care and passion that went into the world I'm in. It's the first time I've been playing a video game and looking at something that evokes the same feeling I get when I'm on a beach at sunset, just taking in the world around me. I didn't know that was possible in a video game, and I still can't really come to terms with it.

Then I get lost. I spend ten minutes stumbling around the map looking for my friends, and it's exciting when we spot each other. Once we meet up, we talk about what we were off doing, what we saw, and what we're going to do next. No matter what we decide on, I'm excited to go do it. 

Then we finish an area and claim whatever the reward for it is. It's always something helpful, and it immediately feels like some massive new potential has unlocked for where we can go and what we can do next. Instead of running right to it, I usually linger, or take the long road there. It's nicer that way. 

I'm about ten hours in and despite the simplicity of this game, it feels like there's so much more for me to do, and I keep itching to play it more with my friends when we all have a free night. I'm realizing as I play it more this game is bringing out the best in all of us. For a few hours at a time, we're forgetting about what's going on in our day-to-day lives and just enjoying a collection of moments as friends. It feels like I've been teleported back in time and we're all just hanging out on Friday nights during summer vacation again, and the world's our oyster. We can go wherever and do whatever we want again. 

When I first heard about this game a couple months before it came out, I thought it was kinda stupid. I didn't understand how something like this would be worth playing. But Big Walk doesn't want me to worry about it, it wants me to interact with my friends. It wants me to remember we all care about each other. It wants me to remember how important they are. It succeeds.

In a time where everything is doom and gloom and nobody has the answers, this is a necessary reprieve where you remember what in your life matters. Big Walk is my Game of the Year.

My friends and I have have known each other for over 10 years at this point, and this may as well have been the ultimate culmination of all the time we've spent together.

Nowhere else I've seen such a great use of an open world for puzzles, all while keeping a good pace with different transport methods that interconnect all of the different parts of the map (without making walking pointless).
The only other example that comes to mind is Outer Wilds, but here the puzzles are a lot more self-contained and are (of course) meant to be completed by two or more people.

It is (probably) the best coop game launched this year, and of the best examples of what a coop game can be (at the same level of other games like Peak, A Way Out and It Takes Two).
It tells a story and presents itself in a way only a videogame can, something that's already hard enough to get right in single-player experiences and becomes even harder when doing a coop game like this.

Of course, if it is played alongside people you don't have much connection with the game can fall off pretty quick, but push through long enough and it can genuinely create a strong bond, or in my case, reinforce an already strong one.

For the sake of fairness, there's a series of puzzle-types that can get repetitive, specially the ones where you're closed in a place with no mic access and have to arrange signs (the game still manages to present new ways and gimmicks to keep this interesting but at times it's just too much), and a few problems with performance that can be a bit jarring at times.

Oh and I guess it's a bit hard to stream this game, or maybe some people just don't know how to deal with themselves and others at the same time.

All in all, this game is something truly special.

- Wave goodbye

It looks like the easiest way to become an expert on AI is to know absolutely nothing about it…

The outrage surrounding Big Walk is a perfect demonstration. House House used an LLM to troubleshoot technical issues, including a rendering problem that even Unity’s own engineers couldn’t resolve. review:
Big Walk might be my game of the year.

I've been looking forward to this game ever since it was announced - puzzles, funky little guys with silly noses, unique music, and all set in my country? I had to play it. Honestly, seeing the Australian scenery in the trailer made me quite emotional - I rarely see a game capture that feeling of home as well as Big Walk does. So when it finally released, my friends and I were regularly stopping and looking at the banksia and grass trees and just appreciating that the place we found ourselves in wasn't as unfamiliar as we thought. 

The graphics themselves are really nice, and the lighting is gorgeous. The mix of the familiarity of Australian bush and the strange shapes and colours dotted throughout the map is such a cool artistic choice! I adore the boldness of the buildings and the characters themselves, they felt odd but never so outlandish that they were an eyesore. And on a personal note, the characters are very fun to draw, I have such a soft spot for them!

The puzzles were as fun as the people I played with (so, quite fun!), and the level of challenge often changes depending on how you decide to solve each one. Since I've played multiple times, every time I played with someone new I chose to try my best and solve the puzzle a new way than before, which led to some fun moments! 

The core theme of communication truly shines brightly the entire time, and as someone who has since finished 3 runs of this game with 3 different groups, and is already planning more with new people, I can say confidently that each playthrough felt so different because of the company I kept and tools we decided to use! Some puzzles were solved quickly, some were skipped entirely, some people liked to stop and watch the sun rise, others liked to kick things off cliffs and make silly noises into the radios. But every single playthrough made me think 3 core things: 

1) This game is absolutely beautiful
2) The puzzles were so fun every time I played them
3) I love my friends very much

So yes, this might be my game of the year. It's a simple premise: you walk, you talk. But you also make some lovely memories with friends, and learn new ways to communicate that you might've never thought of.

I think this game means something more than just completing puzzles. Its about the irrelevant boring times you spend with your friends walking about. Discussing the most random topics, connecting with each other even over immense distance in person. I had so much fun in this game. It's truly a one of a kind coop experience, play it even if you just have 1 friend to play it with. 
Thanks House House

Big Walk is a game about exploring a big island with people you care about.
I like it.  A lot.  Easily my game of the year for 2026, Big Walk is a game that invites you to slow down, explore, enjoy the scenery, do some puzzles, and - most importantly - spend time talking with the people in your life you love.

This game is staunchly multiplayer.  It features myriad ways of making you dependent on others.  I won't speak in detail about what there is to discover throughout the game, but I will give one example of this aspect of the game: character customization.  The characters in this game are simple, and you personalize them by painting the three body segments from an array of colors.  However, you cannot paint yourself.  You have to work with at least one other person to paint each other, and this is evocative of the entirety of the game - you are not meant to be alone.

I've seem some complaints online regarding the rather small range of the proximity chat, but I find that the limitation actually adds to the experience.  Getting separated is easy if members of the group aren't paying attention.  If people are just rushing ahead, someone may soon find themselves left behind, and with the core progression of the game tied to group activities, there's an incentive to make sure that everyone is still there.  So look back.  Check on your friends.  Help them over that rock.  Maybe just carry them for a bit.  You need them, and they need you.

The "puzzles" aren't particularly difficult, rather relying on cooperation and clever communication with others.  Knowing the solution and executing that solution as a group are completely different things.  Just because your friend knows the correct sequence of shapes doesn't mean it's easy to communicate that to you through soundproof glass.  This means that repeated playthroughs still have value, as you always have the opportunity to be on the other side.

Big Walk isn't for everyone, and it doesn't need to be.  The slow pace, low stakes, and peaceful time with others are what made it wonderful for me, but that's not going to be everyone's opinion.
I love this game, and if you're one of the friends I got to journey through it with, I hope you know that I love you, too.

Big Walk is a beautiful gem of a game, lovingly crafted and with a simple premise - it's about walking and talking. I gathered a group of my friends together to play this and we have been having a wonderful time doing just that. So much of this game is designed to require cooperation in a way that it is otherwise almost impossible to achieve most things on your lonesome.
From putting on items you can wear, choosing your character's colour, solving puzzles - these are things that are quickly established as requiring a partner. There are other unsung mechanics as well, though, such as being able to wave your arms around in different patterns or carry people or take items from them. It's the tools you have at your disposal which give rise to such wonderful creative approaches to the problems posed by the game that limit your ability to communicate or interact in various puzzles.

The joy that comes from discovery in this game is also hard to describe - from finding a new item or area or working out how to solve a puzzle with the help of somebody else, every new achievement is wonderful and brings a sense of excitement from everybody at a job well done.

Big Walk is a beautiful snapshot of the Australian outback, one which brings me an unending amount of happiness to see represented in video games. I think this is the first game I've ever played where I actually felt like I was at home - everything is instantly recognisable for me - from the vegetation and the landscape and the soil and leaf litter, to the sound of native animals. The level of detail that has gone in, even down to the squeaking sand as you walk on it - this game has been made with incredible amounts of love and it shows. I do sometimes wish that I could SEE the animals, but I understand that inclusion of these assets poses its own problem.

Overall, though, I HIGHLY recommend Big Walk. Whether you want to play it with a child, parent, friend, partner, or some combination of the above, all are completely fine - I personally recommend 4+ people.
