I’m 30 now, and by a lucky coincidence I managed to get a group of friends back together — people I used to hang out with when we were teenagers. A lot of time has passed since then. Life scattered us in different directions, and now everyone has their own life and their own responsibilities. But here, for a little while, we managed to be together again. And, more importantly, to realize that somewhere inside, we’re still the same teenagers we were back then.

The game is finished now. The experience has been had, and I know perfectly well that it can’t be repeated. You can start over, walk the same paths and solve the same puzzles again, but you can’t get that feeling of discovery back. You can’t face the unknown for the first time again, come up with theories together, argue, make mistakes, suddenly find the answer, and share that moment with your friends.

Long before we reached the end, I already had no doubt that this was the best gaming experience I’ve ever had in my life.

There’s an almost indescribable feeling of genuine discovery here. That moment when, after thinking about something for a long time, a light suddenly goes on in your head and everything finally clicks into place. There are completely unpredictable situations that happen in the middle of a slow, peaceful walk and within seconds turn into stories that your whole group will keep talking about for a long time afterward.

The game constantly finds ways to surprise you. With every new puzzle, you start thinking that you’ve finally understood its language, figured out its rules, and have a pretty good idea of what to expect next. Then it turns everything upside down, and you realize all over again that you know absolutely nothing about this world.

Maybe that’s why it’s so hard to accept the ending.

Every mystery on the island has been solved. Every place has been explored. Every discovery has been made. And now you have to leave behind a world that, not long ago, still felt huge, mysterious, and boundless.

All good things come to an end. And perhaps the saddest part isn’t even that the game is over, but knowing that this exact experience — for the first time, and with these people — will never happen again.

Thank you, House House

The puzzles are repetitive and not interesting, the day/night cycle only purpose is to be annoying, the world feels empty and the inventory management is not great.

Big walk is primarily a co-op puzzle game. The twist is like the name there a lot of walking between destinations, and the indended experiance for communication is using the proximity chat.  THis is because a lot of the puzzles rely on finding creative ways to communicate information as often comm’s will get jammed or you are far enough away that your friend can not hear you. I have spoiler tagged it as a courtesy.

Most of the puzzles are solid and require the whole party from what I can tell they were at least configured to adjust to party size up to at least 4 (I had a party of 3). There was one bad puzzle that stuck out in my mind.

[spoiler] There is one puzzle that just has the party sit in a room and do nothing for 5 minutes (we called it the streamer house). Now I get the intension is to sit and just talk, and if that was the end of the puzzle it would have just been a minor sore point. My problem with the puzzle is after unlocking the advanced puzzles upon initial game completion they add in a version that has you wait for 30 minutes! Which is just ridiculous! My friend group just ended up tabbing out and doing other things while we waited it out, and obviously it was the last one we did, as no one wanted to sit around for that long. Plus the developers already have a reflection room after the advanced puzzles are done so the social aspect is also suspect. This advanced version needs to be removed or changed as it actively wastes the players’ time in a game that already has plenty of ways to accomplish its social interaction goals. [/spoiler]


The other thing I would like to see adjusted is the trains. The player unlocks them usually around halfway through the game, and my guess is they were meant to be a way to travel around the map faster and potentially carry beans (used to progress the game) back to the towers. The problem is that they are way too slow. The speed they move at is the same as player movement, which is good for catching them but that nullifies one aspect of trains. The player also really has no control of the trains either. You can make them stop but you have to constantly hold the brake and even then, as the speed is not an issue this is pointless. Maybe this would not be as bad if there were enough trains passing by but at least for a 3-player game, we only had 3. Either the trains need to be much faster and make stops at the laid-out stations or more need to be added regardless of player count, otherwise it is a useless reward. 


That being said an overall good time with friends.

Big Walk has such a simple concept that is executed perfectly. I thoroughly enjoyed playing this game with a couple of my buddies. The puzzles are genuinely interesting and you feel accomplished after finally solving said puzzles. By the end of the game you have an entire space designated to saying goodbye to the game and the friends you went on this journey with... and I have to say, it was bittersweet. I was happy to see we completed the game but also sad we were done.

There are a couple issues I have with the game, nothing thats overly obstructive, but after 16 hours of playtime, these little things can get on your nerves a bit. At first, the voice chat was annoying for us, then they updated the game to make the voice chat louder, and it got much better. Not perfect, but better. I would say more of my issue actually resides in the jumping mechanics. There are far too many times where you get stuck on small obstacles (not for long but still gets annoying), such as sticks, and small rocks, and not being able to jump onto or over thigns that you should clearly be able to. This wouldn't usually be a big problem, but when a big part of the game is walking and long travel times, these small delays start to add up, and it can get frustrating. I've had a couple times while playing where I get a little loud, lol. 

These complaints are really not that big of a deal, but I felt the need to mention them. The game also heavily relies on the group of people you're playing with. There is a lot of downtime in this game, I mean its in the title, you spend a lot of time simply walking to the next puzzle, so you just end up talking with eachother, arguing over something stupid, or just walking in silence. It's a great time with the right people.

To round off my review, its a very heartwarming game thats simple, with great puzzles, and fun with the right group of friends. Super fun time!

My absolute favourite game in a long time, everything it does, it does exceedingly well. 
TL;DR My game of the year - worth buying even just to go for a little walk in.

For the sheer amount of time you spend walking I was never bored of it, and the environment was a big role in that. The amount of times I found myself just repeatedly saying how beautiful the game was, I genuinely can't count. The sound design of the game is so satisfying as well. It really feels like walking through the Australian bush and reminded me of how beautiful this country is. There are methods to lessen the walking, but they're very well balanced - just inconvenient enough you don't become reliant upon them and just convenient enough that they're there when you really need. Even in the times I wanted the transport but couldn't get it, I wasn't upset I'd have to walk.

Communication is such a blast in this game. In my opinion proximity chat always opens games up for laughs and this was no exception. On my initial playthrough I'd lost my voice and was concerned that not being able to talk would hinder our experience, but the text chat catered well to our needs and the other items within the game that act as alternate forms of communicating completly eliminated my need to speak regardless. Even when my voice came back I was still having just as much fun as I had when I couldn't talk. Each item within the game served it's purpose well, and each had specific enough functions that we often found ourselves working out what we wanted to bring with us and what would work best for what we were trying to achieve.

The puzzles in this game never get old, and while there are several with similar themes or mechanics, each felt unique enough that you never really get tired of any one element. Some puzzles were trickier than others, some required different ways of problem solving and some were significantly more satisfying than others when we finally completed them. 

Overall, this game is one of those cliche' "I wish I could relive playing this for the first time again" types of games, and I'm desperately hoping they expand either on this game, or create a sequel for it.

Edit: I completely forgot to mention that this game screams to me that it was inspired by the "architecture graveyard" and my god do I love it for it because the feeling I get from playing this game is what I'd imagine walking around the graveyard would feel like.

Big Walk is definitely a game of all time. I really appreciate them sticking to their guns and going all in on their vision of creating a "cooperative online walker-talker".

I can't really recommend this though. Walking around results in constantly getting stuck on random map geometry. Talking you'd expect to be fine (and for the most part it is!), but it's pretty rough to be talking in a group and not be able to have a conversation with anyone more than two feet away from me. I get the feeling that this was intentional and intended to split up groups so players can have fun finding each other, but the way our group experienced this was just that we couldn't hear each other even when we were close by. For a game about walking and talking, both felt really bad.

The puzzles were. alright. Most of them were a bit too easy, which is fine given the nature of the game, but there others that just felt incredibly tedious to do. Usually those ones involved sections where it was *reaallly* clear that House House was trying to force players to walk long distances or talk to each other (something we had already been doing the entire time...). There were some particularly strong ones especially during the ending sequence that I enjoyed though!

Other assorted issues: night time is dark as HELL, limited inventory size worsened by the fact that someone needs to carry a light source, dropped items are impossible to find due to the dense underbrush in many areas (funny the first time, just a pain in the ass every time after).

I get it. They had a message and an artistic vision, but they just didn't hit for me and I didn't find the ending worth the trudging it took to get there, despite the fact that it was with friends. The only solace here was the fact that it *was* with friends, so at least while I was holding W for 30 minutes I had nice conversations... that I could've had in discord or in real life doing/playing something more interesting.

If you liked this game, I really think you'd like hanging out with your friends while doing activities more worth your time.

P2 Review: Everyone has a moment growing up where they realize the magic is gone, their toys aren't fun anymore, and the playground is just a playground and not another world. There are many forms of escapist fantasy that adults create in an attempt to re-capture the magic of pretend play. The only thing that has come close to truly immersing me in a sense of adventure and pretend the way I felt as a child is Big Walk. I forgot where I was while I was playing this game. I forgot that the other players weren't actually with me. The adventure felt so simple yet so real. It achieved exactly what it set out to achieve and with so much more to experience towards the end that came completely unexpected. All of the puzzles are challenging and never feel redundant and the map looks incredibly sprawling without being tedious to traverse. By the end, the limitations put on you to communicate through certain puzzles stops feeling like just a barrier set to make something more challenging and begins to feel like something deeper. What are the unique ways someone that you are with will choose to get through to you when you can't hear them, see them, etc.? How will you know what your partner is saying when they are reduced to a blinking light? When they've figured out what you need to do but can only tell you in gestures? How do people share things when they aren't in the same place? Isn't it comforting to know someone's there on the other side even when it seems like you're alone? like a cat meowing back or a wave from the other train platform. There's a little spark of magic here that I can't quite describe.

Work called urgently so I had to leave the preplanned group session of Big Walk.

"No more walking for me big dawg, employment's calling my name."

Came back as soon as I finished my shift. Friendgroup already has hours of completion ahead of me.

I logged in with absolutely no idea of what the game was about. I rushed out and ignored any tutorial and saw something puzzle-like, so if they're finished on one level, I just have to move past the completed stages quickly and reach them, right?

Wrong. It wasn't linear. Went out the door and was baffled by an open world. The sun. The sea. The bush. 

No map. No directions. No communications. Nobody. Me, alone in silence, clinging onto an orb, the only thing I have and know.

I'm lost. I'm big lost.

Lit orbs dotted the map in a vague path, leading to puzzles with signs of prior activity. Traces of people, and a land barren of puzzles, communicating in hostile tone that I was not needed. I was not useful anywhere.

I plunged into the sea in a desperate attempt to die - and hopefully respawn wherever my friends were, if it were to have that mechanic. The waves washed over my floating body, denying me my easy way out from loneliness. 

I swam out into the open sunset as the night robs the light and blanketed me in further confusion. Only following a red blinking dot, my signal to safety. Towards meaning.

I found a railway so I whimseyed my way up. Sat alone with only the ambience as accompaniment. I rushed out into the wilderness, anxious to not wait for a train that will never arrive, but ultimately came wobbling back to the very same station. A sign of civilization was the only possibility I clung onto. I figured out how to read the train sign, I so waited with more patience.

I boarded the slow moving train as it arrived and took to work honking every moment I can to get a response. Messed with the intercoms without knowing if my pleas will ever reach someone.

A small flicker of two person talking. Too busy with puzzles to bother replying to me. Towers colours, signs, I don't get it. 

The train crawled into a station and there was finally someone. Wait, this game doesn't even have name tags? Which friend is this, am I even in the right server? This lone pal hopped onto the train and flickered a flashlight at me. Whether to help me or to screw with me, it didn't matter. 

They hopped off when we reached a ski lift, turned around, and looked at me. Beamed the light in my face. A signal, a hope, and I followed. With a guide I navigated these foreign lands effortlessly. Up a tower, down a valley, I begin to grasp the game even without words between us.

I was led to a small subset of friends and there I found familiarity in their voices. In my glee I accidentally resetted their puzzle and was chided. My new mic wasn't working, and I was mistaken for another silent one in the friendgroup. Still not knowing how to play the game, I apologized and jumped down to another train and left, looking for somewhere I  could be useful.

Wandering, I realized I could do none of the puzzles alone, gained achievements with no one to share with, and in my shameful urgency to leave, I had abandoned my only light. Well, the second to last. The first friend I met left me their flashlight. 

I stumbled onto the Big View and, taking the moment to bask it all in, really figure out what this game was about. My rashness had led me astray, and when I chanced onto a meeting, I immediately ran away in shame. Contemplating the meaning of this game, what it really means to co-op, when-

"We'll be closing the server soon. Everyone, let's meet up at yellow tower." boomed the intercom.

In my panic I rushed to find a station. I wanted to at least see the whole gang, say hello, it's me. Be noticed. 

To find the next lead I decided to break the taboo and headed to the discord call - and bam, everyone was muted. Holy heck, why even host one then. Wait, someone forgot to mute themselves, so I listened in for clues.

One of the coolest co-op puzzle games in years.

If you like environmental puzzle games like The Witness, Big Walk is an easy pick. It hits that sweet spot of open discovery, respects your time, and never overstays its welcome.

A few reasons why it's so good:

Communication is the whole game: The built-in proximity chat and physical tools (walkie-talkies, binoculars, line-of-sight items) make the whole experience. It turns simple coordination into pure comedy and great teamwork.

Fair, satisfying puzzles: The puzzles have good depth without feeling cheap or cryptic. When things click, everyone feels smart instead of having one person carry the rest.

Fits whatever vibe your squad has: I played through this with two totally different groups: one was laser-focused on solving everything efficiently, and the other just wanted to goof off across the island. The game works brilliantly for both. And also has one of the best endings in a co-op game I have experienced without spoiling anything. 

House House nailed the balance between chill exploration and chaotic multiplayer fun. Highly recommended (just make sure to stick to the in-game voice chat instead of Discord for the full effect)!

because when the entire map got unlocked, we split into 2 groups and i found myself doing puzzles with the "stranger", talking about games we liked and how we met the other friends in the lobby, we found out we actually play very simular games and have almost identical play time on some of them, so we added each other on Steam and Discord, i do not think any other game would be able to force 2 strangers to just exchange conversation about real life or different topics THAN the game theyre currently playing,
but Big Walk somehow did,

eventually when all 4 of us met up, we split into 2 groups again, but now exploring the map with a different friend, we would exchange stories of what happened with the other group, what items they found, what puzzles they completed and we just started talking about stuff

and when you get split up by complete accident, the game has so many landmarks or items to help you get back to your group
the feeling of finally seeing someone after being lost for almost half an hour is the biggest relieve

This is genuinely such a beautiful and wonderfully chill game to play and hang out with friends. The scenery? Spectacularly Australian. The sound design? Delightfully joyful. It is so easy to get distracted enroute with a discovery made along the way, and there are suprises hidden everywhere. 
The puzzles make you think, listen to each other, brainstorm and try different ideas. They are all very achievable to succeed in, with some communication. There is no such thing as going backwards progress-wise, and you can always come back and try again later if you get frustrated. 
I have never had so much genuine affection for a game and the way it brings all these elements into something addictively relaxing. The creators have made something very special indeed. I can't wait to go for my next Big Walk with my friends.

[h1]Premium Friendslop Exploration and Puzzle Solving[/h1]

Here is an example of my experience:

I start the game with 7 friends. 3 immediately wander off. Our group of 5 find a cool looking puzzle and work together to solve it. After leaving the area we find the others using the nearest radio and send a flare to show them where we are. We attempt to find each other but our group splits and suddenly I find myself alone. I wander through the now dark forest, hearing distant music playing. Eventually I make my way to the sound to find the 3 people we lost before, now with backpacks, belts, and a walkie-talkie. We team up to do another puzzle. We bring back the little red homunculus to a tower and meet up with the rest of the group by happenstance. The tower unlocks a train that travels around the entire map, with stations at each tower. We find the nearest train station and ride it to the next tower, but lose 2 people who thought it would be funny to jump off. At the next station we leave the train and complete more team building challenges. Eventually we unlock a tunnel system that leads to a nightclub and a secret station that lets you paint your friends metallic colors. We dance and gesture like idiots in a space that feels like we discovered it. Someone grabs the portable radio and attaches it to a backpack so we can vibe to the music we unlocked on our way to the next area, but this time we move as a unit - each person stacked to create one mobile tower with one guy at the top holding a light.

This game is pure magic. It uses cooperation as a tool more effectively than any game I've ever played. At points I felt wonder (for some of the vistas and buildings), anger (at my friends when we had trouble communicating during a puzzle), and joy (when we discovered new silly mechanics). Its hard to describe all the ways I feel about this game, but I have had more fun than I ever was expecting to.

[h1] Is This Game for You? [/h1]

Big Walk is a special case. A game that genuinely benefits from the right expectations and the right mindset. It’s not trying to be everything for everyone, and depending on what you value in games, it may simply not be for you. That’s perfectly fine. But if you are the kind of player it’s speaking to, it becomes something memorable.

[h2] THE FACTS [/h2]

[b]1. Multiplayer Only[/b] — Big Walk requires two or more players to progress. The game is flexible and allows you to swap between 2, 3, or 4+ players when loading in, but it cannot be played solo.

[b]2. Best Played With In‑Game Chat[/b] — The tight built‑in proximity chat is part of the design philosophy. Many puzzles rely on non‑verbal communication, distance, and spatial awareness. Using external voice chat removes a layer of the intended experience.

[b]3. Gameplay Is Slow[/b] — Movement is slow. Progress is slow. You will get lost. You will wait for the sun to rise so you can see where you’re going. You will wait for transportation or for your friends to catch up. The pacing is intentional, but it’s important to know if you’re someone who prefers constant action or deeper mechanics.

[h2] MY OPINION [/h2]

[b]Big Walk belongs in my personal hall of fame as one of the best gaming experiences I’ve ever had.[/b]

It hits several very specific notes for me, and together they create something rare. Here’s why it stands out.

[b]Atmosphere[/b] — Big Walk absolutely nails its tone. At first glance, it looks like it might fall into the “friendslop” category that dominates multiplayer releases lately, but it’s far more intentional than that. The art direction is confident, cohesive, and quietly brilliant. Beneath the simple surface is a thoughtful world with clever design choices that elevate the entire experience.

[b]Immersion[/b] — The proximity chat, the day/night cycle, the slow and deliberate exploration, the environmental storytelling, the puzzles that reward observation and communication — everything works together to pull you into the moment. If you’re willing to be present, the game rewards you with a level of immersion that’s surprisingly rare.

[b]Messaging[/b] — Without spoiling anything, Big Walk has more to say than it initially lets on. It starts as a chill, quirky adventure, but somewhere along the way you realize it’s quietly reshaping how you’re thinking and feeling. It strikes a perfect balance between being a silly game about walking and being a humbling, reflective experience you’ll remember long after you finish it.

[h2] Conclusion [/h2]

If you’re open to a slow, atmospheric, cooperative experience that values presence over speed and communication over mechanics then Big Walk is absolutely worth your time. Bring close friends or your partner, wander the island together, solve puzzles, share discoveries, and enjoy the quiet moments. You might find something deeper waiting for you along the way.

There's gonna be some controversial opinions in this, but bare with me.

Big walk is the sort of game I should like, it's a co-op puzzler with a big player count, and puzzles that aren't frustratingly hard. So why don't I like it?

It comes down to a number of things. The map is probably the most poorly made map I've ever encountered in any game. It's clear almost no time was spent into making the game playable, you will get stuck on geometry, you will find places where you literally need help to get out of spots in the map. There are places on the map that don't actually have a path to get to, requiring you to exploit the map and the poor physics to get to them, and they have items, so they aren't places you aren't meant to go.

The game uses co-op as a crutch, rather than something that benefits the experience. You do not have even a single inventory slot, so you always have to be holding the one item you carry, which gets super annoying as that item can get stuck on geometry, forcing you to keep moving your arms around to keep moving. Even when you get a backpack, or hip holster, you, yourself cannot use it. It becomes an inventory slot for your teammates. The game also forces one player to be the designated light carrier, otherwise you have to wait the entire night out, as it genuinely gets dark in the map.

The physics are just downright poor. Including all the issues mentioned above, there's no or next to no clear answers as to why you can or cannot move on certain parts of the map. And when you fall you are left sitting on your butt for an extended period of time, which is ridiculously long. 

The entire draw of the game seems to be spending time with the people in it, which raises a much bigger issue: If the entire enjoyment to be had in the game is spending time with your friends, then why not do it in a more enjoyable way? Why not have a chat?, why not have a meetup? (if you're playing with IRL friends), why not watch a video together?, and most importantly, why not play a better game?

I didn't get far into the game due to losing a group to play it with a short way in, so I don't know if it does get better at any point. But the puzzles I encountered weren't particularly difficult to solve, nor were particularly interesting in general. This is mostly due to the lack of actual game mechanics. The only real positive aspect I can give to this game is that the atmosphere was pretty good, however it is not a standout even in that area. I am completely confused as to how this game got so well reviewed to be honest. I wouldn't recommend it to anyone.

Honestly, both while playing it and after finishing it, I really don't share the hype around Big Walk.

To me, it is an incredibly tedious game about walking back and forth that stops being interesting after about three minutes. Although, to be fair, the game is literally called Big Walk. I probably should have figured that out before buying it.

The whole idea of "you and your friends are going on a hike and you just talk along the way" sounds cute in theory. In practice, it falls apart because of the absolutely fucking awful in-game VoIP.

It forces everyone to stay within like three meters of each other, constantly making you wait for someone, look for someone who got lost, or realize that you are the one who got lost. And the game gives you a gigantic amount of room for both intentional and completely accidental griefing. I am living proof of that.

I specifically paid attention to this during our last two sessions. In Hunt Showdown, for example, we actually talk about random shit while playing. Then we launch Big Walk and suddenly all conversation disappears. Everything turns into:

"Where's Gosha?"
"Where's Kirill?"
"Has anyone seen Nikita?"
"Borya, where the fuck are you?"
"Van, wait up."

And that's assuming you haven't already wandered off somewhere yourself.

And then there is the whole room where you are apparently supposed to sit around for 5-30 minutes and just talk to your friends. The idea itself isn't even terrible, but the game basically forces you to do it. Sure, you can technically just AFK, but then what is even the point of the whole thing?

The puzzles are probably the best part. Some of them are genuinely funny and actually require everyone to interact. Yes, there are moments where everyone has to mute Discord, but even that could have been handled better. You could just keep the global VoIP and disable it only for the specific puzzles where it actually matters. And, to be fair, that's basically what the game does in some places.

And then there are the shortcuts.

Why the fuck do some shortcuts take roughly the same amount of time as just walking there, while others are actually slower?

Apparently that's one of the great mysteries of Big Walk - clearly worthy of a Nobel Prize.

Ultimately, that's my biggest problem with Big Walk: its main idea - "walk around together and talk to your friends" - works worse because of the game itself.

The world is huge, movement is tedious, the VoIP actively gets in the way of having a normal conversation, and a huge chunk of the experience becomes trying not to lose everyone.

The puzzles are fun. Some moments are genuinely funny. But as an overall experience for a group of friends, the game just did not work for me at all.

After finishing it, I was left with exactly one thought:

"Why the fuck did we spend so much time walking?"

Is big walk... a good game? Or is it piggybacking off the enjoyment I already experience from the personalities of people that I love? that's a hard question to answer because I genuinely had a good time throughout my experience playing this game, but it failed to leave an impression upon me the way actually good games do.

If you like good thought out puzzles with clever solutions Big Walk does have some... However, many puzzles are easily solved by a combination of tedious collaborative guesswork with very little risks or stakes that I cannot call 'fun'. On the other hand other parts of the game provided excellent opportunities for player expression- such as one zone where we had to escort a box outside of a deep pit by throwing and catching it to one another and then traversing up a stairwell and jumping back down to catch it and continue the process. It was moments like these that really lived up to the sell that was promised in the trailer of enjoying the tedium of traversal with friends; which brings me to:

TRAVELING IN BIG WALK SUCKS. I dont know how a game that has the word "walk" literally in the title could f"ck this up. Time and time again we got stuck colliding into small pebbles in the ground that completely disrupted our forward momentum where we had to mash buttons to somehow launch ourselves out via the hardest puzzle in the game: jumping. Some encounters during the game include trying to get to a puzzle up high and theres a couple platforms in front of you (clearly placed at heights that show intention for you to be able to jump from platform to platform to reach the next area) only for each jump to individually be stuck in that same walking problem over and over and over again where it takes substantially longer to reach the goal right in front of you than if it circumnavigated the mountain. Movement in this game is abyssmal and the developers should be ashamed of how bad it is by how obviously encounterably this problem is from 10 mins of organic gameplay.

Luckily there are other ways of getting around the map! oh yippee a train that can take me from place to place and a gondola chair lift that is a focal point of excitement and tunnels that I didnt even know existed before tackling the late game. Because when youre finally done with being frustrated while walking you can elevate yourself to higher means of transportation- or can you? With the exception of the chairlift, the movement rewards felt underwhelming. The train was almost never convenient enough to make much of a difference, in fact the times that we waited for the train at a boarding station its apparent slow movement speed kept us waiting for way longer than expected and oftentimes it wouldve just been faster to start walking. My detractors might mention how it gives an opportunity to appreciate the landscape and relax while in transit, and while i agree that this is a thing I value and is expertly done with the chairlift the train has fairly few good views and an overabundance of bored tunnels that, well, bored us. Speaking of Tunnels, this was a poor decision. A dark, uninspired, ugly, monotonous walk through the backrooms of Big Walk wouldve been way better off as a teleport hub or (I cant believe im saying this) as fast travel. The chair lift is legitimately perfect although: a fantastic view, convenient and constantly running and was always our go to.

Big Walk has two close neighbors in the broad world of video games and Id like to make a moment to address them because I think Big Walk, unfortunately, took the bad aspects from both of these games more than the good. The Witness is an excellent puzzle game that really builds upon an evolution of your understanding of the puzzle mechanics to really challenge you and your understanding while teaching you in tandem; contrary to its steam page however, the Witness DOES NOT TREAT YOUR TIME AS PRECIOUS it wastes it over and over again and I couldn't help but envision the same frustration I felt waiting for boats to come out of the water in the Witness as I waited for the slow and infuriating train in Big Walk. Breath of the Wild needs no introduction but lets talk about what it does well and poor. This Zelda game succeeds tremendously at making traversal constantly interesting and by giving you enhanced toolsets such as climbing, soaring, running, riding horses etc. Shrines however are disappointing and there never seems to be an EVOLUTION OF INTRODUCED IDEAS TO EXPAND UPON THEM IN MORE INTERESTING WAYS.

If we combine from these games we might get a game that has amazing puzzles and excellent exploration, or we get a game with disappointing puzzles and frustrating traversal. Unfortunately Big Walk is the latter and that makes me sad because I had fun playing this game and I'm even sure you may too, but its always going to be in the forefront of what makes this game squander its own potential.

Do you have one friend? Perhaps two friends or more? Well, do I have the game for you! It's Big Walk!

Get your steps in from the comfort of your own home. Enjoy a relaxing walk or slightly faster paced walk through grassy, rocky, or forested terrains. Watch the beautiful water of the ocean glisten in the sun. Hike the trails or make your own path as you seek out your next thrilling little puzzle. When you've had enough walking, hop on the train or the aerial tramway and take in the views from new heights. Take comfort in knowing if you fall off, you will not perish!
 
This game is for you if:
- You find yourself at peace in nature
- You like walking, virtually
- You can laugh at yourself and have fun doing silly things
- You like to have a little dance break in a secret tunnel with strobe lights, flashlights, and shadows
- You appreciate the beauty of simplicity
- You like brainstorming, being creative, and solving puzzles
- You like teamwork or being told what to do or telling other people what to do
- You enjoy a leisurely game with no pressure to fight with anything (other than your friends)

This game may not be for you if:
- You have no sense of direction
- You don't think it would be very fun to get lost in the woods
- You're looking for a fast paced action game
- You don't like to dance in a secret tunnel with strobe lights
- You are bad at puzzles
- You are bad at following instructions

I am what I imagine is about half way through the game now and there is much to do, see, and uncover; perhaps some sort of dark secret? Who can say? I will walk further, see more, and find out!

[h1]A delightful journey for Type B players. A rough experience for Type A players.[/h1]
Big Walk describes itself as a game about walking and talking, which is either its greatest strength or biggest weakness, depending on what you want from it. Type B players will enjoy its relaxing world and laid-back "social-sandbox" design, while Type A players may find themselves solving mentally rewarding puzzles separated by lengthy stretches of walking.

I played Big Walk with various friends across different saves. Depending on who I was playing with, I found myself adopting either a Type A or Type B mindset, and my experiences with the game changed [i]drastically.[/i] This change was so distinct that I consider it two separate game experiences. So rather than give one review, I'm going to give it two: one for the Type A player and one for the Type B player.

[hr][/hr]
[h1]Type A[/h1]
The Type A gamer is driven by goals, mastery, and efficiency. Big Walk has a surprising amount to offer Type As: its world is full of objectives, its puzzles reward coordination and creative thinking, and a clear goal—to collect the oddly-shaped items (my group called them "Plumbuses").

In Big Walk, navigating the world is, in its own way, a puzzle.[i] If we need to be in two places at once, how do we separate and reunite? What's the best route for grabbing as many Plumbuses as possible? How can we use this new item effectively?[/i] I loved planning expeditions with my group. We would look at the map, figure out where we needed to go, divide up responsibilities, and set off.

Unfortunately, planning the expedition is more fun than actually going on it. Once it begins, the stimulation disappears. [i]Walk to the nearest train station or ski lift. Wait for the train or lift (snack break). Wait on the train or lift (bathroom break). Walk to the nearest puzzle. Solve the puzzle. Walk to the nearest Tower. Repeat.[/i]

I've seen Big Walk described as a "Shift + W simulator," and that sentiment isn't entirely wrong. For a Type A player, the time between puzzles can feel like an obstacle that [i]should[/i] be conquerable, but traversal isn't the game's strong suit. The physics don't feel fine-tuned. It's frustrating to get clipped on a tiny branch or discover that a rock you ought to be able to climb is apparently one degree too steep.

My friends and I started optimizing the walking itself. We got excited whenever we discovered movement tech, like pressing Shift + Tab twice for hands-free sprinting, or hugging the terrain while falling to prevent getting dazed. We filled the downtime with pleasant conversation, but sometimes we had to challenge each other to races just to squeeze a little more stimulation out of the journey.

[b]The game wants you to slow down and enjoy the journey. The Type A player just wants to solve the next puzzle.[/b]

[h2]The Puzzles (Spoilers)[/h2]
Thankfully, the puzzles are usually worth walking towards.

Before I discuss any specific ones, I have to say that making [b][i]good[/i][/b] puzzles is [b][i]hard,[/i][/b] and I'm impressed by how many the developers managed to create. Most of the puzzles fall somewhere between good and great, and they were the primary reason my friends and I kept playing.

That being said, some of the puzzles made me [b][i]HATE[/i][/b] this game.

Some aren't particularly good, but are at least inoffensive. Puzzles that require 1–2 people to solve (e.g., basketball) can also be awkward for lobbies with 4+ people. The puzzle where you have to carry a heavy ball up a hill is not exactly a brain teaser, but it's over quickly enough. Unfortunately, there's another "puzzle" where you carry that same heavy ball [i]across the map.[/i] The outside-the-box thinking required here is figuring out how to stay motivated through the tedious task.

Then there's the telescope puzzle, where one player waits while everyone else travels solo across the map to simultaneously press four buttons. The 30-minute waiting-room puzzle was pleasant by comparison; at least there, we were all waiting together. Waiting and walking in silence in this game is not fun.

The issue with these puzzles is the developers made the primary challenge [b]time.[/b] The mental itch isn't there, because the Type A brain isn't stimulated by [i]waiting.[/i] There are several puzzles where the solution is essentially menial work + patience, and because these puzzles take so much longer than the good ones, they can feel disproportionately common.

[h2]The Ending (Spoilers)[/h2]
The ending is [i]perfect,[/i] and all my Type A friends agree. It gave purpose to the puzzles we solved throughout the game beyond objectives to unlock the next area: you learned puzzle mechanics, problem-solving strategies, and established communication methods with each other. The final level puts everything to use. The back-to-back puzzles became the experience we had been asking for the entire time. Once it was over, it got emotional. We each waved goodbye before walking towards the bright light. After spending the entire game working together, we found ourselves separated once again--but closer than ever before.

And then we unmuted on Discord and hopped on Counter-Strike 2.

[hr][/hr]
[h1]Type B[/h1]
The Type B player is all about enjoying the [i]experience,[/i] letting curiosity and spontaneity take the lead. Big Walk feels made for them: its large map, silly character design, and playful mechanics give friends plenty of room to mess around. More importantly, the game is designed to keep them together. Puzzles are cooperative, proximity chat encourages players to stay close, and there are multiple ways to reconnect when someone gets separated.

At the same time, the game lets you take things at your own pace. You can skip puzzles and complete Towers in any order. We came across a stage with a bunch of lawn chairs in front of it. When I saw this as a Type A player, I completely ignored it. As a Type B, I instantly wanted to make a player-chair tower. Someone once went the wrong way on the ski lift and we didn't realize until they contacted us from across the map, and we all laughed. Waiting for the trains, getting lost in the dark, and shooting flares at each other felt as integral to Big Walk as the puzzles. It doesn't need to entertain you every second because [b]you[/b] are the entertainment.

For a Type B player, even rough traversal can become part of the charm. A long train ride isn't downtime if you're telling stories. Falling off a cliff isn't a setback if everyone is shouting "GERONIMOOO!!!" as they fall with you. The game gives you enough freedom for even its rough edges to become part of the experience.

[h2]The Puzzles (spoilers)[/h2]
Still, Type B players aren't immune to Big Walk's problems. The game's worst puzzles are still its worst puzzles. Quality time can't happen if you're walking alone to a telescope halfway across the map. But with the right mindset, even the banality of carrying a ball with someone can be saved by pleasant conversation.

[h2]The Ending (Spoilers)[/h2]
By the end, I wasn't thinking about how fast we'd solved all the puzzles or how much time we'd spent walking. I was thinking about the friends I'd spent all that time walking with. The journey was so beautiful, I didn't want to reach the destination.

This time, as everyone walked towards the light, we left the Discord call one by one, and our Big Walk concluded.

[hr][/hr]
[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
Big Walk is such an interesting game that I could talk about for hours. I enjoyed most of my time with it but would only recommend it to certain people, which is why this is a negative review. If you're a Type B player, you may find the magic I eventually found. If you're a Type A player, you may quit out of sheer boredom. Additionally, repetitive environments, frustrating traversal and inventory, uneven puzzles, and a slightly-too-high pricetag were ultimately enough to outweigh the game's best moments for me.

Lets get one thing straight- I do not dislike this game or the developers. I personally had a good time with it. The reason I am leaving a negative review is because there is room for constructive criticism that I feel others should know about before purchasing the game..

Firstly, the lack of inventory. I'm not saying the game *needs* more inventory, I'm saying I think it would vastly benefit from one extra slot. Sure, the game has backpacks and such, but you cannot interact with them without outside help. This is a cute idea, but it becomes frustrating throughout the game. For example, I need a light to see at night due to how incredibly dark it is on my monitor (with no way to adjust this in the settings, making me completely and totally blind every night without a light source). If I want a light, I have to drop whatever else I've got. Meaning no walkie talkie to interact with my friends, no red glorbo thing you get at the end of puzzles, heck, I can't interact with puzzles at night that require you to hold something since I can't see. With how much the game relies on you using items, it is very difficult to juggle the things you need, even with a large party, as a lot of the items are required for certain puzzles (The blorbos, keys, coordinate box, map, etc) meaning you have to leave your walkie talkies, lights, radio, or other "less important" items somewhere and make the tedious journey back and forth to get your things.
You'll also find yourself getting stuck in the geometry of the world a *lot* while walking around. The game doesn't like rocks for some reason and you'll clip into them often, having to stop and fanagle yourself until you break free. The game itself is rather low resolution with no way of upping the graphics, lighting or shadows in settings. This normally wouldn't bother me so much, but for such a simple game, and it being a whole $20, I would expect to not clip into the floor so frequently in a game revolving so heavily on exploration.
The lack of accessibility settings is also an issue. Don't like the volume level of your friends? Sorry, no settings for that. Can't see at night? Can't up the gamma anywhere. Wouldn't want to break immersion, right?

The game is fun with the right group of people, there's cute little easter eggs to find that keep things interesting, but for $20 per copy in a game that is intended to play with friends ($40 minimum basically to play with someone) it doesn't offer much outside of the "Do a simple puzzle, walk, get stuck in the floor, walk back, walk back again to get your lost friend/item you left, walk again, repeat" loop. It's a decent game and a good time, but much too expensive for what it offers and the lack of polish in certain areas.

Si consideran que League of Legends, Apex Legends, Valorant y demás exponentes de la industria competitiva son capaces de despertar en ustedes un profundo desprecio por la humanidad, permítanme presentarles este juego: una experiencia diseñada para poner a prueba, desde el primer puzzle, no solamente sus capacidades cognitivas, sino también la solidez de sus vínculos interpersonales.

Aquí no hace falta llegar al minuto veinte para comenzar a cuestionar sus decisiones de vida. El juego consigue, prácticamente desde el primer minuto, que uno se pregunte si realmente conoce a la persona con la que está jugando y, más importante aún, cuánto puede insultarla antes de que la amistad llegue oficialmente a su fin.

Cada puzzle constituye una oportunidad inmejorable para contemplar, en tiempo real, la extraordinaria ausencia de capacidad neuronal de nuestros semejantes. Uno comienza diciendo “no pasa nada, vamos otra vez” y termina preguntándose cómo fue posible que esa persona haya logrado llegar hasta la pantalla de inicio de sesión sin asistencia profesional.

Es una experiencia verdaderamente reveladora: permite identificar quiénes son realmente tus amigos, cuánto valoras su amistad y, sobre todo, hasta qué punto estás dispuesto a sacrificar tu estabilidad emocional por seguir jugando con ellos.

Por ello, mi recomendación es contundente:

Si valoras profundamente una amistad, si aprecias a esa persona o si consideras que es alguien cercano a ti, por el amor de Dios, NO JUEGUES ESTO CON ELLA.

Hay amistades que sobreviven a años de convivencia, discusiones, problemas económicos y hasta matrimonios.

The environment is absolutely beautiful, the soundtrack is amazing, the puzzles are really great, they’re not stupidly difficult but still make you feel smart of accomplishing them. The overworld is expansive, there’s all sorts of little quaint areas to chill around, the items are fun to fuck around with, and the ending sequence, oh my god

I cried. What it does is it basically takes away all the player specific colors and mutes everyone so no one knows who’s who.  And then you have to do a tower of puzzles. And, it brought me back to a place where I don’t know what’s happening and why things are going wrong, so I just assume it’s my fault and blame myself. So much to the point that I ended up just hiding behind a wall and just curling up in a ball until they got it done. I had to mute my mic for stream just to cry. It was the mindset of “I can’t do anything right so I should just leave and do nothing.” And then, I started to isolate myself from the crew. I let them do the puzzles, I walked behind everyone, I just honestly wanted to stay out of sight. And then we finished all the puzzles, we all got our colors and mics back, and I just ended up staying silent (while my friend Gina yelled at everyone). Then you have to do this walk to the credits, where you sit down on some chairs and relax, and I did the same thing of walking behind everyone, and when I finally got there I just hear everyone go “There he is!” “Streamer’s missing the credits!”. It felt like getting punched in the chest by Mike Tyson. The snap back to the moment, the realization of, “Holy shit. These are my friends. I have friends. People care for me. I am loved.” 

And then, an absolutely amazing cherry on top. At the end you go up to a rotating door, you press a button and it shows 3 colors on the screens on the side, each one corresponding to a player. That person goes in, waves goodbye, and goes into the light. (Moment would’ve made me cry again if 3 people didn’t get disconnected before going in). And it saved me for last. I got to look back at the 9 hours I had just spent with the most wonderful people in my life. The grueling flare communication, the wonderful gondola rides, all the times I said “I’m a fucking genius” after completing a puzzle, all the miles my friend Echi traveled without moving a god damn inch (because he’s a lazy fuck that doesn’t wanna play the video game and also smells like sulfur and cheese), all the crashes and disconnects because everyone runs the game on donuts, the walks to locations with the whole crew, or with half the crew, or with just one other person, or just trying to find our way back to the others, and just overall, one of the best co-op games I have ever played.

My only issues with this game is some technical stuff. Player collision physics with just about anything feels clunky, the proximity chat could be louder, etc. But overall, I love this game to death and I will 100% be 100%ing it.

There's something special about this combination of prox chat, exploration, and co-op puzzling. PEAK excels in having a clear objective, but doesn't truly enforce cooperation, you can climb the mountain yourself, and it doesn't really feel like hanging out. Other friendslop games lean the other way, mostly hanging out, not much to do. Big Walk does both. There's plenty to do (and unlock, more on that later), and the whole game is about doing them together. You can't even equip your backpack yourself. The game's philosophy is clear.

Other reviews will talk about getting lost and prox chat as negatives. I think it makes the experience. You have to figure out how to communicate if you've ventured away from your friends (find a radio, send up a flare, etc).

Some actual negatives are the performance (this game is not optimized as of this review), movement (getting stuck on things), and a lack of an inventory is a bit annoying (though I don't think this really has much impact and was clearly an intentional choice). I wish the daylight hours were a bit longer. Maybe some weather could be fun too.

Also groups of any size are equally fun. I played one run with I think 10 or so people, and we naturally broke into our own little groups. It's cool just knowing there's others around the map you'll bump into.

Unlocking things in the game as you complete puzzles might be my favorite part about the game. I won't name them specifically and I advise you don't go looking for details, as part of the fun is discovering what the map has to offer for yourself. And this continues all the way to the end of the game. I was continually impressed.

Basically, if you play video games with friends, play this one. Worth every penny.

Big Walk is the game where friendship is measured in miles walked, puzzle-solving ability, and how well you can communicate by violently gesturing with your entire body.

Did we walk a lot? Yes.
Did we solve all the puzzles? Yes.
Did we collect all the beauty blenders like our lives depended on it? Obviously.

What surprised me most is how smart the game is about friendship. Some areas and puzzles basically force you to slow down, hang out, and actually talk to the people you're playing with. Revolutionary concept, apparently.

By the end, the puzzles go completely off the rails in the best possible way. You stop thinking like a normal person and start communicating through jumping, pointing, spinning, crouching, and whatever unholy body-language system your group invents after several hours together.

The final stretch was absolutely insane and genuinely one of the most fun co-op experiences I've had in a while.

My only complaint: I really wish the ending went somewhere more substantial. After you complete the challenging final puzzles, the endings just felt, meh. It left me wanting more. A new area or map to do it all over again but it's a different difficulty or area with new puzzles to do. Also, once you reach the giant Xbox Series X-looking box slapped in the middle of the map like a Game Awards Ad, you open the door, and go on the trip, only one person in our group got to experience it and I wanted every player to be able to experience it, or at least have the ending build into something bigger.

Still, I could easily play this again with completely different groups of friends or my ride-or-die's again. Honestly, half the replay value would be inventing increasingly stupid challenges just to make everything harder on a new playthrough.

In a sea of roguelikes or duo-only puzzle co-ops, this was a super refreshing change of pace. My friend group had been waiting for Big Walk to release since the first trailer, as we're always looking for something new to play together, and this looked super fresh... and it was!

I describe the puzzles in big walk as similar to Portal 2 co-op: they require you to use your brains just the right amount, and can be quite challenging, but are satisfying to complete and enable you to use the skills you gather to solve other puzzles in similar ways. If you like that style of game but want to play it with a committed close friend group, this game is definitely for you!

Further on the puzzles: They don't require a reliance on one tool or methodology, but can instead be solved however you arrive at the puzzle, if you put your heads together. We often left behind things like the walkie-talkies in favour of non-verbal communication when possible, and that forced us to come up with creative methods to complete each puzzle.

As for the map itself and progression through it, we came out the other side having learned our way around intimately, despite the map being quite overwhelming to look at at first! It's expansive, but the way House House created landmarks to use as reference, as well as the ways of getting around the map that you can unlock, made it easy enough to navigate, especially if you got lost from the group!

Finally, I want to give a special mention to both endings of the game. The way the game guides you to the first ending is uniquely fun, as it certainly gives the group something to discuss! No spoilers! But once we got there and completed the "spaceship" puzzles, we sat watching the credits and discussing the experience of that sequence (again, no spoilers) as it was super memorable. The *ending* of both endings hit a really lovely emotional note of collaboration, togetherness, and that lovely feeling you get after a great hangout with friends. The prompts into that state of emotion were expertly done, and have us coming away from the game *very* sad that there isn't more!

Please House House, game devs, more of this! Thank you so much!

There is nothing else like BIG WALK.

House House, creators of 2018’s beloved-yet-short Untitled Goose Game, are back with a new and strange adventure, 100x the size. While that would be an extremely tall order for any studio, the Australians have outdone themselves with wobbling, giggling, flying colors. 

BIG WALK is categorized as a multiplayer puzzle game, but it stretches the genre in new directions. “Friendslop” this ain’t: from first principles, this is a powerful, almost scientific experience about communication between people. Multiplayer is mandatory, and no challenge can be overcome without help. Yet the challenges are barely puzzles at all: press all these buttons at the same time, get this sequence of shapes from one room to another, go there while a friend does that. Seeing the solution is often quite simple, but the -doing- of it, working as a team, is where the difficulty lies. This is because small quirks in the design force players to speak, to gesture and signal, to form internal codes and lingo, and to trust in the actions of teammates whom they cannot see or hear. Voices don’t carry for more than a few meters, so players who get separated (or tear off on their own) will have to resort to other methods to reconnect with the group. Nightfall makes the island deeply, un-navigably dark, so without lamps or flashlights, you can and will get lost. Your bubbly, dog-toy-esque avatars have no distinguishing features besides your color schemes, a limited set of gestures, and your own voices. You must, and will, learn to make use of them.

This game’s design is a triumph of minimalism, structurally and visually. BIG WALK is set in a naturalistic desert island, covered in trees and brush growth, crisscrossed with inch-deep streams, and smashed in the middle of this beautiful landscape are “playlands,” brightly painted and sharply lit jungle gyms, each bearing one of the many challenges for you the players to tackle, lost in the deep drones and gentle percussion of the music. Each one gives the impression of an interactive exhibit at a children’s museum, all primary colors and glimmering glass. The occasional beneficial item is also squirreled away: backpacks, holsters, binoculars, laser pointers, walkie-talkies, everything an intrepid Big Walker could ask for. Yet, those beneficial items can be just as challenging to use, depending on who you and your teammates are. For instance, players wearing backpacks are unable to reach the items inside them, not without another friend to help. Overcoming radio cross-talk, or reading a map, may turn out to be the hardest obstacles of all. In its minimalism, BIG WALK makes its puzzles out of you, the players, and its shortcomings are only as daunting as your own.  

Speaking of friends - do you have friends? Do you enjoy talking to them, hanging out with them? Can you stand it when they walk off in the wrong direction without telling anyone, knowing full well you won’t be able to progress without the key items on their backpack? Does it agitate you when your one friend who can’t sit still keeps opening and closing the doors that make the puzzles reset? Are you coworkers? Lovers? Friends-of-cousins-of-roommates? Are you all turbo-autistic? Doesn’t matter! This game will be a test! A test not only of how well you can talk to each other, but how well you can stand each other, because the interpersonal friction is equally comfortable, crushing, and constant.

So yes, BIG WALK entered my personal Hall Of Fame before we even got to the ending sequence, and what an ending sequence it was. The ultimate test of your teamwork and communications skills will come, as you all march to the first and only final dungeon I’ve seen in a puzzle game, and face twist after twist on your preexisting notions of what you can say, when you cannot say it. Look your friends in the eyes – those weird, doodle-headed, brainless eyes – carry that weight, and take that walk.

Big Walk has numerous Color-based Puzzles with zero accessibility features. No one on the dev team knew or cared, and this is increasingly a problem in Indie spaces. 

Almost every item in Big Walk is based around wasting someone's time. Whether that's the player who stands in one place for a half hour pointing a laser pointer, or the guy who has to schlup all of the red gourds to the towers, even the walkie talkies punish players by forcing them to be unable to carry any other item. These aren't "Trade-Off" mechanics, these are punishment mechanics. While its quaint that they think the modern person can bring 3 of their friends to bear, let alone 10 (the game is inherently designed for as large a group as you can find, despite the assurances otherwise), grabbing all of your friends and several hours out of their busy lives just to tell them to hike alone for an hour or stand alone on a lookout for an hour is a sincerely shitty decision the devs could have just... not done. 

There aren't a lot of 4 player puzzle-venture games out there, and honestly this might be the only one. The graphics look fine, although the horrid clash of the character models and the semi-realistic environment might be a bit much, and my favorite part of the game is the crushing darkness of night, trudging along with nothing but the whims of a laser pointer 4 miles away and the ghostly outline of your friend's eyes beside you. The atmosphere is impeccable. The game design is not.

I recently played [b]Big Walk[/b] with two of my friends, and honestly, it was one of the most enjoyable multiplayer experiences we’ve had in a while. Going into the game, we weren’t entirely sure what to expect, but it quickly turned into a game where we were constantly laughing, messing around, and discovering new things together.

What makes [b]Big Walk[/b] so fun is how much freedom it gives you. There isn’t this constant pressure to rush through objectives or play perfectly. Instead, you can simply explore the world, interact with things, and see what happens. Playing with two friends made this even better because almost every little situation somehow turned into something funny. We would start out trying to complete a simple task and somehow end up completely distracted, experimenting with the environment or doing something completely stupid.

The game is especially good at creating those spontaneous moments that you remember afterwards. A lot of our best moments weren’t even planned. We would randomly find something interesting, start messing around with it, and suddenly all three of us were involved in some ridiculous situation. The game really rewards curiosity, and having friends alongside you makes exploring feel much more entertaining.

I also really liked the overall atmosphere of [b]Big Walk[/b]. It has a relaxed and playful feeling that makes it easy to just sit back and enjoy the experience. The world feels like a place you actually want to explore rather than simply a series of levels that you need to finish. Combined with the humor and the freedom to interact with things, it creates a really unique multiplayer experience.

Of course, [b]Big Walk[/b] probably isn’t a game for someone looking for intense competitive gameplay or a very serious story. But that’s also exactly what I enjoyed about it. It doesn’t take itself too seriously, and it works incredibly well as a game to play with friends when you just want to have a good time.

Overall, playing [b]Big Walk[/b] with two of my friends was a fantastic experience. We laughed a lot, explored a ton, and created plenty of memorable moments. I would definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a fun, relaxed, and genuinely funny co-op game. Playing it with friends is definitely where [b]Big Walk[/b] shines.

Before you buy this game, ask yourself this question: if you were stuck in a room with 1+ of your close friend(s), and you were forced to sit around and talk for five minutes, would you enjoy yourself? If the answer is yes, then you're the intended audience for Big Walk. This isn't a friendslop game where you're going to be inundated with risks and thrills for 2 hours per run, but instead a giant co-op walking sim with puzzles where the fun you have is with your friends.

This game is exactly as the trailer describes: you and your close friends explore an island full of puzzles which all require some form of cooperation between yourselves. These puzzles give strange items that are used to give you more access to the island by unlocking new modes of transportation. During these puzzles, you will be walking from one destination to the other, typically without any form of background music unless you bring the radio. The nights get very dark, and it's not uncommon to get lost for up to half an hour at times.

So where is the fun in this game? It's with your friends: joking around, messing with new items, kicking them into the ocean for giggles, using the walkie talkies like you're tactical soldiers, doing a sick kick that immediately solves a puzzle, and yes, even sitting in a room for five minutes and just having a talk. This game is literally all about the journey, especially since the puzzles have very little variation to their solutions.

It's for that reason that I would only truly recommend this game to a group of friends that either haven't experienced much of the game yet, or who can keep to themselves and let the newer players solve puzzles. In the multiple different playthroughs I've done with different friends, I have seen newer players get annoyed over more experienced players solving puzzles ahead of time. Even I had the most fun when finding something new for the first time, which I feel is muddled when someone else is showing it off to me out of the gate.

This game is definitely one of a kind to me: something that I was able to enjoy with my friends that I feel will be a nice memory in the future. But unlike friendslop like PEAK or R.E.P.O., I find myself unable to jump back into this game immediately. Maybe in a few months, or years, when I'm in the mood for having a big walk with my friends again. If you think you can answer the question at the beginning of this review with a strong yes, then I cannot recommend getting this game enough, and having a great time with your friends.

Big Walk was one of my three most anticipated games of the year, the moment it got announced.
What's funny, is I expected the atmosphere and dynamic that I get from Peak, but got something completely different. Yet I fell in love nonetheless.

My review comes with a BIG disclaimer: coming into Big Walk expecting the same "friendlsop" (god I hate that word) formula will leave you very disappointed. Why?

There is no friendly fire, no way to "harm" your friends or laugh at them get harmed. In short - this game doesn't enforce the chaotic goblin behavior that many friendslop games have become famous for. And personally, it was a nice palate cleanser for my overstimulated brain.

The game is set in a gigantic island, maybe a little too big for the number of puzzles it features, and there are no teleport points. Meaning, you will be walking everywhere, spending stretches of time in between puzzles without immediate dopamine fixes like collecting items, causing chaos, or having any interactables in the evironment. 
Your experience of the game relies HEAVILY on the chemistry between you and your friends. It reveals how well you keep each other company, whether you're comfortable with silence, and how good of a communicator you are. 
Big Walk is seriously just a hiking trip with some friends, with puzzles peppered inbetween.

On the gameplay side, the puzzles are great and innovative in a lot of ways. There were four of us playing, and each contributed in some way. Sure, there were frustrations, but there were also a lot of laughs. Gameplay-wise, my favorite part was, ironically, right at the end (spoilers):

[spoiler] At the start of the game, you get to customize each other's colors, and the entire playthrough, those color schemes become a way to recognize each other. Once you reach the end, you have to complete one final set of puzzles, except, not only are your mics turned off as a way to test your communication skills, but your colors get stripped away too. So there's no way of telling who's who.

That is, until you start recognizing each teammate's movements and behavior, because you've spend the last dozen hours faffing about and going through those same puzzles. From a human behavior standpoint, it was fascinating to catch your brain pinpointing exactly who is who based on nothing but movement and behavior during puzzles. Blew my mind, honestly. [/spoiler] 

The music itself was one of my favorite parts. Big Walk features such a unique soundtrack, and it's been my go-to for work every day for the past few days.

My only gripes with the game: proximity chat is still pretty bad, and my computer crashed three times on one specific puzzle, and I think it's because of the environment load (leaves, bushes, etc). The first crash caused our save to be deleted, so I never hosted again xD BACKUP YOUR SAVES, HOSTS, PLS
Lastly - why can't I use a walkie-talkie when it's on my hip, House House? Makes no goddang sense.

Overall, Big Walk is a huge recommendation for people who don't need constant gameplay stimuli to stay entertained. This is a game for walking, talking, and solving some puzzles along the way. The end credits solidified that intent, and I'm glad House House decided to try something different from the norm.

Allow me to start this review by saying this game is incredible all across the board. BUT! It is not a game made for everyone, and I'm not just talking about people who do not have friends to play this with. Big Walk is one of those games where your entire experience will be based off different factors, the main two being: who you play with and how you all approach the game.

Personally, I completed Big Walk with two other friends (3 people in total). One of them played previously with a much larger group while the other was completely new to the game like me. Considering what I had heard about my friend's experience with the larger group and how our run went, I strongly believe that this game is better with a smaller group of friends (3-4 players is ideal in my opinion). Playing with a larger group may lead to people splitting up more often to cover more ground, which may result in some people missing out on fun puzzles and experiences. In our group, we rarely ever split up unless absolutely necessary. Also, with a game that emphasizes communication in many ways, being in a large group may hinder that intended experience. While you definitely have to communicate with each other for the puzzles, it's important for your Big Walk experience that you converse with one another. It may be possible to still have a good run with a larger group, but once again, it depends on who you play with.

This leads me to my next major point: how you approach the game. While you can definitely attempt to speed run or rush through this game, you won't be able to enjoy it as much in the process (at least for your first run). Big Walk was designed to be taken s l o w. It will reward you whenever you and your friends take your time and actively explore. Some of my own personal favorite moments were the quiet ones where my friends and I just sat and enjoyed the environment for a moment. Rather than focusing solely on progression, it is encouraged to actually talk and interact with one another. In our run, we also avoided looking up puzzle answers as much as possible. We did look up a couple things, just to clear up our own confusion, but overall, we completed 98% of the game without any outside help. This, paired with the game's proximity chat forced us to be immersed in not only the game, but each other's presence. Playing with friends who all wanted a chill, immersive approach to the game really enhanced my own experience overall.

Big Walk is very well made, so much so that it almost feels a little wrong calling it a "friendslop game". When you take your time to explore the nooks and crannies of the map, you will be rewarded with a refreshing, serene experience that you may not be able to easily get in reality. I just know that if this game came out during the COVID-19 pandemic, it would have been praised even more than it is now.

The map itself looks beautiful and it makes you want to stop at times to admire it. Somehow, despite being completely different from the natural environment, the puzzles don't distract or take away from the nature. They're well placed (in my opinion) and force you to really explore the entirety of the map. Something you may have a problem with is how dark the map can become. If you are exploring without a light and it turns night, it may be hard for you to navigate. Personally, my friends and I didn't have too much of a problem with the darkness. There were plenty of lights that we could use throughout the night and even without light, there were plenty of landmarks we would find that helped us navigate. Also, the darkness paired with the incredible sound design really made the game more immersive.

The sound design is so high quality, it's kind of fascinating. The nature sounds like nature. There are no other living beings on the map but the environment still sounds alive and lived in. All of the puzzle sounds are satisfying and fun while the bigger, booming sounds that signify progression feels grand but not loud. The proximity chat is way shorter than most people may be used to, but it encourages you to use items like the megaphone or the walkie-talkies to communicate. I believe the short proximity chat also forces a personal level of intimacy between you and your friends, which is a nice change from usual "friendslop" games. Music is again, a reward, but an incredibly fun reward whenever you stumble upon the tunes (Radio Station I is the best track).

The gameplay is pretty simple and straight forward. Keep in mind though, if you're planning to try and Skyrim walk your way up rocks or mountains, you're not going to get very far. If you can't reach a spot, you probably haven't unlocked the way to it yet. The puzzles are also not too challenging. The real challenge that stems through most of the puzzles is communicating with one another. Even then, however, the puzzles were still pretty manageable. There were a few puzzles that were a bit harder to grasp and understand at first, but we were able to return to them later on and complete them (again, we looked up help for only one of the puzzles on the map). The only "issue" my friends and I had throughout our run was that we would sometimes get stuck on the environment, but it really wasn't that big of a problem. 

Overall, Big Walk is truly an incredible game that was made with so much thought and care. However, not every person's experience with it will be the same. I was incredibly lucky to have had such a positive experience with my first run, and I hope that my review can help you with your own experience. 11/10, I need to play again.

P.S. I believe both endings were super sweet and the perfect ways to finish such a "big walk."
