I genuinely think this game is a strong GOTY contender.

Big Walk fosters genuine conversation and adventure in the most seamless way I have ever seen in a video game. You are constantly put in situations where you are forced to improvise communication. Due to this, over the course of the game, you start to learn the unique patterns that exist in your communication with each other. In a way that you would not ordinarily ever even think about. In turn, you form a shared communication language built on the understanding of each players unique style that is downright magical sometimes. 

Almost none of the puzzles are directly next to each other. This means that following your triumphant puzzle victory you are left with nothing to do other than talk as you head to your next point of interest. The game also does a great job of introducing natural (and sometimes accidental!) breakpoints in that conversation where you get the opportunity to talk more one on one with particular friends. The perfect example of this to me is the gondola. Each seat can only fit two players, which introduces a nice little break from the constant group chatter that can be overwhelming at times. Another example is just straight up getting lost/separated, or going to retrieve a specific item.

While most are rather simple, the puzzles in Big Walk are suited to a variety of players. Some are very structured, and require setting up systematic ways to communicate in the absence of ordinary channels. Others are much more freeform, and encourage creativity and on the spot thinking to accomplish your goal. So far none have left me feeling cheated or unsatisfied with the solutions. Though I can imagine that some groups may become a bit frustrated by certain puzzles.

There is plenty of room for shenanigans in big walk. Between hiding items, kicking stuff off cliffs, playing music over the radios, picking up your friends, and spam clicking everything on and off making annoying clicking sounds, the gremlins of your group will have a blast. There are very few things that can be done in the game that are downright malicious, almost all shenanigans seem highly in the spirit of Big Walk as they tend to encourage more walking and talking.

The inventory management aspect of Big Walk is also rather interesting. While you start out with just your hands, as you explore you gain access to a bit more space. There is always a bit of friction between wanting to carry stuff to help you with exploration and puzzle solving, while also needing to make sure you have enough free space to carry back your puzzle rewards and other tools you find along the way. While it was a rather low friction for my group, I imagine it might become a much larger focus of the game for smaller groups with fewer hands. 

The ability to carry around your friends is super useful, it means that people can take breaks without being left behind. This works if you get disconnected too, you leave behind a body that you will appear in the when you reconnect, so your friends can carry you with them if you are having internet issues! 

I found it super cool that while Big Walk highly encourages talking with your friends, almost everything is also compatible with the in game text chat. Radios re-project your text box to all others when you activate them, and other items that mess with sound have similar compatibility. 

Big Walks ending is both surreal and quite touching, it made several people in our group tear up. It does a great job of offering a bittersweet but satisfying conclusion to your adventure while also presenting the opportunity to put everything you learned throughout your playthrough to the test. 

Despite "finishing" the game, there is still a final (optional?) challenge to complete, so I will likely update this review after we get that done!

puzzle centric game in a nature setting. the game gives you almost no instruction past the controls, and it was super fun to figure everything out on my own very fun if you like coop game, and are able to adapt on the fly, and don't like games that hold your hand. If you have friends to play with definitely give this one a shot. good for anywhere between 20-40 hours of play time, took me about 25 hours to finish everything.

For context I played this with about 6 other of my very close friends, your results may vary especially if you plan to play this in a group smaller than 4 people. 

One of the best game experiences I've had in a long time, while obviously friends improve the experience, big walk is an incredible sandbox to facilitate interactions that feel natural with each other and even by yourself. 

In a pre cell phone world, coordination was extra important because you didn't have a cell phone lifeline to figure things out. There's an inherent trust you have to have that you'll both follow the plan even when you can't easily contact one another to figure things out. That trust comes up often in big walk and it's an incredibly rewarding feeling when everything goes to plan.

Puzzles are often simple yet satisfying to complete, while I've only played through once (and not 100% yet but planning on it), I can imagine these puzzles have good replayability with other groups of people and performing different parts of the puzzle. 

Sometimes you'll get lost in big walk and honestly they're pleasant moments in the game. The game gives the player plenty of tools to find each other, whether it's flares, walkie talkies, laser pointers, or cowbells maliciously put on your friends backpacks. And of course the towers and radio lights across the map show where you can find help and when they turn green maybe you're trying to be contacted. 

Some might call this boring, but I never had a dull moment but only quieter moments that are nice and reflective. Would 100% recommend this to any group of 4+ who have 15 hours to play through this magical experience.

After playing this game in what I think was the most optimal setting: A friend group that is experienced with video games and were 11 people all serious about making forward progress at all times while still able to make be jovial and have fun, I have some thoughts about this one.

Every game journalist, blogger, and I reckon about 60% of gaming youtube (those who seriously engage with art instead of writing games off like these due to being a walking simulator of some kind) will tell you that Big Walk is a transformative game that you should experience with your busy siblings who work 7 days a week, your spouse who thinks video games are weird, your boomer parents, your grandparents and your pets to let them see how great and valid this medium of entertainment is are vastly overselling the accessibility and novelty this game and I think Big Walk is too niche for all of the above statements to be true.

Looking at this from the perspective of someone who doesn't have a lot of experience with gaming in general, I think a lot of those players will struggle. The Controls are a bit too finnicky for people  that are unfamiliar with a controller or using a keyboard as a gaming input. There might be actions that need to be performed that are too precise for people without experience, and in my mind that is pretty damming for a game that is supposed to be recommended for everybody. The overall map is large and unwieldy to navigate; certain paths (that won't appear often) can send them tumbling down a ravine or cliff and navigating back without help will be difficult. When navigating near hills or mountains people with experience will easily pick up on what is traversable or climbable terrain, but for your normie friends they might struggle. Add an aggressive day/night cycle that requires external lights and things will take a lot longer with new players, and their patience might run out before you can make any meaningful progress.

Even without new players, it is basically a requirement that everyone in the group/lobby needs to be on the same page and serious about making progress. This should be a given, but every friend group is different, and the game gives too many tools to troll serious players and seriously hamper forward momentum. At any time someone can steal crucial progress items and drop kick them off a nearby cliff, and while that doesn't permanently disable progress or soft lock the game, someone's gonna have to go get it which can waste a significant amount of time, and aside from kicking people from the lobby, I'm not sure what recourse the host/other serious players actually have. This kind of limits the game from obnoxious younger siblings or immature friends; I think this kind of limiting constrains the optimal experience even further, moreso than other "friendslop games" in the same genre. 

Finally, as a puzzle game first, there are admittedly some real stinkers in the mix here. While I think a decent chunk of them are clever, you'll know these immediately when you see them. While Big Walk makes it a point to show how important verbal and nonverbal communication is, when you stumble upon your 7th puzzle that's just another variation of a game of telephone with buttons, Big Walk starts to overstay it's welcome a bit

I think people who dislike these kinds of games are going to talk about how slow you move and how all the options for faster traversal across the map are still slow, the lack of failure states and how they hate whatever commentary they interpret from the game is "preaching" to them, but I think the reality is that Big Walk is a game 4-6 people who are experienced with video games and are serious about finishing things will find 2-3 play sessions to play a puzzle game with so-so puzzles that is mostly walking around a big map, and pulling that together can be much harder than anyone lets on. Not everyone has a gaming friend group big enough to support this kind of experience these days. I advise you don't play through the entire thing in one sitting. Without spoilers, exercises and experiences that players are supposed to appreciate  will really just start to get on your nerves when you're on your 8th consecutive hour trying to get to the ending.

On that note, this is a $15 experience that you can really only get the most out of once. For those who are willing to do multiple playthroughs with multiple friend groups where you just sit there for another 8-10 hours and just follow instructions and let your friends have all the aha! moments to themselves, you have saint-like patience that I sadly don't possess. The traversal in itself makes it so by the time you're really getting into the main gameplay loop and where the "good" puzzles are, you'll blow right past the refund window. If you decide to buy, you have to ok with that fact going in.

[h1][b]Big Walk is an absolutely phenomenal game that takes its pride in its gameplay with your friends. What makes the game so great? Well, there are a couple of things..[/b][/h1]

Firstly, gameplay. The gameplay of Big Walk is simple, yet entertaining and fun. You and your friends, well, walk around and explore a big open world, solving puzzles to get "gourdes" to unlock towers. The puzzles are all unique and fun that challenge you and your friends to communicate in different ways. There are a total of 5 towers in the game, and each of them unlock a certain part of the game that benefit you and your friends as a team. One of them, for example, unlocks a train that you can use to travel faster. Another unlocks underground tunnels that lead to each tower. Yet another unlocks a ski lift. You see what im getting at. The game gives you goals with the towers, but that does not mean you need to do them. In reality, all you could theoretically do is just walk and talk with your friends aimlessly. And thats what makes this game so powerful; the total freedom you get. The open world is huge and there are many secrets to explore. There are structures that give you items which are rewards for exploration, along with different musical areas where you can unlock new music for your radio. You can just sit down at a beach and hang out with your friends, or play hide and seek with them. The freedom you get is what makes the game truly fun.

Secondly, the graphics. The contrast between the realistic looking world and the cartoonish looking characters is a fantastical art design choice, and it makes the game feel truly unique. This choice feels surprisingly normal and to me, the players dont really look that out of place in the world. Diving deeper into the player characters, they are very expressive. Try stealing an item from your friends hands, and their character gets widened eyes, looking confused. When falling from a large distance, the player character collapses and their eyes start shaking. All of this comes to make up fun, interesting, and expressive player characters that really fit into the world. The realistic graphics themselves are beautiful, as well, and they make the game truly great.

Finally, this is a House House game. Like, this is the creators of Untitled Goose Game were talking about. This company never fails to deliver a banger game, so I would be surprised if this one wasn't worth getting.

Overall. Big Walk is a fantastic game that is insanely fun the game. If you are thinking about getting the game, then I would easily recommend getting it at full price. Its just that good. Absolute masterpiece, 10/10.

Big Walk is art. It is a magical experience that I am sad I will not be able to experience for the first time again. Big Walk is a really simple game, it is just walking around an island and doing puzzles to open up more of the island. Despite this, the wonder of exploring with friends is so enthralling that I am struggling to put into words how genuinely moving this game was.

What makes the experience of the game so magnificent is the serene atmosphere. Quiet crickets at night, bird calls at dusk and dawn, the rustling of gentle leaves, the caress of waves upon sand and rock. It is a sublime place to be where while even alone in the darkest tunnel or veil of night, it is still blissfully tranquil. After the long arduous turmoils of real life I was able to just shed it all away and forget about it while being lost in a new land with my friends. I left work early the Tuesday it came out to play it and ended up staying up too late because it was simply too enrapturing.

The people you play with make a big impact on how the game is. I played it with four people total (including myself), two of which I was already very close to. Every moment the group spent separated where I was only with one other person, it felt intimately personal beyond what I have experienced before. I have been alone with some of these friends in real life before yet it felt so much easier to open up to them here. Something about being under a carpet of stars, aloft a chairlift slowly meandering its way over a forest felt more special than any vacation with them I had previously experienced. As for the other person who I did not know that well, I feel like we were able to learn a lot about each other and embolden our relationship.

Big Walk is not a coop puzzle game, more a collaborative participation in a beautiful craft. There is more downtime traveling than there is actually doing puzzles. Savoring those moments is what makes the game so amazing. It is truly an experience made by the people you play with. The end of the game is rather anticlimactic in the traditional sense as there is no story, no tension, and no rising action. It invites the players to take turns one at a time and say something. It was so unbelievably bittersweet that I found myself in tears watching the people I had grew so close to in 20 hours depart away. It reminded me of the times I had to say goodbye to people in my life for the last time and I am getting lachrymose just typing this.

I cannot recommend this enough to any groups of friends who are willing to be open with each other and experience something truly wonderful. Every few years I play a distinct game during a vulnerable period of my life and never forget how transformative of an experience it is and shapes me as a person. I am fairly resolute in my current position in life yet what this made me feel far surpasses any of those other games.

The audio might be a touch quiet and the climbing may be a tad janky at times but this game truly is something special beyond the praise of my prose.

‘Big Walk’ is a game that shines brightest in the details filled in by the players. At its surface it is a jaunt with friends through lovingly recreated Australian bushland.

The crux of this game is in the small and unspoken ways it requires collaboration. The act of putting on or using a backpack requires the assistance of friends. The puzzles demand group efforts, with most only requiring two players, so that you can split up into pairs and go wandering off on separate journeys. The primary goal is to collect bulbous shapes, which are never given a canonical name, inviting the players to find their own terms for them.

Me and my group speak excitedly of collecting new ‘gourds’, we chant ‘key-key-key’ together when we unlock another section of the map, we sit and listen to the music and watch the sun set, then rise.

As an Australian it is remarkable to see my own landscape so lovingly portrayed. I smile whenever I hear the laugh of the kookaburras (my grandmother believes the soul of my great-grandfather are within them), I cherish the sounds of whipbirds, I love the nostalgic sound of white sand that squeaks underfoot on hot Australian beaches. What a fantastic cultural export.

On more technical details, the game’s VOIP system works flawlessly. Having just experienced ‘The Outlast Trials’ shoddy in-game voice chat it is a joy to have no tech issues on this front. The game works well on a Steam Deck on ‘high’ graphics settings, although the limitations of the device are felt in its inability to use wired headphones and the in-built mic at the same time.

‘Big Walk’ is a big toy. And it’s the best toy I’ve played with in a long time.

EDIT: If you care about the usage of AI to modify 10 lines of code I fear you are perhaps jumping the gun a bit much. Settle down and think about what you really care about.

This is an absolute gem of a co-op game to play with friends, up there with the likes of Portal 2 or It takes Two. My group of three hit credits at about 11.5 hours, and the price felt more than worth it. 

The puzzles were excellently designed, the atmosphere was fun and lighthearted (and sometimes spooky! Even though it is clear there are no actual threats), and the map is laid out in such a way that you can do the puzzles in basically any order, yet there is always a clear sense of progression. Our only very minor complaint is that, due to the way they prevented trying to mountain goat up areas, we would frequently get stuck on bits of terrain. Usually it was only for a brief moment before we'd wiggle free, but occasionally we'd be stuck for 5-10 seconds. 

The game is very dependent on the proximity chat if you choose to use mics, so If you're playing with people in the same house or room as you, everyone will probably need noise cancelling headphones and not to look at each other's screens for the best experience. 

A couple of the puzzles also seemed like they'd be nearly impossible using only text, but it's clear that a ton of thought has gone into the game, so I would be surprised if players without mics haven't been accounted for. My group all had mics though, so I can't say for certain.

All in all, this is a wonderful game that anyone who even remotely enjoys puzzles should consider.

Without doubt, one of, if not the best cooperative experience you can try out at the moment. With such consistent enjoyment and increasing tension, you let creativity take control of various puzzles, communication and signaling. The emphasis on communication is the game’s biggest strength and the whole root of the cooperation. It works exceptionally well, often creating moments that feel completely spontaneous, with everyone naturally pulling together to make progress. It is not, and never feels like, friendslop or any other game built around clipfarming with your friends. In such an oversaturated market, it is refreshing to find something that feels genuinely considered. Whether or not you enjoy this kind of cooperative puzzle-solving is up to individual preferences, but with such confidence, House House really knew how to perfect a thorough experience with friends only. How to catch the funny moments off guard, not causing them yourself, as we mostly do with these games at times. It all happens naturally as exploration takes over and everyone slowly splits up, doing their best to find the next tower and “red fruits?”. We didn’t give them any term or name, but we sure did check every nook and cranny for all we could. If looking outside our sessions, the world looks desolate, empty, a large terrain of nothing but mountains and trees to gaze upon. You do, however, slowly discover colorful little buildings, statues, and towers scattered throughout the otherwise vacant landscape, each one standing out against the world around them. They spark curiosity and give you a reason to keep exploring. Of course it is the entire gameplay loop, but there is something more meaningful here than simply playing to reach the end. It feels less like a game you complete and more like a journey you experience with your friends. Puzzles range from intuitive to deceptively difficult, often requiring creative, out-of-the-box uses of audio, posing, and even directions from friends. I was consistently impressed, particularly by the later-game puzzles and their blend of intuition and complexity. It all culminates in a practically perfect final section that puts you and your friends to the ultimate test, while introducing increasingly surreal elements that subtly hint at something deeper without ever derailing the experience, never losing the charm the game has maintained. Besides gameplay and memorable moments I highly favor the soundscape and use of light in Big Walk. Hearing your voice echo across the mountains before a distorted response comes drifting back is wonderfully executed. Using a light late at night to signal your location or respond to someone far across the landscape is equally satisfying. The way fireworks briefly illuminate the world around you before everything immediately falls back into darkness is one of many small details that feels phenomenal.

At this point of the year, Big Walk is considered my GOTY for 26, because of its originality and creative approach. How it at times gets your brain working, then to give you time for relaxing and comedy. A real gem I am looking forward to seeing getting its praise at TGA later in December.

Unlike many games, it's not one you can just drop into strangers with or complete on your own. This is a game that must be enjoyed with at least one other person and is even more delightful when enjoyed with someone you know. 
It's a game about communicating in difficult situations to reach a common goal and traversing a beautiful landscape with nothing but the company of friends between each new puzzle and landmark. The sound design is masterful in the way it forces you to listen to nature as if you were truly on a hike or fill the void with conversation, and in the rare instances you find music hubs, you're rewarded with a spot to sit and listen. Even the scenery is a love letter to putting on a good pair of shoes and going for a big walk with nowhere in particular in mind because adventure is rewarded with sights of stars over the ocean and sunrises over densely planted landscapes. 
Big Walk is a master class in the ability to mix art and technology for something truly interactive, immersive, and breathtaking with exquisite highlights on the natural world. When I first attended college for computer science out of high school this was the kind of thing I was thinking about wanting to make and something I had begun to think impossible when I later returned to college to complete my art degree. I've never been more inspired to return to thinking about how technology and art can interact. In a time where technology is as inhuman as it's ever been and video games in particular serve as a method of isolation, Big Walk is an innovative and much needed breath of fresh air.

I cannot recommend this enough. 
The artistic style is on point. The environment is highly detailed, but the things you need are in flat colors, making them far easier to find, and adds a childish charm to everything. 
The puzzles are not too complex, but still require you to think. They were clearly well thought out, and making puzzles is difficult. 

There is no music, in general, but you have the option of having music if you want. Instead you get ambient nature sounds that remind me of the tropical environments in zoos and other places. 

The world is your oyster, and you can unlock towers in any order you choose, for the most part (there seem to be a few exceptions). There are no notes to read, except the basic tutorial, so you figure things out along the way. It honestly feels like a giant jungle gym!

If you're worried because the game seems to be centered or aimed for 4 people, worry not. I am playing through it with 1 other person (so we are a 2 person team) and we are doing fine. It may take you longer to get through since you have less hands to carry things, but you can absolutely solve the puzzles with just -2- people. 

The proximity mic is absolutely encouraged, and honestly, makes it more fun. A lot of the features, including the mic, and picking your colors, relies on having another person. They've really thought about how to force cooperation without making it feel tedious or.. well.. forced. 

The game is beautiful, even on low graphics, so you can just sit somewhere and enjoy the music, watch the sun rise, or set, or just listen to the ambience. I can't count the number of times my friend has said "It's so beautiful" as we've wandered around. It really is peaceful.

There is no fall damage. No health bars. No death. It really is a puzzle game with exploration that constantly makes you feel good about finding something (and it feels like you're always finding something new). Puzzles make you feel accomplished. The little things like the train sounds, and the toys you can carry with you, really let you have a blast; you can be a big kid here. 

So if you're waffling on it, I would say get it. It is an absolute treasure. 

My ONLY quibble is that I feel like I am constantly getting stuck on a rock, or a branch or something small in the terrain, or sticking to the terrain. But it doesn't ruin the fun.

review:
Big Walk is a game about going on walks with friends, putting your minds together to figure out puzzles, and getting frustrated because your friend just got lost for the 15th time. It may get infuriating but the beauty of this game is finding that lost friend and bringing them home. To insert the final totem and enter the next area with everyone. To sit by a beach and have a one on one with a close friend, even if just for a little bit. To find meaning in the most trivial things. There's a real sense of togetherness present that only the best of co-op experiences can provide.

What I didn't expect from this game was to get genuinely emotional towards the end of the journey. Not to spoil anything about the endgame, but it challenges you and your friends in new ways that really showcase how much of a bond you've formed over the course of your time together. It's a game that will take you maybe 10 hours to beat, but every second is worth more than words can describe. This is my game of the year, no questions asked, and it's one of the best games I've played in so so long. This is the first time I wouldn't call a game life-changing because it's so much more beautiful than that. In a world that often feels like it priorities negativity above all else, Big Walk serves to remind you of the miracle that is living in the same world and sharing the same experiences with others. It's life-affirming.

Ever since this first got announced a little over 2 years ago now I've been keeping a close eye on it. I just knew it'd be something special, and I'm so, so happy I was right.
If you have a group of friends you want a real special experience with, or even get to know someone better, I cannot recommend Big Walk enough.

So, what'd I like?
The game's core loop is really fun, solving puzzles with friends and figuring out your own ways of communicating information. Even between the challenges, simply chilling out and taking in the nature while occasionally getting updates from your friends over radio is an experience I haven't seen matched with many other games.
Speaking of the puzzles, they're so, so creative. One thing Big Walk does that I haven't seen many other puzzle games try is constantly bringing in new mechanics or gimmicks only present in one or two puzzles. Most of the time this is seen as a bad idea, but the challenge of the puzzles are communicated so quickly and effectively that I found it to be a pleasant surprise rather than an unwanted boon figuring out what a puzzle was even about.
The co-op aspect itself is pushed to its absolute limit with this game, so many puzzles require you to split up and communicate over long distance, or remove talking entirely, which forces you to come up with creative solutions. There were many times while playing I got genuinely giddy over the creativity of our group and how we figured out ways to transfer information without ever speaking a word.

And... what did I dislike?
Not much! I feel that the movement could be pretty clunky at times, although few of the puzzles in the game rely on the movement system so this wasn't much of a disruption. I also couldn't help but feel like the game felt a little unoptimized in a few areas? The framerate of my game fluctuated massively depending on the area I was in. There were also a very small amount of puzzles I felt were more frustrating than fun, although considering how many are in the game, you won't find yourself stuck with these puzzles often, or at all considering you can always go to another puzzle and do that instead.

Overall, a really special experience. The most unfortunate part about puzzle games is they're not replayable, but that just makes the time I put in that much more worthwhile. I highly, highly recommend this title. Please give it a shot with some friends.

To comment on the sound settings, which seems to be the majority of negative reviews, the game DOES have settings for sensitivity & noise compression. However, it does not have a volume control, and automatically adjusts. Yes, this might not work for everyone's setup, however it is done intentionally. The game's audio is impressive, and with the focus on communication, they want to highlight that. 'Earshot' is short range to get people together and listening closely, walls and terrain blocks your voice, caverns carry it. With these intentional limitations, the communications tools like walkie talkies, signs, hand signals, etc., then become so much more engaging to use, and you don't end up defaulting to voice because it's easy.

The game doesn't NEED an individual volume slider, it's an intentional design choice, but if you or a friend is struggling to get their mic working, try running mmsys.cpl and adjusting input device levels. Hopefully that works :)

I loved this game from start to finish. It's sense of exploration is up there with the best games, and playing with friends heightens the experience that much more. I was worried that it would be tough to complete (or 100%) because it's a coop game, but I've now beaten it with one group and I'm nearing the end with another group because everyone else is just as excited to keep playing as I am. The items are super fun and take on different uses with different groups: we had 4 walkie talkies in one group because of how much we split up, but the other stayed together the whole time so we skipped the walkie talkies entirely.

The audio design is FANTASTIC: the nature sounds are so perfect and the little bits of music being location based were so nice to break up the nature sounds... and then the complete silence in sound proof rooms makes you realize just how loud nature is and it's exactly like getting into a car at the end of a night doing astronomy, when I prefer to drive home with no music to enjoy the silence. That said, this game really needs better audio options surrounding the voice chat. The update at least made friends not super quiet, but we still need sliders to actually adjust people, and the mic senstivity option did not work for one of my friends who was echoing the whole time while wearing closed back headphones; an issue he does not have in other games or Discord calls.

There are a few downsides though: While there are some incredible puzzles, a game with this many is bound to have some stinkers, and there are definitely some really bad puzzles, with the ones that can be done by a single person being the main culprits. My other complaint is with the inventory system. I get the point of having limited inventory, and the backpacks and waistbands are a great upgrade. However, not being able to interact with your own backpack is more frustrating than fun, and IMO hinders how creative you can get with exploration and the puzzles you have to split up for.

A simple and focused idea implemented very well. Lovely map and music, in that they are structured well and nothing feels out of place as you wander. It even includes peaceful observation points with great scenery. The voice communication has been excellent; stable and immediately functional, with great ability to tell where people are, including elevation.
Game tutorial is simple and clear, with lots of space to practice. It's a very strong showing of how simple mechanics done well are far more enjoyable than trying to overprovide and therefore overcomplicate.
Points of interest are brightly coloured and geometrically eye catching, so it's very easy to orient yourself. This includes that at night player eyes are a stark, almost glowing, white. A very small decision with a huge impact on players feeling less lost or uncertain, while still being a bit of goofy fun.
The puzzles have been very well structred. Maybe a little obtuse for some, but with very few mechanics and physical objects to work with, it very quickly pares down into a few possible actions.

Minor gripes with collision detection making movement feel a bit janky at times, and the slightly fast voice drop off can make it feel people are moving away very quickly when they are only a few steps ahead. These are actually very minor issues in play, and quick to adjust to.
I will also say the anti-motion-sickness grid added a lot of clutter to my vision that was more distracting than I liked, and made myself more comfortable by reducing my mouse DPI to get much less rapid screen movement if that's something that affects anyone else.

The game gives you tools that work intuitively to set up fun interactions with your friends, and the puzzles are simple yet fun. We played in a group of 10-12 (some had to go to bed :c), and even though it was evident that the puzzles were designed around 4 players, it was still EXTREMELY fun and natural to play. We ended up splitting up into smaller groups, exchanging thoughts on our own puzzles, sharing resources, and planning to reconvene or crossing paths by chance. Its clear that the devs put thought into each feature as the game guides you very naturally, creating a perfectly immersive experience. 

Gripes:

Can't adjust other player's mic output volume individually.

When leaving and rejoining the save, your position is reset back to spawn, and every item that wasn't held by a player is sent to where you found it. Player position and item position saving when you leave is a basic commodity in other games, so I'm left confused on why it wasn't even an option. It was very annoying when our host had connection issues and I had to begin a big walk back to what I was exploring. Our friend also had trouble reconnecting during the final sequence, which threw a wrench in my immersion since we had to take a 10 minute walk back at what was an emotional climax for me.

The train is way too slow to actually find an excuse to use it. I find the train itself very fun, as you can hop on and communicate with your friends to gather and travel with you. However, when you run slightly faster than the train, it feels rather pointless. 

End sequence spoilers: [spoiler] I wish the game intuitively told the players to view each segment of the puzzles before settling into position and beginning attempts. This quickly becomes a necessity after the first puzzle in the tower, yet it took a bit for me to realize that we needed to do so. I get that the lack of verbal communication is the gimmick (which was very fun, don't get me wrong), but it was clouded by the fact that it got in the way of understanding the basic objective instead of the puzzle itself and making a gameplan. Might have been a skill issue, but it wouldn't hurt to give a slight nudge just in the structuring of the rooms. It also made me realize that the game's puzzles are designed around having 4 people, so the limiting factor for solving a puzzle became the 4 smartest people in the room and the rest kind of had to sit out since only one person was needed per segment. Unfortunately, I don't think there is a solution to the 4 player problem without making jobs for each extra person in the session. [/spoiler]

End cutscene: [spoiler] The end cutscene bugged out and we don't know why. We got our first 4 to say goodbye properly, but our 5th friend bugged halfway through the rotation door and had to be pushed the remaining distance. Then, they bugged in the departing hallway and when they were SUPPOSED to be kicked by the game, their body became a corpse indicating that the end cutscene stopped working properly at all. The fps then began to drop harshly and ruined what was supposed to be a sad farewell to Big Walk for our remaining friends. [/spoiler]

[u]My overall opinion:[/u]
The main word I would use to describe this game is sentimental. It's also fun, cute, and even romantic!
One of my favorite aspects of the game is that you cannot access your own backpack or belt. You must trust other players to put a backpack or belt on you, as well as take items on and off of you. It's such a small detail, but it makes the game feel like a trust-building experience. There are similar aspects (such as trusting your friends to paint you the colors you'd like to be painted), but the backpacks and belts are my favorite.

[u]My opinion on replayability:[/u]
I began playing with one of my newer friends (I met her this year), and we spent most of our time talking about our childhoods and sharing stories. She lives in Australia, and I live in the United States, so my first playthrough was made extra special by having someone telling me what all the plants and animal sounds were, since I didn't recognize anything.
Then, I later played a different save file with my partner (someone whom I have known for about 11 years now). Since we already know one another substantially well, we spent most of our time goofing off and trying to make one another laugh. Despite neither of us having anything new to talk about, it was still fun.
The replayability of this game seems to be substantial, because those two playthroughs are already nothing alike - two different people, two completely different paths. I discovered puzzles in one playthrough that I hadn't even seen in the other.
I plan on putting together a group of friends - hopefully, the maximum amount of friends possible - and seeing where that takes us.

[u]Tips for playing:[/u]
In my humble opinion, you'll have the most fun playing this game if you keep the spirit of Big Walk in mind - just walking and talking with your friends.
It's less fun when you only focus on completing puzzles and advancing. The game is the most fun when you take your time, go slow, and open your heart up. I would recommend other players to stop playing when you get tired, bored, or frustrated, and then revisit it again when it feels the most organic to.
Stopping to smell the roses is a must for me. Sprinting is an available game mechanic, but me and my friends don't always end up using it. Sometimes it truly is just best to walk.

[u]Who I think would like/dislike this game:[/u]
If you have ADHD, then I would recommend this game to you. There's a lot of "Look! What's that over there?" moments strung along perfectly between moments of calm. It truly is like taking a walk. I can feel myself relax when I play this, but I don't get too bored too quickly. It's the opposite of the current world of endless scrolling, battle passes, and the version of the Internet that just wants to hold as much of your attention for as long as possible. The game doesn't try to trap you; it just is.
If you like fast-paced competitive games because you want to win win win, then this game might not be for you. There is no winning. Only friendship!

[u]TLDR:[/u]
Sentimental! Fun! Replayable! Relaxing!
A nice break from fast-paced life, and a great way to connect with friends on the other side of the world!

review:
Big Walk is one of my favourite games in decades. I hope you all get a chance to play it. I finished it with my group last night. If you do get to play it, play it end to end with the same people. I really feel that matters.

Here's what got me about the Big Walk: Every night I sat down to play, it didn't feel like playing multiplayer with my friends. I've done that plenty of times with these folks. It felt like being with them. Actually hanging out, the way you do when you're all in a room together. I've only ever had that from VR before, and Big Walk does it without the headset. That's what made it personal instead of just fun. I felt present with them every night. Two of the group I've never even met IRL but I write this now feeling like we have. It's weirdly beautiful in that way.

And it's so much the sum of its parts. No single moment is the game. It's all of them stacked up: the small talk, the problems you work out together, the discoveries, the little arguments about what to do next, the long stretches where you're just in there together catching up on personal life, the stupid little words and language you invent that's just between you and the group, side by side and some times very very lost from each other. I didn't feel the weight of any of that as it happened but I certainly felt it when it stopped.

And I won't spoil it other than to say the ending is just beautifully done. A real masterclass in understanding what its delivered to you and pacing it out for the right emotions to come up and be felt. All four of us shared in the same emotions at that time, and none of it was manufactured. There is no cut scene at the end. The journey was actually over. None of the other co-op games, multiplayer games, or "friendslops" we've played together have left us there. It was exactly like the last day of a big trip: everyone a little quiet, goodbyes at the airport, some sniffles, the group chat going still for a while. I woke up this morning still in it, already wanting to plan the next one. My luggage is still by the door, packed, clothes still stinking, and I want to go again.

The Walk is indeed Big.

This story is a little sad, you have been warned. So for my brothers birthday we got a bunch (10 people) of his friends together to set aside a good chunk of time to hang out. As adults this is quite a special and rare occasion. This game looked perfect, a virtual third space with simple activities to keep us engaged. The game started good, the opening area was just the right size where we were all interacting and socializing. 

After the opening area, it got huge. Each activity requires collaboration, sometimes across the map collaboration. Long story short, I ended up isolated. Tried to find my way back to others by following flairs. I was so far behind they had always left by the time I got there. The session was around 3ish hours, I spent 80% of the play session alone trying to find everyone. Got to the big map, logged off without getting a chance to say goodbye to everyone, and I am now sad.

It seems like everyone is loving this game, I am glad my experience is an outlier!

To the Devs: would have been nice to have gotten a explicit notice "All tasks require another person, be sure to stick in pairs of 2!". That could have made this situation not happen. Giving everyone a radio or having a optional toggleable world chat also would be a nice addition.

That is all, remember to treasure your friends and family!

What can I even say about this game, man...I'll start from what I personally enjoy about the gameplay itself.

1. Puzzles

I love puzzles. I always have, and the puzzles in this game range from simple and satisfying to thought provoking and  time consuming. Luckily there are more than enough puzzles in the game, and since I have yet to do the completionism route at the time of this review, any puzzle you don't like or don't understand can easily be skipped with no consequence to progression, aside from the tutorial area. The puzzle design is at its best when done with 4 people. My group played with 5, which I do not regret one bit, as having 5 of us was still amazingly enjoyable, but when you do some of these puzzles with just four of you? Its like magic.

2. Exploration

After the tutorial area, you can essentially go anywhere. There are ways to get around faster, but this game is called Big Walk for a reason. If you are bored from walking around a lot, then you need to fill that space with conversation. Its a game about walking and talking. My friends and I stayed very entertained and talked about all kinds of stuff while we explored, and it was some of the most memorable moments with them in a long time. Exploration is always more fun with friends along for the ride.

3. Proximity Chat

Yes, it is a little quiet. Yes, it does fade off at a short distance. Yes, individual volume sliders would be nice, but honestly...once I stopped trying to complain about it and just...started playing the game? It really wasn't that bad. You find Walkie Talkie's eventually, and it becomes a non-issue for the most part. I think anyone who plays with speakers instead of headphones would most likely have a much worse time, so I recommend using headphones to hear your friends better. Otherwise...just play the game. Its too good to let one thing stop you from enjoying it.

4. Progression

Personally, I wish there was more towers. I wish it was longer. All in all, without 100% completion, it took about 10-15 hours to complete the game, which is a solid completion time! I am not saying it is too short of a game, but  rather that I liked it so much that I wish there was more! More items to find, more towers to unlock, more secrets to discover....but, the length of the game as it is currently is just fine. As long as you aren't sprinting from one puzzle to the next and aren't ignoring some of the more scenic spots or cool areas, you'll spend plenty of time in the game. Its Big Walk. Not Big Speedrun. Savor it, or you'll regret it.

5. Utility

I didn't find use in some of the utility items, such as the laser pointer or binoculars, and I think part of that has to do with storage. There are only so many ways to carry something, and if you are coming to and from a puzzle, a light or key item will likely take up most of the storage you have. Personally, I wish you could put the Orbs on backpacks to not have to worry about light, and the whiteboards as well would be nice to keep on your back, since its such a cool idea to have them to communicate long distance with someone who has no walkie talkie. I still found use in most items at least once, or at least found myself wishing I had one.

-------------------------------------------------------------

Further Thoughts and Conclusion.

I've been looking forward to this game for the better part of two years. My friends and I are fans of camping and hiking, and we love playing games together. This game seemed right up our alley, and it was. We live relatively close to each other, that being within half and hour or less or each other, but ever since we moved on from high school, we just haven't been able to hang out like we used to. Not as frequently, and not to the same extent anyway. No dumb LAN parties in the media room, no excessive drinking on late nights....we're almost 30 now. We still hang out, and do other dumb sh*t like play Twilight Imperium, but to get together and play this game and just do dumb sh*t and talk about dumb sh*t while hiking and solving puzzles? I don't know, it just kind of made me realize that...even though were older, we can still find reasons to get together and have fun. To take time out of daily life and just...be guys being dudes. To that end, when we finally reached the ending, which I will not spoil...I was genuinely sad. I didn't want it to end. I didn't want them to leave...but every Big Walk has its end sooner or later, and while we'll still be coming back to this game to do 100% completion, it wont be quite the same.

Play this game with your friends. Go on a Big Walk with them before life gets messy. You won't regret it.

Despite blowing the recommended PC specs out of the water, I've been dealing with sub optimal performance as a host. On occasion, the game is very demanding on my rig for some reason, with the game dropping below 10-12 fps for several minutes. It's a cool little game. A team can finish it in 12 hours but it's a low price tag to compensate.

The proximity voice chat is the absolute core of the game, with the difficult of many puzzles entirely dependent on you not being able to talk to each other and having to rely on nonverbal communication; either gestures, movements, or various tools like laser pointers or writing. Do resist the urge to just use Discord chat or something unless someone is truly lost and you have no means of contacting each other.

On the upside, this creates a need for innovative problem-solving and a lot of memorable moments based around suddenly winding up lost, or looking for lost people, or when separate puzzle-solving teams are sharing jokes, stories, or co-ordinating their actions.

On the downside, ending up on your own for too long can be very boring and honestly quite depressing if you know everyone else is having fun without you. You can't see where people are, there's no real fast travel method to get around and check for people, you're extremely unlikely to have a map due to there only being one map item, and extremely unlikely to have a walkie talkie due to those also being very limited. You can't use two of your three possible item slots if you're alone, and you can't solve any puzzles on your own either since they all require multiple players.

Hopefully people will have walkie-talkies so you can find a nearby tower (of which there are several on the skyline) and use the radio at the top of each tower to ask the walkie-talkie bearers where the hell they are.

HOWEVER. There is a section of the game where you cannot do this. This did once result in me spending 30 minutes wandering around on my own, lost, with no map, in silence, trying to reach the location where the others were, then afterwards got to see all the shadowplay clips of how much fun everyone else was having together. So do make sure everyone is together before you go beyond the wall.

We had been sticking together so far, and as we found the walkie talkies, one of my friends, Oli, gives the second one to me. Before we realize it, he’s wondered off. Luckily, our group of three still had both walkie talkies. So I embark on the mission to find him again.

Team home base informs me that one of them, Alex, is going to come pick me up and bring me back to base.

[h1] I've been feeling Video Game Burnout™ [/h1]

Video games have been my entertainment of choice ever since I got my Gameboy Advance SP when I was four years old. I love the worlds, character's stories, gameplay, the feedback of hitting buttons. It's all a great package to unwind and relax.

However, recently I have been feeling less and less interested in playing games as entertainment or relaxation. I have instead taken video games and gaming as a means of socially interacting with people whom I have met playing video games. Call them "gaming buddies", "internet friends", whatever. But these people have changed my life for the better, and any way I can engage with them I hold very near and dear to my heart. Anything from public Minecraft servers, to co-op experiences like Deep Rock Galactic and Helldivers 2, to just meeting people in a random discord server and playing a game we both have. 

I am not a socially developed person in real life. I am awkward, shy, uncomfortable in social environments, and overly stimulated very easily. It's not easy for me to experience human social norms in a healthy, "normal" way, which has led me to escape and hide in these digital spaces. 

Big Walk, at its core, is a cooperative puzzle game for a minimum of two players to a maximum of 12 players. It's about finding a challenge area, discovering what the area's main gimmick is, how to solve it, and collecting the reward at the end. Collecting enough area rewards unlocks a way to travel and explore the world, making finding new areas and puzzles easier. 

As far as the game is concerned, that's about as objective as I can make the description of what everyone's experience will be as I can make it. Because the main draw of the game isn't the puzzles themselves, but how the puzzles are solved.

If you have seen the trailer introduction video for Big Walk, or have seen any videos online (which I don't really recommend watching if you plan on playing), you will understand that this game has proximity voice chat. This is par for the course of "this type of game" (use the word that we're all thinking), and games like Lethal Company and Peak have already done this. 

What sets Big Walk apart is that communication is the main mechanic and gameplay system underlying how the puzzles are solved. Whether it is simply talking to your teammates, using walkie-talkies or megaphones to amplify your range, using laser pointers and flashlights to relay confirmations, or signaling with your hand movements or nodding or shaking your head, the key to solving puzzles is having a clear and concise plan on how to communicate. In contrast to another fantastic co-op puzzles game, the MP campaign of Portal 2, knowing how the puzzle already works ahead of time does not impact how easy or difficult the puzzle itself is, because you will (most likely) be playing with different people who communicate differently, and that makes the challenge uniquely tailored to that person or group of people. 

What this does is pretty self explanatory, but I think it's genius. The joy found in this game is being locked in an isolated, soundproof, signal-proof cage, and having to come up with your own language to solve a problem, and the release of the confetti and the signal of a "job well done" sends serotonin to my brain in a way few games have. The wandering around, the discovery of a new object or point of interest, the uncovering of what or where to place the rewards from each puzzle, it is all absolutely fantastic, with zero instruction or handholding from the game itself. It rewards ingenuity and critical thinking, and holds the player with enough respect to figure out what the game is asking of them.

As for the incredibly small, but equally annoying minority of people complaining and moaning that there is no single-player option to play Big Walk, maybe you could unite and form a group to play amongst yourselves. Problem solved. 

To House House, the developers, thank you for making a fantastic experience that relit the fire of my love for video games. 

And to Jeb, Sonny, and Ariel, who shared this experience with me, thank you for taking a Big Walk with me. As a reminder, you guys rock.

In Big Walk, there are no threats and no HUD elements telling you where to go. Every stone that blocks your path is deliberately placed to subconsciously guide you to the places you need to go to progress, and the game believes the player can use tools in the game to find their own way. The puzzles scattered throughout the world are genuinely fun, and the mechanics they use rarely repeat. You have to gesture, talk, yell, count, sing, guide, signal, and more to complete these creative challenges.

Seeing that burst of confetti when you finally crack a puzzle is incredibly satisfying for the whole group. It makes wandering around the map feel super rewarding, especially since there's something new to solve around every corner.

Because of this deliberate design, Big Walk cannot be grouped into the now-popular genre known as "friendslop." Most well-known friendslop games like REPO, Content Warning, YapYap, and PEAK derive from Lethal Company and base their fun on randomly generated levels filled with threats that act as catalysts for fun moments. Big Walk does not do any of that, making it an absolute friend GEM. I hope other developers get inspired by the thing House House built, and we see more "walk and talk" games.

Big Walk is an amazing breath of fresh air. There is little to say about the bad things in this game because it is made fun by the one thing it tries to do well and succeeds perfectly : Friends. 

And before you think of throwing the term "friendslop" around (a term that means a game is only made to profit off of funny moments with your friends), you need to actually play the game with your friends. This game cannot be played alone and it tells you that everywhere you can look. It does not profit from funny moments because there aren't any, or at least few. It's a game that thrives because of all the different ways you find to communicate with your friends. The puzzles never really have a "forced" way to solve them, they just have a goal that makes you work together and communicate in any way you can come up with. You can group together and decide on hand signals, mimic sounds, or flash light in morse code! As long as the message gets through. 

The game gives you the tools you need to achieve your goals, but its up to you to make the decisions on how you use them. It's not designed to have crazy funny mechanics besides minor things, because it's the friends themselves that make big walk fun. It's the conversations you have, the jokes you make, and the goodbyes at the end. 

That's why big walk is amazing, every experience is completely unique even though the map is completely the same. Take the strange red circles for example, I've seen dozens of names given to them by the players because the game chooses to leave that information out. You create the adventure with your friends and that's the best part.

[h1]Big Walk, a game that focuses on the journey, not the destination.[/h1] 

     [i]Hello![/i] 👋 I have to preface this review: This is genuinely an incredible game, and if possible, you should dive right into this game completely blind. 

     If you enjoy the shrine aspect like in Nintendo's [i]Breath of The Wild[/i], or [i]Tears of The Kingdom[/i], House House's [i]Big Walk[/i] will be a joy for you and your friend(s)! 

     What started off as a [i][b]Big Walk[/b][/i] to collect those little red bulbous-thingies, (that my friend group of seven aptly dubbed "Plingus(es)"), turned into an unforgettable experience that deepened our friendship and gave us lifelong memories. 
     Whether it was our group goofing off and throwing each other off of ledges, going off and getting lost, or simply just enjoying our presences as we all watched the sun rise over the beach, we all had a fantastic time. While there were times were we had gotten split off from the main group, or someone had simply joined into the middle of the session, we made sure to all work together to find each other once again, and having fun while doing so.

     The puzzles in this game vary in difficulty and will challenge how you communicate with each other, similar to Valve's [i]Portal 2[/i]. Nothing in this game has a name or a description, so it's up to your and your friends to come up with names you can all agree upon. Some puzzles may make vocal communication impossible, requiring you to get creative with any tools you can get ahold of—or if you have none—your body.
     
      The graphics and art direction are jaw-droppingly beautiful. I played on the highest graphics setting and had a very okay experience. My framerate was very stable, hanging around ~30FPS, yet would sometime chug for several seconds. Truthfully, I wish the optimization could be a tad better for the highest settings, although you can put your graphics settings to high, and have a more stable result, while still looking great! Shores at sunset have never been so tear-inducing. The clash of the unnatural and wacky landmarks and challenges against the Australian bush offer something that can't be seen in other games. The shadows stretching from players while holding a light source are very well done. 

    There is a vast selection of tools at your disposal to play around with, even something as basic and simple as a lamp can offer a lot of long distance signaling to people around you. While I won't list everything you can get, I have no doubt you'll be content with what you'll be able to get your hands on.
(This game NEEDS a camera item though! Screenshots work well enough, but a dedicated item for it would be incredible!!!)

     I'll be very vague and sparse about the end-game, though I will say that it left me a sniffling, and blubbering mess. Never would I have thought that a game that solely involves walking and talking with your friends could leave such an emotional impact on me, and I WILL be fully completing and replaying this game again in the future. The folks over at House House truly out-did themselves, and you can feel the love and passion oozing from this. If any of them are reading this: Thank you for this incredible game.

[i]Goodbye![/i] 👋

its pretty fun, however, I really dislike the re-use of puzzles. It gives me that same feeling I had in Elden Ring, there's this big map to explore, and every location should be exciting, but when I get to the location, and I see *exact* same cat boss I fought like 10 times, or in this case, seeing a new puzzle location, being excited, and then realizing its the same tile puzzle, again, and it doesn't really require us to change our communication strategy, a couple times it was the same puzzle with a slight change, but there are a few that are just 1:1 the same, copied, which does kill some of the excitement.
 It is still fun though, and the communication is quite entertaining and novel, yet, the best and most fun part of this game, is actually a certain part where you cannot communicate with each other at all, which is interesting and something to think on. 

My only other gripe is the puzzles were all far too easy for our group of 3, there was a singular puzzle we got stuck on, and that was it, the rest were really easy and for the most part we got all of them on the first attempt. I understand it's difficult to make puzzles and have them not be frustrating, or have old PC adventure game moon logic, but some more difficult puzzles would have been nice. What a stunning little (hah) game. Big Walk is everything I wanted it to be and more and I'm so glad I was able to play it in my lifetime. If you want a chill hangout game that has fun, silly puzzles on the side, then Big Walk is the game for you.

The controls are relatively simple and the puzzles can leave you stumped but feel incredibly rewarding to complete once you do finally figure them out with not one puzzle element feeling drawn out or boring despite the reuse of them constantly across the world; it simply made me feel like I was learning how to better solve problems in the group! The music is wonderful and the sound design, whilst a tiny bit spotty when it comes to voice chat, is honestly incredible. I love being able to hear my own voice echo across a cavern... theres nothing else like it... Graphics wise it can be surprisingly demanding, especially to older devices and I had to lower the games graphics to the lowest settings just to get it to stop lagging but it didn't take away from the experience whatsoever.

I didn't have any friends to play it with at the time I purchased because they were all busy or hadn't bought the game yet so I went out on a limb and decided to play with strangers online and its honestly one of the best multiplayer experiences I've had in forever. Most people are just happy to chat and goof around inbetween challenges and it really goes to show how wonderful humanity can be in that, no matter what age we are, we all find joy in the simple things; swinging our arms around and collecting cute little doohickies to play with.

Because of this I now have some new friends I get to learn all sorts of things about! Yay!

The fact that the game forces you to work together to progress yet lets you do whatever you'd like pretty much whenever really adds to the charm of it all because you will slowly start to learn who finds what aspects of the game easier than others in your group and quickly build teams around those strengths and weaknesses to continue unlocking more world to explore.

Despite the heavy puzzle aspect, Big Walk never pressures you to do things in a certain order nor punishes you for getting things wrong or even -hell- purposefully losing the things you'd need for said puzzles; there are built in systems that make is easy for you to find lost items and pick up where you last left off from your previous session and I find it really charming how they implemented everything, especially the backpacks and belts; making those co-op exclusive is incredibly cute and at often times I find myself just giddy with the fact that every aspect of this game is built around helping one another because I feel like there's a lot of negativity around helping strangers nowadays that can lead to unnecessary hate in both the gaming sphere and in real life. Why can't we all just get along and play walking? :( There's no need for it honestly... Come. Take my hand. We will prance through the outback and get lost in the thick meadows... together....

In any case, the contrast between photorealistic scenery, the puzzles and our little guys is just so incredibly cute and I love how animated they are despite being such simple shapes. It really helps everything feel... funny. Like you can't help but laugh at the absurdity going on around you and thats probably the best thing you can take away from any play session; a good laugh.

But yes, I do be poking buttons and playing with mechanical objects like toys in real life like this, thank you for asking.

Overall, Big Walk is just a very joyful and whimsical experience I think everyone should get to enjoy and I can't wait to see what House House develops next <3

Great fun. Chill puzzle game. Don't bother if your friends won't join voice chat in the game, getting lost and having to find each other or work together is the whole point without being in a discord call the whole time.

In a very literal sense, Big Walk is a game about working together with friends to solve puzzles. The world is full of different challenges to complete, but you won't be able to solve them all by yourself. Instead, you'll have to rely on the in-game proximity chat (and some creative arm flailing) to figure it all out together.

At its core, this communication, collaboration, and "together-ness" is what Big Walk is really about. And every single design choice feels thoughtfully and purposefully designed to feed into these central ideas. You will find all sorts of helpful objects along the way, but each person can only carry one at a time, so you will have to coordinate if you want to utilize everything. Someone might find a backpack that lets them carry something else, but they'll need a friend to help them get it off of their back. Even the character customization is a social activity, as you can only change the colors of other players, not your own. When my friends and I played, we lined up single-file and asked for our desired colors as if we were ordering fast food.

The puzzles in Big Walk are all built around this framework of communication. Some puzzles spread us out so much that we couldn't hear each other speak, so we had to assign meaning to our own ridiculous movements and relay information in really fun ways. Solving puzzles felt extra satisfying because it often felt like we found our own unique way of getting to the solution, rather than working out the one "correct" way of doing things.

I could say a lot more about Big Walk, but to end on a more personal note, I had the wonderful opportunity to play this game with two different friend groups together. Seeing some of my closest friends interacting with each other for the first time was an absolute joy. While the puzzles are great, the truly special moments are just completely authentic interactions between friends. The game never feels like it's trying too hard to force any crazy situations on its own, though. It just invites everyone to go for a walk.

The Big Walk is a calm and relaxing game to play with friends. That is, if your friends actually listen! Jokes aside, this game is exactly what the title suggests: a big walking game. However, unlike a traditional "walking sim," this doesn't feel like one. This is due to the shared goal of completing the neat and unique communication puzzles scattered across the map.

Every walk has a purpose. With certain puzzles forcing you to split up, communication can become quite a challenge. Especially if you drop your walkie-talkie! As we progressed through each new challenge, we learned new tricks to use for future puzzles. By the time we completed all the challenges (including the purple ones), we had quite the toolkit of communication methods at our disposal.

(Spoiler for ending)
[spoiler]We then headed to the big orb on the far side of the island, which really put us to the test. Luckily, with our acquired knowledge, we aced the extra puzzles one after another. It was quite fun to hang out on the sofa afterward, debriefing on the puzzles and laughing about who did what.[/spoiler]

All in all, we had a blast and are sad that there are no more puzzles left to solve. To end the review, here is some extra information regarding specific categories:

* Graphics: The graphics are great, featuring good lighting and decent environment textures. The characters are customizable to your liking (unless your friends mess you up).
* Controls: I played with a controller so I could lie back and relax. It works for the most part, but for certain puzzles where more precise aim is needed, I had to switch back to mouse and keyboard.
* Gameplay: The puzzles start easy and increase in difficulty as you explore. I thought it was amazing to see that a puzzle we thought was "hard" later had an even more difficult version that truly challenged our acquired knowledge.
* Sound: The sound is great; however, the lack of sliders for ambient noise caused some minor communication issues. Overall, the ambient noise made me feel as though I were truly in the wild of the "land down under."
* Bugs: We encountered a couple of annoying bugs/issues: [spoiler]
  * Escape Room Unintended Solution: In the escape room puzzle, where after pressing four buttons you and one friend are trapped on one side while the other two are trapped on the other, there is an easy unintended solution. If you simply let someone disconnect, the walls move back up, preventing you from getting stuck. Normally, this would just reset the puzzle, but because the devs "tease" you by releasing the prize before the puzzle is officially finished, you end up completing the puzzle without actually doing the work.
  * "Big Goodbye" Ending: In the final section where you press a button and a specific colored person leaves, I encountered an issue where I tried to leave but got stuck in the gate. I had to quit the game and could not witness the ending. I actually had to use SAM (Steam Achievement Manager) to obtain the achievement. It was quite sad that I couldn't wave goodbye. [/spoiler]

I want to preface this review with the fact that when I first saw the trailers for Big Walk, I thought it was going to mostly about going from point A to B across the wilderness with a few puzzles here and there to find silly items. Instead Big Walk is much more of an open world puzzle game, and one of the best I've seen. It has a 2 player minimum requirement, but I found 3 to 4 is more fun. The entire crux of the game is communication. Every puzzle requires you to transfer information to another ant using the tools provided by the puzzle itself or found elsewhere throughout the island. It can be as simple as using a laser pointer or flare gun to direct a friend to push a button in the distance, or it can mean you have to start assigning hand signs to symbols used in the puzzle to transfer info though sound-proof glass or across great distances. But on top of all the puzzles the game itself is simply a wonderful time wandering though-out the outback with friends. I strongly recommend it. In addition everyone has their own name for the red objects required to be collected to complete the game, and my friends agreed on Donguses.
