[h1] The Walk was Big, but I Had Something Stuck in my Boot the Entire Time [/h1]

Big Walk as a concept is unique and interesting. It's less of a game and more of an [b] Online Friendship Enabler [/b] , something like VR chat - or maybe closer to the magic that can happen occasionally when friends create their own fun by ignoring the intentional rules of a game. 

[h2] The Good [/h2]
[list]
    [*]Simple puzzles 
[/list]
I see lots of complaints about the puzzles being too easy, but I think this works as a design choice. Making them too difficult could be a point of unintended friction between players. One puzzle we played had everyone separated in soundproofed rooms. Each person could only talk to one other person via intercom. If any one of us had misunderstood, we might have been stuck in a frustrating way. 
[list]
    [*] Tools
[/list]
The walkie talkies were fun. Laser pointers being visible across long distances was amusing. The flare gun causing huge gas clouds was great. The map you can find had us plotting our next objective together. 
[list]
    [*]Character design
[/list]
It's fun watching the little ants run around. The nose that moves when you speak is funny and endearing. Character customization comes early at a platform with a paintbrush for your different body segments. 

[h2] The Bad [/h2]
[list]
    [*]Proximity chat
[/list]
One of the selling points of the game. Also one of the bigger points of friction between the players and the devs. It's intentionally set up so that you cannot hear anyone who is further than a few meters away from you. They are completely silent. Far too often you will be walking to a new area and you cannot hear someone who has gone on a slightly different path than you. Some of the puzzles use prox chat in order to force you to find other ways to communicate, and this is quite fun. 
[list]
    [*] Vast, empty world
[/list]
During the design process, at some point a choice was made between a linear, focused experience, and an open world (with certain areas being soft-locked behind unlockable doors). I have to imagine that the devs wanted to encourage the kind of thing that can happen on real life hikes: you wander off from your friends for a few minutes, then come back, excited to show them something that you've found. A fossil, a funny looking bug, a face in a tree. Big Walk has puzzles, and not much else. When you find something in game, odds are it's a new puzzle. There is almost nothing of note to see that doesn't relate to the explicit progression of the game - finding the Kongs, making the keys, opening the doors. Getting lost is a sobering, boring, and rather lonely time - especially at night. 
[list]
    [*]Getting lost/separated
[/list]
The game wants you to split up. There are puzzles which require you to run off on your own, often over distances which take tens of minutes to traverse. You are also very likely to lose your teammates even when you don't intend to. Falling from a short height causes your character to be stunned for a handful of seconds, and you drop anything held in your hands. The underbrush spread over much of the map often causes you to lose your chosen equipment. Searching around for it was funny the first time, but grew very old very quickly. Hope that you're within the very small VC range when this happens, or else you lose track of people who were running ahead of you. A small delay quickly becomes a big headache.
[list]
    [*]Inventory
[/list]
Your character holds one item in their hands. At some point you will come across a backpack or two that allow a friend to place something else on your back (which you yourself cannot use without help). The progression items you need take both hands to hold. At nighttime, you will want a source of light - which uses the same space. I played with four friends at first (later five). Two held radios, one or more was often holding a Kong, one held a light source, and maybe the last person could hold one of the more interesting items. The game gives you very little opportunity to use the fun equipment like laser pointers, due to the simple math of what's needed to progress. A simple solution would be to eliminate the Kongs entirely - the puzzles themselves would unlock the key towers.

[h2] The Ugly [/h2]
[list]
    [*]Movement
[/list]
For a game called Big Walk, where the overwhelming majority of the time you will be walking... movement in this game sucks. First, the walking isn't interesting. You will be holding down the W key and doing little else. There is no double jump, no slide, no movement tech which would break up the monotony of moving through the world. Second, your character's movement is glacially slow. They might have made the world itself smaller, or offer you a temporary movement bonus for whatever reason. I understand that the intent is to provide you with ample opportunity to talk/hang out with friends, but that doesn't excuse the fact that the process of moving is boring. Third, because everyone moves at the same speed and you can't hear beyond a short distance, anything that causes you to slow down will, again, separate you from the group. Fourth, something about the environment or hitboxes is causing characters to get stuck on [b] everything [/b]. Every small rock, every slight incline... Far too much of my playtime was spent spamming the jump button attempting to wiggle off of whatever speck of dust was blocking me. 
[list]
    [*]Day/Night cycle
[/list]
The first time I saw it getting dark, I thought there would be puzzles which required a certain time of day to complete. A light shining through a window like Indiana Jones; a certain perspective which requires twilight; a dim light that is only visible in darkness. I didn't see every puzzle, but in three hours nothing of the sort appeared. 

Night itself is dark. Unbelievably dark. I suppose the devs wanted to have a player who carries the flashlight for the group, but this is problematic, again, due to the small inventories. Either you have someone who holds the light and spends the daytime holding a dead item, or the whole group can't see much of anything for half of your time playing the game. This is entertaining the first time. Every time after you end up simply waiting around until you can see again. 

[h2] A Tedious Slog [/h2]
A majority of the discussion and arguments I see about this game are between people who want it to be a fun game, and those who see it as an experience/adventure. 

"This game isn't worth $20!"
"Out of the five of us, three of us fell asleep." 
"Puzzles designed for kinder-gardeners."

Which is met with responses of: 
"The goal is to make you appreciate the space between moments."
"I had a wonderful chat with a friend I haven't seen in a long time."

I actually agree with the latter crowd. I don't think the design intent was to create an engaging game with goals and quests and deep mechanics. Big Walk is obviously intended to foster fun or intimate moments with people who bring you joy. The problem is, almost all of the mechanics actively oppose this goal. The end result is a lot of time spent by yourself, isolated due to darkness, getting lost, not being able to hear, or anything else I've listed above. I've had deep or memorable conversations with people just sitting in a Discord call, and that was free. 

If people had a wonderful time with friends in Big Walk, that's great. I don't intend to say that they're wrong. For me, I've played far better games that were far cheaper that have fostered the same sort of entertainment.

One of the most memorable and heartfelt games I've ever had the joy to play. 

Our friend group (9ish players) have played social/friend games before, but it doesn't do this game justice to put it in that category. It genuinely felt the same as one of our group holidays where we'd all go to a theme park for a weekend. It's not just about the rides (the puzzles) which are a lot of fun, it's also about the journey around the park, seeing all the cool stuff on the way, deciding what stuff the group wants to do next, waiting for the mandatory toilet break together, working out if we have everyone before moving on to the next thing, singing music stims badly on the way to the next thing (such as tequila, or the Wallace and Gromit theme tune) and the bag check of who has what with them. This game captures that wonderful feeling of simply hanging out with your mates. It has put such attention into naturally allowing those moments to happen in a way that doesn't feel forced at all. 

We now have a collection of screenshots (holiday photos) that we can all look back on after beating the game together. Thank you House House, for what is quite simply the best budget holiday I'll ever have with my friends. NOTHING BEATS A BIG WALK HOLIDAY! (Take that Jet2!)

The perfect game to just relax and chat with friends. I'd been following this game for a few years before it finally released and it gave everything I was hoping for and more. 

The gameplay, while simple, just walking and solving puzzles, gives enough to keep it engaging while leaving plenty of open time to enjoy company and whatnot, it's fun to discuss communication methods and work with your friends to deal with the puzzles, and the packs and belts helped to keep people together in a way by letting people help each other by carrying items. All of the different puzzles manage to strike a good balance, they're easy enough that you don't get too confused while also being able to pose a good challenge, there were some puzzles that left me feeling very excited about managing to figure out how they work. While there were also a couple that I found a little bit annoying to begin with, they were relatively tame to what they could have been, thankfully. 

Traversing the map seemed like it was going to be a pain to start with, lots of hills to walk around and some places long distances away from each other, but the modes of transport serve as a well balanced way to get around a lot easier, especially the gondola lifts. The trains were good if you could catch them at a good time, but if you found yourself waiting at a station for one it was usually better off to just take a... big walk.. 

The storyline(?) is neat, won't say how it ends here for spoiler reasons but it's a very cute and satisfying end, both the regular and completionist endings. 

Overall, good game, great atmosphere, fun gameplay and an all round enjoyable experience.

Wow. Just. Wow. 

It's truly something special to make a game like this. I loved the solving the various challenges and puzzles through teamwork, and I loved just sitting down at the beach and chatting for hours with my friend about the various things that came to mind. I never felt like I was rushed to keep progressing, and I never felt like a second was wasted. Even when the occasional mishap happened, I never saw it as lost time or sighed in exasperation- it was just the continued experience, and I enjoyed every moment of it. 

This game, and more specifically the experiences I shared with my friend in this game, now hold a very special place in my heart. 

To the team at House House, thank you for making this game.

And to my friend, (you know who you are-)

Even if you don't share the nostalgia though, this island's environment is wholly unforgettable, and incredibly charming (and sometimes eerie).

Beyond all that, it's a fantastic experience playing this game with friends- you might hear people call it 'friendslop', but that is a term that does this game an incredible disservice because the quality and heart thats gone into it goes far above and beyond most of the co-op titles on the market from the last decade or so.

My recommendation: Grab the people you most think that you'd enjoy doing an escape room with, especially if they're people you'd be comfortable just hanging out and vibing with, and bring them together to play this game through to completion over a few sittings. You won't regret it, I promise.

-EDIT IN LIGHT OF THE AI FIASCO-

I am strongly against AI on so many fronts, as I prefer to learn and do things on my own. I've learned to draw, to write stories, to make music, and even am starting out game development. I find it important to learn and grow in all our skills so we can teach others about what we've learned.

That being said, my review of this game does not change. Was I disappointed they had used AI? Yes. But they willingly chose to disclose such a minor thing as fixing codes that not even the developers of unity could fix. They even heavily edited that code itself so it fully worked. You know how much code that was? 10 lines of code. Games can have anywhere from thousands to 10s of thousands of code. And all that other code, that 9,990 other lines of code were all made by someone who learned to code.

It's easy for us to get upset at nondisclosure. Yes, I get it. Let ourselves be angry at that. But don't ignore the fact they created a functional, wonderful game that have made so many people grow closer to each other. At the end of the day, they did what they did, because they probably felt they didn't have any other options. And I know that's me just assuming things, but the bottom line of that is-

HouseHouse is a company. They created a game for people to enjoy, and yeah, make a profit off of it. They made a profit BECAUSE it is a good game. And guess what? Though HouseHouse is a company, that company is indeed made of people. People who put so much effort into making a functional game. They went so far as to do QnA testing for over a year. Big company don't do that now-a-days. Rather, they just have the consumer do the "bug testing" for them. I find that to be lazy. HouseHouse, however, did everything in their power to fix the bugs that arose. That, to me, shows character.

So yeah, TLDR: I hate AI, but recognize that HouseHouse did what they felt they had to do to fix a problem at the endstage of development. This doesn't change that their game made me feel immense joy.

Playing this game is almost like a test of the company you keep, if you aren't enjoying the game, then you probably need to talk with the person/people you're playing with..

The ability to explore how you please is excellent. It doesn't just completely drop you off after the tutorial, leaving you in a space very very close to a landmark to unlock and many puzzles, letting you get a feel for what you're meant to be doing on the island without holding your hand throughout the whole thing. It gives you the basic controls, a small and easy to digest tutorial, and puts you out into the rest world with almost no stops or roadblocks while you explore how you want to. Having you figure out yourself where you want to explore, using your own want to see more of the game as motivation.

The puzzles are fun. Some of them are a little to hard or tedious, but having the right person makes the journey a bit better. And only a few of them are unfun, 6 max out of the 45 puzzles in game. A lot of them were very VERY fun and silly and had be laughing. They require a LOT of teamwork to complete and it's satisfying when you're able to complete it using no words, only the movements of your silly little guy. This game is built on friendship and teamwork, you aren't even able to access your backpack without your friend putting and taking the item off it for you. Almost every button and action requires the trust and communication of your teammates, and its extremely charming to see.

This game obviously has a lot of walking, moving from place to place. But its adds to its charm, having to plan and move around the very realistic terrain. It really feels like you are almost hiking. The stark contrast with the hyper real island with the cartoony low poly puzzles and structures is blended seamlessly. Kinda dumb sounding but it is very intentional with how they modeled everything, like they do in fact stand out but not in a bad way at all. Its very sweet and cute, a very pretty looking game.

My only real gripe with the game is HOW DARK IT IS WHEN ITS NIGHTTIME. My goodness I really REALLY don't like how dark it can get. It's insanely hard to see anything in front of you and it always seems you have the most important tasks to complete when it turns night. There are very cute sphere lights scattered around the map so it is nice to look out from a high place and see all of the bright colored lights around the island, but you have to manually light each and every one of them around the map, and they are pretty sparse and only really around puzzles, not the long in-betweens you have to walk through to get from puzzle to puzzle. Having a flashlight is almost a must in exploration and with how little to no backpack space you are given it is HARD to know where you are going early game when you don't have those landmarks lit up. If you have 3+ friends playing with you, I don't see it being hard for someone to always have a flashlight in their hands, but only having one other person makes the planning and backtracking with gourds especially hard. Later on in game you have access to hip-packs and backpacks, but it still puts a strain having to dedicate a whole slot to a required flashlight when you would rather bring along a more fun object on your adventure. I am NOT sitting by a ball light every 5 minutes FOR 5 minutes like its a campfire and I'm huddling for warmth just to be able to see two feet in front of me. Every time me and my friend saw those red or orange lights, we would immediately light that sucker up because we knew they would be our only guide when it turned that harsh.. dark night time..

I give this a 9/10 rating, would highly recommend for any sized group of friends who actually enjoy each other's company <33

Played it with 3-4 friends and had a blast throughout it. The game is already good, but it gets even better thanks to those you play it with, so choose wisely!

The game's design deserves a lot of praise, it really puts your friends at the core of every action both in puzzles and while exploring. Besides the usual multiplayer-designed puzzles, many in-game mechanics help building up the narrative, making any advance a 2+ player endeavour. It's not about "relying on others", it's all about teamwork.

Even simple stuff like having an item in your backpack requires a friend to put it in/take it out, both's connections' cut out whenever 2+ people talk on the radio at the same time, you may need your friend to be the designated street lamp, holding a light buoy for everyone whenever you choose to stroll and get lost overnight. And that is such a great idea, it shows there's been a lot of care and thought out mechanics by House House's team.

The exploration may sometimes feel like a chore, but whatever you do while you traverse it is the biggest plot driver in the game. You all decided to hit the next tower, but you turn around and suddenly someone is already missing. It was nice knowing them and they'll find their way back as you carry on walking. Then there's a milestone up ahead, so you try to point at it and incorrectly (or willingly, nobody will know, I won't tell) bask everyone in the light and smoke of a flare shot at the ground. Your lost friend is sending SOS signals from the radio throughout it, but there's too much chaos to pay any attention. Then someone fell from the chairlifts into the unknown below so now it's just you two. Lastly, your friend keeps waving their arms around with the papaya (or whatever the blorbs are called) and mistakenly kicks it downhill.

"I saw another trial over there!" is a sentence that paves the way to hell.

Credit is also deserved for the really well thought, incredibly funny puzzles you can find towards the end of the game - those had us scratching our heads, trying to align the single neuron each of us had left, and it was all in all a very funny experience.

The world seems somewhat "realistic" but is filled with monochromatic buildings and markings, and your own player's body is made of 3 stacked spheres. The items are also quite simplistic in its shape and colours. While this clash in design is somewhat jarring (and I can't tell why they did so), it's goofy nonetheless, fun and simple in a very good way. Your player's gestures are also quite limited, but it's intentional and it gives so much character and expression nonetheless.

What's the best thing about this game? It'll build up memories you'll cherish.
The worst of it s that you will never be able to experience it fully again along with the joy of hearing a teapot  hitting the ceiling as your colleagues kick it around. There's little replayability after cracking a puzzle, but the world exploration will be different every time, moreso with different teams.

This game is INCREDIBLE. I was a little urked at first since I'm use to friendslop games being cheap and throwaways. This game is not that-- this is a genuine co-op game with a HUGE map and some sort of world lore to solve. Everything in the game utilizes player interaction and making sure to have fun. Some puzzles have the coolest gimmicks, like playing telephone in different rooms to your friends in order to solve the puzzles. Theres a lot of different ways to mess with eachother as well and it makes for a great experience. It's also very relaxing, you dont even have to solve puzzles in the end-- you can just use the game to chill and talk.

However, there are MAJOR CONS:

You will get stuck in every creavass you see. Step over a log? Stuck. Climbing up a rock with a tiny dent? Stuck. Sometimes other players have to come grab eachother to get unstuck. This leads into another issue-- your friends are in a conversation as you run and climb. Suddenly you're stuck-- they're running. Now you're lost. Good luck spending the next 20-30 minutes looking for them, because who knows when you'll actually find them. There are ways to find other players but because the terrain begins to look the same once you go down a mountain it is incredibly easy to get lost without the map or a compass. 

This game really needs a quick respawn reset, and a way to warp back to the base. Too many instances where people get lost including myself and even if you reload the game, you're still lost. It kills immersion and the fun immediately since you're not solving puzzles with friends, you're just mindlessly looking around playing marco-polo hoping they'll shoot a flare. 

Once they fix these bugs, the game is a genuine 5/5, maybe even co-op game of the year.

This is a beautiful game in a way I cannot explain. It is not like any other game I have played, and it doesn't try to be. It is confident in its simplicity, but that simplicity hides an inner layer of perhaps the most effortlessly charming experience a game has given me.
The puzzles are (mostly) not hard. Some are barely puzzles. But that isn't the point. The point is the time you spent doing them with someone you love. 
The long travel times from place to place make this game almost impossible to wantonly boot up for five minutes and then hop off. It wants you to find the time in your week to have fun. 
It asks you to be intentional with your friends, because friends should not be taken for granted. It reminds us that, with all the challenges of life on planet Earth, you should make time to take a big walk.

I will start by saying that the game feels cozy and has some unique and fun ways of communication. The puzzles look fun (so far), and the overall UI feel is nice. 

That being said, there are a few glaring issues that I would like to address:

The game is poorly optimized IMO. I run it on the Deck and the areas with heavy foliage dip to 20-30 fps on medium to low settings. If you play on high settings, it is running at around 30 fps everywhere. For a game that is essentially a walking simulator, this just feels unacceptable. Another issue is the lack of audio controls. The one volume slider is global. If you actually want to hear your friend, you will have to play at 100% volume and you will have to bear other extremely loud environmental noises as well...

Overall, I love the concept. It looks like a cool game that would be very fun to play in a bigger group.

In all the friend-likes, friend-based, and friend-"slop" games I have played. Big Walk will always eternally be the closest to my heart, the 11 hours of my first experience of it were so incredibly meaningful to me. I was hesitant to spend the 13 dollars on the game that I did, and because I did not hesitate, 2 of my friends and I experienced a ton of emotions together, and It sounds cheesy about a game, but I never felt genuinely angry or bored enough to quit unlike many other games in the same/similar genre such as PEAK, R.E.P.O, or Lethal Company. I felt happy throughout it all. This game is a 10/10. I'll get to the technical stuff down below

Art 11/10: I'm not an art person (just like I'm not really a steam review person), but here's this visual contrast between these simple but charming characters and potent colors compared to the more muted, and realistic outdoors in Big Walk, it creates these moments where, when I come out of a long puzzle with the abstract shapes, it feels like I'm moving between a Picasso painting and a Renaissance painting, like. unironically.

Music 10/10: The soundtrack somehow feels... rewarding through gameplay, you have to find and activate radio stations to be able to cycle through the amazing music, which fits both the grounded realistic environments and the crazy abstract places and characters. Big Walk's gameplay is heavy on communication, limiting how you talk or changing the way you communicate, and I think its amazing that (And one of my friends whom I played this game with brought this idea up to me) that a game so heavy on communication has a soundtrack heavy on acapella and voices or voice-like sounds. The music is so incredibly thoughtful and well-crafted.

Gameplay 9/10: The sole reason why this score is not a 10/10 is because the gameplay is half-puzzle and half-collect-a-thon, and the puzzles are outstanding at acting on what they intend to do to the point where me an my friends reluctantly skipped at most 2 out of the nearly endless puzzles they have, every one of them feels fresh and very few have less than 2 solutions, I would also like to bring up the fact that puzzles SCALE with the amount of players you have, so my first playthrough with 3 people will have entirely different puzzles than a gameplay with 4 or 5 or 12 people, which brings up HUGE REPLAY VALUE. The collect-a-thon aspect is where I dislike it, out of all collect-a-thon-ish (collect-a-thon-ish?) games that I've played this one limits where it's useful within gameplay really well, making the puzzles give you things... that you collect... that is how you progress the game. On one hand I don't like that the collecting things is so big (walk?) in this game, but on the other hand it strings together all the puzzles and POIs really well, I think 9/10 is both the highest score and the lowest score I can give gameplay-wise

An average of what I saw, I heard, and I did, brings this game to a PERFECT 10/10. No less, maybe... more, because aside from gameplay, like I said in the beginning, "Playing Big Walk is one of the greatest memories that I have." because I can perfectly remember every time I laughed, got annoyed at one of my friends, got confused on the puzzles, wanted to run directly into a weird structure I found, or wanted to explore the vast environment. I. love. Big. Walk. THANK YOU HOUSE HOUSE PTY LTD! THANK YOU PANIC INC! THANK YOU COMPOSERS SAM GILL AND LUKE NEHER! THANK YOU DESIGNERS STUART GILLESPIE-COOK, NICO DISSELDORP, MICHEAL MCMASTER, JACOB STRASSER! THANK YOU BIG WALK! I LOVE BIG WALK! I LOOOOOOOOOOOOOOVE BIG WAAAAAAAAAALK!

 I would compare Big Walk to something like a late night car ride, it never really matters what's on the road in front of you, you don't really need a destination. The best thing about a late night car ride is the people you're with and the stories you share. That is the best way I can describe how walking around in this game feels, and sure there are puzzles to do, but when you look back, even to the very beginning, all it ever was was just you and your friends, together. 

There is so much in this life that we take for granted, and the time with our friends is sometimes unfortunately one of those things, but this game really makes you appreciate the people you have. Through the week as I've been playing Big Walk with my friends of multiple years, it really made me realize how much I deeply care for these people and their lives. Every time I would get off, I would think to myself "How lucky am I to know all of these people" Even people I haven't seen In a while, Big Walk was the vessel in which I was able to reconnect with an older friend, and that night I had spent playing with them and my friends was one of the best nights I've had in a long time.

 In the 100% ending, when you sit around in the circle of chairs and the cards ask you to reflect on the memories you had made while playing, I didn't want to say it at the time but I was overwhelmed. Not in a bad way at all, but with just pure gratitude, there was really so much I wanted to say and I really only managed to say a few things. To be completely transparent here, I had gotten kind of choked up when the others were talking, because where really was I in that moment if not a circle of my best friends. The text on the card was right, we really did make Big Walk our own experience together, whether it had been finding unique ways to finish a puzzle, or just sitting and talking for hours about mundane things that to us, meant the world.

Coming out of this game has made me feel closer, more grateful, and just incredibly proud of the friends I experienced it with. I have truly never felt more open and comfortable with a group of people, and I truly wouldn't have rather spent my time with anyone else. I haven't just started feeling this way now that its over, to be honest the time I've spent with my friends in Big Walk has been making me think about this all week, and the thought of "How lucky am I" What really are the odds, that In this vast world of billions of people, this small group of friends would all come together from all walks of life, multiple different continents and different ages and would all meet each other through someone about 6 years back and end up right here. I've never been very religious or spectacle at all, but I just couldn't write that off as a coincidence, our paths we're drawn to cross, I fully believe that.

 As much as I've expressed this in recent times, I just can't say it enough, nobody is promised anything, nothing is truly given, and having a friend group like my own is the biggest gift and privilege I have ever had the pleasure of having. Life is as strange as it is incredible, and there is nothing more incredible than to share it with the people you love.

 Big Walk can truly be whatever you make of it, but for me, Big walk is a game about friends, bringing people together, and appreciating who you have.

Thank you House House for making a wonderful experience, and thank you to my wonderful group of friends who could've made something like this so memorable. I couldn't recommend this game enough.

This is an excellent puzzle game! 2 to 12 players for a puzzle co-op game?! I haven't had anywhere near this much fun solving co-op puzzles since Portal 2, and dare I say this is even more fun than Portal 2's co-op was?! The island is so much fun to explore, at its best it has all the excitement the Myst games have, but the puzzles are more clear and contained so it's obvious what is a puzzle (and the art direction means all the puzzles stick out from the background well) and you don't hunt for a button hidden somewhere dumb. The puzzles are largely communication based, so you'll want people you communicate well with. If there is a downside it's that you won't be able to play the game for the first time again, and so (much like Portal or the Myst series) any second time will lack the wonder of figuring out the puzzles, but since they're all varied you'll still have work solving them (unlike, for example, The Witness which is largely full of puzzles that wouldn't be much fun a second time around) and the co-op nature means you could stay silent while the new crew works through it. The art direction is incredible, the natural world contrasts with the bright playground-colored puzzles and infrastructure to the delight of exploration. The lighting and sounds make the world feel alive at any moment, and it's actually nice to sit down and watch the sun rise.
This game is 100% worth the price of entry and deserves to be added to the list of great puzzles games quite near the top!

What an absolutely incredible game! House House, the developers of Untitled Goose Game, have done it again with a game that appears minimalist but has plenty of fun and hilarity baked into it! Big Walk is a game of, well, walking. There's little to no direction whatsoever, and from there you and up to 11 other players can explore the land and uncover its secrets. 

The gist of the game is that it's filled with puzzles that you and your group try to solve together. The puzzles are well crafted with novel ideas where the difficulty may likely be just coordinating with your group. Whoever hosts the game maintains the save file and chooses the number of players (2, 3, 4+) anytime they host a game with that save file. The game world will then alter to account for the number of players, so it's seamless to start a game with multiple people and continue where you left off if more or less people are able to play next time.

My only complaint about the game would be that it's required multiplayer, so there are some that may never have an opportunity to enjoy this game, but multiplayer is what House House was going for. There is no couch co-op; however, a great feature of the game is that it is cross-platform. As of the game's release it was on sale on Switch 2, Steam, and free on PS5 with a PS+ Essentials subscription. That way I could get a copy for free with PS+ and buy it on Steam in order to co-op with my spouse in separate rooms while other friends joined the game using their platform of choice. While you can play with a minimum of 2 players, 3 or more is the sweet spot to experience more of the tools and even the chaos that could ensue with your group.

review:
I usually don't bother writing Steam reviews but having just 100%'d the game, I felt it may be warranted to write something about it. I'll aim to keep the first part of my review [b]informational,[/b] as I just feel like the game can be a bit hard to judge from the Steam page alone. The second part will include my [b]thoughts and criticism.[/b] I will avoid spoilers through out.

[b]Part 1:[/b]
For starters, I absolutely LOVED Big Walk! It's so much fun exploring, progressing and sometimes just screwing around with your friends! My entire playthrough was with a party of 3, taking 9.2 hours to see the credits and 16 hours to do everything.

Regarding party size, you're allowed 2-12 people. If you want to experience everything the game has to offer, you'll likely want to stick to a smaller party (probably 5 or less) so that you don't have others wandering off and progressing or exploring without you. If you crave chaos, silly antics and/or the social aspects, you'll have a blast with a larger group. (Probably 6 or more.)

Gameplay primarily involves traversal, one might even call it... walking (unprecedented, I know) and progressing by solving puzzles! Said progress is completely open ended! Once you leave the tutorial valley, there is no straight line to the end. You complete all objectives as you see fit in any order you want. You do not need to solve every puzzle to see the credits, only to 100% the game. There's even optional secret spots with special stuff to find, so it can be worth exploring points of interest, even if they don't involve a puzzle!

Over the course of a playthrough, you'll find a varied experience ranging from quite, slower moments while walking or watching a sunrise/sunset, big brain 5 head puzzle solutions, fits of frantic fret after losing an important item or rushing to complete a timed puzzle, arguing with your friends over where you are, what you need to do and/or where you need to go, and everything in between!

I don't think this should be a deciding factor for you, but the game has limited replay value. The entire package will be nearly the same, it's how you open it that differs. I'd be willing to play through with different friends but if you've got a small friend group, you'll likely only play through it once. That said, the Big Walk is worth the investment. Just trying to provide what I assume may be useful information.

I highly recommend Big Walk and hope that you've got a better grasp of what you'll be getting in to should you choose to buy the game. The remainder of my review will be my thoughts and criticism.

[b]Part 2:[/b]
I want to take a moment to highlight the laser pointer, as I feel it's one of the more useful and common tools. It will rarely help in solving puzzles but can be invaluable during traversal, specifically for indicating targets, signaling and uniting lost players and even non-verbal communication! It's a high value item with a low risk should it get lost.

The puzzles are what makes the game fun and interesting to me but a fair amount of them rely on sharing information using cards depicting shapes, scribbles and poses. Fortunately, they are implemented with enough diversity as to avoid feeling flat out repetitive but you will likely notice how often they come up. Additionally, the more obscure puzzles can feel a tad arduous to complete in both time and effort. However there are still plenty of unique puzzles offering novel experiences. You'll likely only have puzzle criticism if you 100% the game.

Another criticism that will likely only really matter if you're going for 100% completion but traversal is a little slow. I don't mind the lonely, contemplative moments but when you're trekking across the map looking for something you're missing or to solve a puzzle, you may start to wish you could pick up the pace.

I don't play friend slop games but even I noticed the strange lack of individual player voice adjustment. Your only volume control is the game volume. If you want your friends to be louder, the game must be louder. As of this review, they updated the game to make player voices overall louder but it's still not as good as sliders. You kinda just gotta stick close to anyone you don't want to lose.

[b]Closing thoughts:[/b]
Within the oversaturated, flavor of the week Friend Slop genre that I typically don't engage with, Big Walk is a Friend GEM that caught my eye and proved its worth. Even after the hype has died down and the funny clips stop flowing, I believe Big Walk will continue to shine as not just a Friend Gem but simply a good game. After every play session, my friends and I would comment on how much fun we were having and even if I'm still in the honeymoon phase, I think this experience will become a gaming core memory in my life. <3

My review ran rather long but if you made it to the end, I hope I was able to provide some answers and insight into any questions you may have had. It's currently 3AM, so if I made any writing mistakes, please forgive me. I just wanted to get my thoughts out while they were still fresh.

[b]TL;DR[/b]
Big Walk is my BIG game of 2026!

This year I moved out of my parents house so that my husband and I could live together and start saving for a home. I'm so happy that I get to see my husband every single day after being long distance for five years. Sadly, It hasn't been an easy transition for me since I'm extremely close with my family and suffer from constant anxiety.

Tonight I sat and played this game with my father, my brother, and my brother's friend (who's like a daughter to me). My heart hasn't been this full in so long. We didn't really talk about much, we more solved the puzzles and had fun just being in each other's company. Some parts had us laughing until our bellies hurt and our eyes filled with tears. 

This game is so worth it. If you have people you love, play this with them. <3

This game was really fun and engaging. The entire story and gameplay all felt really fleshed out and prepared. The puzzles were unique and challenging but easy enough to complete. I want more like this, please continue to do more. If you have the money get this game and play it with friends, you won't be upset.

I was following this game for a while, and was very excited for it, especially to play with my friends. However, after 100% completing the game I am rather disappointed. (Spoiler warning)

Pros:
It is a fine way to kill time if you have friends you enjoy being with.
Suitable for every type of person (except when trying to 100% percent the game, because some puzzles are rather challenging).
The lighting does look quite nice

Cons:
It doesn't run very well, sometimes fps would drop to 30 or below while seemingly nothing is happening.
It doesn't look very good, especially the ground textures which are cartoonish to say the least
The puzzles start getting very repetitive, it seemed like 90% of the puzzles are match the shapes 
For a party game 4 people already feels like too much, with some puzzles having them do next to nothing
Although it's called the big walk, there's too much walking, the trains are basically useless even before you unlock the ski-lift. Some other way to quickly go around would be nicer, like a cannon to fling friends far or something
Map design is a little boring, there could have been more meaningless mysterious objects spread around (that would satisfy the mystery tag), and the whole mystery with the ending doesn't make much sense either, it's just strange for the sake of being strange
The day/night section is useless, I had hoped for some day/night specific puzzles but there are none, so by the end of the game it just became annoying to navigate
The terrain is rather stupid to walk through, cause you can get stuck easily and some roads or paths would be nice.

Summary: If it becomes a lot cheaper it may be worth buying, but for 6 years of development it's rather disappointing.

House House say that Big Walk is mainly about two things: walking and talking.
That is clever misdirection!

Big Walk is so much more than that.
Big Walk is about solving problems together—or by yourself—helplessly trying to convince your friends that you have the solution.
Big Walk is about discovering something new because you got separated, then feeling childlike excitement when you see a flare light up the sky, guiding you back to the group.
Big Walk is getting annoyed at a friend who is helplessly trying to convince you that he has the solution.
Big Walk is waiting for the train together, getting lost in deep conversation—then falling off the train and getting lost once again.
Big Walk is finding toys that are fun to play with, only to have them ripped away when you think you need them most.

Big Walk is about connection. It's about becoming closer. It's about cooperation and synchronization. It's about being lost—and found.
It's about excitedly saying hello when seeing each other, flailing your arms in celebration when solving a puzzle, and going in for a hug as your connection deepens.
It's about slowing down, soaking in the ambience, and poignant goodbyes.

Big Walk is also a fantastically playful video game, filled with puzzles that take full advantage of its cooperative premise and the often limited ways you have of communicating.
The puzzles never overstay their welcome, nor do they have solutions we couldn't understand in the end.
I love that the game is fully diegetic, where discovery and the things in the world have this wonderfully grounded feel.

The minimalist, vibrant characters, tools, and structures create a stark contrast to the realistic, detailed environment based on a national park. It's interesting and beautiful.
The ambient sounds of nature are juxtaposed in the same way against the playful, cartoonish sound design and music.
And the music throughout the game creates such a great mood.

Truly a unique game in so many ways. I've never played a co-op game with such a strong vision and intention behind why and how it connects you, even when you're far apart.
And the ending is such a beautiful sequence, where your group becomes one in a profound way.

Update: As you can see, I've near 100%'d the game. And I think I'm going to update my review.

Is the game pleasant? Yes. Is the game fun? Sorta. Does the game respect your time? No. And here is where I decided to change my review.  When a game is overwhelmingly positive, people read the negative reviews.  I think people need to know *why* this game might not be for you. And/or **how** this game might not be for you.

!!! SPOILERS AHEAD !!!
There are 5+ puzzles in the game in working memory that just don't respect your time - and I know there's more.

* There's a "puzzle" where you sit in a room for 5 minutes.
* There's another "puzzle" where you sit in a room for **30** minutes. My friend and I literally just went off to play Slay the Spire instead. We'd already done all this work, "how dare you" force us to just ... sit around.
* There's the golf puzzle - first time, cute. Second time? All the way across the map? Less cute.
* There's another one of those "get the egg timer across a large span". Those are fine; but then, if you fail, you have to jump off a cliff, then swim to shore, then walk ALL THE WAY BACK to the puzzle, which is at the top of said cliff. Several puzzles expect you to have more than 2 people. This game becomes very unpleasant with 2 people. For some of the puzzles, Discord becomes a necessity because you literally can't carry enough items to communicate in-game to a necessary level.

So is it fun? You might enjoy it, genuinely. There were some good times in it. I bet it's **WAY** better with a larger group of friends - maybe 4 or like .... 6+. 2? Use Discord. Don't waste your time 100%ing it.

This game was so masterfully crafted, so artistically inspired, so creativity oriented that it sparked a debate between me and my friends about what is friendslop, and why this game definitely does NOT qualify.

Some quoted supreme court cases, specifically the line "I don't know how to define pornography, but I know it when I see it". Others compared to what you could call "genre-defining" friendslop games, contrasting where the enjoyment comes from and the deeper mechanics within. Me? I thought about the boundaries of a game, whether it's meant to be replayed, or if there's a distinct end.

Big Walk is a game where you drop in, learn the controls, and that's all you get; everything else after that is up to you and your intuition. Everything you do after that is up to you and the friends you brought with you. Now, does that follow along the lines of friendslop? Where the primary enjoyment you get is derived from your friends? Not at all. Big Walk is no more friendslop than putting together a jigsaw puzzle is. Each puzzle is designed in such a way to evoke different perspectives and ideas to solving it while also having one distinct solve where all the pieces fit together just right.

Big Walk is great because it makes you and your friends unwittingly learn more about how each other's take in and process information. Conversely, the downtime between puzzles does the complete opposite, and gives you a chance to ask a buddy what they did today, how that date went, how'd they did on that test, et cetera. It bridges the gap between the "gaming mind" and the "personal mind"; its easy to lock in on the game and not talk about life with your friends, but Big Walk acively works against this, giving you ample time for both.

The game may be short, but the puzzles are fantastic from the outset to the finale. Sixteen hours is what it took for me and my buddies to finish it, but I will definitely cherish those 16 hours together. Big Walk is a fantastic game if you're looking to spend some time and maybe "reconnect" with the homies. I can't think of another game like it out there today. It's relaxing, it's silly, it's moving, and it's ultimately one of my favourite games I've played this year.

I highly recommend you pick it up.

Big walk is a beautiful game with one purpose and one goal: communicating with your friends and having fun. It achieves this perfectly and let's you play at your own pace. The only tutorial is at the very beginning, and that just covers the controls, everything else is up to you. So far, exploring the world has been a blast and the puzzles have felt very well ranged in their difficulty.

I am playing with my girlfriend only, so I can only speak for the 2 player mode. I imagine a bigger lobby with more people could be a bit more hectic and difficult, but also more challenging in a fun way. If you've been enjoying the recent wave of friend games that have come out the past few years, you will probably also enjoy this one. However, the thought and feeling that has gone into making Big Walk feels a lot different from games like Peak, Lethal Company, and REPO. They really want to put the emphasis of the game on players themselves, and have them create the fun inadvertently by simply talking and working with their friends. So, unless you're the really annoying friend people can't stand being around for more than 10 minutes at a time, I'm sure it will be a grand ol time.

Also, thank you devs for putting in a feature that keeps players bodies around after disconnecting (as long as the host keeps the game open). My GF lost power after *just* getting to a button on a long walk where I had to stay at a telescope with another button. I thought the game was going to reset her, but, thankfully, her body stayed put and she was right back where she was standing before when she DC'd and didn't have to do the walk again.

Edit: Who cares if they used AI for 10 lines of code to fix a bug they AND A UNITY ENGINEER couldn't figure out. It didn't replace anyone and was used as a last resort. I am supremely anti-AI, mainly in art and media generation, but this is a case of it being used properly.

Frankly (and my names not Frank), this game is boring - and not the usual boring game that can be covered up with the Redditor label of "cozy." While there is not an ounce of hate in this review for the developers, the game feels lazy. I see their vision for a slow-pace game with your friends to "talk it out" and "enjoy the slow moments" and all that, but in execution its a mundane walking slog of easy puzzles and simple (but somehow annoying) mechanics. Every time I completed one of these puzzles it felt like it was designed for a sickly, simpleminded child who would keel over dead if their turtle walked too quickly in their enclosure. 

The graphics are fine I guess - the best part of this game is the unique style of the characters - but the entire environment felt like it was built with unreal engine generic template world tools in a high school game dev jam. The night portions (marketed as a fun opportunity to turn the game into a rescue party simulator) were just annoying and boring. it doesn't matter if you get lost or separated from your friends because you have to stand 3 feet away from them in order to hear them anyway. Every tool had a single worthless gimmick, and the whole game feels like it was designed for a 5 hour livestream with just enough stimulus for the streamer to overreact or formulate a meek observational joke with their buddies.

It's not that deep - so much so that Its a waste of time and money. Your life could be spent on a game that feels like it was made with some effort instead of single textured baby's-first-building block puzzles. Overall, the whole game feels like a sunk cost fallacy that made me question if it was designed to be some kind of social marketing experiment to see how little they could put in a game for the highest possible price.

I followed this along with my friends who were hyped for it and I kind of got the wrong impressions from the trailers. I was expecting an open-world version of Human Fall Flat where me and my friends could solve fun puzzles with downtime to talk inbetween. Unfortunately, that expectation was shattered pretty quickly.

The puzzles are very simple and linear without any sort of extra creative approaches to solve them (though I did appreciate their dedication to always requiring a friend to fully complete.) The open world, while sometimes pretty, didn't really provide much conversational material inbetween puzzles - something like interesting natural landmarks or art installations would have been cool, but a lot of our time as a group was spent silent after we exhausted regular daily things to talk about, and I don't see that being a problem specific to the friend group I played with.

I think a particular peeve I had with it was how it seems to forego QoL features in favor of the immersive "coziness". There were lots of points where we found interesting tools or objects we wanted to hold onto and play with, but our hands were full with the gourds you get for completing puzzles that you have to lug around until you can physically turn them in. There wasn't really a cohesive way to keep track of our progress, and that was only worsened by the aforementioned lack of landmarks or anything else to naturally track your location without slapping on a minimap GUI. With the environment combined with the low-poly duck models I sometimes felt like I was in that "Mario and the deer in Unreal Engine" image people use to make fun of the "WHAT IF WE MADE THIS AAA?" crowd. 

I think this game feels like an overcorrection to the complaints lodged against the "friendslop" genre of games. People often criticized these games for being so frenetic and focusing on getting clip-worthy moments that they forego more genuine and tender human connection you'd expect in a group experience. While Big Walk does away with those components, it also throws away many of the dynamic features and QoL that made those games fun to return to and hop into with your friends at a moment's notice. 

I can see the appeal of wanting a slower game where you can have more relaxed conversations, but any game can be a vector for that - one of the deepest conversations I've had with a friend group was at 3 am in Fortnite Zero Build while Spider-man swinging around and making our skins hit booty twerk emotes on eachother. I don't see a reason to play just for the puzzles and unless your group specifically needs an environment like this to let loose, I don't see the point of hopping in it compared to other multiplayer games. But everyone and their friends are different, so I can't say my experience is one-size-fits-all.

This has been my most anticipated game since it was announced in 2023. Big Walk is an all-in-one personality test, relationship tester, and teambuilding exercise wrapped in a co-op open world game where you vibe with your friends and solve puzzles. On the outside, it's an easy game with no real stakes and clear goals presented to you and your pals to discover at your own pace. At its core is an experience of self-discovery and a litmus test to who your real friends are. Time after time, with every session played, I found myself trusting people I was not as close to and getting frustrated with the people I thought I knew. 
The puzzles are simple and require all parties to observe and discuss before tackling them together. But what if one or two of your friends don't want to do puzzles? What if they've decided this puzzle isn't worth their time and see a "better one?" What if they sit down and refuse to participate while you work around them? What if you set the game to 4+ players and your 4th and 5th players disappear without a trace, and make the real game about finding them as they run to anywhere with a radio signal to taunt you over the walkie-talkie that you won't find them, thus rendering most puzzles unsolvable without the required number of people? Through all this, everyone has to witness how awful and commanding you are. You sulk through times you aren't even playing the game because this was the game you were looking forward to the most and all you do is throw fits when someone is "ruining" the game experience for you. You, the tyrant, have to deal with the consequences of your actions and realize you are not a good person.
Those moments you spend with the "real" friends you have are some of the best you'll ever have. Solving some of the hardest challenges the game has to offer with someone you trust, understand, and know will see it through to the end has to be the most satisfying accomplishment there is. [h1]A Walk Too Long[/h1]

I've been following Big Walk ever since Geoff Keighley once again trolled us into thinking this was Silksong when it was announced many years ago. This game should never even be in the conversation for a GOTY nomination.

[h3]Open World and Exploration[/h3]

Why is this game open world? That's easily the biggest problem of the game. Big Walk being an open-world game has absolutely no positive effect on the experience. Instead, it turns the whole adventure into a complete slog. If you are going to take inspiration from The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and make an open-world puzzle exploration game, you have to make the walking between puzzles interesting and fun. You also have to provide actual challenges between them.

Instead, the biggest challenge during traversal is your character constantly colliding with tree branches and little rocks, which gets very annoying. The rest of the time, you are just holding W mindlessly until you reach the next puzzle. I don't want to be chatting with my friends in your needlessly huge, empty and extremely boring open world. I can do that any other time. I want to solve puzzles, go on an interesting adventure with my friend and explore. What am I supposed to talk about in this lifeless world? Real-life issues? There aren't even animals in this huge world, lmao.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3782108232

The traversal options are terrible as well. Both the cable car and the train have to be some of the most useless vehicles I have ever used in a game. You're better off sprinting than riding any vehicle and that's not a joke. The map you're carrying should also show the puzzles you've already completed.

[h3]Puzzle Design[/h3]

The game itself is very easy. Once you've completed around five puzzles, you've already seen almost everything the game has to offer challenge-wise. It gets even funnier when the final boss-like puzzles are actually easier than many of the earlier ones.

Don't get me wrong, we had fun with some of the puzzles. But about half of them are either more of the same or extremely similar. The key mechanic that you repeat around five times is a good example. It was fun the first time, but why not evolve it into something more interesting later on? Nope.

There are also some genuinely bad puzzles. One literally asks you to sit in a room for five straight minutes. (I even heard there's another one that lasts around thirty minutes.) Another is basically a fetch quest where you have to find twenty tiny objects scattered around the area and randomly place them into a wall.

[h3]Audio and Atmosphere[/h3]

There is basically no music. Not even while riding the train or the cable car. If you want music, you have to carry a music player with you. The problem is, you also have to carry items that actually matter for puzzles, so nobody ends up carrying the music player. We probably listened to music for less than two minutes during our 10+ hour playthrough. The rest of the adventure is just silence and footsteps. Another bad decision by the developers. Didn't you guys learn anything from Death Stranding?

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3782108347

The day and night cycle is also completely pointless and honestly annoying. There is no reason for it to exist because it adds nothing to the game's design. Instead, it becomes frustrating because nights arrive quickly, visibility becomes terrible, exploration slows down, and it simply wastes your time.

[h3]Graphics and Optimization[/h3]

They clearly aimed for photorealistic visuals, but the render distance is terrible. Everything close to you looks decent, but anything at medium or long distance looks awful. 

The game should look much better considering how badly it runs.
Why is there no upscaling or frame generation? You guys seem lazy when it comes to optimization. Those technologies exist exactly for games like this. To sum it up, technically, the game both looks and runs like ass.

[h3]Final Thoughts[/h3]

The We Were Here series easily clears this game as a coop puzzle experience. Even if Big Walk had been a linear puzzle game, We Were Here would still have been the much better experience. But with this nonsensical semi-open-world design, and many other issues it's not even close.

I only played with 2 people total, and the amount of people you have can vary the enjoyment from this game IMMENSELY, so my review does not speak for 3 or more people AT ALL.

The game starts off as a little fun exploration and puzzle adventure, but a few pain points stick out: Lack of storage, lack of direction, and traversal. The lack of direction is the point, but until you get your bearings it can be a tad confusing. You need to carry important things, but you won't know what exactly is important, or where to carry them - this leads to the next point. The lack of storage will be a constant source of frustration. There's a bunch of cool gadgets that are completely worthless the moment you need to carry something important. This gets addressed but it takes either time or luck. The traversal has no solution. The environment and the rocks can be finnicky to get around, and they stay that way until the end of the game. The day/night cycle is also a huge source of annoyance. Sometimes, you don't have a light (probably because you couldn't afford to carry one) and have to wait out the total darkness. Not a huge deal, but annoying at times and much worse in the early game.

This game is true to its name in that there is a lot of walking. There is no way around it. You will be holding forward and doing nothing else, often. Even once you've figured out the map, you must walk. When you're still exploring this is fun because you might stumble upon a new puzzle! When you've done a bunch of the puzzles, it's not as fun. This game is very chill and relaxing. The puzzles range from literally nothing to fun brain-teasing teamwork challenges. I've heard many people mention that this game would be fun with public lobbies or strangers, and I absolutely agree. I also think that this game has huge horror potential, oddly enough.

It's a game. It's an adventure! It's a team building exercise. It's an experiment. It's an artistic vision, and I respect that! It's.. a lot of walking and doing nothing, if I'm being honest. But when you actually DO things, it's enjoyable. It's not friendslop, it has a goal and some forms of progression that do feel meaningful. I got about 8 hours out of it and might get a few more. If that justifies the price point for you and you have at least one friend to play with, this is worth giving a shot.

This was a much-anticipated game of mine since I first witnessed the very first trailer. I ended up getting unbelievable FOMO due to the fact that one of my closest friends got around to playing the game before me. Luckily, the changes to the game from 4 players to 2 players was substantial enough to offer me and my friend a unique enough experience to keep both of us engaged. The puzzles are a mixed bag and reception will greatly vary from person-to-person. In my opinion, some of the puzzles were genuinely challenging and required some out-of-the-box thinking to solve--which I liked. Other puzzles, such as the telescope ones, were a little bit tedious. A handful of them also gave me and my friend a laugh which is always nice. This game is also surprisingly pretty! The contrast between the realistic environment and the bouncy castle-esque structures you see everywhere is kind of charming. 

This is about where the pros end, though. I will say that the terrain can be quite bothersome to traverse at times. Areas with a lot of small rocks felt choppy and cumbersome. I found myself jumping around the map a lot like I was playing Minecraft or something like that. The darkness during the nighttime is navigable, but with fewer than 4 players it can be a little bit of a hassle to have to carry a light around at all times, especially since the day and night cycle is so rapid. Having a low player count also creates a more intimate experience that kind of muddies the tools that the game gives you to find each other again. The flares at each of the towers were only useful on one occasion and there wasn't really an incentive to split up at all. The game is definitely a more enjoyable experience with 4 to 6 players that you know very well.

It's hard to describe what Big Walk is about. You could say it's a puzzle game or that it's an open world adventure, and you'd be correct; but there's something else. Big Walk isn't just a game, it's an experience. For you, and everyone else that you choose to walk with. I thought this game would be a simple game that we play once and never again. How wrong I was... I can safely say that Big Walk has made a Big Impression on me, and I will play it again and again in the future.

[h2]The repetition's the point[/h2]
Big Walk is a game that asks you to get to know your friends a bit.
The way they talk, the way they think, the way they move through the world.

[b][i][u]As with all games of this nature, it's best to go in blind.[/u][/i][/b] That said, vague reassurances aren't for everyone, so, to try and give some detail to the mechanics at play: Big Walk asks you to complete puzzles with your party, often using a common set of symbols. Not always, but frequently. Sometimes it's a trust exercise across an obstacle course, sometimes it's coordination over radio, sometimes it's a scavenger hunt. Most frequently though, there's information in a locked room, and that information has to leave the room without opening its door to the outside. Can you tell your friends what you see while you're in there? A reset or two with some discussion on strategy may have been required, but they eventually understood you. It was enough to pass.

Now, can you do it again?

Can you do it at a great distance?
Can you do it through interpretive dance?
Can you do it with a laser pointer?
Can you do it via undirected binary input?
Can you do it if they can't hear you?
Can you do it if they can't see you?

And when you're finally stripped of all the tools you've amassed and your ability to provide context, can you trust that your friend knows what you're trying to say? Can you trust that you understand them in turn? You've come all this way, after all.

Some of my favorite parts are when you get lost and have to figure out how to find the others in the pitch black while having no flashlight and no map. The puzzles are fantastic, and creative. There were a few puzzles where we had to start it, realize what we had to do, then cancel it and make a plan on how to solve it. The downtime is especially good in my opinion. My friend claimed the conversations can happen any game, but I think Big Walk does a great job at encouraging you to fill dull or empty moments with conversations. The little rubber duck characters are adorable, emoting with your arms is very expressive if used correctly.

As for my one minor complaint: Carrying the puzzle rewards ("plumbobs" as me and my friends call them) back to the towers can be a little hard, especially because you typically have to 'sacrifice' or leave behind equipment items to have room for the "plumbobs". There is a little bit that can help with this, especially the [spoiler]carrying case that is underneath the blue balloon[/spoiler]. I *think* the devs wanted to encourage you to not get attached to your items, and to grab new ones as you walk.... bigly.....

My suggestion is simple: Make something like Media Player in GMod so we can host little movie nights inside of big walk. Or even just uploading mp4s, anything. I would LOVE to be able to set up a little theater and watch videos with my friends while we chatter as strange rubber creatures.

[h1] Big Walk was Big Fun [/h1]

First, to clear any misunderstanding, this game is NOT a friendslop, imo. While I don't necessarily think the term is outright derogatory, I feel it dramatically undersells what this game is and lumps it into a category many may perceive as lazy or derivative. 

Naturally, any game you play with friends (ones I assume you like, that is) is going to have a bump to the enjoyability meter even if the game is lacking in other ways, but I can confidently say the game on totally its own merits warrants all of the praise it has been receiving and then some. It's an excellent co-op puzzle game.

While I'm still not 100% finished with the game, I have completed the main progression of things and only have loose ends to clean up.

I absolutely loved my time walking, shouting, falling, getting lost, shooting, and interpretive dancing through the unexpectedly gorgeous world. The world design and audio really elevated an already great time. Beautiful sunsetting vistas, the low roar of a moving train, waves crashing on the shore - the game truly caught me off guard with how striking (and comforting) it was. Felt like I really was on a hiking trip with my buds.

The puzzles themselves ranged from incredibly simple to very clever but never anything too difficult to figure out after a few moments thinking it through. I won't spoil it, but the final set of puzzles (you'll know it when you're there) was probably my favorite moment of the entire game. It's a culmination and final test of your teamwork abilities and I loved the callbacks to previous puzzles we had encountered on our journey up to that point.

My only slight negative would be the inability to control individual player's volumes. However, there is a mod out there that completely fixes that issue (Big Voice) that I highly recommend. 

House House has made a pure treat and I could not recommend it more if you have the friends to experience it with.

Updated Review: Post main game completion.

I love this game. Genuinely, fully, love this game. Playing it for the first time brings a similar sense of wonder and sanctity one would feel playing Minecraft for the first time. It's on that level of wonder to me.

The environment is beautiful. The simplistic colorful style of the puzzle buildings in combination with the realistic ecology is something I've not seen before, and it's executed incredibly. The detail within the plants really strikes a chord in me. They look like [and probably actually are!] real species. It seems small, but in a game about running around outside and goofing off, I think it makes a huge difference in how nostalgic it can feel. Maybe it's because I grew up on a coastal region, but this felt like childhood to me. They could have easily made this generic fantasy island beach world and have been fine, but they didn't, and I'm incredibly thankful for it. 

Performance wise, I was able to get away with half resolution and medium graphics. I'm really glad that's an option because I actually like how stuff looks on half res, and being able to see real-time shadows was super cool.  The game chugs a bit at first, but once you're playing it levels off because it's not loading anything new. I'd say I was at or above a comfortable 40 frames for the entirety of my gameplay, save one or two drops. 

The game wasn't really buggy at all, though on my first playthrough my group did accidently 'sequence' break it by getting into an unintended area [with the power of teamwork!], but it didn't break anything. We just came across a puzzle we  didn't really know how to do yet and got a bit confused. We had to go back into the 'tutorial' area and complete it another time because we never actually did that. Kind of a positive, though. There aren't any invisible walls [aside from the ones out in the ocean, which are reasonable] preventing you from getting places. If you want to stack everyone on top of one another to climb stuff you aren't meant to, you can. I appreciate that.

As for everything else... I need more time to think of just how deeply this game effected me. I feel sad having completed it because I'll never get to experience it for the first time again! But there's still more to do, and my friends and I are already thinking of different challenges we can try, and it's able to be replayed to a pretty good extent. 

I'd love to, at some point in the future, see a dlc for this game with more difficult puzzles. Even the higher difficulty area was relatively easy for my group. I completely understand why they are the way they are, and it's SO fun, but I would really love to see my group really struggle on a challenge. We only really struggled on The Button One [and not even the difficult edition of that one, somehow.].

There are so many small details of this game that I love. I would like to write more about it someday. It's touched my soul in an unexpected way. I love you Big Walk.

Played through to the "Standard" ending with my wife. We had fun playing through, and found quite a few puzzles pushed us to "communicate" in the game in unique or interesting ways. The game will test your ability to transmit and interpret information in a number of unique ways, usually with limitations about who has access to different parts of information. Can you pass information to others when you cannot see each other, when only one person can talk, when only one can see at all, or when the tools available are asynchronous? Can you coordinate when you're in different rooms? In different buildings? In completely different parts of the map?

Some particular highlights that we were both laughing about after:
-My wife rapidly slamming her arm in to a soundproof glass pane to try and get me to look at a specific button on the other side
-Us both "waving"/flailing our arms at each other when anything was successful
-"It sounds like it belongs in dubstep" being met with *wildly enthusiastic* flailing
-The "Emotional Support" kettle

The map itself is both interesting to explore, and is filled with a number of visible landmarks to help with navigation. Unsurprisingly in a game based around communication, we ended up having a lot of nicknames for areas, like "sportsball", "green cup", "MONOLITH", or "Fake Moon" - in my opinion, a good sign that they're visually distinct, prominent, and easily referenced in useful ways.

Above and beyond asking us to solve a number of interesting puzzles, I feel this was a good "diagnostic tool" for getting us to reassess a number of fundamental assumptions we were both making with our communication, which was a surprising outcome!

For both of us, there was only one recurring complaint - movement feels just a bit too slow. For us, it felt like too much time is spent on traversal between puzzles, instead of on the puzzles themselves. This isn't limited to walking - we never used some of the things that the puzzles unlock, because they were so slow. Yes, the game is called "the big walk", but with a map so full of interesting puzzles, we wanted to spend more of our time *doing the puzzles* and not just getting to them.

How each group walks through the island in a different way. How each group tackles the same puzzles with sometimes vastly different approaches. The ability to find things that you've missed twice or thrice over just because someone took a different path for fun.

Really weird and really wonderful genre-defining team-building experience!
However, be warned: this is much more of a relaxed co-operative adventure than it is a serious puzzler like Myst. 
If your crew are experienced puzzleheads expecting to be challenged, this might disappoint you quite a bit.

I think it's best to be honest and say that most of the puzzles are really teamwork challenges: you have to figure out how to coordinate around physical barriers, missing information, or restrictions on communication. 
It's not often you encounter something genuinely obtuse that needs thinking and planning to figure out in advance.
However, if you're something like, say, an MMO raider, a Destiny player, then Big Walk would be a great fit.

Best you have friends you like to play and even work with, especially if they're friends who you can schedule time to play together with consistently: this is DEFINITELY meant for one long playthrough, not replay value. So far, we haven't encountered anything that suggests grand headscratchers or easter eggs.
My group intends to 100% every puzzle, and so far we're 15 hours in and still have a ways left to go.

It's a puzzle game at the level of [i]Portal 2[/i], it's a social hangout better than [i]VRChat[/i], it's a walking sim as densely immersive and beautiful as [i]Death Stranding[/i]. The sublime and special thing about [i]Big Walk[/i] is that it is all of these things without ever feeling like it's [i]trying[/i] to be. It's rare to witness a project this effortlessly cohesive. It's a game of journeys big and small: of finding lost items, of wrangling people together from the ends of the earth to solve a puzzle, of splitting back up, of meeting back up, completely unplanned, of regaling the group with tales of the strange and wild things you saw, and what they could mean, and how you could tackle them. Of being lost and found. 

Simply: This is a game tuned firmly towards simple joy. There is a direct line of communication between the developer and player. There's no story or lore and there doesn't need to be. Wade into the iron-rich waters and drink deep of the splendor and majesty of Aussie bush and Fischer-Price-brutalist architecture; experience life on both sides of the soundproof glass, the chirping roar of the wilderness and the stoic silence of the room. It's Babylon. This is the psychic effect video games were meant to have and I never want to hear anyone say the word "content" ever again.
