Going into Big Walk, I honestly wasn't sure what to expect. I was half-expecting another one of those “friend slop” games that is fun for a few hours because you're playing with friends, but doesn't necessarily have much substance on its own.

I am very happy to say that I was completely wrong.

Big Walk is genuinely one of the most thoughtfully crafted co-op games I've played in a while. Everything feels intentional, from the sound design and little musical moments to the puzzles, environments, atmosphere, and overall ambiance of its strange little world. You slowly find yourself becoming immersed in the journey rather than constantly thinking about completing objectives or beating the game.

And that's probably one of my favorite things about it.

The game really encourages you to enjoy the journey with your friends, rather than stressing about getting to the end. You can get as much or as little done as you want at any given time. There is plenty of room to mess around and create your own chaos, but the chaos isn't punishing and it doesn't ruin the experience. It's surprisingly relaxing.

Communication is also a huge part of the game. Not just talking to your friends, but communicating through the environment and using items from a distance. You quickly realize that actually coordinating with the people you're playing with can make a huge difference. In a way you begin forming your own "language" with your friends.

I've also seen quite a few complaints about the voice chat, and I do understand where those came from. Early on, there were definitely some issues with the voice settings. Sometimes you could be standing directly in front of a friend and still struggle to hear them. However, the developers addressed this very quickly, and the voice chat is much better now. 


I recently finished the game with my friends, We still have plenty of gameplay and a lot to accomplish!

I really hope the developers continue expanding Big Walk. I'd love to see another map or additional areas. There's something about this game that feels like it has so much potential for more adventures.

And for anyone wondering about Big Walk because they enjoyed...or didn't enjoy PEAK: this isn't just PEAK with a different coat of paint. There are definitely similarities in the sense that you're surviving and progressing alongside your friends, and teamwork makes things much easier, but Big Walk is significantly more laid-back. You have much more room to simply absorb the world, explore, talk, mess around, and enjoy being with your friends without everything constantly descending into disaster.

And honestly, that was refreshing.

I went into Big Walk expecting something that might be amusing for a little while.

Instead, I got a genuinely charming, relaxing, well-crafted co-op experience that I absolutely loved.

I highly recommend this game!!

The concept behind Big Walk is actually extremely simple: grab at least one friend and walk around the area to keep finding small buildings or structures where you can solve a puzzle. As a reward, you always get a pearlike object that you need to reach new areas on the map.

The game adapts the puzzles based on the number of players. So you can solve every puzzle as a pair, and there arent any puzzles that require a specific number of players. However, you always need at least two players. As far as I have seen, playing solo isnt possible.

It is a stressfree coop game that you can tackle at your own pace. Many puzzles are designed with voice chat in mind, but the game has a very well implemented text chat system that allows everything to be "simulated". So voice chat is by no means a prerequisite, and you can play flawlessly using the ingame text chat.

The only important thing is that you dont cheat by using voice/text chat via Discord, for example. The game uses proximity chat, and you will be locked in soundproof rooms, for instance, and will then have to communicate via gestures or similar methods.

Using 3rd party methods to communicate would render most of the puzzles completely pointless, and you would only be spoiling the fun for yourself.

I'd like to use the walkie talkie more in 2-person co-op but with the amount of items we need to carry it's not reasonable to sacrifice one of our 2-4 item slots between us.

Fun, silly and super chill! Felt like this was specifically made for people who love wandering and exploring with no stakes or danger, finding random things in the wild and solving puzzles—PEOPLE LIKE ME. And of course the best thing is you're doing all of that with friends.

Especially love how puzzles work in this game. There's not always a "right" way to solve them and while the puzzles themselves are usually simple, we've found some super creative ways to communicate, which—who knew there were so many ways you can communicate with each other?? Plus the island is HUGE and the devs put a lot of thought into all the things you can do just in case you get lost or separated.

Although this game is definitely not for everyone. I've seen some comments in places like reddit and twitter asking where the matchmaking was (lol) and trying to create sessions with strangers, which....this is NOT that kind of game and defeats the whole point. This is ALL about the person you play it with. It was made to be played with friends and people you're close to (I do understand that this is trending at the moment and some people just want to play it because a lot of people are playing it a the mo). EDIT: I have seen tons of people on forums set up rooms to play with strangers and it seems like people have been able to bond that way, so honestly good for them! But I do still think the devs' sentiment was to play with those you know because they just recently patched the game so that setting up a password for a session was required now haha.

And unfortunately I have to comment about the proximity chat being super quiet and not having adjustment settings, but there's been a slight improvement (at least in the volume) and it's better-sounding than day one. Hoping the devs can implement those changes soon for newer players. But in the meantime, I'd still highly recommend this game! It does suck that after you finish it there isn't much replayability (although this game does adapt the puzzles depending on how many players and I've done two different sessions so far), but it's still a beautiful one-time experience.

review:
Well, after a 100% run and several side group runs all I can say is: what a bloody delight. A wonderful blend of haphazardly orienteering around a big treasure island, and trying to clack the braincells together simple-but-fun co-operative puzzles with your pals. In such a fast, busy world where we've all moved so far away from each other, it made me remember the most important thing: I f**king love hanging out my idiot friends. 

There were so many little moments where I sat back and just realised this was what it's all about. Firing a flare when I got lost, and feeling the excitement when I finally heard my friends' voices bumbling over the hill towards me. Sitting on a beach watching our 90th sunset to that one soundtrack we loved. Waiting for ages at a train station because the red train is our favourite and we want any excuse to ride it. Big Walk is a great way to grab a bunch of people you love, and find a thousand new ways to love them.

To think that such a tender, pure, joyful experience could come out of the Bastard Goose devs is a real credit to how well the guys at House House have mastered the simple art of whimsy. Made me laugh. Made me cry. Made me feel a nostalgic funny warmth I haven't felt since I beeped at my first companion in 'Journey' back in 2012 and they booped back. Might genuinely be my GOTY.

I've enjoyed my time with Big Walk so far, the puzzles are fun and intuitive, you can see the care put into crafting them with their solutions and how they can be solved uniquely depending on your friend group. The environment is calming and the ambiance is great!

However, I do have some issues:

1) You cannot access the backpack that has been put on you. 

This issue came to light quickly when playing Big Walk. the inability to access your own inventory for necessary items is a rather odd design choice. I understand this is meant to bolster sticking together as a team, but it ends up feeling rather strange and uncomfortable that you are limited in this way, especially when you inevitably get separated from your friends in this massive open world. 

The whole inventory system also feels limited by a "one item at a time" system. Oddly enough, the game PEAK (which this game has a bundle with) seems to strive in it's inventory management system, having a removable backpack that allows players and teammates to access items being carried. I feel Big Walk would benefit from taking notes here. A second inventory slot would not go amiss.


2) A singular sound level?

The only option for turning up / down sound is to raise or lower the game's master volume. For a game emphasising communication between friends, I find it odd that you have no way of filtering what sound level you can have for ambiance, sound effects and talking. Big Walk would again benefit from a change here, especially since people have already made comments about how it's sometimes difficult to hear people in-game.

3) Gamma level slider / night-time illumination options?

Big walk has a very beautiful environment for traversal and problem solving, but the night cycle does feel too... well... dark. It would be very nice to have some ambient lighting (fireflies, glowing flora, etc) that gives the night cycle some oomph and readability. Sunset on the current build leaves you submerged in near-complete darkness in which you have to stumble around trying to find a glowing orb light or rely on a friend having a torch nearby. 

I do understand it's a team game, but some puzzles require your teammates to go long distances from you, and with little to no lighting at night, if you remain separated it does feel like you have to just sit and wait for day to come again before you can progress. 

Having environmental lighting (that isn't the big old orb lights) would be a lovely change, allowing people to see the world the devs have made in (literally) a new light when it comes to night-time exploration.

Despite my issues, I still recommend Big Walk as it hits that perfect level of comfort and exploration with a group of friends. If you're looking for a game to relax with while having a good conversation with a pal, this is for you!

[h2]The perfect co-op hangout[/h2]

Let me get this out of the way: [b][u] THIS GAME IS NOT FRIENDSLOP! [/u][/b]

Big Walk is a fantastic excuse to hang out with friends virtually, and workout your brains together. It's an obvious response to the COVID lockdown, just released a bit late. Getting a group together to wander around a picturesque island was an absolute blast from start to finish. 

The proximity chat isn't just a funny gimmick; it actually adds a fun challenge to the whole experience. While not actually enforceable, my group found no trouble in actually keeping with the challenge of not using outside communication. When one inevitably wanders off and lose the group, frantically trying to communicate and find each other again is challenging, then properly rewarding.

I also really loved the art direction. The map itself has this beautiful realism to it, which creates a striking contrast with the puzzles that use these cartoonishly plain, high-visibility textures. It sounds weird on paper, but it looks [i]great[/i] in practice.

Speaking of the puzzles - they are incredibly well-crafted and balanced. The flow is great, and I have to give a huge shoutout to the ending. Am I a fool for not enjoying *Big Walk*? 
Everyone speaks about this game as if it redefines what it means to play video games with friends, that the experience is unparalleled and revolutionary. I found the game to be a waste of time. 
I think *Big Walk*, at its core, is trying to accomplish something that many games end up accomplishing as a secondary benefit: getting a group of friends together to chat and play video games. I've been playing games for a long time, and almost just as long have I been playing with friends in voice chat. I've played Team Fortress on servers with people I've become friends with, terraria and minecraft ( for countless, *literally* countless hours). All of these games managed to do something we appreciated: they brought friends together to do an activity. Some were more task-oriented. Obviously, not many people are just chatting while trying to coordinate a push in Overwatch. But games like Minecraft excel at this. I can collect wood for the house we're building while my friend mines for diamonds. The tasks can be secondary and menial while chatting: exploring, mining, building. But we can also group up to explore ravines, find resources, and fight bosses together. The game has both aspects of a good game: you can play it as a chatter, or you can play it as a gamer. Then came games designed specifically around friendship, like *Lethal Company*. Proximity voice chat *is* the reason that game works. You can spend time chatting mindlessly with your friends while walking around, when suddenly you get split up. Things become scary, ominous, and sometimes genuinely terrifying. Then you die, join everyone in the deathcam lobby, and laugh about your silly death. Suddenly you're back together, watching the remaining survivor and sharing the experience. I think this is what *Big Walk* wants to accomplish. Unfortunately, I think it fails in almost every aspect, and it's because of a few critical systems that the entire game is founded on. I'm not nitpicking, these are the foundational systems of the game. 
1. The proximity chat. Not only is *Big Walk's* proximity chat one of the shortest-range systems I've encountered, it is also directional and supposedly "accurate to life." Does this make it remotely interesting, functional, or realistic? Hell no. The first area features a puzzle where someone stands in a room and dictates the correct sequence to people outside. Unless both players are literally standing face-to-face at the window, it's impossible to hear each other. If I'm standing at a window, I should be able to talk to my friends five feet away outside it. The voice range is constantly a problem. Any terrain, or even walking forward while chatting with someone behind you, can completely ruin their ability to hear you. And as for its "realism", this isn't real life. When I'm walking with friends irl, I can modulate my speed. I can pull someone aside for a conversation, catch up with the group, or stop while everyone else keeps moving and jog to catch up. In *Big Walk*, everyone essentially moves like a car on a track. If someone gets slightly outside your range, you can't even get their attention to call them back. Which leads to the next problem. 
2. Being lost. One of the defining features of *Lethal Company*-style games is that when you become lost, there is a genuine sense of stakes, fear, or emotion. I suppose in *Big Walk*, the intended emotion is supposed to be beauty, or appreciation of nature. Hypothetically if I'm on a walk in the woods with friends and become separated, that can become an interesting moment. I can meditate, appreciate nature and its beauty, try to use critical thinking to reconnect. In *Big Walk*, there is close to nothing nice about getting separated. It isn't scary or beautiful. It's just annoying and boring. Several times during our playthrough, we became split up. After three to five minutes of silence traveling through low-quality jungle, someone would finally unmute on Discord: "Where are you guys?" "Oh, we're over here." "Oh, okay." Then it's another two or three minutes of walking until we reunite. To do what? The puzzles are supposed to be the Minecraft equivalent of "let's go mining together!": just something to do while chatting. Except the proximity voice means you better be glued to your team, and heaven forbid your group have more than three people, because many challenges require coordination between multiple players. The gameplay experience becomes: walk for a bit, lag behind because of the awful platforming and inability to modulate your speed, lose communication, become lost, wander around, find a puzzle requiring three or more people, reconnect with your friends, tell them about the puzzle, walk all the way back to them, walk all the way to the puzzle, solve it in three seconds, then walk *allllll* the way to where you put the key (which you can't do by yourself, by the way) rinse and repeat.
 3. The movement. There is practically nothing interesting about the movement, and I think this ruins the game. Most of the time, you're supposed to be exploring, right? We can do this in Minecraft. When traveling together through a forest, pathing becomes a skill. Timing jumps, sprinting under trees, navigating terrain can all become ways that people stick together. Because its possible to get caught on world gen, you can modulate your movement with pathing and quickly catch up. Players don't become cars on a track that can only travel ten miles per hour. You can zigzag, jump, cut corners, and meet each other wherever you're at. Movement becomes freedom. In *Big Walk*, the titular activity (walking) is so boring and clunky that it hurts. Navigating terrain may as well be crawling through it, and you can't go anywhere particularly interesting because the landmarks are hardly notable outside of the lego looking buildings. There are very few climbable peaks, solid views, beautiful forests, or beach sunsets despite this being a game that should revolve around those things. Since everyone moves at the same speed, everyone feels like they're on a rail. There is no way to catch up to someone unless they stop, or unless they can hear you (which they can't, because they're outside voice range). And then there's the day-night cycle. During the day, we deal with all of the game's normal annoyances. During the night, everything becomes ten times worse because now we can't hear *or see* each other. The lantern balls are an interesting idea, but their light is so limited, and the views are so vast and covered with jungle clutter, that you can hardly see someone until they're ten feet away. I suppose you could argue that this is "accurate to life." You should have to walk with your group, keep track of everyone, and not leave hearing range. To this I present a counterargument: why am I sitting at my computer for two hours accomplishing absolutely nothing when I could just go on an actual hike in nature? And if the goal is to bring together people who can't physically be together because of distance, unfortunately I think it fails at that too. I've spent many hours catching up with friends over Discord, aimlessly talking about life, joking about memes, and browsing topics together. *There is no danger that I suddenly lose communication with them.* There is no possibility of suddenly spending three to seven minutes sitting in chat by myself because my friends wandered too far away. Because if that's how Discord worked, nobody would use it. And unfortunately, that's exactly what playing *Big Walk* feels like. 
TL;DR: Big Walk felt like a big waste of time. I don't dislike the idea behind the game, but its core is so limiting it infringes on its very concept of purpose: spending time with friends. Almost every system designed to facilitate that idea gets in the way of the thing it's supposed to create, all while putting you in a boring character body with no expression of movement.

I have not yet finished the game but I feel like I've seen enough of it that my opinion is pretty solidified.

The current ecosystem of cooperative multiplayer gaming is largely focused on short, repeatable, randomized gameplay loops. Big Walk is a breath of fresh air in that it offers a handcrafted world that is best enjoyed when taking your time, and its central mechanic is the players you take that time with.

Big Walk's puzzles are distinctly communication dependent. In most circumstances, they require the team to get a little creative to overcome a communication obstacle, whether it be a soundproof window, or being in separate rooms. 

This philosophy even permeates into the inventory management. Players cannot place or remove items from their own backpacks/toolbelts, you need to coordinate with your teammate(s) when you want to use something.

This is simultaneously the game's biggest detriment and its biggest asset. It can only be enjoyed as much as you enjoy the company of your fellow player(s).

With this in mind, it makes sense that Big Walk is a very "hands-off" game. After a brief tutorial zone, players are left to self govern the manner in which they explore the world. It looks like there's a deactivated train over there, maybe we can turn that on somehow? There's a cool looking structure in the distance, I wonder what that is? Hey, it looks like there's a puzzle along the way, maybe we can stop there? There are features of the island to unlock that can expedite travel, but has no bearing on access to content; you can get anywhere on foot.

There is no right or wrong way to approach the puzzles. You can take it head on by hopping into your separate rooms and shutting yourselves in until you figure it out, or you can explore every facet of it and formulate a plan before splitting up.  It's a great feeling when you nail the solution and get to meet back up with the team and celebrate your achievement.

The day-night cycle elevates the sense of adventure by providing a frame of reference for the time you've spent journeying, and passes by quick enough that the darkness of night never feels intrusive. Instead, it offers a great opportunity to stay put for a moment and think about the team's next moves, reflect on progress/goals, or just chat. And even still, you could always just grab a flashlight and continue trekking.

In my experience, getting lost was practically a non-issue, as there are plenty of opportunities to use flares, lights, and radios to take advantage of when you get separated from the pack. You may even discover some neat new structures and locations to tell your friends about when you meet up with them again.

Big Walk is a game about exploring and collaborating with your friends, and is designed to be as unobtrusive to that goal as possible. For me, it has been a memorable experience that I wouldn't hesitate to recommend to anyone.

[h1] Team Building Exercise - The Game. [/h1]

TL;DR The game prioritizes players getting to know more of each other through conversations and their actions as much as completing the tasks, all of which are well-designed to demand every means of communication possible from a player. It leads to a very fantastic and melancholic ending, and it made me love my friends even more.

[h2] Spoiler-free Review [/h2]
In short, it's very much like a co-op multiplayer version of Myst (or Riven), but with much more intuitive puzzles and better traversal QoL.

Let's start with the sense of exploration; it was so good, even in the late game. Some places introduce new mechanics that were already genuinely fun the first time around, and then a separate place will elevate that mechanic to the next level regardless of the order of discovery.
You will also always come across different items at fixed spots in the game, and while that might make some items seem missable, the placement was thought out so well that you will never miss any of the tools they offer despite your very limited inventory.

Communication is the core of this game, and the game will test all the ways you communicate with each other. Puzzles are very easy to understand, but to get it done is actually the main challenge, because the efficiency of your communication is the true hidden difficulty of the puzzles.
The "Aha!" moments didn't arrive from figuring out how the puzzle is supposed to be done, but instead from how to get everyone to work together to get it done, and we found that very engaging.

Also, while I must admit the small-yet-massive map proves to be very challenging to get around due to slow walking speed, the struggle of the traversal quickly melted away when you know you are not alone in this adventure.
Here's the thing: you can always chat with your friend in the meantime to discuss whatever you have in mind. You'll be surprised how many things you will want to talk about during those moments.

I know that many people will call that [i] boring[/i], because there's technically no gameplay in a traditional sense during these moments. But I find that this "boring" part is what makes this game truly precious.

...But why, you may ask?

[h2] Interlude: A Criticism of [b]"Friendslop Games"[/b] [/h2]
To explain that simply, Big Walk is an antidote to the usual [i]chaos[/i] promoted in all of the "friendslops" out there. 

The chaos made those games fun, sure, but also very... exhausting and artificial. 

These friendslops enforce the chaos by constantly forcing the player to do tasks, treating you and your friends as [i]colleagues[/i], without time to genuinely bond together. These tasks ultimately alienate and disconnect players from truly knowing each other, because these friendslop games deem that achieving a common goal and completing tasks by any means are just more important than actually cooperating.

I recently found this forced chaos distasteful, especially when content creators use it to clipfarm to hell and back.

[h2] Why Big Walk is [b]NOT[/b] a Friendslop [/h2]
So, in contrast to friendslops, Big Walk is made so that the goal isn't critical. 

It doesn't rush you to complete and doesn't aggressively punish your failures. It still gives you a place with shared tasks, but without the stress of pressure, while we get to know each other a little bit more.

In failing, everyone got setbacks, but you never end a session feeling like a loser. Big Walk never undermines your effort, and at the harshest, it merely delays your success. You always feel complete every session.

In winning, nobody "[i]clutched[/i]" the win; [b]everyone created those wins[/b]. We all celebrate, share the success, and together move on. After all, the game nurtures your bonds together. With those bonds, you will learn how everyone acts when they cooperate, and these bonds will be tested in a wonderful finale sequence.

Because the whole point of the game is to let you and your friends do something together and celebrate [i]for doing it together, not just for doing it well. [/i]

It eventually led to an emotional ending. A proper conclusion to a wonderful journey.
I sat at the beach, looking at sunset as the credits rolled while chatting with my friends about our adventures. [spoiler]We waved each other goodbye with our little hands as we parted ways one by one.[/spoiler]

It's an experience I will keep near and dear to my heart, that's for sure.

[h2] Final Score [/h2]
So, the reasons above are why I consider this game one of the greatest co-op games of all time, and a true game to replenish your friendship.
[h3] 9.5/10 [/h3]

Yea this is fantastic.

Big Walk already has enough buzz and praise that I don't really even need to tell you that it's fantastic. It was already eye catching on reveal three years ago, announced near the advent of the term "friendslop", delayed to 2026 during the proliferation and usage of such classification, now having arrived as some sort of bright colored knife to cut through the fog. Furthermore, so much of its charm is easily visible on first glance that it requires little words to describe what it's about and even fewer words to describe how good it is.

You solve puzzles on an island with friends. It's fantastic.

However, as simply does Big Walk present itself, its in equal brilliance that it's magic almost only works through that simplicity. Before solving puzzles, Big Walk is about communication. The puzzles are simply the obstacles in which communication is directly stretched and strained. I say this as while I found no one puzzle particularly hard, it's a difficulty that is scaled based on your own ability to communicate with the people you are playing with. Your ability to transcribe, use tools, your ability to understand and interpret. I’d say less than half of Big Walk is puzzles, the majority of the time you're either walking and talking on a stroll to the next objective, trying to get a hold of someone to find out, or simply hanging out!

Big Walk asks,

"How do you personally interpret this symbol, this drawing?"

"How would you describe it to someone who can't see it?"

"Without words, how would you do it?"

And what I mean by simplicity rears its head here. As Big Walk prods your brain about how you perceive and express, the other people people around you pick up on that, they in a sense understand you better. Picking up on ticks, movements, tendencies of the people around you, attributing it to them, all of which is amplified by the limited tools of communication provided. Becoming in sync in such a way does Big Walk not only bring you together for a shared activity, but also bring you together in a sense of understanding.

And it's all in this giant freeform sandbox of what I assume is a loving and endearing ecological recreation of the developer's home country of Australia, sonically backed by an incredibly tender and human soundtrack.

Big Walk doesn't require so many words to illustrate it's brilliance, but there's such a deep understanding and brilliant exercise in, as cheesy as it might sound, what makes us human. We like to walk, we like to talk, we like to work together.

Big Walk is as human as walking. Big Walk is as human as doing a funny little dance. Big Walk is as human as getting lost. Big Walk is as human as getting found. Big Walk is art like Pacman is art. Big Walk isn't about asking the smartest person in the room to solve a puzzle, it's about getting a group of people to work together to achieve a common goal. And I think that’s very human.

It's a fun walking sim, best with friends to keep the chat going! Love the design, music and visuals too.

POSITIVES:
- Incredible sound design! The ambient sounds are spot on, the interaction noises are very fun, and the music is beautiful - my friends and I are happy to sit and listen while talking and joking around.
-Beautiful visuals - the landscapes are beautiful to watch; the day/night cycle, the flora, the sea, it all makes me wish I was really there. It definitely gives you that feeling of climbing up a big rock and calling all your friends over to admire the view.
- Fun interactions - the puzzles are all very simple but fun especially with friends who you can joke with! The things you collect to unlock keys have been christened "the baby" by my friend group, which leads to very funny moments ("I fell down and now I've lost the baby"). There's working walkie-talkie radios. Amazing.

CONS:
- Some of my friends are still quiet despite the patch, and the audio falloff distance is very short by design. IRL you'd be able to shout for your friends if you're just a little bit further away, but alas, in game you just have to run back to them. We also experienced several times where people's audio would just stop working; their mouths moved, we just couldn't hear them. The only fix was for the host to reload. Most of us got slow internet warnings just before, which is very funny considering our internet can regularly support high traffic from discord, streaming and competitive gaming simultaneously.
- Janky collision / softlocking - My friend and I got softlocked and had to quit out of the game when we jumped off a rock into the ocean (another friend had thrown my cowbell into the water so I was trying to retrieve it). You can't swim out far into the ocean and the rocks were too big to climb, so I just got trapped in between some rocks and the sea; couldn't even try and push or jump against the rock to get around it back to shore. Great views, great feeling of inevitable death. Once I quit out, I was unable to rejoin until the host reset. 

Some things it would be nice to see the devs add in future: 
More random sculptures and stuff to see and find; small insects, bugs, beetles, etc to make the place feel alive; more random instruments and the ability to wear hats.

OVERALL RECOMMENDED, ideally buy on sale with your friends and enjoy the nice atmosphere!

I had been waiting for this game to release for over a year. Going into it I was excited and expected to have an interesting map to explore, and fun mechanics to mess around with my friends. Sadly, the Big Walk did deliver on either and was only interesting for the first hour, after that it became repetitive. 

The three main features of the Big Walk are: Walking, Talking and Puzzles.

Walking
The majority of the gameplay is walking. The map is BIG, a little too big. It feels empty and lifeless. The points of interest are primarily puzzle structures. You will spend most of the time walking from Point A to Point B to complete a puzzle then head back to Point A. The worst part is that along with a big map the the movement is horrible. The player collider gets caught on everything, trying navigate up any terrain that isn't a smooth slope is extremely difficult. So exploring is limited to the paths the devs have set for you. It seems like they wanted to discourage climbing since most things are impossible to climb which for me is not fun.

Talking
For a game that uses talking as one of its main selling points and pushes for in game voice chat. The options for communication in game are very lacking from the settings to actual in game methods. The primary method of communication is the in game voice chat. Which has an extremely close fall off range and no volume slider. With voice chat being the main focus, if you happen to end up alone your long range communication options are limited to specific items. If you don't have those items you have to make your way back to a tower and wait for the group or hope they have an item that allows you to find them. This happened a lot during my playtime and made the experience less fun.

Puzzles
Most of them are easy, and can be completed in under 8 minutes. Once a puzzle is completed the structure and area around it become irrelevant. A lot of them are similar so once the group completes one the next ones become trivial. 

With how limited player to player and player to game interaction is, there are very few instances of the game being fun. You can honestly get the same or better experience hopping in a voice call and playing party games. If this game was worth $5 instead of $13.50 (sale). I would be more forgiving but with a price point this high from a game that offers so little, its hard to not be critical.

Truly a masterpiece. Remarkable. Genuis. Despite many games sharing elements, there's nothing quite like Big Walk.

We played with 8 players, with a few more coming and going throughout, and I think that was the perfect amount. 

At first I was worried about some friends running off, some going full ADHD, and some missing out because some friends rush through puzzles while others have a more relaxed pace. I quickly realized this game was designed specifically to accommodate everyone's playstyle, while also requiring teamwork and reconnection in the most rewarding and intuitive ways.

We stuck together, we got lost, we found each other again. At first, getting lost in the bush was scary, or frustrating, or it made me feel like you're missing out, but as the game progressed we all came to enjoy our time separated from the group. 

We naturally came up with our own standard comms, procedures, rituals, and unspoken language. We watched sunrise and sunset. We saw things we wanted to do, and we went and did them. Exploration and discovery are HUGE elements in this game. I'm not lying when I say that we were in awe nearly 100% of the time, and when we weren't we were either laughing or noodling on a puzzle together. Who you play with may have a big impact on this, but the game is built in such a way that even party poopers will have a hard time killing the vibes. Shout out to my Big Walk crew for being the chillest, most adventurous Big Walkers <3

We rolled credits tonight, but didn't 100%. One of our friends is heading out for a month long trip tomorrow, and we all already marked in our calendar the day we'll hop back on to 100% this together, upon their return. 

Couldn't recommend Big Walk more. My personal GOTY, and likely the best multiplayer puzzle game of all time.

Unlocked framerate, crossplay, players can join/leave mid-session (except for the host), text chat, a mute button, host kicking, full controller support, rebindable keybinds, the ability to check FPS and ping in-game (by holding Tab), up to 12 players, and the ability to change the puzzle player requirement from 2, 3, or 4+ without needing to make a new save file.

Big Walk is available on Steam, PlayStation 5, and Switch 2 (although it runs terribly on Switch 2). While I love how this game plays on PC, but it's worth noting that it's free with PlayStation Plus. [h2]Short Review[/h2]
I ended up liking this game more than I expected. You wander around and solve puzzles together in a big national park inspired sandbox. Three to four people has been very fun. My only complaint is how short the voice proximity range is. Also it will get very dark during the night cycles. You must be patient enough to walk around the map and enjoy the environment. 

[h2]Long review[/h2]
[h3]What I expected:[/h3]
A friendslop game for people who don't go outside to hang out at parks and nature conservancies with their friends, with occasional puzzles. I would have hated this.
[h3]What the game actually is:[/h3]
A sandbox game with [b]many puzzles and things to discover[/b] sprinkled around the map. The game drops the player into an island with a very simple visual tutorial area where players can figure out the controls, with nothing else afterward. 

The first hurdle you encounter, maybe even before the puzzles, is that you can only hold one thing in your hand at a time. This adds a layer of challenge where you need friends to be able to use multiple tools or transport multiple items at once. This is resolved by various wearable containers around the map that allow a friend to place some items on your body. The way these interactions work their way into the gameplay feels deliberate, and not like some accident in a poorly thought out system.

The next hurdle is an environmental mechanic: the day/night cycle. The map gets very dark at night, but is littered with pedestals holding lanterns that you can turn on and carry. Every puzzle has a lighting system that can be activated, making it easy to see. Again, a well introduced solution. 

Overcoming the first two hurdles introduces the third and final one. Its a [spoiler]Big Wait[/spoiler]. The map is huge, and players will have to go back to certain areas repeatedly. The environment is varied enough that this has not become too tedious for me personally, but it may for some people. There are shortcuts and travel systems that make moving between old and new areas much faster, but these amount to having to ride a chair lift or train for a minute. 

In summary, the gameplay feels well thought out and intentional. I am excited to continue playing it and will edit this review if that changes. Try it if you are patient and like talking to your friends.

"Friendslop" seems to have a negative connotation because of the massive amounts of shovelware chasing the behemoths of Lethal Company, R.E.P.O. or PEAK. These games work because playing with your friends is a cheat code to having fun, and the gameplay is unintrusive enough that they can serve almost as background noise while you talk. Big Walk feels like the apex predator of these games, since it fully embraces the idea of being a platform to interact with your friends with the gameplay encouraging just talking to eachother in unique ways. The care that clearly went into every minute aspect of this game really sells the passion the devs have for their own game and makes the suffix "slop" feel reductive. 

I played in a group that ranged from 7-9 people. The game feels like it would get better and better for every player you add, since large groups organically split off to go on their own adventures and reform later. I would just say that 4 players is probably the smallest party I'd recommend for this game. There's a lot of puzzles that require four to even start including the entire (excellent) finale. Also, in a larger group that splits off you're likely to miss a decent portion of the puzzles which may be a downside for some, but as soon as our group finished we were immediately talking about when we would do our second playthrough and having a bunch of puzzles I've never seen before sounds excellent to me.

The puzzles themselves were all excellent, just the right level of difficulty to never be too difficult or overstay their welcome but are all very satisfying to figure out what's going on or finish something off. The ending in particular has such a simple twist on the formula which lets it really end on a high note that left my jaw hurting from smiling so hard.

Big Walk is packed with love. It's the ah-ha moments not just from solving a puzzle itself, but the clever walkarounds you'd come up with your friends, using the several simple tools that feels more like toys since they are so fun to play with. It's the fireworks by your friend when you're lost in the dark without a walkie-talkie. It's when you are sitting side by side on a train and the stunning view of the sea at dawn is right outside. It's the stories exchanged after splitting into two groups to survey a new region. It's that one guy who always boards the chairlift going the wrong way and Saving Private Ryan becomes a new adventure.
The only bad thing is this is an one time experience that you can never play it blind again. And yes, there's a sweet spot before the fun becomes tedious or frustrating but I believe the game will end right at the sweet spot, never overstaying the welcome. That's also the bittersweet moment when you realize there are some good things you can only taste them so much in your lifetime, or at least, every few years, before they get sour. I'm grateful that Big Walk has the perfect dosage of this exact kind of fun in it and there are still some people I care about playing this with me.

review: It's not about the walk, it's about the friends you walk along the way.

I played this with my fiance and it's my favorite co op game we've ever played together. It genuinely made me emotional throughout, especially near the end. If you love puzzle games and spending time with people you love, you will enjoy this game. Brava, I hope there is a Big Walk 2 coming. I would play whatever future content this game wants to put out.

Big Walk is comfortably sitting among puzzle giants like Portal 2 or any of the strongest Zelda dungeons for me. The game so effortlessly guides the players through the gorgeous map toward immensely engaging puzzles. Portal has the portal gun, the tool you use to solve the puzzles, Zelda has specific items applied creatively, Big Walk has unique communication and movement. Never have I seen a simple concept like "try to tell your friend how to help solve the puzzle" deconstructed and elaborated on in such meaningful ways.

This is one of the most satisfying co-op experiences I have ever had. Not a single person having a bad time, no annoyances, no frustrations with any piece of game design. The whole experience exudes this thoughtful warmth, this comfortable yearning to just *be* with those around you. Solving puzzles is a lovely time, but so is falling off the ski-lift and getting lost in the dark, huddling around a weird light-orb while silly music plays, reading embarrassing reddit posts while waiting for others to finally make it back. 

Countless games try to nail the feeling you get by spending time with people around you that you care about, but nothing I've ever played has fundamentally struck that chord until now. Constant surprise, constant mystery, constant thought. Countless stories to tell when your friends reunite and so much self-driven fun.

Play this with anyone you care about. Whether it's one person or 11, this game brings out something so magic, so fundamental and pure, it goes beyond words. 

Come for some killer puzzles and cozy moments, but stay for what's broiling underneath; That subtle, ephemeral atmosphere that fills the same space as those perfect late-night hangouts just as the sun sets.

Potentially the greatest Co-op experience ever made. Not much comes close.

review:
The only co-op game that has made me cry (and not just at the end!), this is an all-time great for me. Some co-op games are about putting you into situations that generate wacky, funny moments - this isn't really one of those. The moments that this game tries to build are the frustration of miscommunication or the dread of getting lost, bumped up against how amazing it is to hear your friend's voice in the distance, quietly watching the sun rise or realizing just how well you can understand each other's wordless, nonsensical arm movements. 

For most puzzle games, their mechanics are essentially a conversation with you and the designer. The level has to subtly communicate what it wants you to do, and you're left to interpret that and try to execute it. What I find so interesting about big walk's best challenges is that you aren't working together to communicate with the designer in the traditional way - your friend IS the puzzle. Every playthrough of this game would feel different depending on who you play it with, as the challenges will naturally play out in such a unique way depending on what tools you have at the time, the languages you form with each other or even just how close you are to that person. I'm not sure I've really seen that done in a puzzle game before.

I'm not really sure I've felt this way about a game since I played Outer Wilds - the game that I would consider the best I've ever played. The feeling of having such a wide, unstructured space to explore with surprises and puzzles around each corner feels like it realizes the fantasy I had looking at the box art of Myst which that game really fulfilled for me. In middle school I would often sit on the bus thinking about what my dream game would look like, and I always thought that it would just be a wide open space for me to freely explore, no monsters or danger, just interesting things to find and poke at. It's kind of unbelievable how well this executes on that dream for me. If this game was a solo experience, that fantasy alone would carry it into my favorite games ever - as a co-op game, I think it becomes something like a core memory for me. I don't think this game will hit for a lot of people the same way that it hit for me, but there is something really, really special here.

By the way, I have a complete potato of a computer. Normally, I'd play this kind of thing on Playstation, but with Sony's anti-disc plans, I'm withholding my money and I took a chance that my 8GB of RAM might somehow be able to handle this game despite the 12GB RAM requirement. Great news for my fellow potato-havers: it does, as long as you play on "Very Low" or "Low" graphics settings and have someone else host. House House, if you're reading this, I humbly thank you for every ounce of work you've done to account for no-RAM havers like myself. I got to have a phenomenal date with my LDR because of this.

I don't think I can fully describe the type of experience this game is and what it represents. I can't tell with absolute precision how it feels to play or what kind of quality it has, because it's different based on the people you play it with. It's a social experience unlike anything else.

This is a revolutionary Co-Op game that has unique challenges that I don't believe I've ever seen before. It blends communication in various creative means, giving the player the liberty to discover all the ways they can clear through each puzzle. There are so many unique puzzles in the game that even similar kinds of puzzles don't always play out the exact same way, which puts your creativity to the test.

I don't think I could've had such a thrilling experience with this game if it hadn't been for my friends. We managed to play through the game in quite a large group, we got to share our inability to concentrate, figuring out the puzzles together, having our fun and frustrations and seeing our fruits of effort rewarded time and time again. We got lost, we made dumb decisions and stimmed with all the items until we dropped out of sheer boredom overtaking us, and at the end of the day we could share all of our experiences during our travels in the game.

Then it's all over. 

And I don't think I'd have that any other way. This game, like I said, is a social experience unlike anything else and it will remain part of the best Co-Op games that I have ever played. It is charming, full of heart and passion that also shows that it can be quite sad too that things have to end. But as I keep repeating, that is completely fine... you should play this game with the friends you cherish.

Really fun. None of the puzzles are particularly challenging, but they feel rewarding to complete as they do require solid teamwork and cooperation. Some of the less obvious ones also provide a nice dopamine hit when you end up figuring them out, which again is nice given the non-intimidating difficulty level.

Now that I've finished the game, I will say that while the ending is very grand in style and atmosphere, I found the puzzles and gameplay throughout the finale to be a tad lackluster. They were largely familiar ground relative to the puzzles that appear earlier in the game, and while the difficulty certainly increased slightly, I was expecting something slightly more climactic given the atmospheric and visual build up. While the studio is obviously very small, I feel like this can't be entirely explained through a lack of resources/budget, and is at least partly a conscious decision. I do understand that the game is meant to be approachable for all, but even for me, someone who avoids games that are difficult/challenging/unforgiving, I felt the ending was slightly underwhelming in regards to the lack of novel and challenging gameplay.

There are a disappointing number of bugs and annoyances given how long this has been in development, as well as the amount of playtesting it went through. Despite this, the audio shipped in a pretty bad state, the ability to adjust game and voice chat volume independently still hasn't been added, and I've experienced random crashes as well as unexplained networking errors (the decision to use Epic Online Services, despite this game being exclusively released on Steam for PC/Mac is pretty baffling). I'm just thankful none of the things I've dealt with have necessitated completely abandoning a save, which I've seen some people unfortunately have to do. Movement can also be fairly janky, it is possible for your character to get stuck in places, trying to walk/jump up an incline can be frustrating, and there are some edges (especially the ones on the stairs in the towers) that are annoyingly easy to catch yourself on.

As is, this is a very solid 8/10 game for me, which is not something I say too often. However, if the bugs and issues are addressed, and if the content at the end of the game had some more novel and interesting gameplay flourishes, this would easily be a 9/10 for me. I do think it deserves to be recognised as a bastion of quality amongst the sea of mediocre co-op games that have saturated the market.

Regardless, I did very much enjoy playing this game and I will be completing all of the post-credits content, but I do feel there is potential for this to be even better.

review: It's like The Witness if Jonathan Blow had friends.

Big Walk is a puzzle game, first and foremost. It's like a multiplayer The Witness. As long as you go into it with that in mind, the game is a fun time with friends.

I played it under the assumption that it was more about the walking and exploring and taking in interesting scenery, and was sorely disappointed at first, but I didn't want to bail on my friends so I kept playing to allow the puzzle element to hook me.

The first impression that the game gives isn't very good at the moment. 

For a game where talking with your friends is a key element, the voice chat was very quiet, and the volume falloff too steep.

For a game about walking around in the wilderness, the movement was extremely aggravating, like it hadn't been tested once during all of development. In a game literally called Big Walk. You get stuck to every little rock or slope, and the sprint and jump are underwhelming. Easily the worst part of the game. There is a ton of terrain where your jump will simply fail and a little sound effect plays and your character impotently flails while floating above some rocks. It feels really really bad.

For a game about exploring the wilderness, the environment was dull and felt very lifeless, but it's actually based on a real place. If I'd have known that before playing, the exploration element wouldn't have been as disappointing. Also, because of the aforementioned movement problems, I was disincentivized from straying off the trails since that was the fastest way to get stuck every five feet.

The day/night cycle is very fast, and the night time is pitch black. I spent a lot of time AFK waiting for sunrise. Some moonlight would help, maybe a four day cycle with a full moon night and two half moon nights to simulate a range of night time lighting. A lot of the structure locale had very aesthetic vibes during night time, and would benefit from some ambient moonlight. Some moonlight would also help silhouette the tower structures so they're easier to get back to while travelling at night.

The puzzles. They're really good puzzles; the ones in the beginning are a bit dull and easy, but they really pick up after that. The game is absolutely worth finishing. It's odd that the puzzles are only ever explicitly mentioned in the trailer video which I didn't watch before playing. It should be written down in the description too. They're the best part of the game.

Performance. On an AMD RX 480, the game stuttered like crazy on Medium settings when moving too far too quickly, but was playable otherwise. I restarted my PC before playing and the game consumed all 4GB of VRAM by itself so I definitely recommend having more than that.

More than any other game I've ever played, Big Walk understands why people play cooperative games with their friends. Playing through it with a big group of close friends was one of the most fantastic and memorable gaming experiences of my entire life. It's hard to articulate what makes this game good because it has so much going for it, but the biggest highlights were:

The puzzles. House House has an immaculate understanding of the mechanics of cooperative play - communication, coordination, understanding what others are thinking - and how they can build simple, yet engaging puzzle experiences around them. The game's basic systems allow for a surprisingly wide range of idea expression and will push you to experiment with limited, and often very funny, sets of tools. There are also a lot of great little touches, like how there's a 10 second delay between solving a puzzle and the reward being dispensed so you can celebrate with your friends.

The presentation. The characters are adorable and blend goofiness and earnestness in a way that's hard to come across. There are a ton of little details in the character animations and how your little guy interacts with the world around him. The world itself is a masterclass in prodding players' sense of adventure, giving you little nudges towards interesting locales while still allowing you to explore at your own whims. I don't know how they managed to make "picturesque wilderness dotted with colorful, blocky structures" work, but they did.

The ending. I won't give any details, because spoiling it would be highly immoral. It was incredible and I doubt I will ever forget it.

If you have a couple of friends and a couple free evenings, do yourselves a favor and pick up Big Walk. I would recommend this game even at $50, so at $15 it's an absolute steal.

Game of the year and it's not even close. In a disconnected world filled with distractions and a dying planet with nature burning and being stripped down to make way for endless expansion,

a game about just, walking with your friends in nature, exploring and using tools, and having to do everything together, everything as a group, the concept of just having simple puzzles and sometimes, not even a puzzle, just emergent gameplay for you and your friend(s) to experience is wonderful. 

Upgrades are extremely meaningful and you need your friends to upgrade you, I;e you can't put backpacks on yourself, someone has to help you, you can't customize your character, your friends have to paint you. After you clear the tutorial area, which doesn't feel like one because there's no direction, just "go on a walk" you have access to the entire island and can tackle it in any order you want, and this naturally leads you to getting lost, splitting up, shooting flares, it's dark out and I don't have a light, but I hear my friend playing music in the distance, I see their eyes through the trees. 

I'll never forget how my friend carried the radio with him, at all times because he wanted to listen to the relaxing tunes, he carried it for hours, and near the end of our session, we came across a beach in as the sun was setting, lawn chairs and relaxing warm lights, and a sound stage. Instead of it being a puzzle, it was just an area to relax and have a beach party with your friends, to watch the sun go down. 

So many, beautiful little moments like that, just being able to... walk and experience the world with your friends. There are some negatives, not having a volume slider for every player is bizarre, and while it does make belt and backpack upgrade super important and also impactful, due to how they work, you're going to have plenty of situations where you wish you could hold more on you, and that can make the game feel more limited, as you just sort of "stick with your tool". 

The trains and the towers / other land marks act as sort of natural hubs / gathering points, and it is a fun feeling to suit up / gear up for specific adventures, and I think there's a very deliberate artistic beauty to these decisions, It just requires the player to realize that "we're on a big walk, and that's the point". You do not want to play this game "optimally" or "correctly" you want to bumble around, stumble and slip and fall and get lost. You want to sit in the dark, find a bench and a small station, and wait for the train. You want to accidentally press right click and yeet your precious piece of equipment off the ledge and have to solve the puzzle in a different way. You want one of your friends to get lost in the woods and have to form a search party to find them. 

I can't speak to the lobby size and replayability yet, but there's three gamemodes, 2p 3p and 4+ lobby sizes which change the puzzle mechanics and solutions. But the potential for having individual groups of players lost on the island solving puzzles and unlocking island wide mobility tools, shortcuts and gear? It's such an exciting thing, and I think this game captures that beautifully.

As other's have said, I want to state that I enjoyed the music and atmosphere of Big Walk, and I can respect what it’s trying to do artistically. But honestly, I don’t really get the appeal.

The game markets itself as a big walking/hangout simulator, yet it feels surprisingly linear. The puzzles are mostly boring, and there isn’t enough freedom or discovery to make the exploration itself particularly compelling.

The VOIP is another strange one. The game specifically boasts that “Our proximity voice chat system makes voices fade across distances, echo down corridors, muffle through walls, and crackle through walkie-talkies.” In practice, I frequently couldn’t hear friends who were standing more than five feet away.

I respect anyone who had a genuinely great time with this game, but I absolutely cannot understand the reviews calling it a life-changing experience, talking about crying their eyes out while watching a fake sunset, or wishing they could experience it all over again for the first time. Maybe I’m just missing something, but a lot of that praise feels incredibly exaggerated.

Ultimately, I respect Big Walk for what it is artistically. But as an actual game, I found it pretty underwhelming. At anything above $5, I’d say it’s a waste of money and time. There's better, fairer priced friendslop out there.

That was not the case with Big Walk. With Big Walk, I was enraptured for the entire run time. And now, the day after having finished playing through it with my wife, I'm just kind of sitting here, wishing I could play it more. Wishing I had more reason to go back into that world with the funny little men, and run around with my radio and dance, and run through the woods, and get lost and meet back up, and run to the map and run my little knob-hands against the glass floor and dirt.

I think for most people this will be a fun puzzle game, and will be a solid 10-hour-ish time killer. But for anyone who isn't where they want to be or is perhaps a little more aware of the concept of time than they'd like to be, if they play it with people they cherish and wish they could be just a little bit (or a lot) physically closer to, this game is extremely special. It's extremely special to me, and I say with no exaggeration that it's pretty firmly in my Best Game of 2026, and easily top 5 of my favorite co-op games ever.

I will offer two caveats, though. I think you need to take this game seriously. Not in a "JOKES ARE BANNED" way, but respect it when it asks you to not communicate outside the game. Also there is one puzzle I would outright say is not very good (as it's just tedious), and two I'd argue could use a bit better hint at what you're supposed to do. They weren't terrible to figure out, but I can see these three as being points of frustration for people who are going for the 100%. All the other puzzles are honestly very fun and most are super well crafted. There were a few more puzzles that I struggled with just with how my own brain works, but even as we were walking away with its little gourd, I can say that I did enjoy them.

The standout part of the game ended up being the in-between moments, navigating point to point.  It absolutely nails the feeling of wandering around in a National Park.  Using the interactibles like the walkie talkies, map, and flashlights all felt fantastic.  Gesturing as well.

Gameplay wise it's a game all about communication, where almost every puzzle's solution is learning how to communicate with your partners.  It ends up emphasizing how much .  I played it as a 2 player coop game and we had a great time, I can't really speak to the 3+ player experience.  Finishing the game came out at around 12-13 hours for us at a relaxed pace and that felt about right.

Loved the aesthetic mismatch of the natural landscape and simple toy like shapes of the non-natural world.  Also makes me wonder if the developers were trying to say something about humans not being part of the natural world but maybe I'm reading too much into that.

It did come with a variety of smaller problems.  Movement felt alright, but it feels like you get stuck on terrain too often, particularly on small rocks you're trying to jump over.  Audio was a bit rough on launch, you couldn't really hear anyone, much better now post patch.  I also had pretty bad performance issues with the game on launch, and post patch the game still doesn't run great.  

My biggest complain once the performance was mostly fixed though is the shape of the island.  Everytime you start the game you spawn at the same location.  There's no "correct" way to clear the island, but you can kind of feel it pushing you in a rotation.  If you're doing 2 hours sessions in the game, you're going to spend a lot of time walking to where you left off, if you're doing 1 hour sessions it's going to be a bit rough with the retreading.  There's convenience rewards and you can remove some barriers, but the one that helps the most with this is probably the last one you'd unlock.  I ended up leaving my game on towards the end to avoid the backtracking.

In the end it's a great game because of how everything comes together and it's an easy recommend, I'm going to be finishing the rest of the puzzles later and looking forward to it.

Big walk kicks it to friendslop as a genre and brings back the game's rightful title of cooperative puzzles in a way that makes this game feel so natural and homey. I'm australian, so i have quite a lot of connection towards the biodiversity, the ambient sound, and the environment that feels so nice to immerse myself into.

The gameplay itself is not particularly standout as the game does not revolve around it exlusively, but the puzzles are so enjoyable as they always bring a huge smile to my face and an overwhelming sense of accomplishment for not just me but also the friend(s) i play with. Every puzzle somehow one-ups the last in complexity, uniqueness and cooperative effort without feeling artifical or fustratingly annoying. All puzzles prioritise not just the movement and hand gestures provided by the game but also any possible way you may have of communicating. Some rooms may lock you off with your friends unable to hear eachother and need to communicate another way. Some rooms may effectively blind one friend to information and need another to guide them. These continue to stack up towards the game progresses and no two puzzles feel especially the same.

There's also a good chunk of hidden puzzles that require some kind of very ambiguous solving without holding your hand. Some may just give you some numbers that correlate to a box, a button, or some other device, Some may give you some kind of directional cue, like a flare, or even just the general direction. They all feel pretty fair in the grand scheme of things and not once did i have a moment where i  was angry due to the ambiguity of the directions.

The progression is extremely straightforward. You quickly get accross the point that puzzles get you effigies, effigies get you keys, keys get you progress. Just by walking around you're able to deduce what does what and thanks to the very helpful [spoiler]dynamic map that appears after the red tower,[/spoiler] and can help you pinpoint directions of interest to find.

Speaking of places of interest, the game looks gorgeous, and the contast between the cartoony plastic toy-like players & puzzles with the highly realistic foliage and terrain makes the game very easy to traverse through, with it being clear what's walkable and what isn't, what the buildings are and what obstructions are around. I really appreciated that literally everywhere lights are placed that can be turned on and put back on their podiums. Going around the map and turning on these lights just to put them back on their podium saved me constant times.

The items in this game are super cooperative in the sense that their utility is only measured by how your friends can also use them. I say this in the sense that items like the lantern, item camera, and the Huge Orbs are able to be used exclusively by you and ended up becoming the defacto items for me and my group to use running around the island. Other items are fairly useful, binoculars and laser pointers can let you piece things out but aren't versatile in the sense that you could use them everywhere. What's the point of binoculars if you're in a chasm? I also enjoyed that walkie talkies aren't exactly easy to use but not exactly overly difficult either. I was afraid i would be inclined (or forced to in some cases) to cheese puzzles somehow with walkie talkies but they're all possible without them.

I also like that the "upgrades" you can get are all placed in the same unified structure that can be found in different places over the island. It helped us pinpoint where to go if we really needed a backpack for instance. I don't really enjoy the hip pack for the big part. It's intended to only carry something small, like a map, radio, walkie, etc, but you still require a second person to take it off you in order to use. If you're playing 2 players, you're basically only able to put a map on there and nothing else, as if it was used for walkies, how would you use them in the first place?

The ending was phenomenal. I haven't 100%'d the game as of writing, but this is how long it took me, my brother, and a friend of ours to complete the main portion. It was very satisfying and fufilling. The final building was a huge curveball and I'm not going to spoil the exact thing that happened there but it was not what i was expecting in the slightest. Turned the entire game on its head for one last hurrah and it's for sure something to experience for yourself.

For what is basically house house's second game, This is a swing out the yard by a long shot. It's an absolutely amazing game and I'm so glad that it didn't just boil down to an actual friendslop game. There's actual cooperative substance here. Other games that are "friendslop" can all be done alone and don't neccesarily require a friend to play, but they amplify the social experience of the game. This game takes that socability and rides it to the moon, exploiting it to make it an enjoyable experience for everyone playing.

Genuine GOTY 2026 contender, not even kidding.

Big Walk, a simple game about walking and talking with your friends.

Our group of goofballs stomped around the island finding puzzles and mysteries galore. Every puzzle felt hilariously creative, with new ways to test the cognitive ability of the so called "genius puzzle masters" I call friends. Whether it was rubbing glass, punching shapes, flashing gang signs, or chucking time bombs, every puzzle ended with a celebratory frenzy as we impatiently waited for the red (or purple) blob thingy to drop from the vice. The selection of non-weapon-like objects we came across became weapons of mass destruction as we attacked each other with squishy glowing orbs or radios. Some of the best moments from our gameplay were the in-betweens during our "big walks". Being a clueless radio show host while the group made their way to the towers, playing catch with our newfound red thingies, kicking each other's items off cliffs, dancing at music festivals, and being bored together for 30-minutes in an empty room all came from the simplicity that made this game so interesting. 

Big Walk isn't a game made to entertain you and your friends, it's a game made for you and your friends to entertain each other in.

What a special, amazing, fantastic experience. Not only is the definitely my game of the year, but I think it might be the best co-operative experience I've ever played. Played it with a group of friends who normally just play party games and yell over eachother (you know the vibe), and not only were we all incredibly focused and figuring out all the puzzles in two groups, but at the end multiple people got emotional. I legitimately wanted to cry at the ending of this game as it was just so genuinely beautiful. The entire last section is just absolutely brilliant and elevated it from "one of the best multiplayer games i've played, pure fun" to "a special experience that will never leave my memories or heart".

I can see going into this with the expectation of it being some mindbending puzzle game and being sort of disappointed at the start of the game being pretty easy, but there were some tricky puzzles near the end and we haven't even done them all yet. The game is more about exploration, getting lost, and communicating with friends- mute your discord, use in game comms, and don't be afraid to split up. It truly feels like you're going on a big walk with a bunch of your friends, except the walk is in an island sized "The Site Of Reversible Destiny - Yoro Park". I can't really express in words how fulfilling and special the experience feels in words unfortunately. I'm also surprised at how replayable it felt, since we split up into multiple groups and there's a ton of puzzles I haven't done. Even if you only have 4 players and scale the playercount to 4+, there's many puzzles that only require 2 or 3 people. The island is big enough to get lost in but small enough to find eachother (and there's plenty of tools as well).

The last thing I want to specifically bring up is the absolute love and care put into this game. The characters you play as are so, so, so charming and cute, and it seems that everything was done to make each action they do full of personality. Everything you do has a sound whether it be raising your arms or trying to jump but not being able to, if you AFK for too long you fall asleep and start snoring, if you ALT-TAB or go in the pause menu your eye turns into a square, if you hold a button down and walk away from it your arm makes a stretching noise.... I could go on and on, but seriously, the amount of attention put into Big Walk is stupid crazy. I'm getting emotional again just writing about it, I did not expect something so powerful to come out of playing a game with my party game friends.

[h1] Big Walk is a Big Recommend. [/h1]

There hasn't been a game in a long time that has encouraged unguided exploration, creative communication, and straight genuine fun with any number of friends. Big Walk is so simple, yet so intuitive with its puzzles and world interaction. It's so easy to get lost in this game, but it's also so easy to find each other again through various communicative means using world items or emplacements (like flares, or even the train honk.)

The way the game utilizes communication is so cool, especially when it comes to dealing with puzzles. There isn't always a clear cut solution in how to communicate between each other, so you eventually end up coming up with your own way to tell others how to complete it. Even the most simplest of puzzles becomes so fun due to how the game comes up with new ways to get the curious mind to start coming up with ways to communicate.

The world itself ends up unexpectedly gorgeous despite being simple in nature. The contrast between simple colored buildings and the lush Australian bushland should've been jarring, but it actually ends up being unique and blends into such a nice landscape to explore and interact with. The skybox especially is so beautiful, where me and my friend sometimes end up sitting on top of a tall hill or building, and watch the sun rise or sun set. The way the light interacts with objects in the world (as simple as casting shadows) also lends to a more atmospheric strolls during the night.

[b]Genuinely (*finally finished the game, seriously one of the best games of the year, and of this decade), this is a game unlike any other. It stands out in the co-op genre, up there with the likes of Portal 2.[/b]

[h2]Big Walk is a love letter to friendship. It showcases the truest form of trust and camaraderie between people. And I hope you all enjoy playing it no matter how many people play with you. I played with only one other person, and it was still a grand time. [/h2]

This is the game for the aging discord server, the people who've known each other since teenage years and are now pushing 30. The puzzles are fun, either many requiring you to invent specific communication methods that work for your group. The atmosphere is perfect, which helps prevent the exploration and distance movement from getting stale. If you have the patience for a game that forces you to sit down and chat about the experience, then go for a big walk.

Overall I think it's a really pleasant and fun experience. The sound design of the in-game voice makes it feel like you're in this world with your friends, and it changes the experience of going on long walks or long rides from something boring in a video game to just enjoying being out with your friends. The puzzle difficulty is very easy but requires plenty of communication which means you get to develop a little language with you and your friends and it's fun to imagine how that will be different for others. I only have a few gripes with the game overall:

-First, I'd levy the same criticism at this game that many levy towards the witness... things move way too slow. Even sitting on the ground and sliding is too slow to be worth doing or to be fun. The train should have a variable speed (heck the controls for stop and go already look like a slider!) and the top speed should be at least 2x the current speed. I know the game isn't about getting to the next objective immediately, but the running speed is faster than the train which tells you something.  

-Second, I think two or three of the "late game" bigger challenges that are more involved are a bit much. There are some interesting ideas, but they feel like they are about 20% more tedious than they need to be. 

-Third, major spoilers here, [spoiler]I think the true ending is far more disappointing than the regular ending. I was expecting something more. The emotion of the first ending far exceeded the second one, and I'm not just talking about the puzzle sphere, even the way the game ends with waving goodbye to your friends has much more emotional energy than the true ending. I was shocked to see how much less impactful the true ending was. Instead of reminiscing about the adventure which my friend and I had plenty of time to do on the big walk past the dam, we mostly had less positive things to say as the remainder of the time spent playing the game was doing some of the more involved things that ended up feeling more like chores than fun interactive experiences.[/spoiler]

-Fourth, I know it's a coop game about spending time with friends and working together, but I think games like It Takes Two and Split Fiction showed that occasionally having a little competitive fun can be a nice change of pace. It would've been cool to have a few little competition based optional areas where you can race each other through an obstacle course, or see who can punch the fastest. It doesn't even have to reward you with anything I just think it would be fun. 

That said, there is SO much more good than bad here. I would happily play this with any group, any time. It's just a joy to have a game that makes you really feel like you're hanging with your digital friend group in real life.

Played this when it came out together with 10 friends, and the experience was one of a kind.

And the End, OH MY GOD. The End was maybe one of, if not the best, co-op experiences I've ever had.
