Super frustrating at times, I kept joking with my partner saying it felt like the devs turned evil mid development of the game and went "How do we make the rest of the puzzles as boring and tedious as possible?". Anyway, a positive experience, but I wouldn't recommend. 

I will say that this is definitely a fun game to play with your partner or friends. However, right now, I can't fully recommend it, as there are a few things that made the experience less enjoyable than it could be.

The performance can get pretty stuttery, even on an average-to-high-end PC, especially when you venture deep into forest areas. This seems to get even worse when you go crazy with lanterns/flashlights and start creating more and more shadows. I feel like the foliage could use some optimization as well. I understand that the messy, dense vegetation is supposed to give you that feeling of being "lost," but there is a point where it becomes more frustrating than immersive.

Another thing I didn't like is that the game gives you all these useful tools, but then doesn't really let you carry them with you during your journey. Why can't we carry more tools on our belts? Why can't we quickly swap tools in and out? I don't know if this is the intended way the developers want the game to be played, but not even being able to pull out my own walkie-talkie from my belt or the gourd from my backpack is incredibly annoying, especially when you have to split up for a challenge that requires the team to be in different places at the same time.

This also affects the experience at night. Right now, nighttime feels less like an atmospheric gameplay mechanic and more like an inconvenience because of how ridiculously dark it gets. I honestly wouldn't blame someone for treating nighttime as a nice little "break" to sit back and scroll through TikTok or something.

If the intention is realism, then the glowing eyes on the players already kind of throw that out the window. And if it's supposed to be atmospheric, I think there's still room to make it more enjoyable to actually play through. Moonlight exists, and it does help with visibility in real life, so I'd love to see the developers experiment with just how dark nighttime actually needs to be.

Last but not least, you can get stuck on so many things while hiking up a mountain. I understand that this is probably there to prevent players from bunny-hopping their way out of bounds or reaching places they aren't supposed to, but sometimes you can trip on what feels like a tiny pebble and suddenly your character can't jump or move forward. You're forced to backtrack a few steps and try again. It's a small thing, but it happens often enough to become really annoying, and I think it definitely needs to be looked into.

Other than that, the game is really fun to play with other people. The challenges range from "easy enough" to "what the hell is it asking us to do?" to "just try anything and pray it works," with some genuinely good brain scratchers mixed in. Figuring things out together is definitely where the game shines.

The visuals are also really pretty, especially during sunsets and when morning comes around. Again, I don't have many good things to say about nighttime, but the daytime scenery can look fantastic. The music is another highlight. There are some really good bangers in here, and the soundtrack does a great job of adding to the experience.

If you can overlook the performance issues, clunky controls, and low visibility, I would recommend giving this game a shot if you have a fun group of friends to play with or a special someone you enjoy spending time with.

Hopefully, some of these issues get addressed, because I think there's a really fun game underneath them.

House House had an LLM help troubleshoot a performance bug that they themselves spent time trying to solve and had a Unity engineer spend time trying to solve before they checked with an LLM as a hail mary. This game feels like going to the park or camp with your friends in the best way possible. The puzzles are fresh and don't repeat too hard, the sound design is artful, the level design is fun, and all the lil tools are a blast to play with.

While there are a lot of aspects I really enjoyed about this game I overall thought it was a disappointing experience due to an extremely boring world, inconsistent and repetitive puzzles, and bad traversal

Pros
+ There are some puzzles that are very creative that utilize teamwork and cooperation extremely well
+ Clever progression that doesn't handhold the player and still gets the point across
+ Interesting and unique art style, which is a shame cause I think they didn't use it to its full potential
+ Creative teamwork mechanics
+ Great animation quality

Cons
- My biggest problem with this game is how barren the world is outside of objectives. I know the developers intended for players to make the fun but how am I supposed to make fun out of a world that has literally nothing in it but trees and rocks. I'm not saying there needs to be an activity every 5 steps but just because the game is built around friendship I don't think is a good enough excuse to cut corners with world detail. Literally the only things the world has to offer outside of objectives are chairs to sit in, and speakers that play quiet music. While there are some nice views it gets old quick because of the lack of visual variety, it honestly feels like a tech demo with objectives slapped on to it

- Despite there being some pretty good puzzles none of them will require you to think hard at all and majority of them are way too easy, on top of that you will often repeat the same puzzle just in a different part of the map. There are also some "puzzles" that literally just waste your time but since "friends make the experience" then it's apparently ok. Two examples are where you have to sit in a room for 5 minutes and just wait for the timer to go out, and a fetch quest where you pick up like 20 different things and put them in a wall in no particular order. Thankfully despite a lot of the puzzles being pretty easy they were still enjoyable, I just wish the quality was a lot more consistent especially since puzzles are the only thing to do

- For a game that is literally titled around walking the developers somehow failed in this aspect, your character has some of the worst collision detection I have ever seen in a game, you will get stuck on every piece of geometry which makes traversal feel so janky. On top of this your character cant get up a 35 degree slope without either sliding down or freezing in place, when you mix all of that in with the maps terrain it makes moving around so unenjoyable
Absolute blast with friends, well crafted, and the perfect length such that it doesn't start to feel tiring. Totally worth the one-shot experience.

Big Walk is a game about co-operating. The trailers for this game describe it infinitely better than I could ever, so give those a watch, and you'll have a pretty good idea of what you're getting yourself into. 

It's easy to say that this game is just walking around and solving puzzles, but honestly it's more than that. First off, I would argue that the "puzzles" aren't really puzzles at all. Oftentimes you can spot a solution just from walking around a challenge room briefly. The fun comes from finding obtuse ways to communicate to your friends to work towards the solution.

The gameplay is honestly not anything I can really say I've experienced before in a group, there's a level of teamwork that's required to complete every challenge and finding ways to solve the challenges is unique to every group that makes this game great. Since the challenges require coordination from everyone participating, even if you've done a challenge before, it's still a great time to solve it with your friends, except maybe in a different fashion than you've seen before.

The different tools that you can find around the large open world enrich the experience that much more, since you can use those tools as a form of communication either for a challenge you've run across, or for a way to rendezvous back up with your friends.

All in all, if you have a group to play this with, this is a must-play as far as I'm concerned. Highly recommended!

I don't know how to describe why I love Big Walk so much, but it's managed to become one of my favourite games of all time.

You would think a game about walking around and doing nothing in particular would be extremely boring, but somehow Big Walk is so captivating that it's almost like the most memorable moments of the gameplay is when you're simply walking and talking.

The puzzles are extremely fun and really clever. There were some puzzles that force you to nearly walk across the entire map, and yet the environment is so beautiful and interesting to explore that it honestly doesn't really feel frustrating, but instead almost therapeutic. Many of the puzzles required you to communicate without talking, which were also EXTREMELY well executed and easy to understand what to do, and honestly it was super fun to work out how to use visual cues to communicate.

But in full honesty, the most interesting parts of the game for me were when I got lost from the group and couldn't find them. It was honestly really fun to just explore the map and find places you haven't visited before, and try and find ways to find each other using the tools at your disposal. That, for me, was the best part of the game and I had the most fun trying to find friends after falling down and not knowing where to go.

Big Walk is an excellent game to play with friends who don't know each other that well, as it forces you to find ways to connect in ways you probably haven't thought of before, and yet it executes the puzzles really well and makes them extremely easy to understand. There are also extra challenging puzzles near the end of the game.

I also want to finish off by talking about my thoughts on the ending, and because of that, I will be spoiler marking this section. PLEASE play the game for yourself first. [spoiler]The fact that the game FORCES you to not be able to communicate for the entire ending of the game is honestly such a cool and well executed concept. In the final stretch, your characters are blanked out and lose the personality you gave them for the entirety of the game, now simply acting as husks of the players that still want to help each other succeed. Every single puzzle is unbelievably well executed in the ending, not that they aren't executed well in the rest of the game, but still. And the final goodbye where every player leaves one by one was honestly so heartwarming that it nearly made me cry. I was the first to go, and I said goodbye to my two friends for working together with me, and then I walked into the light and the game ended. Something about that was just so beautiful to me and I honestly think it was a really well done ending for a game like this.[/spoiler]

Overall, Big Walk is an absolute 10/10 multiplayer experience, and I wish I could experience it for the first time again, as those were probably the most fun three days that I've had playing a game with friends in a long time. A huge thank you to House House for developing this game for 6 years, you outdid yourselves, truly.

PS. All of the negative reviews that I've seen about this game are about sound issues, and I can absolutely guarantee that those have been fixed, as the game now adjusts your volume based on how loud or quiet you are automatically.

This game is so good, that I'm gonna make more friends and introduce them to it.

I'm surprised by how well thought out everything seems to be, and I can't wait to explore the island fully with my friends.

review:
Big Walk made me realize puzzles created for three or more players are a rare sight I want more of in the future. The game is heavily focused on strategy and communication, which still works even if you’re typing instead of talking. Some puzzles are much easier with specific tools, but you can still clear them as long as you find alternate ways to communicate.

Speaking of the puzzles, the puzzle design in Big Walk is great, although a bit hit-and-miss. Some involve holding a button while another player goes far away to fetch the pear, or standing still for half an hour. These are rather boring activities considering there were endless opportunities for cooler puzzles, especially ones combining existing elements.

The non-procedural aspect of the game has many upsides, and I’m a huge advocate for thorough level design. But this decision also reduces replayability and doesn’t completely fit the high player count support. Here’s the thing: if you’re playing with a lot of other people, you’re naturally going to split into groups and have to play many times, not to mention convince others to let you go for puzzles you haven’t played yet (which may be very distant from one another).

Something tells me you shouldn’t have to do that in a game built around the thrill of exploration and discovery. The fun part of splitting shouldn’t come with the cost of FOMO. Besides, there simply isn’t going to be enough change to make extra playthroughs interesting.

Yet, what you get to experience once leaves a great impression. And 20 hours of playtime (true ending route) in a co-op adventure/puzzle game is no laughing matter. This let us get acquainted with the gorgeous island and played a big part in our enjoyment of the title, even if we were left with a feeling that some elements deserved better. Holding a button while another player goes far away to fetch the pear, or standing still for half an hour is a boring activity considering there were endless opportunities for cooler puzzles, especially ones combining existing elements.

In many of these multiplayer co-op games, sharing a space with your friends in quirky characters is half of the fun. Big Walk doesn’t disappoint in this regard, and thankfully, doesn’t simply mimic the rest of its genre either.

This might be a contender for one of my favorite co-op multiplayer experiences of 2026. I thoroughly enjoyed every second, and each session went on longer than I had expected. On paper, I expected myself to be amused for the first few hours and get bored, but rather I felt a bittersweet relief upon completing the game with my friends. 

My favorite aspects are the size of the world, the interactive nature of the game between players, and the sheer amount of wonder that came from exploring the world together. And we got lost. Often. The number of times we journeyed to find our missing companions while also being dumbfounded teetered on insanity and hilarity. There's an ambiance that is so calming that it bordered on eeriness at times. Compliments to the sound design for that. (Except for the fixed voice chat issues, which upon playing the hotfix, has been resolved). Having a friend who is directionally challenged get lost for an hour while we try to reconvene and use items found around the world to relocate each other was a wonderful experience. Trudging through a dark forest without a flashlight because somebody misplaced their items was absolutely hilarious. At one point, a friend joined our session late and we only found her because she unknowingly used a megaphone that helped us find her in real time. 

The puzzles. They do not hold your hand, but many heads are better than one. Often times you and your friends will have to come up with a language of your own to communicate solutions to each other, and by the end of our playthrough we had amassed some pretty distinct characteristics for how we relay information to one another. 

My only gripe is that I wish there was more. Often times the novelty of a game disappears after the first few hours but this game gripped it tight with every new puzzle, tower, area, and unlock. We found ourselves marveling at the size of the map no matter what we unlocked. 

I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a game to get lost with friends and looking for a sense of wonder and accomplishment whilst laughing along the way.

In a world where most 2+ player co-op games are functionally derived from Lethal Company - the grandfather of this genre - Big Walk stands out. This is a unique experience unlike anything I've ever played. When a game has you thinking about it after you turn off your computer, you know it's got the sauce. 

Two complaints with this game that you NEED to be aware of prior to playing it: 

1) The voice proximity - in my opinion - is coded incorrectly. As a software engineer I feel qualified commenting on this: it is not difficult, but rather a design choice, to have it be restricted by range.

You will find yourself screaming at people 1 inch too far from you, and they simply can't hear you. You don't sound muffled, they literally can't hear you. This is incredibly frustrating, and really needs to be changed. It is completely possible to have walls (for some of the puzzles) block noise, but not have it restricted by range. 

I am not the first person to comment on this; I also won't be the last. This is a 9/10 game, but can be a 10 if they fix this. 

2) You can only carry one item. Like the voice proximity, this is just un-fun to play with. It's not immersive, it doesn't make the game more challenging, it just wastes your time. It's naive to chalk this up to brain-rot-like patience; if something isn't fun, why have it in the game? Peak is a great example game of what an appropriate item system for this could look like. 

It's worth mentioning that there IS a backpack in this game, but it's also un-fun to use. The person wearing the backup has little-to-no agency in the set-up, and it's also not intuitive that "the small yellow ladder" is a backpack. 

I share my frustrations in this review - and still highly recommend the game- because this game is awesome despite these glaring issues. This game is worth the price and such a novel idea. Mad respect to the developers; they broke the mold for this one and created something awesome they should be proud of.

Great game, and absolutely recommend it for the right group of people.

First the "bad". The audio balance needs adjustment, both in terms of how loud people sound by default as well as in terms of the voice fall off that occurs over distance. The default sound for voices is a bit too quiet, and the falloff is too quick. Devs are apparently working on these and will hopefully render this portion of my feedback moot in short time.

The good is that the game is really engaging between players and brings about a lot of joy from solving puzzles together. I feel like a genius at times when solving a puzzle... and a dunce at times when I can't. So far it's striking a perfect balance. The part that has made me feel like a genius the most is less about how the actual puzzle is solved, but interestingly, it's more about how the communication is solved. At a high level, many puzzles have a similar pattern: person/group A has solved and knows the answer to a puzzle, and person/group B must receive and input that answer to receive the reward. How you communicate the puzzle's answer over distance and/or without vocal audio and/or without visuals is where I have loved this game the most. "When I do this on the left, it means X, but if I do this on the right, it means Y", or sometimes, "If I put something here, it means 10, but if I put it here it means 5, and finally over here it means 1". Those types of self-defined rules for communication are amazing! Because it's completely unique to whatever group is playing the game and not simply repeating a single set of mechanics that the game has chosen for you.

The exploration bit does require that you let go of the dopamine part of your brain that says a game must be thrilling at all times, but if you can do that, I actually enjoy traversing the land. In my case, I'm playing with a 10 year old and a 7 year old. The 10 year old makes the puzzles and traversing a blast. The 7 year old makes me want to rip my hair out and never play with them again. That is, until dinner time when we explain to mom what we did and how funny it was that things didn't work out, and I realized that the moment to moment was indeed frustrating, but the memories that it created between myself and my 7 year old are honestly quite precious to me now. That dinner conversation changed my perspective on playing with them, and I looked forward to attempting (and did attempt) more.

All in all, if you're a person who is looking for a puzzle solving game with downtimes in between, and a game where inter-personal relationship building is understood to be one of the game's "features", then this is a wonderful choice. Highly recommended.

[b]The Big Walk is one of the most inventive and genuinely creative co-op games I’ve played.[/b] House House has somehow taken the simple idea of walking around with your friends and turned it into an entire adventure built around communication, exploration and shared problem-solving. You’re dropped into a beautiful, sprawling world with no great urgency beyond figuring out what the hell you’re supposed to be doing. You walk, you explore, you stumble across strange puzzles, and gradually you start developing your own language for the world around you.

What makes it special is how deeply communication is woven into the experience. Proximity voice chat means your friends disappear when they wander too far away, or echo through tunnels, while walkie-talkies, megaphones, binoculars, flares and whiteboards become essential tools for working together. The puzzles themselves are clever, but the real fun comes from figuring them out [i]with other people[/i]. You’re constantly stumbling into little moments that couldn’t have been scripted.

And that’s ultimately why [b]The Big Walk is so enjoyable with friends: the friendship is the gameplay.[/b]

Falling down a mountain and scrambling around in the dark looking for your gear, spotting a friend’s flare in the distance, inventing names for things — these are the moments you remember. Most multiplayer games give you something fun to do [i]with[/i] your friends. The Big Walk feels like it was designed specifically to let you [i]be[/i] with your friends.

Big Walk is a refreshingly chill game with friends. It throws you into the Australian outback and captures it beautifully, with an almost photo-realistic look while still having its own charm and a question of why are we here and what is that?

At its core, Big Walk is a sandbox puzzle game where "the fun is in the journey". A simple "let's go over there" quickly turns into "oh, what's this?" and you wonder off. You're constantly getting distracted by something new, and that's kind of the whole point.

The puzzles are challenging and require communication in various ways, but they're not so difficult that becomes frustrating. The game feels beautifully paced too. Finding new places and things is always engaging, with everything spaced far enough apart to make exploration feel worthwhile, but never so far that you start losing interest.

Big Walk doesn't push you forward or punish you for taking your time. It just lets you explore at your own pace with friends. No death. No timers. No pressure. It's refreshing.

You could very well just walk around forever if you really felt like it, and it's that non-committal sense of freedom with friends that makes me happy when playing it. At no point did I ever feel any sense of pressure to progress, only curiosity every corner. We could be heading towards something, get completely sidetracked for half an hour, and it never feels like we're playing the game "wrong".

Big Walk also succeeds at allowing multiple types of players to enjoy the game together. There's the problem solver, the helper who carries the group's items, the jester keeping everyone laughing, or the person who doesn't necessarily have much to say and just likes being there and existing with the group. Everyone kind of finds their place without the game forcing them into one.

This game is best enjoyed going into it without knowing what to expect. Avoid spoilers if you can, let yourself explore the world with friends, get distracted, and see where the journey takes you. Big Walk!

Big Walk has got to be the biggest surprise of 2026 for me, so far at least.

The premise is so simple: Get some friends together, Go out and walk, talk, solve puzzles, and just have a general calm and chill time. Now you take that and apply to that to the puzzles and you quickly realize that using your voice might not be the best way to communicate to solve them; it builds this magical moment that crescendos into that sense of relief and celebration once you and your party finally solves it and progress through the adventure. And that's the thing, there is JUST adventure - no story, no annoying npcs, no monsters, nothing. Just you, a massive island, and your best buds, friends, or maybe someone you just met for the first time.

House House knocked their simple pitch right out of the park with Big Walk and my only suggestion to them is PLEASE let "Jumping Voices" (the song that plays in all the trailers) fade in and out every now and then, maybe during those longer treks or during those harder puzzles. OH and a broader puzzle system that randomizes the puzzles on the island and maybe a workshop for the community to create and share their own puzzles, definitely need more replay value for such a joyful game.

review:
There is something almost magical about the sound that plays when you finally place the puzzle reward into the slot and unlock the key on the tower. After all the effort of solving the puzzle, that single moment feels like the game is rewarding you not just with progress, but with a tiny piece of satisfaction. The soft mechanical click as the reward settles into place, followed by the sound of the mechanism activating, creates a feeling that is strangely difficult to describe. It is crisp, deliberate, and perfectly timed.

The sound itself feels like a conclusion—a small musical punctuation mark at the end of a puzzle. It makes the object you have been carrying feel important, as if the game is acknowledging, Yes, you did this correctly. Then, when the key is revealed on the tower, there is an almost ceremonial quality to it. The combination of the visual reward and that satisfying audio cue makes the entire interaction feel far more significant than it technically is.

It is the kind of sound that makes you want to do the interaction again simply to hear it. There is something deeply satisfying about the way the pieces come together: the puzzle is solved, the reward finds its place, the mechanism responds, and the key is finally yours. It is a tiny moment, but it captures exactly what makes good game design so satisfying—the feeling that every action has weight, every solution has a reward, and sometimes, a simple click can feel like an accomplishment.

my biggest gripes:

- lack of earlygame inventory management
- movement is clunky, unpolished, and clashes with gameplay - it sucks to walk in the walking game
- the botw shrine loop where you go to easy puzzle four or five times in order to get mcguffins that unlock another mcguffin in order to progress
- mechanics that the developers have doubled down on despite player feedback indicating that they are not giving the intended experience (a la proximity voice)
- lack of accessibility features. which really, really annoys me
- the general developer mentality, which seems to be controlling the experience to be the same for every person with little to no room for individual adjustment you can see this in their lack of sliders for volume, lack of accessibility features, and the way they patched the low volume issue [which was adjusting an automatic system to normalize mic audio instead of letting players do it themselves]. it is very frustrating and shows a lack of trust in the players)
- not enough walking, ironically! and when you do walk, you have to fight the walking mechanics
- game mechanics that contradict each other, like needing multiple people cooperating in order to do many things (backpacks, customization, puzzles) yet getting lost being an intended feature that happens to every player so they can explore alone and work to find the others
- day-night cycle being very fast and completely fucking you if you're without others and don't have a light on you
- dead world. i see the comparisons to breath of the wild, which i've already made here myself, but a jarring difference between the two is the lack of fauna in this game. there's no environmental storytelling, and the artstyle is done without reason beyond the simple concept of looking artsy and quirky. i was not invested in the world of this game at all, and the bright, geometric structures both served as a beacon encouraging players to run to it (which contradicts Walking and stumbling upon things) and as a tell that this is a video game that exists to be played. it looks like the old roblox starter place worlds with a realistic world that had random bright geometry sprinkled on it by a kid figuring out how to use the studio.

A fun start that falls off quickly - and becomes a frustrating mess by the end. 

If you've seen the trailers for Big Walk and thought that it looked interesting, then you've seen all there is to see. The quirky methods of long distance communication and collaboration showed off in the marketing seemed fun. Signs, radios, pointing lasers, and moving your arms a bit - that's all you ever really do. 

And that itself would not be a bad thing, but in tandem with the extreme lack of puzzle variety, and you end up doing variations of the same puzzle only made slightly more frustrating each time. The only way the game ever finds a way to get "harder" is by hindering your communication with other players more and more, and the devs clearly thing the very minimalistic arm movements you can do are capable of expressing fare more than they actually can. 

Not to mention the fact that most of the geo/models/assets that create the walkable terrain seemed to not be manually clipped AT ALL, and instead are using the default UE clipping method of using the model's exact shape. This results in CONSTANTLY getting stuck, trapped, hemmed, or hung up on terrain, rocks, corners of rocks and mountains. Which are, unfortunately, pretty much 90% of the map. One of the MAIN pathways up to the Blue Tower features a rock path you are meant to ascend like stairs, and not a SINGLE TIME in our session did we pass it and someone not end up stuck. In a game ABOUT WALKING, I feel as though consistent walking should be a standard.

Perhaps most frustratingly of all is the amount of sounds that seem PAINFULLY DEAFENING when other players are dreadfully quiet. I closed this game with a migraine due to a very specific frequency being played for a long period of time. Excruciatingly long. Longer than you are imagining when I say this.

Ultimately, the ending of the game proved to be so frustrating and boring to play for reasons I will not post because of spoilers - I'd say pass. It needs time in the oven to finish, and by the time it is, some other trendy new game will be friendslop of the week.

Big Walk is a game that I would recommend for players who have a close group of friends/family to play with, this game plays better with the more people you have. The entire island that Big Walk takes place on feels as if every inch of the ground, to the sky, has been carefully detailed for you to get absolutely immersed into. To the sound of the sand squeaking beneath your feet, ambient noise of the Australian inspired outback setting. The visual of the sun rising, setting, and the massive amount of stars that dot the night sky. This game has had a lot of sincere care and detail put into every nook and cranny, and it's evident as the game progresses and players discover more.

The gameplay is similar but not exactly the same as any "friendslop" that has come out in the past years. Calling this game a friendslop would be a horrible mislabelling. This game requires a more personal approach to the methods of gameplay that is introduced. Try being bored for a bit when you play Big Walk, just sit down and look around, talk to your fellow friends about what you did this weekend, or show them the cool item you just found when you wandered off in the wrong direction. When you boot the game, it shows a disclaimer every time stressing the importance of NOT using any third party voice communication. The entire game is going to be based on using your voice, and whatever forms of  alternative communication you may find in the world around you. More and more, as you play, the players may find themselves using movements and behaviors that just feel, human.

And that's the difference between Big Walk and friendslops, the human behind the actions you make in the world. While sometimes you might get lost, split up, that's all apart of the experience. Sometimes you'll see hidden objects, buttons, pathways, that maybe someone else didn't find. Maybe someone is already noticed you went missing from the group, and they're trying to find you? All while you're doing this, perhaps a bright flare will light up the sky, signaling that the party is on the search. A laser pointer? Maybe you can use this to let the rest know where the next step of the puzzle is. A megaphone? Now half of the island will able to hear you, better hope it isn't night time, though. And then, when everybody regroups, we can all have a Big Talk about what to do next, or maybe just sit and wiggle our arms around, point at the map, kick some radios around, play catch, or just wait around for the train to arrive to the station.

And honestly, some of the puzzles in Big Walk is unlike anything I've ever seen before, and it only compounds upon itself as you get better at communicating with your fellow players. The end game puzzles, are some of the most memorable moments I have ever had playing video games. I cannot recommend enough, play this with people you care about.

Thank you to House House for spending the last six years polishing this game to be exactly what we wanted it to be, it was worth the wait and we can't wait for whatever is next to come for the studio.

Our friend group had high expectations and were disappointed after only 45 minutes of play.

This game is advertised as a creative focused experience around talking and walking. We did not find either to be entertaining. The player audio in the game is inconsistent and hinders communication instead of facilitating it. Other players may not hear you when you are standing right next to them. Movement also seems off. Your character moves at one pace and is only able to traverse the mildest of inclines. This lead to the open world feeling claustrophobic and reminds me of an early 3D console game.

If the slow movement brought you to interesting places that would be a saving grace. However, the four player opening area is a linear series of simple puzzles. Each puzzle has exactly one obvious optimal way to solve it and will more than likely require most people in the party to complete it.

For example, there's a button placed up high on a crane. When pressed that button releases a required quest item. A friend and I were separated from the others and spent 10 minutes trying to solve the puzzle by ourselves. We picked each other up and tried to press it but we were too short. We also tried kicking balls at it, shooting it with a flare gun, and throwing each other up. None of those were "valid" ways to solve it. Instead we had to turn around and wander around the starting zone yelling into our microphones in hopes that our other party members would hear or see us so we could all go complete the puzzle.

This was the gameplay loop for our entire time playing it. Wander around, split up, find a puzzle, try to solve the puzzle solo or as a smaller group, realize it's not possible, try to find all the other members, go back to puzzle, solve it in one minute.

It's commendable to go for a different vibe than similar co-op games, but it still needs to be fun.

It's the best co op puzzle game. Absolutely no contest. You and all your friends are all placed on an island with no goal other than to explore and have fun. Every puzzle you encounter *will* challenge your cooperation and teamwork skills in a consistently interesting and satisfying way.
The atmosphere reaches heights of playfulness and lows of gentle calm, with their frequency depending on how large your play group between 2 and 12 players is. 

Whether you'll get a bang for your buck playing this game mostly depend on how willing you are to enjoy the journey over the destination. The small celebrations you have when you complete a particularly tricky puzzle or when you finally spot the small part of your group that split off from you 20 minutes ago, for example. Moments like those are equally, if not more valuable than the actual extrinsic moments of major progression through the game. House House have created the perfect sandbox for you to create some of the most memorable moments you might ever have in a co op game, so I'd highly recommend you treat it as such.

Criticisms about the barrier to entry being too steep; needing to have several friends pay $20 for access, for instance, are not totally unfounded. This game isn't going to be for everyone, but in a time where so many of us do enjoy socialising over voice calls, Big Walk seeks to take those connections you already have and only make them stronger.

To put simply: if you have the money and the number of people necessary to give this game a chance you'll wind up enjoying a once in a lifetime experience. It's that simple.

I was struggling to think where I actually stood with Big Walk but I have definitely got my monies worth and I will explain why I had my reservations near the end. 

Big Walks Puzzles focus on group communication and how you interact, puzzles are intuitive and focus on group dynamics to solve them. As you'd expect with the name there is a LOT of walking involved which gives plenty of time to chat the game away and fill that time. The puzzles do scale themselves based on the number of people playing from 2,3 to 4 as far as I understand. I have done a lot of 3 player and a little of 4 so far.

The part that really left me smiling and satisfied for me was the end puzzle. No spoilers but I think it tied together everything so well and it was a really fascinating moment in gaming I have not had for a while. I came out of it smiling and it was really interesting to play.

The reason I was a little on the fence is actually partly a me problem but partly a game problem. 

Firstly the game problem: The walking. For a game centred around it, it can be quite clunky. Odd hitboxes especially around trees, Rocks trapping you in awkward positions and sometimes getting stuck on pebbles. It goes from feeling like an adventure to just feeling a little frustrating. 

The me problem comes down to the Big part: It feels almost slightly too big, especially around the endgame (hunting those last plumbus's). This gives plenty of time to have a chat and enjoy the scenery and such, however it makes it play verrrrry slow. The other forms of transport are equally as slow, for example you can out run the train. I feel like it might need to be a little faster. But hey that's okay! Its just not my personal taste but with the right folks it can still be enjoyable.

To conclude, I would recommend Big walk to those with groups to play with or even partners, its a very interesting game with genuinely amazing calm music and the puzzles are good fun to work out. My only hang ups are really my own personal taste and seeing the same puzzles with similar group sizes but I don't feel as if it was designed for multiple play throughs, and that's okay!

On one hand, a Unity engineer told them it wasn't possible after consulting with other Unity engineers, and so the LLM use was a last-ditch effort. The usage was tiny in comparison, and required so much "extensive" modification that one could argue it was hand-written.

On the other hand, hiding LLM use is an issue. Environmental impacts and award eligibility aside, knowingly concealing LLM use is admittance they knew it would affect sales and cause backlash. Moreover, concealing it only opens up further questions; if they were both willing to use it and willing to hide it, who can say if their late disclosure is actually the full extent of the LLM use? They claim everything else was made by their team, but how can consumers know if that's true since they already kept the now-admitted usage a secret for months after launch?

On the secret third hand, a user on Bluesky figured out the issue House House was having with Unity [url=https://bsky.app/profile/steve-coan.bsky.social/post/3mzxaenu7fs26]in 3 hours without a LLM,[/url] which really begs the question how it was an insurmountable issue to begin with.

While I respect House House for admitting the LLM use to un-nominate themselves for Independent Games Festival awards (unlike others until after they win), the lack of transparency upon release has me now feeling mixed and deceived, and it poisons the studios reputability. Big Walk is a fantastic game with friends that is sure to spawn clones and other similar games in the near future. The LLM usage for a seemingly unsolvable issue is disappointing but also understandable (though I wish they had just delayed it to fix the issues themselves). I'm mostly disappointed that such a wonderous studio of creatives has fallen into the same category as other studios that used it in secrecy (or, indeed, at all) until they were forced to come clean.

I absolutely adore this game. It has been such a treat to play through this game to credits with a close friend of mine (though there is still more to do, and we'll get back to it after a short break). If you are going to play this game, you should go into it as blind as possible. Stop reading reviews, stop looking up gameplay, just grab your most reliable friends and jump into it together.

With new releases, I often fall into the trap of looking up walkthroughs to know which choices to make, how to optimize my builds, etc. etc.. It's how I like to play a lot of modern games (and I guess older games, too, back when physical guidebooks existed). I never once felt like I had to do that with Big Walk (and the game is too new for walkthroughs, anyhow), and I wouldn't have wanted to, either. 

There are an endless amount of "aha" moments where you and your friend(s) figure out a solution to a puzzle, or a way to communicate with only a limited set of tools or, in some cases, without any tools or speech at all. The landscape of the game is set up in a way to invite curiosity and exploration, and unlocking more ways to traverse the terrain feels like a real, hard-won achievement. It's a very rewarding experience.

Just an absolute joy from start to finish. The friend group I played with was I think a little more industrious than most, wanting to move from objective to objective pretty quickly, but there were still plenty of fun moments of discussing what we thought was coming up next, what could've happened to that party that split off a while ago, what we thought was going on with some of the more mysterious aspects of the game, or simply marveling at the beautiful environment design. 

And for the number of puzzles that are in the game, the design is really tight. Most were just the right level of complexity for us: a moment of bewilderment upon discovery --> followed by piecing together the goal or mechanic --> followed by seeing what was blocking us from accomplishing that goal --> followed by coming up with our own (often unique feeling) solution and then celebrating together! It also rarely felt like we were out of our depth or had somehow stumbled into a puzzle we weren't ready for yet.

The ending was truly magical as well, and, for our group, it really lived up to all of the goofy speculation we were having while exploring. I don't know if others will have such a strong reaction, but for me, it was one of those once-in-a-lifetime gaming experiences that I'll be thinking about for a while. Really tied together by the stellar soundtrack.

A few things: in the 4+ player mode, having around 5 or 6 people can be a little awkward. A few of the puzzles are designed strictly for 4 people, so you end up having 1 or 2 friends just sort of standing off to the side or just kinda helping without really being engaged. I think around 7-8 players or above, this was less of an issue since things start becoming more chaotic and you tend to have people split off into 2 or 3 groups that go out and reconvene later.

There were also a couple puzzles that our group wasn't really a fan of. Usually it was because we found the task tedious or were having difficulty figuring out the end goal or primary mechanic. These were in the minority, though.

review:
Big Walk is one of the most creative games I’ve ever played.

The biggest highlight is the co-op gameplay. You find different pieces of information and tools scattered across a massive map, and every puzzle feels completely different from the last. Some require only two players, while others need the entire team, leading to hilarious and spontaneous moments. When something goes wrong, it’s frustrating at first, but you’ll almost always end up laughing about it.

Communication is the heart of the game, and because of that, I think the in-game voice chat could be better. The microphone volume is a bit low, and there’s no option to adjust each player’s volume individually. Thankfully, that’s an easy fix with the Big Voice mod.

Speaking of mods, another one I consider almost essential is Big Actions, which lets you equip your backpack and belt by yourself instead of relying on another player. It was even made by a Brazilian modder. Shoutout to Shiblabi for creating it.

The visuals are simple but beautiful, colorful, and full of charm. For some reason, they also gave me a nostalgic feeling. The soundtrack is fantastic, playing at just the right moments, and the sound effects do a great job of enhancing the atmosphere.

If you prefer games with constant action, this might not be for you. Even so, I’d still recommend giving it a chance. One important tip: play with friends and use the game’s built-in voice chat. Avoid using Discord, TeamSpeak, or any other external voice app, since that takes away a big part of the experience the game is designed to deliver.

Overall, Big Walk does exactly what it sets out to do: bring friends together to explore, solve creative puzzles, and share a lot of laughs. It proves that a game doesn’t need realistic graphics or overly complex mechanics to be unforgettable. Sometimes, keeping things simple is exactly what makes a game special.

Score: 10/10

review:
I cannot fathom how this was in development for six entire years. For a game built around walking and talking, both mechanics feel underbaked. Thanks to no audio sliders, you cannot hear your friends beyond a range of about four meters. You cannot tell me this is intentional. Unless you travel glued together in a clump, you cannot speak to them whatsoever. This means you spend most of your time completely isolated, as you backtrack across the map, watching your inaudible friends 7.01 meters in front of you also struggle to tackle the strangely sticky terrain with their toolbox of an anaemic jump and an egregiously slow walk speed. 

Not that you would have anything to talk about, anyway. The world is a homogenous expanse of forgettable terrain, with some random brightly coloured buildings pasted on the map here and there. There are no animals, or any form of stakes whatsoever. There are no interesting physics based items to troll your friends with, and even if there were you can't die or lose progress. I recognise this is intentional, and the game is designed to be very chill, but it made the game so boring. I don't think the scenery, graphics, or sound design is strong or varied enough to justify the game solely being a walking sim; especially when traversing is so uninteresting. There is no climbing, no real sense of exploration - as you end up sliding off terrain that looked entirely walkable whilst looking for shortcuts, and the map is gated off by key. I would much rather face more creative puzzles that actively engage with the terrain, water, platforming or even mazes, when unlocking sections of the map.

Some people say the fun is when your group meets back up after splitting up, and retell stories of your adventure, 'holding back laughter'. What laughter? If you're not too mesmerised to speak by the outrageously large crosshair sitting in the centre of your screen, your conversation will go as follows - 'Yeah I held a button down for about 4 and a half minutes whilst Jimbob, entirely out of earshot, walked to a lit up location and collected an item'. What a right barrel of laughs. Whilst the puzzles may very well get harder further into the game, the initial puzzles were blindingly obvious to a degree that was almost insulting. There was no sense of gratification to being the first to solve them. I spent 40 minutes clearing through the opening section and beyond, and about 10 seconds of that was spent actively figuring out how to solve the puzzles. You can ease your player base into the core gameplay loop whilst still respecting their time and without treating them as simpletons. It genuinely feels like a game designed for top of the bell curve redditors. 'Me and muh awesomerino wife and kiddo played this and WOW what a heckin' wholesome chungus experience wowowow GOTY!!!'. I think after a few patches (especially with regards to performance, I have a 2080ti and i9 and it ran quite poorly), it will be worth grabbing on sale. I don't really get the current glaze status for this game, if you want to talk with your friends whilst doing BS just play some miscellaneous roblox games for free.

2 hours in - I don't have a big group of friends, I've played (so far) exclusively 2-player co-op with my partner.

EDIT (25 hours later, one full 100% completion playthrough with my partner, another 60%-ish ongoing playthrough with 3 of my college roommates): 
+ Audio sliders added, so the first negative below is eliminated. Kudos to the devs to a) fix the audio in a week or so, FIRST, b) add the requested slider option a few weeks later, and c) do all of this while preserving the heart of the game - "you have to be near each other to hear clearly" really is necessary - if you play the game, it makes sense that it would kinda break without this limitation.
+ The entire endgame sequence is one of my all-time favorite moments in gaming, up there with completing Outer Wilds for the first time in the way that it genuinely had me tearing up without ever once beating me over the head with "THIS IS WHOLESOME - YOU SHOULD CRY NOW" - instead it had me tearing up in appreciation for the experience and the realization that it was now coming to a close.
+ Replayability is interesting - AND I truly think this is a game like Outer Wilds that is not TRYING to be replayed over and over and over. That said, you could absolutely play this multiple times without affecting the experience too much, in my opinion, as long as you are playing with a group where the majority of the group has NOT played before. That's because while yes, you will know the solutions to the puzzles, the actual "puzzles" themselves are more about communicating information than understanding it, so it still requires communication and teamwork that will be different from group-to-group even if one person "knows what to do". The endgame is so good that I find myself thinking of different groups of non-overlapping people in my life I'd like to play with next.

Getting the "negatives" out of the way first:
- Same as nearly everyone else has said, your first reaction is going to be "wow everyone else is quiet" - it's true, and the devs also said they're working on some options there. BUT - playing with my partner, within about 5 minutes we were both completely used to it. It's clear that the game was built on having to be very close by to other players to hear them, so that puzzles requiring you to work around a lack of voice comms actually work.
- It's not the *smoothest* game I've ever played, but turning the graphics from High to Medium instantly took my framerate from a sort of unstable 45 to a rock solid 60+. It's also not a game that really needs ultra-high fidelity graphics, the art design works perfectly well still.

This game is fantastic - I think that for people who [b]haven't[b] played it, it's easy to fall into the trap of "great, another friendslop game". I get it, but the design of Big Walk means that the actual feel of playing it is different from other (also fun) games like Peak, Lethal Company, Content Warning, etc. etc. etc.

Big Walk is much slower paced than those games, and it's very clearly not designed around the slapstick "funny gaming moments". It's more of a hangout space meant for you to work together with people you like just chatting with, and in the middle of all that, you'll be working through almost icebreaker-like puzzles that require you to work around the game's communication distance limitations in different ways by pointing, signaling, using tools, making a plan in advance, etc.

^This is where the fun in Big Walk is, and why it's obvious that the game changes drastically with the number of players playing, but not in a bad way. In a 2-person experience with my partner, it's very focused - we travel together to the different puzzles, and usually the puzzles require us to split up or lose voice comms in some way to complete - we complete the puzzle, meet back up, and go to the next one. In a larger group, it's clear fun dynamics could emerge where you might split up more often - two groups of two solving different puzzles across the map - maybe you have voice comms to let each other know when you're done and where to meet. Or maybe, one group accidentally kicked their walkie talkie off a cliff, but the other group has no idea that happened. You wander around for a while before eventually happening to meet back up at an obvious POI, and chat about what happened, maybe coming up with a new backup plan for how to get back in contact.

These sort of natural communication moments [b]and the world design[b] are what makes Big Walk feel special. Wandering the world feels natural, and beautiful, and whimsical. It's a place that you don't really mind getting lost in (even if you get separated from your friends) and that makes the moments when you meet back up feel rewarding in a subtle way.

Additionally, while certainly it will lose some replay value after playing through once, for a puzzle game, I see it having far more replay value than usual, especially with different groups of friends. The puzzle solutions are (thus far) not remotely difficult to figure out - the emphasis is much more on the "how" - how are you going to communicate the solution back and forth or execute on it - such that different groups of friends will almost certainly have different emergent experiences solving them, even if all or most of them know the puzzles and solutions ahead of time.

At $15, it's an instant buy (for me). Even at the regular price of $20, you'll have a game that you can meet up with a group and spend a few hours in every week for multiple weeks (my partner and I are 2.5 hours in at the time of writing and have explored maybe 15% of the island at absolute most while basically beelining every puzzle we find).

The game is incredibly boring and full of stuff that hasn't had longer than five seconds of thought. For starters, your character is incredibly slow and it's so mundane traversing the world which in itself is a mighty uninteresting environment. You can eventually unlock a train at, what I assume to be, the half way point of the game. It's just too bad the train is somehow slower than the player character in full sprint. Furthermore, there are items in the game to encourage you to split up as a group such as radios and flares, however, most puzzles require all four people (if you're playing with four) to be present and take part in the puzzle. Some items can be useful though such as the flashlight helping out with the day and night cycle which in itself is a terrible idea in my opinion and adds nothing to the game. Don't try to drop more than 5ft with an item though because you will drop it and it will get lost, a terrible feature. In addition, dropping more than 5ft will cause you to be stunned for about 2 seconds, unable to move. It doesn't sound like an issue in theory but when you've played for 5 hours traversing the terrible map, it becomes a frustrating nuisance that just adds nothing of value to the game. Finally, the puzzles. Some of them are fun and interesting and some of them absolutely suck. One puzzle included sitting in a room doing nothing for 5 minutes. That's right, the video game that I paid £12 for restricted me from doing anything apart from sitting in a room talking to my friends which I can do in real life or in Discord, for free. Other puzzles are just super easy or boring and don't require much thought. Which is exactly why I think they suck, the developers put a lack of thought into this game.

There are some good aspects of the game though such as charming music and in true friendslop fashion, it does manage to be an enjoyable experience with friends. However, I think it is a terrible game and a waste of money that I do not recommend buying or playing. There are games 10x better that you can play with your friends, not this slop.

Lastly waving a Big Goodbye to your friends you just spent hours walking with, working together, laughing, getting annoying with, occasonaily getting seperated, and charishing those moments together, as you walk into the light and complete the game is such a beautiful way to end the game.

Planning together how you will tackle a problem, interacting with the world in interesting and intuitive ways is so pleasingly executed.

The audio drop off at short distances felt intentional and acceptable, increasing the chances of becoming seperated from your friend and so again nudging you to use one of the many ways the game allows you to become unlost. It's a system that encouranges you to roll with the game as it evolves in front of you and it is SO rewarding when you let it.

Big Walk is a game about going on a journey with your friends. You'll solve puzzles that require teamwork, find items to aid in your adventure, and unlock new places to explore. That loop is very fun as long as you're sticking in groups. Puzzles can be adjusted to be solvable for 2-4 players, but you can play with more people than that. There is no matchmaking or split-screen, and I don't think either would be a good fit for this game, so you'll need to have friends you play with online.

At the moment there are two flaws. The first is the volume controls. The game uses proximity voice chat, but other players are sometimes too quiet when compared to the ambient volume. A recent patch has resolved this issue to my satisfaction, but other's may still have issues.

The second minor flaw is the lack of replayability. While I think this game has plenty to do the first time around, future playthroughs will be less fulfilling unless you enjoy speedrunning or taking a more watchful role with a new group.
Super fun to discover new things, appreciate simple moments, and spend time working and messing around with friends! Highly recommend

House House has created something truly special a game that proves you don't need constant action to have an amazing multiplayer experience with you and others. When compared to 'friendslop' games like lethal company or Peak, the focus here is on the friend and less on the slop - much more of a slow burn than a whacky zany experience. 

I think the entire game is based on communication - you need to be able to communicate and work together to solve puzzles and navigate. Communicating from a distance requires some signals with light objects, laser pointers, fireworks, flares, etc. Communicating up close is generally talking but also can be pointing or squatting when in a muted room. I'm pretty neutral on these mechanics; because it is the mechanic, it is inherently difficult to communicate because otherwise there wouldn't be a challenge. But in a game with all my friends, I kinda like being able to communicate ... more easily? I found when I played it was easy to get separated or have the distance dropoff be too severe to hear (feel like I always need to shout or be right next to them) so ironically there isn't much talking. 

Light is also quite important as the day night cycle is very persistent. It creates a good atmosphere but if you don't have a light source and are in the overworld, then you might as well go on your phone because it will be very difficult to navigate and you can't really group easily to move on to puzzles.

I never write Steam reviews, but this time I feel like I genuinely have to. I’d been following the development of Big Walk for a while and had high expectations. I was imagining something similar to Peak—a challenging co-op ascent where the group has to split up, making full use of long-distance communication. The concept of using arm gestures, megaphones, lasers, and walkie-talkies looked awesome on paper. But while it has a few cool ideas and funny mechanics, like being able to carry your teammates or a couple of mildly entertaining mini-games, the game completely misses the mark.

The biggest issue is that the core long-distance communication mechanics are practically useless. The challenges almost always require everyone to be in the exact same spot, so you never actually separate from your group. In practice, proximity voice chat is all you need, rendering all the special communication gear totally redundant. You just end up doing mini-games—some of which are tedious and frustrating—without the game ever utilizing its most unique feature.

On top of that, the map is cluttered and horrible to navigate. The island is painful to trek on foot due to endless rocks and dense terrain, the only transport method (the train) doesn't work at the start, and when night falls, you literally can't see anything. There’s a complete lack of clear instructions or objectives, so you just spend ages wandering around without understanding where to go or what you're supposed to do.

Overall, the game feels empty and boring once the initial novelty wears off. You just drag yourself through an impassable jungle to chain together aimless tasks. I played for 3 hours, and my only regret is going past the 2-hour refund window. It is absolutely not worth your time, and I wanted to warn people so they don't waste €19 on a mess like this.

Recent game releases at the time of this review might prompt you to immediately think "Oh, well here comes another friendslop game", but OH BOY would you be wrong to think such a thing. 

Big Walk not only avoids every cliché friendslop-esque mechanic and gameplay loop under the sun but somehow manages to turn playing a game with your friends into creating an extraordinarily memorable story full of experiences you will reminisce and laugh about with them for ages to come.

Whether it's coming up with different methods of communication to complete particular challenges - through voice chat, gesturing, and the items available - frequently leaving you breathless from laughter, or maybe it's figuring out a way to meet back up when the group gets split up, desperately trying to get the attention of anyone who has the slightest chance of noticing your presence by any means, or even simply just getting lost and going on a Big Walk to explore on your own, everything you do in this game feels fulfilling in one way or another.

I not only fully wholeheartedly recommend this game, but I implore anybody reading this to pick it up and give it a try with any number of people because my friends and I cannot believe what we've just experienced.

review: best puzzles ever

There will probably never be an experience like this for quite some time to come.

In all the hostiles of life and the constant struggles, holding onto your friends to find that enjoyment in life despite it all is a staple of making it through. And there are many amazing ways that you can enjoy the time with your friends.

This game is something different. It is a beautiful, hand-crafted experience made by people who know how to take advantage of communication, of that bond between your friends, and highlight it at every moment. It will teach you who is the best as navigating. The best at music and representing it.  The best at executing motions, the best at providing ideas when talking is off the table. The best at solving complex situations, at piecing together the strands the devs leave you.

The gameplay is fantastic. There has not been a puzzle we have yet found annoying or unenjoyable. Everyone has something they enjoyed the most, but everything flows together that it was so hard to put it down on the first night. It does not need to hold your hand, you can just... go. It won't lock you in to any path. Just go, explore, and enjoy it. It is your world to play in.

But the gameplay isn't everything. The world they created, wordless and speechless, somehow begs for you to explore it. The first time you discover the way music guides and marks your journeys, the way you find seats pointing to beautiful scenery and makes you feel a need to sit there with your friends, to simply slow down and embrace it. 

When was the last time a game has made you stop and appreciate something so simple as a sunrise in strange architecture, listening to a melody that is indescribable and yet calming, peaceful? I even went back on my own, just to sit at the site of this music, just to relax and meditate for a while. Maybe that's absurd, but this game has brought a peace like nothing else.

Try it. Grab your friends. Don't spoil yourself on the exploration, be as blind as you can. And laugh, enjoy, play. Just have a good time. This game will be unlike anything else, and everyone deserves to bring their friends into an experience such as this.

First game in a long time to take a leap forward with co-operative game design, very few games set out to reinvent the wheel and fewer succeed. Big Walk has definitely achieved both with its twists of communication between players and freedom to let you get lost and stranded from your friends. There's no invisible rope tying you together, there's nothing stopping anyone from walking off in a random direction to get lost from the group, and there's nothing that tells you where to find your lost friend. This is what sets big walk apart from most multiplayer titles in its genre, fulfilling the promise of an open world through the lens of co-operative design. No doubt we will see many studios inspired by Big Walk in the coming years.

The Big Walk, or Making a Small Friend Into A Big Friend

Whether it's chemistry or spiritual voodoo, nothing will ever beat the energy exchange between two people who meet face to face. The Big Walk comes really damn close. 

Nick and I

The Big Walk is a (big) walking simulator with puzzles and a minimal narrative peppered in. You are thrown into a room that explains everything you can do (unlike life) and when you are ready, thrown into the decent-sized open-world to go explore (just like life). 

While you can roam around by yourself, you'll quickly need a helping hand to progress. At least one, a couple if you can. I played it with my friend Nick, who I met just a couple of months ago in Kyoto, and we hung out every day of the Indie Game Conference BitSummit. Nick then went back to Chicago while I stayed in Asia. That's fifteen hours of time difference. He's sorting his life out, I'm heads-down building things by myself. There isn't a lot of opportunity to meet up.

But present us with a videogame world to explore and an opportunity is suddenly created.

Nick's more of a Hades / Monster Hunter gamer and The Big Walk isn't something he'd normally pick up. I expected an hour, maybe two, before he called it quits. Yet by the time we were finished, ten hours later, he had gone through the same transformation people go through when they've scaled a small mountain. He needed a good one on one social time, a good hang. Something that used to be more available offline.

Videogames are a perfect third space

"Third spaces" are where people socialize, think cafés, bars, restaurants, parks, gyms and so on. While these are still around, the culture of many third spaces has been "optimized" by big data thinking, leaving dehumanized self-service kiosks, robot baristas, and the doom itself, eyes boring into the smartphone. 

Videogames had their own third spaces in MMOs like Runescape, Guild Wars or WoW. Similar to The Big Walk, you could wander around by yourself, but really the genre shined when you befriended other people. The sociable fantasy city trade squares filled with people "/y WTS POTIONS" were replaced with monetized Roblox slot machines and italo-slop brain dumb scooby-doob-doob (don't ask me I don't know either).



Earlier this year I conceptualized a game/app ONMTN, which grew out of an idea about sharing audio messages to maintain long-distance close relationships. That idea evolved into a digital hiking game where you walk, talk, and leave messages along the way. The Big Walk does extremely well in validating my thoughts. Thanks for that.

Another genre The Big Walk could be incorrectly likened to is friendslop, due to the game's simplistic presentation and focus on friend-play. Friend-play. Where friendslop games put simple but deep game mechanics into repeatable environments for players to keep coming back, The Big Walk is one singular thing. A Big Hike you go through once, and you remember it for the moments along the way. It still invites streamer-friendly moments for their wholesomeness rather than absurdity, annoyance and rage. There's no rage in the land of the bright blue, yellow and green.

The colorful geometric shape-filled puzzle island offers situations and tools to ease the journey's troubles. From making it easier to talk and find friends across distances, carrying more than one thing, or finding each other in the pitch dark, the player is never penalized for just having a good time walking around.

The charming neighbour

Now the game at its release is beloved by critics, and I can understand why. It has that nature hike effect, combined with the case of the European girl/boy next door charm. Looks distinctive, sounds unique, but then you see the cracks past the platonic interest: unrewarding dead ends to exploration, one-dimensional transportation unlocks, a narrative sewn in last minute. 

The Big Walk is an adventure you do together as a group. Somehow it is both easy and difficult to find people to go through the whole island. As your group shifts, yet the puzzles remain the same, you don't want to bring in any more people. 

Case in point was a random person who joined about two hours into our game. I'd left the game open for others to find us, but as we progressed further into the island, Nick and I didn't want to have puzzles spoiled by random people jumping in. We ventured together but found it less enjoyable because it felt rushed. When Mr. Rando disconnected, we were happier for it. 

Smile like an idiot

The Big Walk feels like a genuine work between friends who enjoy playing together. Nothing in the game feels forced, maybe misplaced or unintentional, but never aggressively produced to force my attention for a little bit longer. I'm just a big-eyed stick-sphere dude carrying my gourds, in a playful kindergarten-colored environment, enjoying the nature. My motor skills involve bobbing knees, hand gestures and sitting down to watch the beautiful rose-colored sunsets. 

The final stretch of the game has cast the widest smile on my face in a while. After the full-day session, Nick and I had acquired an absolute synergy. I didn't need to talk, he didn't need to talk. We gestured with hands, but understood each other perfectly even without it. One by one, each puzzle of the game fell quicker to our bro-bond. Can you imagine that perfectly choreographed fight scene in any Marvel movie? That was us. Right up to the very last goodbye wave to Nick, I was the sticky-sphery doo-doo dude until I too passed through the white light beyond The Big Wall. That's all it takes for people to meet and connect across vast distances.

Big Walk is a love letter to the co-op puzzle solving genre. It perfectly captures how chaotic communication can be while formatting puzzles in a way that, with calm minds, is suited for a group of friends to organize the chaos. 

This game shines when it takes away your normal means of communication. Its varied gestures allow you and your friends to find out how to breach complexity in outside the box ways. I had been waiting for Big Walk for a long time, and the trailer had completely captivated me, not just for the mechanics and what it was promising, but also for that charming blend of cartoonish characters set against realistic environments. The trailer promised a new social open-world game that would let people connect with each other, have conversations, explore the world together, and maybe even get lost trying to find their way back to the group.

The moment I downloaded the game, I found every single one of those promises fulfilled. The mechanics are delightful and feel remarkably grounded, and I genuinely caught myself giggling like a kid picking up a controller for the very first time. I had an absolute blast exploring every tiny detail: the realistic light and shadow as soon as you switch on a light, finding myself in complete darkness during my first night (something not every game bothers to get right), listening to the ambient sounds, interacting with the world around me. Then I invited a friend for the first time and heard him talking in the distance, only to lose him completely, his voice going muffled the moment I stepped inside a room. And the first time I shouted and heard someone shouting back at me from the mountains, I genuinely got startled, before realising it was my own echo. This game has ECHO! It's something extraordinary, the level of detail and love the developers have poured into this game.

(I can't wait for the low voice volume issue to get fixed. I've already seen you're planning to address it and I'm really grateful for that.)

And don't even get me started on the dynamic sitting animations. When your character sits down, their legs adjust to the surface beneath them. I once sat on a ledge and found my character's legs dangling in mid-air, and another time I sat on some steps and my feet landed exactly where they should on each step. These are details made with genuine love. Another example: when I started pointing at my friend, my character's hand was colliding with every single collider on each section of the other character's body. These are the little things that most people won't even notice, but that tell you exactly how much the developers care. The puzzles are genuinely sweet and very intuitive, and the fact that they're scattered around and hidden makes the whole thing even more intriguing.

Moving on to things I'd love to see in the future. Since the day/night cycle already exists, it would be absolutely wonderful to have variable weather as well. Imagine being in the middle of a light rain while chatting with friends, listening to the sound of the drops around you. Thunderstorms would be incredible too, they would make the most of the dynamic audio system you've already built. Just picture hearing a distant rumble of thunder, seeing the flash first, and then hearing it echo through the mountains.

It would also be amazing to have progressively larger worlds, perhaps with the option to choose bigger maps that allow groups of up to 12 players to genuinely get lost in them as if it were a jungle, finding fun ways to signal their position (which the game already does to some extent). It would also be great to have different types of puzzles that change with each map, both to prevent new players from spoiling the experience for others and to stop people from just memorising solutions, giving everyone a fresh chance every time.

I also know it's not for everyone, and I know that every game that has implemented it has ended up requiring a huge amount of work, but it would be wonderful to have public servers, allowing other people nearby to join and connect based on ping and real-world location. Getting lost and stumbling upon strangers in the game world would be something truly special.

I honestly have so many more ideas, but I've noticed you don't have a Discord and I have absolutely no idea how else to get in touch with you, so I'm using this review not just to recommend the game, but also to catch your attention a little. ♥

In any case, I wish you all the best and thank you again for this wonderful game. 
I can't wait to enjoy new experiences and new additions!
