In their recent book Which Way Up, which I have admittedly not finished at the time of this writing, Jay Foreman and Mark Cooper-Jones point out that our age of always knowing how exactly to get where you’re going, we miss out on the spontaneous pleasures of getting properly lost. This is the kind of sentiment that I feel two ways about. On the one hand, you’ve got the truth that being lost often straightforwardly sucks. Regardless of any valid criticism of the rigidity of our systems, getting lost and going on an adventure can have absolutely dire consequences, and is sometimes just plainly irritating. On the other hand, they’re absolutely right. There is something to be said about being able to navigate a space without being guided, and of figuring out where you need to go from basic tools and then getting there. 
My phone is about one million years old and runs out of battery all the time. It’s gotten to the point where a friend of mine brings an external battery whenever we hang out (especially if I’ve forgotten my own external battery) and makes a running joke of it. Technically, I don’t need my phone to be charged all the time. Most of the time, I know where I’m going, because I live my life close by a major public transport network, and there are very helpful street signs pointing towards the metro blocks away. But sometimes, your battery is just dead, and you need to get from a station to a different station a fifteen-minute walk away, because the line you wanted to take is down for maintenance. 
So you figure things out. And I did figure things out, even if I walked so far in the wrong direction for a bit that I ended up in the next town over. A map in a park, and just good old intuition, with the help of a dim memory of Google Maps before my phone died, meant I not only made it to my destination, I then had a story to tell. The best part was, since I’d given myself more than enough time to get there, I wasn’t even late, and there really were no negative consequences. So even though getting lost was annoying, giving myself the literal time and space to get lost meant I went on a little adventure and was none the worse for it. 
Big Walk opens with a note telling you that you shouldn’t talk to your friends using an out of game VC, because this is a game about talking to your friends. What it doesn’t say, but does strongly imply, is that Big Walk is fundamentally a game about being lost. In real life, being lost in the woods with no way of contacting the outside world is so stressful it feels almost redundant to point it out. Big Walk’s position in the ‘friendslop’ genre of video games means that by definition, this stressful context becomes a zone of play instead. The world is photorealistic, but you and your friends wear silly spherical avatars that cannot be permanently injured and only die when you stop inhabiting them. Big Walk extends an invitation into a ludic space where disorientation, confusion, and discovery are all fun. Because it’s a game, because it’s not real in the same way a city block is real, the carefully crafted island of puzzles and toys finally gives you the time and space to be really, properly lost.
A non-insignificant chunk of my own playthrough of the game has so far involved sitting next to isolated radio broadcasters, desperately calling to see if anyone can hear me. Whether on a tower at the top of the world, or in a halted train near puzzles, these moments of pure isolation, where my only connection to any other living human was a radio, felt incredible. I had no idea when anyone would return, or what they would bring with them, but I knew they were going on incredible adventures, and that when they came back, they could tell me about them. 
I can say for certain that no one in my group has had an entirely identical experience of Big Walk so far. Indeed, one of our friend’s had such a unique experience that whenever it comes up, people immediately start posting Odyssey memes. He was lost for what felt like hours, and even though he wasn’t in any real danger, what was real was the elation and relief the rest of us felt when he finally found a radio and was able to tell us I am here. I am alive. I am coming back. 
(That is the surreal element of a proximity chat-based game like Big Walk. The minimal UI includes no indication of who’s online, so there’s no real way of knowing without breaking the magic circle and messaging them elsewhere that someone’s logged off unless they tell you they’re doing it or someone else passes the message along. Or you can find their empty body. That’s always a possibility. I was half sure we’d find that friend dead halfway down a ravine. Death, loss, the unknown—you can feel all of those, safe in the knowledge that the friend on the other end of the vc isn’t actually dead, isn’t actually lost, isn’t actually alone.)
“Friendslop” at its worst is a genre stuffed with games that are themselves not particularly deep or good or mechanically complex, but which are a fun way of passing an evening with friends who aren’t close enough for twilight softball. Big Walk is absolutely in the same genre, but it’s a much more carefully curated experience than something like Meccha Chameleon.

Big Walk can be played in a way that progresses the game and unlocks things on the island, or you can just walk around discovering things while you chat with your friends. Likely, you'll end up doing both, which is what makes this game so unique. It's an open-world puzzle game and also a walking simulator but one that avoids flip-flopping between the two genres. Instead, it has you embrace both modes simultaneously. 

The decision to model the nature after actual plants and rocks makes the game feel like you're in a familiar place, not on some alien planet. But the solid geometric character models they use for the players as well as the buildings contrast in a way that reminds me of rotoscoped animation from the 70s and 80s where artists would paint over the frames of actual film. For those of us that grew up watching shows like 321 Contact and Sesame Street, there's a nostalgia struck here that adds extra layers to its charm. 
 
While the aesthetic choices alone might be enough to warrant its purchase, there is no lack of solid team-based game mechanisms. They are found everywhere and placed perfectly far apart so just as you've walked in the trees long enough, you come across a colorful structure filled with challenges. The puzzles are very sharp - not hard, but super smart. And their uniqueness will leave you feeling cleaver are rewarded. As long as you can figure out what to do with that gourd you just won.

This minimal movement, low-stim game reminded me what gaming is about at its core. It was the conversations we had while traversing the landscape, carried by beautiful sound design. I hope everyone gets a chance to play this with their friends.

This would be a 10/10 game if the voice audio was adjustable. It's frustrating that we can't carry music with us because it's so loud we can't hear each other. Sometimes even the group's footsteps blast out the prox chat audio. The map is super fun to explore and the puzzles are very satisfying to figure out! Super relaxing, especially given the speed you move around, but it's a great vibe. I also wish I didn't get stuck on so many little bumps and rocks, feels a bit restrictive and clunky to get stuck on the geometry for a game with so much exploration.

In any social setting with more than like 5 people, it inevitably breaks down in to groups of 2 or 3 talking to each other. Big Walk recreates this naturally with the directional voices and splitting up. But it also keeps you connected enough to coordinate across groups with radios and laser pointers and lights, without making these individual cells in the groups too noisy.

The controls are simple enough and accessible, and everything requires some form of teamwork. So far playing in groups ranging from 6 to 8 and I love it! Breaking off into groups of 2 or 3 and coordinating shit is natural and fun, the exploration feels rich and rewarding.

I've had a great time getting lost with friends and feeling a little closer after a half hour of being lost in the woods together. So far this game is everything I wanted it to be and more. It's such a unique experience. I can't wait to play it more!

I am diagnosed with ASD (Autism Spectrum Disorder). I have a hypersensitive nervous system, and I tend to enter flight or fight and shutdown very easily when I'm in said response. This makes it tricky to find a game I don't easily give up on, despite me being very good at gaming compared to the average person.

I also have difficulties with socialization, which can make it hard playing with others and enjoying our time together, especially when there are so many stressers in other co-op games or the Friendslop genre which tend to be long-term roguelikes out of the ones in my library.

Big Walk is the first game that never really triggered my nervous system, and actually helped alleviated a lot of stress through the intuitive mechanics and atmosphere, which made beating it with a friend of mine one of the most blissful and fun experiences I have had with a friend. The environment at every degree is handcrafted to be one big hug.

When I first played, I was too focused on completing things, which stressed me when nobody else cooperated. However, when I realized very early on that the game was just about the people you are with, it eased me into something I just didn't want to leave behind, especially at the end of the main game. 

I WILL be coming back when I play with more people. Thank you for this wonderful game House House!

I saw some streamers playing this and thought it was right up my friends' alley. We generally love puzzle games, and have been looking for some longer form puzzle games. Between us we have MacBooks, Switches, and Windows systems so it can be weird trying to find cross-platform games. We played for 5 hours our first session of the game and it's so fun! I thought we might have had trouble with the in game chat since we usually don't use in-game audio, but even the slightly derpy audio quality hasn't taken away from the game.

This game has potential for being really good, but honestly it just falls flat for me personally. The lighting is terrible, so when it becomes night you literally cannot see anything (Why the hell do you even need a day-night cycle in this game??). But they do provide tools that provide light! Only problem is that it takes up your only held item slot, so they become a bother. Another issue is the voice chat range being far too short and quiet, I literally cannot hear my friend that is less than 2 meters away from me. This makes it very difficult to complete puzzles unless you carry a walkie-talkie which also takes your single held item slot. They also provide transportation within the huge map, but of course they are locked behind several puzzles that you have to complete. The game seems very fun and different, but it just doesn't seem to have the player first in mind.

My Playstation friends recommended we try this game because it's free rn for PS Plus. I am so happy I went in blind because it's one of the most fun gaming experiences I've had in years. Untitled Goose Game creators was enough to get me on board + cooperative + crossplay but I cannot describe how charming the game is. This game made me actually happy and less cynical about gaming. Everything about it felt classy, intuitive, and simple mechanically but with great depth underlying. The respect for both the design and audience was constantly noticeable - from how easy it was to play on crossplay (a simple lobby code and no garbage additional launcher or account required to market my data), all the way to the sound design and visual splendour. This game was clearly made by people who get it and not losers who just wanna market to those sold on shiny graphics. It's pleasant to look at, doesn't feel too frustrating; just enough to have a nice learning curve and to value collaboration and teamwork. It oozes charm - which is rare these days. 

It felt like a real hang with friends playing a new physical game; like a board game or a lawn game, because it requires spatial awareness and sticking together, triangulating, resource management, communication, or survival parameters. A real nice mutual learning experience. So refreshing from games that feel procedural or aesthetically hollow (Arc Raiders). A truly happy experience. I am rambling and repeating myself but me and my 2 buddies with entirely different lives, tastes, and priorities are all sold on finishing this with an actual schedule and plan to do so. Madness! Kudos! Clearly made for the love of the experience. Totally earnest in all regards. Game has soul and is inexpensive or free. Felt like a great hang with buddies. Would be a very nice game to experience with someone new to games or if you had a kid age appropriate. Establishing your communication, landmarks, rendezvous points, etc all so creative and rewarding!

Talking about the bad first, the voice system goes out in what seems 5 meters away making getting lost very easy, which is both fun and sometimes troublesome. You can't change each player sound, or even music, sound effects, and the likes. The train you unlock through the game is a slower option to walking, maybe giving the players the choice for breaking AND accelerating might be a good solution. The only thing that made me frustrated was the getting stuck on what it seems everything. sometimes, walking near objects, paths with rocks, or jumping too short makes the character stuck. 
Now, talking about the good. Every single system design in game makes it an absolute joy to play. I had the pleasure of playing with friends as well as acquaintances, and although we are not that close, it was an absolute blast! We didn't finish every puzzle and we are sure to come back!! THE SOUND DESIGN IS AWESOME! Every little step, every slap/punch on surfaces, dragging your hands through the material makes different noises aiding in the immersion in this simple character design. Since the beginning of the game that cooperation is necessary. For you to be able to change your characters appearance you NEED at least one other person to help you out. It truly embodies co-op in every single aspect of the game. THE GESTURES are a crucial part of the game play. They bring such life to these puppets. As a little spoiler, the end of the game is the best part in my opinion, it blends a bit of every major thing you and your friends did in the island so far, and the actual end hit me in a way i was not expecting at all. 

TL:DR: The game could have very little improvements in my opinion, but its a GREAT, and I repeat a AWESOME experience. As a lover of escape rooms, it was magnific.

Big Walk is a cooperative exploration game developed by House House and published by Panic that reimagines multiplayer adventures by placing communication at the heart of every experience. Instead of focusing on combat, survival, or competitive objectives, it encourages players to work together while traveling across a vast and colorful world filled with puzzles, hidden locations, and unexpected discoveries. The game's relaxed philosophy emphasizes shared experiences, making every journey feel like an adventure created by the players themselves rather than a scripted sequence of missions. This refreshing direction allows the game to stand apart from many modern multiplayer titles by rewarding teamwork, curiosity, and creativity above all else.

One of the game's defining features is its immersive communication system. Voice chat is seamlessly integrated into the gameplay through realistic proximity audio, meaning conversations naturally change depending on where players are standing. Friends can hear one another clearly when close together, but voices gradually fade with distance, echo through large spaces, or become blocked by obstacles. Walkie-talkies and other communication tools help reconnect separated teammates, while certain gameplay situations even require players to rely on gestures and body language instead of spoken words. These mechanics transform simple conversations into meaningful gameplay elements, making every decision about where to go and how to coordinate feel engaging and authentic.

The world itself is designed to reward exploration rather than speed. Every path, landmark, and hidden corner offers opportunities for discovery, encouraging players to slow down and appreciate their surroundings instead of rushing toward objectives. Environmental puzzles require observation and collaboration, while the handcrafted landscapes invite players to experiment, wander, and uncover secrets together. Rather than overwhelming players with constant objectives or endless collectibles, Big Walk creates satisfaction through natural exploration, allowing memorable moments to emerge from spontaneous teamwork and shared curiosity.

The collection of interactive gadgets further enriches the adventure. Players can use items such as binoculars, laser pointers, flares, megaphones, cowbells, whiteboards, and other unusual tools that serve both practical and entertaining purposes. Some assist with navigation and puzzle solving, while others exist simply to encourage playful interactions among friends. This balance between functionality and humor reflects House House's signature design philosophy, where amusing situations often develop naturally through player experimentation instead of scripted events. Even simple activities can become hilarious as groups invent their own games and solutions while exploring the expansive environment.

Big Walk also offers impressive flexibility by supporting groups ranging from two to twelve players with cross-platform multiplayer compatibility. This makes it suitable for both intimate cooperative sessions and larger gatherings where communication becomes increasingly chaotic and entertaining. Unlike many multiplayer games built around endless progression systems, Big Walk delivers a handcrafted adventure with a clear beginning and conclusion. This focused structure allows the experience to maintain a strong sense of purpose while ensuring that exploration remains consistently rewarding throughout the journey.

Visually, the game presents an inviting art style filled with vibrant environments that complement its peaceful atmosphere. The colorful landscapes, distinctive landmarks, and thoughtful environmental design encourage players to slow down and enjoy the scenery while naturally guiding them toward new discoveries. Combined with immersive audio and subtle environmental storytelling, the presentation creates a world that feels alive without relying on excessive visual effects. The overall atmosphere reinforces the game's emphasis on friendship, cooperation, and shared experiences, making the environment just as important as the gameplay itself.

Big Walk may not satisfy players seeking fast-paced action, competitive challenges, or complex progression systems, as its slower pace and cooperative focus require patience and an appreciation for social interaction. However, for groups looking to experience a unique adventure built around communication, exploration, and memorable shared moments, it delivers something genuinely distinctive. House House has crafted a multiplayer experience that values meaningful interaction over constant excitement, resulting in a game that feels both innovative and welcoming. With its imaginative mechanics, charming presentation, and strong emphasis on teamwork, Big Walk successfully offers a fresh take on cooperative gaming.

Two friends and I played the game together. We have now completed the game and are going for 100%. It was a lot of fun, but we still found ourselves reliant on walkie-talkies. Between us, we were able to carry five gourds before having to make a trek back, and we had to keep the day and night cycle in mind. If we wanted to travel at night, four was the most we could manage, while we could carry five during the day.

The puzzles are a lot of fun. Our group found them easy to solve; the trouble came from working out a communication pattern. As most puzzles make you mute, it was mostly just a lot of arm waving. However, we had something worked out by the first puzzle and improved over time. The last puzzles really put this to the test, with all the arm waving and thinking of patterns to explain shapes, as well as yes and no to the other players.

Here's an example:

Left arm flat out = far left
Left arm up = left centre
Both arms flat out = middle
Right arm up = right centre
Right arm flat out = far right
Both arms up = high up

Always work from left to right as well, and keep in mind that if all else fails, just use yes/no head waving and do one at a time.

I do feel, though, that if you have several people in your group with main-character energy, you might struggle, just because of the way the puzzles work. You really need someone to take the lead while the others help out. I can see a lot of problems forming simply because everyone is trying to solve a puzzle in their own way at the same time and getting frustrated. But that's to be expected with some group dynamics. Just remember to share who leads each on each puzzle.

I will say one thing I don't like: the tunnel network. It removes a lot of the walking and talking, and makes things feel very point A to point B. It also takes away a lot of those “Oh, I found something!” moments.

Yeah, the tunnels have some nice secrets, but at the end of the day, they're a massive shortcut to all the towers. The thing with the chairlift and train is that they're very slow, but they give you an amazing, chill time to just sit back, talk, and enjoy the journey.

Overall, House House, you have made an amazing game. Hats off to you!

I'm playing completely blind and so far it's very enjoyable. I was expecting some good friend slop with replayable runs (something like Peak or Lethal Company), but what it seems to be instead is something closer to a multiplayer Outer Wilds or an open world We Were Here game. Pick a group you'll be happy to play through the whole thing with, and hopefully the schedules work so none of you miss out.

A separate volume slider for voices would be handy. I understand the intention is to stop us from hearing each other from too far away - and trivialising some communication - but I found the rustling of my feet through grass was louder than the people right beside me. We can all turn up our own mic gains in our system sound settings, so why not just allow us to do the same in game and not mess up the rest of our setups?

After about 7 hours with a friend, I can honestly say this game completely exceeded our expectations.

We had The Big Walk on our wishlist for a long time because we're absolute suckers for these chill co-op indie games. Walking around, getting lost, solving puzzles, and just messing around with your friends without the game constantly telling you where to go? Sign me up.

Turns out... it's actually even better than we expected.

The whole atmosphere is just awesome. The graphics are simple but somehow super immersive, the world feels peaceful and welcoming, and it genuinely feels like you're just out on a hike with your friends. No pressure, no sweaty gameplay, just exploring this massive island and trying to figure things out together.

The puzzles were another huge surprise. They're all handcrafted, feel really natural, and never made us think "that's just stupid." Some had us scratching our heads for a while, but once we solved them it was always one of those "OHHHH... of course!" moments. Exactly what you want from a puzzle game.

Performance was flawless on my PC too. Smooth the entire time, no crashes, no weird bugs, no performance issues. Love to see it.

I also really like that the game adjusts the puzzles depending on whether you're playing with 2, 3, or 4 players. That's such a nice touch and makes me think there's actually some replay value here. Plus, the island is HUGE. It honestly feels like the devs could keep adding new puzzle areas over time without it feeling forced.

Now... there's one thing that REALLY needs to be fixed.

The game is built around prox voice chat. That's literally one of its core mechanics.

So why on earth can't I separately adjust the volume of the voice chat and the game audio?

When we were only about 5 meters apart, we could barely hear each other. We spent the 15min constantly going:

"Wait... what?"

"Say that again?"

"BRO I CAN'T HEAR YOU."

Eventually we gave up and jumped into Discord.

The problem is... that completely defeats the purpose of the game.

A lot of the puzzles are clearly designed around shouting instructions from a distance, trying to communicate with limited information, or even using emotes when you can't hear each other properly. We tried our best not to just speedrun everything by talking over Discord, but let's be honest—it changes the experience quite a bit.

Honestly, if the devs simply added separate volume sliders for proximity chat and game audio, this issue would probably disappear overnight. It feels like such a small change that would massively improve the experience.

Other than that though?

Absolutely loved it.

For €15, this is an easy recommendation if you've got a couple of friends and enjoy puzzle games that actually make you think. It's relaxing, funny, surprisingly clever, and one of those games where half the fun comes from the random moments you create together.

Highly recommended.

(Just... please give us separate voice chat and game audio sliders. 🙏)

[h1] Review after 100% (spoilers marked): [/h1]
Comparisons to The Witness were more accurate than I initially thought in some ways, and less in others.  There are many different puzzle "languages", and I think the game made at least 1 great puzzle from each of the languages.  However, I wish the number of easy/medium puzzles were cut in half and replaced with challenging ones, as there are a lot of unexplored twists/mashups of these puzzle languages.  Perhaps this is something a level editor could remedy?  I'm ready for some truly devious brain benders!  During early game, a lot of puzzles can be "cheesed" (though you could call this creative problem solving), but thankfully the harder puzzles have lots of limitations, which led to more interesting solutions and hype once we reconvened.  The game is at its absolute best when it's limiting your way to do or communicate something complex, which to some will come off as tedium (and believe me there is some tedium), but if it clicks with you and your friends, it REALLY clicks.   

Here were my Favorite, Least Favorite, Pleasant Surprise, and Biggest Missed Opportunity Puzzles:

[b]- Favorite - [/b] [spoiler] Teapots:  The abstraction between the light patterns with the furniture meant you had to take some real leaps, and having the communication be asymmetrical was a cool changeup [/spoiler]

[b]- Favorite - [/b] [spoiler] Music Tiles Without Voice:  Having to use gestures and motion rather than just copying the sounds was fun and actually led to an initial failure! [/spoiler]

[b]- Least Favorite - [/b] [spoiler] Headphones Radio Hidden Box:  Maybe it's that it used the least interesting or memorable radio station.  Maybe it's that there are way too few handheld radios.  Maybe it's that with 2 players, carrying such a vibes-based item would never happen naturally.  Even if we immediately recognized the snoozy soundscape as Radio Station number whatever, if you don't remember exactly where it is, you'll be going to possibly every station before finding the start of the puzzle.  All the while, your mate is just sitting with the on-hold music putting them to sleep. This really should have used a more interesting station that immediately stands out as a radio clue, or included a radio nearby as a hint. [/spoiler]

[b]- Least Favorite - [/b] [spoiler] Waiting Rooms:  Like I get it, you're meant to just talk to your mates for 5 and then 30 minutes, but the whole game was already about that with its slow pace (trains and gondolas especially).  This is the difference between hanging out and court-ordered hanging out. Feels more like a sTrEaMeR mOmEnT room, and we immediately went like "ok lets hit the bathroom / food and then come back".  Waste of 2 gourds, and reminded me of that god-awful Witness video puzzle but without the video. [/spoiler]

[b]- Pleasant Surprise - [/b] [spoiler] Extreme Golf:  At first we were pissed, then we were in denial (surely it's on this purple zone right?), but once we came to terms with the tedium we actually got tactical and locked in.  It's still barely a "puzzle" and not strictly speaking "good", but it was a much more interesting "main game puzzle made ridiculous" than the Waiting Room.  [/spoiler]

[b]- Pleasant Surprise - [/b] [spoiler] Mask Rooms:  These were so uncomfortable to play, but truly felt like the final test of verbal communication.  Preference for the one with tiles and no death pit, which led to a lot less downtime when a mistake would happen. [/spoiler]

[b]- Missed Opportunity - [/b] [spoiler] Collect All The Tile Types: When we found this puzzle, we had already seen all the tiles before, which meant we spent an hour trudging back through the island trying to remember which building had which types, especially the abstract drawings.  The puzzle building designs were not very memorable to me, so we had a good many wrong guesses and full day/night cycles.  In my dreams, this puzzle would appear very early in the game, like near the Red Tower / Main Hub.  Then, as you complete the puzzles, you'd have to remember to take it back to this mashup puzzle (this would require the tile placement to save between sessions).  Taking it one step further, some of the unique pieces could require extra effort to break them out of their puzzle zone. [/spoiler]

[b]- Missed Opportunity - [/b] [spoiler] The Orb Of Silence:  I really enjoyed the drastic twist of decoloring (would be very interesting in larger groups) and no verbal communication, but I felt like the lower difficulty puzzles were too great of compensation.  It should have felt like a final exam, and it ended up being a breezy victory lap.  Paths too simple, and abstractions not abstract enough. [/spoiler]

Original Thoughts:
------------------------------------------------

Possibly a victim of its own marketing or the landscape it launched in, this is a great blending of The Witness and communication based co-op games like Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes.  The puzzles have ramped up nicely from the too-easy tutorial, and the crunchy-ness of the items and interactions really adds to the feeling of adventure.  I am playing as a duo, which genuinely seems like the best way to play and get the full experience.  

[strike] The biggest negative that hopefully gets patched soon:  no volume sliders for anything.  The environment is way too loud, and even when the game clearly wants my partner to be audible, i find myself needing to talk loudly at 2-3 ft range to effectively communicate.  I can't imagine how much more trouble this will cause when 4-12 people with different microphone setups all have to share 1 volume slider with the world's loudest footsteps. [/strike] This is mostly fixed but I would still prefer some sliders to adjust individual players.

100% recommend, play with a small group, take the game seriously, and go in blind for the best puzzling experience.

The progression is more about map accessibility than power ups, which works really well to ground your progress to the map. Speaking of the map, the sound design is amazing here, with really nice audio cues, which is easily the most immersive part of the game. The juxtaposition between realistic graphics for the terrain, and the flat, blocky puzzle and POI areas really draws you in and makes you feel like you're never really lost. I spent a not inconsiderate amount of time just sat on vistas and viewpoints, listening to the sounds and just taking the world in.

There is only one small complaint, which is the overly short range voice and lack of additional rebound when in rooms, making it feel like sometimes you have to be glued to your friends; but that's only a small complaint in what is otherwise a a perfect experience.

After having 100%-ing the game, I am satisfied to say this is probably the best game I've played in all of 2026. Enjoyment of this game is heavily dependent on having a good consistent social group to play this game with. It is all about the social experiences and turning the sandbox that House House has created for us into a playground. The general gameplay is mostly about exploring the island with your friends, driven by the goals of puzzles. Goof off, enjoy the views, work together to problem solve in creative ways. Big Walk is a much needed hand-designed experience in the flood of PCG "friendslop" social games that focuses on reflection of the experiences and memories we have with other people.

That said, I don't think I can sing the praises enough about the beautiful views and extremely satisfying and tactile sounds. THe tradeoff for graphics fidelity is being quite performance intensive, maxing out my RTX 3060 laptop GPU usage on High and above at 1440p. Dropping down to High from Very High and Highest gets me a decently smooth 60+ fps experience most of the time without reducing quality too noticeably.  It is pretty and can really be successfully used as a virtual "third place". Never once did I want to use external voice chat, the world immersion is fantastic. The biggest immersion break is when hitting invisible walls or having awkward collision issues where you get stuck on certain slopes or nature props in the environment.

The puzzles range from easy to medium in difficulty, with most of the solving being a team effort focused, as advertised, on communication. Their co-op puzzle mechanics are innovative and diverse  despite reusing similar elements and the sandbox has so much potential for custom maps and puzzles, which I hope will develop in the mod community. I think this game is a good base with so much more left to expand upon.

Devs quicikly fixed issue with quieter mics that was present at launch. I understand the voice volume drop-off is designed so that you have to be relatively close to hear each other, but trusting the players by giving them the freedom to choose and accessibility is never wrong in a non-competitive play setting. I believe are mods that help remove these restrictions and add customization. I have similar feelings about the lack of a photo mode with which to help capture and preserve memories and be creative with great views.

We knew there would be walking and puzzles and good vibes but were weren't expecting the sheer scale of the mystery we had to unravel. If you liked "The Witness", there is a real sense that this is a multi-player coop Witness or Myst or something like that. Vast and deep and really unexpected in a good way. 

The good vibes are there but let me tell you, getting lost is a rager and much like the australian bush, you can turn around and find yourself alone so easily. This is made even harder by the one gripe I have with the game. The proximity chat is not the best. You can be standing on the same rooftop a few meters apart & barely hear each other. You could be lost in the bush shouting your friend's name at the top of your lungs and they could be literally just over a hill but they won't hear you. This needs to be fixed asap because it is the one thing ruining the game. 

Having said that, sound issues do little to really dent what is a truly awesome coop adventure experience.

Please, please devs. please add more audio control. the sound design in this game is SO incredible, but if people can't adjust voice volume relative to SFX and music, it truly defeats everything you've clearly worked so hard for in this game.

For those of you that are having audio issues, one fix I found was to go in to my device properties and boost mic volume by +10 or 20 db and have everyone playing do the same, which helped. The footstep and music sounds specifically are still very loud and voices are still quieter than I'd like, but it went from totally unplayable in VOIP to playable.

I have played Big Walk for one day and already it might be my favourite game of 2026.  Escape rooms, cosy vibes, hijinks and friendship.  Co-operation is the name of the game and despite how a lot of Co-op games handle things as basically its single player but your mates there on one side of the spectrum or you can play singleplayer but it absolutely sucks, Big Walk makes co-operation mandatory.  Communication is often made so gestures, writing, codes and shouting to each other are the key to solving puzzles, your given tools and an escalation in how these go, and it is an absolute joy to behold.  

The game is visually stunning and stopping to enjoy vistas, talk with friends, bop to some music or get distracted faffing with the world is delightful. as a man who loves a screenshot I hope a photo mode can be incorporated or a camera added to capture particular moments and take selfies with your friends.

Its important to note this is required multiplayer.  No single player content short of just being able to look at stuff.  You are required to bring a friend if you wish to play.  As that's the concept its not a negative but I think knowing this going in is paramount.

ultimately Big Walk is a lot of fun and a lot of charm.  Its surprisingly engaging and I think could maybe fix my parents relationship if I could get them to play it.... or it would just be a recreation of the "Phogs" incident.... 

Also the Crystal Maze theme should play whenever you enter a puzzle room.

It's very fun to wander around Australia with your friends, occasionally doing puzzles or finding loot. I really love that the game encourages teamwork for even simple things; you cannot take items off your own belt or backpack, one of your friends has to do it for you. This adds another layer of cameraderie to a very relaxing and enjoyable experience.

I was actually looking forward to this game.

Before release, Big Walk was absolutely everywhere. Twitter/X, YouTube, social media... everyone seemed to be talking about it. At first I didn't think much of it, but after release it became obvious what had happened. Unlike games such as Lethal Company or R.E.P.O., which became popular because players themselves created funny clips and viral moments, Big Walk was being heavily promoted before anyone could even buy it. Somehow, a bunch of creators already had access to the game and were calling it "10/10" before it was even released. I honestly don't understand how you can give a game a perfect score before the public has even had the chance to play it.

The marketing definitely worked on me. I was interested in the concept and was waiting for launch.

Then release day came... and I saw the price. Nearly €20 for a game where you mostly just walk around with friends. There isn't much of an objective unless you decide to solve a few puzzles together. Why would I pay €20 for that when I can jump into VRChat for free and have a much more varied social experience?

Still, I bought it to give it a fair chance.

The first thing I noticed was the performance. I have a high-end gaming PC worth around €3000, and the game simply doesn't feel smooth. Turning the camera feels stuttery, almost like it's running at 50–60 FPS, even though my hardware should have no problem running a game that looks like this. For a game with such simple visuals, that's disappointing.

Speaking of visuals, I really don't think the graphics justify the price. The environment has a dull color palette that reminds me of much older games, while the player characters look like they belong in a completely different game. The overall art direction feels inconsistent.

Another thing that surprised me is the lack of basic matchmaking. There's no simple way to find random nearby players. The game is clearly designed around having a group of friends, but not everyone has three or four friends who are all willing to spend €20 on a game that's mostly about wandering around together.

I wanted to like this game, but between the aggressive pre-release marketing, the high price, the disappointing performance, and the lack of basic online features, I just can't recommend it in its current state.

Maybe it will improve over time, but right now I don't think it's worth the asking price.

Some reviews are missing the point entirely, so I'll spell it out here: Big Walk is, at its heart, an experiment in spatial and verbal cooperation amongst friends, which it achieves terrifically like no other game before it.

As the trailer notes, there are just two themes: walking and talking. So people moaning about the lack of physics or ledge-climbing or grandiloquent storytelling or whatever else their hyperactive brains conjured up didn't read the description at all. That's gamers for ya!

You might find tools that you will end up using in creative ways to find each other when you inevitably wander off from your main group. You might solve puzzles with unintended solutions in the way that only groups of people can do. The puzzles themselves are not just problems to be solved: they are social exercises that gently test your ability to communicate and organise as part of a cohesive group. 

If you jive with games like Myst, Riven, The Talos Principle or Portal 2, but want to solve puzzles with friends instead of on your own, Big Walk is exactly the sort of experience you are looking for.

Additionally, the rendering is superb in all three camps: visual, technical, design. The island is a marvel to behold, engine performance on my system is flawless so far and interactable objects (of which there are many, this being a puzzle game) are telegraphed clearly without losing the almost fully diegetic design. 

One item of note that may be addressed in the future is a lack of options for a game so heavily reliant on audio. I have a 4-input audio device and Big Walk's settings could only recognise the first input, which required some manual changes to my usual audio channel arrangements. This is not a problem if you have a minimal audio setup (i.e., headset and microphone), which most people do.

The game is fun. A few hours in, and there is seemingly a staggering amount of content so far. But, it has some minor polish issues, and one major issue. Minor grievances include things like getting stuck on ledges and items very easily, with no unstuck button, so you need a friend to come grab you. Audio balance could use some work, some things are very loud, others are a little quieter. Controls feel good, but take a moment to get used to for sure. The game has a good way of letting you figure things out on your own without making you feel like it's holding your hand, while also providing enough context that you don't feel totally lost constantly. A few puzzles are a little more vague, some are a little more clear, and I think that strikes a good balance.

But good god, there needs to be better player audio balancing. The game opens telling you that you should only use in game audio to communicate with friends once you've started, and I think that's great. Except... you can't hear your friends from more than 3 feet away. Even when their face is pressed directly into yours, they sound as quiet as a mouse. There is no separate audio control for environment, music, and player voice. Want players louder? Turn it all so loud you go deaf. Or, suffer through struggling to hear your friends in the game where the whole point is to communicate. Plus, sound is blocked by objects and seems to be directional, to a point? So in a game where you can already barely hear anyone... you have to find basically clear line of sight to communicate effectively. Would be best to pick one or the other, not both imo. I'd prefer if it was just the latter, with voice being a fair bit louder and carrying a bit farther (as it stands, beyond maybe 15 feet-ish, you no longer get ANY audio from friends)

That being said, I partially understand why it's so limited, and you do somewhat get used to working around it. There are a few puzzles where it definitely feels like it's intended to be part of the struggle, having to run close to your friends to communicate your portion of the solution. Unfortunately, I don't think that lends itself to good game design generally. Which is a shame, because much of the rest of the game so far feels very well done and polished nicely. Fix the apparent audio issue, and I would absolutely say this is a no-brainer purchase. The game definitely goes well beyond expectations for me, and I am glad I picked it up.

It's truly an experience yelling at your friends behind soundproof glass for them not figuring out a puzzle or everyone being confuzzled while staring and sitting at a bunch of hieroglyphs. Sometimes you sit, sometimes you watch, sometimes you busy yourself by playing with whatever's around and on hand, sometimes you take a ride, and sometimes you walk. You either do it in oddly tranquil silence or with boisterous, joyful communication. 

The amount of communication this game has you do, by the way, is insane. All the effort put into making it sound great and actually matter as a gameplay element, both in verbal communication and physical communication (signaling with a laser, light, flare, or just your body), is wild, and the team should be proud of themselves. There's some hiccups with the game in terms of performance every now and then (could be memory cache issues and such), and connection issues may occur rarely, but none of it should get in your way, nor should that ever discourage you from playing this with friends. 

When playing with friends, you will definitely want to pick people who have patience, communication skills, humor, and teamwork. If they don't have that, they better be capable of developing it when playing this game because this game will only work in good company that is willing to lean into the angle this sort of game requires. 

The puzzles are very clever, especially as they ramp up in difficulty, complexity, or remix older, earlier puzzles. And, without a doubt, you constantly get satisfaction throughout the stages of the puzzles; you enter the puzzle room/field, you figuring out what type of puzzle it is and its rules/mechanics rules/mechanics, then you figure out a way to start solving it, and then the actual process of doing the puzzle until you solve it, which results in the satisfaction of completing it. You really get into the whole process, and, before you know it, you're talking about how to wring out the puzzle. There's many tools to help you solve them, but the most important tool is going to be how much you're willing to communicate. Do you try to solve it the moment you enter without exiting? Maybe both sides can swap to get the perspective of the other side. Then swap back or mix the group up based on who thinks they can contribute best to what? Or maybe tour the puzzle as a group and then discuss how to solve it before entering it? There's multiple ways to approach it, and most of these will intersect with each other. But you're always going to be talking things out, even to yourself sometimes (as you may get lost or be on one side of a wall without your group).

Without a doubt, this is game is something special and best experienced with your closest friends. It's a real gem that is unlikely to be copied due to the scope of the game and the effort, care, and passion put into it.

Big Walk has the dubious honor of being the first Steam game I've ever refunded, which is a shame, because I really wanted to like it. Instead, I spent a good 85% of my time in the game being frustrated with it.

Movement in Big Walk feels terrible; the walk speed is far too sluggish for the long distances you have to travel, but you can't even break up the monotony by jumping. If you so much as clip a rock on the way down, your controls will lock up for a full five seconds while you slowly and miserably slide to the ground. Flavor win, I guess?

Night-time in the game is extremely dark, which when combined with the restrictive item system (if you want a light source, it will take up your sole item slot) causes a 50% of game time to be fully unplayable.

The sound system is extremely limited. Others have said plenty about the lack of volume sliders and the poor sound quality, but in my opinion that isn't even the most baffling audio design decision. The proximity chat range is so limited that it actively detracts from immersion. You can't hear people a stone's throw away; talking louder doesn't cause your voice to carry farther; when a puzzle requires you to use a radio to talk to someone the next room over, you clearly feel the hand of the developer making your life harder.

The puzzles in the game were frustrating too, but not because they were difficult. Most were trivially easy, but required the whole party (we played with four people) to be present to solve. Many also involved a baffling amount of walking. Yes, I understand the game is called Big Walk, but when a solid third of the puzzles in it are little more than "walk to this clearly demarcated spot" it starts to become a bit tedious.

Between the puzzles and some of the other design choices, it seems clear to me that the game was intended to be played by traveling around in a single dense clump. Played that way, you'll always be able to hear one other, you'll be able to assign someone to flashlight duty, and you'll be able to solve every puzzle you come across as you move around the map.

What that means, though, is that there is no real reason to split up, explore the map, coordinate over long distances, or develop any meaningful form of non-verbal communication. As an individual, the only way you can meaningfully contribute to progression is to just go where everyone else is going and do what everyone else is doing.

For a game ostensibly about exploration, Big Walk ends up feeling tragically mundane.

This is the longest review I’ve ever written. If you want a summary or a tl;dr I’m not going to supply one. The only way to know how I feel is to read how I feel.

“The nature of a Third Place is one in which the presence of a ‘regular’ is always welcome, although never required. Membership is a simple, fluid process of frequent social contact, renewed each time by choice of the people involved. Eventually, social bonds develop through a type of informal intimacy. The important aspect of these relationships is that they occur outside of any commitment and exist solely in the realm of basic human respect. I ascribe huge importance to this one point because it is slipping away from our isolated modern world. I think that we all miss its presence and this affects us all in very slight, painful ways.” - Ray Oldenburg, The Great Good Place

In the Big Walk OST you'll see one of the EPs is called "Fourth Space." These places are a concept coined by Ray Oldenburg that insists upon the need for a Third Place.

Your First Place is your home. It's where you live, where you come back to each day to sleep, rest, and recover. On its own, our first place does not satisfy social needs. With nothing else it is too isolating and confined, and too familiar. And for many people, such as myself in the past, it may be a hostile environment that is hard to live in, and you may find very little connection with those you live with.

Your Second Place is your job. For most people, you don't have a choice as to whether or not to go. It’s mission driven and not really focused on the individuals. You may form loose friendships, and it does connect you to others, but a lot of it can feel superficial. If you only go between your first place and second place, you can still feel pretty alone and isolated.

The Third Place is considered a social necessity. It is libraries, coffee shops, parks, hobby shops, churches, local game stores, bars. This is not just places that are public. It's places where you organize and gather to share common ground and interests. To find connection, people you can bond with. These are places that help you love those around you, and yourself. Everybody needs these places in their life.

Big Walk styling itself as a Fourth Place is a pretty bold statement, but I think it earned that title. The memories I have playing this game with my friends will live on in my mind for a long time. I bonded both with people I know deeply, and people who are in my friends circles, but I may not have known so much. This became a bridge to deepen my bons in ways many games don't. Most games these days are isolating competitions, meant to drive people against each other. Competition can certainly bring a lot of people together, mostly when you look at games’ grassroots communities such as in speedrunning, some fighting games such as Smash. Splatoon which I was apart of for quite a few years has a vibrant grassroots competitive community. But much bigger competitive games like Counter Strike and League of Legends, the playerbases are infamous for how antisocial they are.

I'm not going to say that Big Walk is a necessity in your life the same way a Third Place is. And certainly not every friend group is going to mesh well playing this game. But maybe yours will. And maybe you struggle to get out to your Third Place. Maybe you have social anxiety, maybe you struggle with transportation, maybe you live in a not so great area, maybe you are one of three people living in Wyoming. If you are craving that connection that the Third Place promises, Big Walk can provide you a taste of that.

I find myself tearing up as I write this review. The moments I shared here are deeply special to me. And I love the people I shared it with, and I want to share it with more people.

The way the game provides connections is simple, yet ingenious. The Ski Lift is the one I want to talk about the most. It’s lumbering and slow, I think it might be the same speed as running or maybe even slower, I don't know. It isolated you with one other person for an extended period. A moment of peace you share together. A moment to ask "hey what's up? What have you been up to lately?" You can make small talk or even Big Talk. You have time and quiet peace to do so.

Maybe your group got separated into at some point. And you're riding the ski lift with a bud and from the other direction you catch two other people on the lift. As you pass you exchange pleasantries "woah fancy seeing you here, hey guys" like two pals bumping into one another at the grocery store. And as the natural forces of the ski lift separate you, you appreciate that you got to see them and may wonder where they may be off to next. Moments like this made the island feel vibrant and alive. This is your space, your Fourth Place.

On release day when plans were being made for our group, I had like four different people ask me if I was joining. I told them, "I'll give it a chance, but it seems like just a hangout space? We have a lot of games for that already." I know, right? Get a load of this guy. I'm glad I gave it that chance. There are the puzzles which facilitate play, but I was overly harsh about the game's hangout element. I did not anticipate the game would be so masterful at bringing people together. Throughout my time with it I started to warmly welcome all its hangout spaces that broke up the time in-between puzzles.

In the trailer they are very genuine about what they set out to create. And you might scoff and roll your eyes and think it can't be that big of a deal. That's the reaction I had and that I know many others had as well. I encourage you, however, to stifle this knee jerk cynical reaction. When you play Big Walk I implore you to do so in earnest, good faith. Turn off the part of you that instinctively shifts into cinema sins critic culture. You don't need to reach some quota of bullet points weighing the pros and cons of a video game. Just let yourself be here, now. If you ever let yourself genuinely and purely enjoy anything, let it be this.

Life's messy. Friends are messy. And sometimes Big Walk is gonna be messy. When you find a puzzle already completed by an offshoot group, don't be frustrated that you missed it. Appreciate the sign of life and activity. Imagine your friends in that situation, finding it, and what they must've went through to solve it. All of it an echo of their presence. Just like how you can't be there for everything in life, sometimes you won't be there for everything in Big Walk, and that's ok.

At one point I was riding the ski lift with a friend, and I told him "this game makes me think about Outer Wilds." Not the puzzles, the vibe.

The most beautiful thing about Outer Wilds to me is the Travelers' Song and the signal scope. This close group of friends, this found family, all separated in different hostile environments. They each pull out their instrument and play their part of the song. Anybody can pull out their signalscope, and listen in no matter how far away. And you might not know what they're up to, but at least you know they're out there still, alive, sharing that connection.

In Big Walk every time you find a puzzle already completed. Every lamp left on but abandoned. Every flicker of the laser pointer in the distance. Every flare shot in the air. Every time the radio towers flash green. This is your Travelers' Song. The heartbeat of yours and their presence. The sign that they are out there, and you are here too.

If you scrolled to the end of this review just to see if I left some closing statement that would give you a tl;dr, then I am sorry. If you want to know my thoughts you will have to scroll back to the top and read it all. Because at the end of the day, it's not about just getting to the end, it's about the Big Walk we took to get there.

review:
I was very excited for Big Walk. After playing it for a little over an hour, i have to say I have a few gripes that are legitimately ruining the game for me. These could be fixed, but as of now, there's some issues that need resolving.

- The terrain sucks. I don't know how else to say it. You'd think a game called big WALK would make the walking part enjoyable. Unfortunately, the terrain is so slippery and easy to get stuck on that you'll find yourself constantly spamming jump and wiggling the stick to get out of invisible weird hitboxes with rocks and to stop yourself from sliding down annoying slopes. I fell off the red bridge into the water and was shocked to find there was no easy way back up or even a "respawn to nearest checkpoint" type of feature. Nope, you fell down this big thing so awkwardly walk alongside the ocean rocks trying to spam jump to get on top of them and waste 10 minutes looping around half a mile until you reach a point you can actually get back up then track all the way back to where you were to try again. This doesn't feel very focused on a casual player base nor do I understand how this type of monotonous punishment of falling down is meant to be fun or engaging.

- The day and night cycle. It's way too fast, and the nights are way too dark. This makes the terrain issue worse, because at night you genuinely have about half a foot of visibility in front of you unless you haul around a light source with you the entire time. Lacking a "tool" slot to free up your hands or even just a hands free flashlight really hurts the enjoyment of the game unless you are ready to have someone be a designated flashlight holder. This also affects the puzzle since so many puzzles are visual based, when it turns night, the puzzle becomes that much more annoying to solve unless you have someone carry around a flashlight for you as you try to solve it or you wait till the morning to actually be able to see. 

- The darkness of night has a second issue I thought warranted its own point. There is no brightness adjustment. If your monitor just sucks or you really have trouble seeing in the dark even with the in-game light sources, you're just screwed. I don't know why game devs are so scared of brightness adjustment in games that are supposed to be casual and fun. So what if someone wants to turn the brightness up so high they "break" the game's darkness? It's a casual game meant to be fun for friends. 

- Zero adjustment for volume of your friend's mics and the mics are all quiet. Even standing next to me, all of my friends mics (who all sound fine in any other game / app) sounded like a whisper. Any farther and I just couldn't hear them. Too bad the game doesn't trust you with a volume adjustment. Much better the game which begs you to not use any outside communication makes their in-game communication borderline unusable and gives you NO tools to fix it. Because what if you turn it up too much and you break the game's VERY delicate balancing. Delicate balancing in a causal fun puzzle game mind you.

I don't know. For how long I was waiting for this game, it really was a let down. These things could be patched. I remember in Peak, the launch build had horrible volume with no adjustment and later added it, but until those issues are fixed, I truly can't recommend the game in its current state

What surprised me most was how quickly it stopped feeling like “just a game” and started feeling like moment I didn’t want to lose. My friends and I would wander without direction, split up just to get lost on purpose or by accident, banter over where we thought we were going, and then laugh when we realized none of it really mattered. There were moments where we’d go quiet, not because there was nothing to say, but because it felt like saying anything would interrupt something fragile and good. It made me realize how rare it is to just be with good people. It reminded me how quickly moments slip away, how easy it is to take time with people for granted, and how you never really notice the “last time” something felt that simple and whole.

[h2] Big Walk isn’t just about reaching a destination, it’s about the people you share the journey with, and the quiet, fleeting feeling of wishing you could stay there just a little longer. [/h2]

There's a lot of grim and gruff games out there with lantern-jawed heroes whose only emotion is vexation, and talk like it's Military Cosplay Hour.  This game is all of that.  Wait, no, sorry, I mistyped.  This game is none of that.

It's bright, cheerful, charming, and built explicitly around coop.  No friends?  Make one before you play this.  Even basic interactions require coop.

The visual style is a bit peculiar, I mean the game takes place in an area that's kind of overgrown, there's trees and a variety of plants and shrubs, and they look good.  They don't look 100% realistic but they do look pretty good, which contrasts sharply with the player characters, which are a stack of three matte rubbery spheres, with pipes for limbs and small spheres for hands and feet.

The game itself is about meandering, together with your group, finding little puzzles to solve.  Those puzzles give you these weird lumplings, and collecting (and securing) enough lumplings gets you a key, which unlocks (pun intended) a bit of a key-cutting challenge, to gain access to another area with greater distances and traversal challenges.

These puzzles have not been hard so far, they mostly require communication.  That communication has its own in-game VOIP, and we elected to use it.  Voice attentuation is severe, with voices dropping off to nothing at 20 meters' distance.  You really need to stick together.  You've got a few gestures you can do but they're basic and not very helpful.  Each player can carry one device, which can be used to help keep the team together:  my wife loved lugging a cowbell along, and at one point I'd chant something and she'd ring the bell to punctuate.  The bell's range sounds farther, perhaps 30 meters.  Glowing balls can be seen even farther, and I'd carry one for illumunation at night, until we decided maybe we could sit around during the darkest hours.

There's no reason why you couldn't use Discord instead, but that's not in the spirit of the game.  And, frankly, the spirit of it is what makes it.  Nothing can hurt you.  There's no real time pressure.  Just scale mountains and gaze out over the (well-rendered) sunrise if you want.  We did at the end of our first streaming session.

So yeah.  Supposing you've got some buddies who don't need to play vexed soldiermans, who maybe like a spot of light puzzling, this is very much the game of the hour in my well-reasoned opinion.  Would that I had an auspicious number in my reviews to give it.

(PS:  The streaming links, and my curator URL, is all up in my profile. There may be others streaming and reviewing, but none so cool as us.  Science fact.   I got my PhD in coolology.)

[u]Full Completion:[/u] This game is a relaxing social experience that is now on my top games of all time. The gameplay itself is a combination of the puzzles from Myst and an open world exploration game like Breath of the Wild, but the way the game encourages positive communication, teamwork, and social connection makes it stand apart. I've discovered everything I think the game had to offer on launch, and have many fond memories going through it blind with my friends. However, I recently was watching a giant group of streamers going through the opening of Big Walk, some of them for the first time, and I had this heartwarming moment of watching these friends experiencing that same joy of discovery I remembered having with my friends. It has a tone that it maintains with very little mechanical effort, and that is a masterstroke of game design.

Even as House House's use of LLMs for debugging and troubleshooting has created controversy (as of Nov 2026), I can't help but feel like the human effort and heart of this game shines through brilliantly, and all I can think is that this game would have been as popular as Animal Crossing if it had come out during COVID.

If you have friends who want a chill time in a combination national park and theme park, making digital memories together, this is a must-play!

This review is a tribute to friendship; a tribute to my best and longest friend, Jason. He was really excited for this game and it was probably one of his most anticipated releases. In his honor: 


8 years ago, I met Jason on some silly roblox game, SCP Anomaly Breach. He played as a D-class, I was an MTF. He had been getting repeatedly killed over and over by all the other MTF in our game, except for me. I talked to him a little bit, and we became friends. We played countless games together, shared what was probably millions of experiences, laughs, and conversations. He was my best friend. He was also just a kid. 


We both had issues, and Jason would have a tendency to get very frustrated when things wouldn't go his way. For 2 or 3 years, I tolerated it. Eventually, though, I cut ties with him. Before I had stopped talking to Jason, I had introduced him to one of my other friends, Michael and after we stopped talking, he and Michael grew closer and closer to the point that Michael was the only person he talked to. Things stayed that way for a while, until Michael had re-introduced us again. I'm glad he did. For the next five or six years, things were fine. My memory is hazy, but as far as I can remember, Jason had been around, he would talk occasionally, some days he would talk a lot, others, we wouldn't see him much. 


A few months ago, Jason had seemingly cut contact with everyone. Not i, nor michael were able to really get in touch with him. From what i was told, he only kind of talked to his IRL friends. I didn't think much of it. He had a habit of going silent sometimes, so i brushed it off. Months passed. I began to get worried about him. I wanted to say something but I didn't want to pressure him in case he was going through something. Occasionally, he would send me a song he made and i'd send one back.


As of writing this review, 30 days ago, on July 5, I had gotten a text from him after about three or four months of silence. It wasn't much, he asked about how things were going and what he had missed since. I caught him up. Told him about some new friends I made and that he probably would have liked to meet them. He told me "I probably would". I told him about games i played, i told him about how we were worried about him. I wanted to tell him that I missed him, that I was happy to hear from him again, but I held back. I figured I could tell him another time. I figured that since he was texting me, he would come back. 
However, soon after he had texted me, Jason took his own life. He was only 19, his birthday in just a month. There's so many things I wish I could say to him, that I regret not having said sooner. I'll just say this:


Jason was a wonderful person, he was intelligent, and a truly creative mind. He had such an immense knowledge on level design. He told me he wanted to be a level designer. Since I’ve known him, Jason has been making maps with a hammer. They were good maps. He never wanted to publish them because he always believed he could one-up his previous map. I suppose he was right, too. Every map he had made was better than the last. Jason also loved music. I don't know how he did it but he was able to teach himself a little bit of music theory, alongside some amateur producing and sound mixing. I was personally never able to get it, so it blew my mind to see him be so comfortable with it. He loved to experience new music. Always open to hearing what people listened to and what they enjoyed. I managed to get him on a couple of my favorite songs. 


Knowing him was a blessing. Being a close friend was even more so. I loved Jason like I love my brother, and since he's been gone, it's felt empty without him. 


When Big Walk was revealed 2 years ago, he and I had watched the trailer, he was really excited to play the game. We talked about what the game would be like, the things we would do, and we'd even started imagining whole bits to do inside the game. It's depressing to think about how I'll never be able to play this game with him now. We've shared so many experiences together, and looking at the game in my library now, I wish so badly that we could have shared just one more experience, this one. I'll miss you, Jason. I hope you're at peace now. I hope that you're able to see how much you were loved. How much you were appreciated. How much you mattered. My life won't be the same without you.

SPOILERS AHEAD!!

From a distance, Big Walk doesn’t look like the kind of video game that’s out to deliver a big emotional payoff. It’s a chilled out co-op game that mostly tasks you and your friends with solving puzzles scattered around an open-world island environment. Any story here is the one you invent with your friend(s) while goofing around. And yet, the “ending” of Big Walk left me speechless — in both a figurative and literal sense. The remarkable sequence snaps House House’s excellent game in place, elevating a carefree multiplayer adventure into one of the most emotionally affecting experiences I’ve ever had with a video game.
For the bulk of Big Walk, you follow a clear structure. The island you’re exploring has multiple towers, each of which holds a key locked in place by a mechanism. You can free those keys by collecting red gourds, which are earned by completing puzzles, and placing them in receptacles within the towers. Once you complete every tower, you can open a giant gate on the island and find out what’s hiding off on the horizon.

Everything that leads up to that final moment is important to the finale. Big Walk’s puzzles require you to effectively communicate with your teammates to complete them. Sometimes that means talking it out to figure out a solution, but House House routinely toys with your ability to hear or see one another. Some puzzles drop a soundproof wall between you and your friends, requiring you to get creative in how you signal to one another. Your characters’ very limited body language becomes crucial to that, as you need to learn how to convey an idea by waving your arms around or squatting. Savvy players can get around these problems with walkie-talkies and laser pointers, but the important thing is that you flex your problem-solving skills together.
Like any great video game, the ending is the ultimate test of those learnings. After walking through the final gate and approaching an orb, your squad is transported to a surreal tower filled with puzzles. The twist? You can no longer hear one another. Not only that, but all the colors that distinguish players from one another have been washed away. Unable to talk or even know who you are waving at, you’re left to solve a suite of puzzles based solely on the trust and communication you’ve built over time.
That might sound like a recipe for frustration, but that wasn’t the case in my playthrough. I quickly found that I no longer needed audio to communicate with the two friends I had spent so much time playing with. I had learned how each one used gestures to communicate over time. When we had to relay symbols to one another to solve a puzzle, I knew exactly what one of my friends meant when they sporadically waved their body around to tell me I had misinterpreted them. I knew that when they threw their arms up in the air, they were telling me I heard them right.
I had learned everyone’s body language to the point where I could tell who was who based on movement alone. The same was true of my teammates. At one point, we found a teapot that was needed to solve a puzzle. I decided to take it with us through the entire tower as a running joke. Later, when we could talk again post-ending, my teammates told me they knew the person carrying the pot was me because I had spent the entire game up to that point hyper fixating on a laser pointer that I refused to get rid of. Of course, I was the guy who wouldn’t drop the pot!
It all culminates in an unexpectedly emotional moment. After finishing the puzzles, you exit the tower and everything returns to normal. Your colors come back, and you can once again speak to each other. Just outside the tower, there’s a couch in front of a projector that rolls the end credits. My team naturally gravitated towards it, using the moment to decompress after the gauntlet. We celebrated our victory, shared all the things we couldn’t say in the tower, and told each other how we were able to identify one another. It was like seeing your best friend for the first time after getting split apart for college; we could have talked forever.
But you can’t, of course. You always have to say goodbye eventually. Big Walk’s final moment drives that home with its final puzzle. Your squad comes up against a turnstile that you can’t pass through. A mechanism on the side lights up, showing three colors. Those colors correspond to the colored body parts of one of your teammates, signaling they can pass through. They cross over and begin to fall out of range of the proximity chat as they pass through into a white light. Each team member exits until no one remains. You’re alone once you cross into the light, greeted only by a splash screen that thanks you for playing. Best video game ive ever played.

Big Walk isn't anything like other recent multiplayer co-op games. The main point of the game is to walk around, complete puzzles, and explore the map with friends. That might sound boring at first, but the puzzle design and general intrigue of exploration makes the experience with friends so much more fun. 

There might be moments where you will be with your group, stumble across a puzzle, then need to work together to find the solution. Maybe a puzzle locks you behind sound-proof glass, so you have to play charades. Maybe you need to press a button on the other side of a valley while one person stays behind to walk through a door.
It's simple, creative puzzle-solving that feels INCREDIBLY rewarding to complete.

The only critiques I have are:
• So far, there isn't any volume sliders in the settings, so the voice volume of your friends might be too quiet, while everything else is too loud. 
• There isn't any online matchmaking, so if you don't really have any friends you can't play it fully. I understand that's intentional, and part of House House's vision is to let you connect with your already-existing friends. I just think it would be nice to meet new people who have the game as well!

Overall, Big Walk is an amazing game that has an interesting premise and a good execution. I can't wait to play more soon!

Still keeping the review as negative because I was expecting/hoping for more. I think the game didn't live up to its hype to me because playing with one friend exaggerates some of the (designed) quirks, that I found more annoying than charming as a result.

Quirks such as having a walkie talkie on your belt but not being able to press the button by yourself. With more people that's fine, yet it kills its use with only 2 players. The same applies to carrying the gourds (puzzle rewards), where we'd often have to choose between multiple round-trips or leaving behind any of the tools you'd might want to use. It's not as much of a problem when you have more people (which simply knowing that makes the problem feel worse when we experience it). Night time often turned into a nuisance, since we're carrying multiple gourds around in complete darkness. Another problem is that we played in two sessions. After rejoining various vital items were lost because we couldn't hold them all, forcing us to backtrack and collect unused gourds. With good friends you can have fun in the worst janky games out there; I don't need to be forced to backtrack or get locked in a room for 30 minutes to have a chat with my friend.

None of these problems I mentioned were big enough to make me want to stop at any point, but all of these add up to a pleasant yet slightly underwhelming experience. With the puzzles being the highlight, co-op puzzle games like the We Were Here series are a better recommendation I can give. Even if those have their own unique problems.
