update on 2026-08-05 (both here and in the comments):

some clarifications about performance:

while i have a graphics card that is almost 10 years old and was even then mid-range - gtx 1050ti - the minimum required gpu is gtx 750ti. while the difference between these two cards is not huge, maybe i expected a bit too much.

game on medium in my case is basically unplayable (at least with 100% render, i haven't tried any other values. i think in this game, where you often need to see things clearly, it's not a good solution to the problem). i get less than 30 fps and the frames are constantly dropping.

so i played on low and very low, and i can play like that. frames are okay (from 60 to 90, but there are also massive drops). however, even in the starting location, my first experience with these presets was the render distance for some objects. a seat in literally 15 meters from me just wasn't visible at all. in normal gameplay some trees, rocks and bushes are appearing from nowhere, requiring me to occasionally reroute.

the drastic difference between medium and anything below is probably because of the lighting and shadows. it would be great if the game had different sliders and more granular settings for graphics: shadows, render distance, maybe even texture resolution.

my cpu is ryzen 5 5600g (integrated graphics are disabled in uefi), so i am not cpu bound (at least i hope so). thinking back, probably this level of performance is expected from my setup.

however, my friends have much more powerful setups, and they also have some performance concerns. for example, one person with 9070xt gpu and 7800x3d cpu (both amd) on windows 11 had frames ranging from 70 to 250 fps on highest settings. while 200+ fps is amazing, these lows with 70 fps are not great.

some clarifications about linux:

performance on linux with proton on my system tends to be better than on windows, but in margins of error, so linux is not an issue. i can guarantee than performance is going to be identical on both systems.

as for launch parameters, probably it's a problem in my specific setup (wayland compositor, xwayland or nvidia drivers), but i was unable to launch the game as-is. if it helps somebody, i needed to use `PROTON_USE_WINED3D=1`.

a clarification about audio:

some people wrote in the comments that "the audio should work this way" and "this simulates real world experience". however, i don't agree with that. you are going to hear people in real life on even further distance. yes, the locations are mostly open, so audio has less objects to reflect from, but the current distance of audio propagation is just absurd.

as a funny solution to this problem, we had a person with a backpack and two radios (walkie-talkie, but i am going to write as radio): one in the backpack and one in the hands. the person talked into the radio, the radio on the backpack repeats his words to us and we can hear them clearly on the distance where we can't hear his words from him directly. i don't think it should work this way.

radio's proximity distance is, what i think, the distance for proximity voice chat should have been. it really is optimal in my experience. and otherwise it doesn't make any sense, because you can circumvent voice chat distance like we did. radio should have the same distance of propagation as a person just talking directly and vice versa.

my review is still positive and i recommend the game, because:

- even with these issues, i still like the game. i haven't elaborated on that much, but the core gameplay is great. i waited for this game's release and, in terms of the gameplay, everything is good so far.

- while the audio problems are still here, they are bearable. and the developers have said that they are already working on the fix.

[h1] We Couldn't Stop Laughing [/h1]

Big Walk proves that not every co-op game needs combat to be fun. The whole idea of getting lost in a huge world with your friends, solving little puzzles, chatting, and figuring things out together sounds simple, but it works surprisingly well. It captures that feeling of going on an adventure without constantly telling you where to go, and that's what makes it so relaxing.

I've been playing it with my friends, and we've been having an absolute blast. Every session turns into a bunch of funny moments that nobody planned. One minute we're trying to figure out where to go, and the next we're completely distracted by something random. It never feels repetitive because every adventure ends up being different.

On the downside, a mic volume slider is badly needed. We couldn't stop laughing, but constantly blowing out each other's headsets quickly became a real issue.

House House has that same charm that made Untitled Goose Game so memorable. The world is full of personality, the interactions are hilarious, and it feels like the game encourages you to create your own stories instead of following a strict path. If you're looking for a co-op game that's more about exploration, laughing with friends, and making memories than winning or grinding, this is an easy recommendation.
